title: Zero-Downtime Amazon EKS Minor & Multi-Version Upgrade (v1.34 → v1.36+)
summary: Production runbook strategy for upgrading Amazon EKS clusters across minor versions (v1.34 → v1.35 → v1.36 → v1.37) with zero application downtime using sequential control plane upgrades, blue/green managed node groups, PDBs, and health validation.
question: Walk me through how you upgraded an Amazon EKS cluster from Kubernetes v1.34 to v1.36 and even after v1.37 without downtime.
intro: In one of my projects, we had a customer-facing application running as microservices on Amazon EKS, and we had a requirement to upgrade Kubernetes from v1.34 to v1.36. Since it was Production, we couldn't afford application downtime, so we followed a proper upgrade runbook.

steps.title: Pre-checks & Compatibility Verification
steps.description: Before touching the cluster, perform a complete pre-flight check of deprecated APIs and dependencies:
items: EKS Upgrade Insights: Checked automated AWS insights for deprecated APIs and cluster readiness.
Deprecated Kubernetes APIs: Audited manifests and Helm charts using API deprecation tools (e.g., Pluto / kubent).
Helm chart and application compatibility: Verified all third-party charts, CRDs, and controllers support the target version.
Core Add-ons: Checked compatibility matrices for VPC CNI, CoreDNS, and kube-proxy for target versions.
AWS Load Balancer Controller: Verified controller version, IAM policies (IRSA), and TargetGroupBinding CRDs.
PDBs and replica counts: Verified PodDisruptionBudgets and replica counts (≥ 2) across all critical services.
Monitoring components: Ensured Prometheus, Grafana, and CloudWatch were operational to capture real-time telemetry.
steps.highlight: Once the pre-checks were clean, we tested the complete upgrade in a lower environment first (Dev → Staging/UAT). We never started directly with Production.

steps.title: Upgrade One Version at a Time
steps.description: Kubernetes minor version upgrades must be performed sequentially. You cannot skip minor versions:
items: For each version, I first upgraded the EKS control plane (AWS handles the multi-AZ control plane upgrade without API downtime).
Once the control plane was healthy, I validated the cluster and then upgraded the required EKS add-ons (VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, EBS CSI driver).

steps.title: Replace Worker Nodes (Blue/Green Node Groups)
steps.description: For worker nodes, we didn't immediately terminate the existing node group:
flow: Drain one node at a time
items: We created a new managed node group with an EKS-optimized AMI compatible with the new Kubernetes version.
Once the new nodes joined the cluster and showed Ready, we started moving the workloads.
Cordon old node: Marked the node unschedulable so new pods were only scheduled on the new node group.
Drain one node at a time: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data.
We didn't drain everything together — we moved workloads gradually to maintain application availability.

steps.title: How Did We Avoid Downtime?
steps.description: Zero downtime was guaranteed because our critical microservices were engineered for High Availability:

pillars.name: Multiple Replicas
pillars.detail: Every critical service had at least 2–3 replicas running across nodes.

pillars.name: PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs)
pillars.detail: Enforced minAvailable / maxUnavailable so the API server blocked evictions that would breach availability.

pillars.name: Readiness Probes & Graceful Shutdown
pillars.detail: Traffic was only routed once newly scheduled pods passed readiness checks; preStop hooks allowed in-flight requests to complete.

pillars.name: Multi-AZ Workload Distribution
pillars.detail: Topology spread constraints ensured pods were distributed evenly across multiple Availability Zones.

steps.highlight: So even when one node was being drained, healthy Pods on other nodes continued serving customer traffic without interruption.

steps.title: Continuous Telemetry & Monitoring
steps.description: Using CloudWatch and Prometheus/Grafana, continuously monitored throughout the upgrade:
items: Node Health: Memory/CPU pressure and kubelet status.
Pod Restarts: Monitored CrashLoopBackOff and restart counts.
Pending Pods: Detected scheduling bottlenecks or resource exhaustion.
CPU and Memory: Monitored cluster-wide headroom and OOM warnings.
ALB Target Health: Confirmed targets remained healthy in AWS Target Groups.
Application Latency: Verified p95/p99 response times did not degrade.
5xx HTTP Errors: Monitored error rates to confirm zero dropped requests.

steps.title: Validate Before Removing Anything
steps.description: Once all workloads were running on the new node group, we didn't immediately remove the old one:
items: We performed smoke testing and validated critical application flows under real traffic.
Once everything was verified stable, we cleanly deleted the old node group.
Then we repeated the same process for subsequent minor version bumps (e.g. v1.34 → v1.35 → v1.36 → v1.37).

keyTakeaway: Zero downtime wasn't achieved just because we carefully upgraded EKS. It was possible because the application was already designed for high availability with multiple replicas, PDBs, readiness probes, Multi-AZ deployment, and controlled node draining.
elevatorPitch: Conducted rigorous pre-checks: EKS Upgrade Insights, API deprecations (Pluto), add-on compatibility, and lower-environment testing.
Upgraded strictly one minor version at a time (v1.34 → v1.35 → v1.36 → v1.37): control plane first, followed by managed add-ons.
Implemented blue/green worker node replacement with new EKS-optimized AMI node groups; cordoned and drained nodes one-by-one.
Guaranteed zero downtime via HA safeguards: replica counts ≥ 2, PodDisruptionBudgets, readiness probes, preStop hooks, and multi-AZ spread.
Monitored CloudWatch/Grafana telemetry (5xx errors, latency, pending pods, ALB target health) throughout.
Executed critical business flow smoke tests before safely decommissioning old node groups.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Draining cluster worker nodes without auditing PodDisruptionBudget availability and replica headroom
mistakesToAvoid.why: Unconditional node draining without checking PDB `maxUnavailable` can evict quorum-critical pods, causing cascading service outages.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Skipping deprecated API manifest validation tools (Pluto, Kubent) prior to initiating cluster upgrades
mistakesToAvoid.why: Kubernetes regularly graduates and removes beta APIs; deploying modern cluster versions with outdated manifest API versions causes immediate deployment rejections.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Initiating control plane upgrades without verifying etcd snapshot backups and quorum health
mistakesToAvoid.why: If control plane state becomes corrupted during an upgrade, restoring etcd snapshots is the sole disaster recovery mechanism.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring kubelet daemon configuration deprecations across newly provisioned worker node instances in eks-upgrade-zero-downtime
mistakesToAvoid.why: Kubelet flags and container runtime interfaces evolve across versions; unvalidated flags prevent worker node registration with the API server.

title: EC2 CPU Suddenly Reaches 100% — Troubleshooting Runbook
summary: Triage runbook for handling sudden 100% CPU utilization on production EC2 instances: telemetry triage, identifying culprit processes, handling legit vs malicious load, and permanent safeguards.
question: EC2 CPU suddenly reaches 100% — how would you troubleshoot?
intro: When a production EC2 instance hits 100% CPU, my priority is two-fold: stop customer impact immediately (mitigation) while capturing telemetry to pinpoint the exact culprit process (root cause analysis).

steps.title: Triage From Outside (CloudWatch & Telemetry)
steps.description: Before logging in, look at multi-dimensional metrics to classify the nature of the spike:
items: Correlate Metrics: In CloudWatch, compare CPUUtilization against NetworkIn, NetworkOut, and DiskReadOps/DiskWriteBytes.

Traffic Surge vs Rogue Process: If high CPU coincides with a 10x spike in NetworkIn and ALB requests, it is likely legitimate or DDoS traffic. If NetworkIn is flat but CPU spiked abruptly, it is likely an internal process, runaway job, or compromised instance.
Check Auto Scaling Group (ASG): Check if ASG target tracking is scaling out instances or if the ASG has hit its max_size limit.

steps.title: SSH / SSM Session & Process Inspection
steps.description: Log into the instance (using AWS Systems Manager Session Manager or SSH) and inspect active processes:
items: uptime: Check load average against total core count (nproc). If 4 cores and load is 40, system is severely saturated.
top -c or htop: Press P to sort by CPU consumption. Note the PID, USER, and COMMAND.
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -10: Print the top 10 CPU-consuming processes with full command-line arguments.
vmstat 1 5: Check if CPU is spending time in user space (us), system/kernel (sy), or I/O wait (wa). High I/O wait indicates a storage bottleneck rather than pure computation.

steps.title: Diagnose the Culprit Process
steps.description: Examine the identified process to determine what it is doing:
items: Thread Inspection: Run top -H -p <PID> to inspect individual threads inside the process.
Syscall Tracing: Run strace -p <PID> -c for 10 seconds to identify spinning loops or repetitive failing syscalls.
Application Thread Dump: For Java/Node/Go runtimes, capture a thread dump (e.g. jstack <PID> or Go pprof) before terminating.
Check Recent Crons: Check /var/log/syslog or /var/log/cron for heavy scheduled backup, antivirus, or indexing tasks.

steps.title: Mitigate and Restore Service
steps.description: Take decisive, safe actions based on the diagnosis:
items: If Rogue Application Process: Issue kill -15 <PID> (SIGTERM) for graceful shutdown. Only use kill -9 if unresponsive.
If Legitimate Traffic Surge: Manually increase ASG desired capacity, or provision a read replica / cache if backend DB queries are choking the app.
If Compromised / Crypto-Miner: Immediately isolate instance: change Security Group to quarantine SG (no outbound/inbound except security audit), capture EBS snapshot for forensics, and terminate.

keyTakeaway: Never reboot an instance blindly. Capture thread dumps and top process telemetry first so you don't lose the smoking gun, and ensure auto-scaling and CPU alarms prevent single-node exhaustion.
elevatorPitch: Check CloudWatch: correlate CPU with NetworkIn and ALB traffic to differentiate traffic surge from rogue process.
Access instance via SSM Session Manager / SSH; run 'top -c', 'uptime', and 'ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -10'.
Check 'vmstat 1 5' for 'us' (app code) vs 'wa' (I/O wait bottleneck) vs 'sy' (kernel context switching).
Inspect threads with 'top -H -p <PID>' and capture thread dump (jstack/pprof) or strace before killing.
Mitigate: graceful SIGTERM, scale out ASG, or quarantine if compromised.
Prevent: CloudWatch Alarm at 75% CPU, ASG auto-scaling, CPU limits (cgroups/Docker), and query optimization.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Jumping straight to SSH/SSM without checking CloudWatch metrics first
mistakesToAvoid.why: Interviewers expect triage from outside the instance first to correlate CPU with NetworkIn, NetworkOut, and ALB requests. Tunnel-visioning straight to terminal access signals reactive server administration rather than cloud architecture and holistic observability.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Recommending an immediate instance reboot or termination
mistakesToAvoid.why: Rebooting destroys the smoking gun: active processes, kernel thread states, CPU profiles, and memory telemetry are permanently lost. Senior engineers isolate the node from the load balancer, capture diagnostics, and attempt graceful mitigation before considering a restart.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring the vmstat breakdown (us vs sy vs wa)
mistakesToAvoid.why: Stating "CPU is 100%" without identifying whether CPU time is spent in user space (application code), kernel/system (syscall churn or lock contention), or I/O wait (EBS volume IOPS/throughput exhaustion) demonstrates surface-level Linux troubleshooting.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Immediately reaching for kill -9 (SIGKILL) instead of kill -15 (SIGTERM)
mistakesToAvoid.why: Unconditional kill -9 corrupts in-flight database transactions, leaves locks dangling, and bypasses application cleanup handlers. Always send SIGTERM first and allow reasonable drain time before escalating to SIGKILL.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to evaluate security compromise or cryptomining malware
mistakesToAvoid.why: A sudden 100% CPU spike with zero corresponding network traffic spike is a classic footprint of a compromised host running an unauthorized crypto-miner. Omitting security containment (security group quarantine, EBS snapshot forensics) is a significant gap in SRE interviews.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting proactive architectural safeguards and auto-remediation
mistakesToAvoid.why: Ending your answer at killing the process shows a reactive break-fix mindset. Senior engineers articulate root-cause prevention: CloudWatch Alarms at 75% CPU, Auto Scaling target tracking policies, container cgroup CPU limits, and database query optimization.

title: EC2 Running but SSH Isn't Working — Layer-by-Layer Diagnostics
summary: Systematic OSI and AWS-layer troubleshooting methodology when an EC2 instance shows 'Running' but SSH connection fails, covering network timeouts, connection refused, key issues, and SSM rescue.
question: EC2 is running but SSH isn't working — what would you check?
intro: When SSH fails while EC2 shows 'Running', the very first step is to observe the exact error message: 'Connection timed out' means a networking/firewall block, whereas 'Connection refused' or 'Permission denied' means you reached the OS but sshd or auth failed.

steps.title: Differentiate Network Timeout vs Connection Refused
steps.description: Run verbose SSH: ssh -vvv -i key.pem user@ip to see where the handshake stalls:
items: Connection Timed Out: Packet dropped before reaching EC2 (Security Group, Route Table, NACL, or my public IP changed).
Connection Refused: Packet reached the instance, but no process is listening on port 22 (sshd stopped or crashed).
Permission Denied (publickey): Network and sshd are working, but authentication credentials or file permissions failed.

steps.title: AWS Network & VPC Checks (If Timed Out)
steps.description: Verify the packet path from internet to instance ENI:
items: Security Group Inbound Rules: Is port 22 allowed from my current external IP? (Did office VPN or ISP change my public IP?).
Public IP & Subnet Route Table: Does the subnet route table route 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway (IGW)? (If private subnet, you must connect via Bastion host or AWS Client VPN).
Network ACLs (NACL): Verify NACL allows inbound port 22 AND allows ephemeral ports (1024–65535) outbound for the return traffic.
Instance Status Checks: Check AWS Console: System Status Check (AWS hardware) and Instance Status Check (OS kernel). If Instance check fails, OS is frozen.

steps.title: OS, Key Pair & Disk Checks (If Refused or Denied)
steps.description: Verify host-side configuration and authentication:
items: Key Permissions: Local private key must have chmod 400 key.pem (SSH client rejects overly permissive keys).
Correct Username: Amazon Linux (ec2-user), Ubuntu (ubuntu), Debian (admin), CentOS (centos), RHEL (ec2-user).
Disk Space 100% Full: If the root EBS disk is 100% full, sshd cannot allocate a PTY session or write to /var/log/auth.log, causing instant drops.
EC2 System Log / Screenshot: In AWS Console, select Actions → Monitor and troubleshoot → Get system log / Get instance screenshot to see kernel panics or boot errors.

steps.title: Rescue Strategies Without SSH
steps.description: How senior SREs regain access when SSH is dead:
items: AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Session Manager: Connect via browser/CLI (bypasses port 22 and SSH keys entirely using the SSM Agent and IAM role).
EC2 Serial Console: Connect directly to the serial port if enabled on Nitro instances.

EBS Volume Detach Rescue: Stop the EC2 instance, detach the root EBS volume, attach it as a secondary drive to a healthy rescue EC2 instance, mount it, fix /etc/ssh/sshd_config or ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, reattach, and start.

keyTakeaway: Categorize the error immediately: 'Timed out' is AWS network/SG; 'Connection refused' is sshd/port; 'Permission denied' is key/username. Always have AWS SSM Session Manager enabled as a zero-SSH out-of-band management backdoor.
elevatorPitch: Check error type: 'Timed out' = network/firewall; 'Connection refused' = sshd dead; 'Permission denied' = key/user error.
If timed out: Check Security Group IP whitelist, subnet route table (IGW attached), NACLs (ephemeral return ports).
If refused/hung: Check EC2 Instance Status Check, EC2 console screenshot, and system log for kernel panic or 100% disk.
If permission denied: Verify key permissions (chmod 400), correct OS username (ec2-user vs ubuntu).
Rescue path: Use AWS SSM Session Manager (no port 22 needed), or detach EBS root volume to a rescue instance to fix config.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Purging compromised IAM user credentials immediately prior to querying CloudTrail forensic event logs when addressing layer-by-layer
mistakesToAvoid.why: Deactivating a compromised key prevents abuse while preserving identity records for CloudTrail forensic queries to assess blast radius.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Conflating local IAM Permissions Boundaries with organizational Service Control Policies (SCPs)
mistakesToAvoid.why: SCPs define maximum permission guards at the AWS Organization level across accounts, whereas permission boundaries limit delegate privileges within a single account.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Deploying single-AZ cloud infrastructure for production workloads without multi-AZ failover resilience
mistakesToAvoid.why: Availability Zone hardware failures or localized network partitions cause complete service downtime when resources are not distributed across >=2 AZs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Jumping straight to SSH or instance restarts without reviewing CloudWatch metrics and AWS Systems Manager logs
mistakesToAvoid.why: Senior SREs triage control plane and hypervisor metrics via CloudWatch and SSM Session Manager before executing invasive host-level actions.

title: ALB Starts Returning 5xx Errors — Identifying Root Cause
summary: Production runbook for isolating Application Load Balancer (ALB) 5xx errors: distinguishing ELB-generated vs Target-generated codes, debugging 502/503/504, and querying access logs with Athena.
question: ALB starts returning 5xx errors — how would you identify the root cause?
intro: When an ALB starts throwing 5xx errors, my immediate first goal is to differentiate between errors generated by the ALB itself versus errors generated by backend application targets.

steps.title: CloudWatch Metrics Differentiation (ELB vs Target)
steps.description: Look at CloudWatch metrics for the load balancer immediately:
items: HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count: The ALB itself generated the error before receiving a response from targets (502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout).
HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count: The backend application generated a 5xx response (e.g. unhandled 500 internal server error or database crash), and the ALB simply forwarded it to the client.
HealthyHostCount / UnHealthyHostCount: Check if backend targets are failing health checks.

steps.title: Diagnose Specific 5xx Error Codes
steps.description: Apply targeted root cause analysis based on status code:
items: HTTP 502 (Bad Gateway): Target closed the TCP connection before sending full HTTP headers. Classic cause: Keep-Alive timeout mismatch (backend web server keep-alive must be set GREATER than ALB idle timeout, e.g. backend 65s vs ALB 60s).
HTTP 503 (Service Unavailable): No healthy targets available in the Target Group (all targets failed health checks), or ALB capacity exceeded during extreme traffic spikes.
HTTP 504 (Gateway Timeout): Target took longer to respond than the ALB idle timeout. Check for slow database queries, thread pool exhaustion, or locked worker processes.
HTTP 500 (Target Generated): Application code threw an uncaught exception, or database/Redis connection failed.

steps.title: Query ALB Access Logs with Amazon Athena
steps.description: Analyze ALB S3 access logs to extract exact failing requests, targets, and response times:
items: Check elb_status_code vs target_status_code.
Check target_processing_time: If high (>30s), target application is hanging.
Identify offending request paths, client IPs, or specific unhealthy backend target IP addresses.

steps.title: Remediate and Safeguard
steps.description: Immediate mitigation and permanent safeguards:
items: If 503 (unhealthy targets): Inspect target health check path (e.g. /healthz) in Target Group. Are targets returning 404 or failing DB ping?
If 502: Align keep-alive timeout: set Nginx/Node.js/Gunicorn keep-alive to 65s+ and ALB timeout to 60s.
If 504: Temporarily bump ALB idle timeout to relieve immediate pressure while developers optimize slow DB queries.
Configure CloudWatch Alarms on HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count > 10 with SNS to PagerDuty.

keyTakeaway: Always split ELB 5xx from Target 5xx in CloudWatch first. If it's ELB 502, check Keep-Alive timeout mismatches; if 503, check Target Group healthy host count; if 504, check target processing latency.
elevatorPitch: Check CloudWatch: HTTPCode_ELB_5XX (ALB fault) vs HTTPCode_Target_5XX (app fault).
If Target 5XX: App is throwing 500s; inspect app logs and database connectivity.
If ELB 502: Target closed TCP prematurely; fix Keep-Alive timeout (backend keep-alive must exceed ALB 60s).
If ELB 503: Zero healthy targets in Target Group; verify health check path (/healthz) and target capacity.
If ELB 504: Gateway timeout; target query took >60s. Check target_processing_time and database locks.
Query ALB Access Logs via Athena to isolate failing URLs, client IPs, and specific target instance IDs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Confusing ALB 502 Bad Gateway (target connection reset) with 504 Gateway Timeout (upstream response timeout) when configuring Starts Returning Errors
mistakesToAvoid.why: 502 indicates the backend target closed the TCP connection prematurely or returned malformed HTTP, whereas 504 means the target failed to respond before idle timeout.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Setting target deregistration delay to zero instead of allowing connection draining when configuring Starts Returning Errors
mistakesToAvoid.why: Instant target deregistration severs in-flight HTTP requests during auto-scaling scale-in or rolling deployments, causing immediate user-facing drops.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to query CloudWatch ELB metrics (`HTTPCode_ELB_5XX` vs `HTTPCode_Target_5XX`) during load balancer outages when configuring Starts Returning Errors
mistakesToAvoid.why: Comparing load balancer generated errors against target generated errors immediately isolates whether the issue lies in the proxy tier or application runtime.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Overlooking Security Group rules on backend EC2/ECS instances that block health check traffic from the ALB when configuring Starts Returning Errors
mistakesToAvoid.why: Target instances must explicitly permit inbound HTTP/HTTPS traffic from the ALB security group on the configured container/application port.

title: App Works Internally but Not from Internet — Network Tracing
summary: Outside-in OSI network layer troubleshooting model for resolving private VPC services that remain inaccessible over the public internet.
question: AWS app works internally but not internet — how would you troubleshoot?
intro: When an AWS app works internally but not internet, the compute instance and container runtime are verified healthy. The root cause is isolated strictly along the outside-in ingress network boundary between the public internet and the AWS VPC.

steps.title: DNS & IP Resolution (Outside-in Step 1)
steps.description: Verify public DNS mapping from an external workstation to ensure client traffic reaches AWS edge endpoints:
items: Execute dig +short app.example.com and nslookup app.example.com against public recursive resolvers (e.g. 8.8.8.8 or 1.1.1.1).

Verify Route 53 Public vs Private Hosted Zones: A common failure occurs when an internal record resolves to a private VPC IP (10.0.x.x) because only a private hosted zone was configured, leaving the public hosted zone missing or pointing to a stale endpoint.
Confirm the public A/AAAA Alias record correctly maps to the Application Load Balancer canonical DNS name (dualstack.app-alb-xxxx.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com).
steps.codeBlock:
# 1. Inspect public DNS resolution against authoritative resolvers
dig +noall +answer app.example.com @8.8.8.8

# Expected stdout: Public ALB IP or CNAME
# app.example.com.    300 IN  CNAME   dualstack.app-alb-102938475.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com.
# dualstack.app-alb-102938475.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com. 60 IN A 52.204.142.89

steps.title: Entry Point Topology & Subnet Routing (Step 2)
steps.description: Audit Internet Gateway (IGW) attachments and subnet routing table associations:
items: Public Subnet Route Table Verification: The subnets hosting the Application Load Balancer must have an explicit route table entry: 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-xxxx (Internet Gateway). If an ALB is mistakenly deployed into private subnets, inbound packets cannot cross the VPC perimeter.
Load Balancer Scheme Audit: Confirm the ALB scheme is configured as internet-facing rather than internal. An internal ALB only receives private ENI IPs without public routability.
Avoid NAT Gateway Confusion: NAT Gateways only enable outbound egress from private subnets to the internet; they do not accept inbound ingress from the public internet.
steps.codeBlock:
# 2. Verify subnet route table target points to an Internet Gateway
aws ec2 describe-route-tables \n  --filters "Name=association.subnet-id,Values=subnet-0123456789abcdef0" \n  --query "RouteTables[].Routes[?DestinationCidrBlock=='0.0.0.0/0'].[DestinationCidrBlock,GatewayId]" \n  --output text

# Expected clean output (no ASCII formatting):
# 0.0.0.0/0    igw-0123456789abcdef0

steps.title: Firewalls: Security Groups & Stateless NACLs (Step 3)
steps.description: Inspect AWS stateful Security Groups and stateless Network Access Control Lists (NACLs) across ingress and egress paths:
items: ALB Security Group: Must explicitly allow inbound TCP port 80/443 from 0.0.0.0/0 (Public Internet).

Target Security Group Chaining: Backend EC2 or ECS tasks in private subnets must allow ingress from the ALB's Security Group ID (e.g. sg-alb123), preventing direct unauthorized access while permitting forwarded traffic.

Stateless NACL Ephemeral Return Ports: Network ACLs evaluate inbound and outbound rules independently without connection tracking. The subnet NACL must allow inbound 80/443 AND allow outbound ephemeral traffic on ports 1024–65535 to return SYN-ACK packets to client browsers.

matrix.title: AWS VPC Ingress Diagnostic Matrix: Layer-by-Layer Triage
rows: NXDOMAIN or private 10.x IP returned to public clients
SYN packet dropped before entering VPC boundary
Traffic blackholed if 0.0.0.0/0 points to NAT instead of IGW
ALB created as 'internal' scheme with private ENIs only
Client connection hangs on TCP SYN (SYN packet dropped at ENI)
Inbound SYN allowed, but outbound SYN-ACK dropped on ephemeral ports
Immediate HTTP 403 Forbidden with WAF rule token header

steps.title: AWS WAF & VPC Reachability Analyzer (Step 4)
steps.description: Inspect perimeter firewall rules and mathematically prove network path connectivity using AWS VPC Reachability Analyzer:
items: AWS WAF Inspection: Review CloudWatch metrics for BlockedRequests. Common false positives stem from aggressive IP rate limiting thresholds, geographic restrictions, or overly sensitive AWS Managed Core Rule Set (CRS) SQLi rules.

VPC Reachability Analyzer: Run an automated diagnostic path between the Internet Gateway (igw-xxxx) and the load balancer or target instance ENI. The tool computes hop-by-hop configuration analysis and pinpoints the exact misconfigured route or security rule without injecting live probe packets.

Cross-reference operational runbooks with our companion guides: inspect the AWS ALB 5XX Troubleshooting Runbook, review the AWS EC2 SSH Access Diagnostics, and explore the AWS DevOps Architecture Guide for enterprise VPC landing zones.
steps.codeBlock:
# 4. Mathematically prove network path using AWS VPC Reachability Analyzer
aws ec2 create-network-insights-path \n  --source igw-0123456789abcdef0 \n  --destination eni-0123456789abcdef0 \n  --protocol TCP \n  --destination-port 443

# Expected result: PathFound: false (or true once rules are resolved)
# Explanations: Security group sg-0123 does not allow inbound TCP on port 443

keyTakeaway: When an AWS app works internally but not internet, the compute tier is healthy. Methodically trace outside-in: Route 53 public DNS -> Internet Gateway route (0.0.0.0/0) -> Public Subnet ALB -> Security Group (80/443 from 0.0.0.0/0) -> Stateless NACLs (inbound 80/443 + outbound ephemeral 1024-65535) -> AWS WAF. Use VPC Reachability Analyzer to mathematically pinpoint the blocking rule in seconds.
elevatorPitch: First, isolate the failure layer: since the app works internally on private VPC IPs, compute and application processes are proven healthy.
Trace outside-in starting at DNS: run dig app.example.com to verify public DNS resolves to the ALB CNAME rather than a private 10.x IP.
Check subnet route tables: ensure the ALB is deployed in public subnets containing an active 0.0.0.0/0 route to an Internet Gateway (IGW), not a NAT Gateway.
Audit Security Groups: verify the ALB SG permits inbound ports 80/443 from 0.0.0.0/0, and backend instance SGs permit ingress chained from the ALB SG.
Verify stateless Network ACLs: confirm both inbound 80/443 allow rules and outbound ephemeral return rules (ports 1024–65535) are active.
Execute AWS VPC Reachability Analyzer: trigger an automated network insights path between the IGW and ENI to mathematically identify the exact blocking security rule.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Deactivating a compromised key prevents abuse while preserving identity records for CloudTrail forensic queries to assess blast radius.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Conflating local IAM Permissions Boundaries with organizational Service Control Policies (SCPs) when configuring Works Internally Internet
mistakesToAvoid.why: SCPs define maximum permission guards at the AWS Organization level across accounts, whereas permission boundaries limit delegate privileges within a single account.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Deploying single-AZ cloud infrastructure for production workloads without multi-AZ failover resilience when configuring Works Internally Internet
mistakesToAvoid.why: Availability Zone hardware failures or localized network partitions cause complete service downtime when resources are not distributed across >=2 AZs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Jumping straight to SSH or instance restarts without reviewing CloudWatch metrics and AWS Systems Manager logs when configuring Works Internally Internet
mistakesToAvoid.why: Senior SREs triage control plane and hypervisor metrics via CloudWatch and SSM Session Manager before executing invasive host-level actions.

title: Kubernetes Pod Stuck in Pending: 6 Common Root Causes & Step-by-Step Triage Runbook
summary: Step-by-step diagnostic workflow for pods stuck in Pending state: decoding kube-scheduler events, capacity exhaustion, taints/tolerations, PVC binding, and autoscaling response.
question: Pod is stuck in Pending — what would you check?
intro: A Pod stuck in Pending means the kube-scheduler cannot find a node that meets all the pod's constraints, or volume mounting / admission controllers are blocked. My primary tool is immediately 'kubectl describe pod <pod-name>'.

steps.title: Inspect Scheduler Events First
steps.description: Run kubectl describe pod <pod-name> and look directly at the Events section at the bottom:
items: FailedScheduling message: The scheduler explains in plain English why each node was rejected (e.g. 0/6 nodes available: 3 Insufficient cpu, 3 node(s) had untolerated taint).
FailedMount / FailedAttachVolume: Storage subsystem is blocked attempting to attach or format an EBS/NFS volume.

steps.title: Root Cause 1: Insufficient Node Capacity (CPU/Memory)
steps.description: Scheduler calculates fit based on requests, not actual usage:
items: Run kubectl describe nodes | grep -A 8 'Allocated resources' to see node allocation percentages.
If pods have huge CPU/memory requests (e.g. cpu: 4 on 4-core nodes), no single node can fit them.
Fix: Adjust application requests, or ensure Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter is provisioning new nodes.

steps.title: Root Cause 2: Node Selectors, Affinity & Taints
steps.description: Filter constraints that eliminate eligible nodes:
items: spec.nodeSelector: Label typo (e.g. disk: ssd when nodes are labeled disktype: ssd).
nodeAffinity / podAntiAffinity: Hard anti-affinity (requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution) preventing pods from running on the same node/AZ.
Taints without Tolerations: Nodes tainted with dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule or uncordoned maintenance taints.

steps.title: Root Cause 3: Unbound PVCs & Missing Config
steps.description: Check persistent storage and required configuration:
items: Check PVC state: kubectl get pvc. If Pending, check StorageClass and CSI provisioner.
Volume Multi-AZ Trap: In AWS, an EBS volume lives in us-east-1a. If nodes in us-east-1a are full, scheduler cannot place the pod in us-east-1b.
Check referenced ConfigMaps/Secrets: If a volume references a non-existent ConfigMap, pod cannot start.

keyTakeaway: Always run 'kubectl describe pod' and read the Scheduler Events. Differentiate resource request starvation (fit calculation) from affinity/taint rules and AZ-locked EBS volume binding.
elevatorPitch: Run 'kubectl describe pod <name>' and read the Events section: FailedScheduling tells you why.
Check Resources: verify node allocated requests ('kubectl describe nodes') vs pod spec.resources.requests.
Check Constraints: nodeSelector, nodeAffinity, and taints/tolerations that block placement.
Check Storage: verify PVC status ('kubectl get pvc') - check if volume is locked to a different AWS AZ.
Verify Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter logs to ensure nodes are actively spinning up.
Fix: Tune requests, correct label selectors, add tolerations, or trigger node autoscaling.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Restarting a crashing container without examining preceding termination logs via kubectl logs --previous when configuring Kubernetes Stuck Pending
mistakesToAvoid.why: Restarting the pod flushes ephemeral container runtime state, destroying vital panic stack traces and fatal initialization logs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Misdiagnosing an application boot crash as a failure of aggressive liveness probes when configuring Kubernetes Stuck Pending
mistakesToAvoid.why: Liveness probes with short timeouts or high failure thresholds kill slow-starting applications repeatedly, causing false `CrashLoopBackOff` loops.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Neglecting node taints, tolerations, and resource quotas when diagnosing pods stuck in Pending when configuring Kubernetes Stuck Pending
mistakesToAvoid.why: Pods remain `Pending` when scheduler predicates fail; `kubectl describe pod` reveals whether CPU/memory exhaustion or taints prevent placement.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Invoking kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0 indiscriminately on unready pods when configuring Kubernetes Stuck Pending
mistakesToAvoid.why: Forced deletion bypasses kubelet cleanup and can cause multi-attach errors on PersistentVolumes (PVs) or split-brain on stateful workloads.

title: Pod in CrashLoopBackOff — Diagnostic & Root Cause Workflow
summary: Exhaustive triage process for debugging CrashLoopBackOff: decoding container exit codes (137 OOMKill, 1 app error, 143 SIGTERM), fetching previous container logs, and fixing probe failures.
question: Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff — how would you troubleshoot?
intro: CrashLoopBackOff means the container started, crashed, and Kubernetes is backing off before restarting it. My troubleshooting sequence always follows: Exit Code analysis -> Previous container logs -> Liveness probe evaluation.

steps.title: Inspect Exit Code via kubectl describe
steps.description: Run kubectl describe pod <pod-name> and examine the Last State: Terminated block:
items: Exit Code 137 (OOMKilled): Reason: OOMKilled. The Linux kernel OOM Killer terminated the container for exceeding its limits.memory. Fix: bump memory limit or fix memory leak.
Exit Code 1 or 255 (App Error): Application code crashed (uncaught exception, syntax error, missing environment variable, failed DB connection).
Exit Code 127 (Command Not Found): Container CMD/ENTRYPOINT executable does not exist inside the image.
Exit Code 143 (SIGTERM): Graceful shutdown signal was received, often from a failing liveness probe or preStop hook.
Exit Code 0 (Completed): Container finished its task and exited normally, but pod restartPolicy is Always instead of OnFailure/Never.

steps.title: Fetch Previous Container Logs (--previous)
steps.description: Because the crashing container has already terminated, standard logs may be empty or only show startup lines:
items: kubectl logs <pod-name> --previous: The golden command — reads the stdout/stderr from the crashed instance before it restarted.
If multi-container pod: kubectl logs <pod-name> -c <container-name> --previous.
Look at the last 20 lines for stack traces, database connection timeouts, or missing config keys.

steps.title: Check Liveness & Startup Probes
steps.description: A misconfigured liveness probe will actively kill a healthy container during slow startup:
items: Check events for: Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 500.
If an app takes 45 seconds to initialize but initialDelaySeconds is 10, Kubernetes kills it repeatedly!
Fix: Implement a startupProbe with generous failureThreshold, giving the app time to start before liveness checks engage.

steps.title: Interactive Debugging with Ephemeral Containers
steps.description: If logs are silent and container crashes instantly:
items: Override entrypoint in a local manifest: change command to ['sh', '-c', 'sleep 3600'] to keep container alive, then kubectl exec -it to inspect files and environment.
Use kubectl debug -it <pod-name> --image=busybox --target=<container> to attach an ephemeral debugging container sharing the process namespace.

keyTakeaway: Look at the Exit Code first (137 = OOM, 1 = App crash). Use 'kubectl logs --previous' to capture the crash stack trace. Verify startupProbe isn't killing slow-starting applications.
elevatorPitch: Run 'kubectl describe pod <name>' -> inspect Last State: Exit Code (137 = OOMKill, 1 = code exception, 127 = binary missing).
Run 'kubectl logs <name> --previous' to retrieve the stack trace from the crashed instance.
If Exit Code 137: Increase spec.resources.limits.memory or profile memory leak.
Check Probes: Verify livenessProbe isn't timing out during slow boots; add startupProbe.
If container crashes instantly: Override command with 'sleep 3600' or attach ephemeral container via 'kubectl debug'.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Restarting the pod flushes ephemeral container runtime state, destroying vital panic stack traces and fatal initialization logs.

title: Pod Running but Service Inaccessible — End-to-End Network Approach
summary: Systematic networking approach for when pods report Running/Ready but the Kubernetes ClusterIP/NodePort/LoadBalancer Service cannot be reached.
question: Pod is running but Service isn't accessible — what's your approach?
intro: When a Pod is Running but its Service isn't accessible, I isolate the failure across 5 discrete layers: Service Selector/Endpoints -> Port mapping -> Readiness probes -> Cluster DNS -> NetworkPolicies.

steps.title: Step 1: Check Endpoints & EndpointSlices (The #1 Culprit)
steps.description: Services do not route to Pods directly; they route to Endpoints populated by label matching:
items: Run: kubectl get endpoints <service-name> and kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<service-name>.
If Endpoints is <none>: The Service's spec.selector does NOT match the Pod's labels! Compare kubectl get svc <svc> -o yaml against kubectl get pods --show-labels.
Common typos: app: web in service vs app: frontend or tier: web on pod.

steps.title: Step 2: Check Pod Readiness Probes
steps.description: A pod can be 'Running' but failing its readiness probe:
items: Check kubectl get pods: Is the pod showing 0/1 READY?
If a readiness probe fails, Kubernetes removes the pod's IP from the Service Endpoints to prevent traffic from hitting unready pods.
Check kubectl describe pod for readiness probe failures.

steps.title: Step 3: Verify Port & TargetPort Mapping
steps.description: Confirm the port translation pipeline:
items: port: 80: The port clients connect to on the Service ClusterIP.
targetPort: 8080: The port the container is actually listening on.
Verify the app is listening inside the container: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- ss -tulpn or curl localhost:8080.
If targetPort is a named port (e.g. http), verify containerPort: 8080 in pod spec matches the name.

steps.title: Step 4: Test In-Cluster DNS & NetworkPolicies
steps.description: Spin up a temporary debug pod inside the cluster:
items: kubectl run curl-test --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh
Test by IP first: curl -Iv http://<ClusterIP>:<port>. If IP works, problem is CoreDNS resolution.
Test by FQDN: curl -Iv http://<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local:<port>.
Check NetworkPolicies: Run kubectl get netpol. If an ingress default-deny NetworkPolicy exists on the namespace without an allow rule for the client, all traffic is dropped silently at the CNI layer.

keyTakeaway: Always check 'kubectl get endpoints <svc>' first. If endpoints are empty, it's either a label selector mismatch or a failing readiness probe. Then test port mappings and NetworkPolicies.
elevatorPitch: Check Endpoints: 'kubectl get endpoints <svc>'. If empty, Service selector doesn't match Pod labels.
Check Readiness: If pod is 0/1 READY, failing readiness probe stripped pod IP from endpoints.
Check Port Translation: Verify service port -> targetPort matches the port the container is listening on (ss -tulpn).
Test via curl container: Test ClusterIP directly, then FQDN (service.ns.svc.cluster.local) to rule out CoreDNS.
Check NetworkPolicies: 'kubectl get netpol -n <ns>' - verify ingress allow rules exist between namespaces.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Overlooking CoreDNS query amplification caused by high ndots search path configurations
mistakesToAvoid.why: Default `ndots:5` triggers multiple sequential failed DNS lookups for external domains against cluster local search paths, overloading CoreDNS.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Applying restrictive NetworkPolicies that block CoreDNS egress UDP/TCP port 53 lookups
mistakesToAvoid.why: Blocking egress DNS traffic prevents pods from resolving internal cluster services or external database endpoints.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Confusing Service exposure ports with container targetPort definitions in Kubernetes manifests
mistakesToAvoid.why: Mismatched ports forward traffic to unlistening container ports, resulting in immediate `connection refused` errors.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring MTU packet size mismatches between physical host interfaces and CNI overlay encapsulation
mistakesToAvoid.why: Overlay encapsulation headers (VXLAN/Geneve) exceed standard MTU without proper clamping, causing silent packet drops on large TCP payloads.

title: New Deployment Breaks Production — Fast & Safe Rollback
summary: Fast-response production incident runbook for rolling back broken Kubernetes deployments across native kubectl, GitOps (ArgoCD/Flux), and handling database migration traps.
question: New deployment breaks production — how would you rollback?
intro: When a new deployment causes production degradation, the priority is mean time to recovery (MTTR). The rollback path depends on whether you run imperative deployments or declarative GitOps.

steps.title: Immediate Imperative Rollback (kubectl rollout undo)
steps.description: If using native Kubernetes deployments:
items: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<deployment-name> -n <ns>: Instantly rolls back to the previous revision.
kubectl rollout status deployment/<deployment-name>: Monitor the rollback progress in real-time.
To target a specific revision: kubectl rollout history deployment/<name> followed by kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> --to-revision=3.
How it works under the hood: Kubernetes points the Deployment back to the previous healthy ReplicaSet, scaling it up while scaling down the broken ReplicaSet.

steps.title: GitOps Rollback (ArgoCD / Flux Reality)
steps.description: In GitOps, manual kubectl rollouts will be reverted by self-healing:
items: The GitOps Trap: If you run kubectl rollout undo while ArgoCD has auto-sync + self-heal enabled, ArgoCD will detect drift and immediately re-deploy the broken version!
Proper GitOps Rollback: Run git revert HEAD && git push origin main in the manifest repository. ArgoCD syncs and restores the previous commit cleanly.
Emergency Fast-Path: In ArgoCD UI/CLI, click Disable Auto-Sync, roll back revision, then fix Git repository.

steps.title: The Database Migration Trap
steps.description: Can code be safely rolled back if database schema migrated?
items: If the release included destructive database schema migrations (e.g. dropped a column or renamed a table), rolling back application code will crash the previous version because old code expects the old schema.
The Rule: Production deployments must follow Expand and Contract database migrations (additive changes first, deploy code, cleanup in next release).
If a migration broke backward compatibility: Coordinate with DBAs to apply a compensating forward migration or restore DB snapshot before reverting code.

steps.title: Post-Incident & Blameless Post-Mortem
steps.description: Preventing the same failure in future releases:
items: Conduct blameless post-mortem: Why didn't automated CI tests or staging catch this?
Implement Canary Deployments with Argo Rollouts or Flagger: Route 5% traffic to canary; automatically abort if 5xx errors spike without human intervention.
Add automated smoke tests and readiness probe validation.

keyTakeaway: Know your deployment mechanism: In pure K8s, use 'kubectl rollout undo'; in GitOps (ArgoCD), disable auto-sync or 'git revert' to prevent self-heal fighting. Never do destructive DB migrations in single-step releases.
elevatorPitch: Immediate action: Run 'kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>' to revert to previous ReplicaSet.
If GitOps (ArgoCD/Flux): Disable auto-sync immediately or 'git revert HEAD && git push' so self-heal doesn't re-break it.
Database check: Verify if DB migrations ran. If additive, rollback is safe. If destructive, apply compensating migration.
Verify recovery: Monitor 'kubectl rollout status', ALB 5xx metrics, and application logs.
Post-mortem: Implement progressive delivery (Argo Rollouts/Canary) with automatic metric-based rollback.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Over-granting cluster-admin permissions to pod ServiceAccounts instead of scoping namespace Roles when configuring Deployment Breaks Fast
mistakesToAvoid.why: Over-granting cluster-wide permissions violates least-privilege principles and allows compromised pods to escalate privileges across namespaces.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Referencing mutable latest container tags across production Kubernetes Deployment specs when configuring Deployment Breaks Fast
mistakesToAvoid.why: Deployments referencing `:latest` risk inconsistent versions across replica pods and break deterministic rollback capabilities.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting pod readiness probes, causing traffic to hit uninitialized application containers when configuring Deployment Breaks Fast
mistakesToAvoid.why: Readiness probes gate traffic delivery; missing probes cause Kubernetes to route user requests to pods before dependencies or caches are loaded.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Executing diagnostic triage without analyzing chronological cluster events and describe outputs when configuring Deployment Breaks Fast
mistakesToAvoid.why: Cluster events provide sequential timestamps of scheduler decisions, probe failures, and image pull timeouts essential for rapid root-cause isolation.

title: CI/CD Pipeline Succeeds but New Version Isn't Deployed — Debugging
summary: Diagnostic guide for when CI/CD logs show green checkmarks but the target production environment continues running old code: image tag caching, branch rules, and GitOps sync gaps.
question: Pipeline succeeds but the new version isn't deployed — how would you debug?
intro: When a CI/CD pipeline shows green but production is unchanged, the issue lies in artifact immutability, deployment trigger conditions, or GitOps reconciliation gaps.

steps.title: Verify What is Actually Running in Production
steps.description: Start by inspecting the live cluster/server before checking pipeline scripts:
items: Run: kubectl get deployment <app> -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'.
Check the image tag and digest. Does it match the newly built Git commit SHA?
Hit the application's version endpoint: curl https://app.example.com/version.

steps.title: The ':latest' Tag & imagePullPolicy Trap
steps.description: The single most common root cause in container CI/CD:
items: If the pipeline pushes myapp:latest and the Kubernetes Deployment manifest says image: myapp:latest with imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent:
Kubernetes checks if a tag named latest exists locally on the node. If yes, it never pulls the new image from the registry!
Furthermore, Kubernetes detects no change in the Deployment manifest (the image string is still myapp:latest), so it triggers zero rollout!
Fix: Always use immutable image tags based on Git SHA or semantic release (e.g. myapp:sha-7f3a9b2).

steps.title: Pipeline Step Conditions & Environment Mismatch
steps.description: Audit pipeline execution steps:
items: Skipped Deploy Step: Did the build/test job succeed, but the deploy job was skipped because of a condition like if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' when building a feature branch?
Target Environment Mismatch: Did the pipeline deploy to Staging instead of Production due to environment variable configuration?
Manual Approval Gate: Is the pipeline waiting on manual approval in GitHub Actions Environments / GitLab Protected Environments?

steps.title: GitOps Manifest Repo & Controller Audit
steps.description: If using a separate manifest repository (ArgoCD / Flux):
items: Did the CI pipeline successfully commit and push the updated image tag to the config repo? (Check git credentials and branch protection rules).
Check ArgoCD sync status: Is the application in OutOfSync or Sync Failed state? Is auto-sync paused?
Check for Kubernetes manifest validation failure (e.g. invalid YAML or unaccepted CPU limit).

keyTakeaway: Check the live running image tag first. Avoid mutable ':latest' tags that bypass k8s rollouts. Verify pipeline conditions, approval gates, and GitOps manifest commit chains.
elevatorPitch: Verify running container image: 'kubectl get deploy <app> -o jsonpath={..image}'.
Check image tagging: Avoid ':latest' with 'imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent' which ignores new image pushes.
Audit CI logs: Ensure the deploy job actually executed and was not skipped by branch/tag conditions.
Check GitOps repo: Verify CI successfully pushed new image tag commit to the manifest repository.
Check ArgoCD/Flux: Inspect sync status, controller errors, or paused auto-sync.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Promoting application releases to production without an automated, canary-validated rollback mechanism when configuring CI/CD Pipeline Succeeds
mistakesToAvoid.why: Pipelines that lack automated rollback mechanisms force engineering teams to scramble manual hotfixes during severe production regressions.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running concurrent deployment pipeline jobs without stage mutex locking on shared target environments when configuring CI/CD Pipeline Succeeds
mistakesToAvoid.why: Concurrent pipeline runs on the same environment race to apply state changes, causing out-of-order commits and unpredictable deployment state.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting dependency lockfiles (package-lock.json, go.sum, Cargo.lock) from continuous integration builds when configuring CI/CD Pipeline Succeeds
mistakesToAvoid.why: Omitting lockfiles allows upstream package updates to break builds unpredictably without any changes to application codebase.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to define dynamic cache invalidation keys for CI package managers and layer caches when configuring CI/CD Pipeline Succeeds
mistakesToAvoid.why: Stale build caches mask underlying dependency incompatibilities or pull outdated libraries, while un-cached runs slow feedback loops.

title: Production Deployment Fails Halfway — Rollback & Blast Radius
summary: Engineering strategy for recovering from halfway-failed deployments: rolling update halts, automated canary rollback, and protecting stateful databases.
question: Production deployment fails halfway — what's your rollback strategy?
intro: A deployment failing halfway means your system is in a hybrid state — some nodes or pods are running the new version while others run the old version. The strategy depends on deployment pattern and data compatibility.

steps.title: Stop Forward Rollout & Contain Traffic
steps.description: Halt the release immediately before more instances degrade:
items: In Kubernetes: Rolling updates halt automatically if new pods fail readiness checks or crash (governed by maxUnavailable).
In Canary (Argo Rollouts / Flagger): Issue an abort command (kubectl argo rollouts abort <app>) to shift 100% traffic back to the stable baseline.
In AWS CodeDeploy / ECS: Click Stop and roll back deployment.

steps.title: Execute Safe Rollback
steps.description: Restore all instances to the previous known-good state:
items: Run kubectl rollout undo deployment/<app> to revert to previous ReplicaSet.
If Blue/Green: Traffic router never switched over, or can be instantly routed back to Blue target group with 0 rebuild time.
Verify target health: Ensure all healthy pods are receiving traffic and serving 200 OK.

steps.title: Verify Database & Stateful Dependencies
steps.description: The most dangerous aspect of partial failures:
items: Did a migration script execute before the application containers failed?
If code rolled back but DB schema remains in new state: verify application is backward-compatible.
Golden Rule: Never deploy breaking DB schema changes and application code in the same release. Always use the Expand/Contract (Parallel Run) pattern.

steps.title: Automated Guardrails to Prevent Recurrence
steps.description: Architectural improvements for future releases:
items: Add synthetic canary health analysis: evaluate Prometheus 5xx error rate and latency over 5-minute intervals before promoting each traffic step.
Add pre-deployment health checks and automated database rollback scripts.

keyTakeaway: Halt forward rollout immediately. Revert traffic to the stable baseline. Never couple breaking database migrations with application deployments — use Expand/Contract.
elevatorPitch: Halt rollout immediately: Abort canary or rolling update to prevent further degradation.
Revert instances: Use 'kubectl rollout undo' or flip traffic router back to 100% stable version.
Check Database: Verify if migrations ran; ensure schema changes follow Expand/Contract so old code remains functional.
Validate: Confirm healthy targets in ALB and verify application error metrics stabilize.
Prevent: Introduce automated Canary analysis (Argo Rollouts/Flagger) with automated rollback thresholds.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Pipelines that lack automated rollback mechanisms force engineering teams to scramble manual hotfixes during severe production regressions.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running concurrent deployment pipeline jobs without stage mutex locking on shared target environments when configuring Deployment Fails Halfway
mistakesToAvoid.why: Concurrent pipeline runs on the same environment race to apply state changes, causing out-of-order commits and unpredictable deployment state.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting dependency lockfiles (package-lock.json, go.sum, Cargo.lock) from continuous integration builds when configuring Deployment Fails Halfway
mistakesToAvoid.why: Omitting lockfiles allows upstream package updates to break builds unpredictably without any changes to application codebase.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Stale build caches mask underlying dependency incompatibilities or pull outdated libraries, while un-cached runs slow feedback loops.

title: Secure Secrets Management in CI/CD & Production
summary: Enterprise secrets management architecture: eliminating secrets from Git and CI logs, integrating HashiCorp Vault / AWS Secrets Manager with Kubernetes, and using SOPS/External Secrets Operator.
question: How would you securely manage secrets?
intro: Secure secrets management requires defense-in-depth across three stages: in Git repositories (at rest), during CI/CD execution (in transit), and inside production runtime environments.

steps.title: Pillar 1: Never Commit Plaintext Secrets to Git
steps.description: Enforce strict pre-commit and repository-level prevention:
items: Pre-commit Hooks & Secret Scanning: Run git-secrets, TruffleHog, or GitHub Secret Scanning to block commits containing API keys, private certs, or AWS tokens.
Encrypted In-Repo Secrets (GitOps): If secrets must be stored in Git for GitOps, use Mozilla SOPS (encrypted with AWS KMS / GCP KMS) or Bitnami Sealed Secrets (asymmetric public key encryption).

steps.title: Pillar 2: Centralized Secrets Store of Record
steps.description: Use dedicated secret management services:
items: Store canonical secrets in AWS Secrets Manager, AWS SSM Parameter Store, or HashiCorp Vault.
Enable automated rotation for database passwords and API tokens.
Enforce IAM least privilege and audit every secret read with AWS CloudTrail / Vault audit logs.

steps.title: Pillar 3: Runtime Injection into Kubernetes
steps.description: How applications consume secrets securely in production:
items: External Secrets Operator (ESO): Best practice — synchronizes secrets from AWS Secrets Manager / Vault into native Kubernetes Secrets declaratively.
Secrets Store CSI Driver: Mounts secrets directly from AWS Secrets Manager into container memory volumes without creating native K8s Secret objects.
Cluster Security: Enable etcd encryption-at-rest using KMS provider to ensure raw secrets aren't stored unencrypted on disk.

steps.title: Pillar 4: CI/CD Pipeline Hygiene
steps.description: Protecting secrets during automated builds:
items: Use OIDC (OpenID Connect): GitHub Actions / GitLab CI authenticates to AWS via IAM roles without long-lived static AWS access keys!
Mask all environment variables in pipeline logs.
Scoped permissions: Pipeline runners should only have access to secrets needed for build/deploy, never admin credentials.

keyTakeaway: Store secrets in AWS Secrets Manager / Vault, inject into K8s via External Secrets Operator, encrypt in Git using SOPS, use OIDC for CI/CD instead of static keys, and encrypt etcd at rest.
elevatorPitch: Repository level: Block secrets with TruffleHog / pre-commit hooks; use SOPS/KMS if storing in GitOps repos.
Storage of record: AWS Secrets Manager / HashiCorp Vault with automated rotation and CloudTrail audit logging.
Kubernetes integration: Use External Secrets Operator (ESO) or Secrets Store CSI driver; enable etcd encryption-at-rest.
CI/CD pipeline: Eliminate static AWS keys using OIDC federated IAM roles; mask all secrets in logs.
Access control: Enforce strict RBAC on K8s secrets; disable automountServiceAccountToken where not needed.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Promoting application releases to production without an automated, canary-validated rollback mechanism when configuring Secure Secrets Management
mistakesToAvoid.why: Pipelines that lack automated rollback mechanisms force engineering teams to scramble manual hotfixes during severe production regressions.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running concurrent deployment pipeline jobs without stage mutex locking on shared target environments when configuring Secure Secrets Management
mistakesToAvoid.why: Concurrent pipeline runs on the same environment race to apply state changes, causing out-of-order commits and unpredictable deployment state.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting dependency lockfiles (package-lock.json, go.sum, Cargo.lock) from continuous integration builds when configuring Secure Secrets Management
mistakesToAvoid.why: Omitting lockfiles allows upstream package updates to break builds unpredictably without any changes to application codebase.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Stale build caches mask underlying dependency incompatibilities or pull outdated libraries, while un-cached runs slow feedback loops.

title: Implementing Blue-Green vs Canary Deployments in Production
summary: Architectural blueprints for Blue-Green and Canary deployments: traffic routing mechanics, automated metric verification, database migration considerations, and rollback triggers.
question: How would you implement Blue-Green/Canary deployment?
intro: Both strategies aim for zero downtime, but they serve different risk profiles: Blue-Green is all-or-nothing environment switching, while Canary is progressive, metric-driven traffic shifting.

steps.title: Implementing Canary Deployments (Progressive Delivery)
steps.description: Deploy new version alongside stable, route a small percentage of real traffic:
items: Tooling: Argo Rollouts or Flagger integrated with an Ingress controller (NGINX, ALB, or Istio service mesh).
Traffic Step Plan: Route 5% traffic → wait 5 minutes → 20% → 50% → 100%.
Automated Analysis (AnalysisTemplate): During each step, Argo Rollouts queries Prometheus for metrics: HTTP error rate < 1% and p99 latency < 250ms.
Automatic Rollback: If error rate spikes, the controller automatically aborts and restores 100% traffic to the stable version without human intervention.

steps.title: Implementing Blue-Green Deployments (Environment Isolation)
steps.description: Maintain two identical production environments (Blue = Live, Green = Idle):
items: Step 1: Deploy new release to Green environment. Zero production user traffic hits Green yet.
Step 2: Run comprehensive automated smoke tests, health checks, and synthetic user journeys against Green.
Step 3 (Traffic Flip): Update the router (Kubernetes Service selector, ALB weighted target group, or Route 53 weighted record) to point 100% traffic to Green.
Step 4: Keep Blue running for 30–60 minutes as an instant zero-downtime rollback target. Once stability is proven, decommission or repurpose Blue.

steps.title: Database Schema Strategy for Both
steps.description: How to handle databases when two different application versions run simultaneously:
items: In both Canary and Blue-Green, old and new versions run concurrently against the same production database.
You must use the Expand and Contract pattern: Schema migrations must be backward-compatible with the old version.
Never drop or rename columns in the same release as application updates.

keyTakeaway: Canary uses Argo Rollouts/Flagger for metric-driven progressive traffic shifting (5% -> 100%). Blue-Green uses dual environments with a router flip. Both require backward-compatible Expand/Contract database schemas.
elevatorPitch: Canary: Progressive rollout using Argo Rollouts or Flagger. Incremental traffic shift (5% -> 20% -> 100%) with Prometheus metric analysis for auto-rollback.
Blue-Green: Dual identical environments. Deploy to Green, run smoke tests, flip Service selector or ALB Target Group weight, keep Blue alive for fast rollback.
Traffic Routing: Managed at Ingress/Service Mesh layer (Istio, NGINX Ingress, or AWS ALB weighted target groups).
Database requirement: Backward-compatible Expand/Contract schema migrations to support both versions running concurrently.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Confusing ALB 502 Bad Gateway (target connection reset) with 504 Gateway Timeout (upstream response timeout)
mistakesToAvoid.why: 502 indicates the backend target closed the TCP connection prematurely or returned malformed HTTP, whereas 504 means the target failed to respond before idle timeout.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Setting target deregistration delay to zero instead of allowing connection draining
mistakesToAvoid.why: Instant target deregistration severs in-flight HTTP requests during auto-scaling scale-in or rolling deployments, causing immediate user-facing drops.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to query CloudWatch ELB metrics (`HTTPCode_ELB_5XX` vs `HTTPCode_Target_5XX`) during load balancer outages
mistakesToAvoid.why: Comparing load balancer generated errors against target generated errors immediately isolates whether the issue lies in the proxy tier or application runtime.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Overlooking Security Group rules on backend EC2/ECS instances that block health check traffic from the ALB in cicd-blue-green-canary-implementation
mistakesToAvoid.why: Target instances must explicitly permit inbound HTTP/HTTPS traffic from the ALB security group on the configured container/application port.

title: terraform plan Shows Unexpected Changes — Investigation Steps
summary: Deep investigation runbook for unexpected terraform plan diffs: distinguishing configuration drift, provider upgrade defaults, dynamic attributes, and preventing accidental destruction.
question: terraform plan shows unexpected changes — what would you investigate?
intro: When 'terraform plan' shows unexpected changes — especially destruction or in-place modifications — my absolute first rule is: STOP. Do not run 'terraform apply'. Investigate the diff systematically.

steps.title: Analyze the Diff & Action Symbols
steps.description: Read the exact plan output carefully:
items: ~ update in-place: Non-destructive attribute change.

-/+ replace (forces replacement): High danger — Terraform must DESTROY the existing resource and recreate a new one! Look for the # ... forces replacement comment next to the specific attribute that triggered it (e.g. EC2 AMI change, VPC CIDR, or EBS volume type).
- destroy: Resource is being deleted because it was removed from code or renamed.

steps.title: Check for Out-of-Band State Drift
steps.description: Did someone modify the cloud resource manually in the AWS Console or CLI?
items: Run: terraform plan -refresh-only.
This compares the Terraform state file directly against real-world cloud infrastructure without proposing changes to match the code.
If -refresh-only shows drift: Someone touched the resource out-of-band.
Check AWS CloudTrail: Filter event history by resource name to identify who modified the resource, when, and via which API call.

steps.title: Provider Upgrades & Variable Drift
steps.description: Inspect underlying dependencies:
items: Provider Version Changes: Check .terraform.lock.hcl. Did a provider update (e.g. AWS provider v5.0 → v5.2) change default attributes, deprecate tags, or modify schema defaults?
Variable & tfvars Mismatch: Was a different .tfvars file passed? Did an engineer override variables via TF_VAR_* environment variables?
Dynamic Inputs: Is code using dynamic functions like timestamp() or uuid() that produce new diffs on every single run?

steps.title: Resolve and Prevent Recurrence
steps.description: How to resolve safely:
items: If code was renamed: Use moved { from = ... to = ... } blocks (Terraform 1.1+) instead of destroying and recreating!
If manual change was intentional: Update Terraform code to match reality, run terraform apply -refresh-only.
If manual change was rogue: Run terraform apply to overwrite manual changes and restore code enforcement.
Add lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } to critical databases and VPCs.

keyTakeaway: Never apply an unexpected plan. Look for '# forces replacement' flags. Run 'terraform plan -refresh-only' to isolate cloud drift from code changes, and check CloudTrail for out-of-band console edits.
elevatorPitch: Freeze: Do not apply. Inspect plan diff for '~' (in-place) vs '-/+' (destroy and recreate - forces replacement).
Isolate drift: Run 'terraform plan -refresh-only' to identify out-of-band manual changes in AWS Console.
Check CloudTrail: Identify who modified the resource outside Terraform and when.
Check provider & variables: Check '.terraform.lock.hcl' for provider upgrades and verify correct .tfvars file.
Use moved blocks: If refactoring, use 'moved' blocks to prevent destroy/recreate cycles.
Safeguards: Add 'lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }' on critical production resources.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Unpinned provider versions automatically download breaking major upgrades during CI runs, introducing unexpected schema validation failures.

title: Someone Manually Changes Terraform Infrastructure — What Happens?
summary: Exhaustive breakdown of configuration drift in Terraform: what happens during refresh, how Terraform resolves divergence, and how to eliminate console access in production.
question: Someone manually changes Terraform-managed infrastructure — what happens?
intro: This is known as 'Configuration Drift'. What happens depends on whether the resource was modified, added, or deleted, and when the next Terraform execution runs.

steps.title: What Happens During Next Terraform Run
steps.description: During the next terraform plan or apply, Terraform performs a refresh:
items: State Refresh: Terraform queries the cloud provider API (e.g. AWS API) for all resources tracked in terraform.tfstate.

If a tracked resource was modified manually: Terraform compares the real-world state against the code. It flags drift and proposes an in-place update to revert the resource back to the code definition.
If a tracked resource was deleted manually: Terraform state detects the missing resource and proposes recreating it from scratch.

If unmanaged sub-resources were added manually: For example, someone manually added tags or security group rules: Depending on resource arguments, Terraform may delete the extra rules, ignore them, or fail with conflict errors.

steps.title: Two Remediation Paths
steps.description: The team must choose between restoring code or adopting the change:
items: Path A (Enforce Code / Revert Drift): Run terraform apply. Terraform will overwrite the manual console changes and restore the infrastructure to the version-controlled state of truth.

Path B (Adopt the Manual Change into Code): If the manual change was an emergency hotfix: update the .tf code to match the new configuration, run terraform plan to verify 0 proposed changes, and commit the code.

steps.title: How to Prevent It from Happening Again
steps.description: Enterprise governance safeguards:
items: Remove Write Access in Production: Developers and DevOps engineers should have ReadOnlyAccess in the AWS Production Console. Only the CI/CD pipeline's IAM role should have write permissions.

Automated Drift Detection: Run a scheduled daily CI/CD pipeline (e.g. at 2 AM) executing terraform plan -detailed-exitcode. If exit code is 2 (drift detected), send an automated alert to Slack/PagerDuty.
Use SCPs (Service Control Policies): Enforce AWS Organizations SCPs preventing direct edits to mission-critical VPC, IAM, or KMS resources.

keyTakeaway: On next run, Terraform detects drift during refresh and proposes reverting the manual change back to match code. Prevent it by removing AWS console write access and running automated daily drift detection in CI.
elevatorPitch: What happens: On next 'terraform plan', refresh detects divergence between cloud reality and state. Terraform proposes reverting manual edits to match code.
If resource deleted manually: Terraform proposes recreating it.
Remediation: Either 'terraform apply' to overwrite manual changes, or update code to match reality and commit.
Root prevention: Restrict IAM - zero human write access in Production AWS Console; only CI/CD IAM role has write access.
Detection: Schedule daily automated 'terraform plan -detailed-exitcode' in CI; alert team on exit code 2 (drift).
