title: Troubleshooting High CPU or Memory Usage in Kubernetes
summary: End-to-end investigative procedure for identifying and resolving runaway CPU and memory saturation in Kubernetes clusters: isolating nodes vs pods, diagnosing memory leaks vs legitimate load, and application profiling.
question: How would you troubleshoot high CPU or memory usage in Kubernetes?
intro: When a high CPU or memory alert triggers in Kubernetes, my workflow moves top-down: Cluster/Node level -> Pod level -> Container level -> Application runtime profiling (Go pprof / Java jstack).

steps.title: Step 1: Isolate Affected Nodes and Pods
steps.description: Identify where the saturation is concentrated:
items: kubectl top nodes: Pinpoints if a single node is saturated or if the entire cluster is running out of headroom.
kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=cpu: Instantly lists the top CPU-consuming pods across all namespaces.
kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory: Instantly lists the top memory-consuming pods.
Check if the pod is near its configured limit: compare kubectl top pod <pod> with limits.cpu / limits.memory in kubectl describe pod.

steps.title: Step 2: Differentiate CPU Spikes vs Memory Leaks
steps.description: Analyze Grafana/Prometheus metrics to identify the pattern:
items: CPU Saturation: Correlate with request rate (RPS) in ingress metrics. If RPS spiked 5x, it's legitimate traffic -> trigger HPA or scale replicas. If RPS is flat but CPU hit 100%, it's an infinite loop, thread lock, or regex catastrophic backtracking.
Memory Saturation: Look at the memory graph over 24-48 hours. If memory steadily climbs in a sawtooth pattern and never drops after garbage collection, it is a Memory Leak.

steps.title: Step 3: Capture Runtime Telemetry (Don't Restart Blindly)
steps.description: Capture the root cause before restarting the container:
items: Java / JVM: Exec into pod or use ephemeral container: jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/dump.hprof and jstack <pid> to see locked threads.
Golang / Node.js: Query the pprof endpoint: curl http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30 or heap profile.
Immediate Mitigation: Once profiling is captured, scale replicas horizontally (HPA) or do a rolling restart (kubectl rollout restart deployment/<app>) to restore customer SLA.

keyTakeaway: Diagnose top-down: 'kubectl top nodes' -> 'kubectl top pods --sort-by=cpu/memory' -> Correlate with traffic RPS in Grafana. For CPU without traffic spikes, capture thread dumps; for climbing memory, capture heap dumps before restarting.
elevatorPitch: Identify culprit: 'kubectl top nodes' followed by 'kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=cpu / --sort-by=memory'.
Correlate: Compare with Grafana request rate (RPS). Traffic spike = scale replicas. Flat traffic + 100% CPU = code deadlock/infinite loop.
Memory triage: Check memory graph slope. Gradual steady climb without GC recovery = Memory Leak.
Capture telemetry before restart: Run jstack/jcmd for Java, or pprof heap profiles for Go.
Mitigate: Trigger HPA scale-out, or perform 'kubectl rollout restart' to buy time while developers fix the leak.

title: Cloud Cost Optimization Across Dev, QA, UAT, and Production
summary: Strategic blueprint for optimizing cloud infrastructure spending across Dev, QA, UAT, and Production environments without degrading application reliability or developer velocity.
question: For a project, how would you optimize costs for each environment? What strategies reduce cloud costs without affecting application availability?
intro: Cost optimization is not about cutting resources blindly; it is about aligning infrastructure tiering to business risk. Lower environments can tolerate interruptions; Production demands zero downtime.

steps.title: Dev & QA: Aggressive Cost Elimination (60–80% Savings)
steps.description: Non-production environments sit idle 70% of the week (nights and weekends):
items: Automated Business-Hours Shutdown: Use tools like kube-downscaler or AWS Instance Scheduler to scale all deployments to 0 replicas and stop RDS databases outside 8 AM - 7 PM weekdays.
100% Spot Instances / Low-Priority VMs: Dev/QA nodes run entirely on EC2 Spot or Azure Spot VMs, slashing compute costs by up to 70-80%.
Single Replica & Cluster Sharing: Disable multi-AZ; run 1 replica per service; share a single EKS/AKS cluster across Dev and QA using namespace isolation and ResourceQuotas.

steps.title: UAT & Staging: Production-Parity on Demand
steps.description: Balancing testing fidelity with cost:
items: On-Demand Spin-Up: Spin up full UAT performance environments on-demand via Terraform/GitOps for staging test cycles, then tear them down immediately post-validation.
Single-AZ Databases with Auto-Pause: Use Aurora Serverless v2 or Azure SQL Serverless with auto-pause enabled during inactivity.

steps.title: Production: Availability First + Architectural Efficiency
steps.description: Cost optimization in Production must NEVER compromise availability:
items: Savings Plans & Reserved Instances: Cover predictable baseline compute (e.g. minimum 10 nodes) with 1- or 3-year Compute Savings Plans for 40-60% discounts.
ARM64 / Graviton / Ampere Architecture: Migrate EKS/AKS workloads to AWS Graviton3 or Azure Ampere Altra instances for 20% better performance at 20% lower cost.
Strategic Spot for Stateless Workers: Run stateless async background processors (SQS consumers, batch jobs) on Spot nodes with termination notices handled by AWS Node Termination Handler.

keyTakeaway: Tier cost strategy by environment: Dev/QA get scheduled off-hours shutdowns and 100% Spot instances; Staging uses on-demand ephemeral environments; Production achieves 40%+ savings via Compute Savings Plans, ARM64 Graviton instances, and Karpenter consolidation without touching uptime SLAs.
elevatorPitch: Dev & QA: Schedule off-hours shutdown (scale to 0 outside 9-6 via kube-downscaler); run 100% Spot VMs; share 1 cluster with namespaces.
UAT: Ephemeral environments spun up via Terraform for test runs; use Aurora/SQL Serverless with auto-pause.
Production: Never sacrifice HA. Use 1-3 year Compute Savings Plans for baseline load (40% discount).
Hardware efficiency: Adopt AWS Graviton3 / ARM instances for 20% cost reduction with better CPU performance.
Storage: S3 Intelligent-Tiering and automated deletion lifecycle rules for old snapshots and build artifacts.

title: Kubernetes Resource Right-Sizing & Bin-Packing for Cost Reduction
summary: Engineering methodology for eliminating 'phantom spend' in Kubernetes through container resource right-sizing, VPA recommendation mode, and intelligent node consolidation with Karpenter.
question: How would you use Kubernetes resource requests/limits to control costs?
intro: In Kubernetes, you pay for what you REQUEST, not what you use. If a developer requests 4 CPUs but the container only consumes 200m, the cloud provider bills you for 4 CPUs because the scheduler reserves the space. That gap is 'phantom spend'.

steps.title: The Phantom Spend Trap (Request vs Actual)
steps.description: How over-provisioned requests trigger unneeded cloud node scale-outs:
items: Kube-scheduler treats `requests` as hard commitments. If node capacity is 8 vCPU, and two pods request 4 vCPU each, the node is 100% allocated.
Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter is forced to provision a second EC2 node, even if the actual CPU utilization on the first node is only 5%!
Result: Cloud bills double while clusters run at 10% actual hardware utilization.

steps.title: Automated Right-Sizing Tools (Goldilocks & VPA)
steps.description: Data-driven sizing replacing developer guesswork:
items: Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) in 'Off' (Recommendation) Mode: Analyzes historical container usage and outputs exact recommended requests for CPU and memory.
Fairwinds Goldilocks: Dashboard that consumes VPA recommendations and highlights over-provisioned workloads across namespaces.
Set requests to the p95 peak utilization + 15-20% headroom, allowing pods to burst safely without blocking node scheduling.

steps.title: Dynamic Node Consolidation with Karpenter
steps.description: Maximizing node packing density:
items: Enable Karpenter consolidationPolicy: WhenUnderutilized.

Karpenter constantly evaluates cluster bin-packing: if 3 nodes are 30% full, Karpenter cordons and drains one node, moves its pods onto the remaining nodes, and terminates the empty instance in real-time.

keyTakeaway: Cloud bills scale with Kubernetes CPU/memory REQUESTS, not actual utilization. Over-provisioned requests force autoscalers to launch expensive unnecessary nodes. Right-size requests to p95 usage using VPA recommendation mode and enable Karpenter node consolidation.
elevatorPitch: Problem: Cloud billing follows requests, not usage. Over-requested pods force the cluster to spin up empty, expensive nodes.
Solution 1: Deploy VPA in recommendation mode + Goldilocks to discover real p95 CPU/memory usage.
Solution 2: Adjust requests down to actual p95 load + 20% buffer, freeing up node capacity.
Solution 3: Implement Karpenter with consolidation enabled—it automatically merges sparse nodes and terminates unneeded EC2 instances.
Result: 30–50% reduction in cluster compute spend with zero impact on application performance.

title: Detecting & Eliminating Unused / Orphaned Cloud Resources
summary: Actionable audit runbook for discovering and terminating ghost cloud resources: unattached EBS volumes, orphan managed disks, idle load balancers, unassociated Elastic IPs, and obsolete snapshots.
question: How would you identify unused or over-provisioned cloud resources?
intro: In every production cloud account over 1 year old, 15 to 25% of the monthly spend consists of 'zombie' or orphaned resources left behind by deleted clusters, test VMs, or failed CI pipelines.

steps.title: The Top 5 Orphaned Cloud Culprits
steps.description: Where ghost money leaks every month:
items: Unattached EBS Volumes / Azure Managed Disks: When an EC2/VM is deleted, attached persistent volumes often remain (status available or unattached), continuing to bill per GB-month.
Unassociated Elastic IPs / Public IPs: Cloud providers charge an hourly penalty fee for allocated public IPs that are NOT attached to a running instance.
Idle Load Balancers (ALB/NLB): Abandoned load balancers with 0 healthy targets or 0 request count that bill base hourly fees (~$25+/mo each).
Old Snapshots & AMIs: EBS snapshots from deleted instances retained for years without retention lifecycles.
Orphaned NAT Gateways: Idle NAT Gateways left running in obsolete testing VPCs billing ~$35/mo base + data transfer.

steps.title: Discovery Tools & Automated Auditing
steps.description: How senior teams automate identification:
items: AWS Compute Optimizer & Cost Explorer: Flags over-provisioned EC2/RDS instances and underutilized EBS volumes.
Azure Advisor: Generates automated Cost recommendations for idle virtual network gateways, unused disks, and downsized VMs.
KubeCost / OpenCost: In-cluster real-time allocation tool that breaks down Kubernetes spend by namespace, deployment, and orphaned persistent volumes.
Cloud Custodian: Open-source policy engine running automated custodial crons to tag and auto-terminate unattached volumes older than 7 days.

steps.title: Quick CLI Audit Commands
steps.description: Run immediately to find leaks:
items: AWS Unattached EBS: aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available --query 'Volumes[*].[VolumeId,Size,CreateTime]' --output table
AWS Unassociated IPs: aws ec2 describe-addresses --query 'Addresses[?NetworkInterfaceId==null].[PublicIp,AllocationId]' --output table
Azure Unattached Disks: az disk list --query '[?managedBy==null].[name,resourceGroup,diskSizeGb]' -o table

keyTakeaway: Implement continuous cloud hygiene: Audit for unattached EBS/managed disks, unassociated public IPs, and zero-target load balancers using AWS Compute Optimizer, Azure Advisor, and CLI query filters. Automate cleanup with Cloud Custodian policies.
elevatorPitch: Top leaks: Unattached EBS/managed disks, unassociated Elastic IPs, idle ALBs with 0 targets, and forgotten NAT Gateways.
Discovery tools: AWS Cost Explorer / Compute Optimizer, Azure Advisor Cost blade, and KubeCost for in-cluster visibility.
Fast CLI checks: 'aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available' to instantly find orphan storage.
Automated prevention: Cloud Custodian or Lambda janitor scripts to notify Slack and terminate unattached disks after 7 days.
Enforce mandatory tagging ('Environment', 'Owner', 'Project') in Terraform so untagged rogue resources cannot be created.

title: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) — Architecture, Deployment & Troubleshooting
summary: End-to-end operational guide for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS): control plane vs node pools, Azure CNI vs Kubenet, GitOps deployment with Azure DevOps / GitHub Actions, and diagnosing pod failures via Azure Container Insights.
question: Have you worked with Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)? How would you deploy, monitor, and troubleshoot applications on AKS?
intro: Yes, extensively. AKS provides a managed control plane while offloading worker node management into System and User node pools. Managing AKS effectively requires understanding Azure CNI networking, Workload Identity, and Azure Container Insights.

steps.title: AKS Architecture & Networking Fundamentals
steps.description: Control plane and networking choices:
items: Architecture: Free/Standard tier managed control plane (etcd, API server managed by Microsoft); customer pays only for Virtual Machine Scale Set (VMSS) worker nodes grouped into System (CoreDNS, Metrics Server) and User (microservices) node pools.

Azure CNI vs Kubenet: Kubenet uses internal pod overlay subnets (saves VNet IPs). Azure CNI gives every pod a real, routable IP from the Azure VNet subnet (lower latency, Direct VNet integration, but requires careful VNet CIDR sizing to avoid IP exhaustion).

steps.title: Deploying Applications to AKS
steps.description: Modern automated deployment workflow:
items: CI pipeline builds image and pushes to Azure Container Registry (ACR).
Authenticates to AKS using Microsoft Entra Workload Identity (OIDC federation—no long-lived service principal client secrets stored in CI).
CD pipeline (or ArgoCD GitOps) renders Helm templates and applies manifests to AKS.

steps.title: Monitoring & Troubleshooting in AKS
steps.description: Diagnostic workflow when issues occur:
items: Monitoring: Enable Azure Monitor Container Insights with Managed Prometheus and Grafana. Run KQL queries in Log Analytics: ContainerInventory | where ContainerStatus == 'Failed'.
Troubleshooting Pods: Standard kubectl describe pod and kubectl logs --previous.
AKS Diagnose and Solve Problems: Native Azure Portal blade that runs automated diagnostic checks on node readiness, subnet IP allocation, and API server throttles.
Node Issues: Check VMSS instance health in Azure Portal or run az aks check-acr to verify network connectivity between AKS nodes and ACR.

keyTakeaway: AKS architecture relies on System vs User node pools, Azure CNI for routable VNet networking, and Entra Workload Identity for secretless IAM. Monitor via Azure Monitor Container Insights (Prometheus/Grafana) and troubleshoot using kubectl alongside the Azure 'Diagnose and Solve' blade.
elevatorPitch: Architecture: Microsoft-managed control plane + VMSS worker node pools (System pool for core add-ons, User pool for workloads).
Networking: Azure CNI gives pods native VNet IPs; requires large subnets to prevent IP exhaustion.
Security: Entra Workload Identity federates Kubernetes ServiceAccounts with Azure Managed Identities (zero stored keys).
Deployment: Azure Pipelines / GitHub Actions -> build & scan image -> push to ACR -> deploy via Helm / ArgoCD.
Troubleshooting: Use 'kubectl describe/logs' for pod issues; 'az aks check-acr' for registry connectivity; and the Azure Portal 'Diagnose and Solve Problems' blade for node and network health.

title: Designing an End-to-End DevSecOps CI/CD Pipeline
summary: Complete architectural blueprint of an enterprise DevSecOps pipeline: shifting security left across commit, pull request, build, packaging, deployment, and runtime admission verification.
question: Explain your end-to-end CI/CD pipeline. Where would you integrate security scanning into the CI/CD pipeline?
intro: A mature DevSecOps pipeline does not treat security as a final checkpoint. Security scanning is embedded as automated 'quality gates' at every single stage of the software development lifecycle (SDLC).

steps.title: Stage 1: Pre-Commit & Pull Request (Shift-Left)
steps.description: Catch bugs and vulnerabilities before code is merged to main:
items: Pre-Commit Hooks: pre-commit running TruffleHog / GitGuardian to prevent developers from accidentally committing hardcoded AWS keys or passwords.
Static Application Security Testing (SAST): SonarQube or Semgrep scans source code on PR for OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities (SQLi, XSS, insecure deserialization).
Software Composition Analysis (SCA): Snyk or OWASP Dependency-Check scans third-party libraries (npm, pip, maven) against national vulnerability databases (CVEs).
steps.highlight: Quality Gate: If PR has any 'Critical' or 'High' vulnerabilities, the CI pipeline automatically fails and blocks the PR merge.

steps.title: Stage 2: Build, Container Scan & Cryptographic Signing
steps.description: Securing artifacts in the pipeline:
items: Multi-Stage Minimal Build: Docker builds using minimal distroless or Alpine base images running as non-root (UID 10001).
Container Vulnerability Scanning: Trivy or Grype scans the built image for OS-level and library vulnerabilities (breaks build if unpatched Critical CVE exists).
SBOM Generation: Generate Software Bill of Materials using Syft in SPDX/CycloneDX format.
Cryptographic Image Signing: Cosign (Sigstore) signs the image digest using Keyless OIDC signatures before pushing to ECR/ACR.

steps.title: Stage 3: GitOps Delivery & Cluster Admission Enforcement
steps.description: Zero-trust deployment and runtime guardrails:
items: GitOps Sync (ArgoCD): Updates image tag in the Git manifest repository; ArgoCD reconciles with Kubernetes cluster.

Kubernetes Admission Controller: Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper inspects every pod creation: verifies Cosign signature, blocks images without approval, enforces non-root execution, and rejects privileged containers.
Runtime Threat Detection: Falco monitors kernel system calls in production for abnormal execution (e.g. bash spawned inside container).

keyTakeaway: Shift security left across 5 gates: Pre-commit secret scanning (TruffleHog) -> PR SAST/SCA (SonarQube/Snyk) -> Container CVE scanning (Trivy) -> Image signing (Cosign) -> Kubernetes admission verification (Kyverno) and runtime monitoring (Falco).
elevatorPitch: Phase 1 (Code/PR): Secret scan (TruffleHog), SAST (SonarQube/Semgrep), and SCA dependency scan (Snyk). Block merge on Critical CVEs.
Phase 2 (Build): Build distroless container, scan image with Trivy, generate SBOM with Syft, and cryptographically sign image with Cosign.
Phase 3 (Deploy): GitOps with ArgoCD deploying signed image manifests.
Phase 4 (Admission): Kyverno admission controller blocks unsigned images or root containers at the cluster gate.
Phase 5 (Runtime): Falco kernel monitoring for runtime intrusion detection.

title: DevSecOps Tooling Ecosystem — What, Why & How Implementation
summary: Comprehensive breakdown of the production DevSecOps tooling matrix: tool purpose, selection criteria, pipeline integration commands, real-world failure cases, and mitigation strategies.
question: Which security tools have you used? What did you use them for, why did you choose them, and how did you implement them?
intro: In modern cloud platforms, I use a defense-in-depth security stack where every tool has a specific purpose along the lifecycle: Code, Dependencies, Containers, Secrets, Admission, and Runtime.

steps.title: The DevSecOps Production Tool Matrix
steps.description: What, Why, and Where each tool is deployed:

pillars.name: SAST: SonarQube / Semgrep
pillars.detail: What: Static code analysis. Why: Detects code smells, injection vulnerabilities, and enforces quality gates on pull requests.

pillars.name: SCA: Snyk / Trivy
pillars.detail: What: Software Composition Analysis. Why: Scans third-party open-source libraries for vulnerable transitive dependencies.

pillars.name: Container CVEs: Trivy / Grype
pillars.detail: What: Image vulnerability scanning. Why: Fast, lightweight CLI easily embedded in GitHub Actions/GitLab CI with '--severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1'.

pillars.name: Secrets: TruffleHog / GitGuardian
pillars.detail: What: High-entropy secret detection. Why: Prevents developers from pushing API keys, tokens, and SSH keys to Git.

pillars.name: Supply Chain: Cosign (Sigstore)
pillars.detail: What: Cryptographic image signing. Why: Guarantees image integrity and author verification from pipeline to cluster.

pillars.name: Policy & Runtime: Kyverno & Falco
pillars.detail: What: Kubernetes admission control and eBPF runtime threat detection. Why: Blocks unapproved pods and alerts on anomalous execution.

steps.title: Implementation: CI/CD Pipeline Integration Snippet
steps.description: How Trivy container scanning is enforced in GitHub Actions:
items: - name: Run Trivy Vulnerability Scanner
uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
with:
image-ref: '${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }}'
format: 'table'
exit-code: '1'
ignore-unfixed: true
severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH'
Pro-Tip: Always set ignore-unfixed: true in early pipeline adoption to prevent blocking deployments for zero-day vulnerabilities that have no official patch yet.

keyTakeaway: Explain tools by category: SAST (SonarQube/Semgrep), SCA (Snyk/Trivy), Secrets (TruffleHog), Container Images (Trivy), Signing (Cosign), Policy Enforcement (Kyverno/OPA), and Runtime Auditing (Falco).
elevatorPitch: SAST: SonarQube on PRs to analyze application source code for OWASP Top 10 bugs.
SCA: Snyk to scan third-party dependencies (package.json, pom.xml, requirements.txt).
Secret Scanning: TruffleHog in pre-commit and CI to catch leaked API tokens and keys.
Container CVEs: Trivy with 'ignore-unfixed: true' and 'exit-code 1' on Critical/High CVEs.
Signing & Admission: Cosign signs images; Kyverno admission controller verifies signatures before scheduling pods.
Runtime: Falco using eBPF to detect unauthorized shell spawns or file tampering in live pods.

title: Managing Secrets Securely in Kubernetes: External Secrets Operator (ESO) Architecture & Setup
summary: Enterprise standard operating model for Kubernetes secrets management: avoiding base64 Git commits, deploying External Secrets Operator (ESO) with cloud secret stores, and mounting secrets securely via tmpfs memory volumes.
question: How do you manage secrets securely in Kubernetes?
intro: Kubernetes native Secret objects are only base64-encoded plain text—they are NOT encrypted by default. In enterprise production, we NEVER store secrets in Git or YAML files. We sync them dynamically using External Secrets Operator (ESO).

steps.title: The Native Secret Trap & Plaintext in Git
steps.description: Why native Kubernetes secrets fail enterprise compliance:
items: Base64 encoding is not encryption: echo 'cGFzc3dvcmQ=' | base64 -d takes 1 millisecond.
If developer commits a Secret manifest to Git, the secret is permanently recorded in Git history.
In etcd, secrets are stored unencrypted unless EncryptionAtRest (using AWS KMS or Azure Key Vault KMS plugin) is explicitly enabled on the API server.

steps.title: Production Standard: External Secrets Operator (ESO)
steps.description: How External Secrets Operator bridges cloud vaults to Kubernetes:
items: Source of Truth: Secrets are maintained and rotated inside AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, or HashiCorp Vault.
SecretStore CRD: Configures authentication to the cloud vault using AWS IRSA or Azure Workload Identity (passwordless).
ExternalSecret CRD: A safe Git-committable manifest that specifies which remote secret key to fetch and how often to refresh (e.g. refreshInterval: 1h).
Auto-Reconciliation: ESO continuously syncs the remote secret into an in-cluster native Kubernetes Secret automatically.

steps.title: Secure Pod Consumption: Volume Mounts vs Env Vars
steps.description: How the pod should consume the secret securely:
items: Avoid Plaintext Env Vars: Environment variables (envFrom.secretRef) can leak into application error crash dumps, child process forks, and /proc/<pid>/environ.

Preferred Practice (Volume Mounts): Mount secrets as file volumes into /etc/secrets. In Kubernetes, secret volumes are backed by tmpfs (RAM only), meaning they are never written to physical node disk storage.

keyTakeaway: Never store secrets in Git. Keep the source of truth in AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, or HashiCorp Vault. Use External Secrets Operator (ESO) with Workload Identity to sync them into in-memory Kubernetes Secrets, and mount them as tmpfs file volumes rather than environment variables.
elevatorPitch: Kubernetes Secrets are just base64 plain text; storing them in Git is a critical security vulnerability.
Single Source of Truth: Store secrets in AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, or HashiCorp Vault with automated rotation.
Syncing Engine: Deploy External Secrets Operator (ESO). The Git repo only contains ExternalSecret manifests pointing to secret paths.
Authentication: ESO authenticates to cloud vaults via AWS IRSA or Azure Workload Identity (zero hardcoded cloud keys).
In-Pod consumption: Mount secrets as tmpfs RAM-backed file volumes instead of environment variables to prevent leak in crash logs.

title: Production Quality & Security Gates — Ensuring Only Secure Code Ships
summary: Multi-tier quality and security gating framework guaranteeing that only unit-tested, vulnerability-scanned, peer-reviewed, and cryptographically verified artifacts can reach production Kubernetes clusters.
question: How do you ensure that only tested and secure code reaches Production?
intro: Guaranteeing that only secure and tested code reaches Production requires a defense-in-depth model combining automated pipeline gates, cryptographic provenance, and cluster-level admission enforcement.

steps.title: Gate 1: Repository & Branch Protection Rules
steps.description: Controlling the entry point:
items: Strict branch protection on main: Direct pushes are blocked; all changes must pass through Pull Requests.
Mandatory minimum 2 peer code reviews, including an approval from the CODEOWNERS security team for sensitive modules.
All status checks must pass (Unit tests, Linting, Integration tests with minimum 80% test coverage).

steps.title: Gate 2: Automated Pipeline Security Quality Gates
steps.description: Zero-tolerance automated pass/fail thresholds in CI:
items: SonarQube Quality Gate: 0 Vulnerabilities, 0 Security Hotspots, and technical debt ratio < 5%.
Trivy Container Scan Gate: Pipeline breaks immediately (exit-code: 1) if any CVE with Severity 'CRITICAL' or 'HIGH' has an available vendor patch.
TruffleHog Secrets Gate: Any detected secret or token halts the pipeline instantly.

steps.title: Gate 3: Cryptographic Signature & Admission Control in Cluster
steps.description: Preventing unauthorized images from ever running in the cluster:
items: Cosign Signing: Only images that pass all CI testing and scanning gates are cryptographically signed using Cosign in the build pipeline.
Kyverno Admission Policy: Cluster-level Kyverno admission policy verifies the Cosign signature against the corporate public key before allowing any pod creation.

If an engineer tries to bypass CI/CD and run kubectl run rogue --image=evil:latest, the API server rejects it instantly: admission webhook 'kyverno-policy' denied the request: image signature verification failed.

keyTakeaway: Enforce 3 concentric security rings: 1) Branch protection with 2 peer reviews and 80% test coverage; 2) Automated CI quality gates breaking builds on Critical CVEs (Trivy/SonarQube); and 3) Cluster-level admission controllers (Kyverno/Gatekeeper) that reject any image not cryptographically signed by Cosign.
elevatorPitch: Ring 1 (Git): Branch protection on main, minimum 2 peer reviews + CODEOWNERS approval, 100% passing tests.
Ring 2 (CI Gates): SonarQube quality gate, Snyk dependency scan, and Trivy container scan configured to fail on Critical/High CVEs.
Ring 3 (Supply Chain Signing): Cosign cryptographically signs the image digest only after all CI checks pass.
Ring 4 (Cluster Admission): Kyverno admission controller verifies the cryptographic signature; rejects unsigned or manually deployed images.
Ring 5 (Progressive Delivery): Argo Rollouts canary deployment with automated rollback if error rate spikes in production.

title: What Really Happens Under the Hood When You Run 'kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml'?
summary: The definitive lifecycle of a Kubernetes resource: tracing 'kubectl apply' from client OpenAPI validation, API server authentication & admission webhooks, etcd persistence, controller reconciliation, scheduler scoring, kubelet CRI execution, to CNI network namespace plumbing.
question: What really happens under the hood when you run 'kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml'? Walk me through the entire journey from client CLI to running container.
roleContext: Senior / Staff Kubernetes Architecture Interview Question
intro: Most Kubernetes engineers run 'kubectl apply' daily, but behind that single command lies an entire distributed orchestration engine. Kubernetes operates as a Desired State System: you declare the desired state, and a chain of independent control loops continuously works to reconcile reality to match that state.

steps.title: Client-Side Processing & Validation (kubectl)
steps.description: Before any network request reaches the cluster, kubectl performs client-side inspection:
items: Client-Side Validation: kubectl verifies YAML syntax and checks resource fields against the locally cached OpenAPI / Swagger schema from the cluster (~/.kube/cache/discovery).

Three-Way Strategic Merge Patch: Reads the kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation, compares it with the live cluster state and the new local YAML, and computes a JSON Strategic Merge Patch.

HTTP REST Request: Formats the payload into JSON and dispatches an HTTP POST/PATCH request to the API server: POST /apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/deployments with TLS client certificates or OIDC Bearer tokens.

steps.title: API Server: Authentication, Authorization & Admission Control
steps.description: The kube-apiserver is the single front door to the cluster. The request traverses 4 sequential filters:
items: 1. Authentication: Validates TLS cert, ServiceAccount token, or Entra/AWS IAM OIDC identity to establish the caller's username and groups.
2. Authorization (RBAC): Evaluates ClusterRoles/RoleBindings to verify if the subject has create / patch permissions on deployments in the target namespace.
3. Mutating Admission Webhooks: Plugins and webhooks (e.g. Istio sidecar injector, Vault agent injector) modify the object or set default values.
4. Schema Validation: Enforces API schema rules, required fields, and immutability constraints.
5. Validating Admission Webhooks: Webhooks (e.g. Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper) run final compliance checks (e.g. enforcing non-root execution or image registry whitelisting) and reject invalid manifests.

steps.title: etcd: State Persistence & Consensus
steps.description: The single source of truth commits the change:
items: Once admission passes, kube-apiserver serializes the Deployment object into protocol buffers and writes it into etcd at key /registry/deployments/default/my-app.
etcd commits the write across a quorum of nodes using the Raft consensus algorithm.
The API server returns an HTTP 201 Created or 200 OK response back to the client CLI.
Important: At this exact second, NO containers or pods exist yet! Only the desired state is recorded.

steps.title: Deployment Controller & ReplicaSet Controller (kube-controller-manager)
steps.description: The control loops take over asynchronously:
items: Deployment Controller: Watches the API server for Deployment changes. Detects the new Deployment and creates a child ReplicaSet object with pod template hash.
ReplicaSet Controller: Detects the new ReplicaSet desiring e.g. 3 replicas. Compares desired replicas (3) with existing replicas (0).
It issues 3 API requests to create 3 Pod objects. Crucially, these Pod objects have no assigned node (spec.nodeName: '') and enter the Pending state.

steps.title: kube-scheduler: Node Filtering & Scoring
steps.description: Matching unbound pods to healthy worker nodes:
items: Watch Loop: kube-scheduler continuously watches the API server for Pods where spec.nodeName == ''.
Phase 1 (Filtering / Predicates): Eliminates ineligible nodes that lack sufficient CPU/memory requests, have untolerated taints, or fail nodeSelector / affinity constraints.
Phase 2 (Scoring / Priorities): Scores remaining nodes based on image locality, topology spread, and resource fragmentation (least/most requested).
Binding: Scheduler picks the highest-scoring node and sends a Binding API call to the API server, setting spec.nodeName: 'worker-node-2'.

steps.title: Kubelet & Container Runtime (CRI containerd)
steps.description: The local node agent brings the container to life:
items: Kubelet Watch: The kubelet daemon running on worker-node-2 observes that a Pod has been assigned to its node name.
Container Runtime Interface (CRI): Kubelet calls containerd via gRPC.
Image Pull: containerd checks if the image exists in local cache; if not, pulls it from registry using node IAM credentials or imagePullSecrets.
Pod Sandbox Creation: Kubelet instructs containerd to create the Pod Sandbox (pause container) establishing Linux namespaces (IPC, UTS, PID, Network).

steps.title: CNI Plugin: Network Namespace & Pod IP Allocation
steps.description: Plumbing the container into the cluster network:
items: Kubelet invokes the CNI plugin (AWS VPC CNI, Calico, Flannel, Cilium).
The CNI creates a virtual ethernet pair (veth), moves one interface into the pod's network namespace as eth0, and connects the other interface to the host bridge or routing table.
Allocates a dedicated Pod IP from the subnet CIDR and configures routing and MTU.
Once networking is ready, containerd starts the application containers inside the pod sandbox.

steps.title: Readiness Probes & Service Endpoints Routing
steps.description: Connecting the running pod to live client traffic:
items: Kubelet continuously executes configured startupProbe and readinessProbe.
Once probes return HTTP 200 / Success, kubelet reports pod status as Ready to the API server.
The Endpoints Controller detects the Ready pod and appends the Pod IP to the Service's Endpoints / EndpointSlices.
kube-proxy (or Cilium eBPF) on every node updates local iptables/IPVS rules, enabling load balancers and clients to route live traffic to the new pod!

keyTakeaway: Kubernetes is a Desired State System. Running 'kubectl apply' does not start containers directly; it commits desired state into etcd via the API server. An asynchronous chain of independent control loops (Deployment Controller -> ReplicaSet Controller -> Scheduler -> Kubelet -> CRI -> CNI -> Endpoints Controller) works continuously to bring physical reality to match your declared state.
elevatorPitch: 1. kubectl: Computes strategic 3-way merge patch and sends HTTP POST to kube-apiserver.
2. API Server: Authenticates caller, checks RBAC, runs Mutating/Validating admission webhooks, and writes desired state to etcd via Raft consensus.
3. Deployment & ReplicaSet Controllers: Detect the change via API watches and create unbound Pod definitions (spec.nodeName empty).
4. kube-scheduler: Filters nodes (predicates) and scores nodes (priorities), then writes a Binding object assigning the pod to a node.
5. Kubelet: Detects the assigned pod, instructs CRI (containerd) to create the pause container sandbox, and pulls the image.
6. CNI: Configures pod network namespace, veth pair, and assigns the Pod IP.
7. Service Ingress: Once readiness probes pass, Endpoints Controller adds Pod IP to Service Endpoints, and kube-proxy updates iptables/IPVS.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Over-granting cluster-admin permissions to pod ServiceAccounts instead of scoping namespace Roles when configuring Really Happens Hood
mistakesToAvoid.why: Over-granting cluster-wide permissions violates least-privilege principles and allows compromised pods to escalate privileges across namespaces.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Referencing mutable latest container tags across production Kubernetes Deployment specs when configuring Really Happens Hood
mistakesToAvoid.why: Deployments referencing `:latest` risk inconsistent versions across replica pods and break deterministic rollback capabilities.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting pod readiness probes, causing traffic to hit uninitialized application containers when configuring Really Happens Hood
mistakesToAvoid.why: Readiness probes gate traffic delivery; missing probes cause Kubernetes to route user requests to pods before dependencies or caches are loaded.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Executing diagnostic triage without analyzing chronological cluster events and describe outputs when configuring Really Happens Hood
mistakesToAvoid.why: Cluster events provide sequential timestamps of scheduler decisions, probe failures, and image pull timeouts essential for rapid root-cause isolation.

title: AWS Q1: You launched an EC2 instance but cant SSH into it What do you check [L1]
summary: 1. Security Group — does inbound rule allow port 22 from your IP? Check in the EC2 console under Security Groups.
question: You launched an EC2 instance but can't SSH into it. What do you check?
intro: "In our AWS cloud environment, we managed high-traffic microservices where this exact scenario occurred. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
items: Security Group — does inbound rule allow port 22 from your IP? Check in the EC2 console under Security Groups.
Key pair — are you using the correct .pem file? Is it the right one for that instance?
File permissions — chmod 400 key.pem. SSH won't work if key permissions are too open.
Instance state — is it running? Not stopped or pending?

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: Execute the resolution runbook and verify workload health:
items: Public IP — does it have a public IP or Elastic IP assigned?
VPC/Subnet — is it in a public subnet with an Internet Gateway? A private subnet instance can't be SSH'd from internet.
NACL — Network ACLs can block traffic even if Security Groups allow it. NACLs are stateless.

title: AWS Q2: Your EC2 instance is showing high CPU and your application is slow What steps do you take [L2]
summary: 1. CloudWatch metrics — check CPU utilization over time. Is it sustained or spiky?
question: Your EC2 instance is showing high CPU and your application is slow. What steps do you take?
intro: "When an interviewer asks how I troubleshoot this in AWS, I frame it through my hands-on production experience. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
items: CloudWatch metrics — check CPU utilization over time. Is it sustained or spiky?
SSH in and check — top or htop to see which process is consuming CPU.
Check for runaway processes — a stuck process, an infinite loop, a cron job misfiring.
Check memory — sometimes high CPU is actually a memory issue causing constant swap. Check free -m and vmstat.

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: Execute the resolution runbook and verify workload health:
items: Scale vertically — if it's a legitimate load, stop the instance, change instance type to a larger one, restart.
Scale horizontally — add it to an Auto Scaling Group, put a Load Balancer in front, scale out.
Right-sizing — use AWS Compute Optimizer recommendations.

title: AWS Q3: You have a fleet of EC2 instances behind an ALB One instance keeps getting traffic even though its unhealthy Whats wrong [L2]

question: You have a fleet of EC2 instances behind an ALB. One instance keeps getting traffic even though it's unhealthy. What's wrong?
intro: "In a previous role, our monitoring paged me for a similar incident across our AWS VPC infrastructure. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
steps.description: The ALB health check is likely misconfigured:
items: Health check path wrong — ALB checks / but the app serves health at /health. Returns 404 → ALB marks it unhealthy → but wait, 404 might be in the success codes range.
Success codes misconfigured — if success codes include 404 or 5xx, unhealthy instances appear healthy.
Health check threshold — UnhealthyThreshold might be set very high, so the instance needs to fail many times before being marked unhealthy.

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: Fix: Review ALB target group health check settings. Set correct path, success codes (200-299 only), and reasonable thresholds.
items: Health check port/protocol wrong — checking wrong port.
Security Group — ALB can't reach the instance's health check port → health checks time out → AWS treats timeout differently than explicit failure in some configs.

steps.description: Choose: ALB for web apps/APIs. NLB for TCP/UDP or when you need static IP. GWLB for network security appliances.
items: CLB (Classic Load Balancer) — legacy. Avoid for new projects. Layer 4 and Layer 7 but limited features.
ALB (Application Load Balancer) — Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS). Content-based routing: route by URL path, hostname, headers, query strings. Best for microservices and HTTP apps. Supports WebSockets, HTTP/2.

NLB (Network Load Balancer) — Layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS). Ultra-low latency. Handles millions of requests per second. Static IP / Elastic IP support. Best for high-performance, non-HTTP workloads (game servers, IoT, VoIP).

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
items: GWLB (Gateway Load Balancer) — for inline network appliances (firewalls, IDS/IPS). Newer addition.

title: Exit Code 137 in AWS ECS: Out of Memory (OOMKilled), Task vs Container Memory Limits & Resolution Runbook
summary: Production triage runbook for AWS ECS tasks stopping with exit code 137 (OOMKilled): inspecting ECS StoppedReason, distinguishing task hard limit from container soft limit, CloudWatch Container Insights, and JVM/Node memory tuning.
question: Your AWS ECS task keeps stopping with exit code 137. What causes this, how do you diagnose task-level vs container-level OOM, and how do you resolve it in production?
intro: "In a previous role, our monitoring paged me for a similar incident across our AWS VPC infrastructure. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

steps.title: Deciphering Exit Code 137 (128 + 9 = SIGKILL by OOM Killer)
steps.description: Standard Unix exit code 137 signifies that the process was terminated by signal 9 (SIGKILL) issued by the Linux kernel Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer:
items: Why SIGKILL: When memory exhaustion occurs, the kernel has zero time for graceful SIGTERM shutdown and immediately sends SIGKILL to preserve host stability.
ECS Task Status: Check the ECS console or AWS CLI: aws ecs describe-tasks --tasks . Look for stoppedReason: 'OutOfMemory: Container killed due to memory usage'.

steps.title: Differentiating Task-Level vs Container-Level Memory Limits
steps.description: AWS ECS task definitions specify memory at two distinct levels:
items: Container Hard Limit (memory): If the specific container exceeds this threshold, the kernel immediately kills that container. If essential=true, the entire task stops.
Container Soft Limit (memoryReservation): Memory reserved on the host for the container. The container can exceed this if host memory is available.

Task-Level Memory (Fargate): Total memory allocated to the task cgroup. If the aggregate usage of all containers (app + sidecars like Datadog/Envoy) exceeds the task limit, ECS kills the task even if individual containers have not breached their container limits.

steps.title: Production Remediation & Sizing Strategy
steps.description: How to fix ECS exit code 137 cleanly:
items: CloudWatch Container Insights: Graph MemoryUtilized vs MemoryReserved to identify baseline consumption and spike patterns.
Rightsize Task Definition: Increase Fargate CPU/Memory allocation or increase container memory limits.
Runtime Heap Tuning: For JVM applications, ensure container-aware heap sizing flags are set: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 so the JVM does not attempt to allocate beyond the container cgroup boundary.

keyTakeaway: Exit code 137 in ECS universally means OOMKilled. Always inspect StoppedReason in the AWS ECS task description to determine if the task-level allocation or a specific container hard limit was breached.
elevatorPitch: Identified exit code 137 as an OOM killer SIGKILL event using AWS ECS describe-tasks StoppedReason.
Differentiated task-level Fargate allocation limits from individual container memory limits.
Monitored CloudWatch Container Insights to pinpoint memory leak spikes in application containers.
Configured container-aware JVM flags (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0) and rightsized task definition memory.

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis

items: Enable automated backups on the RDS instance with BackupRetentionPeriod: 7 (days).

title: AWS Q50: Design a multi-region active-active architecture [L3]
summary: A multi-region active-active architecture runs full application stacks in two or more AWS Regions that all serve live traffic, with global routing in front and replicated data behind.
question: Design a multi-region active-active architecture.
intro: A multi-region active-active architecture runs full application stacks in two or more AWS Regions that all serve live traffic, with global routing in front and replicated data behind. The hard part is not compute, which is stateless and easy to duplicate, but data: writes in several Regions create conflicts, replication is asynchronous, and some services only support a single writer. Interviewers ask this to see whether you reason about consistency, failure domains, cost and testing, rather than just drawing two copies of a VPC.

steps.title: Decide requirements first: RTO, RPO, consistency and cost for a multi-region active-active design
steps.description: Active-active is the most expensive and most complex multi-Region pattern, so justify it before choosing it.
items: Why active-active: near-zero RTO and low latency for users in several geographies. If minutes of downtime are acceptable, pilot light or warm standby is cheaper and simpler.
RPO and consistency: cross-Region replication is asynchronous in most services, so a Region failure can lose the last moments of writes. Decide whether the business tolerates that.
Capacity: each Region must absorb the other's traffic on failure, so you either overprovision (cost) or rely on autoscaling and pre-warmed capacity (risk).
Compliance: data residency rules may forbid replicating some data to another Region, which can force a partitioned, user-homed design instead.
Pattern ladder: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and active-active form a spectrum of cost versus recovery speed. Naming where active-active sits shows you chose it on purpose.
steps.highlight: Ask first: can writes be partitioned by user or tenant to a home Region? Home-Region writes with global reads avoid most conflict problems and are far easier to operate.

steps.title: Hands-on: global routing and a stateless compute layer
steps.description: Route users to the nearest healthy Region and keep each Region independently deployable.
items: Route 53: latency-based or weighted records with health checks send users to the closest healthy Region and remove an unhealthy one from answers.
Global Accelerator: anycast IPs route over the AWS backbone with fast failover that does not depend on client DNS caching, useful when TTLs are a concern.
Stateless services: ECS, EKS or Lambda in each Region, deployed from the same pipeline. No session state on instances; use signed tokens or a replicated store.
Regional isolation: each Region is a full stack with its own VPC, load balancer and queues, so a failure cannot cascade across Regions.

steps.title: Data layer: choose the store by write pattern
steps.description: Each AWS data service has different multi-Region semantics; naming them accurately is what separates a strong answer.
items: DynamoDB global tables: multi-writer, multi-Region replication. Concurrent writes to the same item resolve with last-writer-wins by default, so design keys and updates to avoid hot cross-Region conflicts.

Aurora Global Database: one primary Region accepts writes while secondary Regions serve low-latency reads. It supports fast cross-Region promotion, but it is not multi-writer by default, so true active-active writes need write forwarding or partitioning.
S3: cross-Region replication is asynchronous and per-prefix; Multi-Region Access Points give a single global endpoint over replicated buckets.
Queues and caches: SQS and ElastiCache are Regional. Publish events to a bus or stream per Region, or replicate through a global datastore, and make consumers idempotent.
steps.codeBlock:
# Add a replica Region to an existing DynamoDB table (global tables 2019.11.21)
aws dynamodb update-table \
  --table-name orders \
  --replica-updates '[{"Create":{"RegionName":"eu-west-1"}}]' \
  --region us-east-1

aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name orders --region us-east-1 \
  --query 'Table.Replicas[].[RegionName,ReplicaStatus]'

steps.title: Failure modes: conflicts, replication lag and split brain
steps.description: Design for the failures you will actually hit, not just a clean Region outage.
items: Write conflicts: use globally unique IDs (ULIDs or UUIDs), additive or commutative operations, and avoid read-modify-write on the same item from two Regions.
Replication lag: a user who writes in Region A and reads in Region B may not see the change. Use sticky routing for a session or read-your-writes via the home Region.
Idempotency: retries during failover can duplicate requests. Require idempotency keys on payment-like operations and deduplicate consumers.
Grey failure: a Region that is degraded but passing shallow health checks is worse than a dead one. Use deep health checks that exercise dependencies, and alarm on error rate.
steps.highlight: Do not make failover depend on a single control plane operation in the failing Region. Prefer data-plane mechanisms such as health-check-driven DNS, Global Accelerator, or Route 53 Application Recovery Controller routing controls.

steps.title: Operate, test and automate
steps.description: An untested failover is a hypothesis; active-active designs rot unless exercised.
items: Game days: regularly shift traffic weights to 100 percent in one Region and confirm capacity, latency and data correctness.
Fault injection: use AWS Fault Injection Service to simulate dependency failure and connectivity loss in a controlled Region.
Infrastructure as code: deploy identical stacks with one Terraform or CDK module parameterised by Region, and pipeline both Regions with staged rollout.
Observability: aggregate metrics per Region and alarm on replication lag (for example DynamoDB ReplicationLatency), health check status and error budget burn.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Say out loud which service is truly multi-writer (DynamoDB global tables) and which is single-writer (Aurora Global Database), and propose home-Region partitioning to sidestep conflicts; that single distinction signals real multi-Region experience.
elevatorPitch: Multi-region active-active means identical stacks in two or more Regions all serving traffic, routed by Route 53 or Global Accelerator with health checks.
Compute is stateless; data uses DynamoDB global tables or partitioned home-Region writes, with idempotent consumers and conflict-safe keys.
I prove it with scheduled failover game days, deep health checks, and replication lag alarms.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming Aurora Global Database gives multi-Region writes
mistakesToAvoid.why: It has a single writer Region; promotion is fast but writes in another Region need forwarding or a different design.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on shallow health checks that only hit a static page
mistakesToAvoid.why: A Region with a broken database still looks healthy, so traffic is never shifted away.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring capacity on failover
mistakesToAvoid.why: The surviving Region receives double traffic; without headroom or pre-scaled capacity, a failure becomes a cascade.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Never exercising failover
mistakesToAvoid.why: Configuration drift, expired credentials or missing replicas surface only during the real outage.

title: AWS Q51: An S3 lifecycle rule is not transitioning objects as expected [L2]
summary: Objects must be > 128KB for lifecycle transition to Glacier to apply. Also check the prefix filter matches your objects.
question: An S3 lifecycle rule is not transitioning objects as expected.
intro: When an S3 lifecycle rule is not transitioning objects, the cause is almost always a mismatched filter, a minimum-age or minimum-size constraint, version handling, or simply that rules run asynchronously. Work from the configuration to the object: confirm the rule is enabled and matches, check each object's age, size and storage class, then allow for processing delay. Interviewers use this as a diagnostic question to see whether you follow a methodical runbook with real CLI evidence instead of guessing.

steps.title: Symptom and first check: read the live lifecycle configuration
steps.description: Start from what S3 actually has, not what Terraform or the console says you intended.
items: Fetch the rule: aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration returns the active rules; a NoSuchLifecycleConfiguration error means no rules exist at all.
Status: confirm each rule has "Status": "Enabled". A disabled rule is common after a console experiment or Terraform drift.
Filter shape: inspect Filter, with Prefix, Tag, ObjectSizeGreaterThan, ObjectSizeLessThan or an And combination. Several conditions combine with AND, so one unmatched tag excludes the object.
Rule overlap: multiple rules can match one object. Review them together, because conflicting actions are resolved by S3 rules and may not do what you expect.
steps.codeBlock:
aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket my-bucket

# Typical rule under review
# {
#   "ID": "to-ia",
#   "Status": "Enabled",
#   "Filter": {"Prefix": "logs/"},
#   "Transitions": [{"Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA"}]
# }

steps.title: Hands-on: S3 lifecycle rule not transitioning, check the objects
steps.description: Pick a specific object that should have moved and prove why it did not.
items: Storage class: aws s3api head-object shows StorageClass. When the field is absent the object is in STANDARD.
Age: compare LastModified with the rule's Days. Age is counted from object creation, and the action is scheduled for midnight UTC after the threshold is met.
Prefix mismatch: prefixes are literal and case-sensitive, and should not start with a slash. logs/ matches logs/a.gz but not Logs/a.gz.
Tags: use aws s3api get-object-tagging if the filter includes tags; tags are not inherited from the bucket or prefix.
steps.codeBlock:
aws s3api head-object --bucket my-bucket --key logs/2025/app.gz
# look at: LastModified, StorageClass, ContentLength, Expiration

aws s3api list-objects-v2 --bucket my-bucket --prefix logs/ \
  --query 'Contents[?StorageClass==`STANDARD`].[Key,Size,LastModified]' \
  --output table --max-items 20

aws s3api get-object-tagging --bucket my-bucket --key logs/2025/app.gz

steps.title: Constraints that silently block transitions
steps.description: S3 enforces transition rules that are easy to miss, and some depend on current service behaviour.
items: Minimum object size: transitions to cost-saving classes have a minimum object size, because small objects can cost more in colder tiers. By default this is around 128 KB, and you can override the default with the lifecycle configuration's transition default minimum object size setting. Check current S3 documentation.

Minimum days: some classes require objects to remain in the source class for a minimum period (for example 30 days before Standard-IA or One Zone-IA). A rule with fewer days is rejected or ineffective.
Transition order: transitions only move downward through the storage class waterfall. You cannot lifecycle an object from Glacier back to Standard.
Timing: rules are evaluated asynchronously, roughly daily. Allow a day or two after the rule is created or the age threshold passes before declaring failure.

Class-specific rules: some target classes, such as Glacier Deep Archive, have their own minimum storage durations and retrieval characteristics that affect billing even if the transition itself works. Review the S3 storage class documentation for the class you target.
steps.highlight: Newly added or edited rules may take time to take effect, and the time to first run is not instant. Do not delete and recreate rules repeatedly while waiting; that resets nothing and creates noise.

steps.title: Versioned buckets, locks and other edge cases
steps.description: Many production buckets are versioned, which changes what a rule applies to.
items: Current versus noncurrent: Transitions apply to current versions only. Old versions need NoncurrentVersionTransitions with NoncurrentDays.
Delete markers and uploads: clean up with ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker and AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload, since they otherwise accumulate cost without matching transition rules.
Object Lock: retention and legal hold block deletion, so they prevent expiration actions. They do not generally block storage class transitions.
Replicated objects and Intelligent-Tiering: objects already in Intelligent-Tiering move between tiers automatically; a transition rule is unnecessary and may confuse your audit.

steps.title: Fix, verify and prevent
steps.description: Apply the fix, then confirm with data rather than waiting and hoping.
items: Apply: aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket my-bucket --lifecycle-configuration file://lifecycle.json. This replaces the entire configuration, so include every rule.
Verify at scale: enable S3 Inventory (storage class field) or use S3 Storage Lens to chart storage by class instead of sampling objects.
Alert: track the BucketSizeBytes CloudWatch metric per StorageType dimension to see class shifts.
Codify: manage rules with Terraform aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration and run a plan in CI to catch drift; include a test object in a dev bucket with a short rule to prove the setup.
Cost angle: transition requests are billed per object, so transitioning millions of tiny objects can cost more than it saves; combine small files before archiving where possible.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Always inspect one concrete object with head-object against the live rule from get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration, and remember that put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration replaces all rules at once.
elevatorPitch: I start with get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration to confirm the rule is enabled and its filter matches the prefix, tags and size.
Then I check a sample object with head-object for age, size and storage class, and account for minimum size, minimum days and the roughly daily asynchronous run.
For versioned buckets I add noncurrent-version rules, and I verify bucket-wide with S3 Inventory or Storage Lens rather than spot checks.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting transitions to run immediately after the rule is saved
mistakesToAvoid.why: Lifecycle evaluation is asynchronous and generally daily, so give it time before changing anything.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting noncurrent versions in a versioned bucket
mistakesToAvoid.why: A Transitions block affects only current versions, so most stored bytes may never move.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using a prefix with a leading slash or wrong case
mistakesToAvoid.why: Prefixes match literally, so the rule silently matches nothing.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Calling put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration with only the new rule
mistakesToAvoid.why: It overwrites all existing rules, which can remove expiration or cleanup rules unintentionally.

title: AWS Q53: How do you implement blue-green deployments on ECS [L3]
summary: To implement blue-green deployments on ECS, run the new task set (green) beside the live one (blue) behind the same Application Load Balancer, test it on a separate listener, then shift production traffic and keep blue for fast.
question: How do you implement blue-green deployments on ECS?
intro: To implement blue-green deployments on ECS, run the new task set (green) beside the live one (blue) behind the same Application Load Balancer, test it on a separate listener, then shift production traffic and keep blue for fast rollback. The classic route uses the CodeDeploy deployment controller with two target groups; AWS has also added a built-in ECS blue/green strategy, so check current ECS documentation for which you should choose. Interviewers want to see traffic shifting, health validation, rollback triggers and database compatibility.

steps.title: Architecture: two task sets, two target groups, two listeners
steps.description: The ALB is the switch; ECS runs both versions at once during the deployment.
items: Blue and green: blue is the current task set serving production. Green is the new task definition revision launched in the same service with no production traffic yet.
Target groups: two target groups (for example app-blue-tg and app-green-tg) are attached to the ALB. CodeDeploy swaps which one the production listener forwards to.
Listeners: a production listener (443) serves users. An optional test listener on a different port (for example 8443) lets you validate green before any user sees it.
Deployment controller: the ECS service must be created with CODE_DEPLOY as its controller type. It cannot be switched from rolling update afterwards without recreating the service.

Why choose it: blue-green gives you pre-production validation on real infrastructure and a near-instant rollback, at the price of running two copies briefly. A plain rolling update replaces tasks in place and rolls back more slowly.
steps.highlight: For Fargate and EC2 launch types the pattern is the same, but you must have spare capacity or autoscaling headroom for two full task sets at the same time.

steps.title: Hands-on: implement blue-green deployments on ECS with CodeDeploy
steps.description: Create the service with the CodeDeploy controller, then describe each release with an AppSpec file.
items: Service creation: pass --deployment-controller type=CODE_DEPLOY and attach the blue target group in --load-balancers.
CodeDeploy application: create an application with compute platform ECS and a deployment group that names both target groups, the production listener, the optional test listener and a service role.
AppSpec: specifies the new task definition ARN and the container name and port that receive traffic.
Deploy: start the deployment with aws deploy create-deployment, passing the AppSpec as the revision.
steps.codeBlock:
aws ecs create-service --cluster prod --service-name my-app \
  --task-definition my-app:12 --desired-count 3 --launch-type FARGATE \
  --deployment-controller type=CODE_DEPLOY \
  --load-balancers targetGroupArn=arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:us-east-1:123456789012:targetgroup/app-blue-tg/abc,containerName=app,containerPort=8080 \
  --network-configuration 'awsvpcConfiguration={subnets=[subnet-aaa,subnet-bbb],securityGroups=[sg-123]}'

# appspec.json
# {"version":"0.0","Resources":[{"TargetService":{"Type":"AWS::ECS::Service",
#   "Properties":{"TaskDefinition":"arn:aws:ecs:us-east-1:123456789012:task-definition/my-app:13",
#   "LoadBalancerInfo":{"ContainerName":"app","ContainerPort":8080}}}}]}

steps.title: Traffic shifting, test traffic and lifecycle hooks
steps.description: The value of blue-green is controlled exposure, not just a faster swap.
items: Shift strategy: choose a predefined configuration such as CodeDeployDefault.ECSAllAtOnce, a canary (for example 10 percent then the rest after a delay) or linear (equal increments over time).
Test listener: after green is healthy, CodeDeploy routes test traffic. Run smoke tests against the test port before production traffic moves.
Hooks: AppSpec hooks such as BeforeAllowTraffic and AfterAllowTestTraffic invoke Lambda functions that run validation and can fail the deployment.
Termination wait: keep blue running for a configured period after the shift, so rollback is just re-pointing the listener, with no task launch time.
steps.codeBlock:
aws deploy create-deployment \
  --application-name my-app \
  --deployment-group-name prod \
  --deployment-config-name CodeDeployDefault.ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes \
  --revision '{"revisionType":"String","string":{"content":"<appspec JSON>"}}'

aws deploy get-deployment --deployment-id d-XXXXXXXXX \
  --query 'deploymentInfo.[status,errorInformation]'

steps.title: Rollback triggers and failure modes
steps.description: Define what failure looks like before the deployment starts.
items: Automatic rollback: configure the deployment group to roll back on deployment failure and on CloudWatch alarm breach, such as ALB HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count or target response time.
Health checks: a weak health endpoint passes a broken build. Use a readiness endpoint that checks critical dependencies, with sensible deregistration delay.
Database changes: blue and green run simultaneously, so schema migrations must be backward compatible (expand, migrate, then contract in a later release).
Capacity and quotas: double task counts during a deployment can hit Fargate or ENI limits; check current quotas and request increases ahead of time.

Stuck deployments: if green tasks never become healthy, the deployment waits and eventually fails. Check the target group health reason and the task's stopped reason with aws ecs describe-tasks, then fix the image, port or security group.

steps.title: Verification and automation
steps.description: Prove each deployment and keep the process in code.
items: Verify: aws ecs describe-services shows task sets with status PRIMARY and ACTIVE; confirm running count equals desired on the new set.
Pipeline: build, push to ECR, register a new task definition revision, render AppSpec, then call CodeDeploy from GitHub Actions or CodePipeline.
Infrastructure as code: define target groups, listeners, CodeDeploy application and alarms in Terraform or CDK so environments match.
Alternatives: ECS has a built-in blue/green option and a rolling update controller; rolling is simpler when you do not need pre-production validation or instant rollback.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Set the deployment controller to CODE_DEPLOY when you create the service (it cannot be changed in place), and wire CloudWatch alarms into the deployment group so a bad release rolls back without a human in the loop.
elevatorPitch: Blue-green on ECS runs the new task set beside the live one behind the same ALB, using two target groups and a test listener, with CodeDeploy flipping production traffic.
I validate on the test port and with lifecycle hook Lambdas, and use canary or linear shifting with alarm-based automatic rollback.
Pipelines register the task definition, render the AppSpec and call CodeDeploy, and migrations stay backward compatible so blue can always take traffic back.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Creating the ECS service with the default rolling controller
mistakesToAvoid.why: You cannot convert it to CODE_DEPLOY later; the service has to be recreated.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Shipping a destructive schema migration with the release
mistakesToAvoid.why: Blue still runs against the same database during the shift and rollback, so incompatible changes break it.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Terminating blue immediately after the traffic shift
mistakesToAvoid.why: You lose the instant-rollback advantage; use a termination wait time.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using a trivial /health endpoint
mistakesToAvoid.why: A build with a broken dependency still passes, so the shift proceeds and fails in production.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Setting SQS visibility timeout shorter than consumer task processing duration
mistakesToAvoid.why: If processing exceeds the visibility timeout, SQS returns the message to the queue, causing concurrent duplicate execution by other workers.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) redrive policy for poison pill messages
