title: AWS Q55: SNS topic notification not being received [L2]
summary: When an SNS topic notification is not being received, work the path in order: was the message published, is the subscription confirmed, does a filter policy drop it, can SNS actually deliver to the endpoint, and is it failing.
question: SNS topic notification not being received.
intro: When an SNS topic notification is not being received, work the path in order: was the message published, is the subscription confirmed, does a filter policy drop it, can SNS actually deliver to the endpoint, and is it failing silently after delivery. SNS reports success for a publish regardless of what happens next, so you need metrics and delivery logs to find the break. Interviewers use this to test whether you can use CloudWatch evidence, IAM and resource policies, and encryption keys to isolate a messaging failure methodically.

steps.title: Symptom: confirm the message was published and counted
steps.description: Split the problem in half: did SNS accept the message, and did SNS deliver it?
items: Publish result: aws sns publish returns a MessageId on success. An authorization or KMS error here means the problem is on the publisher side.
Topic metrics: in CloudWatch check NumberOfMessagesPublished, NumberOfNotificationsDelivered, NumberOfNotificationsFailed and NumberOfNotificationsFilteredOut for the topic.
Reading the pattern: published up but delivered flat points to subscriptions or filters; failed up points to endpoint permissions or availability.
Right Region and ARN: confirm the publisher uses the topic ARN in the same Region; a typo creates confusion because a different topic may exist.
steps.codeBlock:
aws sns publish --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789012:alerts \
  --message "test" --subject "diag"

aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/SNS \
  --metric-name NumberOfNotificationsFailed \
  --dimensions Name=TopicName,Value=alerts \
  --start-time $(date -u -v-1H +%FT%TZ) --end-time $(date -u +%FT%TZ) \
  --period 300 --statistics Sum

steps.title: Hands-on: SNS topic notification not being received, check subscription and filters
steps.description: Most real cases are an unconfirmed subscription or a filter policy that excludes the message.
items: Subscription status: aws sns list-subscriptions-by-topic shows PendingConfirmation for unconfirmed email, HTTP and HTTPS endpoints. Unconfirmed subscriptions receive nothing.

Filter policy: aws sns get-subscription-attributes reveals FilterPolicy and FilterPolicyScope. By default the policy matches message attributes; with MessageBody scope it matches the JSON body instead.
Attributes must be set: publishers must send the attributes the filter expects, with the right data type (String or Number). Missing attributes mean the message is filtered out.
Raw message delivery: for SQS and HTTP endpoints, this changes the payload format. A consumer expecting the SNS JSON envelope will fail to parse a raw message, and vice versa.
FIFO topics: FIFO topics only deliver to SQS queues, and the message group and deduplication settings can cause a message to be treated as a duplicate and dropped within the deduplication window.
steps.codeBlock:
aws sns list-subscriptions-by-topic \
  --topic-arn arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789012:alerts \
  --query 'Subscriptions[].[Protocol,Endpoint,SubscriptionArn]' --output table

aws sns get-subscription-attributes --subscription-arn <arn> \
  --query 'Attributes.[FilterPolicy,FilterPolicyScope,RawMessageDelivery,RedrivePolicy]'

steps.title: Permissions: SQS, Lambda and KMS
steps.description: SNS needs explicit permission to deliver to cross-service endpoints, and encryption adds another policy.
items: SQS queue policy: the queue must allow sqs:SendMessage from principal sns.amazonaws.com, ideally with an aws:SourceArn condition equal to the topic ARN.
Lambda: add a resource-based permission with aws lambda add-permission for principal sns.amazonaws.com and the topic as source ARN; otherwise invocations are denied.

Encrypted topic or queue: if you use a customer managed KMS key, its key policy must allow SNS to use it (and the publisher to kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt). The AWS managed aws/sns key cannot be extended to grant other services access.
Cross-account: the topic policy must allow the other account to subscribe, and the endpoint's own policy must allow SNS to deliver.
steps.codeBlock:
aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url <url> --attribute-names Policy

aws lambda add-permission --function-name my-fn \
  --statement-id sns-invoke --action lambda:InvokeFunction \
  --principal sns.amazonaws.com \
  --source-arn arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789012:alerts

steps.title: Delivery status logs, retries and protocol-specific causes
steps.description: When metrics show failures, delivery status logging tells you why.
items: Delivery status logging: enable it per protocol (Lambda, SQS, HTTP and others) with an IAM role, then read the failures in CloudWatch Logs for the exact status and error message.
HTTP and HTTPS: endpoints must return a 2xx response and be reachable from the internet. Failed deliveries retry according to the delivery policy, then are dropped unless a DLQ is set.
Email: confirm the subscription, then check spam and filters. Corporate mail systems often quarantine messages from no-reply@sns.amazonaws.com.
SMS: new accounts can be in the SMS sandbox with verified destinations only, and recipients who opted out will not receive messages. Check account SMS settings and spending limits.
steps.highlight: Attach a subscription-level dead-letter queue via RedrivePolicy. It turns silent drops into inspectable messages.

steps.title: Prevention and automation
steps.description: Make delivery observable before the next outage.
items: Alarms: alarm on NumberOfNotificationsFailed greater than zero and on DLQ depth.
Infrastructure as code: define the topic, subscriptions, queue policy and KMS grants together in Terraform so permissions never drift apart.
Synthetic test: publish a heartbeat message on a schedule and alarm if the consumer does not record it.
Idempotent consumers: SNS standard topics deliver at least once, so consumers should tolerate duplicates and not treat missing duplicates as errors.
Runbook link: keep this checklist next to the alarm so on-call engineers check subscription status, filter policy, permissions, then delivery logs in the same order every time.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Compare NumberOfMessagesPublished, NumberOfNotificationsFilteredOut and NumberOfNotificationsFailed first; the one that moved tells you whether to look at filters, permissions or the endpoint.
elevatorPitch: SNS accepts a publish independently of delivery, so I split the problem using the topic's published, filtered-out, delivered and failed metrics.
I check subscription confirmation, FilterPolicy and scope, queue or Lambda resource policies and KMS key policy, and read delivery status logs for the exact error.
I prevent repeats with failure alarms, subscription DLQs and Terraform that defines topic, subscription and permissions together.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming a successful publish means delivery
mistakesToAvoid.why: SNS returns a MessageId before delivery happens; failures and filtering are visible only in metrics and logs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting the SQS queue policy for the SNS principal
mistakesToAvoid.why: SNS cannot send to the queue, and the subscription looks fine in the console.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using the AWS managed aws/sns key with cross-service subscribers
mistakesToAvoid.why: You cannot edit its key policy to grant other services access; use a customer managed key.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Publishing without the attributes the filter policy expects
mistakesToAvoid.why: Messages are silently filtered out and counted in NumberOfNotificationsFilteredOut.

title: AWS Q56: What is the difference between SQS and SNS [L1]
summary: The difference between SQS and SNS is delivery model: SQS is a pull-based message queue where one consumer group processes each message, while SNS is a push-based publish/subscribe topic that copies each message to every.
question: What is the difference between SQS and SNS?
intro: The difference between SQS and SNS is delivery model: SQS is a pull-based message queue where one consumer group processes each message, while SNS is a push-based publish/subscribe topic that copies each message to every subscriber. Interviewers ask this because the two are constantly combined, and candidates who can only recite definitions miss the real design question: how do you decouple producers from consumers, absorb bursts, and fan out one event to several independent workflows without losing messages? A strong answer gives the mental model, shows the SNS-to-SQS fan-out pattern, and names the failure modes such as poison messages and missing queue policies.

steps.title: Mental model: queue (SQS) vs topic (SNS)
steps.description: SQS stores messages until a consumer asks for them; SNS does not store anything for you, it pushes to whoever is subscribed at publish time.
items: SQS: a durable buffer. Consumers poll (ReceiveMessage), process, then delete. Unprocessed messages wait until retention expires (4 days by default, configurable up to 14). Each message is handled by one consumer, so adding consumers scales throughput, not the number of recipients.

SNS: a topic with many subscribers. A publish is delivered to every subscription (SQS, Lambda, HTTPS, email, SMS, mobile push, Firehose). SNS retries according to the protocol's delivery policy but is not a long-term store.

Coupling: with SQS the consumer controls the pace and can fall behind safely. With SNS the subscriber must keep up or lose the delivery after retries, which is why durable subscribers are usually SQS queues.
Ordering and duplicates: standard queues and topics are at-least-once with best-effort ordering. FIFO variants add strict ordering per message group and deduplication.
Rule of thumb: if you can name the consumers in advance and each needs its own copy, think SNS; if you only care that the work eventually gets done by someone, think SQS.
steps.highlight: Short answer for the room: SQS decouples in time (buffering), SNS decouples in recipients (fan-out). Together they do both.

steps.title: Hands-on: SNS-to-SQS fan-out with the AWS CLI
steps.description: Create one topic and two queues, allow the topic to write to each queue, then subscribe them.
items: Queue policy is mandatory: an SQS queue only accepts messages from SNS if its access policy allows sqs:SendMessage from the topic ARN. A missing policy is the top cause of 'subscription confirmed but nothing arrives'.
Raw message delivery: set RawMessageDelivery=true on the subscription if consumers should receive the original body rather than the SNS JSON envelope.
Filter policies: attach a FilterPolicy to each subscription so billing only receives order_placed events, for example, instead of filtering in code.
Cross-account: add the publisher or subscriber account to the topic and queue policies explicitly.
steps.codeBlock:
TOPIC_ARN=$(aws sns create-topic --name orders --query TopicArn --output text)
Q_URL=$(aws sqs create-queue --queue-name orders-billing --query QueueUrl --output text)
Q_ARN=$(aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url "$Q_URL" \
  --attribute-names QueueArn --query Attributes.QueueArn --output text)

# Allow only this topic to send to the queue
cat > policy.json <<EOF
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow",
 "Principal":{"Service":"sns.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sqs:SendMessage",
 "Resource":"$Q_ARN",
 "Condition":{"ArnEquals":{"aws:SourceArn":"$TOPIC_ARN"}}}]}
EOF
aws sqs set-queue-attributes --queue-url "$Q_URL" \
  --attributes "$(jq -n --slurpfile p policy.json '{Policy: ($p[0]|tojson)}')"

aws sns subscribe --topic-arn "$TOPIC_ARN" --protocol sqs --notification-endpoint "$Q_ARN" \
  --attributes '{"RawMessageDelivery":"true","FilterPolicy":"{\"event\":[\"order_placed\"]}"}'

aws sns publish --topic-arn "$TOPIC_ARN" --message '{"id":42}' \
  --message-attributes '{"event":{"DataType":"String","StringValue":"order_placed"}}'

steps.title: Verify delivery and consumption
steps.description: Confirm the message landed, was received once by a consumer, and was deleted.
items: Peek at the queue: aws sqs receive-message --queue-url "$Q_URL" --wait-time-seconds 10 uses long polling, which reduces empty responses and cost compared with short polling.
Delete after success: aws sqs delete-message --queue-url "$Q_URL" --receipt-handle <handle>. If you never delete, the message reappears once the visibility timeout expires.
Queue depth: watch ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible and ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage in CloudWatch; the age metric is the best backlog alarm.
SNS side: check NumberOfNotificationsFailed and enable delivery status logging for non-SQS endpoints.
steps.codeBlock:
# Long-poll, process, then delete
aws sqs receive-message --queue-url "$Q_URL" --wait-time-seconds 10 \
  --attribute-names ApproximateReceiveCount --max-number-of-messages 1
aws sqs delete-message --queue-url "$Q_URL" --receipt-handle "<receipt-handle>"

# Attach a DLQ so poison messages stop cycling (DLQ_ARN from get-queue-attributes)
aws sqs set-queue-attributes --queue-url "$Q_URL" \
  --attributes '{"RedrivePolicy":"{\"deadLetterTargetArn\":\"'"$DLQ_ARN"'\",\"maxReceiveCount\":\"5\"}","VisibilityTimeout":"60"}'

steps.title: Failure modes and when to use which
steps.description: Choose by the question 'who needs this message and what happens if they are down?'.
items: Use SQS alone: one worker fleet processes jobs (image resize, email send) and you need buffering, retries and a dead-letter queue (DLQ) with maxReceiveCount.
Use SNS alone: notify humans or HTTP endpoints (email, SMS, push) where a missed delivery is acceptable or handled elsewhere.
Use SNS to SQS: several independent services must each process every event at their own pace. Each gets its own queue and DLQ, so one slow or broken consumer never blocks the others.
FIFO: SNS FIFO topics can fan out to SQS FIFO queues when order and deduplication matter. Throughput is lower than standard, so check current quotas.
Poison messages: without a DLQ a bad message cycles forever. Set a redrive policy and alarm on DLQ depth.
Cost and scale: both are fully managed and scale without capacity planning, so choice rests on semantics, not throughput; check current quotas for FIFO.

steps.title: Production practice
steps.description: Codify the wiring and make backlog visible.
items: IaC: define topic, queue, policy and subscription together in Terraform or CloudFormation so the queue policy cannot be forgotten.
Encryption: if the topic or queue uses a customer managed KMS key, grant sns.amazonaws.com permission to use it, otherwise publishes fail silently from the producer's view.
Idempotency: design consumers to tolerate duplicates; at-least-once delivery makes this unavoidable on standard queues.
Alarms: alert on oldest-message age and DLQ depth, not just queue length.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Always fan out with one SQS queue per consuming service behind a single SNS topic, and put a DLQ plus a queue policy scoped to the topic ARN on every queue.
elevatorPitch: SQS is a pull-based queue that buffers work for one consumer group; SNS is a push-based topic that copies each message to every subscriber.
I verify by checking the queue policy, long-polling a receive, and watching message age and DLQ depth in CloudWatch.
I automate topic, queues, policies and filter policies in IaC and design consumers to be idempotent because delivery is at-least-once.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Subscribing a queue to a topic without a queue access policy
mistakesToAvoid.why: SNS gets denied when sending, so the subscription looks healthy but the queue stays empty.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using SNS directly to a Lambda or HTTP endpoint for work that must not be lost
mistakesToAvoid.why: SNS is not a durable backlog; a queue in between gives buffering, retries and a DLQ.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting to delete messages or setting the visibility timeout shorter than processing time
mistakesToAvoid.why: Messages reappear and are processed again, producing duplicates and runaway retries.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting strict ordering from standard queues and topics
mistakesToAvoid.why: Only FIFO provides ordering per message group; standard is best-effort.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Raising provisioned read/write capacity blindly instead of isolating hot partition keys in DynamoDB
mistakesToAvoid.why: Individual DynamoDB partitions enforce hard throughput limits (1,000 WCU / 3,000 RCU); table-level capacity increases cannot resolve single-key hot partitions.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting strongly consistent reads from a Global Secondary Index (GSI)
mistakesToAvoid.why: DynamoDB GSIs are updated asynchronously and only support eventually consistent reads; code demanding immediate read-after-write consistency will read stale data.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Storing large unstructured payloads (>400KB) directly in DynamoDB items instead of offloading to Amazon S3
mistakesToAvoid.why: DynamoDB strictly caps item size at 400KB; storing large attributes inflates RCU/WCU consumption and degrades throughput compared to S3 claim-check patterns.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using scan filters with projection expressions expecting reduced RCU consumption in aws-q057-dynamodb-read-latency-suddenly-incr
mistakesToAvoid.why: DynamoDB charges RCUs based on the total size of items evaluated before the filter expression is applied, not the filtered payload returned to the client.

title: AWS Q59: CloudFront is serving stale content after you updated S3 [L2]
summary: When CloudFront is serving stale content after you updated S3, the cause is almost always caching, not S3: S3 gives strong read-after-write consistency, so the origin is correct while an edge location, or the user's browser,.
question: CloudFront is serving stale content after you updated S3.
intro: When CloudFront is serving stale content after you updated S3, the cause is almost always caching, not S3: S3 gives strong read-after-write consistency, so the origin is correct while an edge location, or the user's browser, still holds the old object until its TTL expires. The fast fix is an invalidation; the lasting fix is versioned asset names and sane cache headers. Interviewers use this scenario to see whether you diagnose methodically (is it the browser, the edge, or the origin?) rather than blindly invalidating /* and hoping.

steps.title: Symptom to cause: three caches in the path
steps.description: Work out which layer is serving the old bytes before changing anything.
items: Browser cache: governed by Cache-Control returned to the client. A long max-age means the browser never even asks CloudFront.

CloudFront edge (and regional edge) cache: governed by the cache policy's minimum, default and maximum TTL combined with the origin's Cache-Control/Expires. The default TTL is typically 24 hours when the origin sends no headers.
Origin: confirm S3 really holds the new object. An upload to a different key, bucket or prefix than the origin path is a surprisingly common cause.
Query strings, headers, cookies: if they are not part of the cache key, differing requests collapse into one cached object.
Practical order: test with curl first (no browser), then compare edge versus origin, then inspect cache policy. This sequence takes minutes and avoids unnecessary invalidations.
Rule out replication delays: if you use a multi-origin or cross-region replicated bucket, confirm the object reached the bucket CloudFront actually reads.

steps.title: Hands-on: CloudFront serving stale content, inspect the headers
steps.description: Use response headers to prove which layer answered.
items: X-Cache: Hit from cloudfront means the edge served a cached copy; Miss from cloudfront means it fetched from the origin.
Age: seconds the object has lived in the edge cache. A large value on a file you just updated confirms an edge cache problem.
ETag / Last-Modified: compare with aws s3api head-object to prove edge and origin differ.
Bypass the browser: use curl so browser caching is excluded from the test.
Cache-Control from S3: S3 returns whatever metadata was set at upload. Re-uploading with the same key but without the header resets it, so check the object's metadata after each pipeline change.
Compare with a cache-busting request: adding ?v=2 only proves a difference if query strings are in the cache key; use it as a hint, not as proof.
steps.codeBlock:
# What does the edge say?
curl -sI https://cdn.example.com/app.js | egrep -i 'x-cache|age|etag|cache-control|last-modified'
# x-cache: Hit from cloudfront
# age: 61342

# What does the origin say?
aws s3api head-object --bucket my-assets-bucket --key app.js \
  --query '{ETag:ETag,LastModified:LastModified,CacheControl:CacheControl}'

# What caching rules apply to the distribution?
aws cloudfront get-distribution-config --id E123EXAMPLE \
  --query 'DistributionConfig.DefaultCacheBehavior.CachePolicyId'

steps.title: Fix now: create an invalidation and wait for it
steps.description: An invalidation removes objects from edge caches before TTL expiry.
items: Targeted paths: invalidate only what changed, for example /index.html and /app.js. Wildcards like /* work but are wasteful; check current pricing and free-path allowances.
Wait for completion: invalidations are not instant. Use aws cloudfront wait invalidation-completed before telling stakeholders it is fixed.
Paths are case sensitive and must match the cached URL, including a leading slash. Query strings are part of the cached key if forwarded.
Browser copies are not purged: users with a long max-age still need a hard refresh or a changed URL.
Verify afterwards: a first request after invalidation should report Miss from cloudfront and return the new ETag; the next should be a Hit with the new content.
steps.codeBlock:
INV=$(aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id E123EXAMPLE \
  --paths "/index.html" "/app.js" --query Invalidation.Id --output text)

aws cloudfront wait invalidation-completed --distribution-id E123EXAMPLE --id "$INV"
curl -sI https://cdn.example.com/app.js | grep -i x-cache   # expect: Miss then Hit
steps.highlight: An invalidation is a repair tool, not a deployment strategy. If every release needs one, your caching design is wrong.

steps.title: Root causes and edge cases
steps.description: Match the symptom to a configuration fault.
items: Long TTL on mutable names: app.js served with max-age=31536000 will be stale in browsers for a year.
Wrong origin or path: the behavior's origin path or a different origin group points at an older bucket or prefix.
Cache policy too aggressive: a high minimum TTL overrides short origin headers. Review the policy rather than the object.
Multiple behaviors: a more specific path pattern may match your file with different caching than the default behavior.
Origin Shield or regional cache: additional layers delay propagation, which is why a verified invalidation matters.

steps.title: Production practice: versioned assets and cache headers
steps.description: Make staleness impossible by design.
items: Content-hashed filenames: publish app.3f9c1a.js with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable; a new build means a new URL, so nothing needs invalidating.
Short TTL for the entry document: keep index.html at a low max-age or no-cache (revalidate) and invalidate only that file in the deploy pipeline.
Set headers at upload: aws s3 sync dist/ s3://my-assets-bucket --cache-control ... per file type, or use a response headers policy.
Pipeline step: end the deploy job with the invalidation and wait command, and fail the job if it errors.
Stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error: CloudFront can honor these directives; useful for resilience, but they also deliberately serve old content, so set them knowingly.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Read the X-Cache and Age headers first to locate the stale layer, then ship hashed asset filenames with long TTLs and invalidate only index.html.
elevatorPitch: S3 is strongly consistent, so stale content means an edge or browser cache is still holding the old object until its TTL ends.
I confirm with curl -I for X-Cache and Age, compare against aws s3api head-object, then run a targeted invalidation and wait for it to complete.
I automate content-hashed filenames, explicit Cache-Control headers and a post-deploy invalidation of only the entry file.

title: AWS Q61: Route 53 health check is failing for your endpoint but the endpoint seems fine [L2]
summary: When a Route 53 health check is failing while the endpoint looks fine from your laptop, the usual reason is that the checkers cannot reach or satisfy it the way you do: their source IPs are blocked by a security group, NACL or.
question: Route 53 health check is failing for your endpoint but the endpoint seems fine.
intro: When a Route 53 health check is failing while the endpoint looks fine from your laptop, the usual reason is that the checkers cannot reach or satisfy it the way you do: their source IPs are blocked by a security group, NACL or WAF, the Host header or SNI is wrong, the response is too slow or the string match fails. Route 53 health checkers run from multiple AWS regions, so your own browser test proves little. Interviewers want a diagnostic runbook: read the per-region status, reproduce the probe exactly, fix the blocking layer and prevent a false failover.

steps.title: Read the evidence: per-region checker status
steps.description: Start with what Route 53 itself reports instead of guessing.
items: Console and CLI: aws route53 get-health-check-status --health-check-id <id> lists each checker region with a status report such as a connection timeout or HTTP status. If only some regions fail, suspect geo or IP filtering.
Review the config: aws route53 get-health-check --health-check-id <id> shows type, port, path, FullyQualifiedDomainName, EnableSNI, SearchString, RequestInterval and FailureThreshold.
CloudWatch: the HealthCheckStatus metric lives in us-east-1; create alarms there regardless of where the endpoint runs.
Remember the semantics: the endpoint is healthy only if enough checkers (default: more than 18% of them) report it healthy, and it flips after the failure threshold of consecutive failed checks.

Interpret the pattern: all regions failing with timeouts points to an unreachable or slow endpoint; mixed results suggest partial blocking or a flapping backend; HTTP 4xx from every region suggests the path or Host header.

steps.title: Hands-on: Route 53 health check failing, reproduce the probe
steps.description: Replicate what the checker sends rather than what your browser sends.
items: Host header and SNI: for HTTPS the checker sends the configured domain name or the IP-with-host-header combination; if EnableSNI is off, a multi-cert or ALB endpoint may return a default certificate or error.
Path and status: the endpoint must return 2xx or 3xx within a few seconds. A login redirect chain, 401 or 403 on /health counts as failure.
String matching: Route 53 searches only the first 5,120 bytes of the body, so a marker placed late in a large page is never seen.
Speed: connection and response have short fixed timeouts; a slow health endpoint that queries a database often fails intermittently.
Redirects: do not rely on the checker following a redirect to a healthy page; point it at a direct 200 path.
steps.codeBlock:
# Reproduce as the checker would (replace host/path)
curl -sv -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} connect=%{time_connect}s total=%{time_total}s\n' \
  -H 'Host: app.example.com' --resolve app.example.com:443:203.0.113.10 \
  https://app.example.com/health

aws route53 get-health-check-status --health-check-id abcdef11-2222-3333-4444-555555fedcba \
  --query 'HealthCheckObservations[].[Region,StatusReport.Status]' --output table

steps.title: Allow the Route 53 health checker IP ranges
steps.description: Public AWS publishes the source addresses; your firewall layers must permit them.
items: Fetch the ranges: the ROUTE53_HEALTHCHECKS service in ip-ranges.json lists the CIDRs.
Every layer: check the security group, subnet NACL, host firewall (iptables, ufw), on-prem firewall, WAF rules and rate limits. Bot-protection rules commonly block the checkers.
Right port and protocol: a TCP check on 443 differs from an HTTPS check; mismatch with the listener is a classic mistake.
Keep it current: subscribe to the AWS IP range change notification SNS topic or generate rules from the JSON in your pipeline.
Verify after the change: wait a few intervals (default 30 seconds each, 10 seconds for fast checks) and re-run get-health-check-status; every region should flip to Success.
steps.codeBlock:
curl -s https://ip-ranges.amazonaws.com/ip-ranges.json \
 | jq -r '.prefixes[] | select(.service=="ROUTE53_HEALTHCHECKS") | .ip_prefix' | sort -u

# Example: allow 443 from one range (repeat per CIDR, or use a managed prefix list)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-0abc1234 \
  --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 15.177.0.0/18   # use a real CIDR from the list above

steps.title: Root causes and special cases
steps.description: Tie observed symptoms to a fix.
items: Private endpoint: health checkers cannot reach private IPs or private hosted zone targets. Use a CloudWatch-alarm-based health check driven by metrics from inside the VPC.
Wrong health path: checking / which redirects to a login, or a path that exists only on one backend.
Target group vs DNS name: the check hits the ALB DNS name, whose backend instances may be unhealthy; evaluate target health separately.
Fail-open behavior: if all records in a set are unhealthy Route 53 returns them all, so you may not see an outage even though checks are red.
Calculated or inverted checks: verify no inversion flag or parent aggregate check explains the status.
Cert problems: an expired or mismatched certificate fails HTTPS checks even though browsers on your machine may have cached exceptions.

steps.title: Prevention and alerting
steps.description: Make health checks reliable and observable.
items: Dedicated health endpoint: fast, unauthenticated, shallow (process alive and critical dependency reachable) and under the timeout.
Alarm on the metric: CloudWatch alarm on HealthCheckStatus < 1 notifies via SNS before DNS failover surprises anyone.
Define in IaC: manage aws_route53_health_check with Terraform alongside the firewall rules so port and path stay in sync.
Test failover: deliberately fail the endpoint in staging to confirm routing policy and TTL behave as expected.
Document ownership: record who owns the health path and what 'healthy' means so application changes do not silently break DNS failover.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Run aws route53 get-health-check-status first; if only some checker regions fail, you have a firewall, WAF or geo filter blocking the ROUTE53_HEALTHCHECKS ranges.
elevatorPitch: Route 53 health checkers probe from many AWS regions, so a healthy endpoint for me can still fail for them.
I verify with get-health-check-status per region, then reproduce the probe with curl using the right Host header, SNI and path.
I automate the checker IP allowlist from ip-ranges.json, define checks in Terraform and alarm on HealthCheckStatus in us-east-1.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Declaring the endpoint healthy because it loads in a browser
mistakesToAvoid.why: The checkers come from other IPs and regions and may be blocked by security groups, NACLs or WAF.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Pointing a public health check at a private IP
mistakesToAvoid.why: Route 53 checkers are on the internet and cannot reach private addresses; use a CloudWatch alarm check instead.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Putting the match string deep in a large response
mistakesToAvoid.why: Only the first 5,120 bytes of the body are searched.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Making the health endpoint call slow dependencies
mistakesToAvoid.why: Timeouts are short, so the check flaps and can trigger needless failover.

title: AWS Q64: Your Lambda function is doing the same cold start every invocation because it initializes a big ML model How do you fix it [L2]
summary: To fix a Lambda cold start with a big ML model, load the model once in the init phase (outside the handler), shrink and cache it, and pay to keep environments warm with provisioned concurrency where latency matters.
question: Your Lambda function is doing the same cold start every invocation because it initializes a big ML model. How do you fix it?
intro: To fix a Lambda cold start with a big ML model, load the model once in the init phase (outside the handler), shrink and cache it, and pay to keep environments warm with provisioned concurrency where latency matters. If the function seems to cold start on every invocation, either the model is loaded inside the handler, or concurrency is so spiky that each request gets a new execution environment. Interviewers ask this to test whether you understand the Lambda lifecycle (init, invoke, freeze) and the real options: global scope reuse, packaging choices, provisioned concurrency, SnapStart where the runtime supports it, and when Lambda is the wrong tool.

steps.title: Understand the lifecycle: what repeats and what does not
steps.description: Only code outside the handler runs once per execution environment; the handler runs per invocation.
items: Init phase: downloads code, starts the runtime and runs top-level code. A cold start is this phase plus the first invoke. It appears as Init Duration in the REPORT log line only on cold starts.
Warm invokes: reuse the same environment, its global variables and /tmp, until it is idle long enough to be reclaimed.
Diagnosis question: if every REPORT line shows Init Duration, either each request lands on a new environment (bursty concurrency or low traffic) or you are not caching anything.
Memory is CPU: more memory gives proportionally more CPU, which often shortens model deserialization considerably.

Why it looks like every call: at low or very spiky traffic, Lambda scales out new environments for concurrent requests, and idle ones are eventually reclaimed, so sparse traffic means frequent cold starts.

steps.title: Hands-on: measure the Lambda cold start with Logs Insights
steps.description: Quantify how often cold starts happen and how long init takes before optimizing.
items: Cold start ratio: count REPORT lines that include an init duration versus the total.
Where time goes: add timing logs around model download, deserialization and first inference.
X-Ray or Lambda Insights: enable active tracing to see the initialization subsegment.
Set a target: decide an acceptable p95 for first-request latency before choosing between code fixes and paid warm capacity.
steps.codeBlock:
# CloudWatch Logs Insights query (run against /aws/lambda/my-ml-fn)
fields @timestamp, @initDuration, @duration, @maxMemoryUsed
| filter @type = "REPORT"
| stats count() as invokes, count(@initDuration) as cold_starts,
        avg(@initDuration) as avg_init_ms, pct(@initDuration, 95) as p95_init_ms
  by bin(1h)

steps.title: Fix 1: load the model once, in init scope
steps.description: Move heavy initialization out of the handler and make it lazy-safe.
items: Global variable: load at module import so later invocations reuse it.
Local artifact: bake the model into the container image, or fetch from S3 to /tmp once and check for the file before downloading again (ephemeral storage is configurable up to 10 GB).
Smaller model: quantize, prune or export to ONNX; load only what inference needs. Package size affects init time.
Container image: images up to 10 GB are supported and avoid zip size limits, but a large image still needs to be loaded on first use.
Thread-safety: the loaded object is shared across invocations in one environment, but each environment handles one request at a time, so ordinary inference code is safe.

steps.title: Fix 2: remove the cold start from the user path
steps.description: When init cannot be shortened enough, pre-initialize environments.
items: Provisioned concurrency: keeps a set number of environments initialized, including your top-level model load. It must target a version or alias, not $LATEST, and is billed while configured; use Application Auto Scaling to schedule it.

SnapStart: snapshots the initialized environment and resumes from it. Support depends on runtime (Java originally, with Python and .NET added later) and region, so verify current support before relying on it.
Not a fix: reserved concurrency only caps or guarantees capacity; it does not keep anything warm. Periodic ping hacks are fragile compared with provisioned concurrency.
Right tool: for multi-GB models or GPU needs, a SageMaker endpoint or container service is usually better than Lambda.
Autoscale warm capacity: register the alias with Application Auto Scaling using target tracking on utilization, or scheduled actions for known peaks.
steps.codeBlock:
aws lambda publish-version --function-name my-ml-fn
aws lambda create-alias --function-name my-ml-fn --name live --function-version 7
aws lambda put-provisioned-concurrency-config --function-name my-ml-fn \
  --qualifier live --provisioned-concurrent-executions 5
aws lambda get-provisioned-concurrency-config --function-name my-ml-fn --qualifier live
# Status should become READY; point callers at the alias ARN

steps.title: Verify and operate
steps.description: Prove the improvement and keep it.
items: Re-run the Insights query after deployment; cold_starts should fall and p95 latency should drop. Metric ProvisionedConcurrencySpilloverInvocations shows traffic exceeding the pre-warmed pool.
Init limits: the init phase has its own time limit, so a model that loads too slowly will fail outright rather than just be slow. Check current limits in the docs.
Version the model: deploy new model versions through new function versions so aliases shift traffic gradually.
Cost check: compare provisioned concurrency spend against the latency requirement; scheduled scaling covers business hours only.
Layers and dependencies: trim heavy libraries (full TensorFlow or PyTorch) in favor of lighter runtimes such as ONNX Runtime to cut package size.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Put the model load in global init scope and pre-warm it with provisioned concurrency on an alias, then confirm with a Logs Insights query on @initDuration.
elevatorPitch: Cold start cost is the init phase, so a big ML model must load once at module scope, not inside the handler.
I measure with Logs Insights on Init Duration, shrink the model, cache it in the image or /tmp, then use provisioned concurrency on an alias.
I automate scheduled provisioned concurrency scaling and alarm on spillover invocations and p95 latency.

title: AWS Q69: How do you enable encryption for an existing unencrypted RDS instance [L2]
summary: You cannot toggle encryption on an existing unencrypted RDS instance; instead you snapshot it, copy the snapshot with a KMS key to produce an encrypted snapshot, restore that into a new instance and cut traffic over.
question: How do you enable encryption for an existing unencrypted RDS instance?
intro: You cannot toggle encryption on an existing unencrypted RDS instance; instead you snapshot it, copy the snapshot with a KMS key to produce an encrypted snapshot, restore that into a new instance and cut traffic over. Interviewers ask this because it tests whether you know encryption at rest is fixed at creation time, can plan the downtime or replication window, and remember everything a restore does not carry over: security groups, parameter groups, endpoints and monitoring. A senior answer also covers verification and the guardrails that stop unencrypted databases from being created again.

steps.title: Why there is no in-place switch and what the options are
steps.description: Storage encryption is applied when the DB instance volumes are created, so the data must be copied into encrypted storage.
items: Snapshot-copy-restore: the standard path. Simple, supported for all engines, and requires a write freeze (or a catch-up strategy) at cutover.
Logical migration: create a new encrypted instance and use AWS DMS or native logical replication to sync, then cut over with minimal downtime. More moving parts but shorter outage.
What encryption covers: data on the underlying storage, automated backups, snapshots and read replicas. It does not replace TLS in transit, which you enable separately.
Decide the key: the AWS managed key aws/rds works but cannot be shared cross-account; a customer managed KMS key allows key policy control, rotation and snapshot sharing.

Downtime expectation: state it honestly in the interview: snapshot-restore means a write outage covering the final snapshot, copy and restore time, which grows with database size, so measure it in a rehearsal.

steps.title: Hands-on: encrypt an existing unencrypted RDS instance with snapshots
steps.description: Create a snapshot, copy it with a KMS key, then restore into a new instance.
items: Take a fresh snapshot and wait until it is available. For Multi-AZ, the snapshot is taken from the standby without impacting the primary on most engines.
Copy with a KMS key: specifying --kms-key-id during copy-db-snapshot produces the encrypted copy.
Restore into a new identifier and set the same instance class, subnet group, security groups and parameter group explicitly; restores do not reuse your old settings automatically.
Copy tags and options: use --copy-tags-to-snapshot and re-apply option groups as needed.
Time to restore: the first read from a restored volume can be slower while blocks hydrate lazily, so warm critical tables or run representative queries before cutover.
steps.codeBlock:
aws rds create-db-snapshot --db-instance-identifier prod-db \
  --db-snapshot-identifier prod-db-pre-enc
aws rds wait db-snapshot-available --db-snapshot-identifier prod-db-pre-enc

aws rds copy-db-snapshot --source-db-snapshot-identifier prod-db-pre-enc \
  --target-db-snapshot-identifier prod-db-enc \
  --kms-key-id arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:111122223333:key/EXAMPLE-KEY-ID
aws rds wait db-snapshot-available --db-snapshot-identifier prod-db-enc

aws rds restore-db-instance-from-db-snapshot \
  --db-instance-identifier prod-db-encrypted \
  --db-snapshot-identifier prod-db-enc \
  --db-instance-class db.r6g.large \
  --db-subnet-group-name prod-db-subnets \
  --vpc-security-group-ids sg-0abc1234 \
  --db-parameter-group-name prod-pg15 --multi-az

steps.title: Plan the cutover to avoid data loss
steps.description: Anything written to the old instance after the snapshot will be missing from the new one.
items: Quiesce writes: put the app in maintenance mode or read-only, then take a final snapshot and repeat the copy and restore so no data is lost. This is the simplest correct path.
Shorter outage: set up DMS ongoing replication (or engine-native logical replication) from the old to the new encrypted instance, then switch when lag is zero.

Endpoint swap: either point applications at the new endpoint through a Route 53 CNAME or secret, or rename instances with modify-db-instance --new-db-instance-identifier so the old name moves to the new database. A DNS indirection is safer and reversible.
Keep the old instance stopped or renamed for rollback until the new one has proven itself, then delete it and its unencrypted snapshots.
Secrets and connection strings: if credentials live in Secrets Manager with rotation tied to the old instance, update the secret's host field and rotation configuration for the new instance.

steps.title: Verify encryption and parity
steps.description: Check the flag, key and operational settings before declaring success.
items: Encryption flag: StorageEncrypted must be true and KmsKeyId populated.
Settings parity: compare parameter groups, backup retention, maintenance window, Performance Insights, enhanced monitoring, IAM auth, deletion protection and alarms with the old instance.
Functional test: run schema and row-count checks, then the application smoke tests against the new endpoint.
Replicas: create new read replicas from the encrypted instance; they inherit encryption.
Backups: confirm automated backups are enabled on the new instance and that a first encrypted snapshot completes successfully.
steps.codeBlock:
aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier prod-db-encrypted \
  --query 'DBInstances[0].[DBInstanceIdentifier,StorageEncrypted,KmsKeyId,DBInstanceStatus]'
# ["prod-db-encrypted", true, "arn:aws:kms:...", "available"]

aws rds describe-db-instances \
  --query 'DBInstances[?StorageEncrypted==`false`].DBInstanceIdentifier'
# anything listed still needs migrating

steps.title: Failure modes and guardrails
steps.description: Handle common surprises and stop recurrence.
items: KMS permissions: the restoring principal needs access to the key; a restrictive key policy causes a confusing KMSKeyNotAccessible failure.
Cross-region or cross-account: copying across regions needs a key in the destination region; sharing encrypted snapshots needs a customer managed key and key policy grants.
Detect: enable the AWS Config managed rule rds-storage-encrypted to flag unencrypted databases.
Prevent: add an SCP or IAM condition denying rds:CreateDBInstance when rds:StorageEncrypted is false, and set storage_encrypted = true in Terraform modules.
Test the runbook: rehearse in staging and time each phase so the production window is a known quantity.
Aurora note: Aurora clusters follow the same principle, restoring an encrypted copy of a cluster snapshot into a new cluster, and cluster members share the cluster's key.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Rehearse the snapshot, encrypted copy and restore in staging, front the database with a DNS CNAME for a reversible cutover, and add an SCP so no new unencrypted instance can be created.
elevatorPitch: RDS encryption is set at creation, so for an existing database I snapshot it, copy the snapshot with a KMS key and restore into a new encrypted instance.
I verify with describe-db-instances for StorageEncrypted and KmsKeyId, then check parameter groups, security groups and application smoke tests.
I automate detection with the rds-storage-encrypted Config rule and prevention with an SCP and encrypted-by-default Terraform modules.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Rows written after the snapshot are silently lost on the new instance.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming the restored instance inherits security groups and parameter groups
mistakesToAvoid.why: Restores need those specified explicitly, or the new database launches with defaults.

mistakesToAvoid.why: The AWS managed key cannot be shared; use a customer managed KMS key.

title: AWS Q73: How does Auto Scaling determine when to scale in vs scale out [L2]
summary: EC2 Auto Scaling scale in vs scale out decisions come from CloudWatch alarms and scaling policies: when a metric crosses a threshold the group adds instances (scale out), and when it stays well below the target for long enough.
question: How does Auto Scaling determine when to scale in vs scale out?
intro: EC2 Auto Scaling scale in vs scale out decisions come from CloudWatch alarms and scaling policies: when a metric crosses a threshold the group adds instances (scale out), and when it stays well below the target for long enough the group removes them (scale in), always bounded by minimum and maximum size. Interviewers ask this to find out whether you know the asymmetry: scale out is aggressive, scale in is deliberately cautious, and different policy types behave differently. A good answer explains target tracking, step scaling, warmup and cooldown, and how Auto Scaling chooses which instance to terminate.

steps.title: Decision model: metric, alarm, policy, capacity limits
steps.description: Every dynamic decision is a CloudWatch alarm triggering a policy that changes desired capacity.
items: Desired capacity: the number of instances the group tries to run; always clamped between MinSize and MaxSize.
Target tracking: you pick a metric and target (for example average CPU 50%). Auto Scaling creates and manages the alarms and computes capacity to keep the metric near the target.
Step scaling and simple scaling: you define alarms and adjustments yourself. Step scaling can apply bigger adjustments for bigger breaches; simple scaling waits for a cooldown after each action.
Scheduled and predictive scaling: change capacity by calendar or forecast, complementing reactive policies.

Evaluation periods: an alarm needs several consecutive datapoints in breach, so brief spikes under a minute or two rarely trigger action. Detailed monitoring (1-minute metrics) makes decisions faster than the 5-minute basic default.

steps.title: Hands-on: scale out vs scale in with target tracking
steps.description: Create a policy and inspect the alarms it generates.
items: Scale-out alarm: fires when the metric exceeds the target for a short evaluation window, so capacity rises quickly.
Scale-in alarm: fires only when the metric is below the target by a comfortable margin for a longer window; the exact thresholds are managed by AWS and are intentionally conservative.
Multiple policies: the group scales out if any policy asks for it, but scales in only when all target tracking policies agree, with the largest capacity winning.
Disable scale in: the option DisableScaleIn lets a policy only scale out, useful for stateful or slow-draining workloads.

Math behind target tracking: it scales proportionally to how far the metric is from the target, for example roughly doubling capacity when the metric is double the target, rather than adding a fixed step.
steps.codeBlock:
cat > tt.json <<'EOF'
{
  "TargetValue": 50.0,
  "PredefinedMetricSpecification": {"PredefinedMetricType": "ASGAverageCPUUtilization"},
  "DisableScaleIn": false
}
EOF
aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg \
  --policy-name cpu50 --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling \
  --target-tracking-configuration file://tt.json

# See the alarms Auto Scaling created and the policy details
aws autoscaling describe-policies --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg
aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-name-prefix TargetTracking-web-asg

steps.title: Timing controls: warmup, cooldown and scale-in protection
steps.description: These settings stop flapping and premature termination.
items: Instance warmup: for target tracking and step scaling, newly launched instances are excluded from the aggregated metric until warmup ends, so the group does not over-provision while they boot.
Cooldown: applies to simple scaling and also as a default; after an activity, further simple-scaling actions wait. Default is 300 seconds unless changed.
Scale-in protection: mark instances so they are not selected during scale in, for example while processing a long job.
Lifecycle hooks: pause termination to drain connections or upload logs before the instance goes away.
Health checks: unhealthy instances are replaced independent of scaling policies; a failing ELB health check causes replacement, not scale in.
Cooldown vs warmup: they solve different problems; warmup keeps new instances out of the metric, cooldown spaces out simple scaling actions.

steps.title: Which instance gets terminated on scale in
steps.description: The default termination policy balances first, then ages.
items: Step 1: select the Availability Zone with the most instances, to keep the group balanced across zones.
Step 2: within that zone, prefer the instance with the oldest launch template or configuration, which phases out old versions.
Step 3: if still tied, choose the instance closest to the next billing hour (relevant for per-hour billed usage); otherwise pick randomly.
Override: set termination policies such as OldestInstance, NewestInstance or OldestLaunchTemplate if you need different behavior, and combine with scale-in protection.
steps.codeBlock:
# Protect a busy instance from scale in, then set a termination policy
aws autoscaling set-instance-protection --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg \
  --instance-ids i-0abc1234def567890 --protected-from-scale-in

aws autoscaling update-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg \
  --termination-policies OldestLaunchTemplate Default

aws autoscaling describe-scaling-activities --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg --max-items 5 \
  --query 'Activities[].[StartTime,StatusCode,Cause]' --output table

steps.title: Verify and operate
steps.description: Read the activity history and tune from evidence.
items: Activity log: aws autoscaling describe-scaling-activities --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg --max-items 10 shows cause strings such as an alarm breach and the capacity change.
Flapping: frequent out-then-in cycles suggest a target too tight, warmup too short or a spiky metric; widen the target or use a request-count metric.
Pick the right metric: CPU suits compute-bound apps; ALBRequestCountPerTarget suits web tiers; use SQS backlog per instance (custom metric) for workers.
Limits: if the group sits at MaxSize or capacity is unavailable, scale out silently stalls; alert on that condition.

Capacity rebalancing and Spot: with mixed instance groups, Spot interruptions and AZ rebalancing launch and terminate instances independently of scaling policies, so do not read every activity as a policy decision.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Use target tracking on ALBRequestCountPerTarget for web tiers, set a realistic instance warmup, and read describe-scaling-activities before touching thresholds.
elevatorPitch: Auto Scaling changes desired capacity when CloudWatch alarms driven by scaling policies fire, bounded by min and max size.
Scale out reacts quickly; scale in waits for the metric to stay well below target and, with several target tracking policies, requires all to agree.
I verify with describe-scaling-activities, tune warmup and metrics, and protect instances or use lifecycle hooks to drain safely.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Scale in is intentionally conservative with a longer window and margin to avoid flapping.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Setting instance warmup too short
mistakesToAvoid.why: Booting instances report low metrics and cause over-provisioning or premature scale in.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using CPU for an I/O-bound or queue-driven worker fleet
mistakesToAvoid.why: The metric does not reflect load, so the group scales at the wrong times.

title: AWS Q75: Your SQS consumer occasionally processes the same message twice How do you handle this [L2]
summary: If an SQS consumer processes the same message twice, treat it as expected behavior to design for, not a bug to eliminate: standard queues guarantee at-least-once delivery, and a message can reappear when the visibility timeout.
question: Your SQS consumer occasionally processes the same message twice. How do you handle this?
intro: If an SQS consumer processes the same message twice, treat it as expected behavior to design for, not a bug to eliminate: standard queues guarantee at-least-once delivery, and a message can reappear when the visibility timeout expires before deletion or when the delete call fails. The senior answer is to make the consumer idempotent, tune the visibility timeout and batch handling so duplicates are rare, and use FIFO deduplication only where its limits fit. Interviewers want to hear the causes, a concrete idempotency pattern with a conditional write, and the monitoring that exposes duplicate rates.

steps.title: Why duplicates happen
steps.description: Know the three common sources before choosing a fix.
items: At-least-once delivery: standard queues are distributed; in rare cases a message is delivered more than once even if you deleted it correctly.
Visibility timeout too short: when processing takes longer than the timeout, the message becomes visible again and another worker (or the same one) receives it while the first is still working.
Delete failure or crash: the worker finishes the side effect but crashes or times out before DeleteMessage, so the message returns.
Lambda partial batch failure: if one record in a batch fails and you throw, the whole batch is retried unless you return batch item failures.
Interview framing: exactly-once processing is built from at-least-once delivery plus idempotent handling; no queue gives it for free end to end.

steps.title: Hands-on: SQS consumer processes the same message twice, find out why
steps.description: Use message attributes and queue metrics to confirm the cause.
items: Receive count: request ApproximateReceiveCount; values above 1 mean redelivery.
Compare timeout and duration: if p99 processing time exceeds VisibilityTimeout, that is your cause.
Metrics: watch ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage, NumberOfMessagesDeleted versus NumberOfMessagesReceived; a persistent gap implies messages are received but not deleted.
Log the MessageId and your business key at consume time to quantify duplicates.
Heartbeat check: if a long job extends visibility, confirm the extension actually runs; a stalled heartbeat thread is a classic hidden cause.
Rule out duplicate producers: two different MessageIds with the same payload mean the producer published twice, which a consumer-side timeout fix will not cure.
steps.codeBlock:
aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url "$Q_URL" \
  --attribute-names VisibilityTimeout ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds RedrivePolicy

aws sqs receive-message --queue-url "$Q_URL" --max-number-of-messages 1 \
  --attribute-names ApproximateReceiveCount --message-attribute-names All

# Raise the timeout (must exceed worst-case processing time; for Lambda, use at least
# 6x the function timeout as AWS recommends)
aws sqs set-queue-attributes --queue-url "$Q_URL" --attributes VisibilityTimeout=120

steps.title: Fix: make the consumer idempotent
steps.description: Record a unique key atomically so a second delivery becomes a no-op.
items: Choose the key: a business identifier such as order ID or an idempotency key set by the producer, not the SQS MessageId (a producer retry creates a new MessageId).
Atomic claim: a DynamoDB conditional PutItem with attribute_not_exists succeeds for exactly one caller.
TTL: expire keys after a retention window longer than the maximum redelivery period.
Process then mark, or mark then process: mark first with a status of IN_PROGRESS and update to DONE, so crashed attempts can be retried safely. Prefer naturally idempotent operations such as upserts.
Powertools option: in Lambda, the AWS Lambda Powertools idempotency utility implements this pattern with DynamoDB, including payload hashing and expiry, so you need not hand-roll it.
steps.codeBlock:
import boto3, time
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError
table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("processed-messages")

def handle(record):
    key = record["order_id"]
    try:
        table.put_item(
            Item={"pk": key, "status": "IN_PROGRESS", "ttl": int(time.time()) + 7*86400},
            ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(pk)")
    except ClientError as e:
        if e.response["Error"]["Code"] == "ConditionalCheckFailedException":
            return  # duplicate, safe to delete the message
        raise
    do_work(record)
    table.update_item(Key={"pk": key}, UpdateExpression="SET #s=:d",
                      ExpressionAttributeNames={"#s": "status"},
                      ExpressionAttributeValues={":d": "DONE"})

steps.title: Fix: tune queue and Lambda settings
steps.description: Reduce how often redelivery occurs.
items: Visibility timeout: set above worst-case processing time; for long jobs, extend dynamically with ChangeMessageVisibility heartbeats.
Partial batch response: in the Lambda event source mapping set FunctionResponseTypes=[ReportBatchItemFailures] and return only failed itemIdentifiers so successful records are not retried.

FIFO queues: provide MessageDeduplicationId (or enable content-based deduplication); duplicates sent within the 5-minute deduplication interval are dropped. This stops producer-side duplicates but not consumer-side redelivery, and has lower throughput limits.
DLQ: add a redrive policy with maxReceiveCount so poison messages move aside instead of cycling.
Long polling: set ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds to 20 to reduce empty receives; it does not change duplicates but lowers cost and noise when you analyze logs.

steps.title: Verify and monitor
steps.description: Prove duplicates are harmless and measurable.
items: Replay test: send the same message twice to staging and assert the side effect happens once.
Metrics: emit a custom metric on each duplicate skipped, and alarm on a sudden rise, which signals a timeout regression.
Downstream calls: pass your idempotency key to payment or email APIs that support it so external effects are deduplicated too.
Outbox note: for database-plus-queue consistency, use the transactional outbox pattern rather than hoping a single publish is exactly once.
Capacity of the dedup table: on-demand DynamoDB billing avoids throttling the consumer when traffic spikes.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Treat duplicates as normal, key your idempotency check on a business identifier with a DynamoDB conditional write, and set the visibility timeout above worst-case processing time.
elevatorPitch: Standard SQS is at-least-once, and a message also reappears if processing outlasts the visibility timeout or the delete fails.
I check ApproximateReceiveCount and compare processing duration with the timeout to find the cause.
I make handlers idempotent with a conditional write keyed by business ID, report partial batch failures, add a DLQ, and use FIFO dedup only where needed.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using the SQS MessageId as the idempotency key
mistakesToAvoid.why: A producer retry creates a new MessageId for the same business event, so duplicates slip through.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on FIFO deduplication to protect consumers
mistakesToAvoid.why: It only drops duplicate sends within a 5-minute window; consumer redelivery after a timeout still occurs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Throwing on one bad record in a Lambda batch
mistakesToAvoid.why: The entire batch is retried, re-running successful records unless partial batch responses are enabled.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Check-then-act without an atomic write
mistakesToAvoid.why: Two workers can both pass the check; use a conditional write or unique constraint.

title: AWS Q78: A CloudFormation stack is in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED state How do you recover [L2]
summary: A CloudFormation stack in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED means an update failed and then the automatic rollback also failed on one or more resources.
question: A CloudFormation stack is in `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` state. How do you recover?
intro: A CloudFormation stack in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED means an update failed and then the automatic rollback also failed on one or more resources; you recover by fixing the underlying cause and running continue-update-rollback, skipping a resource only as a last resort. The stack is frozen: you cannot update it until the rollback completes. Interviewers use this to test calm, ordered diagnosis: read the stack events, identify why a resource could not return to its previous state, repair that cause, retry, and understand the drift risk that skipping creates.

steps.title: What UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED means
steps.description: Rollback tries to restore every changed resource to its previous configuration; one of those restores failed.
items: State: the stack is stuck; allowed actions are continue-update-rollback or deleting the stack. A normal update-stack is rejected.
Typical trigger: something outside CloudFormation changed, such as a resource deleted by hand, an IAM role removed, or a dependency in use.
Two failures: the original update failure (the first UPDATE_FAILED) is not the one blocking you; the blocker is the resource failing during rollback.
Priority: do not delete the stack in a hurry, as that may destroy production resources.

Contrast with other states: UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE is a healthy, updatable state after a successful rollback; UPDATE_FAILED with rollback disabled is different again, and you must handle each correctly.

steps.title: Hands-on: UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED, find the failing resource
steps.description: Read events in reverse chronological order for the status reason.
items: Locate failed resources: filter events for UPDATE_FAILED that occurred during rollback and read ResourceStatusReason.

Common reasons: resource does not exist, not authorized or role assume failure, resource in use or dependency conflict, S3 bucket not empty, or service stabilization timeout such as an ECS service that cannot reach a steady state.
Nested stacks: open the child stack that failed; the parent only reports the nested stack failure.
CloudTrail: search for manual changes to that resource around the time of the incident.
Console route: the Stack actions menu offers Continue update rollback with an advanced section listing which failed resources you may skip, which is handy when you cannot recall logical IDs.
Read in order: sort events by timestamp and look for the earliest rollback-phase failure, because later failures often cascade from it.
steps.codeBlock:
aws cloudformation describe-stack-events --stack-name my-stack \
  --query "StackEvents[?ResourceStatus=='UPDATE_FAILED'].[Timestamp,LogicalResourceId,ResourceType,ResourceStatusReason]" \
  --output table

aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name my-stack \
  --query 'Stacks[0].[StackStatus,StackStatusReason]'

steps.title: Fix the cause, then continue the rollback
steps.description: Make the resource restorable and retry.
items: Resource deleted manually: recreate it with the same physical identity where possible, or restore from backup, so rollback can proceed.
Permissions: if the service role or your principal lost permissions, restore them or supply --role-arn with a role that has the needed access.
In use or not empty: detach the dependency or empty the bucket (carefully), then retry.
Retry: run continue-update-rollback and wait for UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE.
Service role considerations: if the stack was created with a service role, rollback uses it, so a deleted or trust-broken role is a frequent blocker.
steps.codeBlock:
aws cloudformation continue-update-rollback --stack-name my-stack
aws cloudformation wait stack-rollback-complete --stack-name my-stack

# Last resort when the resource cannot be repaired: skip it
aws cloudformation continue-update-rollback --stack-name my-stack \
  --resources-to-skip MyBrokenResourceLogicalId
# nested stack resources use the form NestedStackLogicalId.ResourceLogicalId

steps.title: Skipping resources and what it costs
steps.description: Skipping tells CloudFormation to mark the resource as successfully rolled back without touching it.
items: Result: the skipped resource is marked as complete, but its real configuration may not match the previous template, so the stack is out of sync.
After skipping: run drift detection (aws cloudformation detect-stack-drift), reconcile manually or by importing, and only then deploy.
Which resources: only resources in a failed state can be skipped; others are not eligible.
Retry the original change: once the stack is UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, correct the template or parameters that caused the first failure and deploy again, preferably using a change set.
Document the skip: record which resources were skipped and why in the incident notes, so the later reconciliation is deliberate.

steps.title: Verification and prevention
steps.description: Confirm health and stop it recurring.
items: Verify: stack status is UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, critical resources respond, and drift detection is clean.
Change sets and previews: review replacement and delete actions before executing updates.
Stack policy and termination protection: shield critical resources from accidental updates and the stack from deletion.
Stop console edits: restrict manual changes to managed resources through IAM and detect them with scheduled drift detection.
Rollback triggers: attach CloudWatch alarms so bad updates roll back automatically in a controlled way.
Pipelines: make CI deploy through aws cloudformation deploy with change sets and fail fast, so a stuck stack is noticed immediately rather than at the next release.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Find the rollback-time UPDATE_FAILED event first, repair that resource, and only use --resources-to-skip as a last resort followed by drift detection.
elevatorPitch: UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED means the rollback itself failed on a resource, leaving the stack frozen until rollback completes.
I read describe-stack-events for the failing resource and reason, fix the cause such as a deleted resource or missing permission, then run continue-update-rollback.
I skip resources only as a last resort, run drift detection afterwards, and prevent repeats with change sets, stack policies and restricted console access.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Deleting the stack to get unstuck
mistakesToAvoid.why: It can destroy production resources that were fine; recover the rollback instead.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Reaching for --resources-to-skip immediately
mistakesToAvoid.why: It leaves the stack out of sync with reality and hides the real defect.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Debugging only the parent of a nested stack
mistakesToAvoid.why: The actual failure is in the child stack's events.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Redeploying the same template after recovery without finding the original failure
mistakesToAvoid.why: The first update failure will happen again and roll back again.

title: AWS Q84: What is Amazon EventBridge and how does it differ from SNS [L2]
summary: Amazon EventBridge is a serverless event bus that routes JSON events from AWS services, your applications and SaaS partners to targets using content-based rules, while SNS is a high-throughput pub/sub topic that pushes each.
question: What is Amazon EventBridge and how does it differ from SNS?
intro: Amazon EventBridge is a serverless event bus that routes JSON events from AWS services, your applications and SaaS partners to targets using content-based rules, while SNS is a high-throughput pub/sub topic that pushes each message to its subscribers. The key difference between EventBridge and SNS is routing intelligence versus raw fan-out: EventBridge matches rich patterns on event content, supports schema discovery, archive and replay, whereas SNS excels at simple, fast fan-out and endpoints like SMS, email and mobile push. Interviewers ask this to see whether you can pick the right messaging primitive for event-driven architecture rather than defaulting to SNS for everything.

steps.title: Mental model: event bus with rules vs topic with subscriptions
steps.description: Both decouple producers from consumers, but they differ in where routing decisions live.
items: EventBridge: producers put events on a bus; rules with event patterns decide which targets receive each event. Rules can match on any field in the JSON body, including nested values and numeric ranges.
SNS: producers publish to a topic; every subscription gets the message unless a filter policy (on message attributes, or on the payload if configured) excludes it.
Event sources: the default EventBridge bus receives events from AWS services (EC2 state changes, CodePipeline, GuardDuty and more) automatically; SNS only carries what you publish.
Extra features unique to EventBridge: schema registry, archive and replay, event buses across accounts and regions, SaaS partner buses, API destinations, Pipes and Scheduler.
Typical examples: 'when a GuardDuty finding has severity above 7, start a Step Functions workflow' is natural in EventBridge; 'text the on-call phone when an alarm fires' is natural in SNS.

steps.title: Hands-on: Amazon EventBridge rules and put-events
steps.description: Create a bus rule matching on payload content and send a test event.
items: Pattern first: test it with aws events test-event-pattern before wiring targets.
Targets: add Lambda, SQS, Step Functions, ECS tasks, API destinations and many other services. Give each target a dead-letter queue and a retry policy.
Permissions: Lambda needs a resource-based permission for events.amazonaws.com; other targets use an IAM role specified on the target.
Custom events: use a source name you own, for example my.app.orders, and a stable detail-type.
Verify end to end: after put-events, check the rule's Invocations and FailedInvocations metrics and read the target queue or function logs to confirm the event arrived with the expected shape.
steps.codeBlock:
aws events create-event-bus --name orders-bus

aws events put-rule --event-bus-name orders-bus --name big-orders \
  --event-pattern '{"source":["my.app.orders"],"detail-type":["OrderPlaced"],"detail":{"total":[{"numeric":[">",1000]}]}}'

aws events put-targets --event-bus-name orders-bus --rule big-orders \
  --targets '[{"Id":"fraud-queue","Arn":"arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:111122223333:fraud-review",
              "DeadLetterConfig":{"Arn":"arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:111122223333:eb-dlq"}}]'

aws events put-events --entries '[{"EventBusName":"orders-bus","Source":"my.app.orders",
  "DetailType":"OrderPlaced","Detail":"{\"id\":\"42\",\"total\":1500}"}]'

steps.title: Archive, replay and schema discovery
steps.description: Features that make EventBridge suited to evolving event-driven systems.
items: Archive: store events from a bus, optionally filtered by pattern, with a retention period.
Replay: re-send archived events to a bus within a time window to reprocess after a bug fix or to seed a new consumer. SNS has no equivalent; once delivered, messages are gone.
Schema registry and discovery: infer schemas from events and generate code bindings, helping teams agree on contracts.
Careful with replay: consumers must be idempotent, and replays go back through the rules so side effects can repeat.
Cost angle: archives and replays are billed separately from event ingestion, so set a retention period deliberately.
steps.codeBlock:
aws events create-archive --archive-name orders-archive \
  --event-source-arn arn:aws:events:us-east-1:111122223333:event-bus/orders-bus \
  --retention-days 30

aws events start-replay --replay-name fix-2026-10 \
  --event-source-arn arn:aws:events:us-east-1:111122223333:archive/orders-archive \
  --destination '{"Arn":"arn:aws:events:us-east-1:111122223333:event-bus/orders-bus"}' \
  --event-start-time 2026-10-24T00:00:00Z --event-end-time 2026-10-25T00:00:00Z

steps.title: When to use which
steps.description: Choose based on routing needs, scale and endpoints.
items: EventBridge: reacting to AWS service events, content-based routing, SaaS integrations, cross-account event sharing, schedules, and architectures where you want replay and discoverable schemas.
SNS: very high fan-out volume with low latency, direct delivery to SMS, email and mobile push, and the classic SNS-to-SQS fan-out pattern with FIFO ordering where needed.
Quotas and latency: they differ in throughput limits, targets per rule and delivery latency; check current quotas rather than assuming, and load test if volume is high.
Together: a common design is EventBridge for routing and SNS or SQS as targets for downstream fan-out.
Ordering and dedupe: EventBridge does not offer FIFO ordering semantics; if you need strict order per key, route to an SQS FIFO queue or use SNS FIFO.

steps.title: Production practice
steps.description: Operate the bus like an API.
items: Contracts: version detail-type or add a version field, and avoid breaking changes to detail shape.
Failure handling: configure retry policy and target DLQs, and alarm on FailedInvocations and DLQ depth.
Least privilege: restrict who can PutEvents to a bus with resource policies, especially for cross-account access.
Observability: use CloudWatch metrics per rule and consider X-Ray or correlation IDs in the event detail.
IaC: define buses, rules and targets in Terraform or CloudFormation so patterns are reviewed in pull requests.
Cross-account pattern: a central bus in a platform account with rules forwarding to team buses keeps ownership clear.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Pick EventBridge when you need content-based rules, AWS service events or replay, and keep SNS for lightweight fan-out and notification endpoints; always add a DLQ to each target.
elevatorPitch: EventBridge is a serverless event bus with content-based rules, schemas, archive and replay; SNS is a fast pub/sub topic for simple fan-out and notifications.
I validate patterns with test-event-pattern, send a put-events test and check target metrics and DLQs.
I define buses and rules in IaC, version event contracts, and use replay for recovery with idempotent consumers.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating EventBridge as a drop-in SNS replacement for high-volume fan-out
mistakesToAvoid.why: Quotas, latency and delivery endpoints differ; SNS is better for simple massive fan-out and SMS or email.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Skipping target DLQs and retry policies
mistakesToAvoid.why: Events that exhaust retries are dropped without a trace.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Replaying archived events into non-idempotent consumers
mistakesToAvoid.why: Replays re-trigger side effects such as emails or charges.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Writing patterns without testing them
mistakesToAvoid.why: A subtle mismatch means events silently match nothing; use test-event-pattern.
