title: AWS Q89: How do you implement infrastructure drift detection [L3]
summary: To implement infrastructure drift detection, run an automated comparison between declared state (Terraform, CloudFormation) and real resources on a schedule, alert on any difference, and route each finding to a decision: revert.
question: How do you implement infrastructure drift detection?
intro: To implement infrastructure drift detection, run an automated comparison between declared state (Terraform, CloudFormation) and real resources on a schedule, alert on any difference, and route each finding to a decision: revert the change or codify it. Drift happens when someone changes a resource in the console or with a script, or when an external system mutates it. Interviewers ask this at senior level because detection is easy to demo but hard to operationalize: you need scheduling, noise control, ownership and prevention, so that drift becomes an exception rather than a monthly clean-up.

steps.title: Define drift and choose detectors per layer
steps.description: Different tools see different kinds of change.
items: Terraform: terraform plan refreshes state against the provider and shows differences from configuration. Use -refresh-only to see out-of-band changes without proposing config changes.
CloudFormation: built-in stack drift detection compares actual properties with the template for supported resource types; not every type is supported, so check the docs.
AWS Config: records configuration changes over time and evaluates compliance rules, giving a timeline of who changed what and a drift-like signal for rule violations.
Event-driven: CloudTrail plus EventBridge can alert in near real time on console or CLI write calls by humans.
Layered answer: no single tool sees everything, so combine a scheduled IaC diff for declared resources with Config and CloudTrail for resources and actors outside the code.
Scope first: list which accounts, environments and state files are in scope; unmanaged accounts cannot be checked by a plan job.

steps.title: Hands-on: infrastructure drift detection with Terraform in CI
steps.description: Schedule a plan and use its exit code as the signal.
items: Exit codes: with -detailed-exitcode, 0 means no changes, 1 means error, 2 means changes present (drift or unapplied code).
Read-only credentials: the drift job needs only read access plus state read; do not give it apply rights.
Separate real drift from pending code: run against the default branch so any diff means drift, not unmerged work.
Ignore noise deliberately: use lifecycle { ignore_changes = [...] } for attributes legitimately managed elsewhere, such as autoscaling desired capacity.
State access: the drift role needs read access to the remote state bucket and lock table; grant nothing broader.
Matrix by workspace: use a job matrix over each root module or workspace so one noisy stack does not hide others.
steps.codeBlock:
name: drift-detection
on:
  schedule: [{cron: "0 6 * * *"}]
  workflow_dispatch: {}
permissions: {id-token: write, contents: read}
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with: {role-to-assume: "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/tf-drift-readonly", aws-region: us-east-1}
      - run: terraform init -input=false
      - id: plan
        run: |
          set +e
          terraform plan -refresh-only -detailed-exitcode -input=false -no-color | tee plan.txt
          echo "code=${PIPESTATUS[0]}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - if: steps.plan.outputs.code == '2'
        run: echo "Drift detected" && exit 1   # replace with Slack/ticket notification

steps.title: Hands-on: CloudFormation drift detection
steps.description: Start detection, poll it, then list differing resources.
items: Start: detection is asynchronous and returns a detection ID.
Review: filter resource drifts to MODIFIED and DELETED and read the property differences.
Schedule: trigger it from EventBridge Scheduler and a Lambda, or a CI job, and publish results to your alert channel.
Limits: it covers properties the template defines; changes to properties not specified in the template may not be reported.
Consolidate output: post a summary listing stack, resource logical IDs and the property differences so reviewers need not open the console.
steps.codeBlock:
ID=$(aws cloudformation detect-stack-drift --stack-name my-stack --query StackDriftDetectionId --output text)
aws cloudformation describe-stack-drift-detection-status --stack-drift-detection-id "$ID" \
  --query '[DetectionStatus,StackDriftStatus]'

aws cloudformation describe-stack-resource-drifts --stack-name my-stack \
  --stack-resource-drift-status-filters MODIFIED DELETED \
  --query 'StackResourceDrifts[].[LogicalResourceId,StackResourceDriftStatus,PropertyDifferences]'

steps.title: Triage and remediation: revert or codify
steps.description: Every finding needs an owner and a decision.
items: Revert: if the manual change was wrong or an incident hot-fix that is over, run terraform apply (or update the stack) to restore declared state.
Codify: if the change should stay, update the code to match; for resources created outside IaC use Terraform 1.5+ import blocks and terraform plan -generate-config-out as a starting point.
Accept and ignore: document attributes that are expected to differ and ignore them in code.
Track: open a ticket or message in a channel with the plan summary, resource addresses and the CloudTrail principal who made the change.
Hot-fix etiquette: during incidents, allow break-glass changes, but require a follow-up pull request within an agreed period so drift is reconciled, not forgotten.

steps.title: Prevention and guardrails
steps.description: Reduce drift at the source.
items: Least privilege: give humans read-only production access; make changes through pipelines with a break-glass role that is audited.
SCPs and Config rules: deny or flag high-risk manual changes such as opening security groups to the world.
Real-time alerts: EventBridge rule on CloudTrail write events from non-pipeline principals.
Measure: track drift count and time-to-resolve as team metrics.
Avoid abandoned tools: prefer maintained mechanisms such as the scheduled plan above; community tools like driftctl are no longer actively developed.
Tags for ownership: tag resources with a team and repo so alerts route to the right people automatically.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Run a daily read-only terraform plan -refresh-only -detailed-exitcode on the default branch and treat exit code 2 as an alert with a named owner.
elevatorPitch: Drift is when real infrastructure differs from the declared IaC state, usually from manual changes.
I detect it with a scheduled terraform plan using detailed exit codes, CloudFormation drift detection and AWS Config, plus CloudTrail alerts.
I triage each finding as revert or codify, use import blocks for adoption, and prevent drift with read-only access and SCPs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running drift checks from a feature branch
mistakesToAvoid.why: Unmerged changes appear as differences and drown real drift in noise.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Giving the drift job apply permissions
mistakesToAvoid.why: A detection job should be read-only; auto-applying hides unreviewed changes and risks outages.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Detecting drift without an owner or SLA
mistakesToAvoid.why: Alerts get ignored and the backlog grows until nobody trusts the report.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming CloudFormation drift covers every resource and property
mistakesToAvoid.why: Unsupported resource types and unspecified properties are not reported.

title: AWS Q91: What is Amazon Inspector and when would you use it [L2]
summary: Amazon Inspector is AWS's managed vulnerability management service: it continuously scans EC2 instances, container images in ECR and Lambda functions for known software vulnerabilities (CVEs) and unintended network exposure, and.
question: What is Amazon Inspector and when would you use it?
intro: Amazon Inspector is AWS's managed vulnerability management service: it continuously scans EC2 instances, container images in ECR and Lambda functions for known software vulnerabilities (CVEs) and unintended network exposure, and produces prioritized findings. You use it when you need always-on, automated coverage of workloads against known CVEs without running your own scanners. Interviewers ask about it to check you understand the security tooling landscape: Inspector finds vulnerable packages, while GuardDuty detects threats, Config tracks configuration and Security Hub aggregates findings. A good answer covers setup, how scanning works, triage and where it fits in CI and operations.

steps.title: What Inspector scans and how
steps.description: Inspector (the current generation, often called Inspector v2) is continuous and event-driven.
items: EC2: uses the SSM Agent to inventory installed packages and compares them to a vulnerability database; instances must be SSM managed. An agentless option scans EBS snapshots for instances without SSM. It also reports network reachability findings.
ECR images: scans on push and re-scans continuously when new CVEs are published, once enhanced scanning is enabled for the registry.
Lambda: scans function dependencies, and with Lambda code scanning can also flag code-level issues in your own function code.

Output: findings with a severity and an Inspector score that adjusts for context, with exploit information included, sent to the console, EventBridge and Security Hub, plus SBOM export for supported resources.
When to use it: any account running EC2, containers in ECR or Lambda where compliance (patching SLAs, audit evidence) or security hygiene needs continuous, centralized CVE visibility.

steps.title: Hands-on: enable Amazon Inspector and read findings
steps.description: Turn it on for the resource types you run, then query findings.
items: Enable per account and region: scanning is regional, so enable in every region you use.
Organizations: designate a delegated administrator to enable Inspector for all member accounts and see findings centrally.
Coverage check: list-coverage shows which instances, repositories and functions are actually scanned and why others are not.
Filter findings: narrow to critical, fixable and in-use vulnerabilities first.
Scan latency: new resources are typically discovered automatically, but allow time for the first scan; do not assume instant results in the first minutes.
steps.codeBlock:
aws inspector2 enable --resource-types EC2 ECR LAMBDA --account-ids 111122223333
aws inspector2 batch-get-account-status --account-ids 111122223333

aws inspector2 list-coverage \
  --filter-criteria '{"resourceType":[{"comparison":"EQUALS","value":"AWS_EC2_INSTANCE"}]}' \
  --query 'coveredResources[].[resourceId,scanStatus.statusCode,scanStatus.reason]'

aws inspector2 list-findings \
  --filter-criteria '{"severity":[{"comparison":"EQUALS","value":"CRITICAL"}],"fixAvailable":[{"comparison":"EQUALS","value":"YES"}]}' \
  --query 'findings[].[title,resources[0].id,inspectorScore]' --output table

steps.title: Containers: enhanced scanning and CI
steps.description: Move detection left and keep images watched after release.
items: Registry setting: switch ECR from basic to enhanced scanning to use Inspector; choose scan-on-push and continuous scan filters per repository.
Pipeline gate: after pushing an image, query findings for that repository and fail the pipeline on critical fixable CVEs; Inspector also offers a CI/CD scanning integration for build systems.
Continuous value: an image that was clean at build time gets findings later when a new CVE is disclosed, which one-off scanners miss.
Remediate: rebuild on an updated base image and redeploy; patch EC2 through Systems Manager Patch Manager.
What it cannot see: findings reflect packages Inspector can inventory; custom-compiled or vendored binaries may be missed, so pair with SBOM and software composition analysis in CI.
steps.codeBlock:
aws ecr put-registry-scanning-configuration --scan-type ENHANCED \
  --rules '[{"scanFrequency":"CONTINUOUS_SCAN","repositoryFilters":[{"filter":"*","filterType":"WILDCARD"}]}]'

# Fail a pipeline step if critical fixable findings exist for one repo
COUNT=$(aws inspector2 list-findings --filter-criteria \
  '{"ecrImageRepositoryName":[{"comparison":"EQUALS","value":"my-app"}],"severity":[{"comparison":"EQUALS","value":"CRITICAL"}],"fixAvailable":[{"comparison":"EQUALS","value":"YES"}]}' \
  --query 'length(findings)')
[ "$COUNT" -eq 0 ] || { echo "Critical fixable CVEs: $COUNT"; exit 1; }

steps.title: Inspector vs GuardDuty, Config and Security Hub
steps.description: Knowing what it does not do is part of the answer.
items: Inspector: finds vulnerable software and exposure before an attacker exploits it.
GuardDuty: detects suspicious activity and threats, such as credential misuse or malware communication, in logs and runtime.
AWS Config: records and evaluates resource configuration, for example an unencrypted volume or public bucket; Inspector does not audit those settings.
Security Hub: aggregates findings from all of these into one view and supports automated response.
Legacy: the older Inspector Classic with assessment runs and agents has been replaced by the current service.
Ownership: security owns enablement and policy, but service teams own remediation; align on severity-based SLAs.

steps.title: Operate it day to day
steps.description: Make findings actionable rather than noisy.
items: Prioritize: start with critical or high findings that have a fix available, are network reachable, or run in production.
Suppression rules: create filters with action SUPPRESS for accepted risks, with a documented reason and review date.
Automate response: route findings through EventBridge to tickets, chat or an SSM automation that patches instances.
Track SLAs: measure time-to-remediate by severity and report coverage gaps, such as instances without a working SSM Agent.
Cost awareness: pricing is based on scanned resources; check current pricing before enabling everywhere and use the free trial to estimate.
Evidence for audits: export findings and SBOMs to S3 on a schedule to show continuous coverage.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: After enabling Inspector, run list-coverage first; unmanaged EC2 instances without SSM Agent are the silent blind spot, and filter findings to critical plus fixable before anything else.
elevatorPitch: Amazon Inspector is a continuous vulnerability scanner for EC2, ECR images and Lambda that reports CVEs and network exposure with prioritized scores.
I verify coverage with list-coverage and review findings filtered by severity and fix availability.
I automate enablement through Organizations, gate pipelines on critical fixable findings, and route findings to Security Hub and EventBridge for remediation.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming Inspector scans every EC2 instance by default
mistakesToAvoid.why: Instances need SSM management (or agentless eligibility), so unmanaged ones go unscanned; check coverage.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting it to catch misconfigurations or active threats
mistakesToAvoid.why: That is the role of AWS Config and GuardDuty; Inspector focuses on vulnerabilities and exposure.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Leaving ECR on basic scanning
mistakesToAvoid.why: Basic scanning does not provide the continuous, Inspector-powered re-scan when new CVEs appear.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Enabling it in one region only
mistakesToAvoid.why: Inspector is regional; workloads elsewhere are not covered.

steps.description: Historically, in S3, the AWS account that uploads the object retains explicit ownership and full control of that object, even if the bucket itself belongs to a different account. title: AWS Q118: A fleet of 5000 Lambda functions in a private VPC aggressively scrape data from the public internet Randomly hundreds of them begin crashing with bizarre Connection Timed Out networking errors despite the internet destination being perfectly healthy What AWS bottleneck is occurring [L3]
summary: This is classic SNAT (Source Network Address Translation) Port Exhaustion on the NAT Gateway.
question: A fleet of 5,000 Lambda functions in a private VPC aggressively scrape data from the public internet. Randomly, hundreds of them begin crashing with bizarre `Connection Timed Out` networking errors, despite the internet destination being perfectly healthy. What AWS bottleneck is occurring?
intro: "When an interviewer asks how I troubleshoot this in AWS, I frame it through my hands-on production experience. The interviewer is testing: NAT Gateway SNAT Port Exhaustion.. I structure my answer around systematic triage first, root cause analysis second, and permanent remediation third."

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: This is classic SNAT (Source Network Address Translation) Port Exhaustion on the NAT Gateway. A single AWS NAT Gateway utilizes a single public Elastic IP. TCP allows a theoretical maximum of ~65,000 ephemeral outbound ports per IP addressing a single destination. When 5,000 highly concurrent Lambda functions open thousands of individual API connections to the exact same external internet API simultaneously, the NAT Gateway completely runs out of ephemeral routing ports. It violently drops any new outbound connection attempts until old ones close. *Fix:* Heavily deploy multiple NAT Gateways across multiple public subnets and route traffic dynamically to distribute the SNAT allocation, or deploy dedicated NAT instances.

steps.description: Legacy Redshift nodes (like DC2/DS2) tightly coupled Compute and Storage physically onto the single instance. title: CI/CD Q26: How do you enforce code coverage requirements in your CI pipeline [L2]
summary: Enforce code coverage requirements in your CI pipeline using pull request diff gates, automated threshold checks, and branch protection rules.
question: How do you enforce code coverage requirements in your CI pipeline?
intro: Enforcing code coverage requirements in your CI pipeline ensures that new software changes do not silently erode test suite quality. Rather than relying on rigid overall percentages that penalize legacy codebases, production engineering teams implement pull request diff coverage gates alongside baseline thresholds. This approach mandates that all newly authored or modified lines meet defined testing standards before automated branch protections permit merging.

steps.title: Enforce Code Coverage Requirements in CI via Quality Gates
steps.description: A key distinction in CI pipelines is differentiating between repository-wide code coverage and pull request diff coverage.
items: Global threshold gates: Evaluates the entire project (e.g. minimum 80% total statements). While simple, this can block critical hotfixes in legacy repositories with historical technical debt.
Diff coverage (patch coverage): Evaluates only lines altered in the active pull request. Legacy code is grandfathered in, while new features must maintain 85% to 90% coverage.
Branch protections: Combine automated CI test runs with GitHub or GitLab status checks, preventing pull requests from merging when code coverage checks fail.

steps.title: Generate coverage reports and enforce CLI gates in CI runners
steps.description: Configure unit test runners to generate machine-readable coverage reports (LCOV, Cobertura, or XML) and exit with a non-zero code if thresholds are breached.
steps.codeBlock:
# Python: Fail if overall coverage drops below 80%
pytest --cov=src --cov-report=xml --cov-report=term --cov-fail-under=80 tests/

# Node.js (Jest): Enforce global line and branch thresholds
npx jest --coverage --coverageReporters="text" "cobertura"

# Go: Generate profile and parse coverage percentage
go test -race -coverprofile=coverage.out -covermode=atomic ./...
go tool cover -func=coverage.out | grep total | awk '{print $3}'
items: pytest-cov: Uses --cov-fail-under=80 to immediately fail the step in CI runners if coverage falls below the threshold.
Jest config: Define coverageThreshold: { global: { branches: 75, functions: 80, lines: 80, statements: 80 } } inside jest.config.js.
Go coverage: Use go tool cover to inspect statements and automate custom bash gates against coverage.out.

steps.title: Integrate automated PR status checks and branch protection rules
steps.description: Upload test artifacts to code quality platforms (such as Codecov, Coveralls, or SonarQube) that report patch coverage back to pull requests as blocking commit statuses.
steps.codeBlock:
# GitHub Actions workflow snippet
- name: Run Unit Tests with Coverage
  run: pytest --cov=app --cov-report=xml:coverage.xml tests/

- name: Upload coverage report to Codecov
  uses: codecov/codecov-action@v4
  with:
    file: ./coverage.xml
    fail_ci_if_error: true
    token: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}
items: Automated PR commenting: The coverage service posts a dynamic summary table highlighting exactly which modified lines lack unit tests.
Strict status checks: Configure GitHub branch protection rules to require passing status checks from codecov/patch before the merge button becomes active.
Informational vs blocking: Keep global project coverage as an advisory comment while making pull request patch coverage strictly required.

steps.title: Common failure modes: Mock abuse, test gaming, and brittle thresholds
steps.description: Enforcing numbers without code review discipline creates perverse incentives where developers game metrics instead of verifying logic.
items: Assertion-free testing: Executing code paths without asserting return values achieves 100% line coverage while catching zero regressions. Pair coverage tools with static analysis or mutation testing.
Over-mocking external boundaries: Mocking out database drivers, third-party APIs, and message brokers inflates coverage without validating real failure handling.
Fragile threshold drops: Deleting dead code can paradoxically cause total coverage percentage to decline if the deleted code had high coverage. Diff coverage eliminates this paradox.

steps.title: Production best practices: Path exclusions and phased rollout
steps.description: Establish sustainable test coverage requirements by scoping enforcement to core business logic and excluding auto-generated assets.
items: Exclude non-business code: Exclude migrations, auto-generated protobuf/gRPC files, mock fixtures, and build configurations in .coveragerc or codecov.yml.
Ratchet mechanism: Automatically raise the global coverage baseline whenever new milestones are achieved, preventing downward regression.
Emergency bypass policy: Maintain a documented emergency override path for production P1 hotfixes using administrative approvals or repository bypass tags.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Enforce diff coverage on pull requests rather than rigid global repository percentages to prevent blocking critical hotfixes in legacy code.
elevatorPitch: Enforce patch coverage on pull requests to ensure all new code is tested without penalizing legacy debt.
Generate standardized XML/LCOV reports in CI and connect them to blocking branch protection status checks.
Pair automated coverage thresholds with code review to verify test assertions rather than superficial line execution.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Focusing exclusively on global line coverage instead of pull request patch coverage
mistakesToAvoid.why: Global repository percentages penalize developers touching untested legacy modules and incentivize avoiding necessary refactoring.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating line execution as proof of correct validation without requiring assertions
mistakesToAvoid.why: Tests that execute functions without asserting edge case returns provide false confidence while passing CI coverage gates.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to exclude auto-generated files, protobufs, and database migrations from coverage calculations

title: CI/CD Pipeline for Database Migration: Zero-Downtime Schema Changes, Flyway & Rollback Strategies
summary: Engineering zero-downtime database migrations inside automated CI/CD pipelines using Flyway/Liquibase, Kubernetes PreSync Jobs, the Expand-Contract schema pattern, and backward-compatible DDL.
question: How do you design an automated CI/CD pipeline for database migration without downtime or data corruption? Walk me through tool selection, expand-contract patterns, and safe rollback strategies.
intro: "During a high-stakes release, we hit a similar deployment challenge and resolved it with automated safeguards. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

steps.title: Decouple Migration from Application Startup (Never Use Init Containers)
steps.description: Running migrations inside app init containers creates severe race conditions when multiple replicas spin up simultaneously and causes slow pod startups:
items: Dedicated Pipeline Stage: Execute database migrations in a dedicated CD pipeline step (or ArgoCD PreSync Hook Job) strictly before deploying new application pods.
Advisory Locking: Ensure migration engines like Flyway or Liquibase acquire distributed database locks to guarantee single-execution idempotency.
Ephemeral Runner / K8s Job: Run the migration container using dedicated database service credentials with DDL permissions, isolating application runtime credentials (which only need DML).

steps.title: The Expand-Contract (Parallel Run) Schema Pattern
steps.description: Never introduce breaking schema changes in a single release. Follow three backward-compatible phases:
items: Phase 1 (Expand): Add the new column as nullable or with defaults. Deploy Application v2 which writes to both old and new columns, but reads from the old column.
Phase 2 (Backfill): Run an asynchronous background batch job to backfill existing historical rows without locking active transactional tables.
Phase 3 (Contract): Switch Application v2.1 to read and write exclusively to the new column. Once verified stable, drop the legacy column in a subsequent release.

steps.title: Zero-Data-Loss Rollback & Shadow Testing
steps.description: In CI/CD, rolling back application code must not crash because of forward database changes:
items: Backward Compatibility Testing: In staging CI, run the new migration, then run automated regression tests against the previous version of the application code to guarantee non-breaking compatibility.
Non-Destructive DDL: Prohibit table drops or column renames in forward migrations; deprecate fields first before removing them.
Pre-Migration Snapshots: For critical stateful databases, trigger automated storage snapshots (e.g. AWS RDS snapshot or Aurora volume restore point) prior to executing high-risk DDL.

keyTakeaway: Zero-downtime database migrations in CI/CD require decoupling migrations from container boot via dedicated PreSync jobs and enforcing the Expand-Contract pattern so application versions n and n-1 can concurrently query the database.
elevatorPitch: Decoupled migration execution into an isolated CI/CD step or ArgoCD PreSync Job rather than pod init containers.

Employed Flyway/Liquibase with advisory locking to ensure idempotent, serialized execution across environments.

title: CI/CD Q33: What is a build matrix in CI [L2]
summary: Run the same job with multiple combinations of parameters (OS, Python version, Node version). Useful for testing cross-compatibility.
question: What is a build matrix in CI?
intro: A build matrix in CI is a way to define one job template and have the CI system expand it into many parallel jobs, one for every combination of variables such as operating system, language version or database. It replaces copy-pasted jobs and proves your code works on every supported target. Interviewers ask about it to see if you can balance coverage against cost, handle failures sensibly, and avoid traps like unstable required status check names and cache collisions between matrix legs.

steps.title: Mental model: one template, many jobs
steps.description: The matrix is the cartesian product of the variables you list, minus exclusions, plus inclusions.
items: Expansion: Two operating systems and three Node versions produce six jobs. Each job gets its own runner, workspace and result.
Independence: Legs share nothing unless you pass artifacts or caches, which makes them safe to run in parallel.
Good fits: Library compatibility (Python 3.10 to 3.12), cross-OS builds, multiple Kubernetes versions for chart tests, or per-service builds in a monorepo.
Bad fits: Huge cartesian products. Ten versions across four OS and three databases is 120 jobs, so prune to the combinations users actually run.
Variables beyond version: A matrix can also carry feature flags, target architectures or cloud regions, and include lets one leg carry extra settings such as a coverage upload flag.
steps.highlight: Matrix size is a cost decision: every added dimension multiplies runner minutes.

steps.title: Hands-on: build matrix in GitHub Actions and GitLab CI
steps.description: Define the matrix once and reference its values with matrix.<name>.
items: GitHub Actions: Put strategy.matrix under the job and reference values as ${{ matrix.node }}.
Exclude and include: exclude removes unsupported pairs; include adds extra legs or extra variables for one combination.
fail-fast and max-parallel: fail-fast: false lets all legs finish so you see every failure; max-parallel caps concurrency to protect runner quotas.
GitLab CI: Use parallel: matrix: with lists of values; each combination becomes its own job.
Dynamic values: You can reference matrix values in names, environment variables and conditions, for example if: matrix.coverage to run an upload step on one leg only.
steps.codeBlock:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      max-parallel: 4
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
        node: [18, 20, 22]
        exclude:
          - os: windows-latest
            node: 18
        include:
          - os: ubuntu-latest
            node: 22
            coverage: true
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci && npm test

# .gitlab-ci.yml
test:
  image: python:$PY
  parallel:
    matrix:
      - PY: ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12"]
  script: [pip install -r requirements.txt, pytest]

steps.title: Verify the matrix expanded the way you intended
steps.description: Check job names, counts and cache behaviour before trusting green checks.
items: Count the legs: The Actions run page lists each combination in the job name, for example test (ubuntu-latest, 20); confirm excluded pairs are absent.
Print the context: Add a debug step that echoes matrix.os and the tool version so each leg proves what it ran on.
Cache keys: Include matrix values in cache keys, such as key: ${{ runner.os }}-node${{ matrix.node }}-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}, so legs do not restore incompatible dependencies.
Artifact names: In actions/upload-artifact@v4, artifact names must be unique per run, so append the matrix values to the name.
Summary visibility: Write a short job summary per leg with versions and timings so you can spot a slow leg that dominates total pipeline time.
steps.codeBlock:
# Aggregate gate job: use this single name as the required status check
  ci-ok:
    needs: [test]
    if: always()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: |
          if [ "${{ needs.test.result }}" != "success" ]; then
            echo "matrix failed: ${{ needs.test.result }}"; exit 1
          fi

# Per-leg cache key including matrix values
# key: ${{ runner.os }}-node${{ matrix.node }}-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}

steps.title: Failure modes and edge cases
steps.description: Matrices fail in subtle ways, mostly around gating and naming.
items: Required checks: Branch protection needs exact check names. If you rename or resize a matrix, required checks become pending forever. Use one aggregate job that depends on all legs.
Aggregate job pattern: A final job with needs: [test] and if: always() that fails when needs.test.result != 'success' gives branch protection a single stable name.
Flaky legs: With fail-fast: true one flaky leg cancels the others and hides real failures; for compatibility testing turn it off.
Experimental legs: Use continue-on-error: ${{ matrix.experimental }} for nightly or pre-release toolchains so they inform without blocking.

steps.title: Production practice: cost and signal
steps.description: Keep the matrix focused so the feedback loop stays fast.
items: Tiering: Run a minimal matrix on pull requests and the full matrix on merges or a nightly schedule.
Dynamic matrices: Generate JSON in a prior job (for example only changed services in a monorepo) and feed it with fromJSON(needs.plan.outputs.matrix).
Pin versions: Prefer explicit supported versions over latest so the matrix is reproducible; add a scheduled leg for the newest release to get early warning.
Reuse: Combine the matrix with reusable workflows so the matrix definition lives in one place across repos.
Review regularly: Drop end-of-life runtimes from the matrix when you stop supporting them, otherwise you pay for jobs that protect nothing.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Add one aggregate gate job that needs every matrix leg and use that single name as the required status check, so you can change the matrix without breaking branch protection.
elevatorPitch: A build matrix in CI expands one job definition into parallel jobs for each combination of variables like OS and runtime version.
I verify the expanded job names, include matrix values in cache keys and artifact names, and check excluded pairs are really gone.
I automate with tiered matrices, dynamic monorepo matrices and an aggregate gate job for branch protection.

mistakesToAvoid.why: One failing leg cancels the rest, so you only learn about one incompatibility at a time.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Renaming a version changes the check name and leaves pull requests blocked on a check that never reports.

title: CI/CD Q35: How do you implement zero-downtime deployments for a stateful service [L3]
summary: Zero-downtime deployments for a stateful service mean updating one replica at a time while the rest keep serving, so the data tier never loses quorum or the primary.
question: How do you implement zero-downtime deployments for a stateful service?
intro: Zero-downtime deployments for a stateful service mean updating one replica at a time while the rest keep serving, so the data tier never loses quorum or the primary. Unlike stateless apps you cannot just surge extra pods: each pod owns identity and data. The answer combines a StatefulSet rolling update, readiness that reflects replication health, a PodDisruptionBudget, graceful shutdown and backward-compatible schema changes. Interviewers ask to see whether you recognise that the data layer, not the container image, is the hard part.

steps.title: Mental model: why stateful is different
steps.description: A stateful pod has a stable identity, its own volume, and a role in a replication or consensus group.
items: Ordered updates: A StatefulSet with RollingUpdate updates pods in reverse ordinal order (db-2, then db-1, then db-0) and waits for each to be Ready before continuing.
No surge: There is no extra pod created during the update; capacity temporarily drops by one, so you need enough replicas to tolerate that.
Data attached: The PersistentVolumeClaim follows the pod name. Restarting is quick only if the volume reattaches quickly.
Roles matter: Updating a primary first causes a failover. A good rollout updates replicas, then switches over, then updates the old primary.
Client behaviour: Clients must retry or reconnect during a leader change. Connection poolers and driver retry settings are part of the zero-downtime story.
steps.highlight: Zero downtime depends on the application tier supporting at least N-1 availability, such as a 3-node quorum that stays healthy with one node down.

steps.title: Hands-on: zero-downtime deployments for a stateful service
steps.description: Configure the StatefulSet for controlled, canary-style updates.
items: Use partition for canary: updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.partition: N updates only pods with ordinal greater than or equal to N. Lower it step by step.
Readiness must be truthful: A pod should become Ready only after it has caught up with replication, not merely when the port opens.
Graceful shutdown: A preStop hook and terminationGracePeriodSeconds let the node flush, step down as leader or drain connections.
Protect quorum: A PodDisruptionBudget with maxUnavailable: 1 stops node drains from taking two replicas at once.
Services: Use a headless Service for stable pod DNS plus a separate read or write Service whose selector or endpoints follow the current primary.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata: {name: db, namespace: prod}
spec:
  replicas: 3
  serviceName: db
  podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      partition: 3          # hold all pods; lower to roll out
  template:
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120
      containers:
        - name: db
          image: registry.example.com/db:2.1.0
          readinessProbe:
            exec: {command: ["/bin/sh","-c","/opt/check-replication-lag.sh"]}
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec: {command: ["/bin/sh","-c","/opt/graceful-stepdown.sh"]}
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata: {name: db, namespace: prod}
spec:
  maxUnavailable: 1
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: db}}

steps.title: Roll out in stages and verify each step
steps.description: Lower the partition gradually and prove health between steps.
items: Canary one replica: Set partition to 2 so only db-2 updates; watch replication lag, errors and latency.
Continue: Set partition to 1, then 0. At each stage confirm kubectl rollout status statefulset/db completes.
Check the application: Query the cluster's own status (replication state, leader, quorum) rather than relying only on Kubernetes Ready.
Switch over deliberately: Before updating the current primary, trigger a controlled switchover with your database tooling or operator.
Pause points: Wait several minutes of steady metrics at each partition value before continuing, because replication problems often surface only under load.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl patch statefulset db -n prod --type merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"updateStrategy":{"rollingUpdate":{"partition":2}}}}'
kubectl rollout status statefulset/db -n prod
# validate replication, then continue
kubectl patch statefulset db -n prod --type merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"updateStrategy":{"rollingUpdate":{"partition":0}}}}'
kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=db -o wide

steps.title: Failure modes and edge cases
steps.description: Most outages here come from data compatibility and ordering, not Kubernetes.
items: Schema changes: Use expand and contract. Deploy additive changes first, then code that uses them, then remove old structures in a later release, so N and N-1 both work.
Stuck rollout: If a new pod never becomes Ready, a StatefulSet halts and does not roll back automatically; fix forward or revert the image and delete the broken pod.
RWO volume reattach delay: If a pod moves to another node, the volume must detach and attach first, which can add minutes during node failure.
Downgrade impossibility: Some storage formats cannot be read by older versions after upgrade, so take a backup or snapshot before the canary and test restore.
Split brain risk: If readiness is too lenient, a lagging replica can be promoted during failover and lose recent writes; tune probes and failover thresholds together.

steps.title: Production practice
steps.description: Automate the safety net and consider an operator.
items: Operators: Mature operators for databases handle switchover, version upgrades and backups, and encode the ordering that raw StatefulSets cannot.
Pre-flight checks: CI should run an upgrade test from the previous version on a staging cluster with real data volume.
Backups: Take a VolumeSnapshot or logical backup before each production upgrade and verify restores regularly.
Observability: Alert on replication lag, leader changes and under-replicated partitions during rollout windows.
Practice failure: Rehearse killing a replica mid-upgrade in staging so the team knows whether the system recovers on its own.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Treat the StatefulSet partition as a canary dial and gate every step on application-level health such as replication lag, not on pod Ready alone.
elevatorPitch: Zero downtime for a stateful service means updating one replica at a time while quorum and the primary stay available, using a StatefulSet rolling update, PDB and graceful shutdown.
I verify using replication lag, leader status and rollout status at every partition step, and I take a snapshot first.
I automate with operators, upgrade tests in CI and expand-and-contract migrations.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Updating the primary first
mistakesToAvoid.why: It forces an unplanned failover and write interruption; update replicas and switch over deliberately.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: A readiness probe that only checks the port
mistakesToAvoid.why: A pod that has not caught up with replication receives traffic and serves stale or missing data.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Skipping a PodDisruptionBudget
mistakesToAvoid.why: A node drain can evict two replicas at once and break quorum.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running a destructive migration in the same release
mistakesToAvoid.why: The previous version cannot read the new schema, which removes your ability to roll back.

title: CI/CD Q36: What is artifact management and why do you need it [L2]
summary: Artifact management is the practice of storing, versioning, securing and promoting the outputs of your build, such as container images, packages, Helm charts and binaries, in a dedicated repository instead of rebuilding them.
question: What is artifact management and why do you need it?
intro: Artifact management is the practice of storing, versioning, securing and promoting the outputs of your build, such as container images, packages, Helm charts and binaries, in a dedicated repository instead of rebuilding them. You need it so that what you tested is exactly what you deploy, so you can roll back to a known version, and so you can trace a running service back to a commit. Interviewers ask to confirm you understand build-once-promote-many, immutability and supply chain controls, not just where files are stored.

steps.title: Mental model: build once, store immutably, promote
steps.description: An artifact is a build output with an identity; a repository is its system of record.
items: Artifact types: Container images (registry), language packages (npm, PyPI, Maven), Helm charts (OCI registry), and installers or binaries.
Immutability: A version, once published, never changes. This is what makes deployments reproducible and rollbacks trustworthy.
Promotion, not rebuild: The same digest moves from dev to staging to prod by retagging or copying. Rebuilding for production means you ship something you never tested.
Metadata: Store commit SHA, build ID, SBOM and provenance with the artifact so it is traceable.
Why it matters: Without a repository, teams rebuild from source, pick up different dependency versions, and cannot prove which binary is in production during an audit or incident.
steps.highlight: CI artifacts (short-lived files passed between jobs) are different from release artifacts (long-lived, versioned, in a registry).

steps.title: Hands-on: artifact management with a registry
steps.description: Publish an immutable image, sign it, and promote it by digest.
items: Immutable tags: For ECR use aws ecr put-image-tag-mutability --image-tag-mutability IMMUTABLE.
Push with a unique tag: Tag with the commit SHA so every build has a distinct identity.
Sign: cosign sign --yes <image>@<digest> attaches a signature, with keyless signing available when your CI provides OIDC identity.
Promote: crane copy copies by digest between repositories without pulling to the runner.

Authentication: Log in with short-lived credentials, for example aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <registry>, rather than static passwords. Inspect what you published: docker buildx imagetools inspect <image>:<tag> prints the manifest digest and platforms, which is the value to record in deployment manifests.
steps.codeBlock:
aws ecr put-image-tag-mutability --repository-name my-app \
  --image-tag-mutability IMMUTABLE

docker build -t 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-app:${GIT_SHA} .
docker push 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-app:${GIT_SHA}

cosign sign --yes 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-app@sha256:<digest>

# Promote the same digest to a prod repository
crane copy 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-app@sha256:<digest> \
  123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-app-prod:1.4.2

steps.title: CI job artifacts versus release artifacts
steps.description: Use the right store for the right lifetime.
items: Job artifacts: actions/upload-artifact@v4 and GitLab artifacts: pass files between jobs and expire by retention settings. They are for test reports and intermediate builds.
Release artifacts: Push to a registry or package repository (ECR, GHCR, Artifactory, Nexus) with retention measured in releases, not days.
Caches: Dependency caches speed builds but are not artifacts; they can be evicted at any time and must never be a source of truth.
Retention policy: Keep every released version and the last N untagged builds; never delete an image that a cluster still references.

Naming: Include the run ID or commit SHA in job artifact names so parallel matrix jobs do not collide. Language packages: Proxy public registries like npm and PyPI through an internal repository so builds keep working during upstream outages and so you can block bad versions.
steps.codeBlock:
- uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  with:
    name: test-report-${{ github.run_id }}
    path: reports/
    retention-days: 14

steps.title: Failure modes and edge cases
steps.description: Problems appear when artifacts are mutable, unscanned or pruned too early.
items: Mutable tags: Overwriting latest or a version tag makes two nodes run different code under the same name.
Over-aggressive cleanup: Lifecycle rules that delete by age can remove the image you need for rollback. Exempt tags matching release patterns.
Registry as single point of failure: A registry outage blocks scale-up and deploys; consider pull-through caches or replication.
Credentials sprawl: Long-lived registry passwords in CI leak easily; use OIDC and short-lived tokens.
Compliance: Retain release artifacts for as long as audit rules require, and document where they live and who can delete them.

steps.title: Production practice: provenance and security
steps.description: Make artifacts verifiable.
items: SBOM and provenance: Generate an SBOM and build attestations in CI and attach them to the image so audits can see contents.
Scan on publish and on schedule: New vulnerabilities appear after release, so rescan stored images regularly.
Admission policy: Enforce signature verification in the cluster (for example with Kyverno or Sigstore policy controller).
Access control: CI gets push rights; clusters get pull-only roles; humans rarely get either.

Lifecycle policies: In ECR, aws ecr put-lifecycle-policy with a JSON policy can expire untagged images while keeping tagged release images; test the policy preview before applying. Disaster recovery: Replicate critical repositories to a second region or registry and test pulling from it, so a regional outage does not stop deployments.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Promote by digest between environments and enforce immutable tags, so the artifact in production is provably the bytes that passed your tests.
elevatorPitch: Artifact management stores, versions, secures and promotes build outputs in a repository so you deploy exactly what you tested.
I verify by digest, signature and SBOM, and I trace each running image back to a commit.
I automate immutable tags, signing in CI, retention policies that protect released versions, and cluster-side signature enforcement.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Rebuilding the image for production
mistakesToAvoid.why: The production image differs from the tested one, which breaks the guarantee of testing.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using mutable latest as a deploy reference
mistakesToAvoid.why: You cannot tell what is running or roll back to what ran yesterday.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Retention policy that prunes by age only
mistakesToAvoid.why: It can delete a release image still referenced by a cluster, causing ImagePullBackOff on scale-up.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating the dependency cache as storage
mistakesToAvoid.why: Caches can be evicted anytime, so builds become non-reproducible.

title: CI/CD Q37: How do you trigger a pipeline only when a tag is pushed [L2]
summary: GitHub Actions: on: push: tags: ['v']. GitLab: rules: - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG.
question: How do you trigger a pipeline only when a tag is pushed?
intro: To trigger a pipeline only when a tag is pushed, filter on tag refs: in GitHub Actions use on.push.tags, in GitLab CI use rules: - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG, and in Jenkins use when { buildingTag() }. Release automation depends on this, because a tag is an immutable marker of a version. Interviewers ask to test whether you know the syntax and the gotchas: glob versus regex patterns, tags created by the default token not triggering workflows, and ensuring a tag came from a protected branch.

steps.title: Mental model: a tag push is its own event
steps.description: A tag is a ref under refs/tags/, so CI systems can distinguish it from a branch push.
items: Event types: Pushing a commit to a branch and pushing a tag are separate push events with different refs.
Pattern language: GitHub uses glob patterns such as v*.*.*, not full regex; GitLab can use regex with $CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/.
Intent: Tag pipelines are typically release pipelines: build, sign, publish artifacts, create a release.
Separation: Keep normal branch CI on branch events and put publishing only in the tag workflow.
Annotated versus lightweight: Annotated tags (git tag -a) store an author, date and message, which is useful for release notes; both kinds trigger tag pipelines.

steps.title: Hands-on: trigger a pipeline only when a tag is pushed
steps.description: Configuration for GitHub Actions, GitLab CI and Jenkins.
items: GitHub Actions: Specify tags under push and no branches so only tag pushes run.
GitLab CI: Use rules with $CI_COMMIT_TAG; the variable is only set for tag pipelines.
Jenkins: In a multibranch pipeline enable tag discovery and add when { buildingTag() } or tag pattern: 'v*', comparator: 'GLOB'.
Create the tag: Use an annotated tag and push it explicitly.
Shallow clones: Tag pipelines may need full history for changelogs. Set fetch-depth: 0 in actions/checkout@v4 when you generate release notes.
steps.codeBlock:
# GitHub Actions
on:
  push:
    tags:
      - 'v[0-9]+.[0-9]+.[0-9]+'
    # no 'branches:' key, so branch pushes do not trigger this workflow

# GitLab CI
release:
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/'
  script: ./release.sh

# Jenkinsfile (declarative)
# stage('Release') {
#   when { buildingTag() }
#   steps { sh './release.sh' }
# }

git tag -a v1.4.2 -m "Release 1.4.2"
git push origin v1.4.2

steps.title: Verify only tags trigger it
steps.description: Prove both the positive and negative cases.
items: Positive test: Push v1.4.2 and confirm a run appears with the ref refs/tags/v1.4.2; in GitHub use gh run list --workflow release.yml.
Negative test: Push a commit to main and a tag like test-1; neither should start the release workflow.
Inspect context: Print github.ref_name or $CI_COMMIT_TAG in the first step so logs show which tag fired it.
Boundary cases: Confirm v1.10.0 matches, and decide deliberately whether pre-releases such as v1.4.2-rc1 should trigger the release workflow or a separate one.
Deleting tags: Deleting a tag does not cancel a running pipeline; cancel the run manually if the tag was pushed by mistake.
steps.codeBlock:
gh run list --workflow release.yml --limit 5
git ls-remote --tags origin | tail -3

steps.title: Failure modes and gotchas
steps.description: Most surprises are about who pushes the tag and where it points.
items: Default token does not trigger: A tag pushed using GITHUB_TOKEN inside a workflow will not start another workflow. Use a GitHub App token or a dedicated PAT, or call the release workflow with workflow_call.
Tag on the wrong commit: Anyone with write access can tag any commit. Verify in the pipeline that the tagged commit is reachable from main using git merge-base --is-ancestor.
Branch and tag both match: If a workflow lists both branches and tags, either event triggers it; omit branches if you want tags only.
Moving tags: Force-pushing a tag re-triggers or confuses releases. Treat release tags as immutable and protect them.
Duplicate runs: If a tag is pushed with a branch in the same git push, both events fire; keep release logic in the tag-only workflow and keep tests in the branch workflow.

steps.title: Production practice
steps.description: Make tag-driven releases safe and repeatable.
items: Protected tags: Use tag protection or repository rulesets so only maintainers can create v* tags.
Derive versions from the tag: Set the image tag and chart version from the tag name so there is no second source of truth.
Environment approvals: Gate production deployment with environment protection rules even though the tag triggered the build.
Automate tagging: Tools like release-please or semantic-release create the tag after merging, which removes manual mistakes.

Idempotent publishing: Make release steps safe to re-run, for example by skipping a push when the image tag already exists, because tag pipelines are retried after transient failures. Audit trail: Create a GitHub or GitLab release from the tag with generated notes so each version links to the commits, pipeline run and artifacts.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Verify inside the pipeline that the tagged commit is an ancestor of main, because a tag filter alone cannot tell you whether the code was reviewed.
elevatorPitch: To trigger only on tags, filter on tag refs: on.push.tags in GitHub Actions, rules with CI_COMMIT_TAG in GitLab, buildingTag in Jenkins.
I test the positive case with a real tag and the negative case with branch pushes and non-matching tags.
I automate tagging with release tooling, protect the tag namespace and derive versions from the tag.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Listing both branches and tags in the trigger
mistakesToAvoid.why: Either event starts the workflow, so release steps run on ordinary pushes.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Creating the tag with GITHUB_TOKEN and expecting a run
mistakesToAvoid.why: Events caused by the default token do not start new workflows.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using full regex syntax in a GitHub tag filter
mistakesToAvoid.why: GitHub filters use glob-style patterns, so constructs like \d are not understood and the workflow never fires.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Allowing anyone to push release tags
mistakesToAvoid.why: A tag on an unreviewed commit publishes unreviewed code.

title: CI/CD Q40: Your Docker push to ECR fails in CI no basic auth credentials [L2]
summary: When a Docker push to ECR fails with no basic auth credentials, the Docker client has no valid credential stored for that exact registry hostname.
question: Your Docker push to ECR fails in CI: `no basic auth credentials`.
intro: When a Docker push to ECR fails with no basic auth credentials, the Docker client has no valid credential stored for that exact registry hostname. Nearly always the fix is to run aws ecr get-login-password piped into docker login for the right account and region in the same job and user context that runs the push. Interviewers use this scenario to test whether you debug methodically: identity, region, credential store, token lifetime and IAM permissions, instead of retrying the pipeline and hoping.

steps.title: Symptom and mental model
steps.description: The error comes from the Docker client before AWS permission checks, so it is about credentials being absent, not about IAM denial.
items: Typical output: no basic auth credentials on docker push, often right after the build succeeded. A permissions problem usually shows denied or not authorized instead.
How ECR auth works: ECR does not use your AWS keys directly. ecr get-login-password returns a temporary token (valid for 12 hours) that you give to Docker as the password for user AWS.
Registry host is the key: Credentials are stored per hostname such as 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com. A login for another account or region does not apply.
Order of checks: Who am I, which registry, did I log in, where were credentials stored, does the role have push rights, does the repository exist.
Quick triage question: Did this ever work on this runner? If yes, suspect token expiry or a changed environment; if never, suspect a missing login step.

steps.title: Hands-on: fix the Docker push to ECR login
steps.description: Verify identity first, then log in explicitly with AWS CLI v2.
items: Confirm identity: aws sts get-caller-identity shows the account and role the job is using; the account must match the registry hostname.
Log in: Pipe the password to docker login --password-stdin so it never appears in process lists.
Match region: Use the region of the repository in both --region and the registry host.
Retry the push: Tag with the full registry path and push.
Windows and Mac helpers: Desktop installs may use credential helpers such as osxkeychain or wincred, which behave differently from the plain auths file on Linux runners.
steps.codeBlock:
aws sts get-caller-identity

REGION=us-east-1
ACCOUNT=123456789012
REGISTRY=${ACCOUNT}.dkr.ecr.${REGION}.amazonaws.com

aws ecr get-login-password --region $REGION \
  | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $REGISTRY
# Login Succeeded

docker tag my-app:1.4.2 $REGISTRY/my-app:1.4.2
docker push $REGISTRY/my-app:1.4.2

steps.title: Ordered diagnostic checks when login looks correct but push still fails
steps.description: Walk the list from the most common cause to the least.
items: Login in a different context: The credential file belongs to a user. A login as one user and a push through sudo docker, a different Jenkins agent or another container will not share credentials. Check ~/.docker/config.json for the registry under auths or a credsStore or credHelpers entry.
Custom DOCKER_CONFIG: If the pipeline sets DOCKER_CONFIG to a temp directory, login and push must use the same one.
Wrong registry string: The image tag must start with the exact host used in login. A typo, a different region or a different account gives this same error.
Token expired: A cached login from a long-lived runner is older than 12 hours. Always log in at the start of the job.
Buildx or docker-in-docker: A build that pushes from a separate builder container needs credentials available to that builder, and a DinD service has its own empty config.
steps.codeBlock:
cat ~/.docker/config.json | jq '.auths | keys, .credsStore, .credHelpers'
echo "$DOCKER_CONFIG"
docker info | grep -i -A2 registry
docker buildx ls

steps.title: Permissions, repository and public ECR edge cases
steps.description: After authentication works, the next layer is IAM and repository settings.
items: Required IAM actions: ecr:GetAuthorizationToken (resource *) plus push actions on the repository: BatchCheckLayerAvailability, InitiateLayerUpload, UploadLayerPart, CompleteLayerUpload and PutImage.
Repository must exist: ECR does not create repositories on push; you will see a repository-does-not-exist error. Create it with aws ecr create-repository.
Immutable tags: Pushing an existing tag to an immutable repository fails with a tag-invalid error, which is different from the auth failure.
ECR Public: It uses aws ecr-public get-login-password --region us-east-1 and the host public.ecr.aws, and the API is only in us-east-1.
Cross-account pushes: Pushing to another account's repository needs a repository policy there allowing your principal, in addition to your own IAM policy.

steps.title: Prevention: keyless, repeatable login in CI
steps.description: Make the login a standard first step with short-lived credentials.
items: GitHub Actions OIDC: Use aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 with role-to-assume, then aws-actions/amazon-ecr-login@v2, instead of storing access keys.
Least privilege role: Scope push permissions to specific repository ARNs, and give deploy clusters pull-only roles.
Fail fast: Add aws sts get-caller-identity and a login step before the build so credential problems fail in seconds, not after a 10-minute build.
Mask and avoid logging: Never echo the password; use --password-stdin and keep debug output free of tokens.
Observability: Check CloudTrail for GetAuthorizationToken events to confirm the job actually requested a token and which role made the call.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: The registry host in docker login, the image tag and the repository region must be the same string; compare them character by character before touching IAM.
elevatorPitch: no basic auth credentials means Docker has no stored login for that registry host; the fix is aws ecr get-login-password piped into docker login for the right account and region.
I verify with sts get-caller-identity, the auths section of the docker config, and a test push of a small tag.
I automate with OIDC role assumption, the amazon-ecr-login action and a fail-fast login step at the start of each job.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Logging in once on a long-lived runner
mistakesToAvoid.why: The ECR token expires after about 12 hours, so later jobs fail with the same error.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Logging in as one user and pushing as another
mistakesToAvoid.why: Docker stores credentials per user config, so sudo or a different agent user has none.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Logging in to the wrong region or account host
mistakesToAvoid.why: Credentials apply only to the exact registry hostname, so the push still lacks auth.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Adding broad ecr:* permissions to fix it
mistakesToAvoid.why: The error is about missing credentials, so wider IAM does not help and weakens security.

title: CI/CD Q42: What is a release train model [L3]
summary: Multiple teams' features are collected over a sprint and released together on a fixed schedule (e.g., every 2 weeks). Good for coordinating large teams. Downside: a broken feature blocks the whole train.
question: What is a release train model?
intro: "When developers encounter this build or release bottleneck, my first goal is unblocking velocity safely. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

title: CI/CD Q43: How do you version Docker images in a way thats safe for rollbacks [L2]
summary: To version Docker images so rollbacks are safe, give every build an immutable, unique identity: tag with the git commit SHA (and a semantic version for releases), enforce immutable tags in the registry, and deploy by digest.
question: How do you version Docker images in a way that's safe for rollbacks?
intro: To version Docker images so rollbacks are safe, give every build an immutable, unique identity: tag with the git commit SHA (and a semantic version for releases), enforce immutable tags in the registry, and deploy by digest. Never rely on latest. The goal is that any running pod can be traced to a commit and that an older version can be redeployed byte for byte. Interviewers ask this because many rollback failures are caused by mutable tags, pruned images or ambiguity about what was actually running.

steps.title: Mental model: tag for humans, digest for machines
steps.description: A tag is a movable label; a digest is the content hash of the manifest and cannot change. Think of the tag as the name on the box and the digest as the serial number stamped on the contents; rollback safety comes from relying on the serial number.
items: Tag: my-app:1.4.2 is a pointer in the registry that can be repointed unless the registry enforces immutability.
Digest: my-app@sha256:... identifies exact bytes. Deploying by digest guarantees what runs.
Two tags per build: A SHA tag such as my-app:3f9c2ab for traceability and a semver tag such as 1.4.2 for release communication.
Allowed characters: Docker tags allow letters, digits, underscore, period and hyphen and are at most 128 characters; semver build metadata with + is not valid, so use a hyphen.
Why not only semver: A semver tag says what a release is called but not which commit built it. The SHA closes that gap, and pre-release builds can use 1.5.0-rc.1 style tags.
steps.highlight: The tag you promote must be the tag that you tested. Version at build time and never rebuild per environment.

steps.title: Hands-on: version Docker images in CI
steps.description: Build once, label with metadata and push both tags. This takes seconds in CI and means every image carries its own provenance, which saves time during incident triage.
items: Compute the identity: Short SHA from git rev-parse --short=7 HEAD and the version from a git tag or VERSION file.
Add OCI labels: org.opencontainers.image.revision and .version make the image self-describing.
Push and record the digest: Capture the digest after push and write it into your deployment manifest or values file.
Use metadata-action in GitHub: docker/metadata-action generates tags and labels consistently.
Dockerfile ARGs: Pass --build-arg GIT_SHA=$SHA if the application should report its own version at runtime through a /version endpoint, which makes support and incident triage faster.
steps.codeBlock:
SHA=$(git rev-parse --short=7 HEAD)
VERSION=1.4.2
IMG=registry.example.com/my-app

docker build \
  --label org.opencontainers.image.revision=$SHA \
  --label org.opencontainers.image.version=$VERSION \
  -t $IMG:$SHA -t $IMG:$VERSION .
docker push $IMG:$SHA
docker push $IMG:$VERSION

docker buildx imagetools inspect $IMG:$VERSION | grep Digest
# Digest: sha256:<digest>   <- put this in the Deployment

steps.title: Deploy by digest and roll back
steps.description: Reference the digest in manifests and treat rollback as redeploying an earlier digest.
items: Manifest reference: image: registry.example.com/my-app:1.4.2@sha256:<digest> keeps a readable tag while the digest is what Kubernetes actually pulls.
Rollback: Revert the commit that changed the digest in GitOps, or run kubectl rollout undo for an emergency.
Verify what runs: Check .status.containerStatuses[*].imageID on pods against your record.
Trace back: docker inspect --format '{{ index .Config.Labels "org.opencontainers.image.revision" }}' <image> returns the commit.
Helm and Kustomize: Store the digest in values.yaml or a Kustomize image override, so a Git revert rolls the whole release back with the same review process.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl set image deployment/my-app \
  my-app=registry.example.com/my-app@sha256:<previous-digest> -n prod
kubectl rollout status deployment/my-app -n prod
kubectl get pods -n prod -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.containerStatuses[*].imageID}'

steps.title: Failure modes and edge cases
steps.description: These choices look fine until a rollback is needed. Each of these shows up only when you need to recover quickly, which is the worst time to discover them.
items: latest in production: Two nodes can pull different content under the same tag, and the previous version is unrecoverable by name.
Mutable semver tags: Rebuilding 1.4.2 to fix a typo breaks every record that referred to it. Publish 1.4.3 instead.
Registry cleanup: Lifecycle policies must keep the last N release images and anything referenced by a live deployment.
Multi-arch images: A tag points to an index of per-platform manifests; pin the index digest so every node architecture resolves consistently.
Pull policy: With a digest reference imagePullPolicy matters less, but a tag-only reference with IfNotPresent can leave nodes on stale cached content; this is another reason to pin digests.

steps.title: Production practice
steps.description: Enforce the rules in the registry and pipeline, not by convention.
items: Immutable tags: Enable tag immutability on ECR or an equivalent setting on other registries.
Admission policy: Reject pods that use latest or tag-only references with Kyverno or Gatekeeper.
Automated versions: Tools like semantic-release or release-please derive semver from commit history.
Sign and attest: Sign digests with cosign so you can prove the artifact that rolled back is the one you built.
Retention rule of thumb: Keep every released version indefinitely or per compliance, keep the last N commit-SHA builds, and expire untagged manifests after a grace period.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Publish a commit-SHA tag for traceability and a semver tag for humans, but let the digest in Git be the single source of truth for what runs.
elevatorPitch: Safe versioning means every build gets an immutable identity: commit SHA and semver tags, with deployments pinned by digest.
I verify by comparing the running imageID with the recorded digest and reading the revision label from the image.
I automate semver generation, immutable registry tags, admission rules against latest, and retention that protects released images.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Deploying latest
mistakesToAvoid.why: The tag moves, so you cannot identify or reproduce what is running.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Re-pushing an existing version tag
mistakesToAvoid.why: Rollback targets and audit records no longer match the actual bytes.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using + from semver build metadata in a tag
mistakesToAvoid.why: Docker tags do not allow +, so the push fails or tags get mangled.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Pruning old images by age alone
mistakesToAvoid.why: The previous version may be deleted just when you need to roll back.

title: CI/CD Q46: What is SBOM and why does your CI pipeline need to generate one [L2]
summary: An SBOM in your CI pipeline is a machine-readable inventory (a software bill of materials) of every package and library inside a build artifact.
question: What is SBOM and why does your CI pipeline need to generate one?
intro: An SBOM in your CI pipeline is a machine-readable inventory (a software bill of materials) of every package and library inside a build artifact. Generating it on each build gives you provenance and lets you answer "are we affected?" within minutes when a new vulnerability is published, instead of re-scanning old images. Interviewers ask this to test supply chain security awareness: format choice (CycloneDX or SPDX), where the SBOM is generated, how it is stored with the image, and how it is used to gate releases.

steps.title: What an SBOM is and why CI should produce it
steps.description: The SBOM is evidence tied to a specific build.
items: Content: package names, versions, licenses, hashes and dependency relationships, for OS packages and language dependencies.
Formats: CycloneDX and SPDX are the two common standards; most scanners read both.
Incident response: when a new CVE appears, search stored SBOMs instead of pulling and scanning every old image.
Compliance: customers and auditors increasingly request SBOMs and license data per release.

steps.title: Generating the SBOM from the built image
steps.description: Scan the final artifact, not just the source tree, so base image packages are included.
items: Syft: catalogues an image, directory or archive and emits CycloneDX or SPDX JSON.
BuildKit attestation: docker buildx build --sbom=true attaches an SBOM attestation to the pushed image.
Pin by digest: record the image digest in the SBOM metadata so the file maps to one exact artifact.
Artifact upload: keep the SBOM as a build artifact even if it is also attached to the registry.
steps.codeBlock:
# Generate from the pushed image
syft registry.example.com/my-app:1.4.2 -o cyclonedx-json=sbom.cdx.json

# Or let BuildKit attach it during build
docker buildx build --sbom=true --push -t registry.example.com/my-app:1.4.2 .

# Quick sanity check: component count
jq '.components | length' sbom.cdx.json

steps.title: Scanning the SBOM and gating the pipeline
steps.description: Use the SBOM as input to vulnerability and license checks.
items: Grype: scans an SBOM directly and can fail the build above a severity threshold.
Trivy: trivy sbom scans an existing SBOM file.
Policy: fail on fixable high or critical findings, allow documented exceptions with expiry.
Rescan later: run the same scan on a schedule, because new CVEs affect old SBOMs.
steps.codeBlock:
grype sbom:sbom.cdx.json --fail-on high
trivy sbom sbom.cdx.json --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1
steps.highlight: A clean scan today is not permanent: re-scan stored SBOMs on a schedule so newly disclosed vulnerabilities in already shipped releases are found.

steps.title: Attaching and signing the SBOM
steps.description: An unsigned file next to an image proves little.
items: cosign attest: binds the SBOM to the image digest as a signed in-toto attestation stored in the registry.
Verification: consumers or admission controllers verify the attestation before deployment.
Retention: keep SBOMs for as long as the release is supported.
Workflow example: a GitHub Actions step produces and uploads the file for every build.
steps.codeBlock:
cosign attest --yes --key cosign.key --type cyclonedx \
  --predicate sbom.cdx.json registry.example.com/my-app@sha256:<digest>

cosign verify-attestation --key cosign.pub --type cyclonedx \
  registry.example.com/my-app@sha256:<digest>

# GitHub Actions
- uses: anchore/sbom-action@v0
  with:
    image: registry.example.com/my-app:1.4.2
    format: cyclonedx-json
    output-file: sbom.cdx.json

steps.title: Limits and production practice
steps.description: An SBOM is inventory, not proof of safety.
items: Accuracy limits: statically linked binaries or vendored code can be missed; compare tools when completeness matters.
Vulnerability context: combine with VEX statements to mark findings as not exploitable.
Admission control: enforce signed attestations with Kyverno or Sigstore policy-controller.
Reproducibility: generate in the same pipeline run that builds, never later from a mutable tag.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Generate the SBOM from the pushed image digest, sign it with cosign attest, and re-scan stored SBOMs nightly so new CVEs in old releases are caught without rebuilding.
elevatorPitch: An SBOM is a machine-readable list of all components in a build, in CycloneDX or SPDX format, generated per build in CI.
I generate it from the final image digest with Syft or BuildKit, then validate it by scanning with Grype or Trivy.
I sign and attach it with cosign, fail the pipeline on fixable high findings, and re-scan stored SBOMs on a schedule.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Generating the SBOM from source manifests only
mistakesToAvoid.why: It misses OS packages from the base image, so scans under-report real exposure.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Referencing the image by a mutable tag
mistakesToAvoid.why: The SBOM may describe a different artifact than what is deployed; use the digest.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Generating an SBOM but never storing or scanning it again
mistakesToAvoid.why: The value is in looking up affected releases later when new CVEs are published.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Shipping the SBOM unsigned
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without an attestation bound to the digest nobody can trust it was produced by your pipeline.
