title: CI/CD Q48: How do you implement progressive delivery [L3]
summary: Progressive delivery releases a change to a growing slice of traffic while automated analysis decides whether to continue or roll back.
question: How do you implement progressive delivery?
intro: Progressive delivery releases a change to a growing slice of traffic while automated analysis decides whether to continue or roll back. You implement it with a controller such as Argo Rollouts or Flagger, a traffic-shifting layer (ingress, service mesh or Gateway API), and metrics that define success. It goes beyond a plain rolling update because the decision is driven by real user-facing signals, not only pod readiness. Interviewers ask to see whether you can design the loop: exposure steps, metrics, thresholds, abort behaviour and the data compatibility that makes it safe.

steps.title: Mental model: exposure, measurement, decision
steps.description: Progressive delivery is a feedback loop around a release. Without that loop you only have a slower deployment, not a safer one.
items: Strategies: Canary (small percentage first), blue-green (full parallel stack and switch), and feature flags (decouple deploy from release).
Control loop: Shift weight, wait, query metrics, then promote or abort automatically.
Traffic control: Without a mesh or ingress integration, a canary weight is approximated by replica ratio, so 10 percent needs enough pods to be meaningful.
Decision data: Success rate, latency percentiles and saturation compared against a baseline or fixed threshold.
Compared with rolling update: A Kubernetes rolling update gates on readiness only. Progressive delivery adds weighted exposure, metric analysis and automatic rollback on top.

steps.title: Hands-on: progressive delivery with Argo Rollouts
steps.description: A Rollout replaces the Deployment and defines canary steps and analysis. Keep the Rollout, AnalysisTemplate and Service in the same Git path so they are reviewed and promoted together.
items: Steps: setWeight shifts traffic, pause waits, and analysis runs checks inline.
AnalysisTemplate: A reusable query with a success condition and failure limit.
Traffic routing: Add trafficRouting for NGINX, Istio, Gateway API or other supported providers for exact percentages.
Operate it: The kubectl plugin shows live status and supports promote and abort.
Blue-green variant: Setting strategy.blueGreen with autoPromotionEnabled: false runs the new version beside the old one, lets you test the preview Service, and then switches on promotion.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata: {name: my-app, namespace: prod}
spec:
  replicas: 5
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: my-app}}
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 10
        - pause: {duration: 5m}
        - analysis:
            templates: [{templateName: success-rate}]
            args: [{name: service-name, value: my-app}]
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: {duration: 10m}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: my-app}}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: my-app
          image: registry.example.com/my-app:1.5.0
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata: {name: success-rate, namespace: prod}
spec:
  args: [{name: service-name}]
  metrics:
    - name: success-rate
      interval: 1m
      count: 5
      failureLimit: 1
      successCondition: result[0] >= 0.99
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
          query: |
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="{{args.service-name}}",status!~"5.."}[2m]))
            / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="{{args.service-name}}"}[2m]))

steps.title: Operate, observe and verify the rollout
steps.description: Watch each step and confirm both the controller state and the user-facing metrics.
items: Watch: kubectl argo rollouts get rollout my-app -n prod --watch shows the current step, weights and analysis runs.
Promote or abort: promote skips a pause, and abort returns traffic to the stable version immediately.
Cross-check dashboards: Compare canary and stable error rate and latency, since an analysis query can be wrong or too lenient.
Confirm final state: After the last step the new ReplicaSet becomes stable and the old one scales down after the configured delay.
Pre-promotion checks: You can also run analysis before any traffic shifts, using smoke-test Jobs as a metric provider, to catch obvious breakage cheaply.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl argo rollouts get rollout my-app -n prod --watch
kubectl argo rollouts promote my-app -n prod
kubectl argo rollouts abort my-app -n prod
kubectl argo rollouts undo my-app -n prod

steps.title: Failure modes and design trade-offs
steps.description: The mechanism only protects you if signals and data are sound. A good design review asks what happens when each of these goes wrong, and answers it before production does.
items: Low traffic: If 10 percent of traffic is a handful of requests, metrics are noise. Use longer pauses or synthetic probes for low-volume services.
Bad metrics: A query that returns no data may pass or fail depending on configuration; test analysis templates against a deliberately broken release.
Stateful and schema changes: Two versions run at once, so database changes must be backward compatible.
Sticky sessions and caches: Users may flip between versions; make APIs and cached payloads compatible across both.
Rollback speed: Abort is fast for canary because stable pods are still running, whereas in-place rolling updates must pull and start old pods again.

steps.title: Production practice
steps.description: Standardise it so teams get safe defaults.
items: GitOps integration: Argo CD manages the Rollout manifest; the controller manages the traffic steps.
Flagger alternative: Flagger watches a normal Deployment and creates the canary resources for you, with provider support for Istio, Linkerd, NGINX and Gateway API.
Feature flags: Ship code dark, then release gradually per cohort without redeploying.
Notifications: Send abort events to chat and paging so a failed canary is investigated rather than silently retried.
Define SLO-based gates: Tie thresholds to your error budget so promotion rules reflect what the business tolerates and not arbitrary numbers.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Test your analysis template by deploying a deliberately failing version; a progressive delivery pipeline that has never aborted is unproven.
elevatorPitch: Progressive delivery shifts traffic to a new version in steps while automated analysis on real metrics decides whether to promote or abort.
I verify with the rollout watch output, canary versus stable dashboards and a deliberate failure test.
I automate it with Argo Rollouts or Flagger, Prometheus analysis, GitOps and abort notifications.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using replica ratio as exact traffic percentage
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without traffic routing a 10 percent canary of 3 pods is really 33 percent.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Analysis queries that never produce data
mistakesToAvoid.why: Empty results can be treated as pass or inconclusive, so a broken release is promoted.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running incompatible schema changes with canary
mistakesToAvoid.why: Both versions share the database, so a breaking migration affects stable users too.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Promoting on a timer alone
mistakesToAvoid.why: Pauses without analysis are just a slow rollout and catch nothing.

title: CI/CD Q49: What is the purpose of a Dockerfile dockerignore file [L2]
summary: In a pipeline, .dockerignore in CI/CD controls which files from the checked-out workspace are sent to the builder and made available to COPY. Its purpose is to keep the build context small, deterministic and free of secrets.
question: What is the purpose of a Dockerfile `.dockerignore` file?
intro: In a pipeline, .dockerignore in CI/CD controls which files from the checked-out workspace are sent to the builder and made available to COPY. Its purpose is to keep the build context small, deterministic and free of secrets. CI workspaces are messier than laptops: they contain .git, test reports, coverage output, downloaded artifacts and sometimes credential files written by earlier steps. Interviewers ask this to see whether you connect an old Dockerfile feature to cache hit rate, build time and supply-chain safety.

steps.title: Why CI Workspaces Need Filtering
steps.description: The pipeline's workspace is the build context, so everything earlier steps wrote is a candidate for the image.
items: Noise from earlier steps: test reports, coverage/, .pytest_cache, built binaries and downloaded caches appear before the Docker step runs.
Credential files: steps that write .npmrc, ~/.aws style files or kubeconfigs into the workspace can leak into a layer through COPY . ..
Cache invalidation: a changing file, such as a timestamped report, invalidates the COPY . . layer and every layer after it on each run.
Upload cost: remote builders and BuildKit services receive the context over the network, so size directly adds to job time.

steps.title: Configure .dockerignore and the Build Step
steps.description: Keep the ignore file in the repo and build with BuildKit and a registry cache.
items: Ignore pipeline artifacts: list report, cache and CI directories explicitly.
Copy dependency files first: order the Dockerfile so manifests are copied and installed before sources, then ignore rules protect that cache.
Same behaviour everywhere: BuildKit and Buildx honour the file, so local and CI builds match.
Registry cache: cache-from and cache-to persist layers across stateless runners.
steps.codeBlock:
# .dockerignore
.git
.github
.env*
coverage/
test-results/
*.log
node_modules
dist

# .github/workflows/build.yml (excerpt)
- uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
- uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
  with:
    context: .
    push: true
    tags: registry.example.com/team/my-app:${{ github.sha }}
    cache-from: type=registry,ref=registry.example.com/team/my-app:buildcache
    cache-to: type=registry,ref=registry.example.com/team/my-app:buildcache,mode=max

steps.title: Verify Context Size and Image Contents in the Pipeline
steps.description: Add cheap checks so a regression in the ignore file is caught in review.
items: Read the context size: docker build --progress=plain . logs the "transferring context" size; compare it with the previous run.
List the image filesystem: run ls -la on the app directory of the built image and fail the job if forbidden names appear.
Scan for secrets: Trivy can scan an image for secrets with --scanners secret.
Review layers: docker history --no-trunc shows the instructions that created each layer.
steps.codeBlock:
docker build --progress=plain -t my-app:ci . 2>&1 | grep -i "transferring context"

# Fail the job if sensitive files are present
docker run --rm --entrypoint sh my-app:ci -c \
  'find /app -name ".env*" -o -name "*.pem" | grep . && exit 1 || exit 0'

trivy image --scanners secret --exit-code 1 my-app:ci

steps.title: Failure Modes in Pipelines
steps.description: Over-ignoring breaks builds; under-ignoring breaks caching and security.
items: Build passes locally, fails in CI with "not found": a generated file such as dist/ is ignored but the Dockerfile expects it; build inside a stage instead of copying artifacts.
Cache never hits: check for volatile files in context, for example a generated version.txt or reports; ignore them or copy them in a late layer.
Wrong ignore file: with a custom -f Dockerfile, a <name>.dockerignore beside it takes precedence under BuildKit.
Git context builds: when the context is a remote Git reference, only committed files are present, so behaviour differs from a workspace build.
steps.highlight: A leaked secret removed in a later RUN rm is still in the earlier layer. Prevention is the ignore file plus BuildKit --mount=type=secret, not cleanup.

steps.title: Make It Part of the Delivery Standard
steps.description: Treat the ignore file like code that gets reviewed and tested.
items: Template per language: keep a baseline .dockerignore in your project template so new services start safe.
Review rule: any new top-level directory must be reviewed against .dockerignore in the same pull request.
Policy checks: a CI lint step can fail when the file is missing from a repository that has a Dockerfile.
Multi-stage builds: pair with a lean final stage so build tools and sources never ship.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Track the "transferring context" size in pipeline logs; a sudden jump is an early signal that a build artifact or secret file is about to enter your image.
elevatorPitch: .dockerignore filters the CI workspace before it becomes the Docker build context, keeping reports, .git and credential files out of COPY.
I verify it from the transferring-context size, a filesystem check on the built image and a Trivy secret scan.
I standardise a baseline file per language, combine it with registry layer caching and BuildKit secret mounts, and review changes alongside the Dockerfile.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Letting COPY . . run after earlier steps wrote reports or credentials into the workspace
mistakesToAvoid.why: They become part of the image and constantly invalidate the layer cache.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring dist/ while the Dockerfile copies it
mistakesToAvoid.why: The build fails only in CI where the artifact path is expected; build artifacts in a stage instead.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Deleting a secret with a later RUN rm
mistakesToAvoid.why: The earlier layer still contains it and can be extracted; keep it out of the context entirely.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Having no .dockerignore in repositories with a Dockerfile
mistakesToAvoid.why: Every CI run uploads .git and workspace noise, slowing builds and risking leaks.

title: CI/CD Q50: Your Jenkins pipeline uses credentials stored in Jenkins Credentials Store How are they accessed in the pipeline [L2]
summary: A Jenkins pipeline accesses secrets from the Jenkins Credentials Store by referencing a credential ID, either with the withCredentials step or the credentials() helper in an environment block.
question: Your Jenkins pipeline uses credentials stored in Jenkins Credentials Store. How are they accessed in the pipeline?
intro: A Jenkins pipeline accesses secrets from the Jenkins Credentials Store by referencing a credential ID, either with the withCredentials step or the credentials() helper in an environment block. Jenkins injects the value into environment variables or temporary files only for that scope and masks it in the console log. Interviewers ask this to check that you know the binding types, understand that masking is not a security boundary, and can avoid classic leaks such as Groovy string interpolation, secrets in the Jenkinsfile and overly broad credential scopes.

steps.title: Mental model: IDs, types, scopes and the Credentials Binding plugin
steps.description: The Jenkinsfile never contains the secret, only the ID that points to it.
items: Credential types: Secret text, username with password, secret file, SSH username with private key, and certificate. Each has its own binding.
Store and scope: Credentials live in the controller's encrypted store at system (global) scope or in a folder or user domain. Folder scope limits which jobs can see them.
Binding: The Credentials Binding plugin resolves the ID at runtime and exposes the value only inside the bound block.
Credential IDs: Use stable, descriptive IDs like ecr-push-role or github-token since pipelines depend on them.

Where values go: Secret text becomes an environment variable, a file credential becomes a temporary path on the agent, and the file is removed when the block ends, so avoid copying it elsewhere on disk.
steps.highlight: Secrets are decrypted on the controller and sent to the agent that runs the step; protect both controller and agents.

steps.title: Hands-on: using the Jenkins Credentials Store in a pipeline
steps.description: Use withCredentials for fine scope, or the credentials() helper for stage-wide variables.
items: String credential: string(credentialsId: 'api-token', variable: 'API_TOKEN') sets an environment variable inside the block.
Username and password: usernamePassword(...) sets two variables; credentials('id') in environment also creates _USR and _PSW variables.
Files and SSH keys: file(...) and sshUserPrivateKey(...) write a temporary file and give you its path.
Use single quotes in sh: Let the shell expand the variable, instead of Groovy, so the secret is not interpolated into the command text.
Scripted pipelines: The same withCredentials([...]) { ... } step works in scripted syntax; the credential is available only to code inside the closure.

steps.title: Verify bindings work and secrets stay hidden
steps.description: Confirm the pipeline authenticates correctly without exposing values.
items: Functional check: The login or API call succeeds; a missing or mistyped ID fails fast with a credential-not-found error.
Masking check: Console output shows **** where the secret would print. Verify with a harmless test credential.
Scope check: Run a job in another folder and confirm it cannot resolve the ID.
Lint warning: Jenkins warns when Groovy interpolation is used with a secret: A secret was passed to sh using Groovy String interpolation. Treat it as a defect.
Audit trail: Credential usage is recorded in the build's fingerprints for supported types, so you can see which builds used a given credential before rotating it.

steps.title: Failure modes and leak paths
steps.description: Masking only matches the exact string, so transformed output can escape it.
items: Encoded output: Printing a base64 or reversed secret is not masked. Anyone who can edit a Jenkinsfile can exfiltrate secrets, so restrict who can change pipelines.
Pull request builds: Untrusted forks must not run with real credentials; disable credentials for external PRs.
Debug options: set -x in shell can print expanded commands, and env or printenv dumps variables; avoid both inside bound blocks.
Wide scope: Global credentials are visible to every job. Move sensitive ones into folders per team.
Agents as risk: Any build on a shared agent can read other builds' workspaces if cleanup is poor; use ephemeral agents (for example Kubernetes pod agents) and cleanWs().

steps.title: Production practice: reduce long-lived secrets
steps.description: Prefer dynamic and external secret sources where possible.
items: External stores: Use the HashiCorp Vault plugin or the AWS Secrets Manager credentials provider so Jenkins reads secrets without storing them.
Short-lived cloud access: Assume an IAM role from an agent with an instance profile instead of storing access keys.
Rotation and audit: Rotate regularly, record who can use each credential, and check the Credentials usage and audit logs.
Configuration as code: Manage credential definitions through JCasC with values injected from the secret manager, not committed to Git.
Pipeline-as-code review: Require code review on the Jenkinsfile and use shared libraries for steps that handle credentials, so one audited implementation is reused everywhere.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Reference credentials by ID, use single-quoted shell steps and bind them in the narrowest block possible, because Jenkins masking only hides exact matches.
elevatorPitch: Jenkins pipelines read secrets from the Credentials Store by ID using withCredentials or the credentials() helper, which inject them only for that scope.
I verify binding by a successful authenticated call, confirm masking in the log, and check folder scoping.
I automate with external secret managers, short-lived cloud roles, JCasC and restricted pipeline edit rights.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using double-quoted sh steps with a secret
mistakesToAvoid.why: Groovy interpolates the secret into the command, which can leak it into logs and process listings.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Putting secrets in the Jenkinsfile or environment block as plain text
mistakesToAvoid.why: They are committed to Git and visible to everyone with repo access.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running untrusted PR code with credentials
mistakesToAvoid.why: A malicious Jenkinsfile can print or send the secret elsewhere.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating console masking as protection
mistakesToAvoid.why: Masking only matches exact text, so encoded output is not hidden.

title: Trunk-Based Development vs Gitflow: Branching Strategies, Feature Flags & Merge Conflict Prevention
summary: Comparing Trunk-Based Development vs Gitflow branching strategies: lifecycle of feature branches, eliminating merge conflicts, feature flags, release cadence, and DORA metrics alignment.
question: Explain trunk-based development vs Gitflow. When would you choose one over the other, and how do high-performing DevOps teams prevent merge hell while releasing multiple times per day?
intro: "During a high-stakes release, we hit a similar deployment challenge and resolved it with automated safeguards. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

steps.title: Gitflow: Structure, Strengths & Failure Modes
steps.description: Gitflow revolves around persistent, long-lived branches (main, develop, feature/*, release/*, hotfix/*):
items: Workflow: Developers branch off develop, work in isolation for days or weeks, and open PRs back to develop. Release branches freeze code for QA before merging into main and tagging.
Strengths: Clear structure for legacy software with scheduled, rigid release cadences (e.g., quarterly embedded firmware or enterprise desktop software).
Failure Modes: High risk of merge hell, delayed integration feedback, stale branches, and painful cherry-picking when production hotfixes must be synchronized back into develop.

steps.title: Trunk-Based Development (TBD): Continuous Integration at Scale
steps.description: All developers merge small, frequent commits into a single shared branch (main or 'trunk') at least once per day:
items: Short-Lived Branches: Feature branches live for less than 24–48 hours and typically contain fewer than 300 lines of code.
Continuous Integration: Automated pipelines run unit tests, linting, and security scans on every pull request within 5–10 minutes, catching bugs immediately.
Pair Programming & Fast PRs: Code reviews happen continuously rather than batch-reviewing thousands of diff lines right before release day.

steps.title: The Key Enablers of Trunk-Based Development
steps.description: How do you deploy unfinished features to production without exposing them to users?
items: Feature Flags / Toggles: Code paths for in-progress features are wrapped in runtime toggles (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, or open-source flag engines). Code is in main and deployed to production, but inactive for users.
Branch by Abstraction: When refactoring major subsystems, build an abstraction layer, implement the new version alongside the old one, and gradually swap callers before removing the old code.
Robust Automated Rollbacks: If an issue occurs, roll back or toggle the feature flag off in seconds without requiring git reverts or code rollbacks.

keyTakeaway: Trunk-Based Development is the proven gold standard for high-performing DevOps teams (accelerating DORA Lead Time for Changes and Deployment Frequency). Gitflow introduces unnecessary friction and merge conflicts in modern cloud-native environments.
elevatorPitch: Championed Trunk-Based Development with short-lived branches (< 24h) and daily merges to main.
Decoupled deployment from release using runtime feature flags to safely push code continuously without user exposure.
Cut merge conflict resolution overhead by 80% and increased deployment frequency from bi-weekly to multiple times daily.
Reserved Gitflow strictly for scheduled, versioned shrink-wrapped software where continuous delivery is impractical.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Promoting application releases to production without an automated, canary-validated rollback mechanism when configuring Trunk Based Development
mistakesToAvoid.why: Pipelines that lack automated rollback mechanisms force engineering teams to scramble manual hotfixes during severe production regressions.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running concurrent deployment pipeline jobs without stage mutex locking on shared target environments when configuring Trunk Based Development
mistakesToAvoid.why: Concurrent pipeline runs on the same environment race to apply state changes, causing out-of-order commits and unpredictable deployment state.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting dependency lockfiles (package-lock.json, go.sum, Cargo.lock) from continuous integration builds when configuring Trunk Based Development
mistakesToAvoid.why: Omitting lockfiles allows upstream package updates to break builds unpredictably without any changes to application codebase.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to define dynamic cache invalidation keys for CI package managers and layer caches when configuring Trunk Based Development
mistakesToAvoid.why: Stale build caches mask underlying dependency incompatibilities or pull outdated libraries, while un-cached runs slow feedback loops.

title: CI/CD Q52: How do you manage Helm chart versioning in CI/CD [L2]
summary: Helm chart versioning in CI/CD means treating the chart as its own artifact: version in Chart.yaml is the chart's SemVer and changes whenever templates or defaults change, while appVersion describes the application it deploys.
question: How do you manage Helm chart versioning in CI/CD?
intro: Helm chart versioning in CI/CD means treating the chart as its own artifact: version in Chart.yaml is the chart's SemVer and changes whenever templates or defaults change, while appVersion describes the application it deploys. CI packages the chart with explicit versions, pushes it to an OCI registry or chart repository as an immutable release, and environments pin the exact chart version. Interviewers ask to see whether you understand the two version fields, SemVer rules for chart changes, and how to avoid overwriting released versions.

steps.title: Mental model: chart version versus appVersion
steps.description: These fields change for different reasons and must not be confused. Keeping them separate lets you ship a chart-only fix, such as a new probe default, without pretending the application changed.
items: version: Required SemVer 2 version of the chart. Bump it for any chart change: templates, values defaults, dependencies.
appVersion: Informational version of the app, typically the image tag. It does not affect Helm's version resolution.
SemVer meaning: Major for breaking changes to values or behaviour, minor for backward-compatible features, patch for fixes.
Dependencies: The dependencies section pins subchart version ranges; Chart.lock records the resolved versions for reproducible builds.
Chart.yaml example: apiVersion: v2, name: my-app, version: 1.8.0 and appVersion: "1.5.0"; quote appVersion so YAML treats it as a string.
steps.highlight: Helm's package, push and install commands use version; two different charts with the same version in one repository is an error waiting to happen.

steps.title: Hands-on: Helm chart versioning in CI
steps.description: Package with versions injected from the pipeline and publish to an OCI registry (Helm 3.8 and later supports OCI by default). Because the pipeline injects the versions, nobody edits Chart.yaml by hand and the published artifact always matches the build that produced it.
items: Lint and render: helm lint and helm template validate before packaging.
Package with explicit versions: --version sets the chart version and --app-version sets appVersion, overriding the file.
Authenticate and push: helm registry login then helm push to oci://.
Install a pinned version: helm install my-app oci://registry.example.com/charts/my-app --version 1.8.0.
Verify the artifact: After pushing, helm pull oci://registry.example.com/charts/my-app --version 1.8.0 and helm show chart confirm the published content matches what CI built.
steps.codeBlock:
helm dependency update charts/my-app
helm lint charts/my-app
helm template my-app charts/my-app -f values-prod.yaml > /dev/null

CHART_VERSION=1.8.0
APP_VERSION=1.5.0       # image tag built earlier in the pipeline
helm package charts/my-app --version $CHART_VERSION --app-version $APP_VERSION
# Successfully packaged chart and saved it to: my-app-1.8.0.tgz

echo "$REGISTRY_PASSWORD" | helm registry login registry.example.com -u ci --password-stdin
helm push my-app-1.8.0.tgz oci://registry.example.com/charts

steps.title: Automate version bumps and promotion
steps.description: Choose one deterministic rule so humans do not edit versions by hand.
items: Tag-driven: Push a git tag like chart-1.8.0 and let the pipeline derive the chart version from it.
Conventional commits: Tools such as release-please can compute the next SemVer from commit types for charts and apps.
Pre-releases for branches: Publish 1.8.0-rc.1 or 1.8.0-pr123.1 for testing; SemVer orders these before the final release.
Promotion: Environments reference the version in GitOps, for example Argo CD targetRevision: 1.8.0 on the chart source, and promotion is a pull request changing that value.
Monorepo charts: When several charts share a repo, trigger versioning only for changed paths so unrelated charts do not receive empty releases.
steps.codeBlock:
# Argo CD Application (excerpt)
# source:
#   repoURL: registry.example.com/charts
#   chart: my-app
#   targetRevision: 1.8.0
helm show chart oci://registry.example.com/charts/my-app --version 1.8.0 | grep -E 'version|appVersion'

steps.title: Failure modes and edge cases
steps.description: The common bugs are overwritten versions and version drift. Each of these is cheap to prevent in CI and expensive to untangle after clusters have pinned the wrong content.
items: Republished version: Overwriting 1.8.0 breaks clusters that cached or pinned it and makes audits impossible. Block re-push in CI by checking the registry first.
Forgetting to bump: Changing templates without bumping version means CI publishes nothing new or collides. Enforce with a CI check on chart path changes.
Plus signs in OCI tags: SemVer build metadata using + is converted to _ for OCI tags, which surprises people comparing versions.
Floating ranges: Subchart ranges like ^1.2.0 drift unless you commit Chart.lock and run helm dependency build.
CRDs: Helm does not upgrade files in the crds/ directory on helm upgrade, so chart version bumps that change CRDs need a separate, documented upgrade step.

steps.title: Production practice
steps.description: Make chart releases auditable and safe. The aim is that anyone can answer which chart version is running in each environment, and why, from Git history alone.
items: Immutable registry settings: Enable tag immutability for the chart repository where supported.
Sign charts: Use cosign on OCI chart artifacts or Helm provenance files with helm package --sign.
Test upgrades: Run helm upgrade --install from the previous released version in a kind cluster and validate with helm test.
Document breaking changes: A major bump should come with migration notes and a values schema (values.schema.json) to fail fast on bad input.
Rollbacks: helm rollback my-app <revision> restores a previous release revision in the cluster, while pinning an earlier chart version in Git is the durable rollback in GitOps.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Bump the chart version for every chart change and let appVersion follow the image tag, then pin the exact chart version per environment so promotion is a one-line Git change.
elevatorPitch: Helm chart versioning treats the chart as a SemVer artifact where version tracks chart changes and appVersion tracks the application.
I verify with helm lint, helm template, helm show chart on the published version and an upgrade test from the previous release.
I automate bumps from tags or commit history, push to OCI with immutable versions, and pin versions in Argo CD.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating appVersion as the chart version
mistakesToAvoid.why: Helm resolves charts by version, so bumping only appVersion creates confusion and collisions.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Republishing an existing chart version
mistakesToAvoid.why: Clusters and audits can no longer rely on the version to identify content.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Leaving dependency ranges without Chart.lock
mistakesToAvoid.why: Subcharts drift between builds and break reproducibility.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Changing values defaults in a patch release
mistakesToAvoid.why: It breaks consumers who rely on SemVer to signal compatibility.

title: CI/CD Q56: How do you handle a situation where a dependencys latest version breaks your build [L2]
summary: When a dependency's latest version breaks your build, first restore a green pipeline by pinning the last known good version, then diagnose and fix properly.
question: How do you handle a situation where a dependency's latest version breaks your build?
intro: When a dependency's latest version breaks your build, first restore a green pipeline by pinning the last known good version, then diagnose and fix properly. Start by comparing the lockfile or resolved versions between the last passing and failing build, pin the offender, merge, and only then investigate the upstream change or report it. Interviewers ask this because it exposes whether your builds are reproducible: if an unchanged commit can fail tomorrow, you have unpinned dependencies and no lockfile discipline.

steps.title: Triage: confirm it is the dependency, not your code
steps.description: Establish what changed between the last green and the first red build.
items: Same commit, new failure: If rerunning an old commit now fails, an external input changed, most likely a floating dependency range, a base image tag or a tool version.
Diff the resolved versions: Compare the lockfile in git, or the logged install output of the passing and failing runs, to find updated packages.
Read the error: Type errors, removed APIs or peer-dependency conflicts after install point to a major or minor update that changed behaviour.
Reproduce locally: Use a clean clone and fresh install, because local caches can hide the problem.
Communicate early: Tell the team the build is red because of an upstream release and that a pin is coming, so people stop retrying and stop merging into a broken main.

steps.title: Hands-on: when the latest version breaks your build, pin and lock
steps.description: Restore green first by pinning to the last good version in your ecosystem.
items: npm: npm install pkg@1.4.2 --save-exact and commit package-lock.json; CI should use npm ci, which fails if the lockfile and manifest disagree.
Transitive dependency: Use overrides in package.json (npm), resolutions (Yarn) or constraints files to force a safe version.
Python: Pin pkg==1.4.2 in requirements or a constraints file, and consider pip install --require-hashes for locked installs.
Go and Maven: go get example.com/pkg@v1.4.2 updates go.mod; Maven uses explicit versions or dependencyManagement.
Bisect versions: If several packages changed, revert half of the lockfile changes at a time, or use git bisect on the lockfile history, to isolate the single culprit quickly.
steps.codeBlock:
# Find what changed
git diff HEAD~1 -- package-lock.json | grep -E '^[+-].*"version"'
npm ls pkg                      # who pulls it in

# Pin and lock
npm install pkg@1.4.2 --save-exact
npm ci && npm test

# package.json: force a transitive version
# "overrides": { "transitive-pkg": "2.3.1" }

# Python
pip install "pkg==1.4.2"
pip freeze | grep -i pkg

steps.title: Verify the fix and make the build reproducible
steps.description: Prove that the build is deterministic again.
items: Clean build: Run the full pipeline from scratch with an empty cache; it should pass on repeated runs.
Check the lockfile in CI: Use npm ci, pip install -r requirements.txt --require-hashes or go mod verify so CI never silently re-resolves.
Confirm actual versions: Print npm ls --all or pip freeze in the log for future diffs.
Scan again: If the new version was a security patch, track the upgrade debt so the pin does not hide a vulnerability.
Check peers: Peer dependency warnings after the fix tell you whether the pinned version still satisfies other packages that expect a newer range.

npm ls --all | grep pkg

steps.title: Edge cases and failure modes
steps.description: Not every breakage is a version bump you control.
items: Yanked or republished packages: An upstream maintainer can unpublish or replace a release; mirror dependencies in an internal registry so you keep a copy.
Floating base images: A FROM node:lts or latest changes underneath you; pin to a version or digest.
Transitive conflicts: Overrides can mask incompatibilities; add a test and a TODO to remove the override when upstream fixes it.
Supply chain risk: A sudden breaking update can also be a compromised package; read the changelog and diff before accepting, not just pin.
Private mirrors: An internal proxy such as Artifactory, Nexus or CodeArtifact retains the versions you used, so builds survive upstream removal.

steps.title: Prevention: controlled upgrades
steps.description: Move updates into pull requests so breakage hits a branch, not your release.
items: Renovate or Dependabot: Open automated update PRs that run the full CI; group minor and patch updates and review majors individually.
Cooldown: Configure a minimum release age (Renovate minimumReleaseAge) so brand-new versions get time to be flagged.
Contract tests: Test the integration points your code relies on, so API changes fail early with a clear message.
Report upstream: File a reproducible issue with the versions involved, and track it until you can drop the pin.
Time-box the pin: Record the pin with a ticket and review date; remove it as soon as the upstream fix or your code change lands.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Fix the red build by pinning the last good version, and fix the process by committing lockfiles and moving upgrades into Renovate or Dependabot pull requests.
elevatorPitch: When a dependency's latest version breaks the build, I pin the last known good version to restore green, then diagnose the upstream change.
I verify by diffing resolved versions between passing and failing builds and by running a clean install with the lockfile in CI.
I automate with committed lockfiles, npm ci or hash-locked installs, an internal mirror and Renovate pull requests with release-age delays.

mistakesToAvoid.why: An unchanged commit can fail tomorrow, which removes reproducibility.

title: CI/CD Q61: Your team heavily utilizes GitHub Actions but the monthly bill for GitHub-hosted runners has skyrocketed You want to switch to self-hosted runners but are worried about security and state poisoning if runners are reused How do you implement this safely [L2]
summary: You must undeniably use Ephemeral Runners combined with Auto-Scaling (e.g., Actions Runner Controller in Kubernetes).
question: Your team heavily utilizes GitHub Actions, but the monthly bill for GitHub-hosted runners has skyrocketed. You want to switch to self-hosted runners, but are worried about security and state poisoning if runners are reused. How do you implement this safely?
intro: "In our delivery pipeline supporting multiple engineering squads, pipeline reliability was paramount. The interviewer is testing: Ephemeral self-hosted CI agents.. I structure my answer around systematic triage first, root cause analysis second, and permanent remediation third."

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: You must undeniably use Ephemeral Runners combined with Auto-Scaling (e.g., Actions Runner Controller in Kubernetes). A standard self-hosted runner executes a job and remains alive to accept the next one. This means a malicious PR could execute docker run crypto-miner in the background, or leave behind hidden malware in the /tmp directory that instantly infects the next team's build. By passing the --ephemeral flag when registering the runner, the runner mathematically guarantees it will cleanly accept only one single job. The moment the job finishes, the runner aggressively unregisters itself and the underlying Pod or EC2 instance is completely destroyed, guaranteeing an immutable, clean slate for every build.

question: In GitLab CI, you have 5 independent stages. Stage 3 logically cannot begin until Stage 2 finishes. However, Job X in Stage 3 relies strictly on Job A in Stage 1, completely ignoring Stage 2. How do you optimize the pipeline heavily so Job X isn't needlessly waiting?
intro: "In our delivery pipeline supporting multiple engineering squads, pipeline reliability was paramount. The interviewer is testing: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAG) in CI.. I structure my answer around systematic triage first, root cause analysis second, and permanent remediation third."

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: You would utilize a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) by implementing the needs: keyword. By default, GitLab CI fundamentally operates sequentially: all jobs in Stage 1 must absolutely finish before *any* job in Stage 2 can begin. By defining needs: [job_a] explicitly heavily on Job X, you break the rigid stage barrier. GitLab will instantly execute Job X the millisecond that Job A finishes, entirely ignoring the fact that Stage 2 jobs are still slowly churning. This dramatically accelerates parallel execution and drastically reduces overall pipeline wall-clock time.

title: CI/CD Q90: Your infrastructure team uses Terraform Cloud for remote state and applies In CI developers run terraform plan on every PR You discover that two developers PRs simultaneously modified the same resource — when both were merged the second apply overwrote the first silently What mechanism prevents this Terraform race condition [L3]
summary: This race condition is prevented by state locking. Terraform backend implementations (S3+DynamoDB, Terraform Cloud, etc.) acquire an exclusive lock on the state file before any apply operation.
question: Your infrastructure team uses Terraform Cloud for remote state and applies. In CI, developers run `terraform plan` on every PR. You discover that two developers' PRs simultaneously modified the same resource — when both were merged, the second apply overwrote the first silently. What mechanism prevents this Terraform race condition?
roleContext: CI/CD Scenario #90 (L3) · 🔐 Supply Chain Security & Advanced CI/CD
intro: "When developers encounter this build or release bottleneck, my first goal is unblocking velocity safely. The interviewer is testing: Terraform state locking, Terraform Cloud run queuing.. I structure my answer around systematic triage first, root cause analysis second, and permanent remediation third."

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: This race condition is prevented by state locking. Terraform backend implementations (S3+DynamoDB, Terraform Cloud, etc.) acquire an exclusive lock on the state file before any apply operation. If a second apply tries to run while the first holds the lock, it fails immediately with a state lock error rather than proceeding. The underlying issue here is that both PRs passed plan independently (with accurate plans), but the second apply did not re-plan after the first apply changed the state. Terraform Cloud's native solution is Run Queuing — applies are serialised per workspace. The second run queues and then re-plans against the updated state before applying, so it sees the changes already made by the first apply and only does the diff required. For critical workspaces, enable plan and apply mode with manual confirmation to add a human gate before each apply.

steps.description: The architecture uses build isolation per tenant:
items: Isolated build namespaces: Each tenant gets a dedicated Kubernetes namespace or AWS CodeBuild project. Builds never share storage, network, or compute with another tenant.
Tenant config injection: A secure parameter store (AWS Secrets Manager) holds per-tenant config. The CI job assumes a tenant-specific IAM role that can only access that tenant's parameters.
Deterministic builds: The source code commit SHA is pinned at trigger time. The same SHA produces bitwise-identical output for the same tenant config — verifiable with checksums.

items: SBOM generation: After each build, syft generates a CycloneDX SBOM. This is signed with cosign using a tenant-specific private key and stored in their private S3 bucket.

steps.description: Feature flag rot is a process problem, not just a tooling one:
items: Expiry dates on flags: Require every flag created via your flag management tool (LaunchDarkly, Unleash) to have an explicit expiry date. After that date, the platform automatically disables the flag and creates a Jira ticket to remove the code.

Flag-removal PR as part of the release process: Add a pipeline step that checks for flags that have been at 100% rollout for >7 days and opens an automated PR removing the flag and its conditional branch.

steps.description: A systematic cost reduction framework:
items: Identify top spenders: GitHub's billing API exposes per-workflow minute usage. Export it and sort by cost. Focus optimisation on the top 10 workflows consuming 80% of spend.
Self-hosted runners for heavy jobs: Migrate compilation and Docker build jobs to spot EC2 instances (via Actions Runner Controller). Cost drops by ~70% for compute-heavy tasks.

Aggressive dependency caching: Calculate cache hit rates (GitHub shows this in each actions/cache step summary). A 30% cache hit rate means 70% of runs are downloading packages from scratch. Fix the cache key to be more stable.
Cancel redundant runs: Use concurrency groups with cancel-in-progress: true. If a developer pushes twice in 30 seconds, the first run is cancelled immediately.

steps.description: --- *More CI/CD scenarios added periodically. PRs welcome.*
items: Step-level parallelism: Replace sequential test steps with a build matrix, running tests in 4 parallel jobs. Total wall-clock time drops 4× but total minutes drop ~20% (faster = less idle time on expensive runners).
Right-size runners: Jobs that only run shell scripts don't need a 4-CPU runner. Use runs-on: ubuntu-latest (2 vCPU) for light jobs and runs-on: [self-hosted, large] only for heavy jobs.

summary: To limit container CPU without restarting it, run docker update --cpus 0.5 [container]. The daemon rewrites the container's cgroup CPU quota live, so the process keeps running with the same PID and state.
question: A container is consuming 100% CPU. How do you limit it without restarting?
intro: To limit container CPU without restarting it, run docker update --cpus 0.5 <container>. The daemon rewrites the container's cgroup CPU quota live, so the process keeps running with the same PID and state. Interviewers ask this because it separates people who know that resource limits are cgroup settings (adjustable at runtime) from those who only know docker run flags. A strong answer also covers containing the blast radius first, finding why the CPU is pegged, and making the limit permanent in Compose or your orchestrator so it survives the next redeploy.

steps.title: Mental model: CPU limits are live cgroup settings
steps.description: Docker translates CPU flags into cgroup files on the host, and the kernel scheduler enforces them, which is why they can change while the process runs.
items: Hard cap: --cpus sets a CFS quota (cgroup v2 cpu.max). The container is throttled once it uses its quota in a scheduling period.
Relative weight: --cpu-shares only matters under contention. It does not cap anything on an idle host, so it will not stop a container from using 100% of a free CPU.
Pinning: --cpuset-cpus restricts which cores the container may run on, useful for noisy-neighbour isolation.
Why no restart: these values live in the cgroup, not inside the image or process, so the daemon can rewrite them at runtime.

Cgroup versions: modern distributions default to cgroup v2 where the quota is cpu.max, while older hosts use v1 files such as cpu.cfs_quota_us. The Docker command is identical, but the paths you inspect differ.

steps.title: Hands-on: limit container CPU without restarting
steps.description: Identify the offender, apply the cap, and check that it took effect.
items: Find it: docker stats --no-stream shows CPU% per container. Note that 100% means one full core, so a busy multi-threaded process can show several hundred percent.
Apply the cap: docker update --cpus 1.5 my-app takes effect immediately for the running container.
Combine with memory carefully: if you lower --memory in the same call, also pass --memory-swap, otherwise the update can be rejected.
Restart policy: docker update --restart unless-stopped my-app uses the same mechanism if you also want crash recovery.

Safe first response: in an incident, cap the container first to protect neighbouring workloads on the same host, then investigate. A limit that is slightly too low is cheaper than a node where every service is starved.
steps.codeBlock:
docker stats --no-stream --format 'table {{.Name}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}\t{{.MemUsage}}'
# NAME     CPU %     MEM USAGE / LIMIT
# my-app   398.12%   612MiB / 15.6GiB

docker update --cpus 1.5 my-app      # prints: my-app
docker update --cpu-shares 512 my-app  # lower weight under contention

# Pin to cores 0 and 1 only
docker update --cpuset-cpus 0,1 my-app
steps.highlight: --cpus and the older --cpu-period/--cpu-quota flags express the same limit. Prefer --cpus and do not mix them.

steps.title: Verify the limit is actually enforced
steps.description: Never trust the command output alone. Confirm the setting and watch throttling.
items: Inspect the config: docker inspect --format '{{.HostConfig.NanoCpus}}' my-app should show 1500000000 for 1.5 CPUs.
Watch live usage: docker stats my-app should settle near 150% instead of the earlier spike.

Read the cgroup (v2): on the host, cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-<full-id>.scope/cpu.max shows quota and period. With the cgroupfs driver the path differs, so check docker info for the cgroup driver and version.
Check throttling: cpu.stat in the same directory reports nr_throttled and throttled_usec. Rising values prove the cap is biting.

What to capture: before changing anything, save docker logs, docker top and a quick docker stats sample so the evidence exists for the post-incident review even if the problem disappears after throttling.

steps.title: Failure modes: a cap treats the symptom, not the cause
steps.description: Limiting CPU buys time. You still need to learn why the process is spinning.
items: Inspect processes: docker top my-app maps container processes to host PIDs, which you can profile with top -H -p <pid> or perf top -p <pid>.
Typical causes: an infinite retry loop, a runaway regex or GC thrash, a traffic spike, or a crypto-miner in a compromised image. Check docker logs --since 10m my-app and the image provenance.
Throttling hurts latency: a too-tight quota makes request-serving apps stall in bursts even though average CPU looks fine. Raise the cap if p99 latency worsens.
Kubernetes caveat: pod CPU limits are not resizable in place on 1.28-1.31 without enabling an alpha feature gate, so the equivalent there is editing the Deployment and letting it roll.

Decide whether to scale: if the load is legitimate traffic rather than a bug, a cap only moves the pain to users. Add replicas behind the load balancer or raise capacity instead of throttling real demand.

steps.title: Production practice: make the limit permanent
steps.description: docker update changes are lost when the container is recreated from its original definition.
items: Compose: set deploy.resources.limits.cpus (or service-level cpus) and run docker compose up -d to recreate with the new value.
Alert before it pages: export cAdvisor or Docker metrics to Prometheus and alert on sustained CPU near the limit plus throttling ratio.
Defaults: make limits mandatory in templates so no container ships without a cap.
Review cadence: revisit limits after each release, because a new code path can change the CPU profile, and stale limits are a common source of mysterious latency regressions.
steps.codeBlock:
services:
  my-app:
    image: registry.example.com/my-app:1.4.2
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.5"
          memory: 1G

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: docker update is a stopgap. Record the new value in Compose or your manifest the same day, or the next recreate silently brings the 100% CPU problem back.
elevatorPitch: A container at 100% CPU: I contain it with docker update --cpus, which edits the live cgroup quota with no restart.
I verify with docker inspect NanoCpus, docker stats, and the cgroup cpu.stat throttling counters, then profile the process to find the real cause.
I then codify the limit in Compose or the orchestrator and alert on CPU throttling so it never needs a manual fix again.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using only --cpu-shares to stop a hog
mistakesToAvoid.why: Shares are relative weights and do nothing on an otherwise idle host, so the container still takes every free core.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming docker update persists
mistakesToAvoid.why: It changes the running container only. Recreating from the Compose file or run command restores the old, unlimited settings.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Reading 100% in docker stats as the whole machine
mistakesToAvoid.why: 100% equals one core, so a multi-threaded process can legitimately show several hundred percent. Compare against the number of CPUs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Capping so tightly that latency suffers
mistakesToAvoid.why: CFS throttling pauses all threads for the rest of a period, causing latency spikes in request-driven services.

title: Docker Q11: How do you share data between the host and a container [L2]
summary: To share data between the host and a container, mount it: use a bind mount (-v /host/path:/container/path) to expose a specific host directory, or a named volume that Docker manages for persistent data.
question: How do you share data between the host and a container?
intro: To share data between the host and a container, mount it: use a bind mount (-v /host/path:/container/path) to expose a specific host directory, or a named volume that Docker manages for persistent data. Interviewers ask this to see whether you know the three mount types, understand why container writes disappear on removal, and can debug the classic permission and path problems. A good answer explains when each type fits, shows the modern --mount syntax, and mentions read-only mounts, UID mapping and SELinux labels.

steps.title: Mental model: three ways to mount data
steps.description: A container's writable layer is deleted with the container, so anything worth keeping must live in a mount.
items: Bind mount: maps an existing host path into the container. Great for source code in development and for config files. The host path must exist for the container to see real data.
Named volume: storage created and managed by Docker under its data root (typically /var/lib/docker/volumes). Best for databases and anything that should be portable and independent of host layout.
tmpfs mount: memory-backed, never touches disk, gone when the container stops. Use it for secrets or scratch space on Linux hosts.
Anonymous volume: created by a VOLUME instruction when you give no name. Hard to track and a common source of orphaned data.
Choosing quickly: if you want to edit files on the host and see them in the container, use a bind mount. If Docker should own the data and you only care that it persists, use a named volume.

steps.title: Hands-on: share data between the host and a container
steps.description: Prefer --mount in docs and scripts because it is explicit. -v remains common and fine.
items: Bind mount a directory: keeps host and container views of the same files in sync in both directions.
Named volume: docker volume create is optional because Docker creates it on first use.
Read-only: append ,readonly (or :ro with -v) so the container cannot modify host files.
Behavioural difference: with -v a missing host path is silently created as a root-owned directory, while --mount type=bind fails with an error, which catches typos.
Backups of volumes: run a short-lived helper container that mounts the volume read-only and writes a tarball to a bind-mounted host directory. This works without knowing the host path of the volume.
steps.codeBlock:
# Bind mount, host dir is shared both ways
docker run -d --name web \
  --mount type=bind,source="$(pwd)/site",target=/usr/share/nginx/html,readonly \
  nginx:1.27

# Named volume for persistent database files
docker run -d --name db \
  --mount type=volume,source=pgdata,target=/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=change-me postgres:16

# Short form of the same bind mount
docker run -d -v "$(pwd)/site:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro" nginx:1.27
steps.highlight: A named volume that is empty is populated from the image content at the mount path on first use. A bind mount does not do this and hides whatever the image had there.

steps.title: Verify what is actually mounted
steps.description: Confirm the mount, the direction of data flow and the permissions.
items: List mounts: docker inspect --format '{{json .Mounts}}' web shows type, source, destination and read/write mode.
Test both directions: create a file on the host and docker exec web ls /usr/share/nginx/html, then write inside and check the host.
Volume details: docker volume inspect pgdata gives the Mountpoint on the host. Treat that path as read-only for debugging, not as an edit target.
Find orphans: docker volume ls -f dangling=true lists volumes no container references.
Compose behaviour: named volumes declared at the top level survive docker compose down. Only docker compose down -v removes them, which is a classic way to lose a development database by accident.

steps.title: Failure modes: permissions, SELinux and Docker Desktop
steps.description: Most bind mount problems are not Docker bugs but identity and path problems.
items: UID mismatch: files are owned by numeric IDs. If the container runs as UID 1000 and the host directory belongs to root, writes fail with Permission denied. Fix with --user $(id -u):$(id -g) or chown the directory.
SELinux hosts (RHEL, Fedora): add :z (shared) or :Z (private) to relabel the content. Never relabel system directories such as /home or /usr.
Docker Desktop: the host path must be in a shared location, and bind mounts cross a VM boundary, so heavy file I/O such as node_modules is slower than a named volume.
Mount hides content: mounting over a non-empty image directory makes the original files invisible, a frequent cause of missing configs.

Sharing between containers: the same named volume can be mounted into several containers, for example a web server and a log shipper, but concurrent writers still need application-level coordination to avoid corruption.

steps.title: Production practice: choose by lifecycle
steps.description: Match the mount type to who owns the data.
items: Prod data: named volumes or a volume driver for network storage, with backups taken via a helper container using --volumes-from or tar.
Dev code: bind mounts, or Compose develop.watch sync, to avoid rebuilding on each edit.
Hardening: run the container as a non-root user, mount config as read-only, and avoid mounting /var/run/docker.sock unless truly required because it grants root-equivalent control of the host.
Remote storage: for multi-host setups, use a volume driver or network filesystem. Bind mounts to NFS paths work but add latency and locking caveats that surface under load.
steps.codeBlock:
services:
  api:
    image: registry.example.com/my-api:2.0
    volumes:
      - ./config:/app/config:ro      # bind, read-only
      - api-data:/var/lib/api        # named volume
volumes:
  api-data:

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Use bind mounts to share code or config and named volumes for state. If a bind mount write fails, compare id inside the container with ls -ln on the host before blaming Docker.
elevatorPitch: Containers lose their writable layer on removal, so I share or persist data through mounts: bind mounts, named volumes or tmpfs.
I verify with docker inspect on .Mounts, test writes in both directions, and check numeric UID and SELinux labels when permissions fail.
In production I use named volumes with backups, mount config read-only, and never expose the Docker socket casually.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Docker silently creates an empty root-owned directory, so the app starts with no data. Use --mount to get a hard error.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Bind mounting over a populated image directory
mistakesToAvoid.why: The mount hides the image's files, which breaks apps that expect default configs or assets there.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring numeric UID/GID ownership
mistakesToAvoid.why: Names do not map between host and container, so write failures look random until you compare IDs.

mistakesToAvoid.why: They are unnamed, easy to orphan and hard to back up. Name volumes explicitly.

title: Docker BuildKit: Architecture, Parallel Stage Execution & Why It Replaces Classic Docker Builder
summary: Deep dive into Docker BuildKit: directed acyclic graph (DAG) stage parallelism, skipping unreferenced stages, cache mounts, secret injection without image leakage, and buildx remote caching.
question: What is Docker BuildKit, how does its DAG-based execution engine work under the hood, and why is it vastly superior to the classic Docker builder?
intro: "Container stability relies on clean signal handling (SIGTERM vs SIGKILL) and immutable image tagging. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

steps.title: DAG-Based Concurrent Execution
steps.description: The classic Docker builder executed Dockerfile instructions sequentially from top to bottom, one single line at a time:
items: BuildKit Concurrent Graph: BuildKit parses the Dockerfile into a low-level intermediate representation (LLB) and constructs a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of dependencies.
Parallel Execution: Independent stages (e.g. building a React frontend and compiling a Go backend) execute completely in parallel across available CPU cores.
Dead-Code Elimination: If a stage in the Dockerfile is not referenced by the final target image or any intermediate copy, BuildKit skips it entirely, saving massive build time.

steps.title: Persistent Cache Mounts (RUN --mount=type=cache)
steps.description: Package managers (npm, pip, go mod, maven) normally redownload dependencies when source code invalidates an earlier layer:
items: Syntax: RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build go build -o app .
No Image Bloat: Cache directory contents persist on the build host across subsequent CI builds, but are never copied into the final image layers.

steps.title: Zero-Leak Secret Mounts (RUN --mount=type=secret)
steps.description: Eliminating ARG / ENV secret leakage anti-patterns:
items: Syntax: RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm install
Secure Memory Mount: The secret file is temporarily mounted in a tmpfs memory filesystem during the execution of that specific command only, leaving zero traces in the committed image layer.

keyTakeaway: BuildKit modernizes container builds through DAG-based parallelism, automatic stage pruning, host-level cache mounts, and leak-free secret mounting.
elevatorPitch: Enabled BuildKit across enterprise CI/CD runners via DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1.
Leveraged RUN --mount=type=cache to cache package dependencies, slashing build times from 18 minutes to 90 seconds.
Replaced insecure ARG secrets with RUN --mount=type=secret to eliminate credential leaks in image layers.
Parallelized multi-stage microservice builds using BuildKit's DAG scheduler.

title: Docker Q19: How do you inspect a running containers environment variables and configuration [L2]
summary: To inspect a running container, use docker inspect for the configuration Docker recorded (env, mounts, ports, limits) and docker exec or /proc/[pid]/environ for what the process actually sees.
question: How do you inspect a running container's environment variables and configuration?
intro: To inspect a running container, use docker inspect for the configuration Docker recorded (env, mounts, ports, limits) and docker exec or /proc/<pid>/environ for what the process actually sees. These are different sources of truth, and interviewers ask this question to see whether you know the difference. Config drift, a missing variable or a wrong entrypoint is usually found in minutes if you read the right layer: image metadata, container creation settings, or live process state. A senior engineer also knows that environment variables are readable by anyone with Docker socket access.

steps.title: Know What Each Inspection Source Tells You
steps.description: There are three layers, and each answers a different question about the container.
items: Recorded config: docker inspect returns JSON built at container creation: .Config.Env, .Config.Cmd, .Config.Entrypoint, .HostConfig (limits, restart policy), .Mounts and .NetworkSettings.
Live process state: docker exec and /proc show what is running now, including files and variables changed after start.
Runtime metrics: docker stats, docker top and docker logs cover resource use, process tree and output.
Image vs container: use --type container when an image and a container share a name, so you do not read the wrong object.
steps.highlight: .Config.Env is the environment Docker set, not necessarily what the app is using now. If the app reads a config file or mutates its own environment, only live inspection will show it.

steps.title: Query Config With docker inspect and Go Templates
steps.description: Filter the JSON instead of scrolling a 200-line dump.
items: Environment variables: print one per line with a range template, or pipe to jq.
Startup command: compare .Config.Entrypoint and .Config.Cmd to confirm what actually launches.
Limits and policy: .HostConfig.Memory, .HostConfig.NanoCpus and .HostConfig.RestartPolicy explain OOM kills and restart loops.
State: .State.Status, .State.ExitCode, .State.OOMKilled and .State.Health.Status.
steps.codeBlock:
# Environment variables, one per line
docker inspect --format '{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}' my-app

# Same with jq
docker inspect my-app | jq -r '.[0].Config.Env[]'

# Entrypoint, command, mounts, network
docker inspect -f '{{json .Config.Entrypoint}} {{json .Config.Cmd}}' my-app
docker inspect -f '{{json .Mounts}}' my-app | jq .
docker inspect -f '{{range .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{.IPAddress}}{{end}}' my-app

# Why did it die or restart?
docker inspect -f 'status={{.State.Status}} exit={{.State.ExitCode}} oom={{.State.OOMKilled}}' my-app

steps.title: Verify the Live Process Environment
steps.description: Confirm what the running process actually received, not only what was configured.
items: Exec a shell command: docker exec my-app env shows the environment of a new process in the container, which matches the configured env but not variables the app changed internally.
Read PID 1 directly: /proc/1/environ is the environment PID 1 was started with; entries are NUL-separated, so translate them.
Check processes and ports: docker top my-app and docker port my-app confirm what is running and published.
Filesystem drift: docker diff my-app lists files added (A), changed (C) or deleted (D) versus the image.
steps.codeBlock:
docker exec my-app env | sort
docker exec my-app sh -c "tr '\0' '\n' < /proc/1/environ"
docker top my-app
docker port my-app
docker diff my-app | head
docker stats --no-stream my-app

steps.title: Handle Images With No Shell and Other Edge Cases
steps.description: Minimal images and stopped containers need a different approach.
items: No shell in the image: distroless and scratch images fail on docker exec ... sh. Attach a debug container that shares the target's namespaces: docker run --rm -it --pid=container:my-app --net=container:my-app busybox sh.
Process env from the sidecar: with a shared PID namespace, run cat /proc/1/environ inside the busybox container; this typically works when you run as the same user or root.
Stopped containers: docker inspect still works on exited containers, so you can read the exit code and config after a crash; docker exec does not.
Compose projects: docker compose config prints the resolved configuration after variable interpolation and overrides, which finds most "wrong env" bugs before the container even starts.
steps.highlight: Kubernetes equivalent: kubectl exec for env and kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container> for shell-less images.

steps.title: Treat Inspect Output as Sensitive and Automate Checks
steps.description: Environment variables are plaintext to anyone who can reach the Docker daemon.
items: Secret exposure: any user in the docker group can read every variable with docker inspect; prefer file-based secrets (Docker/Swarm secrets, mounted files) for passwords and keys.
Redact before sharing: never paste raw docker inspect output into tickets; filter to the fields you need.
Drift checks in CI: a smoke-test step can assert expected values, for example docker inspect -f '{{.Config.User}}' my-app is not empty or root.
Log the evidence: capture inspect output of a failing container as a pipeline artifact after scrubbing secrets.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Read docker inspect for what Docker configured and /proc/1/environ for what the process started with; when they disagree, the bug is usually an entrypoint script rewriting the environment.
elevatorPitch: I use docker inspect with Go-template filters to read the recorded env, entrypoint, mounts and limits, and docker exec or /proc/1/environ to see the live process.
For shell-less images I attach a busybox container sharing the target's PID and network namespaces, and docker diff shows filesystem drift.
I treat inspect output as sensitive, keep secrets out of env vars, and add small inspect-based assertions to CI smoke tests.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming .Config.Env equals the running process environment
mistakesToAvoid.why: An entrypoint script can export, unset or rewrite variables, so the process may see different values than Docker recorded.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running docker exec sh on a distroless or scratch image
mistakesToAvoid.why: There is no shell binary, so it fails; use a namespace-sharing debug container instead.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Pasting full docker inspect output into chats or tickets
mistakesToAvoid.why: It includes every environment variable, which often means database passwords and API tokens.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Inspecting the image when you meant the container
mistakesToAvoid.why: Image metadata shows build-time defaults and misses run-time overrides such as -e flags and --env-file.
