title: Docker Q21: How do you get a shell inside a running container [L1]
summary: docker exec -it <container> bash or sh if bash isn't available.
question: How do you get a shell inside a running container?
intro: To get a shell inside a running container, run docker exec -it <container> sh (or bash when the image ships it). exec starts a new process in the container's existing namespaces, so leaving the shell does not stop the container. Interviewers ask this to check you know the difference from docker attach and docker run, and what to do when there is no shell at all, as in distroless or scratch images. Strong answers cover debugging safely without changing production state.

steps.title: Mental model: exec starts a second process
steps.description: A container is just processes isolated by namespaces and cgroups. docker exec joins those namespaces with a new process.
items: exec: spawns an additional process (your shell) inside a running container. Exiting it does not affect the main process.
attach: connects your terminal to the container's main process (PID 1) stdin/stdout. Pressing Ctrl+C or exiting can stop the container, so it is rarely what you want for debugging.
run: creates a brand-new container. docker run -it image sh is for exploring an image, not the live instance.
Flags: -i keeps stdin open, -t allocates a TTY. Use both for interactive shells.
Choosing the shell: to learn what is available, try docker exec my-app sh -c 'echo $0; ls /bin' or inspect the image with docker image inspect for its default command and user.

steps.title: Hands-on: get a shell inside a running container
steps.description: Pick the shell that exists in the image and the user you need.
items: Alpine and BusyBox images: only sh exists by default, so bash fails with executable file not found.
Run as root: --user 0 (or -u root) helps when the app user cannot install or inspect things. Use it sparingly on production.
Set context: -w /app sets the working directory and -e KEY=value adds a variable for that session only.
Compose: docker compose exec web sh targets a service by name without finding the container name.

Environment differences: an exec session does not run the container's entrypoint script, so variables set by that script may be missing. Use docker exec my-app env and compare with the application's own view.
steps.codeBlock:
docker ps --format 'table {{.Names}}\t{{.Image}}\t{{.Status}}'
docker exec -it my-app sh                 # BusyBox/Alpine
docker exec -it my-app bash               # Debian/Ubuntu based
docker exec -it -u 0 -w /app my-app sh    # root, in /app
docker exec my-app cat /etc/os-release    # one-off, no TTY needed

docker compose exec web sh

steps.title: When the image has no shell
steps.description: Distroless and scratch images deliberately omit shells and package managers, so exec sh fails.
items: Share namespaces from a debug container: start a tooling image attached to the target's PID and network namespaces.
Docker Debug: docker debug <container> is available in recent Docker Desktop and CLI releases (check your subscription and version) and injects a toolbox without modifying the image.
Kubernetes equivalent: kubectl debug -it pod/my-app --image=busybox:1.36 --target=app adds an ephemeral container.
Copy files out instead: sometimes docker cp and reading logs is all you need.
Non-interactive use: in scripts drop -t and use -i only when piping input. A TTY in CI logs produces carriage returns and breaks automation.
steps.codeBlock:
# Debug sidecar sharing the target's PID and network namespaces
docker run --rm -it \
  --pid=container:my-app --net=container:my-app \
  nicolaka/netshoot sh
# ps aux  -> shows the app's processes
# ss -tlnp -> shows its listening sockets
steps.highlight: The debug container sees the target's processes and network but not its filesystem by default. Reach it through /proc/<pid>/root when your privileges allow.

steps.title: Verify and handle common errors
steps.description: Read the error text, because each one points at a different cause.
items: Container is not running: docker exec only works on running containers. Check docker ps -a and docker logs. For a crashed one, start a copy with docker run -it --entrypoint sh image.
OCI runtime exec failed: usually means the binary (bash) is not in the image. Try sh.
Confirm where you are: inside the shell, hostname equals the container ID and ps shows few processes, proving you are in the container, not the host.
Garbled terminal: missing -t causes odd line handling. Resize problems often fix with stty rows 40 cols 120.
Exited containers: to look inside a crashed container's files, either docker cp out the paths you need or create an image from it with docker commit and run that image with an overridden entrypoint.

steps.title: Production practice: debug without drift
steps.description: Shell access in production is a change surface, so treat it that way.
items: Immutable mindset: do not install tools or edit files in a live container. They vanish on redeploy and hide the true state.
Audit access: limit who can reach the Docker socket or kubectl exec, and log exec events through audit tooling.
Prefer observability: logs, metrics and traces answer most questions, leaving exec for last-resort inspection.
Remote hosts: use a Docker context or SSH to reach the daemon, for example docker --context prod exec -it my-app sh, rather than sharing the daemon port unauthenticated over the network.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Use docker exec rather than attach, and for distroless images join the target's namespaces with a debug container instead of rebuilding the image with a shell.
elevatorPitch: I run docker exec -it container sh, which starts a new process in the running container's namespaces and leaves the main process untouched.
If bash is missing I use sh, and for distroless images I attach a debug container with --pid and --net, or use kubectl debug in Kubernetes.
I treat the session as read-only inspection and move fixes into the image or manifest.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using docker attach to get a shell
mistakesToAvoid.why: It connects to PID 1, so exiting or Ctrl+C can stop the container.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming bash exists in every image
mistakesToAvoid.why: Alpine and many slim images only have sh, producing an executable-not-found error.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Installing debug tools in a live container
mistakesToAvoid.why: Changes are lost on recreate and make the running state diverge from the image.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting that exec needs a running container
mistakesToAvoid.why: A crash-looping container cannot be exec'd into. Inspect logs or run the image with an overridden entrypoint instead.

title: Docker Q22: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container [L1]
summary: Image = read-only template (blueprint). Container = running instance of an image.
question: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?
intro: The difference between a Docker image and a container is that an image is an immutable, layered template (filesystem plus metadata), while a container is a running or stopped instance of that image with its own writable layer, process and network. Interviewers use this basic question to check whether you understand why containers are disposable, why data needs volumes, and why one image can start many containers. Good answers go beyond the class and object analogy to layers, copy-on-write and content-addressable IDs.

steps.title: Mental model: template versus instance
steps.description: The image is what you build and ship. The container is what you run. Interviewers often follow up by asking where data lives, so keep the layer picture in mind throughout your answer.
items: Image: an ordered stack of read-only layers plus a config (default command, environment, exposed ports). It is identified by a content digest such as sha256:... and by tags that are movable labels.
Container: a process (or set of processes) started from an image, isolated with namespaces and limited by cgroups, with a thin writable layer on top.
Copy-on-write: reads fall through to image layers. When a container modifies a file, it is copied into the writable layer, and the image stays untouched.
One to many: a single image can back hundreds of containers that share the same read-only layers on disk.

Image identity: an image ID is derived from its configuration and layer digests, so identical content has the same ID wherever it is built or pulled. A container ID is random and unique to that instance.

steps.title: Hands-on: image vs container in practice
steps.description: List each with the right command and watch the relationship.
items: Images: docker images or docker image ls shows repository, tag, ID and size.
Containers: docker ps -a shows running and stopped containers and the image each came from.
Create versus start: docker create makes the container (writable layer) without running it, docker start runs it, and docker run does both.
Trace the link: docker inspect --format '{{.Image}}' my-app returns the image ID the container was created from.
Lifecycle states: an image is either present or absent. A container moves through created, running, paused, exited and removed, and each state is visible in docker ps -a.
steps.codeBlock:
docker pull nginx:1.27
docker run -d --name a nginx:1.27
docker run -d --name b nginx:1.27     # second container, same image

docker images nginx                   # 1 image
docker ps --filter ancestor=nginx:1.27 --format '{{.Names}}'
# a
# b

docker history nginx:1.27 | head      # image layers, read-only

steps.title: Verify the writable layer and immutability
steps.description: Prove that changes land in the container, not the image.
items: Make a change: docker exec a sh -c 'echo hi > /tmp/x'.
See the diff: docker diff a lists added (A), changed (C) and deleted (D) paths in that container's layer only.
Check the sibling: container b does not have /tmp/x, and the image is unchanged.
Remove it: docker rm -f a deletes the writable layer and the file with it. This is why state belongs in volumes.
Size accounting: docker ps -s shows the writable layer size and the virtual size including the image. A large writable layer is a hint that the app writes data that should be in a volume.
steps.codeBlock:
docker exec a sh -c 'echo hi > /tmp/x'
docker diff a
# A /tmp/x
docker exec b ls /tmp/x
# ls: cannot access '/tmp/x': No such file or directory
docker rm -f a    # writable layer gone

steps.title: Edge cases and common confusions
steps.description: Interviewers often probe the corners of the model. Check each symptom against the evidence before changing anything.
items: Committing a container: docker commit turns a container's layer into a new image. It works but is not reproducible. Prefer a Dockerfile.
Tags are not images: re-pushing app:latest moves the tag. The old image loses its tag and may become dangling.
Stopped is not gone: an exited container still holds its writable layer and keeps the image from being removed until you docker rm it.
Not a VM: containers share the host kernel. An image holds userland files, not a kernel.
Layer sharing: ten containers from one image do not use ten copies of the base layers. Only each container's own changes consume extra space, which is why starting many containers is cheap.

steps.title: Production practice: build once, run many
steps.description: The distinction drives release and operational habits.
items: Immutable deploys: promote the same image digest through dev, staging and prod rather than rebuilding per environment.
Pin by digest: image: repo/app@sha256:... guarantees the exact bytes run.
Housekeeping: remove exited containers with docker container prune and unused images with docker image prune, scheduled on build hosts.
Registry view: registries store images, never containers. To move a container's state elsewhere you must export its data, not push the container.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Say it in one line: an image is a read-only filesystem template, a container is that template plus a writable layer and a running process. Then demonstrate it with docker diff.
elevatorPitch: An image is an immutable, layered template identified by a digest. A container is a runtime instance of it with a thin writable layer and isolated processes.
I show the relationship with docker ps --filter ancestor and docker diff, which proves writes stay in the container.
I automate by building once, pinning by digest and pruning stopped containers and unused images on build hosts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating a container as a place to store data
mistakesToAvoid.why: Its writable layer is deleted on docker rm, so data written there is lost. Use volumes.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Saying images contain a kernel
mistakesToAvoid.why: Containers use the host kernel. Images only carry userland files and metadata.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Confusing a tag with an image
mistakesToAvoid.why: Tags are mutable pointers. The same tag can reference different content over time, so pin by digest for reproducibility.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using docker commit as a build process
mistakesToAvoid.why: The result is undocumented and not reproducible, unlike an image built from a versioned Dockerfile.

title: Docker Q23: How do you copy a file from a container to the host [L2]
summary: docker cp <container>:/path/to/file /host/path.
question: How do you copy a file from a container to the host?
intro: To copy a file from a container to the host, use docker cp <container>:/path/in/container /path/on/host. It works on running and stopped containers and does not need a shell or tar in the image. Interviewers ask it because it is an everyday debugging task with several traps: ownership, symlinks, mounted paths and the fact that you can pull files from a crashed container for forensics. A thorough answer lists alternatives such as bind mounts, streaming tar and BuildKit --output for build artifacts.

steps.title: Mental model: docker cp talks to the daemon
steps.description: Unlike exec cat, docker cp reads the container filesystem through the Docker API, so the container does not have to run or contain any tools. Choose the method by whether the container is running, how big the data is, and whether the task will repeat.
items: Direction: either way works. docker cp c:/src dest copies out, and docker cp src c:/dest copies in.
Stopped containers: the writable layer persists until removal, so you can recover logs and dumps from an exited container.
Directories: they copy recursively. A trailing /. on the source copies the contents rather than the directory itself.
No shell required: works with distroless and scratch images, where exec cannot help.
Path rules: the container path is always absolute inside the container filesystem, and relative host paths resolve against your current directory, so check pwd before copying large trees.

steps.title: Hands-on: copy a file from a container to the host
steps.description: Basic forms and the flags that matter.
items: Single file: copy to the current directory with ..
Directory contents: use /. to avoid nesting an extra folder.
Preserve ownership: -a (archive) copies UID/GID information. By default files on the host end up owned by the invoking user.
Follow symlinks: -L follows a symlink in the source path instead of copying the link.
Overwrite behaviour: copying onto an existing host file replaces it without prompting. Copy into a new directory when you are collecting evidence to avoid clobbering earlier captures.
steps.codeBlock:
docker cp my-app:/var/log/app/error.log ./error.log
docker cp my-app:/etc/nginx/. ./nginx-conf/        # contents only
docker cp -a my-app:/data ./data-backup           # keep UID/GID

# Works on a stopped container too
docker ps -a --filter name=my-app
docker cp my-app:/tmp/core.1234 ./core.1234

steps.title: Alternatives when cp is not enough
steps.description: Pick the method that fits automation, large trees or build artifacts.
items: Stream with tar: docker exec my-app tar -C /data -cf - . | tar -xf - -C ./out handles many files and lets you compress. It needs tar in the image.
Pipe a single file: docker exec my-app cat /etc/hosts > hosts.txt is simple but requires a running container and a cat binary.
Bind mount up front: if you know you will need the output, mount a host directory so files appear without copying.
Build artifacts: with BuildKit, docker build --output type=local,dest=./out . exports files from a build stage (for example a FROM scratch stage) with no container to manage.
Compose services: docker compose cp web:/app/out.txt ./out.txt addresses the service by name, which is convenient when container names include project prefixes.
steps.codeBlock:
# Stream a directory with compression
docker exec my-app tar -C /data -czf - . > data.tgz

# Export build output directly to the host (BuildKit)
docker build --target artifacts --output type=local,dest=./out .
ls ./out

steps.title: Verify the copy and avoid pitfalls
steps.description: A successful exit code does not guarantee you copied the right thing. Check each symptom against the evidence before changing anything.
items: Check integrity: compare sha256sum of the host file with docker exec my-app sha256sum /path when it matters.
Special mounts: files under tmpfs mounts and under /proc or /sys cannot be copied with docker cp. Read them with exec.
Permissions: unreadable output often means root ownership with -a. Fix with sudo chown.
Large or sensitive files: copying core dumps or database files can expose secrets. Store them with restricted permissions and delete after use.
Size awareness: copying a multi-gigabyte directory goes through the daemon and can fill the host disk. Check docker exec my-app du -sh /path first.

steps.title: Production practice: avoid manual copies
steps.description: Repeated copying is a sign that output should go somewhere durable.
items: Ship logs and dumps out: write logs to stdout and use a log driver or agent. Mount a volume for heap dumps.
Kubernetes: kubectl cp ns/pod:/path ./path requires tar in the container. kubectl exec with cat or ephemeral containers works otherwise.
CI artifacts: use BuildKit --output or your CI artifact upload rather than docker cp from a leftover container.
Remote daemons: with a remote Docker context the file lands on your local machine, not the remote host, which is useful for pulling diagnostics but slow over poor links.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: docker cp works on stopped containers and needs no shell, which makes it the first move for pulling logs or dumps from a crashed container before you remove it.
elevatorPitch: I use docker cp container:/path ./dest, which reads through the daemon so it works on stopped containers and shell-less images.
I verify with a checksum and use -a when ownership matters, or tar streaming for large trees.
For repeat needs I mount volumes or use BuildKit --output instead of manual copying.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Removing a crashed container before copying its files
mistakesToAvoid.why: The writable layer disappears with the container. Copy logs and dumps first.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting docker cp to read tmpfs or /proc
mistakesToAvoid.why: It does not support those mounts, so you get errors or empty results. Use exec to read them.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting the trailing /. on directories
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without it you copy the directory itself, creating an unexpected nested folder.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using exec cat on binary files via a TTY
mistakesToAvoid.why: Allocating a TTY (-t) can corrupt binary output. Use docker cp or no -t.

title: Docker Q24: Your container image build is failing on apt-get update Whats likely wrong [L2]
summary: A build failing on apt-get update is usually a network or repository problem, not an apt bug: DNS or proxy settings inside the build, an end-of-life release whose repos moved, an expired or missing GPG key, or a clock mismatch.
question: Your container image build is failing on `apt-get update`. What's likely wrong?
intro: A build failing on apt-get update is usually a network or repository problem, not an apt bug: DNS or proxy settings inside the build, an end-of-life release whose repos moved, an expired or missing GPG key, or a clock mismatch. Interviewers ask it to see whether you troubleshoot in order, using the exact error text rather than guessing. The runbook is to reproduce outside the build, read the specific error, isolate network from repository issues, fix the root cause and then harden the Dockerfile so it stays reliable.

steps.title: Symptom to cause map
steps.description: Start from the message, because each one points at a different layer.
items: Temporary failure resolving 'deb.debian.org': DNS. The build container cannot resolve names, often due to a corporate resolver or a broken /etc/docker/daemon.json DNS setting.
Could not connect / connection timed out: proxy, firewall, or an IPv6 route that does not work.

404 Not Found or 'does not have a Release file': the distribution is end of life and its repos moved. For example EOL Debian releases go to archive.debian.org and EOL non-LTS Ubuntu releases to old-releases.ubuntu.com.
NO_PUBKEY, invalid signatures, 'Release file is not valid yet': missing or expired key, or clock skew, often on a Docker Desktop VM after sleep.
Hash Sum mismatch: a caching proxy or mirror in the middle serving partial content.

steps.title: Hands-on: reproduce a build failing on apt-get update
steps.description: Remove Docker build noise and test the failing step in isolation. Change one variable at a time so the result is attributable.
items: Full output: rerun with docker build --progress=plain --no-cache . to see every line and bypass a cached bad layer.
Same base, interactively: run the base image and execute the command by hand.
Test DNS and connectivity: check resolution and an HTTPS fetch from a throwaway container.
Try the host network: docker build --network host . tells you whether Docker's bridge networking is the culprit.

Architecture mismatch: on ARM builders or emulated builds some third-party repositories do not publish the architecture you need, and apt-get update warns or fails for that source only. Check dpkg --print-architecture.
steps.codeBlock:
docker build --progress=plain --no-cache -t test .

docker run --rm -it debian:bookworm bash -c 'apt-get update'
docker run --rm busybox nslookup deb.debian.org
docker run --rm curlimages/curl -sSI https://deb.debian.org

# Is it Docker's bridge network?
docker build --network host -t test .

steps.title: Fix the root cause
steps.description: Apply the fix that matches the diagnosis.
items: DNS: set resolvers in /etc/docker/daemon.json (for example {"dns": ["10.0.0.2", "8.8.8.8"]} using your resolver), then restart the daemon.
Proxy: pass --build-arg HTTP_PROXY=... --build-arg HTTPS_PROXY=.... These are predefined build args and do not need an ARG line. Add your corporate CA with ca-certificates if TLS is intercepted.
EOL release: the real fix is a supported base image tag. As a stopgap point sources at the archive host.
Clock or keys: restart Docker Desktop to resync the VM clock. For third-party repos, install the signing key into /etc/apt/keyrings with signed-by= instead of the deprecated apt-key.
IPv6 problems: if the build host has a broken IPv6 route, apt may hang trying AAAA addresses first. Forcing IPv4 with -o Acquire::ForceIPv4=true confirms it as the cause.
steps.codeBlock:
# Stopgap for an EOL Debian release (prefer upgrading the base image)
RUN sed -i 's|deb.debian.org|archive.debian.org|g' /etc/apt/sources.list

# Proxy at build time
# docker build --build-arg HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.example.com:3128 .

steps.title: Harden the Dockerfile pattern
steps.description: Many intermittent failures come from how the step is written. Treat the Dockerfile as code that runs on many networks, not only yours.
items: Combine in one layer: apt-get update && apt-get install in one RUN. A separate cached update layer goes stale and later installs hit 404 on outdated package indexes.
Non-interactive: set DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive for the step only and use -y.
Retries: -o Acquire::Retries=3 smooths over transient mirror hiccups.
Clean up: remove /var/lib/apt/lists/* in the same layer to keep the image small.
Ownership of the fix: network and proxy issues belong to platform or network teams, so bring them the exact failing hostname and command output rather than a vague report that the build is broken.
steps.codeBlock:
RUN apt-get update -o Acquire::Retries=3 \
 && DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
      ca-certificates curl \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

steps.title: Verification and prevention
steps.description: Confirm the fix and keep it from recurring.
items: Verify: a clean docker build --no-cache passes, and CI passes on a fresh runner, not only on your cached laptop.
Mirror dependencies: use an internal package mirror or pull-through registry so builds do not depend on public mirrors.
Track base image EOL: schedule base image upgrades and scan for unsupported distributions.
Pin and rebuild regularly: pin base images by digest and rebuild weekly so repo drift shows up early.
BuildKit secrets: if a private repository needs credentials, pass them with a BuildKit secret mount, never as a build argument that gets stored in image history.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Always copy the first error line from --progress=plain output. DNS, EOL repo and GPG errors look similar in a failing build but need entirely different fixes.
elevatorPitch: I reproduce the failure with --progress=plain --no-cache and by running apt-get update by hand in the base image.
I classify by message: DNS or proxy, EOL repositories, GPG or clock, or a bad mirror, and test DNS and HTTPS from a throwaway container.
I fix the cause, keep update and install in a single layer with retries, and use a supported, pinned base image with an internal mirror.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Putting apt-get update in its own RUN layer
mistakesToAvoid.why: The layer is cached, so a later install can use a stale index and fail with 404 errors.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Staying on an EOL base image and patching sources forever
mistakesToAvoid.why: Repos move and eventually stop updating, so security fixes are gone. Upgrade the base image.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using apt-key add or disabling signature checks
mistakesToAvoid.why: apt-key is deprecated and bypassing signatures removes supply-chain protection. Use signed-by keyrings.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Debugging only with cached builds
mistakesToAvoid.why: A cached layer hides the failure on your machine while a clean CI runner breaks. Use --no-cache when diagnosing.

title: Docker Q29: What is the purpose of dockerignore [L2]
summary: A .dockerignore file lists paths that Docker leaves out of the build context, so they are never sent to the builder and cannot be copied into the image by COPY or ADD. It works much like .gitignore but applies to docker build.
question: What is the purpose of `.dockerignore`?
intro: A .dockerignore file lists paths that Docker leaves out of the build context, so they are never sent to the builder and cannot be copied into the image by COPY or ADD. It works much like .gitignore but applies to docker build. Interviewers ask about it because it affects three things at once: build speed, layer cache hits and accidental secret leakage. A good answer shows you know the context is uploaded before the first instruction runs, and that patterns have rules that differ from .gitignore.

steps.title: How .dockerignore Fits Into a Build
steps.description: The build context is the directory you pass to docker build, and .dockerignore filters it before anything else happens.
items: Context transfer: the client packages the context and sends it to the builder; without a filter, .git, node_modules and build output all go too.
Location: the file sits at the root of the context. With BuildKit, a file named <Dockerfile-name>.dockerignore next to the Dockerfile takes precedence for that Dockerfile.
Scope: it affects COPY, ADD and the context upload only. It does not change bind mounts at docker run time.
Matching: patterns are relative to the context root, a later rule overrides an earlier one, and ! re-includes a path.

steps.title: Write a Practical .dockerignore
steps.description: Start from what the image does not need at runtime, then verify nothing required is excluded.
items: VCS and editor files: .git, .idea, *.swp add size and change often.
Dependencies and artifacts: node_modules, target/, __pycache__ should be rebuilt inside the image for the right OS and architecture.
Secrets: .env, *.pem, .aws and *.tfstate must never enter a layer, because layers are permanent and extractable.
Recursive match: *.md matches only at the root; use **/*.md to match at any depth.
steps.codeBlock:
# .dockerignore
.git
.gitignore
.env
.env.*
*.pem
node_modules
**/__pycache__
**/*.log
coverage/
dist/
Dockerfile
.dockerignore
docker-compose*.yml

# Re-include a file that a broader rule excluded
!README.md

steps.title: Use an Allowlist and Verify the Result
steps.description: The safest pattern for large repos is to exclude everything and re-include only what the build needs.
items: Allowlist style: start with *, then add !package.json, !src. New files stay out by default.
Check context size: run docker build --progress=plain . and read the "transferring context" line; a drop from hundreds of MB to a few MB confirms the filter works.
Inspect what landed: a throwaway stage with COPY . /ctx and RUN find /ctx lists exactly what the builder received.
Cache effect: with COPY . . any changed file in the context invalidates that layer, so ignoring noisy files keeps later layers cached.
steps.codeBlock:
# .dockerignore (allowlist)
*
!package.json
!package-lock.json
!src/

# Debug stage: see what the builder actually received
# FROM busybox AS ctx
# COPY . /ctx
# RUN find /ctx -maxdepth 2

docker build --progress=plain --target ctx .
docker build --progress=plain -t my-app:dev .

steps.title: Failure Modes and Edge Cases
steps.description: Most .dockerignore bugs are over-exclusion or wrong pattern scope.
items: Build fails with "not found": a COPY source is excluded. Re-include it with !path after the broad rule.
Rule order: the last matching pattern wins, so a ! line placed before the exclusion has no effect.
Ignoring the Dockerfile: allowed; the builder still reads it, it is just not available to COPY.
Different from .gitignore: there is no per-directory file and no automatic recursion for patterns like *.log.
steps.highlight: Excluding .git is usually right, but tooling that stamps a version from git describe inside the build will break; pass the version as a --build-arg instead.

steps.title: Keep It Maintained in Production
steps.description: Treat the file as part of your supply-chain hygiene.
items: Review with the Dockerfile: change both in the same pull request when directory layout changes.
Secrets belong in build secrets: use RUN --mount=type=secret with BuildKit, not files copied into the context.
Monorepos: use a per-Dockerfile ignore file so each service sends only its own sources.
Defence in depth: combine it with multi-stage builds so build tooling and credentials stay out of the final image.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Prefer an allowlist (* then !src) in monorepos, and confirm it by checking the "transferring context" size in --progress=plain output.
elevatorPitch: .dockerignore excludes files from the build context so they are not uploaded to the builder or copied into the image.
It speeds builds, keeps COPY layers cached and stops secrets such as .env and keys leaking into permanent layers.
I verify it by checking the transferred context size, and in monorepos I use an allowlist plus per-Dockerfile ignore files.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using *.md and expecting it to match nested files
mistakesToAvoid.why: Patterns are anchored at the context root; nested matches need **/*.md.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Putting a ! re-include before the broad exclusion
mistakesToAvoid.why: The last matching rule wins, so the exclusion overrides the re-include.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on .dockerignore to hide secrets that are used at build time
mistakesToAvoid.why: If the file is excluded the build cannot use it, and if it is copied it stays in a layer; use BuildKit secret mounts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming it affects docker run -v bind mounts
mistakesToAvoid.why: It only filters the build context; mounted host paths are fully visible to the container.

title: Docker Q30: How do you implement health checks in Docker [L3]
summary: In Dockerfile: HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD curl -f http://localhost/health || exit 1. Docker marks container as healthy or unhealthy. Compose and orchestrators use this for readiness.
question: How do you implement health checks in Docker?
intro: "In an interview, I explain how we diagnosed container runtime failures without guessing. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: In Dockerfile: HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD curl -f http://localhost/health || exit 1. Docker marks container as healthy or unhealthy. Compose and orchestrators use this for readiness.

Run targeted verification commands before modifying configuration.
Automate permanent guardrails (CI check, alerts, IaC policy) to prevent recurrence.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Copying code before package manifests (`package.json`, `go.mod`, `requirements.txt`) invalidates the build cache on every commit, forcing slow full reinstalls.

title: Docker Q31: How do you build an image for multiple CPU architectures (AMD64 and ARM64) [L2]
summary: To build an image for multiple CPU architectures such as AMD64 and ARM64, use docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push.
question: How do you build an image for multiple CPU architectures (AMD64 and ARM64)?
intro: To build an image for multiple CPU architectures such as AMD64 and ARM64, use docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push. Buildx (BuildKit) produces one image per platform and publishes them under a single multi-platform manifest list, so each host pulls the matching variant automatically. Interviewers ask this because ARM servers and Apple Silicon laptops are common. They want to hear about emulation versus cross-compilation, base image support, and verifying the manifest.

steps.title: Mental model: manifest list plus per-platform images
steps.description: A tag like my-app:1.0 can point to an index that references several platform-specific images. Keep in mind that the build host and the target host may differ, which is the whole reason the platform flag exists.
items: Manifest list (image index): maps platforms such as linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 to image digests. The runtime picks the right one.
Three build strategies: QEMU emulation (simple, slow), cross-compilation in one builder (fast, needs language support), and native builders per architecture (fastest, more setup).
Base image must support every target: check that your FROM image publishes both platforms.

Local storage limit: with the classic image store the local daemon cannot hold a multi-platform image, so use --push or an OCI output. The containerd image store (optional in recent Docker releases) lifts this.
Why it matters: Apple Silicon laptops, AWS Graviton and other ARM nodes are common, and a single-architecture image forces developers to emulate or breaks deployment on mixed clusters.

steps.title: Hands-on: build an image for multiple CPU architectures
steps.description: Create a builder, enable emulation and push.
items: Create a builder: the default docker driver cannot do multi-platform builds on the classic store, so use a docker-container driver builder.
Register QEMU: binfmt handlers let an AMD64 host run ARM64 binaries during the build.
Build and push: authenticate to the registry first with docker login.
Single platform load: to test locally use --platform linux/arm64 --load for one architecture.
Tags and promotion: push one tag that resolves to the multi-platform index rather than separate -amd64 and -arm64 tags, so Kubernetes and Compose files stay architecture-agnostic.
steps.codeBlock:
docker buildx create --name multi --driver docker-container --use
docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install arm64   # QEMU handlers

docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  -t registry.example.com/my-app:1.0 \
  --push .

# Local test of one architecture
docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64 -t my-app:arm --load .

steps.title: Make it fast: cross-compile instead of emulate
steps.description: Running the compiler under QEMU can be many times slower. Let the build stage run natively and target the other platform.
items: Pin the build stage to the builder's platform: FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM.
Use automatic args: BuildKit sets TARGETOS, TARGETARCH and BUILDPLATFORM. Declare them with ARG to use them.
Final stage runs on target: copy the compiled binary into a small base image for each platform.
Works best for Go, Rust and similar: interpreted stacks and native dependencies (Python wheels, Node addons) may need an emulated or native build.
Pull behaviour: if a platform is missing from the index, the runtime reports no matching manifest. This error is the signature of a build that only produced one architecture.
steps.codeBlock:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang:1.22 AS build
ARG TARGETOS TARGETARCH
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=$TARGETOS GOARCH=$TARGETARCH go build -o /out/app ./cmd/app

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12
COPY --from=build /out/app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]

steps.title: Verify the manifest and run each variant
steps.description: A push succeeding does not prove both platforms work. Check each symptom against the evidence before changing anything.
items: Inspect the index: docker buildx imagetools inspect registry.example.com/my-app:1.0 lists each platform and digest.
Run each platform: docker run --rm --platform linux/arm64 registry.example.com/my-app:1.0 uname -m should print aarch64.
Check emulated run speed: if tests pass only slowly under emulation, run them on real hardware before release.
Common error: exec format error means a binary for the wrong architecture ended up in the image, often from a missing --platform or a hard-coded download URL.

Testing strategy: run the unit tests natively and a smoke test per platform, since architecture-specific bugs such as alignment, SIMD code paths or native dependencies only surface on the real target.

steps.title: Production practice: CI and native runners
steps.description: Automate the build and keep it fast and secure.
items: GitHub Actions: use docker/setup-qemu-action, docker/setup-buildx-action, docker/login-action and docker/build-push-action with platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64.
Cache: use cache-from and cache-to with type=gha or a registry cache to avoid rebuilding every layer.
Native builders: for heavy builds, run one job per architecture on native runners and merge with docker buildx imagetools create.
Supply chain: sign the index digest and attach SBOM and provenance attestations.
Builder cleanup: remove stale builders with docker buildx rm multi and prune the builder cache with docker buildx prune so build hosts do not accumulate gigabytes of layers.
steps.codeBlock:
- uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v3
- uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
- uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
  with:
    platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
    push: true
    tags: registry.example.com/my-app:1.0
    cache-from: type=gha
    cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Use QEMU only for the final-stage assembly. Cross-compile with $BUILDPLATFORM and TARGETARCH so the slow compile step runs natively on the builder.
elevatorPitch: Multi-arch images are a manifest list pointing at per-platform images, and I build them with docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push.
I verify with buildx imagetools inspect and run each variant to confirm uname -m, watching for exec format error.
In CI I use setup-qemu and setup-buildx with a registry cache, or native runners per architecture for heavy builds.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Building the whole toolchain under QEMU
mistakesToAvoid.why: Emulated compilers are much slower. Cross-compile on the native build platform when the language supports it.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using a base image that lacks one platform
mistakesToAvoid.why: The build fails or silently falls back. Check the base image's published platforms first.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Hard-coding an AMD64 binary download in the Dockerfile
mistakesToAvoid.why: The ARM64 image then contains an AMD64 binary and crashes with exec format error. Use TARGETARCH in the URL.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Trying to --load a multi-platform build into the classic store
mistakesToAvoid.why: It is not supported, so push to a registry or use an OCI output.

title: Docker Q32: How do you push a Docker image to a private registry [L2]
summary: docker login <registry>. docker tag myimage:latest <registry>/myimage:latest. docker push <registry>/myimage:latest.
question: How do you push a Docker image to a private registry?
intro: To push a Docker image to a private registry, authenticate with docker login, tag the image with the registry host in its name, then run docker push. The tag matters because Docker decides where to push by the hostname prefix. Interviewers ask this to check that you understand image naming, credential storage, TLS trust and how clusters later pull the image. Most real failures are one of four things: a missing prefix in the tag, expired credentials, an untrusted certificate, or a repository that does not exist yet.

steps.title: Understand Image Names and Where a Push to a Private Registry Goes
steps.description: A reference is registry-host[:port]/namespace/repo:tag, and the host part selects the destination.
items: No host means Docker Hub: my-app:1.0 would target docker.io/library/my-app, which is almost never what you want.
Tags are mutable: pushing 1.4.2 twice overwrites the tag unless the registry enforces immutability; the digest (sha256:...) is the permanent identifier.
Auth is per registry host: credentials are stored by hostname in ~/.docker/config.json, preferably through a credential helper.
Tag is just an alias: docker tag adds a name to the same image ID; it copies nothing.

steps.title: Login, Tag and Push
steps.description: The standard flow for a registry such as Harbor, GitLab, Nexus or a self-hosted registry:2.
items: Login without leaking the password: use --password-stdin so the secret does not land in shell history or the process list.
Tag with the full path: include host, project and version.
Push and note the digest: the last line of the output prints the digest of the pushed manifest.
Multi-arch: docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push builds and pushes a manifest list in one step.
steps.codeBlock:
echo "$REGISTRY_TOKEN" | docker login registry.example.com -u ci-bot --password-stdin

docker build -t my-app:1.4.2 .
docker tag my-app:1.4.2 registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.4.2
docker push registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.4.2
# 1.4.2: digest: sha256:<digest> size: 1573

# Build and push multi-arch directly
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  -t registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.4.2 --push .

steps.title: Verify the Image Landed Correctly
steps.description: Do not trust the push exit code alone; confirm the manifest from a clean state.
items: Inspect remote manifest: docker buildx imagetools inspect reads the registry without pulling layers and lists platforms.
Pull from a clean host: remove the local copy and pull by digest to prove the registry serves what you pushed.
Registry API check: a registry v2 endpoint such as /v2/team/my-app/tags/list lists tags (authentication required).
Cluster pull test: for Kubernetes create a pull secret and run a test pod before relying on it.
steps.codeBlock:
docker buildx imagetools inspect registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.4.2

docker image rm registry.example.com/team/my-app:1.4.2
docker pull registry.example.com/team/my-app@sha256:<digest>

# Kubernetes pull credentials
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred -n prod \
  --docker-server=registry.example.com \
  --docker-username=ci-bot --docker-password="$REGISTRY_TOKEN"
# then set imagePullSecrets: [{name: regcred}] on the pod spec

steps.title: Diagnose Common Push Failures
steps.description: Read the error string; each maps to a specific cause.
items: denied: requested access to the resource is denied: not logged in, wrong account, no push permission, or the tag lacks the registry prefix and went to Docker Hub.
no basic auth credentials: login is missing for that exact hostname, including the port if one is used.
x509: certificate signed by unknown authority: install the CA at /etc/docker/certs.d/registry.example.com/ca.crt; avoid insecure-registries outside a lab.
Large layer rejected or timeouts: a reverse proxy body-size limit (nginx client_max_body_size) or idle timeout often sits in front of the registry.
Repository not found: some registries, such as Amazon ECR, require creating the repository first.
steps.highlight: Amazon ECR: aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <account-id>.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com. The token is short-lived (12 hours), so refresh it in every pipeline run.

steps.title: Production Practice in CI
steps.description: Automate the push and make it traceable.
items: Short-lived credentials: prefer OIDC federation or scoped robot accounts over a personal password in CI.
Immutable, unique tags: tag with the git SHA or release version; deploy by digest.
Scan and sign: run an image scanner before promotion and sign with a tool such as cosign if your policy requires it.
Retention: configure registry lifecycle rules so old CI tags do not grow storage without bound.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Deploy by digest, not by tag; a tag can be overwritten, while the sha256 digest printed by docker push identifies exactly what you tested.
elevatorPitch: I log in with --password-stdin, tag the image with the registry host and path, and docker push it; the host prefix decides the destination.
I verify with buildx imagetools inspect and a pull by digest from a clean machine, and give Kubernetes an imagePullSecret.
In CI I use short-lived credentials, immutable SHA tags, a vulnerability scan before promotion, and lifecycle rules for cleanup.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Tagging as my-app:1.0 and pushing
mistakesToAvoid.why: With no host prefix Docker targets Docker Hub, so the push fails or lands in the wrong place.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Adding the registry to insecure-registries to fix x509 errors
mistakesToAvoid.why: It disables TLS verification for that host; install the registry CA under certs.d instead.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Passing the password with -p on the command line
mistakesToAvoid.why: It is visible in shell history and process listings; use --password-stdin.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Reusing a mutable tag like latest for deployments
mistakesToAvoid.why: Nodes can pull different content for the same tag, making rollbacks and audits unreliable.

title: Docker Q33: What does EXPOSE do in a Dockerfile [L2]
summary: EXPOSE in a Dockerfile records which port the container is expected to listen on as image metadata; it does not open or publish that port to the host. Publishing happens at run time with -p or -P.
question: What does `EXPOSE` do in a Dockerfile?
intro: EXPOSE in a Dockerfile records which port the container is expected to listen on as image metadata; it does not open or publish that port to the host. Publishing happens at run time with -p or -P. This is a classic interview trap, because many candidates say EXPOSE makes a port reachable. Knowing the distinction helps you debug "connection refused" problems, understand what tools such as docker run -P and some reverse-proxy integrations read, and avoid accidentally exposing services to the network.

steps.title: What EXPOSE Actually Does
steps.description: It adds an entry to the image config under ExposedPorts, and nothing else.
items: Documentation: it tells the reader and tooling which port the app uses, like a comment that can be queried.
Protocol: default is TCP; write EXPOSE 53/udp for UDP, or list both.
No networking effect: containers on the same user-defined network can reach each other on any listening port, whether or not it is exposed.
Used by -P: docker run -P publishes every exposed port to a random high host port.

steps.title: Compare EXPOSE and Publishing in Practice
steps.description: Run the same image with and without publishing to see the difference.
items: Only EXPOSE: the host cannot reach the app by localhost:8080.
Explicit publish: -p 8080:8080 maps host port to container port.
Random mapping: -P uses the exposed ports and picks free host ports; docker port shows the result.
Restrict the interface: -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 keeps it local to the host.
steps.codeBlock:
# Dockerfile
FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
EXPOSE 80/tcp

docker build -t my-web:1.0 .
docker run -d --name web1 my-web:1.0          # reachable only inside Docker networks
docker run -d --name web2 -p 8080:80 my-web:1.0
docker run -d --name web3 -P my-web:1.0
docker port web3
# 80/tcp -> 0.0.0.0:32768

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:8080   # 200

steps.title: Verify Exposed and Published Ports
steps.description: Check metadata, runtime mappings and the real listener separately.
items: Image metadata: docker inspect --format '{{json .Config.ExposedPorts}}' my-web:1.0.
Published mappings: docker ps PORTS column or docker port <container>.
Real listener: docker exec <container> ss -ltn (or netstat -ltn) shows what the process is bound to; EXPOSE can name a port nothing listens on.
Compose: expose: is equivalent metadata, while ports: publishes.
steps.codeBlock:
docker inspect --format '{{json .Config.ExposedPorts}}' my-web:1.0
# {"80/tcp":{}}
docker ps --format 'table {{.Names}}\t{{.Ports}}'
docker exec web2 ss -ltn

steps.title: Failure Modes and Security Surprises
steps.description: Most problems come from the bind address or from assuming EXPOSE publishes.
items: Bound to 127.0.0.1 inside the container: a published port forwards to the container's network interface, so an app listening only on loopback is unreachable. Bind to 0.0.0.0.
Port mismatch: EXPOSE says 3000 but the app listens on 8080; the metadata is not enforced.
Firewall bypass: -p binds 0.0.0.0 by default and Docker writes its own iptables rules, so host firewall tools such as ufw may not block it. Publish to 127.0.0.1 or use a reverse proxy.
Kubernetes: EXPOSE is ignored; use a Service for access, and treat containerPort mostly as documentation.
steps.highlight: Seeing the page work from another container but not from your laptop almost always means the port was never published with -p, regardless of EXPOSE.

steps.title: Use EXPOSE as Good Practice, Not Security
steps.description: Keep the instruction accurate and let run-time configuration control access.
items: Declare the real port: keep it in sync with the app's default; use an ARG or ENV for configurable ports and EXPOSE the default.
Publish deliberately: prefer explicit -p host:container and bind to a specific interface in production.
Review in CI: a linter such as hadolint plus an inspect assertion can verify the metadata.
Least exposure: expose only application ports, never debug or admin ports, in the image.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Treat EXPOSE as documentation and -p as the real switch; when a published port refuses connections, check whether the app listens on 0.0.0.0 rather than 127.0.0.1.
elevatorPitch: EXPOSE records a port in the image metadata; it does not publish it or change any firewall behaviour.
Publishing happens with -p or -P, and I verify with docker port plus ss inside the container to see the real listener.
I bind published ports to a specific interface in production and make sure the app listens on 0.0.0.0, not loopback.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Believing EXPOSE makes the port reachable from the host
mistakesToAvoid.why: Only -p or -P publishes a port; EXPOSE is metadata.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running the app bound to 127.0.0.1 in the container
mistakesToAvoid.why: Traffic arriving through a published port comes via the container's interface, so loopback-only apps refuse it.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using -p 5432:5432 for a database on a public host
mistakesToAvoid.why: It listens on all interfaces and Docker's iptables rules can bypass the host firewall; bind to 127.0.0.1 or use a private network.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Letting EXPOSE drift from the application's real port
mistakesToAvoid.why: Nothing validates it, so misleading metadata sends operators and tooling to the wrong port.

summary: Docker Compose is not recommended for production at scale. For production: Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS), ECS, or Docker Swarm (simpler than K8s). Compose is for local development and simple single-host deployments.

intro: "In an interview, I explain how we diagnosed container runtime failures without guessing. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

steps.description: Docker Compose is not recommended for production at scale. For production: Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS), ECS, or Docker Swarm (simpler than K8s). Compose is for local development and simple single-host deployments.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Docker Compose is not recommended for production at scale. For production: Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS), ECS, or Docker Swarm (simpler.

title: Docker Q35: How do you override the default CMD when running a container [L2]
summary: To override the default CMD when running a container, put the new command after the image name: docker run my-app:1.0 python manage.py migrate. Whatever follows the image replaces CMD.
question: How do you override the default CMD when running a container?
intro: To override the default CMD when running a container, put the new command after the image name: docker run my-app:1.0 python manage.py migrate. Whatever follows the image replaces CMD. The twist interviewers look for is ENTRYPOINT: if the image defines one in exec form, your arguments are appended to it instead of replacing it, and you need --entrypoint to change the program itself. Getting this right matters for running migrations, one-off admin tasks and opening a debug shell in production images without rebuilding them.

steps.title: Understand the Default CMD and ENTRYPOINT Together
steps.description: The two instructions combine; the combination decides what runs.
items: CMD only: arguments after the image name replace CMD completely.
ENTRYPOINT (exec form) plus CMD: CMD supplies default arguments; run-time arguments replace CMD and are appended to ENTRYPOINT.
ENTRYPOINT shell form: ENTRYPOINT command arg runs under /bin/sh -c and ignores CMD and run-time arguments, which also stops signals reaching your app.
Overriding CMD never clears ENTRYPOINT: only --entrypoint changes it.

steps.title: Override CMD in Practice
steps.description: One image, three different invocations.
items: Default run: uses ENTRYPOINT plus CMD from the image.
Replace CMD: arguments after the image name become the new CMD.
Replace ENTRYPOINT: --entrypoint takes a single executable; its arguments follow the image name.
Clear ENTRYPOINT: --entrypoint "" makes the trailing arguments the whole command.
steps.codeBlock:
# Dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
ENTRYPOINT ["python", "-m", "app"]
CMD ["serve", "--port", "8080"]

docker run --rm my-app:1.0                      # python -m app serve --port 8080
docker run --rm my-app:1.0 migrate              # python -m app migrate
docker run --rm --entrypoint sh my-app:1.0 -c 'env | sort'   # replaces ENTRYPOINT
docker run --rm -it --entrypoint "" my-app:1.0 python --version

steps.title: Verify What Will Actually Run
steps.description: Check the effective command before and after starting the container.
items: Image defaults: docker inspect --format '{{json .Config.Entrypoint}} {{json .Config.Cmd}}' my-app:1.0.
Running container: docker ps --no-trunc shows the COMMAND column; docker inspect on the container shows .Path and .Args.
Process tree: docker top <container> confirms PID 1 is your program and not a shell wrapper.
Exit status: docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}}' for one-off jobs, which CI should assert on.
steps.codeBlock:
docker inspect --format '{{json .Config.Entrypoint}} {{json .Config.Cmd}}' my-app:1.0
# ["python","-m","app"] ["serve","--port","8080"]
docker run -d --name job1 my-app:1.0 migrate
docker inspect -f '{{.Path}} {{.Args}}' job1
docker wait job1

steps.title: Edge Cases and Failure Modes
steps.description: Most surprises come from quoting and from the ENTRYPOINT interaction.
items: Executable not found: exec: "migrate": executable file not found in $PATH means the image has no ENTRYPOINT and you passed an argument expecting one; either name the full command or use --entrypoint.
Shell features: pipes, && and variable expansion need sh -c '...'; exec form does not invoke a shell.
Debug shell: docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh my-app:1.0 works even when ENTRYPOINT starts the server; it fails on distroless images with no shell.
Compose: command: overrides CMD and entrypoint: overrides ENTRYPOINT; setting entrypoint also discards the image's default CMD.
steps.highlight: Kubernetes mapping: command overrides ENTRYPOINT and args overrides CMD. If you set command but not args, the image's CMD is ignored.

steps.title: Production Practice
steps.description: Design images so overrides are safe and predictable.
items: Exec form always: use JSON arrays so the app is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM for graceful shutdown.
Subcommand pattern: ENTRYPOINT as the binary and CMD as the default subcommand lets the same image run serve, migrate and worker.
Jobs: run migrations as a Kubernetes Job or a CI step with an overridden command rather than baking them into startup.
Guardrails: avoid entrypoint scripts that swallow arguments; end them with exec "$@" so overrides still work.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: With an ENTRYPOINT in exec form, extra arguments after the image name are appended to it; to run a different program (for example a shell), you must add --entrypoint.
elevatorPitch: Anything after the image name in docker run replaces CMD; ENTRYPOINT stays unless I pass --entrypoint.
I confirm the effective command with docker inspect on Config.Entrypoint and Config.Cmd, and docker ps --no-trunc on the running container.
I design images with exec-form ENTRYPOINT plus a default CMD so migrations and debug shells run from the same image, and I map this to command and args in Kubernetes.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Passing sh as an argument to an image with an ENTRYPOINT
mistakesToAvoid.why: The argument is appended to the entrypoint instead of replacing it; use --entrypoint sh.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using shell-form ENTRYPOINT or CMD
mistakesToAvoid.why: The command runs under /bin/sh -c, so the app is not PID 1 and may miss SIGTERM; CMD and arguments can also be ignored.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting pipes or && in a docker run override to work directly
mistakesToAvoid.why: There is no shell by default; wrap the command in sh -c '...'.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Writing an entrypoint script that does not end with exec "$@"
mistakesToAvoid.why: The script swallows the override, or leaves a shell as PID 1.

title: Docker Q36: What is an init container (not Kubernetes) Why might you use --init in Docker [L2]
summary: docker run --init runs a tiny init process (tini) as PID 1. This properly handles zombie process reaping and signal forwarding. Without init, if PID 1 doesn't forward signals, docker stop becomes slow and unreliable.
question: What is an `init` container (not Kubernetes)? Why might you use `--init` in Docker?
intro: "Container stability relies on clean signal handling (SIGTERM vs SIGKILL) and immutable image tagging. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."
