title: Docker Q41: What is a dangling image in Docker [L2]
summary: A dangling image in Docker is an image with no tag and no remaining reference from a tagged image, shown as none:none in docker images.
question: What is a "dangling image" in Docker?
intro: A dangling image in Docker is an image with no tag and no remaining reference from a tagged image, shown as <none>:<none> in docker images. It typically appears when you rebuild an image under the same tag: the tag moves to the new build and the previous one is left untagged. Interviewers ask this to see whether you can reclaim disk space on build hosts without deleting images that are still needed. The key distinction is dangling versus unused, and knowing which prune command removes which.

steps.title: Mental model: how an image becomes dangling
steps.description: Tags are movable pointers to image IDs. When a tag moves, the old image keeps existing but loses its name. Cleaning too aggressively on a shared host can slow the next build because cached images must be pulled again.
items: Cause: docker build -t my-app:latest . run twice. The second build takes the latest tag and the first becomes dangling. Pulling a newer image for the same tag does the same.
Dangling: untagged and not a parent layer of any tagged image.
Unused: a tagged image that no container currently references. Not dangling, and removed only with prune -a.
Not the same as build cache: BuildKit cache is separate and is cleaned with docker builder prune.
Why they accumulate: CI agents that rebuild the same tag on every commit create one dangling image per build, so a busy runner can collect dozens of them in a day, each holding its own layers.

steps.title: Hands-on: find a dangling image in Docker
steps.description: List them with a filter and see how much space is involved.
items: Filter: docker images -f dangling=true shows only dangling images.
IDs only: add -q for scripting.
Disk summary: docker system df reports reclaimable space for images, containers, volumes and build cache.
Reproduce one: build the same tag twice with a changed file and watch the first image turn into <none>.
Shared layers: deleting a dangling image only frees the layers that no other image uses. The reclaimed space is often smaller than the listed sizes added together.
steps.codeBlock:
docker images -f dangling=true
# REPOSITORY   TAG       IMAGE ID       CREATED        SIZE
# <none>       <none>    3f2a9c1b7d44   2 hours ago    187MB

docker images -f dangling=true -q
docker system df

steps.title: Remove dangling images safely
steps.description: Use the narrowest command that does the job.
items: Dangling only: docker image prune asks for confirmation and removes dangling images. Add -f in scripts.
Everything unused: docker image prune -a also removes tagged images with no container. Be careful on hosts that rely on pre-pulled images.
Age filter: --filter "until=168h" keeps anything newer than seven days.
Whole system: docker system prune removes stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images and build cache. Volumes are removed only with --volumes.
Seeing the parents: docker images -a additionally lists intermediate images on the classic builder. With BuildKit these are hidden, so an empty dangling list does not mean the disk is clean.
steps.codeBlock:
docker image prune                          # dangling only, prompts
docker image prune -f --filter "until=168h" # older than 7 days, no prompt
docker image prune -a --filter "until=720h" # all unused older than 30 days

docker builder prune --filter until=168h    # BuildKit cache
docker system df                            # confirm space reclaimed
steps.highlight: docker system prune --volumes deletes unused volumes, which may contain data you need. Never run it on a host with database volumes unless you have a backup.

steps.title: Edge cases and verification
steps.description: Not everything labelled none is safe to delete blindly. Check each symptom against the evidence before changing anything.
items: Images pulled by digest: they can show <none> as the tag and still be in use. Check docker images --digests and running containers before removing manually.
In-use images are protected: removal of an image used by a container fails. Remove the container first.
Intermediate layers: with BuildKit, intermediate build steps do not appear as dangling images. They live in the build cache.
Verify: rerun docker images -f dangling=true and docker system df to confirm the reclaimable figure dropped.
Inspecting before deleting: docker image inspect <id> shows creation time, labels and the original command, which helps decide whether an untagged image is worth keeping for a rollback.

steps.title: Production practice: stop dangling images piling up
steps.description: Treat cleanup as scheduled housekeeping and reduce how many are created.
items: Tag builds uniquely: use commit SHA or version tags so nothing silently overwrites latest and leaves orphans.
Scheduled cleanup: run docker image prune -f --filter until=168h from cron or a systemd timer on build agents.
Alert on disk: monitor /var/lib/docker usage so a full disk does not break builds.
Registry side: apply registry retention policies, because local pruning does not clean remote repositories.
Registry parity: pushing to a registry does not create dangling images remotely, but untagged manifests can remain there, and registry garbage collection is a separate job.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: docker image prune removes only dangling images, while -a removes every unused image. On shared build hosts add an until filter so you do not delete images someone just pulled.
elevatorPitch: A dangling image is untagged and unreferenced, shown as <none>:<none>, usually left behind when a rebuild moves a tag.
I list them with docker images -f dangling=true and check reclaimable space with docker system df.
I automate docker image prune with an age filter and use unique tags so rebuilds do not create orphans.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Confusing dangling with unused
mistakesToAvoid.why: Dangling means untagged. A tagged image that no container uses is only removed by prune -a, which may delete images you wanted cached.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running docker system prune --volumes casually
mistakesToAvoid.why: It deletes unused volumes, which can contain database files and cannot be recovered.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring BuildKit cache when disk fills up
mistakesToAvoid.why: Dangling images are only part of the picture. Build cache can be large and needs docker builder prune.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Deleting every none image by ID in a script
mistakesToAvoid.why: Some untagged images are referenced by digest or by other images, and removal can fail or break deployments.

title: Docker Q42: How do you set resource limits for a Docker Compose service [L2]
summary: To set resource limits for a Docker Compose service, add deploy.resources.limits with cpus and memory to the service in compose.yaml. Docker Compose v2 applies these on docker compose up, while reservations declare a minimum.
question: How do you set resource limits for a Docker Compose service?
intro: To set resource limits for a Docker Compose service, add deploy.resources.limits with cpus and memory to the service in compose.yaml. Docker Compose v2 applies these on docker compose up, while reservations declare a minimum. Interviewers ask this to test whether you know the Compose Specification syntax, how limits behave at runtime (CPU throttling versus memory OOM kills), and how to verify enforcement. Mentioning the older mem_limit style shows you can read legacy files.

steps.title: Mental model: limits, reservations and what they do
steps.description: Compose maps these keys to the same cgroup controls as docker run flags. Remember that limits protect the host and neighbouring services, so a missing limit on one container is a risk to every other container on that machine.
items: limits.cpus: a hard cap in CPU units, for example "0.5" is half a core, enforced by CFS throttling.
limits.memory: a hard cap. If the process exceeds it the kernel OOM killer terminates it and Docker reports exit code 137.
reservations: a soft minimum used for scheduling in Swarm. On a single host, a memory reservation acts as a soft limit under memory pressure.
Legacy keys: mem_limit, cpus, mem_reservation and pids_limit at service level are still supported by the Compose Specification.

Where it is enforced: limits are applied by the Docker Engine through cgroups on the host running the container, so they work the same in a laptop or a single-server deployment as they do for plain docker run.

steps.title: Hands-on: set resource limits for a Docker Compose service
steps.description: A complete example with CPU, memory and process limits.
items: Quote CPU values: write cpus: "0.50" as a string for portability.
Apply: run docker compose up -d. Changing limits recreates the container.
Preview the merged config: docker compose config shows what Compose will actually apply.
Swap and PIDs: memswap_limit and pids_limit at the service level cap swap use and fork bombs.
Memory plus swap: by default a memory limit may allow equal swap on some hosts, which delays OOM kills but slows the app badly. Set memswap_limit equal to the memory limit to disable extra swap.
steps.codeBlock:
services:
  api:
    image: registry.example.com/my-api:2.0
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.50"
          memory: 512M
        reservations:
          cpus: "0.25"
          memory: 256M
    pids_limit: 200

  worker:
    image: registry.example.com/my-worker:2.0
    cpus: 1.0          # legacy-style service-level keys
    mem_limit: 1g
steps.highlight: Do not set both deploy.resources.limits.memory and mem_limit for the same service with different values. Compose rejects conflicting definitions in many versions, so pick one style.

steps.title: Verify the limits are enforced
steps.description: Confirm what Docker applied, not only what the file says.
items: Live usage: docker stats --no-stream shows MEM USAGE / LIMIT, which should read 512MiB for api.
Inspect HostConfig: docker inspect --format '{{.HostConfig.Memory}} {{.HostConfig.NanoCpus}}' <container> prints bytes and nano-CPUs, here 536870912 500000000.
OOM check: docker inspect --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.ExitCode}}' <container> returns true 137 after a memory kill.
Stress test: run a memory hog in a staging container to see the kill behaviour before production does.
Docker Desktop: containers share the resources assigned to the Desktop VM, so a service limit above the VM allocation is meaningless. Raise the VM memory in settings first.
steps.codeBlock:
docker compose up -d
docker compose config | grep -A4 limits
docker stats --no-stream --format 'table {{.Name}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}\t{{.MemUsage}}'
# NAME      CPU %   MEM USAGE / LIMIT
# app-api-1 0.4%    120MiB / 512MiB
docker inspect --format '{{.HostConfig.NanoCpus}}' app-api-1

steps.title: Failure modes and version caveats
steps.description: Most surprises come from syntax history and runtime semantics. Check each symptom against the evidence before changing anything.
items: Compose v1 and the deploy key: old docker-compose 1.x ignored deploy outside Swarm unless run with --compatibility. Compose v2 (docker compose) honours it.
Silent OOM kills: a container restarting every few minutes with exit code 137 is usually hitting its memory limit. Raise it or fix the leak.
Runtime awareness: JVM, Node and Go may size heaps from host memory. Set JVM flags such as -XX:MaxRAMPercentage so the heap fits inside the cgroup limit.
Throttled latency: a tight CPU cap throttles bursts. Check for slow requests when CPU looks low.
Sizing method: run a realistic load test, record peak working set, and set the limit with headroom while keeping the reservation near typical usage.

steps.title: Production practice: defaults and observability
steps.description: Make sizing a measured, reviewed decision.
items: Measure first: base limits on observed peak usage from docker stats or cAdvisor with headroom, not guesses.
Use extension fields: define common limits once with a YAML anchor under an x- key and reuse it in services.
Alert: track memory near limit, OOMKilled events and CPU throttling in Prometheus.
Orchestrators: in Kubernetes translate these to resources.requests and resources.limits in the pod spec.
Profiles per environment: keep dev with generous limits in an override file such as compose.override.yaml and enforce stricter production values in compose.prod.yaml.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Verify limits with docker inspect and docker stats after up, and treat exit code 137 with OOMKilled=true as the signal that a memory limit is too low or the app leaks.
elevatorPitch: I set deploy.resources.limits with cpus and memory in the Compose file, plus reservations, and apply it with docker compose up -d.
I confirm with docker compose config, docker stats and docker inspect for HostConfig.Memory and OOMKilled.
I size from measured peaks, align runtime heap settings with the limit and alert on OOM kills and CPU throttling.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on deploy limits with Compose v1
mistakesToAvoid.why: The legacy docker-compose 1.x ignored deploy outside Swarm, so containers ran unlimited. Use Compose v2.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Setting memory limits below the runtime's heap needs
mistakesToAvoid.why: The JVM or Node may try to exceed the cgroup limit and get OOM killed, even though the host has plenty of RAM.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Unquoted or wrong CPU units
mistakesToAvoid.why: cpus is a fraction of cores, not a percentage, so 50 means fifty cores. Use a quoted decimal like "0.5".

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Never checking exit codes
mistakesToAvoid.why: Exit 137 with OOMKilled true is the only clear sign that limits killed the process. Without checking it, restarts look like random crashes.

title: Docker Q43: How does container networking work at the Linux kernel level [L3]
summary: Container networking at the Linux kernel level is built from a few primitives: each container gets its own network namespace, a veth pair connects it to a Linux bridge (docker0 or a user-defined bridge) on the host, and iptables.
question: How does container networking work at the Linux kernel level?
intro: Container networking at the Linux kernel level is built from a few primitives: each container gets its own network namespace, a veth pair connects it to a Linux bridge (docker0 or a user-defined bridge) on the host, and iptables or nftables rules provide NAT and port publishing. Interviewers ask this to find out whether you can debug when docker run -p does not work, because the answer lives in kernel objects you can inspect. A strong answer names each component, shows the packet path, and gives commands to verify every hop.

steps.title: Mental model: namespaces, veth, bridge, NAT
steps.description: Docker does not implement networking itself. It configures standard Linux features.
items: Network namespace: an isolated copy of the network stack (interfaces, routes, iptables, sockets). Each container normally gets its own.
veth pair: a virtual cable. One end sits inside the container as eth0, the other end is on the host and attached to a bridge.
Bridge: a software switch (docker0 by default, or br-<id> for user-defined networks) that forwards frames between containers on the same network.
NAT and filtering: outbound traffic is masqueraded to the host IP, and published ports use DNAT rules. Both depend on IP forwarding being enabled.
Namespace plumbing: Docker keeps its namespaces under /var/run/docker/netns, so ip netns list shows nothing by default. Use the container PID with nsenter, or symlink the files into /var/run/netns.

steps.title: Hands-on: inspect container networking at the Linux kernel level
steps.description: Follow a single container from Docker down to kernel objects.
items: Find the container's PID: docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' my-app.
Enter its namespace from the host: nsenter -t <pid> -n ip addr shows eth0 with the container IP and the peer index.
Find the host end: ip link on the host lists vethXXXX@ifN. bridge link shows it attached to the bridge.
Routes: nsenter -t <pid> -n ip route shows the default gateway pointing at the bridge IP.
Same-network traffic: two containers on one bridge talk through the bridge's forwarding table using MAC learning, exactly like machines on an Ethernet switch, with no routing or NAT involved.
steps.codeBlock:
PID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' my-app)
sudo nsenter -t $PID -n ip addr show eth0
# eth0@if12: inet 172.17.0.2/16 ...
sudo nsenter -t $PID -n ip route
# default via 172.17.0.1 dev eth0

ip -br link | grep veth       # host side of the pair
bridge link                    # veth attached to docker0
ip addr show docker0
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward     # must be 1

steps.title: Packet path: NAT, published ports and DNS
steps.description: Trace outbound and inbound traffic through netfilter.
items: Outbound: a MASQUERADE rule in the nat table rewrites the container source IP to the host IP. See it with iptables -t nat -L POSTROUTING -n -v.
Inbound published port: -p 8080:80 adds a DNAT rule in the DOCKER chain sending host port 8080 to container port 80. A docker-proxy process may also handle loopback and hairpin cases.
Container to container: on a user-defined bridge, traffic stays inside the bridge with no NAT, and names resolve through Docker's embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11.
Other drivers: host shares the host namespace, macvlan gives containers their own MAC on the LAN, and overlay uses VXLAN tunnels between hosts.

Isolation between networks: separate bridges are isolated by iptables rules in the DOCKER-ISOLATION chains, so containers on different user-defined networks cannot reach each other unless connected to both.
steps.codeBlock:
sudo iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n -v      # DNAT for published ports
sudo iptables -t nat -L POSTROUTING -n -v # MASQUERADE for outbound
docker network inspect bridge --format '{{json .IPAM.Config}}'
docker exec my-app cat /etc/resolv.conf   # nameserver 127.0.0.11 on user-defined nets
sudo conntrack -L | head                  # active NAT'd flows (needs conntrack-tools)
steps.highlight: Rule layout differs between iptables-legacy, iptables-nft and nftables hosts. Use nft list ruleset if iptables output looks empty.

steps.title: Failure modes: where the packet path breaks
steps.description: Map symptoms to kernel layers.
items: Published port unreachable: check the DNAT rule, that the container listens on 0.0.0.0 (not 127.0.0.1) and that the host firewall allows it.
No outbound internet: ip_forward is 0, the MASQUERADE rule is missing, or a firewall manager flushed Docker's chains. Restarting Docker recreates them.
ufw and firewalld surprises: Docker inserts its own rules and published ports can bypass ufw rules. Restrict exposure with -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 or by using the DOCKER-USER chain.
Subnet overlap and MTU: a VPN using the same range as 172.17.0.0/16 breaks routing. Set default-address-pools in daemon.json. Overlay networks may need a lower MTU.
Performance notes: every published-port packet crosses netfilter and conntrack, which is fine for most workloads but is why host networking is chosen for very high packet rates.

steps.title: Production practice: observability and hardening
steps.description: Know where to look and reduce exposure.
items: Packet capture: nsenter -t $PID -n tcpdump -i eth0 captures inside the container namespace without installing tools in the image.
User-defined networks: prefer them to the default bridge for DNS by name and for isolation between app tiers.
Least exposure: publish only required ports and bind them to specific interfaces, and use --internal networks for backends.
Kubernetes link: the same primitives sit under CNI plugins, which add routing or eBPF instead of a simple bridge.
IPv6: IPv6 is disabled for bridge networks by default and needs explicit daemon configuration, so a container with no IPv6 route is expected rather than a bug.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Debug in layers. Check the container namespace with nsenter -n, then the veth and bridge, then the iptables nat chains. The failing hop is almost always visible with plain ip and iptables output.
elevatorPitch: Each container has its own network namespace, joined to a host bridge by a veth pair, with iptables doing NAT and port publishing.
I verify by entering the namespace with nsenter, checking ip addr, the veth on the bridge, ip_forward and the nat table rules.
I use user-defined networks, bind published ports narrowly and capture packets with tcpdump inside the namespace.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming Docker has its own network stack
mistakesToAvoid.why: It uses Linux namespaces, veth, bridges and netfilter. Not knowing that makes debugging guesswork.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Trusting ufw to block published ports
mistakesToAvoid.why: Docker's rules are inserted ahead of ufw's, so ports can stay exposed. Bind to localhost or use the DOCKER-USER chain.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using the default bridge for multi-service apps
mistakesToAvoid.why: It has no automatic DNS by container name. Use a user-defined network.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring subnet overlap with VPNs
mistakesToAvoid.why: Docker's default ranges can collide with corporate networks, causing routes that silently go to the wrong place.

title: Docker Q44: How do you rebuild only a specific service in Docker Compose [L2]
summary: To rebuild only a specific service in Docker Compose, name the service: docker compose up -d --build --no-deps web rebuilds the image for web and recreates just that container.
question: How do you rebuild only a specific service in Docker Compose?
intro: To rebuild only a specific service in Docker Compose, name the service: docker compose up -d --build --no-deps web rebuilds the image for web and recreates just that container. Without --no-deps, Compose also starts dependencies, and without --build, up reuses the existing image. Interviewers ask this to check you understand how Compose decides to rebuild, how it detects configuration changes and how to avoid needless downtime in the rest of the stack.

steps.title: Mental model: build versus recreate
steps.description: Two separate actions are often confused: building an image and recreating a container from it. Knowing which of these commands touches running containers is what keeps a quick fix from becoming an outage.
items: docker compose build: only builds images for services with a build: section. It does not touch running containers.
docker compose up: creates or recreates containers whose configuration or image changed. It builds missing images, but does not rebuild an existing image unless asked with --build.
Dependencies: naming a service on up also starts services it depends_on. --no-deps prevents that.
Image-only services: services with just image: are pulled, not built, so rebuilding does not apply. Use docker compose pull.
Several services: list more than one name, such as docker compose up -d --build --no-deps web worker, to rebuild a subset while leaving databases and caches untouched.

steps.title: Hands-on: rebuild only a specific service in Docker Compose
steps.description: The typical commands, from slowest to most targeted.
items: Build only: docker compose build web prepares the new image and leaves containers running.
Build and replace: docker compose up -d --build --no-deps web rebuilds and recreates only web. Other containers keep running.
Force a fresh build: add --no-cache to build, and --pull to refresh the base image first.
Force recreate: --force-recreate replaces the container even if nothing changed, for example after changing a mounted file the app reads only at start.
Build arguments: pass --build-arg through docker compose build, or define args in the service's build section, so version stamps change the layer and trigger a real rebuild.
steps.codeBlock:
docker compose build web                          # build image only
docker compose up -d --build --no-deps web        # rebuild + recreate web only
docker compose build --no-cache --pull web        # clean rebuild, fresh base
docker compose up -d --no-deps --force-recreate web

# Image-only service (no build:), pull instead
docker compose pull redis && docker compose up -d --no-deps redis

steps.title: Verify that only the right service changed
steps.description: Check image IDs and container timestamps rather than assuming.
items: Container ages: docker compose ps should show web as recently created while others show their original uptime.
Image identity: docker compose images lists the image ID and age for each service.
Build output: docker compose build --progress=plain web shows CACHED for unchanged steps, so you can see which layers actually rebuilt.
Behaviour: hit the service and compare the version endpoint or file content to the change you made.
Downtime expectation: recreating a container stops the old one before starting the new one, so a single replica has a brief gap. Use multiple replicas behind a proxy if you need zero downtime.
steps.codeBlock:
docker compose ps --format 'table {{.Name}}\t{{.Image}}\t{{.Status}}'
docker compose images web
docker inspect --format '{{.Created}}' $(docker compose ps -q web)

steps.title: Failure modes and cache behaviour
steps.description: If the change did not appear, one of these is usually why. Check each symptom against the evidence before changing anything.
items: Layer cache hides the change: COPY . . placed before dependency install invalidates the cache too often, while a late COPY might not include what you changed. Check .dockerignore and layer order.
No rebuild happened: plain docker compose up -d web reused the old image. Add --build.
Bind-mounted code: if source is mounted into the container, you may not need a rebuild at all, only a restart or a watch-mode sync.
Environment changes: editing environment or ports needs a recreate, which up -d does automatically, not a rebuild.
Project scoping: commands act on the current project name. If a rebuild seems to do nothing, check docker compose ls and the -p flag to be sure you are targeting the right stack.

steps.title: Production practice: faster loops and safer deploys
steps.description: Use Compose features that avoid manual rebuild commands.
items: Compose Watch: docker compose watch (Compose 2.22 and later) syncs files or rebuilds a service on change using develop.watch rules.
Dependency order: use depends_on with condition: service_healthy so a recreated service waits for its database.
CI builds: build and push tagged images in CI, and on servers run pull then up -d --no-deps for one service to avoid building on production hosts.
Rollbacks: keep the previous image tag so you can set it and recreate quickly.
Cleaning up: repeated rebuilds leave dangling images behind, so run docker image prune occasionally on development machines.
steps.codeBlock:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    develop:
      watch:
        - action: sync
          path: ./src
          target: /app/src
        - action: rebuild
          path: package.json

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Remember the trio: --build to force an image rebuild, --no-deps to leave neighbours alone, and a service name to limit scope. Then confirm with docker compose ps timestamps.
elevatorPitch: I run docker compose up -d --build --no-deps web, which rebuilds the image and recreates only that service.
I verify through docker compose ps and images and by reading build output for CACHED layers.
I automate with Compose Watch in development and CI-built, pulled images for servers.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running up without --build after changing the Dockerfile
mistakesToAvoid.why: Compose reuses the existing image, so the container keeps running old code.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting --no-deps and restarting databases
mistakesToAvoid.why: Naming a service starts its depends_on services too, which can create unplanned churn.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting build to restart containers
mistakesToAvoid.why: docker compose build only makes an image. You still need up to replace the running container.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting that image-only services cannot be built
mistakesToAvoid.why: Services without a build section need pull, so rebuild commands do nothing for them.

title: Docker Q47: How do you roll back to a previous Docker image version in Kubernetes [L2]
summary: To roll back to a previous Docker image version in Kubernetes, run kubectl rollout undo deployment/my-app (optionally with --to-revision=N), or redeploy the known-good image digest from Git.
question: How do you roll back to a previous Docker image version in Kubernetes?
intro: To roll back to a previous Docker image version in Kubernetes, run kubectl rollout undo deployment/my-app (optionally with --to-revision=N), or redeploy the known-good image digest from Git. A Deployment keeps old ReplicaSets, so a rollback is just scaling an older ReplicaSet back up under the same rolling-update rules. Interviewers ask this to see whether you understand revision history, immutable image references and what a rollback does not undo, such as ConfigMaps, database schema changes and anything managed by GitOps controllers that will simply put the bad version back.

steps.title: Mental model: Deployments, ReplicaSets and revisions
steps.description: Every change to the pod template creates a new ReplicaSet; a rollback re-activates one of the old ones.
items: Revision = ReplicaSet: Changing spec.template (image, env, resources) creates a new ReplicaSet and a new revision number. Scaling or changing replicas does not.
History limit: spec.revisionHistoryLimit defaults to 10. If it is set to 0, old ReplicaSets are garbage collected and rollout undo has nothing to roll back to.
Strategy still applies: A rollback uses the same maxSurge and maxUnavailable settings as a forward rollout, so it is gradual and respects readiness probes.
Revision numbers move: Rolling back to revision 3 makes that pod template the newest revision (for example revision 6); revision 3 disappears from the list because it is now the current one.
steps.highlight: A rollback only reverts the pod template. It does not revert ConfigMaps, Secrets, Services, HPA settings or database migrations.

steps.title: Hands-on: roll back to a previous Docker image version in Kubernetes
steps.description: Inspect history first, then undo to the last revision or to a specific one.
items: See what you can return to: kubectl rollout history deployment/my-app -n prod lists revisions; add --revision=N to print the image and env of that revision.
Undo the last change: kubectl rollout undo deployment/my-app -n prod goes back exactly one revision.
Pick a specific revision: --to-revision=N is safer during incidents because a failed forward fix can leave the previous revision also bad.
Pin an exact image: If history is gone, kubectl set image with a digest deploys a known-good build directly.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl rollout history deployment/my-app -n prod
# REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
# 4         release 1.4.2
# 5         release 1.5.0

kubectl rollout history deployment/my-app -n prod --revision=4 | grep Image
#   Image:  registry.example.com/my-app:1.4.2

kubectl rollout undo deployment/my-app -n prod --to-revision=4

# Fallback when history is unavailable: deploy by immutable digest
kubectl set image deployment/my-app \
  my-app=registry.example.com/my-app@sha256:<known-good-digest> -n prod

steps.title: Verify the rollback actually completed
steps.description: A successful command only means the API accepted the change; confirm the pods are running the old image and healthy.
items: Wait for convergence: kubectl rollout status deployment/my-app -n prod --timeout=180s exits non-zero if the rollout stalls, which makes it usable in scripts.
Check the running image ID: Compare .status.containerStatuses[*].imageID against the digest you expect, because a mutable tag can resolve to a different build.
Read the events: kubectl describe deployment my-app shows the ReplicaSet scale-up and scale-down sequence, and kubectl get rs -n prod confirms the old ReplicaSet owns the desired replica count.
Watch golden signals: Error rate and latency on your dashboards should return to baseline; Kubernetes health alone does not prove the service is correct.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl rollout status deployment/my-app -n prod --timeout=180s
kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=my-app \
  -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.status.containerStatuses[0].imageID}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl get rs -n prod -l app=my-app

steps.title: Failure modes and edge cases
steps.description: Most failed rollbacks come from state outside the pod template or from tags that are not immutable.
items: Mutable tags: If my-app:stable was overwritten, undoing to a revision that references that tag may pull the new bad content when imagePullPolicy: Always is set. Immutable tags or digests avoid this.
Schema changes: If the new version ran a forward-only migration, the old code may crash against the new schema. Use expand/contract migrations so the previous version stays compatible.
GitOps fights you: With Argo CD or Flux self-heal enabled, a manual rollout undo is reverted to the Git state within minutes. Revert the commit instead, or pause sync.
Registry pruning: A lifecycle policy that deletes old images can leave a ReplicaSet pointing at an image that no longer exists, producing ImagePullBackOff.
Paused Deployments: A Deployment with spec.paused: true will not roll back until you run kubectl rollout resume.

steps.title: Production practice: make rollback boring
steps.description: Design the pipeline so that rolling back is the same code path as rolling forward.
items: Git revert as the source of truth: In GitOps, revert the commit that changed the image; the controller applies it with audit history.
Record intent: Annotate releases with kubectl annotate deployment/my-app kubernetes.io/change-cause="release 1.5.0" (the older --record flag is deprecated) so history is readable.
Automate the trigger: Argo Rollouts or Flagger can abort and roll back automatically when Prometheus analysis fails, removing human delay.
Rehearse: Run a rollback in staging regularly and keep revisionHistoryLimit at 5 to 10, and retain the last several release images in the registry.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Deploy by image digest and keep the last several images in the registry, so kubectl rollout undo and a Git revert both land on content that is guaranteed to be identical to what ran before.
elevatorPitch: A rollback in Kubernetes re-activates an older ReplicaSet, using the Deployment's normal rolling-update rules, via kubectl rollout undo with an optional --to-revision.
I verify with rollout status, the running imageID digest and error-rate dashboards, and I check that GitOps will not revert my change.
I automate it by reverting in Git, using immutable digests, and letting Argo Rollouts or Flagger abort failing releases automatically.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Setting revisionHistoryLimit to 0 to reduce clutter
mistakesToAvoid.why: Old ReplicaSets are deleted, so there is no revision to undo to and recovery requires a full redeploy.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Rolling back with kubectl while Argo CD self-heal is on
mistakesToAvoid.why: The controller reapplies the Git state and silently reinstates the bad image.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming the rollback also reverts the database
mistakesToAvoid.why: Forward-only migrations leave the schema incompatible with the older code, causing crashes after the undo.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Trusting a mutable tag like stable or latest
mistakesToAvoid.why: The tag may now point to different content, so the previous revision does not run the previous build.

title: Docker Q48: What is Docker Swarm and how does it compare to Kubernetes [L2]
summary: Docker Swarm is Docker Engine's built-in clustering and orchestration mode: you join several hosts into one swarm, declare services, and Swarm schedules, load-balances and restarts the containers.
question: What is Docker Swarm and how does it compare to Kubernetes?
intro: Docker Swarm is Docker Engine's built-in clustering and orchestration mode: you join several hosts into one swarm, declare services, and Swarm schedules, load-balances and restarts the containers. Compared with Kubernetes it is much simpler to set up and uses the familiar Docker CLI and Compose files, but it has a smaller feature set and ecosystem. Interviewers ask this to check that you can compare orchestrators on facts such as scheduling, networking, extensibility and operations, rather than repeating that Kubernetes has won.

steps.title: Mental model: what Docker Swarm actually is
steps.description: Swarm mode is a feature of the Docker daemon, not a separate product to install.
items: Managers and workers: Manager nodes hold cluster state in a Raft log and schedule tasks; worker nodes only run tasks. Use 3 or 5 managers (an odd number) for quorum.
Service and task: A service is the desired state (image, replicas, ports); each replica is a task that runs in one container on one node.
Overlay networking and routing mesh: Overlay networks span nodes, and published ports are reachable on every node through the ingress routing mesh.
Built-in secrets: docker secret stores encrypted data in the Raft log and mounts it as files under /run/secrets in the container.

Scheduling: The default strategy spreads tasks across nodes by load; you steer it with placement constraints such as node.labels.disk==ssd and preferences, but there is no equivalent of Kubernetes affinity, taints or priority classes.
steps.highlight: Swarm needs TCP 2377 (management), TCP and UDP 7946 (node gossip) and UDP 4789 (overlay VXLAN) open between nodes.

steps.title: Hands-on: Docker Swarm cluster, service and stack
steps.description: Create a cluster, deploy a replicated service and then a stack from a Compose file.
items: Initialise: docker swarm init --advertise-addr <manager-ip> prints a join token for workers.
Join nodes: Run the printed docker swarm join command on each worker, then check docker node ls.
Create a service: docker service create --replicas 3 -p 80:80 nginx:1.27 schedules three tasks across the nodes.
Deploy a stack: docker stack deploy -c compose.yaml mystack uses the Compose file format with a deploy: section for replicas and update policy.

Day-two commands: docker service update --image nginx:1.27.1 web performs a rolling update, docker service logs web aggregates task logs, and docker node update --availability drain <node> evacuates a node for maintenance.
steps.codeBlock:
docker swarm init --advertise-addr 10.0.0.10
docker node ls
docker service create --name web --replicas 3 -p 80:80 nginx:1.27
docker service ls
docker service ps web          # which node runs which task

# compose.yaml (stack)
# services:
#   web:
#     image: nginx:1.27
#     ports: ["80:80"]
#     deploy:
#       replicas: 3
#       update_config: {parallelism: 1, delay: 10s, order: start-first}
docker stack deploy -c compose.yaml mystack

steps.title: Docker Swarm vs Kubernetes: the real differences
steps.description: Compare on capabilities that matter in operations rather than popularity.
items: Setup: Swarm is one command per node. Kubernetes needs a control plane, a CNI plugin, an ingress controller and usually a managed service.
Scaling and autoscaling: Swarm scales manually with docker service scale; Kubernetes has HPA, VPA and cluster autoscalers.
Extensibility: Kubernetes has CRDs, operators, admission webhooks, RBAC and NetworkPolicy. Swarm has no equivalent extension model.
Rollouts: Swarm supports rolling updates and rollback via docker service update --rollback; Kubernetes adds probes-driven rollouts and progressive delivery tooling.

Ecosystem: Managed offerings, Helm charts, and vendor support target Kubernetes almost exclusively. Networking model: Swarm gives each service a virtual IP with built-in DNS load balancing; Kubernetes separates Service, Ingress or Gateway API and NetworkPolicy, which is more flexible but more to learn.

steps.title: Operational caveats and failure modes
steps.description: Know the places Swarm bites in production.
items: Quorum loss: If a majority of managers fail, you cannot change cluster state until quorum returns; recover with docker swarm init --force-new-cluster on a surviving manager only as a last resort.
Routing mesh surprises: Client source IPs are NATed unless you use host-mode publishing; this affects logging and allow-lists.
Health checks: Define HEALTHCHECK or a service health check; otherwise a running but hung process counts as healthy.
Stateful data: Volumes are local to a node by default, so pin stateful tasks with placement constraints or use a volume plugin.
Upgrades: Upgrade managers one at a time and confirm docker node ls shows them Reachable before touching the next one, otherwise you risk losing quorum during the upgrade.
steps.codeBlock:
docker node ls                                   # managers show Leader / Reachable
docker node update --availability drain worker-2  # evacuate before maintenance
docker service update --rollback web              # revert last service update
docker service inspect --pretty web | grep -A3 UpdateConfig
# Last resort on a surviving manager after quorum loss:
docker swarm init --force-new-cluster --advertise-addr 10.0.0.10

steps.title: When to use which
steps.description: The decision is mostly about team size, features required and ecosystem.
items: Choose Swarm: A small team, a handful of stateless services, existing Compose files, and no need for operators or autoscaling.
Choose Kubernetes: Multi-team platforms, autoscaling, policy and multi-tenancy, or any dependency on cloud-native tooling.
Migration path: Compose files can be converted as a starting point (for example with Kompose), but expect to rewrite networking and secrets.
Check support status: Swarm mode ships with Docker Engine, but confirm current maintenance and roadmap before betting a new platform on it.
Observability: Both work with Prometheus and Grafana, but Kubernetes has far more ready-made exporters, dashboards and operators; account for that when estimating effort.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Frame the answer as simplicity versus extensibility: Swarm gives you orchestration with the Docker CLI in minutes, while Kubernetes pays an operational cost to get autoscaling, policy and an operator ecosystem.
elevatorPitch: Docker Swarm is Docker Engine's native clustering mode where managers keep Raft state and schedule replicated services across workers.
I verify with docker node ls, docker service ps and checking that three or five managers keep quorum and the required ports are open.
I automate with stack files in Git and rolling update settings, and I would pick Kubernetes once autoscaling, policy or operators are required.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running two managers
mistakesToAvoid.why: Raft needs a majority, so two managers tolerate zero failures; use three or five.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Opening the Docker API on TCP without TLS
mistakesToAvoid.why: It gives root-equivalent control of the host to anyone who can reach it.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming volumes follow tasks between nodes
mistakesToAvoid.why: Local volumes stay on one node, so a rescheduled task starts with empty data.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Declaring Swarm dead or Kubernetes always better
mistakesToAvoid.why: The correct answer depends on scale, team skills and required features.

title: Docker Q54: What does docker save and docker load do [L2]
summary: docker save writes one or more images, with all layers, tags and history, into a tar archive, and docker load reads that archive back into the local image store.
question: What does `docker save` and `docker load` do?
intro: docker save writes one or more images, with all layers, tags and history, into a tar archive, and docker load reads that archive back into the local image store. They are how you move images to air-gapped hosts, back up a build, or hand an image to a tool that cannot reach a registry. Interviewers ask this to see whether you can distinguish images from containers, and save/load from export/import, which flatten a container filesystem and drop image metadata.

steps.title: Mental model: images versus containers
steps.description: Save and load operate on images; export and import operate on containers.
items: docker save: Packages the image layers, manifest, config and tags. The result keeps layer sharing, so saving several related images in one archive stores common layers once.
docker load: Restores those layers and tags into the local daemon; images with the same layers are not duplicated.
docker export / import: export dumps a container's flattened filesystem; import creates a new single-layer image without CMD, ENTRYPOINT, ENV or history.
Not a registry: The archive is a transport format. It has no access control, no signature verification and no pull semantics.
Typical use cases: Offline installs for secure networks, shipping a release to a customer environment, caching images between CI jobs, and preserving a build before a registry migration.
steps.highlight: Use save/load when you need to preserve the image as built. Use export only when you really want a flattened filesystem snapshot.

steps.title: Hands-on: docker save and docker load
steps.description: Create an archive, compress it, move it and load it on another host.
items: Save one image: docker save -o my-app.tar registry.example.com/my-app:1.4.2.
Save several at once: Pass multiple image names to one command so shared base layers are stored once.
Compress in a pipe: docker save my-app:1.4.2 | gzip > my-app.tar.gz and gunzip -c my-app.tar.gz | docker load avoid writing an intermediate file.
Load: docker load -i my-app.tar prints Loaded image: ... for each tag restored.
Output to stdout: Without -o, docker save writes the tar stream to standard output and refuses to write to a terminal, so redirect or pipe it.
steps.codeBlock:
docker save -o stack.tar my-app:1.4.2 postgres:16
ls -lh stack.tar

# Transfer, then on the target host
scp stack.tar user@airgapped-host:/tmp/
docker load -i /tmp/stack.tar
# Loaded image: my-app:1.4.2
# Loaded image: postgres:16

# Stream over SSH without a temp file
docker save my-app:1.4.2 | gzip | ssh user@host 'gunzip | docker load'

steps.title: Verify the image arrived intact
steps.description: Confirm tags, image ID and checksums, because the archive travels outside registry integrity checks.
items: Checksum the archive: Publish sha256sum my-app.tar beside it and verify on the target before loading.
Compare image IDs: docker image inspect --format '{{.Id}}' my-app:1.4.2 should match on both hosts, since the image ID is the config digest.
Check the layers: docker history my-app:1.4.2 shows the build steps are preserved, unlike an imported container export.
Smoke test: Run docker run --rm my-app:1.4.2 --version or your health endpoint before promoting.
Inspect without loading: tar -tf my-app.tar lists manifest.json and the layer blobs, and tar -xOf my-app.tar manifest.json shows the tags stored in the archive.
steps.codeBlock:
sha256sum my-app.tar
docker image inspect --format '{{.Id}}' my-app:1.4.2
docker images --digests | grep my-app

steps.title: Failure modes and edge cases
steps.description: Archives behave differently from registry pulls in a few important ways.
items: Saved by ID loses tags: If you save using an image ID rather than a name, the loaded image has no tag and shows as <none>; always save by name:tag.
Registry digest is not preserved: The registry manifest digest used by image@sha256:... references can differ after load, so do not use load as proof of the registry artifact.
Platform mismatch: An archive built for one architecture will fail with exec format error on another; verify docker image inspect --format '{{.Architecture}}'.
Large archives: Images with big layers produce huge tar files; check disk space on both ends and prefer a local registry when you transfer repeatedly.

Daemon storage backend: Behaviour with multi-platform images can depend on whether the classic or the containerd image store is enabled in your Docker version, so test the round trip before relying on it.

steps.title: Production practice and security
steps.description: Treat the archive as an untrusted artifact until proven otherwise.
items: Kubernetes nodes: To preload an image for containerd run ctr -n k8s.io images import my-app.tar; kind and minikube offer kind load image-archive and minikube image load.
Air-gapped mirrors: Prefer pushing to an internal registry after loading, so nodes pull normally and policy checks still apply.
Supply chain: Scan the image after load with your scanner and verify signatures before transfer, because docker load performs no signature check.
Retention: Store archives with the build ID and checksum in your artifact repository so disaster recovery does not depend on a single registry.
CI caching: Saving an image to a CI cache works for small bases, but registry-backed BuildKit cache (--cache-to type=registry) is usually faster and avoids multi-gigabyte tar files.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Save by name and tag, record a checksum with the archive, and push the loaded image into an internal registry so air-gapped clusters still pull through normal policy and scanning.
elevatorPitch: docker save serializes images with layers, tags and history into a tar archive; docker load restores them into the daemon.
I verify with sha256sum on the archive, matching image IDs on both hosts and a smoke run before use.
I avoid ad hoc archives by pushing to an internal registry, and keep export/import only for container filesystem snapshots.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Export flattens a container and drops CMD, ENV and history, so the result behaves differently.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Saving by image ID
mistakesToAvoid.why: The loaded image has no repository or tag, which makes deployment and cleanup confusing.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Loading archives from unknown sources
mistakesToAvoid.why: docker load performs no signature or provenance check, so a malicious image runs as soon as it is started.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring CPU architecture
mistakesToAvoid.why: An amd64 archive loaded on an arm64 host fails at runtime with exec format error.

summary: Docker bypasses UFW by design.
question: You set up a strict UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) on your Ubuntu server to block all incoming traffic to port 8080. You then run a Docker container `docker run -p 8080:80 myapp`. Miraculously, a hacker easily accesses your app on port 8080 from the internet. Why did the firewall fail?
intro: "In an interview, I explain how we diagnosed container runtime failures without guessing. The interviewer is testing: Docker networking vs. Host iptables/UFW integration.. I structure my answer around systematic triage first, root cause analysis second, and permanent remediation third."

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: Docker bypasses UFW by design. When Docker starts, it actively manipulates the Linux iptables directly by inserting its own rules at the absolute top of the PREROUTING chain in the nat table (in a chain called DOCKER). Because UFW operates primarily in the INPUT chain, the traffic hitting port 8080 is intercepted by Docker's PREROUTING rule *before* UFW ever sees it, and routed directly into the container. *Fix:* Never rely on host OS firewalls to protect exposed Docker ports. You must either not publish the port 8080 to the internet (bind it to localhost -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80), or modify the Docker daemon configuration to set "iptables": false (which breaks many standard Docker networking features).

question: A developer submits a Dockerfile that copies a 5GB file, runs a command to compress it to 100MB, and then runs `rm` to delete the original 5GB file in the next step. Why does the final Docker image still weigh over 5GB?
intro: "In an interview, I explain how we diagnosed container runtime failures without guessing. The interviewer is testing: Intersecting image layers natively, Copy-on-Write storage.. steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: Dockerfile instructions like COPY, RUN, and ADD create immutable, read-only layers. When the developer copied the 5GB file in Layer 1, it was permanently baked into the image history. When they deleted it in Layer 3 using a subsequent RUN rm command, Docker merely created a new layer with a "whiteout" marker hiding the file. The original 5GB file still exists underneath and is physically downloaded by anyone pulling the image. *Fix:* Operations that download, process, and delete temporary files must be chained together within a single RUN instruction using &&: RUN wget massive.tar && compress massive.tar && rm massive.tar

intro: "Container stability relies on clean signal handling (SIGTERM vs SIGKILL) and immutable image tagging. The interviewer is testing: Daemonizing background processes inside containers.. I structure my answer around systematic triage first, root cause analysis second, and permanent remediation third."

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: A Docker container strictly lives only as long as its primary PID 1 process is running. If the CMD or ENTRYPOINT in the Dockerfile starts an application in the background (e.g., executing service nginx start or appending an & to a script), the script will start the daemon, successfully finish its execution, and return an exit code of 0. Because the foreground script finished, PID 1 terminates, and Docker shuts down the container, killing everything inside it. *Fix:* You must run the main process in the foreground. Use nginx -g 'daemon off;' or execute the application binary explicitly without backgrounding it.

title: Docker Q69: What happens if your CI pipeline repeatedly builds the exact same Dockerfile using the latest tag and pushes it to an AWS ECR registry every day for a year [L1]

intro: "When containerizing our microservices stack, container lifecycle and resource management were critical. The interviewer is testing: Tag mutability, dangling references, registry bloat.. steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: Using the latest tag makes it a mutable tag. Every time the CI pipeline pushes, AWS ECR will overwrite the latest tag to point to the brand new image manifest. The older images from previous days will lose their tag and become Untagged (Dangling) images in the registry. If no Lifecycle Policy is configured to garbage-collect untagged images, you will accumulate 365 orphaned 1GB images, paying AWS for useless storage bloat. (Also, deploying latest in Kubernetes is dangerous as it breaks rollback determinism). Always use Git SHAs or Semantic Versioning tags.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: No, Docker containers natively are not Virtual Machines. It isolates processes locally using Linux features like Namespaces (for isolating visibility of network/PIDs) and Cgroups (for capping CPU/Memory limits). Containers are vastly lighter because they don't load a 1GB kernel to simply run a 50MB Python app.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: Use Rootless Docker, which runs the Docker daemon and all containers entirely within a user's namespace without requiring root privileges on the host. Installation: dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh install (ships with Docker 20.10+). steps.description: Use the --read-only flag to make the entire root filesystem read-only: With --read-only, any write attempt to an unmounted path returns a "Read-only file system" error. steps.description: When Docker sends SIGTERM via docker stop, it delivers the signal to PID 1 inside the container. If PID 1 is a shell script (/bin/sh or /bin/bash), the shell does NOT forward signals to its child processes by default. The shell itself ignores SIGTERM, so nothing happens for 10 seconds until Docker sends SIGKILL.
items: Use exec to replace the shell with the main process: the last line of your entrypoint script should be exec ./my-worker instead of ./my-worker. This makes the worker PID 1 and it receives SIGTERM directly.
Trap signals in the shell script if you must manage multiple processes:
Use --init flag (docker run --init) to inject tini as PID 1, which properly forwards signals and reaps zombie processes.

./worker1 &
./worker2 &
wait

items: Log Rotation: Immediately configure logrotate to compress and delete logs older than a few hours or when they exceed a certain MB threshold. This caps the maximum disk usage.

Decoupling State: In modern DevOps (e.g., Docker/Kubernetes), applications shouldn't manage log files on disk at all. Applications should log purely to STDOUT and STDERR. A DaemonSet or sidecar agent (like Fluentbit or Filebeat) acts as a pipe, reading those streams and shipping them entirely off the host to a centralized aggregator (Datadog/Elasticsearch) preventing local disk exhaustion completely.

title: General DevOps Q4: Explain the difference between Blue/Green deployment and Canary deployment [L1]
summary: Blue/Green: You maintain two identical production environments. The current live environment is "Blue".
question: Explain the difference between Blue/Green deployment and Canary deployment.
roleContext: General DevOps Scenario #4 (L1) · General DevOps — Scenario-Based Interview Questions
intro: "Senior DevOps is about building reliable automated feedback loops between code commit and production observability. The interviewer is testing: Deployment strategies, risk mitigation.. I structure my answer around systematic triage first, root cause analysis second, and permanent remediation third."

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
items: Blue/Green: You maintain two identical production environments. The current live environment is "Blue". You deploy the new code to the "Green" environment, run integration tests against it in isolation, and when ready, you instantaneously flip the router/load balancer to send 100% of user traffic to Green. If something goes wrong, you instantly flip the router back to Blue for a zero-downtime rollback. It requires 2x the infrastructure capacity.

Canary: You deploy the new code to a small subset of servers (the "canary"), and route only a tiny percentage of traffic (e.g., 5%) to it. You monitor the error rates and metrics on the canary. If stable, you gradually increase traffic (10%, 25%, 100%). If it fails, only 5% of users are impacted, and it automatically rolls back. It requires complex traffic routing (like a Service Mesh or ALB weighted rules).

At 2 AM the next night, the cron job fires again. Now two heavy backups are running simultaneously, locking the DB. How do you prevent this in the script?
roleContext: General DevOps Scenario #12 (L2) · General DevOps — Scenario-Based Interview Questions
intro: "Senior DevOps is about building reliable automated feedback loops between code commit and production observability. steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: Cron jobs must be designed to be self-aware of overlapping executions. This is solved using File Locking. The script must attempt to acquire an exclusive lock before running the heavy operation. If it cannot get the lock, it immediately exits. In Linux, the standard tool is flock: 0 2 * * * /usr/bin/flock -n /var/run/backup.lock /path/to/backup_script.sh The -n (non-blocking) flag tells flock to immediately fail if the lock file is currently held by a previous, still-running instance of the script. This guarantees only one backup can ever run at a time.

title: Ansible Q1: You have an architecture running 50 identical EC2 instances You need to deploy a rapid emergency patch Using Ansible what is the problem with running the playbook against the inventory sequentially and how do you speed it up [L2]
summary: By default, Ansible processes tasks with a concurrency of 5 forks. When patching 50 instances, sequential execution causes severe delay (20+ minutes). Overriding with -f 50 spawns 50 parallel worker processes, slashing turnaround down to ~2 minutes.
question: You have an architecture running 50 identical EC2 instances. You need to deploy a rapid emergency patch. Using Ansible, what is the problem with running the playbook against the inventory sequentially, and how do you speed it up?
roleContext: Senior DevOps / SRE Scenario #1 · Ansible Performance & Scale
intro: "In production operations, maintenance windows during SEV-1 outages are measured in minutes. The interviewer is testing understanding of Ansible's execution model, process architecture, and concurrency limits. I structure my response around immediate triage, parallel fork optimization, and Day-2 configuration guardrails."

steps.title: Analyze Default Fork Bottlenecks
steps.description: By default, Ansible runs with forks = 5 in ansible.cfg. When executing against 50 hosts, Ansible divides the fleet into 10 sequential batches (50 / 5 = 10). If an emergency patching task takes 2 minutes per host, the entire deployment requires 20 minutes of critical lead time.
items: Default Concurrency: 5 worker sub-processes handling SSH connections.
Sequential Grouping: Each task waits for all 5 current hosts to complete before dispatching to the next 5 hosts.
Blast Radius / Time Risk: Extended exposure window where instances run mixed versions.

steps.title: Immediate Remediation: Override Forks at Runtime
steps.description: To achieve instantaneous fleet-wide patching, override the worker forks count directly from the CLI to match the total instance count:
items: ansible-playbook -i inventory/aws_ec2.yml patch.yml -f 50
This instructs the Ansible controller to spawn 50 parallel Python worker processes simultaneously.
Execution duration drops from 20 minutes down to ~2 minutes (single execution cycle).

steps.title: Controller Capacity & SSH Multiplexing Tuning
steps.description: Spawning 50 parallel SSH sessions requires tuning the Ansible controller OS limits and SSH configuration:
items: File Descriptor Limits: Ensure ulimit -n 65535 on the controller to avoid socket exhaustion.
SSH Pipelining: Enable pipelining = True in ansible.cfg to execute Python modules directly via stdin without file copies.
ControlMaster: Configure ssh_args = -C -o ControlMaster=auto -o ControlPersist=60s to reuse persistent TCP connections.

keyTakeaway: Concurrency in Ansible is governed by the forks parameter. During emergency patches, scale worker forks to match node count (-f 50), enable SSH pipelining, and tune controller file descriptors to achieve near-instantaneous fleet-wide deployment.
elevatorPitch: Default Ansible concurrency is capped at 5 forks, forcing 50 instances into 10 sequential 2-minute batches (20 min total).
Immediately override concurrency on CLI using: ansible-playbook -i inventory patch.yml -f 50 to execute all nodes in parallel.
Verify Ansible controller has adequate file descriptors (ulimit -n 65535) and memory headroom for 50 worker processes.
Enable SSH pipelining = True in ansible.cfg to eliminate intermediate Python script SFTP writes.
Use SSH ControlMaster multiplexing to persist open TCP sockets across consecutive tasks.
Establish permanent guardrails in ansible.cfg setting default forks = 25 or 50 for CI/CD runners.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running playbooks with default 5 forks during active P1 outages
mistakesToAvoid.why: Extends incident duration by 10x. Interviewers expect senior engineers to immediately identify the concurrency parameter as the primary bottleneck.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Increasing forks to 100+ without verifying controller CPU, memory, and ulimit
mistakesToAvoid.why: Spawning too many forks on an undersized controller (e.g. t3.micro) causes fork bomb kernel OOM kills and dropped SSH handshakes.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Confusing forks with the serial keyword
mistakesToAvoid.why: Forks controls task parallelism across hosts; serial controls rolling batch deployment sizes across entire plays.

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
steps.description: This is called a Cache Stampede (or Thundering Herd). It happens when a highly popular cached key expires. Instantly, thousands of concurrent requests hit the cache, find a miss, and *all* of them simultaneously bypass the cache and query the database to regenerate the exact same data, crashing the database.
items: Adding Jitter: Instead of setting a strict 1-hour expiration on keys, add random jitter (e.g., 60 minutes + random 0 to 5 minutes) so keys expire staggeringly, preventing massive simultaneous purges.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: Serverless functions (like AWS Lambda) scale highly concurrently. If 5,000 requests come in, 5,000 ephemeral Lambda containers spin up, and *each one* attempts to open a separate, direct TCP connection to the PostgreSQL database. To fix this, you must introduce a Connection Pooler between the Lambdas and the Database. In AWS, the best managed solution is Amazon RDS Proxy. The Lambdas connect to the RDS Proxy, and the proxy multiplexes those thousands of requests over a small, stable pool of persistent connections to the database, protecting it from being overwhelmed.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: In microservices, Service A often calls Service B. If Service B becomes unresponsive, Service A will continuously wait for timeouts, backing up its own queues and exhausting its threads until Service A also crashes. This causes a "cascading failure" across the entire system. The Circuit Breaker pattern prevents this. If Service B fails a certain number of times in a row, Service A's circuit breaker "trips" (opens). Service A stops trying to call Service B entirely, instantly returning a fallback response or an error, protecting its own resources. It periodically sends a test request (half-open state) and if Service B is healthy again, the circuit closes and normal traffic resumes.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: In Traditional CI/CD (Push), the CI runner (like Jenkins or GitHub Actions) lives outside the Kubernetes cluster. To deploy, the CI runner must be granted highly privileged API credentials to reach *into* the cluster and push changes. If Jenkins is compromised, the attacker has god-mode access to the production cluster. In GitOps (Pull), an operator (like ArgoCD) runs *inside* the cluster itself. It proactively monitors a Git repository for changes and pulls them in, applying them locally. Security Difference: The cluster never exposes its API credentials to the outside world. The Git repository becomes the single source of truth, and if CI is compromised, attackers can only push code, not execute direct cluster commands, significantly reducing the blast radius.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: In distributed architectures (where data is replicated across multiple servers or regions for high availability), it takes time for a write on Node A to propagate to Node B. Eventual Consistency means that if you update a record and immediately try to read it back from a different replica, you might get the old data for a few milliseconds (or seconds). However, the system guarantees that absent of any further updates, eventually all replicas will synchronize, and all readers will see the latest correct value. It is a tradeoff sacrificing immediate strict consistency in exchange for massive scalability and uptime.

steps.title: Understand Git Conflict Markers & Enable diff3 Mode
steps.description: Decode the standard conflict markers and activate diff3 or zdiff3 to reveal the common base ancestor commit.
items: <<<<<<< HEAD: Marks lines currently present on your checked-out branch (ours).
||||||| base: Present when merge.conflictstyle=diff3 (or zdiff3) is configured. Displays the original code from the common ancestor commit before divergence.
=======: The horizontal divider separating your local branch changes from the incoming branch changes.
>>>>>>> feature-branch: Marks lines coming from the branch being merged into your current branch (theirs).

matrix.title: Git Conflict Marker Tokens & Diff3 Inspection

steps.title: Resolve Hunks, Remove Markers & Execute Test Suites
steps.description: Edit each conflicted file, combine valid business logic, remove all marker tokens, and execute local unit tests.
items: Synthesize logic: Read both changes in context. Never blindly accept --ours or --theirs without validating business intent.
Verify zero leftover markers: Search working tree with grep -rnE '(<<<|>>>|===)' src/ to ensure no syntax errors slip through.
Run test suite: Execute local linting and unit test suites before staging.

# Verify no remaining conflict markers in codebase

# Run language unit tests to verify merged logic
go test -v ./...

steps.title: Stage Resolved Files & Finalize the Merge Commit
steps.description: Mark conflicts resolved using git add and finalize the merge commit.
items: Stage resolved files: Run git add <file> to move resolved files from unmerged stage 1/2/3 to the index stage 0.
Inspect staged diff: Run git diff --staged to review the clean consolidated merge patch.
Commit: Conclude with git commit (Git automatically populates the default merge message referencing the merged branch).

git diff --staged
git commit -m "Merge feature/auth-v2 into main: resolve router and config conflicts"

steps.title: Production Safeguards: git rerere & Trunk-Based Practices
steps.description: Automate repetitive conflict resolution with git rerere and prevent drift with short-lived branches.
items: Enable git rerere: Run git config --global rerere.enabled true so Git records resolved conflict hunks and automatically reapplies them when rebasing long-lived branches.
Short-lived feature branches: Enforce pull requests merged within 24-48 hours to minimize merge blast radius.
Automated merge conflict CI checks: Configure GitHub Actions / GitLab CI to run mergeability dry-runs on every pull request update.

title: Git Q4: When should you use git rebase instead of git merge and what is the one rule you must never break [L2]
summary: Both integrate changes from one branch into another, but they produce very different histories.
question: When should you use `git rebase` instead of `git merge`, and what is the one rule you must never break?
intro: "Git is an immutable directed acyclic graph (DAG); knowing commands like git reflog means you never truly lose commits. The interviewer is testing: Workflow tradeoffs, understanding the danger of rewriting shared history.. I structure my answer around systematic triage first, root cause analysis second, and permanent remediation third."

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
steps.description: Both integrate changes from one branch into another, but they produce very different histories.
items: Merge preserves the actual branching history (creates a merge commit). Good for main/release branches where the history of *when things converged* matters.

Rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch, producing a linear history with no merge commits. Good for cleaning up your local feature branch *before* opening a PR — it makes review easier and git log readable.

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: The one rule: never rebase commits that have been pushed and that other people are working on. Rebase rewrites commit hashes. If a teammate has pulled the old commits and you force-push rewritten ones, their next pull is a mess and they may re-introduce the old commits. Rebase your private branch all you want; never rebase shared branches like main or develop. Common workflow: rebase your feature branch onto latest main (git pull --rebase origin main), squash interactively (git rebase -i), force-push to your *own* feature branch, then merge the PR.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: You can't reset main — it's shared and 15 other commits have built on top. The right tool is git revert, which creates a *new* commit that undoes the changes. For a merge commit you need -m to tell Git which parent to revert to (the "mainline"): -m 1 means "treat parent 1 (the main side) as the mainline, and revert everything that came in from the feature side." -m 2 would do the opposite. Push the revert. Now main is back to a working state and the 15 unrelated commits are preserved. Gotcha: if later you want to re-merge the fixed version of that feature branch, a plain merge will appear to do nothing because Git thinks those changes are already on main (they were, then reverted). You either revert the revert (git revert ) before re-merging, or rebase the feature branch onto current main so the commits get fresh hashes.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: A --hard reset moves the branch pointer and discards working-tree changes — but the commits themselves are not deleted. They're orphaned (no branch points to them) and will sit in the object database until garbage collection runs (default: ~30 days for unreachable objects, 90 days if reachable from reflog). Recovery via the reflog, which is a per-clone log of every move HEAD (and each branch ref) has made: You'll see something like: def5678 is the tip of the work that was wiped. Restore it: Two important caveats: (1) the reflog is local — it doesn't help if the commits never existed on this clone (e.g. teammate's machine). (2) Run recovery *before* git gc runs. If you suspect a teammate already ran git gc --prune=now, the objects may genuinely be gone. As a habit, alias reset --hard to require confirmation, and teach the team git stash and git switch -c backup before risky operations.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: git pull is two commands stitched together: git fetch (download new commits and tags from the remote into origin/) followed by git merge origin/ into your current branch. If your local branch has commits the remote doesn't, that merge produces a merge commit ("Merge branch 'main' of …"), which clutters history with bookkeeping commits that don't represent real work. git pull --rebase replaces the merge step with a rebase: your local commits are temporarily set aside, the new remote commits are applied first, and then your commits are replayed on top. Result: a clean linear history with no noise commits. Many teams set git config --global pull.rebase true so this becomes the default. title: Git Q13: Explain the four states a file can be in inside a Git repo untracked modified staged committed Why does Git have a separate staging area [L1]

question: Explain the four states a file can be in inside a Git repo: untracked, modified, staged, committed. Why does Git have a separate staging area?

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
steps.description: A file moves through these states:
items: Untracked — exists in your working directory but Git has never been told about it. Shows up under "Untracked files" in git status.
Modified (tracked) — Git knows about the file, and the working-tree version differs from what's in the last commit. Shows under "Changes not staged for commit."
Staged — you ran git add , copying its current content into the *index* (staging area). Shows under "Changes to be committed." git commit will record exactly this snapshot.

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: The staging area exists so you can build the *next* commit deliberately instead of having every saved file immediately become part of it. You can edit ten files, but git add only the three related ones, then git commit a focused logical change. git add -p takes this further — letting you stage individual hunks within a file. Without the index, you'd have to commit everything at once or stash/branch around it.
items: Committed — the staged content has been written into a commit object. Working tree, index, and HEAD all agree.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: Use git bisect — a binary search over commits. Git checks out a commit roughly halfway between them. You build/test it and report: Each step halves the search space. steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
steps.description: Three orthogonal techniques solve three different problems:
items: Partial clone — defers downloading file blobs until they're actually accessed:
Sparse-checkout — limits which paths exist in your working tree:

Git LFS for large binaries — design files, ML model artifacts, video. LFS stores a small pointer file in Git and the actual blob on a separate object store, fetched on demand. Adopt this *going forward*; converting historical large blobs requires git lfs migrate import plus a force-push, which rewrites history.
Partial clone makes operations like git log -p, git blame, and bisect across many files trigger on-demand fetches that can be slow or fail offline. Engineers on flaky networks suffer.

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: Fetches all commits and trees but no file contents. When you checkout or log -p a path, Git lazily fetches just those blobs. Cuts initial clone from 25 GB to a few hundred MB. Requires a server that supports it (GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, Gitea all do). You still have the full history, but only the directories you listed materialize on disk. IDE indexing now sees 5% of the tree. Combine with partial clone for maximum effect (git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse ). Where they fall short: The pragmatic recipe for most teams: sparse + partial clone via a git clone wrapper script for new hires, LFS adopted for any binary > a few MB, and a "no committing build artifacts" lint in CI.
items: Sparse-checkout doesn't help operations that *traverse* the repo — git grep over a sparse checkout misses files you didn't materialize, which can be surprising. Cone mode mitigates but doesn't eliminate this.

LFS adds operational dependency on the LFS server, increases hosting cost, and storage isn't free or fast for huge blobs. It's not a silver bullet — for truly large binary pipelines (e.g. game asset workflows), Perforce or a content-addressed object store is sometimes a better fit than Git.

None of these address the *root* problem on Git itself: extremely deep histories on a few hot files (think: lockfiles touched by everyone) can still slow blame and log. At true Google/Microsoft scale you eventually outgrow vanilla Git and look at VFS for Git, Scalar, or Piper-style virtual filesystems.
