steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
steps.description: By default, Git's Author and Committer headers are unauthenticated free-text — anyone can run git config user.email "ceo@company.com" and produce commits that look like the CEO. Signing fixes that with cryptographic proof.
items: Signing keys per developer. Either GPG (traditional) or SSH signing (Git ≥ 2.34, much simpler — reuse the SSH key engineers already have):
Allowed-signers file mapping email → public key, distributed via your IDP / SSO so trust is centralized, not per-laptop.
Upload the public key to GitHub/GitLab under "Signing key." Now the platform shows a "Verified" badge and exposes verification status via the API.
Branch protection on main — require signed commits, require linear history, require status checks. Block merges where any commit is unsigned.

CI verification — a pre-merge job that runs git verify-commit against each commit in the PR, failing if any commit isn't signed by a key in the allowed-signers list. Don't rely solely on the platform UI badge.
CODEOWNERS to require domain-expert review on sensitive paths (e.g. /infra/, /auth/, CI workflows themselves).

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: Implementation: What this actually prevents: What it does not prevent: Signing answers "who wrote this commit?" with cryptography. It does not answer "is this code safe?" — that's a separate problem.
items: Author spoofing — an attacker who compromises one developer's laptop can no longer forge commits as a different developer (different key).
Tampering with merged history — if someone with repo-admin access tries to silently rewrite a past commit, the signature on the original commit chain breaks and CI rejects it.
Compromised CI tokens pushing arbitrary code as humans — unsigned commits are blocked, so a leaked PAT can't ship merge-able changes without a key.

A compromised developer laptop with their key on it — the attacker's commits will sign correctly. Mitigations: hardware-backed keys (YubiKey for GPG, or SSH keys in ssh-agent with confirmation), short-lived keys via SSO-issued certificates, and behavioral monitoring.
Malicious code that's *legitimately* authored and signed (insider threat, social-engineered review). That's what CODEOWNERS, mandatory review, and SCA tooling are for.

steps.description: Compliance auditors essentially want to see: every change to main is reviewed by someone other than the author, every change is traced to a ticket, every change runs the same controls, and the history is tamper-evident.
items: No direct pushes — pushes only via PR. Restrict who can push to matching branches set to no one (not even admins, with Do not allow bypassing enabled).
Linear history required — no merge commits. Forces squash- or rebase-merge, making each main commit a single reviewable, revertable unit.
Required reviews — minimum 1 for low-risk paths, 2 for sensitive paths via CODEOWNERS. Dismiss stale reviews on new commits so a reviewer's approval doesn't carry over after the author force-pushes.
CODEOWNERS mapping critical paths (/infra/, /auth/, /billing/, /.github/workflows/) to specific owners. Workflows-on-workflows is a common attack vector — protect .github/ aggressively.

Required status checks — CI must pass: unit tests, integration tests, SAST (e.g. Semgrep), dependency scan (Dependabot/Snyk/Trivy), secret scan (gitleaks), license scan, and the duplicate-Q&A or contract-tests if relevant. Pin the exact check names so they can't be renamed away.
Signed commits required — see prior answer.
Conversation resolution required — every PR comment must be resolved before merge.
No bypass for admins — auditors will ask. The tradeoff: a real emergency (rare) requires temporarily lifting the rule, which is logged in the audit trail and is itself a finding to triage.
Ticket linking — PR title regex enforced to include JIRA-1234 (or similar). The commit-msg hook on the server rejects PRs without it. Auditors get traceability from ticket → PR → commit → deployment.

items: PR templates — checkboxes for "tests added," "security impact considered," "rollback plan." Required for sensitive areas via CODEOWNERS-driven PR templates.

Two reviewers required on /auth/ slows urgent fixes — mitigate with a documented break-glass process and clear on-call ownership.
Required signed commits adds setup friction for new hires — build it into the laptop bootstrap script and have the onboarding checklist verify a signed test commit before they get repo write access.

Many required checks → slow merges. Invest in CI parallelism and selective testing (run only the affected service's tests when paths under services/foo/ change). Without this, developers will route around the system, defeating the policy.

steps.description: git clone does not initialize submodules by default — it clones the parent repo and creates the submodule directory, but leaves it empty. The fix:
items: The parent repo stores a .gitmodules file (URL + path mapping) and a special tree entry recording the *exact* commit SHA the submodule should point to.
git submodule update checks out that pinned commit inside the submodule directory — it puts the submodule in detached HEAD state.
To update the submodule to its latest upstream commit: cd && git pull origin main, then go back to the parent repo and git add && git commit to record the new SHA.
Forgetting --recurse-submodules on clone, pull, and checkout — configure globally: git config --global submodule.recurse true.

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: Or clone with submodules from the start: How submodules work: Common pitfalls: Many teams eventually migrate away from submodules to package managers (npm, pip, Maven) or monorepo approaches because submodules add significant cognitive overhead.
items: Committing without updating the submodule pointer — you update the library but forget to commit the new SHA in the parent repo. Other developers don't get the update.
Nested submodules — always use --recursive.

title: Git Q35: Explain how Git stores data internally What are blobs trees commits and tags at the object level [L3]
subCategory: Pull updates from an incremental bundle:
summary: Git is fundamentally a content-addressable filesystem. Every piece of data is stored as an object identified by its SHA-1 (or SHA-256) hash. There are four object types:.
question: Explain how Git stores data internally. What are blobs, trees, commits, and tags at the object level?
roleContext: Git Scenario #35 (L3) · Pull updates from an incremental bundle:
intro: "During a major release branch cut, we encountered this exact scenario and used Git internals to recover cleanly. The interviewer is testing: Deep understanding of Git's content-addressable object model.. I structure my answer around systematic triage first, root cause analysis second, and permanent remediation third."

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
steps.description: Git is fundamentally a content-addressable filesystem. Every piece of data is stored as an object identified by its SHA-1 (or SHA-256) hash. There are four object types:
items: Blob — stores file content (just the raw bytes, no filename or permissions). Two files with identical content share the same blob object, regardless of filename or location. This is how Git deduplicates storage.

Tree — represents a directory. Contains entries mapping filenames → blob SHAs (for files) or other tree SHAs (for subdirectories), along with file mode (permissions). A tree is a snapshot of a directory at a point in time.

Commit — points to one tree (the root tree of the project at that moment) and zero or more parent commits. Contains author, committer, timestamp, and message. The first commit has no parent; merge commits have two or more parents. The commit's SHA is a hash of all this — changing anything (message, author, parent, tree) produces a different SHA.

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: How a commit represents a full snapshot: Each commit stores a complete snapshot, not a diff. Git computes diffs on the fly by comparing two commits' trees. This is why checkout is fast (just materialize one tree) and why branches are cheap (a branch is a 41-byte file containing a commit SHA). Packfiles: for efficiency, Git periodically packs loose objects into packfiles (.pack + .idx), using delta compression (storing diffs between similar blobs) to reduce disk usage. git gc triggers this. Packing is a storage optimization — the logical model is still immutable, content-addressed objects.
items: Tag (annotated) — points to a commit (or any object) and adds tagger identity, date, message, and optional signature.

commit abc123
  └── tree def456 (root directory)
       ├── blob 111aaa  README.md
       ├── tree 222bbb  src/
       │    ├── blob 333ccc  main.py
       │    └── blob 444ddd  utils.py
       └── tree 555eee  tests/
            └── blob 666fff  test_main.py

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
steps.description: git gc (garbage collection) performs housekeeping on the Git object database:
items: Packs loose objects into packfiles — individual objects in .git/objects/ are compressed into efficient .pack files with delta compression.

Packs refs — consolidates individual ref files in .git/refs/ into a single packed-refs file.
Prunes old reflog entries — entries older than 90 days (reachable) or 30 days (unreachable) by default.

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: When Git runs it automatically: Git triggers gc --auto after certain operations (e.g., when there are more than 6700 loose objects or more than 50 packfiles). Only useful occasionally (e.g., after importing from another VCS). Don't run it routinely — the default compression is good enough and --aggressive is slow. Caution: --prune=now immediately deletes unreachable objects. If you're recovering lost commits via reflog, run recovery *before* GC.
items: After large history rewrites (filter-repo, mass deletions) to reclaim disk space.
When the repo feels slow and .git/ is unusually large.
Before creating a bundle or archive — ensures maximum compression.

items: Enable Git tracing:

Server-side hooks are slow? — pre-receive or update hooks (code scanning, large file checks, CI triggers) run synchronously. Check with the platform admin.

title: Kubernetes Q10: Your init container is stuck and the main container never starts How do you debug [L2]
summary: Debug a stuck Kubernetes init container by inspecting pod events with describe, checking init container logs, and verifying blocking service dependencies.
question: Your init container is stuck and the main container never starts. How do you debug?
intro: When an init container is stuck, the Kubernetes kubelet halts pod initialization because init containers must complete sequentially and exit with code 0 before app containers start. The pod status remains frozen in Init:0/1, Init:CrashLoopBackOff, or PodInitializing. To diagnose the failure quickly, senior engineers follow a structured triage path: check pod status and termination exit codes, extract init container logs, test network dependencies, and resolve deadlocks.

steps.title: Triage Why Your Init Container is Stuck Using Kubectl Logs
steps.description: Init containers execute sequentially in the exact order declared under spec.initContainers. Understanding status codes is critical for triage.
items: Init:N/M status: In a pod with M init containers, N have successfully completed with exit code 0. If stuck at Init:0/1, the first init container is either hanging or actively running.
Init:CrashLoopBackOff: The init container completed with a non-zero exit code. Kubelet restarts it with an exponential backoff delay (10s, 20s, up to 5m).
Main container dormancy: The primary application containers in spec.containers remain in Waiting state with reason PodInitializing until all init containers succeed.

steps.title: Step 1: Inspect pod status, container exit codes, and recent events
steps.description: Execute kubectl describe to extract the init container's current state, last termination reason, exit code, and cluster events.
steps.codeBlock:
# Identify pods stuck in Init state
kubectl get pods -l app=payment-api

# Detailed inspection of container state and events
kubectl describe pod payment-api-7b89df5c4-x8k9l

# Extract exact state and exit codes via jsonpath
kubectl get pod payment-api-7b89df5c4-x8k9l -o jsonpath='{range .status.initContainerStatuses[*]}{.name}{"\t"}{.state}{"\n"}{end}'
items: State inspection: Look under Init Containers in the describe output. Check if State: Running (process is hanging) or State: Waiting with CrashLoopBackOff.
Termination reason & exit code: Exit code 1 indicates runtime script failure; code 137 indicates an OOMKilled event or SIGKILL; code 127 indicates command not found.
Pod events section: Check if image pull errors (ErrImagePull, ImagePullBackOff) or volume mount failures are blocking the init container from even launching.

steps.title: Step 2: Fetch stdout and stderr logs for the specific init container
steps.description: Standard kubectl logs queries default to the first app container, which does not exist yet. You must explicitly target the init container by name.
steps.codeBlock:
# Target init container logs explicitly
kubectl logs payment-api-7b89df5c4-x8k9l -c wait-for-postgres

# Stream logs in real-time if init container is currently running
kubectl logs -f payment-api-7b89df5c4-x8k9l -c wait-for-postgres

# If container crashed, inspect previous instance before restart
kubectl logs payment-api-7b89df5c4-x8k9l -c wait-for-postgres --previous
items: Specify container name: Always pass -c <init-container-name>. Running kubectl logs <pod> without -c fails with container not found.
The --previous flag: When an init container crashes and enters backoff, inspect the logs of the crashed instance using --previous to see uncaught stack traces.
Common log patterns: Look for connection refused errors, database authentication timeouts, missing environment variables, or database migration syntax errors.

steps.title: Step 3: Test network reachability, DNS, and service dependencies
steps.description: A frequent root cause of stuck init containers is waiting indefinitely for an upstream service or database migration lock.
steps.codeBlock:
# Launch an interactive debug container in the same network namespace
kubectl debug -it payment-api-7b89df5c4-x8k9l --image=curlimages/curl --target=wait-for-postgres

# Test DNS resolution for upstream database inside cluster
nslookup postgres-service.database.svc.cluster.local

# Test TCP connectivity on database port
nc -zv -w 5 postgres-service 5432
items: CoreDNS resolution failure: Verify the init container can resolve external and in-cluster hostnames. Check if /etc/resolv.conf contains valid nameservers.
NetworkPolicy blockage: Check if Kubernetes NetworkPolicies or cloud security groups prevent egress from the pod's namespace to the target service.
Deadlocked migration locks: Database migration tools (e.g., Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic) maintain lock tables. If a previous deployment crashed mid-migration, the lock may remain held.

steps.title: Production remediation: Implement timeouts, bounded loops, and probes
steps.description: Prevent indefinite pod hangs by building defensive retry logic and failure limits into init container commands.
steps.codeBlock:
# Resilient init container with bounded timeout
initContainers:
- name: wait-for-db
  image: busybox:1.36
  command: ['sh', '-c']
  args:
    - |
      timeout=60
      until nc -z -w 2 postgres-service 5432 || [ $timeout -le 0 ]; do
        echo "Waiting for PostgreSQL on port 5432... ($timeout s remaining)"
        sleep 2
        timeout=$((timeout - 2))
      done
      if [ $timeout -le 0 ]; then
        echo "ERROR: Timeout reached waiting for PostgreSQL!"
        exit 1
      fi
items: Bounded timeout wrappers: Never run unbounded while true; do sleep 1; done loops. Always enforce a hard timeout that exits non-zero so Kubernetes can alert on the failure.
Active readiness probes on upstream: Verify dependent services have valid endpoints in kubectl get endpoints <service> before pod scheduling.
Resource limits on init containers: Explicitly set CPU and memory limits on init containers to prevent cluster eviction or silent node OOM panics.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: When debugging a stuck init container, use kubectl logs <pod> -c <init-container> --previous and inspect the pod's termination exit code in describe output.
elevatorPitch: Run kubectl describe pod to inspect the init container's state, termination reason, and cluster events.
Fetch stdout and stderr logs by explicitly specifying the init container name with kubectl logs -c <init> --previous.
Verify network reachability and database migration locks, and ensure all init scripts enforce bounded timeouts.

title: Kubernetes Q15: You want to make sure two pods of the same app NEVER run on the same node How [L2]
summary: Use Pod Anti-Affinity:
question: You want to make sure two pods of the same app NEVER run on the same node. How?
intro: To make sure two pods of the same app never run on the same node, add a requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution pod anti-affinity rule that matches the app's own labels and uses kubernetes.io/hostname as the topologyKey. The scheduler will then refuse to place a second matching pod on any node that already runs one. Interviewers ask this to see whether you know the difference between a hard guarantee and a preference, and whether you have thought about what happens when replicas outnumber nodes or when a rolling update needs surge capacity.

steps.title: Mental Model: Hard Anti-Affinity vs Soft Preference
steps.description: Pod anti-affinity is evaluated by the scheduler at placement time, against pods that already exist in a topology domain.
items: Required (hard): requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution is a filter. If no node satisfies it, the pod stays Pending. This is the only form that gives a true guarantee.

Preferred (soft): preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution only adds a score weight (1 to 100). The scheduler may still co-locate pods when nothing else fits, so it does not satisfy a NEVER requirement.
topologyKey: defines what counts as the same place. kubernetes.io/hostname means one node; topology.kubernetes.io/zone means one availability zone.
IgnoredDuringExecution: the rule is not re-checked after scheduling. If someone relabels a pod or a node, running pods are not evicted.
Why hostname: every node carries the well-known label kubernetes.io/hostname with a unique value, so using it as the topologyKey makes each node its own domain.
steps.highlight: A hard rule is a trade of availability for isolation: if you run 4 replicas on a 3 node cluster, the fourth pod will sit in Pending forever. That is the correct behaviour for a NEVER requirement, so size the cluster for it.

steps.title: Hands-on: Pods Never Run on the Same Node (YAML)
steps.description: The labelSelector must match the labels of the pods being created, otherwise the rule constrains nothing.
items: Selector match: the labelSelector below matches app: my-app, which is also in the pod template labels. A typo here is the most common reason the rule silently does nothing.
Scope: without namespaces or namespaceSelector in the term, only pods in the pod's own namespace are considered.
Apply and watch: after applying, kubectl get pods -l app=my-app -o wide should show a different value in the NODE column for every replica.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-app
    spec:
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            - labelSelector:
                matchLabels:
                  app: my-app
              topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      containers:
        - name: my-app
          image: registry.example.com/my-app:1.4.2
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }

steps.title: Verify Placement and Read Scheduler Events
steps.description: Never trust the manifest alone; confirm what the scheduler actually did.
items: Check node spread: kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=my-app -o custom-columns=POD:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName lists each pod with its node. Any duplicate node name means the rule is not in effect.

Read the Pending reason: kubectl describe pod <pod> shows an event like 0/3 nodes are available: 3 node(s) didn't match pod anti-affinity rules. That message confirms the rule is working and capacity is the issue.
Confirm the rendered spec: kubectl get deploy my-app -n prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.affinity}' proves what was actually applied, which matters when Helm or Kustomize patches are involved.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=my-app \
  -o custom-columns=POD:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName,STATUS:.status.phase

# Count replicas per node, anything above 1 is a violation
kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=my-app -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.spec.nodeName}{"\n"}{end}' \
  | sort | uniq -c

steps.title: Failure Modes: Rolling Updates, Replica Count and Autoscaling
steps.description: Hard anti-affinity interacts badly with default rollout settings and with small clusters.
items: Rolling update deadlock: during a rollout, old and new ReplicaSet pods share the app label, so a surge pod repels itself from every node that holds an old pod. With replicas equal to node count and the default maxSurge: 25%, the surge pod can stay Pending. Set maxSurge: 0 and maxUnavailable: 1, or keep at least one spare node.

Replicas greater than nodes: extra pods stay Pending. With Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter, a new node will be provisioned if one is allowed to satisfy the rule; check the autoscaler logs when pods are Pending but the node group has headroom.
Taints and selectors: if only some nodes are eligible (nodeSelector, taints, GPU pools), the effective limit is the eligible node count, not the cluster node count.

Alternative: topologySpreadConstraints with maxSkew: 1 and whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule keeps pods evenly spread and scales better, but it limits imbalance rather than forbidding sharing, so it is not a strict NEVER.

Node drains: with hard anti-affinity and no spare node, a drained pod cannot be rescheduled elsewhere and stays Pending until the node returns or capacity is added, so plan maintenance windows with one node of headroom.

steps.title: Production Practice: Spread, Budgets and Cost of Scheduling
steps.description: Anti-affinity is one control; availability needs a few more around it.
items: Pair with a PodDisruptionBudget: spreading pods does not stop a node drain from evicting two of them in sequence. A PDB with minAvailable protects voluntary disruptions.
Layer zone spread: use required hostname anti-affinity plus a soft or topology-spread rule on topology.kubernetes.io/zone so a single zone failure does not take out the service.

Example — block direct traffic to Service C except from Service B: This says: "Only accept incoming traffic to pods labeled app: service-c if it comes from pods labeled app: service-b." title: Kubernetes Q44: How do you handle configuration that differs between environments (dev staging prod) in Kubernetes [L2]
summary: Two main approaches:
question: How do you handle configuration that differs between environments (dev, staging, prod) in Kubernetes?
intro: Handle configuration that differs between environments by building one immutable image and injecting everything environment-specific from outside it: ConfigMaps, Secrets, and per-environment overlays (Kustomize) or values files (Helm), all stored in Git and applied by a GitOps controller. Interviewers ask this because the wrong answer, rebuilding images per environment or copying whole manifests, causes drift and untested production artifacts. A strong answer separates non-secret config from secrets and explains how config changes trigger pod restarts.

steps.title: Principles: Build Once, Configure Per Environment
steps.description: Start from the rule that the artifact tested in staging is byte-for-byte the artifact that runs in prod.
items: Image: identical across dev, staging and prod, referenced by tag or preferably digest. Environment names must never be baked into the image.

Non-secret config: ConfigMaps consumed as environment variables or mounted files, differing in values such as log level, feature flags, replica counts and hostnames. Keep the ConfigMap for values the application can safely log, and put anything that grants access, such as tokens and passwords, in a Secret so RBAC can restrict who may read it.
Secrets: Kubernetes Secrets are only base64 encoded, so do not commit them as plain manifests. Use an external secret store synced in, or encrypt them in Git.
Structure: keep a shared base and thin per-environment differences, so a change to a common field is made once and reviewed once.
Twelve-factor view: store config in the environment, not the code, which is what lets one build serve dev, staging and prod without modification.
steps.highlight: Cluster per environment (strong isolation) versus namespace per environment (cheaper, weaker isolation) is a separate decision. The config pattern works for both, but prod should at least be a separate cluster or account for blast radius reasons.

steps.title: Hands-on: Configuration That Differs Between Environments with Kustomize
steps.description: Kustomize patches a common base without templates, which keeps the diff between environments small and readable.
items: Layout: base/ holds the Deployment, Service and a configMapGenerator; overlays/dev, overlays/staging, overlays/prod each hold one kustomization.yaml. Keep overlays small: if an overlay patches more than a handful of fields, the base probably has the wrong abstraction.
Generator behaviour: configMapGenerator appends a content hash to the ConfigMap name, so changing a value renames the ConfigMap and automatically triggers a rollout of pods that reference it.
Preview before applying: kubectl kustomize overlays/prod renders the final YAML, and kubectl diff -k overlays/prod shows what would change in the cluster.
steps.codeBlock:
# overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - ../../base
namespace: prod
replicas:
  - name: my-app
    count: 4
images:
  - name: registry.example.com/my-app
    newTag: "1.4.2"
configMapGenerator:
  - name: my-app-config
    behavior: merge
    literals:
      - LOG_LEVEL=warn
      - FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT=false

# Render and diff
kubectl kustomize overlays/prod | head -40
kubectl diff -k overlays/prod
kubectl apply -k overlays/prod

steps.title: Helm Values Files and Secret Handling
steps.description: If the team ships a Helm chart, the same idea is expressed with layered values files.
items: Layering: helm upgrade --install my-app ./chart -n prod -f values.yaml -f values-prod.yaml. Later files override earlier ones, so values.yaml holds safe defaults.
Render check: helm template my-app ./chart -f values.yaml -f values-prod.yaml and helm lint catch mistakes before they reach a cluster.
Secrets option A: External Secrets Operator reads from AWS Secrets Manager or Vault and creates the Kubernetes Secret, so Git only holds a reference.
Secrets option B: SOPS or Sealed Secrets lets you commit encrypted values and decrypt in-cluster or in the GitOps tool.
steps.codeBlock:
# values-prod.yaml
replicaCount: 4
image:
  tag: "1.4.2"
env:
  LOG_LEVEL: warn
ingress:
  host: app.example.com

helm template my-app ./chart -n prod -f values.yaml -f values-prod.yaml | kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f -
helm upgrade --install my-app ./chart -n prod -f values.yaml -f values-prod.yaml --atomic --timeout 5m

steps.title: How Config Changes Reach Running Pods
steps.description: A ConfigMap update does not always restart anything, which surprises people in production.
items: Environment variables: read once at container start. Editing a ConfigMap does not change them until the pod is recreated.
Mounted files: the kubelet refreshes ConfigMap volumes eventually, but not for subPath mounts, and the application must re-read the file.
Hash-suffixed names: the Kustomize generator approach, or a Helm checksum annotation on the pod template, forces a rolling restart on every config change.
Immutable ConfigMaps: setting immutable: true prevents accidental in-place edits and reduces API server watch load.

Checksum annotation in Helm: add checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }} to the pod template annotations so the Deployment rolls whenever the rendered ConfigMap changes.

steps.title: Verification, Drift Control and GitOps
steps.description: The goal is that what Git says is what runs.
items: GitOps controller: Argo CD or Flux apply each environment directory and report drift. Manual kubectl edit in prod gets reverted or flagged.
Promotion: promote by changing the image tag in the next overlay via pull request, with CI running kubectl kustomize and a schema validator such as kubeconform.
Runtime check: kubectl get cm my-app-config -n prod -o yaml and kubectl exec deploy/my-app -n prod -- env | grep LOG_LEVEL confirm the value the container actually sees.
Policy checks: run kubeconform and a policy engine such as Kyverno or conftest in CI so a prod overlay cannot, for example, drop resource limits or enable debug flags by accident.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Let Kustomize configMapGenerator or a Helm checksum annotation rename or re-hash config so every config change triggers a rollout, instead of relying on pods to notice edits.
elevatorPitch: One image everywhere, with a shared base and thin per-environment overlays or values files in Git.
Secrets come from an external store or are encrypted in Git, never plain base64 in a repo.
I render and diff in CI, apply via Argo CD or Flux, and use hashed ConfigMap names so config changes roll pods.

mistakesToAvoid.why: The artifact promoted to prod is then not the one that was tested, and bugs hide in the differences.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Committing Secret manifests with base64 values
mistakesToAvoid.why: Base64 is encoding, not encryption, so anyone with repo read access gets production credentials.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Copy-pasting whole manifests per environment
mistakesToAvoid.why: Copies drift apart over time, and a fix applied to one environment is forgotten in the others.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming a ConfigMap edit restarts pods
mistakesToAvoid.why: Env vars are read at start, so the cluster keeps running old values until something recreates the pods.

title: Kubernetes Q47: Explain how the Kubernetes scheduler makes a placement decision for a new pod [L3]
summary: The scheduler goes through two phases:
question: Explain how the Kubernetes scheduler makes a placement decision for a new pod.
intro: "In one of our high-traffic production clusters, our SRE team handled this incident using a standardized runbook. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
steps.description: The scheduler goes through two phases:
items: Does the node have enough CPU and memory?
Does the node match the pod's nodeSelector?
Does the pod tolerate the node's taints?
Are the required volumes available in that zone?
Does the pod's affinity/anti-affinity rule allow this node?

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: Phase 1: Filtering (Predicates) Eliminate nodes that can't run the pod: Phase 2: Scoring (Priorities) Rank the remaining nodes: The highest-scoring node wins. If tied, a random one is picked. The scheduler then writes the chosen node name into the pod's spec (nodeName field), and the kubelet on that node picks it up and starts the pod.
items: Least requested resources (prefer emptier nodes for better bin-packing).
Affinity preference scores.

items: Liveness probe — "is this container still alive?" If it fails, Kubernetes restarts the container. Use for detecting deadlocks or infinite loops where the process is running but not making progress.
Scenario: A Java app has a thread deadlock. The JVM is running but requests hang forever. Liveness probe detects no HTTP response → restarts container.

Readiness probe — "is this container ready to serve traffic?" If it fails, the pod is removed from Service endpoints. Use for apps that need warmup time or temporarily can't serve (e.g., during a DB connection retry).

title: Kubernetes Q63: How do you roll back a Helm release [L2]
summary: bash
question: How do you roll back a Helm release?
intro: To roll back a Helm release, run helm history <release> to find a known-good revision, then helm rollback <release> <revision>. Helm re-applies that revision's stored manifest and records the result as a brand-new revision, so history is never rewritten. Interviewers ask this to see whether you understand that Helm tracks releases as numbered Secrets in the release namespace, and that a rollback only restores what Helm manages: it does not undo database migrations, deleted PVC data or CRD changes.

steps.title: Mental model: revisions behind a Helm rollback
steps.description: Helm 3 stores every install and upgrade as a release Secret (type helm.sh/release.v1) containing the rendered chart, values and manifest.
items: Revisions are immutable: a rollback to revision 3 from revision 5 creates revision 6 whose content equals revision 3.
Default target: omitting the revision number rolls back to the immediately previous revision.
Scope: only resources in the stored manifest are patched; anything created outside Helm is left alone.
History limit: Helm keeps 10 revisions by default (--history-max), so very old revisions may no longer exist.
steps.highlight: A rollback is a forward move in history. Always read the new revision's description, which says Rollback to N.

steps.title: Hands-on: helm history and rolling back a Helm release
steps.description: Find the last good revision, compare what changed, then roll back and wait for readiness.
items: List revisions: helm history my-app -n prod shows status (deployed, superseded, failed) per revision.
Compare values: helm get values my-app -n prod --revision 3 shows what was supplied then.
Roll back safely: add --wait --timeout 5m so the command fails if pods never become ready.
Rehearse first: --dry-run renders the plan without touching the cluster.
steps.codeBlock:
helm history my-app -n prod
# REVISION  STATUS      CHART         DESCRIPTION
# 4         superseded  my-app-1.3.0  Upgrade complete
# 5         deployed    my-app-1.4.0  Upgrade complete

helm get values my-app -n prod --revision 4
helm rollback my-app 4 -n prod --dry-run
helm rollback my-app 4 -n prod --wait --timeout 5m --cleanup-on-fail
# Rollback was a success! Happy Helming!

steps.title: Verify the rollback actually restored service
steps.description: A success message from Helm only means the API accepted the manifests; confirm workload health separately.
items: Release state: helm status my-app -n prod should show deployed and a new highest revision.
Rollout: kubectl rollout status deploy/my-app -n prod confirms new ReplicaSet pods are Ready.
Image check: read the live image with kubectl get deploy my-app -n prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'.
Signals: check error rate and latency dashboards, not only pod status.
steps.codeBlock:
helm status my-app -n prod | head -n 8
kubectl rollout status deploy/my-app -n prod --timeout=180s
kubectl get deploy my-app -n prod \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}{"\n"}'

steps.title: Failure modes: what helm rollback cannot undo
steps.description: Most failed rollbacks come from state that lives outside the release manifest.
items: Data and schema: database migrations and PVC contents are not reverted; an old app version may not start against a newer schema.
CRDs: Helm installs CRDs from the crds/ directory once and never upgrades or rolls them back.
Hooks: pre-rollback and post-rollback hooks run, but upgrade hooks (such as migration Jobs) do not run in reverse. Use --no-hooks only deliberately.
Stuck release: an interrupted operation leaves status pending-upgrade and blocks further commands; roll back to the last deployed revision to recover.
Immutable fields: changes to e.g. a Service clusterIP or StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplates can make patching fail; --force recreates resources and causes downtime.

steps.title: Production practice: make rollback automatic and auditable
steps.description: Do not rely on someone remembering the revision number at 3 a.m.
items: Auto-rollback on upgrade: helm upgrade --install --atomic --wait --timeout 5m rolls back by itself if the upgrade fails.
Keep history: set --history-max 10 or higher so you have somewhere to go back to.
GitOps: with Argo CD or Flux the Git revert is the source of truth; a manual helm rollback will be reverted by the next sync.
Audit: log helm history output in the pipeline for each deploy.
steps.codeBlock:
helm upgrade --install my-app ./chart -n prod \
  -f values-prod.yaml --atomic --wait --timeout 5m --history-max 15

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Use helm upgrade --atomic --wait in CI so failed upgrades revert themselves, and remember that helm rollback never reverts CRDs, migrations or PVC data.
elevatorPitch: A Helm rollback re-applies a stored earlier revision of a release and records it as a new revision, using helm rollback <release> <revision>.
I pick the target from helm history, compare values with helm get values --revision, and verify with --wait plus kubectl rollout status.
I automate it with --atomic in CI and keep in mind CRDs, schema migrations and PVC data are not rolled back.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming rollback reverts database migrations
mistakesToAvoid.why: Helm only restores Kubernetes manifests. A migration Job that ran on upgrade is not undone, so the old image may crash against the new schema.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Rolling back without --wait
mistakesToAvoid.why: The command returns once manifests are applied, so a broken revision can look successful while pods crash-loop.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting CRD changes to roll back
mistakesToAvoid.why: Helm does not manage CRDs in the crds/ folder after first install, so new CRD schemas stay in place.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running helm rollback on a GitOps-managed release
mistakesToAvoid.why: Argo CD or Flux will sync back to the Git state and silently undo your rollback; revert the commit instead.

title: Kubernetes Q69: Describe the Container Storage Interface (CSI) and why it replaced in-tree volume plugins [L3]
summary: In-tree volume plugins (like the old AWS EBS plugin built into kubelet) had problems:
question: Describe the Container Storage Interface (CSI) and why it replaced in-tree volume plugins.
intro: "In our production Kubernetes clusters running microservices on EKS/AKS, this was a classic operational challenge. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
steps.description: In-tree volume plugins (like the old AWS EBS plugin built into kubelet) had problems:
items: They had to be updated with Kubernetes releases.
Bugs in storage plugins could crash kubelet.
Storage vendors couldn't release independently of Kubernetes.
PVC created → external-provisioner (CSI sidecar) calls the CSI driver to provision a volume.

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: CSI (Container Storage Interface) is a standard API that lets storage vendors write drivers that run as pods in the cluster, independent of Kubernetes core. Flow: Vendors like AWS (EBS CSI), Azure Disk, GCP PD, and Portworx all now have CSI drivers. In-tree plugins are deprecated and being removed.
items: Pod scheduled → node-driver-registrar mounts the volume on the node.
Container starts with the volume attached.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: They had to be updated with Kubernetes releases..
elevatorPitch: They had to be updated with Kubernetes releases.

Storage vendors couldn't release independently of Kubernetes.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Over-granting cluster-admin permissions to pod ServiceAccounts instead of scoping namespace Roles when configuring Describe Container Storage
mistakesToAvoid.why: Over-granting cluster-wide permissions violates least-privilege principles and allows compromised pods to escalate privileges across namespaces.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Referencing mutable latest container tags across production Kubernetes Deployment specs when configuring Describe Container Storage
mistakesToAvoid.why: Deployments referencing `:latest` risk inconsistent versions across replica pods and break deterministic rollback capabilities.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting pod readiness probes, causing traffic to hit uninitialized application containers when configuring Describe Container Storage
mistakesToAvoid.why: Readiness probes gate traffic delivery; missing probes cause Kubernetes to route user requests to pods before dependencies or caches are loaded.

title: Kubernetes Q71: Pod shows ErrImagePull [L1]
summary: Image not found or wrong tag. Check image name/tag. For private registry, ensure imagePullSecret is configured.
question: Pod shows `ErrImagePull`.
intro: A pod that shows ErrImagePull means the kubelet tried to pull the container image and failed; after retries the status flips to ImagePullBackOff, which is the same problem with an exponential delay (up to 5 minutes). The fix is always in the event message: wrong name or tag, missing credentials, registry rate limit, network or DNS trouble. Interviewers ask this to see if you start from kubectl describe pod rather than guessing.

steps.title: Read the exact ErrImagePull error first
steps.description: The Events section names the failing image and the registry's reason.
items: Describe: kubectl describe pod <pod> -n prod and read the last Failed events.
Typical messages: manifest unknown or not found (bad tag), unauthorized or pull access denied (credentials), toomanyrequests (rate limit), no such host or timeout (DNS or network).
Namespace events: kubectl get events -n prod --sort-by=.lastTimestamp.
Spec image: confirm the image string in the pod spec, not in your Git repo.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl describe pod my-app-6f7d9-abcde -n prod | sed -n '/Events:/,$p'
# Failed to pull image "registry.example.com/my-app:1.4.O":
#   rpc error: code = NotFound ... not found
kubectl get pod my-app-6f7d9-abcde -n prod \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}'

steps.title: Fix credentials with imagePullSecrets
steps.description: Private registries need a Secret of type kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson in the pod's namespace.
items: Create the Secret: kubectl create secret docker-registry with registry server, user and token.
Reference it: add imagePullSecrets to the pod spec or patch the ServiceAccount so all pods in the namespace use it.
Namespace scope: Secrets do not cross namespaces; create one per namespace.
Cloud registries: ECR tokens expire after 12 hours, so use node IAM roles, kubelet credential providers or a refresh job.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred -n prod \
  --docker-server=registry.example.com \
  --docker-username=ci-bot --docker-password="$REGISTRY_TOKEN"

kubectl patch serviceaccount default -n prod \
  -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}'
kubectl rollout restart deploy/my-app -n prod

steps.title: Verify from the node, not only the API
steps.description: Reproduce the pull exactly where the kubelet runs.
items: Which node: kubectl get pod -o wide shows the node.
CRI pull: on a containerd node run crictl pull <image> to see the registry response.
DNS and egress: check the node resolves and reaches the registry (proxy, firewall, NAT, VPC endpoint).
Image exists: query the registry for the tag directly, for example crane manifest or docker manifest inspect.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get pod my-app-6f7d9-abcde -n prod -o wide
# on the node:
sudo crictl pull registry.example.com/my-app:1.4.0
getent hosts registry.example.com
docker manifest inspect registry.example.com/my-app:1.4.0 >/dev/null && echo exists

steps.title: Less obvious causes
steps.description: When the name and credentials look right:
items: Rate limits: anonymous Docker Hub pulls are limited per IP; authenticate or use a registry mirror or pull-through cache.
Architecture: a no matching manifest for linux/arm64 message means the image lacks that platform, common on mixed Graviton and x86 clusters.
Digest pins and tags: a tag deleted by a retention policy returns not found though it worked yesterday.
Policy: imagePullPolicy: Always forces a registry contact on every start; a registry outage then blocks restarts.
TLS: private CAs must be trusted by the container runtime on every node.

steps.title: Production practice: prevent pull failures
steps.description: Treat image delivery as a dependency.
items: Pin versions: deploy immutable tags or digests built by CI; never rely on latest.
Pre-flight: CI verifies the tag exists in the registry before applying manifests.
Mirror: use a pull-through cache or in-region registry for resilience and speed.
Alert: alert on pods in ImagePullBackOff via kube-state-metrics kube_pod_container_status_waiting_reason.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Run crictl pull on the node that hosts the pod, since it reproduces the kubelet's exact credentials, DNS and network path in seconds.
elevatorPitch: ErrImagePull means the kubelet failed to pull the image; ImagePullBackOff is the same failure being retried with backoff.
I read kubectl describe pod events, then confirm the tag, credentials and reachability, testing with crictl pull on the node.
I prevent it with pinned tags, a CI tag-exists check, pull-through caching and an alert on waiting reason.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating ImagePullBackOff as a different problem from ErrImagePull
mistakesToAvoid.why: It is the same pull failure with a growing retry delay; the cause is in the original event.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Creating the pull secret in the wrong namespace
mistakesToAvoid.why: imagePullSecrets are namespaced; a secret in default does nothing for pods in prod.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Debugging only from your laptop
mistakesToAvoid.why: Your workstation has different credentials, DNS and network than the node; reproduce on the node.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring architecture mismatch
mistakesToAvoid.why: A single-platform image fails on nodes of another CPU architecture with a manifest error, not an auth error.

title: Kubernetes Q72: Deployment has 0 ready pods but desired is 3 [L2]
summary: All pods failing readiness. Check probe config and app logs.
question: Deployment has 0 ready pods but desired is 3.
intro: When a Deployment has 0 ready pods but desired is 3, find which stage the pods are stuck in: not created, not scheduled, not started, or started but failing the readiness probe. Work from the Deployment down to the ReplicaSet, then the Pod, then its events and logs. Interviewers use this scenario to see whether you triage in a repeatable order instead of guessing, and whether you know that READY counts only pods whose readiness probe passes, not pods that merely exist.

steps.title: Symptom and Triage Order
steps.description: Classify the failure before touching anything: the pod count and phase tell you where to look.
items: Start at the top: kubectl get deploy my-app -n prod shows READY 0/3, UP-TO-DATE and AVAILABLE. UP-TO-DATE 0 suggests the ReplicaSet could not create pods; UP-TO-DATE 3 with AVAILABLE 0 suggests pods exist but are not ready.
No pods at all: look at the ReplicaSet. Quota exceeded, a rejecting admission webhook, a Pod Security violation or a missing ServiceAccount all surface as FailedCreate events there, not on pods.
Pods present: read STATUS: Pending (scheduling), ContainerCreating (image, volume or CNI), ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, or Running with READY 0/1 (probe failing).

Read the counts correctly: READY compares ready pods to desired; UP-TO-DATE counts pods on the newest ReplicaSet; AVAILABLE counts pods ready for at least minReadySeconds. The three numbers together identify the stage.

steps.title: Hands-on: Deployment 0 Ready Pods, Ordered Checks
steps.description: Run the same sequence every time. Each command answers one question and narrows the next.
items: Events first: kubectl get events -n prod --sort-by=.lastTimestamp often names the cause in one line, such as insufficient CPU or a failed mount.
Describe the pod: the Conditions block (PodScheduled, Initialized, ContainersReady, Ready) tells you the first stage that is False.
Logs of the previous run: for a crash loop, --previous is essential because the current container may have no output yet.

Quick filter: kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=my-app grouped by STATUS tells you immediately whether all three pods fail the same way, which suggests a configuration or image problem, or differently, which suggests node or capacity problems.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get deploy,rs,pods -n prod -l app=my-app -o wide
kubectl describe deploy my-app -n prod | sed -n '/Conditions/,/Events/p'
kubectl describe rs -n prod -l app=my-app | tail -20      # FailedCreate shows here
kubectl describe pod -n prod -l app=my-app | grep -A15 Events
kubectl logs deploy/my-app -n prod --previous --tail=50
kubectl get events -n prod --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20

steps.title: Root Causes Mapped to Symptoms
steps.description: Most cases fall into a short list, each with a distinct signature.
items: Pending, unschedulable: event 0/N nodes are available: Insufficient cpu, untolerated taints, unbound PVC, or node selector mismatch. Fix requests, add capacity, correct tolerations or the storage class.

ImagePullBackOff: wrong tag, private registry without imagePullSecrets, or rate limiting. kubectl describe pod gives the exact registry error. Pulling the wrong tag or a registry outage looks identical across all three replicas, which is the clue that the problem is shared rather than node-specific.
CrashLoopBackOff: application exits at start: missing env var, bad config, unreachable dependency, or OOMKilled (check lastState.terminated.reason).
Running but 0/1 Ready: readiness probe wrong path or port, app slow to start, or dependency down. A startupProbe prevents slow starters from failing early.
No pods created: ResourceQuota, LimitRange, admission webhook denial, or Pod Security Admission restricted rejecting the spec.

steps.title: Fix, Verify and Roll Back Safely
steps.description: Apply the narrowest fix, then prove recovery with the rollout status rather than by eye.
items: Fix forward or revert: if the last change caused it, kubectl rollout undo deploy/my-app -n prod restores the previous ReplicaSet quickly while you investigate.

Wait for convergence: kubectl rollout status deploy/my-app -n prod --timeout=180s exits non-zero on failure, which makes it usable in scripts. Prefer a fix that changes the manifest in Git, because a manual kubectl edit during an incident is easily overwritten by the next pipeline run.
Confirm traffic: kubectl get endpointslices -n prod -l kubernetes.io/service-name=my-app should list ready addresses; an empty list means the Service still has no backends.

Probe debugging: run the probe by hand: kubectl exec deploy/my-app -n prod -- wget -qO- localhost:8080/healthz. A different response from the one the kubelet expects means the probe path, port or scheme is wrong.
steps.codeBlock:
# Is the probe the problem? Compare the probe config with what the app serves
kubectl get deploy my-app -n prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].readinessProbe}'
kubectl get pod -n prod -l app=my-app -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"  "}{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.reason}{"\n"}{end}'
# Expected for an OOM crash: OOMKilled

steps.title: Prevention and Alerting
steps.description: Make the next failure visible before users report it.
items: Progress deadline: the default progressDeadlineSeconds is 600, after which the Deployment gets a ProgressDeadlineExceeded condition. Tune it to your startup time.
CI gate: run kubectl rollout status after deploy and fail the pipeline if it times out, triggering an automatic undo.
Alerts: with kube-state-metrics, alert on kube_deployment_status_replicas_available being below kube_deployment_spec_replicas for several minutes.
Dry run: kubectl apply --dry-run=server surfaces quota and admission rejections before the real rollout.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: The ReplicaSet is where FailedCreate events live, so when a Deployment shows no pods, describe the ReplicaSet before hunting through pod logs that do not exist.
elevatorPitch: READY 0 of 3 means no pod passes its readiness probe, so I locate the stage: not created, not scheduled, not started, or unready.
I go Deployment, ReplicaSet, Pod, events, then logs with --previous, and read the first failing condition.
I confirm with rollout status and EndpointSlices, and prevent repeats with a CI gate, progress deadline and kube-state-metrics alerts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Reading only pod logs when no pods exist
mistakesToAvoid.why: Quota or admission failures are reported on the ReplicaSet, so pod logs will never show them.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Restarting or deleting pods repeatedly
mistakesToAvoid.why: It destroys the evidence in events and previous logs and does not change the underlying cause.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting --previous on crash loops
mistakesToAvoid.why: The current container is freshly restarted and often shows nothing, while the crash output is in the prior instance.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating a failing readiness probe as an application crash
mistakesToAvoid.why: The pod can be healthy but probing the wrong port or path, so the fix is probe configuration, not code.

title: Kubernetes Q73: How do you scale a deployment to 5 replicas [L1]
summary: kubectl scale deployment <name> --replicas=5 or update spec.replicas.
question: How do you scale a deployment to 5 replicas?
intro: To scale a deployment to 5 replicas, run kubectl scale deployment my-app --replicas=5, or better, set spec.replicas: 5 in the manifest in Git and let your pipeline apply it. This looks like a trivial L1 question, but interviewers use it to hear whether you know the difference between imperative and declarative changes, what happens when an HPA or GitOps controller also manages the replica count, and how to verify that five pods are actually ready and not merely requested.

steps.title: Mental Model: Scaling Changes Desired State Only
steps.description: Scaling edits the replica count on the Deployment's scale subresource; the controllers do the rest.
items: No new revision: scaling does not create a new ReplicaSet and does not appear in kubectl rollout history. Only pod template changes do.

Controller loop: the Deployment controller updates the ReplicaSet's replicas; the ReplicaSet creates pods; the scheduler places them. Any of those steps can stall. After the ReplicaSet is updated, pod creation is asynchronous, so the command returning does not mean the pods exist yet.
Who owns the number: exactly one actor should own spec.replicas: a human or Git, or an HPA. Two owners will fight.
Scale subresource: kubectl scale talks to the /scale subresource, which is why it also works on ReplicaSets, StatefulSets and custom resources that expose it.

steps.title: Hands-on: Scale a Deployment to 5 Replicas
steps.description: Three ways to do it, with different audit trails.
items: Imperative: kubectl scale is fastest in an incident. The --current-replicas flag adds a precondition so the command fails if someone else already changed the count. Add -n prod every time or set the namespace in your context, because scaling the same-named Deployment in the wrong namespace is a classic incident cause.
Patch: kubectl patch against the Deployment works in scripts and uses the same API field.
Declarative: change replicas in the manifest, commit, and apply. This is the production default because it is reviewed and reproducible.
steps.codeBlock:
# Imperative, with a guard against concurrent edits
kubectl scale deployment my-app -n prod --current-replicas=3 --replicas=5

# Patch equivalent
kubectl patch deployment my-app -n prod -p '{"spec":{"replicas":5}}'

# Declarative: edit spec.replicas: 5 in deployment.yaml, then
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

# Expected
# deployment.apps/my-app scaled

steps.title: Verify That Five Replicas Are Actually Ready
steps.description: Scaled is not the same as ready, so check the whole chain.
items: Rollout status: kubectl rollout status deploy/my-app -n prod waits until all replicas are available.
Counts: kubectl get deploy my-app -n prod should read 5/5 in READY. If it reads 3/5, inspect the missing pods.
Pending pods: kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=my-app --field-selector=status.phase=Pending lists those waiting for capacity, and kubectl describe pod gives the scheduler reason.
Service backends: five ready endpoints should appear in kubectl get endpointslices -n prod -l kubernetes.io/service-name=my-app.
Why READY lags: new pods must pull the image, start, and pass their readiness probe, so READY rising from 3 to 5 over several seconds or minutes is normal. A stall is the signal to investigate.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get deploy my-app -n prod
# NAME     READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE
# my-app   5/5     5            5
kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=my-app -o wide

steps.title: Failure Modes: HPA, GitOps and Capacity
steps.description: Most 'scaling did not stick' reports come from a second controller.
items: HPA present: if a HorizontalPodAutoscaler targets the Deployment, it will overwrite your manual value on its next evaluation. Change minReplicas/maxReplicas on the HPA instead, and omit spec.replicas from the manifest so applies do not reset it.
GitOps reverts: Argo CD or Flux with self-heal will set it back to the Git value within minutes. Commit the change rather than running the imperative command.
No room: pods stay Pending due to insufficient CPU or memory, ResourceQuota, or anti-affinity. Scaling the number does not create capacity unless the Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter adds nodes.
Downstream limits: five replicas multiply database connections and rate limits; check connection pool sizes before scaling out.
StatefulSets differ: scaling a StatefulSet adds pods one at a time in order by default, and scale-down removes the highest ordinal first, so it behaves differently from a Deployment.

steps.title: Production Practice
steps.description: Make scaling safe and observable.
items: PDB and spread: a PodDisruptionBudget and topology spread keep the new replicas from landing on one node.

Readiness probes: new pods receive traffic only after their probe passes, so scale-out under load is safe only with correct probes. For planned events, scale out ahead of the load rather than reacting, and scale back after verifying error rates and latency are stable.
Audit: imperative scaling should be rare and visible; API audit logs record the scale subresource update.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Before running kubectl scale, check kubectl get hpa for the same target; if an HPA or GitOps self-heal owns the replica count, your manual 5 will be reverted.
elevatorPitch: kubectl scale deployment my-app --replicas=5 changes desired state on the scale subresource, with no new rollout revision.
I verify with rollout status, READY 5/5 and five ready EndpointSlice addresses, and read events for Pending pods.
In production I change replicas in Git, or the HPA bounds, because HPA and GitOps otherwise overwrite manual scaling.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Scaling manually while an HPA targets the same Deployment
mistakesToAvoid.why: The HPA recalculates the count and overwrites your value, so the change silently disappears.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Declaring success when the command prints scaled
mistakesToAvoid.why: That only means desired state changed; pods may be Pending for lack of capacity or failing readiness.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Keeping spec.replicas in a manifest that an HPA manages
mistakesToAvoid.why: Every kubectl apply resets the count to the manifest value and causes a scaling flap.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Scaling out without checking downstream connection limits
mistakesToAvoid.why: More replicas can exhaust database connections and turn a capacity fix into an outage.

title: Kubernetes Q74: NodePort service not reachable from outside [L2]
summary: Check firewall/security group rules allow the NodePort (30000-32767) range.
question: NodePort service not reachable from outside.
intro: A NodePort service not reachable from outside almost always fails in one of four places: the Service has no endpoints, kube-proxy has not programmed the node port, a firewall or cloud security group blocks the port, or you are using an address that is not routable from your client. Test from the inside out: pod, ClusterIP, node itself, then external client. Interviewers ask this because it tests whether you understand that a NodePort is only a port opened on every node, forwarded by kube-proxy rules to pod endpoints.

steps.title: Symptom and the Four Layers to Check
steps.description: Reachability is a chain; find the first broken link instead of changing things at random.
items: Layer 1, Service and endpoints: does the Service select ready pods, and does targetPort match the container port?
Layer 2, node dataplane: has kube-proxy (iptables, IPVS or nftables mode) created rules for the node port on that node?
Layer 3, network path: does a host firewall, cloud security group, NACL or on-prem firewall allow the port from your client to the node IP?
Layer 4, addressing and policy: is the node IP reachable from the client, and does externalTrafficPolicy or a NetworkPolicy change which pods answer?
What the rule does: kube-proxy matches traffic to any node IP on the node port and rewrites it to a pod endpoint, which may be on another node; the Service object itself runs no process.

steps.title: Hands-on: NodePort Service Not Reachable From Outside
steps.description: Run these in order. The first one that fails is your root cause.
items: Endpoints: an empty ENDPOINTS list means a selector or readiness problem, not a network problem.
Inside the cluster: if the ClusterIP works from a debug pod but the NodePort does not, the problem is outside the Service object.
On the node: curl to localhost:<nodePort> on the node isolates host rules from the external network path.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get svc my-app -n prod -o wide          # TYPE NodePort, PORT(S) 80:30080/TCP
kubectl get endpointslices -n prod -l kubernetes.io/service-name=my-app
kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=my-app -o wide   # note node names and IPs

# From inside the cluster
kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- \
  curl -sv http://my-app.prod.svc.cluster.local:80

# On a node (SSH or SSM)
curl -sv http://127.0.0.1:30080
sudo iptables -t nat -S KUBE-NODEPORTS | grep 30080    # iptables mode
# From your laptop
curl -sv --max-time 5 http://<node-external-ip>:30080

steps.title: Root Causes and Fixes
steps.description: Each failure has a signature that points to the fix.
items: Empty endpoints: selector does not match pod labels, or pods fail readiness. Fix labels or the probe; the NodePort cannot work with no backends.
Wrong targetPort: the Service forwards to a port the container does not listen on, giving connection refused or reset. Align targetPort with the container port or its name.

Firewall or security group: a timeout (no response) points here. On AWS, the node security group must allow inbound TCP on the node port; the default range is 30000-32767 unless changed with --service-node-port-range. a timeout points to a firewall or routing problem, while connection refused points to a reachable host with nothing listening on the target, which is typically a targetPort or pod issue.
Private node IP: using an internal address from the internet times out. Use the node's public address, a bastion, or put a LoadBalancer or Ingress in front.
externalTrafficPolicy: Local: only nodes that run a ready pod answer; other nodes drop the traffic. Query a node that hosts a pod, or use Cluster and accept source IP masquerading.

steps.title: Verification and Special Environments
steps.description: Confirm the fix from the same place that failed.
items: Retest externally: a successful curl -sv from the original client is the only real proof; node-local success is not enough.
Local clusters: on minikube, kind or Docker Desktop the node IP is inside a VM or Docker network. Use minikube service my-app --url, extra port mappings in kind, or kubectl port-forward.
kube-proxy health: kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-proxy and its logs reveal a crashed or misconfigured proxy; some CNIs replace kube-proxy entirely, so rules look different.
NetworkPolicy: a policy selecting the pods can block the traffic; remember NodePort traffic may arrive with the node's IP after SNAT.
steps.codeBlock:
# Which mode is kube-proxy running, and are there rules for the port?
kubectl -n kube-system get cm kube-proxy -o jsonpath='{.data.config\.conf}' | grep -E 'mode|nodePortAddresses'
sudo ipvsadm -Ln | grep 30080          # ipvs mode
# AWS: is the port open on the node security group?
aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --query 'SecurityGroups[].IpPermissions[?FromPort<=`30080` && ToPort>=`30080`]'

steps.title: Production Practice: Prefer Load Balancer or Ingress
steps.description: NodePort is a building block, not an internet-facing design.
items: Front with a load balancer: use a LoadBalancer Service or Ingress/Gateway so clients do not depend on individual node IPs that change with autoscaling.
Restrict exposure: limit the source CIDR in security groups and use nodePortAddresses on kube-proxy if only specific interfaces should listen.
Pin the port deliberately: set nodePort explicitly only when an external system needs it, and document it to avoid collisions.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Test the NodePort with curl on the node itself first; success there with failure from your laptop proves the problem is the network path, and you can stop debugging Kubernetes.
elevatorPitch: A NodePort opens one port on every node and kube-proxy forwards it to the Service endpoints.
I check endpoints, ClusterIP from a debug pod, curl on the node, then the external path and security groups.
In production I avoid raw NodePort for public traffic and use a load balancer or Ingress with restricted source ranges.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Debugging firewalls before checking endpoints
mistakesToAvoid.why: A Service with no ready endpoints fails no matter how open the network is.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Confusing port, targetPort and nodePort
mistakesToAvoid.why: Traffic is forwarded to targetPort on the pod, so a mismatch gives refused connections that look like network issues.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using the node's private IP from outside the VPC
mistakesToAvoid.why: That address is not routable from the internet, so every test times out regardless of cluster health.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring externalTrafficPolicy: Local
mistakesToAvoid.why: Nodes without a local pod drop the traffic, so the Service works on some nodes and not others.

title: Kubernetes Q75: Two pods cant communicate even though NetworkPolicy allows it [L2]
summary: CNI plugin may not support NetworkPolicy. Check CNI (Flannel doesn't, Calico does).
question: Two pods can't communicate even though NetworkPolicy allows it.
intro: When two pods can't communicate even though NetworkPolicy allows it, the rule you are staring at is rarely the problem. Check that your CNI enforces policies at all, that the source pod has a matching egress rule if egress is restricted, that DNS is allowed, that selectors mean AND not OR, and that the port is the pod port, not the Service port. Interviewers ask this because NetworkPolicy semantics are additive, directional and easy to misread, and debugging needs a methodical approach.

steps.title: Mental Model: How NetworkPolicy Really Decides
steps.description: A connection needs permission on both ends, and policies only restrict pods they select.
items: Selection: a pod is isolated for ingress or egress only if some policy selects it for that direction. Otherwise it allows everything.
Both directions: if the source pod is egress-restricted, you need an egress rule on the source and an ingress rule on the destination. Allowing only one side blocks traffic.
Additive: policies are unions of allows; there are no deny rules in the core API, so a stray default-deny policy in the namespace can be the cause.
Enforcement: the API server accepts NetworkPolicy objects regardless; only a CNI that implements them (Calico, Cilium, Antrea and others) enforces them. Plain Flannel does not.
Stateful tracking: established return traffic is allowed automatically by the CNI, so you only describe who may initiate the connection, in each direction where isolation applies.

steps.title: Hands-on: Pods Can't Communicate Even Though NetworkPolicy Allows It
steps.description: Reproduce the failure from the client pod, then list every policy that selects either pod.
items: List policies: kubectl get netpol -A and kubectl describe netpol -n prod show which pods each policy selects and what it allows.
Check labels: kubectl get pods -n prod --show-labels and kubectl get ns --show-labels; policies match labels, and a typo makes a rule select nothing.
Test with the right tool: an ephemeral debug container avoids changing the app image.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get netpol -A
kubectl describe netpol -n prod
kubectl get pods -n prod --show-labels
kubectl get ns --show-labels | grep -E 'prod|staging'

# Test from the client pod's network namespace
kubectl debug -it -n prod pod/client --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=client -- \
  sh -c 'nslookup backend.prod.svc.cluster.local; nc -zv backend.prod.svc.cluster.local 8080'

steps.title: The Usual Culprits: Why Allowed Traffic Still Fails
steps.description: These account for most real cases.
items: Missing egress or DNS: a default-deny egress policy blocks DNS to CoreDNS in kube-system (UDP and TCP 53), so names fail even if the target IP is allowed.
AND versus OR in from/to: a single list item containing both namespaceSelector and podSelector means AND; two separate dash items mean OR. Mixing them up opens too much or too little.
Namespace labels: a namespaceSelector needs a label on the namespace itself. Kubernetes sets kubernetes.io/metadata.name automatically, which is the reliable one to use.
Wrong port: policies match the destination pod's container port, not the Service port. If the Service maps 80 to 8080, allow 8080.

Not the CNI you think: check which plugin is installed with kubectl get pods -n kube-system; a non-enforcing plugin means policies are ignored and the real block is elsewhere (Service selector, readiness, mesh).
steps.codeBlock:
# Correct AND semantics: pods labelled app=client in namespaces labelled team=payments
ingress:
  - from:
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels:
            kubernetes.io/metadata.name: payments
        podSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: client
    ports:
      - protocol: TCP
        port: 8080

steps.title: Verification with CNI Flow Tools
steps.description: Ask the dataplane what it dropped instead of reasoning from YAML alone.
items: Cilium: hubble observe --namespace prod --verdict DROPPED shows dropped flows and the policy reason; cilium monitor --type drop works on the node.
Calico: enable policy logging with a Log action in a staged policy, or inspect with calicoctl and the node's iptables counters.
Control test: in a non-production namespace, remove one policy at a time to find the culprit, then restore it.
Pod IP versus Service: test the pod IP directly; if that works and the Service name fails, the issue is the Service, DNS or kube-proxy, not NetworkPolicy.
Host and probe traffic: kubelet health probes and hostNetwork pods are treated specially by many CNIs, so a policy that looks correct can still behave differently for node-originated traffic.

steps.title: Production Practice
steps.description: Make policy changes testable and reversible.
items: Default deny plus explicit allows: include DNS egress in the baseline policy so teams do not break name resolution.
Test in CI: tools such as cyclonus or Cilium connectivity tests validate that policies behave as intended in a kind cluster.
Observability: keep flow logs (Hubble or equivalent) enabled so a dropped connection is a query, not a guess.
Review checklist: for every new policy ask which pods it selects, which direction it covers, whether DNS is allowed, and what a test connection from an unauthorised pod should show.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Look for a default-deny egress policy on the source pod and for missing DNS egress first; allowing ingress on the destination alone never fixes a connection that dies at the client's egress.
elevatorPitch: NetworkPolicy is directional and additive, and only a CNI that implements it enforces it.
I list every policy selecting either pod, check egress and DNS, verify label and port matches, then test with a debug container.
I confirm drops with Hubble or Calico logs and bake a DNS-allowing default-deny baseline into CI-tested policies.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Only writing an ingress rule on the destination
mistakesToAvoid.why: If the source is egress-restricted, its own egress policy still blocks the connection.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Putting namespaceSelector and podSelector in separate list items
mistakesToAvoid.why: That is OR, not AND, so the rule allows far more than intended or something else than expected.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using the Service port in the policy
mistakesToAvoid.why: Policies are evaluated against the pod's target port after Service translation.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming the cluster enforces NetworkPolicy
mistakesToAvoid.why: On a CNI without policy support the objects are accepted but do nothing, which sends you debugging the wrong layer.

title: Kubernetes Q76: How do you upgrade Kubernetes version with zero downtime [L3]
summary: Upgrade control plane first (API server, etcd, scheduler). Then drain, upgrade, uncordon worker nodes one by one.
question: How do you upgrade Kubernetes version with zero downtime?
intro: "Kubernetes is a declarative desired state system; understanding the reconciliation loop is how you diagnose this quickly. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: Upgrade control plane first (API server, etcd, scheduler). Then drain, upgrade, uncordon worker nodes one by one.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Upgrade control plane first (API server, etcd, scheduler). Then drain, upgrade, uncordon worker nodes one by one..
elevatorPitch: Immediate Triage: Upgrade control plane first (API server, etcd, scheduler). Then drain, upgrade, uncordon worker
Run targeted verification commands before modifying configuration.
Automate permanent guardrails (CI check, alerts, IaC policy) to prevent recurrence.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Attempting multi-minor Kubernetes version jumps directly during cluster upgrades when configuring upgrade Kubernetes version
mistakesToAvoid.why: Kubernetes explicitly does not support multi-minor version jumps; control plane and worker components require sequential hops to validate API deprecations.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Upgrading kube-apiserver while leaving critical cluster add-ons and CNI plugins desynchronized when configuring upgrade Kubernetes version
mistakesToAvoid.why: Upgrading kube-apiserver without synchronizing CNI daemonsets or CoreDNS manifests causes silent pod networking failure and DNS timeouts immediately post-upgrade.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Replacing worker node pools simultaneously rather than adopting sequential rolling node group updates when configuring upgrade Kubernetes version
mistakesToAvoid.why: In-place or simultaneous node pool replacements risk cluster-wide capacity starvation if new AMIs or kubelet versions encounter bootstrapping errors.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Overlooking terminationGracePeriodSeconds when evicting stateful database or queue consumer pods when configuring upgrade Kubernetes version
mistakesToAvoid.why: Prematurely terminating stateful pods before in-flight transactions commit causes data corruption and unclean lock releases.

title: Kubernetes Q77: Ingress shows Address <pending> [L2]
summary: No LoadBalancer IP assigned yet. On bare-metal, need MetalLB. On cloud, wait 1-2 min for cloud LB provisioning.
question: Ingress shows `Address: <pending>`.
intro: When an Ingress shows Address pending (or an empty ADDRESS column), no controller has written a load balancer address to the Ingress status. That means the controller is missing, is ignoring the Ingress because of the class, or its own Service of type LoadBalancer never received an external IP. Interviewers ask this because an Ingress object is only configuration; without a running controller and a reachable entry point it does nothing, and candidates should trace the chain from Ingress to controller to Service to cloud.

steps.title: What Populates the Ingress Address
steps.description: The ADDRESS field is written by the controller, not by Kubernetes core.
items: Controller required: creating an Ingress without an ingress controller (NGINX, AWS Load Balancer Controller, Traefik, GCE and others) leaves ADDRESS empty indefinitely.

Class selection: a controller only reconciles Ingresses whose spec.ingressClassName matches its IngressClass (or that match its legacy annotation rules). This is why creating an Ingress alone, with no IngressClass in the cluster, never produces an address, no matter how correct the rules are.
Address source: controllers such as ingress-nginx copy the external IP or hostname from their own LoadBalancer Service. If that Service is pending, the Ingress stays pending.
Cloud-managed controllers: the AWS Load Balancer Controller creates an ALB and writes its DNS name, so IAM, subnet tags and quotas matter.
Quick triage rule: if the Ingress has events but no address, look at the controller; if it has no events at all, look at the class, because no controller is even considering it.

steps.title: Hands-on: Ingress Address Pending Triage
steps.description: Walk down the chain and stop at the first thing that is wrong.
items: Ingress events: kubectl describe ingress often contains controller errors in Events at the bottom.
