Controller present: list IngressClasses and the controller pods; none means you need to install one. For a cloud-managed controller, also read the controller's own logs because address assignment depends on a successful call to the cloud API.
Controller Service: look at EXTERNAL-IP of its LoadBalancer Service; <pending> there is the real issue.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get ingress my-app -n prod
kubectl describe ingress my-app -n prod | tail -15
kubectl get ingressclass
kubectl get pods -A | grep -Ei 'ingress|traefik|alb|haproxy'
kubectl get svc -n ingress-nginx
# EXTERNAL-IP <pending> on the controller Service is the common root cause
kubectl describe svc ingress-nginx-controller -n ingress-nginx | tail -15
kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx deploy/ingress-nginx-controller --tail=50

steps.title: Root Causes and Fixes
steps.description: Match the signature to the cause.
items: No controller installed: no IngressClass and no controller pods. Install one with Helm or manifests, then recreate or wait for reconciliation.

Class mismatch: the Ingress uses an ingressClassName that does not exist, or none is set and there is no default IngressClass (annotation ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"). Fix the class name.

Controller Service pending, bare metal or on-prem: no cloud provider exists to fulfil type LoadBalancer. Install MetalLB or kube-vip, or expose the controller with NodePort or hostNetwork and put an external load balancer in front.

Cloud provisioning failure: events on the Service or Ingress show quota exhaustion, missing subnet tags (for AWS, kubernetes.io/role/elb on public subnets), or missing IAM permissions for the controller. check kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/aws-load-balancer-controller for subnet discovery or IAM errors, and make sure the Ingress annotations select the intended scheme (internet-facing or internal).
Local clusters: minikube needs minikube tunnel or the ingress addon; kind needs extra port mappings and a ready controller.

steps.title: Verification
steps.description: Prove the address exists and routes.
items: Address populated: kubectl get ingress my-app -n prod -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress}' returns an IP or hostname. Remember that an ADDRESS shown for a pending-then-fixed Ingress can take a short while to appear after the controller Service receives its IP, so re-run the command a few times before concluding the fix failed.
Route test before DNS: curl -sv -H 'Host: app.example.com' http://<address>/ checks routing without waiting for DNS changes.
Backends: a 503 or 404 after the address appears points to the backend Service or the host and path rules, which is a different problem.
DNS follow-up: once the address exists, point the host name at it with a CNAME or A record, ideally automated by ExternalDNS.
steps.codeBlock:
# Confirm routing without touching DNS
ADDR=$(kubectl get ingress my-app -n prod -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].hostname}{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip}')
curl -sv -H 'Host: app.example.com' "http://$ADDR/healthz"
# Expect 200, or a 404 from the controller if host or path rules do not match

steps.title: Production Practice and Alternatives
steps.description: Keep the entry point declarative and monitored.
items: Declare the class explicitly: always set ingressClassName so the intended controller reconciles the Ingress. Declaring the class also makes the manifest portable across clusters where a different default exists.
Alert on pending: monitor controller Service external IP assignment and controller error logs in infrastructure tests.
Check controller lifecycle: project maintenance status changes over time, so verify the support status of your controller (including ingress-nginx) and evaluate Gateway API for new designs.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Read EXTERNAL-IP on the controller's own LoadBalancer Service before anything else; the Ingress address is just a copy of it, so a pending Service is the root cause most of the time.
elevatorPitch: An Ingress is only configuration, and its address is written by a controller after its entry point exists.
I check IngressClass, controller pods and logs, then the controller Service EXTERNAL-IP and cloud events.
I set ingressClassName explicitly, use MetalLB on bare metal, and test routing with a Host header before DNS.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Editing the Ingress YAML repeatedly
mistakesToAvoid.why: The Ingress is rarely wrong; the missing piece is the controller, class or load balancer.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Leaving ingressClassName unset with no default class
mistakesToAvoid.why: No controller claims the Ingress, so it stays unreconciled and pending.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting type LoadBalancer to work on bare metal
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without a cloud provider or MetalLB nothing assigns the external IP.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring controller logs and cloud events
mistakesToAvoid.why: Quota, IAM and subnet tag errors are only reported there.

title: Kubernetes Q78: How do you get logs from all pods of a deployment [L1]
summary: kubectl logs -l app=<label> or use label selector.
question: How do you get logs from all pods of a deployment?
intro: To get logs from all pods of a deployment, select them by label: kubectl logs -l app=my-app --all-containers --prefix --tail=100. Running kubectl logs deployment/my-app reads from only one pod, which surprises many people. Interviewers ask this to check that you know labels and selectors, the default limits of the selector mode, and when kubectl is the wrong tool and a log pipeline is needed instead.

steps.title: Why kubectl logs deployment/name shows only one pod
steps.description: A Deployment owns ReplicaSets, which own Pods. kubectl logs deploy/x resolves to a single pod and streams that one.
items: Single pod: kubectl picks one pod of the Deployment and prints a hint line about the chosen container.
Label selector: -l key=value fetches logs from every matching pod, so use the Deployment's spec.selector.matchLabels.
Find the labels: kubectl get deploy my-app -n prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector.matchLabels}'.
Defaults: in selector mode kubectl shows only the last 10 lines per pod unless you pass --tail.

steps.title: Hands-on: logs from all pods of a Deployment
steps.description: Combine selector, prefix and tail flags so you can tell the pods apart.
items: Prefix: --prefix adds [pod/name/container] to each line.
All containers: --all-containers includes sidecars and init containers' output where available.
Follow: -f streams live. kubectl opens at most 5 concurrent streams by default; raise it with --max-log-requests.
Time window: --since=15m or --since-time limits output.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get deploy my-app -n prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector.matchLabels}'
# {"app":"my-app"}

kubectl logs -l app=my-app -n prod --all-containers --prefix --tail=100 --since=15m
kubectl logs -l app=my-app -n prod --prefix -f --max-log-requests=20

steps.title: Verify coverage and narrow down the noise
steps.description: Make sure you actually saw every replica, then filter.
items: Count pods: compare the pod list with the prefixes you see: kubectl get pods -l app=my-app -n prod.
Filter: pipe to grep -i error or use jq if logs are JSON.
Single pod deep dive: use kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> for one container.
Quiet pods: a pod with no lines inside the window may simply be idle; widen --since.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get pods -l app=my-app -n prod -o name
kubectl logs -l app=my-app -n prod --prefix --tail=500 | grep -i "error"
kubectl logs my-app-7d9c8b6f5-abcde -n prod -c app --tail=50

steps.title: Failure modes and edge cases
steps.description: Selector-based logs are a convenience, not a complete record.
items: Crashed containers: add --previous to read the last terminated instance; selector mode supports it per pod that has one.
Deleted pods: logs vanish with the pod and are also rotated by the kubelet on the node, so completed history is lost.
Stream cap: with more than 5 replicas and -f you get an error unless --max-log-requests is increased.
Overlapping labels: a broad selector such as app=web may pull in pods from other Deployments; add more labels.
RBAC: you need get on pods/log.
steps.highlight: kubectl logs reads from the node's container log files via the kubelet. If the pod or node is gone, so are the logs.

steps.title: Production practice: ship logs off the node
steps.description: For anything beyond a quick check, use a log pipeline.
items: Stern: the open-source stern my-app -n prod tails all matching pods with colors and picks up new pods automatically.
Central logging: ship stdout to Loki, Elasticsearch or a cloud logging service with a DaemonSet agent such as Fluent Bit.
Structure: log JSON with a request ID so you can correlate across replicas.
Retention: central storage keeps logs after pod rescheduling and node replacement.
steps.codeBlock:
stern my-app -n prod --since 15m --tail 50
# or, using only kubectl:
kubectl logs -l app=my-app -n prod --prefix --tail=-1 > /tmp/my-app-all.log

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Always pair -l with --prefix and an explicit --tail, since selector mode defaults to 10 lines per pod and hides which replica spoke.
elevatorPitch: kubectl logs deploy/x only reads one pod, so for all replicas I use kubectl logs -l app=x --all-containers --prefix --tail=100.
I confirm coverage by comparing prefixes with kubectl get pods -l and raise --max-log-requests when following many pods.
For real operations I ship logs to a central store and use stern for live tailing.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming kubectl logs deployment/name covers every replica
mistakesToAvoid.why: It selects a single pod, so you may debug the one healthy replica while the failing one stays unread.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting --tail in selector mode
mistakesToAvoid.why: kubectl returns only the last 10 lines per pod by default, so earlier errors are missed.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Following more than 5 pods without --max-log-requests
mistakesToAvoid.why: kubectl refuses concurrent streams beyond the default limit of 5 and errors out.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on kubectl logs as the only log retention
mistakesToAvoid.why: Logs are tied to pod and node lifecycle and are rotated by the kubelet, so evidence disappears after restarts or evictions.

title: Kubernetes Q79: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler shows unknown/50% for current metric [L2]
summary: metrics-server not installed or pods have no resource requests set.
question: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler shows `unknown/50%` for current metric.
intro: When the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler shows unknown/50% as the current metric, the HPA controller cannot obtain a usable metric for the target pods, so it will not scale. The usual causes are no metrics-server (or an unhealthy metrics API), missing CPU requests on the pods, pods that are not ready yet, or a wrong target or selector. Interviewers ask this because utilization targets are relative to resource requests, a detail many engineers forget.

steps.title: How the HPA Gets Its Metric
steps.description: The HPA reads from the metrics API; the chain has several single points of failure.
items: Resource metrics: CPU and memory come from metrics-server through the metrics.k8s.io API, which is registered as an APIService.

Utilization is a percentage of requests: a 50% CPU target means 50% of the summed container CPU requests. No request, no percentage, so the value is unknown. If a pod has two containers and only one defines a CPU request, the HPA cannot compute pod utilization and reports the metric as unknown.
Custom and external metrics: these need an adapter such as prometheus-adapter or KEDA, which exposes custom.metrics.k8s.io or external.metrics.k8s.io.

Readiness and age: the HPA ignores recently started or unready pods in its calculation, which can briefly show unknown on a new deployment. A deployment that was just created can show unknown for the first scrape interval, usually under a minute, so wait before treating it as a fault.
Formula: desired replicas = ceil(current replicas x current metric / target metric), with a default tolerance of 10% around the target, which is why small fluctuations do not trigger scaling.

steps.title: Hands-on: HPA Shows unknown/50% Diagnosis
steps.description: The HPA's own conditions usually state the reason in plain text.
items: Read conditions: kubectl describe hpa lists AbleToScale and ScalingActive; a False ScalingActive with FailedGetResourceMetric names the missing piece. Look at the Events section too: repeated FailedGetResourceMetric and FailedComputeMetricsReplicas entries include the underlying API error text, such as the metrics API being unavailable.
Test the metrics API: kubectl top pods works only if metrics-server is healthy; an error means fix that first.

Check the APIService: kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io should be Available True. If the APIService reports FailedDiscoveryCheck or MissingEndpoints, metrics-server is not reachable by the API server, often because of a webhook-style network policy or firewall between the control plane and the pod network on managed clusters.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get hpa my-app -n prod
kubectl describe hpa my-app -n prod | sed -n '/Conditions/,/Events/p'
# Typical message: missing request for cpu in container my-app of Pod my-app-...

kubectl top pods -n prod
kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io
kubectl -n kube-system get deploy metrics-server
kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/metrics-server --tail=30

steps.title: Root Causes and the Matching Fix
steps.description: Each signature has a one-step remedy.
items: Metrics-server missing or unhealthy: install it, or fix its kubelet connection. --kubelet-insecure-tls exists for lab clusters only; in production fix kubelet serving certificates. Check the version-specific install: metrics-server must run and be registered; on managed Kubernetes it is sometimes an add-on you must enable explicitly.

Missing CPU request: add resources.requests.cpu to every container in the pod, including sidecars, because the pod-level utilization needs all of them. On Kubernetes 1.30 and later the ContainerResource metric type can target a single container.
Wrong scaleTargetRef or selector: the HPA must reference the right Deployment name and kind, whose selector matches running pods.
Pods not ready or crashing: unready pods are excluded, so fix the pod health first.
steps.codeBlock:
# Deployment container
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 200m
    memory: 256Mi

# HPA
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: prod
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: my-app
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 50

steps.title: Verification Under Load
steps.description: Do not stop when the number appears; prove it scales.
items: Value appears: after a minute kubectl get hpa -w should show a real value such as 12%/50%.

Generate load: run a short load test (for example with hey or k6) and watch replicas rise and fall, remembering the scale-down stabilization window of 5 minutes by default. Compare against kubectl top pods during the test to see whether the metric the HPA uses matches what you observe, and remember that the HPA evaluates on a sync period of 15 seconds by default.
Events: SuccessfulRescale events confirm the controller acted.

steps.title: Production Practice
steps.description: Autoscaling is only as good as requests and metrics health.
items: Set requests from data: base them on observed usage; unrealistic requests make utilization targets meaningless. Set requests close to typical steady-state usage so 50% means a meaningful amount of headroom, not an arbitrary number.
Monitor the metrics pipeline: alert when the metrics APIService is unavailable or when HPA reports ScalingActive false.
Tune behavior: use spec.behavior to control scale-up and scale-down speed and avoid flapping.
Min and max sanity: if min equals max the HPA can never move, and if the target Deployment is scaled to zero by hand the HPA is disabled until replicas are above zero.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Read the HPA conditions with kubectl describe first; FailedGetResourceMetric usually says exactly whether metrics-server or a missing CPU request is the cause.
elevatorPitch: Unknown means the HPA cannot compute utilization, usually because metrics-server is down or CPU requests are missing.
I describe the HPA, run kubectl top, check the metrics APIService, then confirm requests on every container.
I alert on the metrics API and HPA conditions and load-test to confirm scaling up and down.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Setting a CPU utilization target without CPU requests
mistakesToAvoid.why: Utilization is calculated relative to requests, so there is nothing to divide by and the metric stays unknown.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting a sidecar without requests
mistakesToAvoid.why: One container missing a request makes the pod-level value incomputable.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using --kubelet-insecure-tls in production
mistakesToAvoid.why: It disables certificate verification between metrics-server and kubelets.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting instant scale-down
mistakesToAvoid.why: The default stabilization window delays scale-down, so waiting a few minutes is normal and not a failure.

title: Kubernetes Q80: etcd backup failed Recovery steps [L3]
summary: etcdctl snapshot save backup.db. Restore: stop API server, restore snapshot, restart.
question: etcd backup failed. Recovery steps?
intro: "Kubernetes is a declarative desired state system; understanding the reconciliation loop is how you diagnose this quickly. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: etcdctl snapshot save backup.db. Restore: stop API server, restore snapshot, restart.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: etcdctl snapshot save backup.db. Restore: stop API server, restore snapshot, restart..
elevatorPitch: Immediate Triage: etcdctl snapshot save backup.db. Restore: stop API server, restore snapshot, restart.
Run targeted verification commands before modifying configuration.
Automate permanent guardrails (CI check, alerts, IaC policy) to prevent recurrence.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Applying exclusive-lock DDL table migrations on live production databases during peak traffic windows when configuring etcd backup failed
mistakesToAvoid.why: DDL migrations that acquire an exclusive table lock block all concurrent queries, queuing connections until the database connection pool exhausts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Allowing high-frequency queries to trigger full table scans without appropriate composite indexing when configuring etcd backup failed
mistakesToAvoid.why: Sequential table scans saturate database CPU and disk I/O, evicting frequently queried data from the buffer cache and causing cascading timeouts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Disabling referential integrity constraints during bulk ETL imports without post-import consistency validation when configuring etcd backup failed
mistakesToAvoid.why: Skipping relational consistency checks risks introducing orphaned records and referential integrity violations into production tables.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on database snapshot backups that have never been verified through automated restoration drills when configuring etcd backup failed
mistakesToAvoid.why: Backups that have never been tested with automated restore verification frequently fail during real disaster recovery scenarios.

title: Kubernetes Q81: A developer accidentally deleted a namespace How do you recover [L2]
summary: From backup/GitOps. There's no undo in kubectl. This is why GitOps (ArgoCD/Flux) matters — re-apply the Git state.
question: A developer accidentally deleted a namespace. How do you recover?
intro: To recover a deleted namespace in Kubernetes, first stop further damage and protect any surviving volumes, then rebuild the namespace from a backup (Velero or an etcd-derived snapshot) or from Git via GitOps, and restore data from volume snapshots. There is no undelete: deleting a namespace removes every namespaced object in it, including Deployments, ConfigMaps, Secrets and PersistentVolumeClaims. Interviewers ask this to test incident discipline, backup literacy and whether you know what happens to persistent volumes.

steps.title: Contain the Incident and Understand What Was Lost
steps.description: Spend the first minutes limiting damage and measuring the blast radius, not restoring blindly.
items: What is deleted: all namespaced resources: workloads, Services, Ingresses, ConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCs, RBAC bindings, custom resources. Cluster-scoped objects and PersistentVolumes are not namespaced. Write down exactly what existed, using Git, Helm releases, and Velero or Argo CD inventories, because that list becomes your restore checklist.
Volumes depend on reclaim policy: a PV with Retain survives as Released; with Delete the backing disk is removed along with the PVC, unless you intervene first.
Still Terminating? if kubectl get ns my-ns shows Terminating, controllers are still cleaning up. Quickly patch PVs to Retain before the volumes are deleted.
Find the cause: Kubernetes audit logs or cloud audit logs show who issued the delete. Freeze the pipeline or credentials involved so it is not repeated.
steps.highlight: Do not force-remove namespace finalizers as a first reaction. That skips cleanup controllers and can orphan cloud resources such as load balancers and disks.

steps.title: Hands-on: Recover a Deleted Namespace with Velero
steps.description: With a recent backup, restore is a single command and the quickest path to a known-good state.
items: List backups: pick the newest backup that contains the namespace and predates the delete.

Restore selectively: include only the namespace; Velero recreates objects and, with CSI or file-system backup, volume data. Prefer restoring into the original name only after confirming the namespace is fully gone, otherwise a half-terminated namespace causes conflicts and partial restores.
Watch the restore: velero restore describe shows warnings and errors for skipped objects.
Cross-cluster option: Velero can restore into a different cluster, which is useful if the damage is wider or you want to validate the restore before touching production.
steps.codeBlock:
# Protect surviving volumes first
kubectl get pv | grep my-ns
kubectl patch pv <pv-name> -p '{"spec":{"persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy":"Retain"}}'

# Restore from the latest suitable backup
velero backup get
velero restore create restore-my-ns \
  --from-backup daily-20260101020000 \
  --include-namespaces my-ns
velero restore describe restore-my-ns --details
velero restore logs restore-my-ns | tail -30

steps.title: Rebuild from Git, Secrets and Data
steps.description: If infrastructure is declared in Git, the namespace is rebuilt from source of truth rather than from a backup.
items: GitOps resync: recreate the namespace and sync the Argo CD Application or Flux Kustomization. Declared Deployments, Services and Ingresses return exactly as defined.

Secrets: if they come from an external store (External Secrets Operator, Vault, cloud secret manager) they are regenerated automatically. Secrets created by hand or by kubectl create are gone unless backed up.

Persistent data: restore from VolumeSnapshots or cloud disk snapshots, create PVs and PVCs that bind to them, then start the workloads. For databases, prefer restoring the application's own logical backups over raw volume copies.

Last resort: an etcd snapshot restored into a separate scratch cluster, with etcdutl snapshot restore, lets you export the needed objects with kubectl and re-apply them. Never restore etcd over a live production cluster for one namespace.
steps.codeBlock:
# Rebuild from Git instead of backup
kubectl create namespace my-ns
kubectl label namespace my-ns team=payments
argocd app sync my-app-prod      # or: flux reconcile kustomization my-app -n flux-system --with-source
kubectl get all,cm,secret,pvc -n my-ns

steps.title: Verify the Recovery
steps.description: Confirm both control plane objects and application behaviour.
items: Objects back: kubectl get all,cm,secret,pvc,ingress -n my-ns compared against Git or a previous inventory.

Pods ready and data intact: check kubectl rollout status, application health endpoints and a data sanity check such as a row count. Run an application-level check, not just kubectl: log in, read a known record, and confirm background jobs resume.
Dependencies: verify DNS, certificates (cert-manager reissues them), and Ingress addresses, which may have changed after recreation.
RBAC and quotas: RoleBindings, ResourceQuotas and NetworkPolicies are namespaced, so confirm they were restored too.
Cloud leftovers: load balancers and DNS records created by controllers may have been deleted too; check ExternalDNS and the cloud console for orphaned or missing resources.

steps.title: Prevention: Backups, Guardrails and Access
steps.description: Make the next accident hard or harmless.
items: Scheduled backups: velero schedule create daily --schedule="0 2 * * *" --ttl 720h, and test restores regularly in a scratch cluster.
Retain volumes: use a StorageClass with reclaimPolicy: Retain for critical data and keep cloud disk snapshots.
Admission guardrail: a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (stable in 1.30) or Kyverno policy can deny DELETE on namespaces carrying a protection label.
Least privilege: developers rarely need namespace delete; grant it only to platform automation and require review for prod.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Patch the PersistentVolumes to Retain the moment you notice the delete, since a Delete reclaim policy removes the underlying disks while the namespace is still terminating.
elevatorPitch: Deleting a namespace removes all namespaced objects and there is no undelete, so recovery means restoring from backup or Git.
I protect PVs with Retain first, then restore with Velero or resync GitOps, and rebuild secrets and data from snapshots.
I prevent repeats with scheduled and tested backups, Retain classes, admission policy and least-privilege RBAC.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forcing namespace finalizers off immediately
mistakesToAvoid.why: It bypasses controller cleanup and can orphan load balancers and disks.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Not checking PV reclaim policy
mistakesToAvoid.why: A Delete policy removes the backing disk with the PVC, turning an object loss into a data loss.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming Git contains everything
mistakesToAvoid.why: Secrets, manually created resources and data are not in manifests unless backed up elsewhere.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Never testing restores
mistakesToAvoid.why: An untested backup often fails on missing CRDs, storage classes or cross-namespace dependencies during the real incident.

title: Kubernetes Q82: Pod shows Terminating for hours and wont delete [L2]
summary: Force delete: kubectl delete pod <name> --grace-period=0 --force. Usually caused by finalizers or stuck volumes.
question: Pod shows `Terminating` for hours and won't delete.
intro: When a pod shows Terminating for hours and won't delete, the API object has a deletion timestamp but something is blocking its removal: a finalizer, a kubelet that cannot confirm the container stopped, a volume that will not unmount, or a process ignoring SIGTERM past a long grace period. Diagnose which of these applies before you force anything. Interviewers ask this because the lazy answer, force delete, can leave a StatefulSet pod running twice, and a senior answer explains the safe path.

steps.title: How Pod Deletion Works and Where It Blocks
steps.description: Deletion is a sequence; stuck pods are stuck at a specific step.
items: Sequence: the API sets deletionTimestamp, the kubelet runs preStop hooks and sends SIGTERM, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30), sends SIGKILL, unmounts volumes, and reports back so the object can be removed.
Finalizers: any string in metadata.finalizers keeps the object until its controller removes it.

Node dependency: only the kubelet on the pod's node can confirm termination; if the node is NotReady or unreachable the pod stays Terminating. This is why pods on a failed node show Terminating while a Deployment has already created replacements elsewhere, and why StatefulSet replacements wait.
Volumes and runtime: a hung CSI unmount or an unresponsive container runtime stalls the kubelet's cleanup.
Grace period surprises: a pod can legitimately be Terminating for as long as its grace period, so confirm terminationGracePeriodSeconds is not set to hours before assuming it is stuck.

steps.title: Hands-on: Pod Stuck in Terminating Diagnosis
steps.description: Collect four facts: finalizers, node health, grace period and events.
items: Finalizers and timestamps: if finalizers are present, find the owning controller and why it is not clearing them.
Node state: NotReady or missing nodes explain most hours-long cases. A node that is NotReady will not respond at all; check it from the cloud console or SSM before assuming Kubernetes is the problem.
Events and kubelet logs: unmount and kill errors appear on the pod or in the node's kubelet journal.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get pod my-pod -n prod -o jsonpath='{.metadata.deletionTimestamp}{"\n"}{.metadata.deletionGracePeriodSeconds}{"\n"}{.metadata.finalizers}{"\n"}'
kubectl get pod my-pod -n prod -o wide      # which node?
kubectl get node <node-name>
kubectl describe pod my-pod -n prod | tail -20

# On the node
sudo journalctl -u kubelet --since "1 hour ago" | grep -i my-pod
sudo crictl ps -a | grep my-pod

steps.title: Root Causes and Targeted Fixes
steps.description: Fix the cause, not the symptom, where you can.
items: Finalizer owner not running: a deleted controller or webhook leaves finalizers behind. Restore the controller, or if it is truly gone, remove only that finalizer. Typical examples are controllers for storage protection or custom resources that were uninstalled before the objects they guarded were cleaned up.

Node NotReady: recover the node, or drain and delete the Node object after confirming it is really down. For planned shutdowns that were not graceful, Kubernetes 1.28 made non-graceful node shutdown GA: taint the node node.kubernetes.io/out-of-service=nodeshutdown:NoExecute to let pods and volume attachments be cleaned up.
App ignores SIGTERM: the process runs as a shell child or never handles the signal, so it waits until SIGKILL after a long grace period. Fix the entrypoint with exec form or an init such as tini.
Stuck volume unmount: inspect VolumeAttachments with kubectl get volumeattachment and CSI driver logs.
Foreground deletion: an owner deleted with foreground propagation waits for dependents, so a Terminating parent object may simply be waiting on children with their own finalizers.

steps.title: Force Deletion: When and How
steps.description: Force delete removes the API object without kubelet confirmation, so use it deliberately.
items: Command: kubectl delete pod my-pod -n prod --grace-period=0 --force removes the object immediately; the container may still run on the node.
StatefulSet risk: StatefulSets guarantee at most one pod per identity; force deleting while the old pod may still be running can create two writers to the same volume. Be sure the node is down first.
Finalizer removal: kubectl patch pod my-pod -n prod -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}' --type=merge is the last resort for orphaned finalizers.
Verify: kubectl get pod returns NotFound, a replacement is Running and Ready, and no orphaned container remains in crictl ps on the old node.
steps.highlight: Force delete only after you know the old container is dead (node powered off or fenced). For stateful workloads, an unconfirmed force delete risks data corruption.
steps.codeBlock:
# Last-resort sequence (after confirming the node is down or fenced)
kubectl delete pod my-pod -n prod --grace-period=0 --force
# Orphaned finalizer only
kubectl patch pod my-pod -n prod --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'
kubectl get pod my-pod -n prod

steps.title: Prevention
steps.description: Design pods so termination is fast and observable.
items: Handle SIGTERM: stop accepting work, drain, exit; keep the grace period just above real drain time.
Keep preStop short: a sleep or hook that hangs delays termination for the full grace period.
Monitor: alert on pods with a deletionTimestamp older than a threshold, and use node problem detector for runtime and kubelet failures.
Control finalizers: uninstall controllers cleanly so they release resources and finalizers first.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Check metadata.finalizers and the node status before forcing, because those two facts decide whether a force delete is a safe shortcut or a StatefulSet data hazard.
elevatorPitch: A Terminating pod has a deletion timestamp but is blocked by a finalizer, an unreachable node, a stuck volume or an unhandled SIGTERM.
I read finalizers, node health, grace period and events before acting.
I force delete only when the old container is confirmed dead, and I fix SIGTERM handling and monitoring to prevent repeats.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running force delete as the first step
mistakesToAvoid.why: It hides the cause and on StatefulSets can create duplicate writers to one volume.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Stripping finalizers without finding their owner
mistakesToAvoid.why: The owner controller may then leave external resources behind.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring node health
mistakesToAvoid.why: A NotReady node can never confirm termination, so no pod-level fix will work.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using a shell-form entrypoint
mistakesToAvoid.why: SIGTERM goes to the shell, not the app, so the app only dies at SIGKILL after the full grace period.

title: Kubernetes Q83: Service mesh vs NetworkPolicy — when do you use each [L3]
summary: Service mesh vs NetworkPolicy is not an either-or choice: NetworkPolicy is a built-in L3/L4 firewall enforced by the CNI that decides which pods may connect, while a service mesh adds identity, mutual TLS, L7 authorization,.
question: Service mesh vs NetworkPolicy — when do you use each?
intro: Service mesh vs NetworkPolicy is not an either-or choice: NetworkPolicy is a built-in L3/L4 firewall enforced by the CNI that decides which pods may connect, while a service mesh adds identity, mutual TLS, L7 authorization, retries and telemetry through proxies. Use NetworkPolicy for baseline isolation in every cluster and add a mesh when you need encrypted service-to-service traffic, request-level policy or traffic management. Interviewers ask this to check you can weigh capability against operational cost.

steps.title: Mental Model: Two Different Layers
steps.description: They answer different questions and are enforced by different components.
items: NetworkPolicy: built into the Kubernetes API, enforced by the CNI (Calico, Cilium, Antrea). Matches pods, namespaces and IP blocks on TCP/UDP/SCTP ports. Allows or isolates connections; it does not encrypt or inspect HTTP.

Service mesh: Istio, Linkerd or Cilium service mesh. Sidecar proxies, or ambient mode in Istio with node-level ztunnel and optional waypoint proxies, enforce mTLS and L7 rules. Linkerd and ambient mode reduce the sidecar overhead, but you still operate additional control plane components and certificates.
Identity: NetworkPolicy relies on labels and IPs. A mesh issues workload identities (for example SPIFFE IDs) tied to certificates, so rules can say which service account may call which endpoint.
Cost: NetworkPolicy has near-zero runtime cost. A mesh adds control plane components, proxy resources, upgrade work and debugging complexity.
Cilium note: Cilium implements both: standard NetworkPolicy via eBPF, plus its own L7-aware policies and optional mesh features, so the boundary between the two is blurring in some stacks.

steps.title: Hands-on: Service Mesh vs NetworkPolicy Configs Side by Side
steps.description: The same intent, only the backend may call the database, expressed at two layers.
items: NetworkPolicy: default deny ingress in the namespace, then allow pods with label app: backend to reach the database on port 5432. Default deny is added with an empty podSelector and policyTypes Ingress; then each service gets an explicit allow rule, so the namespace is closed by default.
Istio AuthorizationPolicy: allow only the backend service account identity, which survives pod IP changes and works with mTLS.
PeerAuthentication: STRICT mode rejects plaintext traffic between meshed workloads.
steps.codeBlock:
# L3/L4: NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: db-allow-backend
  namespace: prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: db }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app: backend }
      ports:
        - { protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }
---
# Identity and L7: Istio
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: db-allow-backend
  namespace: prod
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: db }
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
    - from:
        - source:
            principals: ["cluster.local/ns/prod/sa/backend"]
---
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: prod
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT

steps.title: When to Use Which
steps.description: Decide from requirements, not trends.
items: NetworkPolicy only: you need namespace and pod isolation, default deny, and tier separation, and your compliance does not demand in-cluster encryption or per-route authorization.

Mesh needed: you must encrypt east-west traffic with mTLS, authorize by workload identity or HTTP method and path, do canary traffic splitting, or collect uniform golden-signal metrics. Request-level rules such as allowing only GET on /api/orders are only possible with an L7-aware layer.
Both: the common production answer. NetworkPolicy provides a kernel-level backstop that works even for pods without a proxy, and the mesh provides identity and L7 control.
Neither alone is enough: a mesh can be bypassed by pods that are not injected or by hostNetwork pods, so do not treat it as a replacement for network isolation.
Compliance angle: if a regulation requires encryption in transit between services, a mesh with STRICT mTLS (or CNI-level transparent encryption such as WireGuard) is the control, not NetworkPolicy.

steps.title: Failure Modes and Interactions
steps.description: The two layers interact; plan for it.
items: Policy blocks the mesh: a default-deny policy must allow DNS and the traffic needed by proxies and the control plane, such as webhook and xDS ports for your mesh, or injection and certificate issuance fail.
Source IP and ports: with sidecars, NetworkPolicy sees proxy traffic and mesh ports. Test policies after enabling the mesh.
Partial rollout: PERMISSIVE mTLS during migration allows plaintext; track and move to STRICT.
Operational load: proxy upgrades, resource overhead and extra hops affect latency and incident debugging; measure before committing cluster-wide.
steps.codeBlock:
# Verify enforcement from an unauthorised pod
kubectl run probe -n prod --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot --restart=Never -- nc -zv -w 3 db 5432
# Expect a timeout (NetworkPolicy drop) or an RBAC: access denied response (mesh)
istioctl x describe pod <db-pod> -n prod

steps.title: Production Practice and Verification
steps.description: Roll out in stages and verify enforcement.
items: Baseline first: default-deny NetworkPolicy plus DNS allow in each namespace, tested in CI.
Adopt mesh incrementally: start with namespaces that handle sensitive data, in PERMISSIVE then STRICT mode.
Verify: attempt a blocked call from an unauthorized pod and confirm it is dropped (hubble observe or mesh access logs); confirm mTLS with istioctl or linkerd viz tooling.
Cost check: estimate per-pod proxy CPU and memory and the added upgrade burden before rollout; in ambient mode the cost shifts to node-level components but still exists.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Treat NetworkPolicy as the always-on L3/L4 floor and the mesh as the identity and L7 layer on top; running a mesh without default-deny leaves un-injected pods wide open.
elevatorPitch: NetworkPolicy is a CNI-enforced L3/L4 allowlist; a service mesh adds mTLS identity, L7 authorization and traffic control via proxies.
I use NetworkPolicy everywhere and add a mesh only when encryption, per-route policy or traffic management justify the cost.
I verify with blocked-call tests, flow logs and mTLS status tools, and roll out STRICT mode in stages.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating a mesh as a replacement for NetworkPolicy
mistakesToAvoid.why: Un-injected and hostNetwork pods can bypass it, so network-level isolation is still needed.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Adopting a mesh only for observability
mistakesToAvoid.why: Lighter tools such as eBPF-based flow visibility may meet the need without proxy overhead.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Applying default-deny without allowing mesh and DNS traffic
mistakesToAvoid.why: Sidecar injection, certificate issuance and name resolution then fail in confusing ways.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Staying on PERMISSIVE mTLS indefinitely
mistakesToAvoid.why: Plaintext traffic remains accepted, so the encryption benefit is never realised.

title: Kubernetes Q84: How do you make a pod restart on config change without a code change [L2]
summary: A pod restart on config change is not automatic: Kubernetes only rolls pods when the Pod template changes, so you must make the config change show up in the template (a checksum annotation, a hashed ConfigMap name) or trigger a.
question: How do you make a pod restart on config change without a code change?
intro: A pod restart on config change is not automatic: Kubernetes only rolls pods when the Pod template changes, so you must make the config change show up in the template (a checksum annotation, a hashed ConfigMap name) or trigger a rollout explicitly with kubectl rollout restart. Interviewers ask this because ConfigMap and Secret updates are a classic source of silent drift: the object changes, the running pods do not. A strong answer explains how each consumption mode behaves (env vars, volume mounts, subPath), then picks a repeatable, GitOps-friendly mechanism instead of manually deleting pods.

steps.title: Mental model: why pods ignore config updates
steps.description: Before choosing a trigger, know how the container actually consumes the config, because that decides whether a restart is needed at all.
items: Env vars: values from env.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef or envFrom are resolved once at container start. Editing the ConfigMap never changes a running process, so a restart is mandatory.

Volume mounts: files in a mounted ConfigMap or Secret volume are refreshed by the kubelet after a delay (sync period plus cache TTL, so it can take a minute or more). The application must re-read the file or watch for changes.
subPath mounts: a ConfigMap mounted with subPath is never updated in place. This surprises many teams, and a restart is the only fix.
Immutable objects: if the ConfigMap has immutable: true you cannot edit it at all. You create a new object and point the workload at it, which naturally triggers a rollout.

steps.title: Hands-on: pod restart on config change with rollout restart
steps.description: The fastest option is a rolling restart, which respects readiness probes, maxUnavailable and PodDisruptionBudgets, unlike deleting pods by hand.
items: Trigger: kubectl rollout restart deployment/my-app stamps a kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt annotation on the Pod template, which creates a new ReplicaSet. It also works for StatefulSets and DaemonSets.
Watch it: kubectl rollout status blocks until the new ReplicaSet is fully available, so you can use it as a CI gate.
Limitation: it is imperative. Nothing in Git records that a restart happened, and it does not detect config drift by itself.
Rollback: kubectl rollout undo returns to the previous ReplicaSet if the new config is bad.
steps.codeBlock:
# 1. Update the config
kubectl -n prod apply -f app-config.yaml

# 2. Roll the pods so they pick it up
kubectl -n prod rollout restart deployment/my-app

# 3. Wait for the rollout to finish (non-zero exit on failure/timeout)
kubectl -n prod rollout status deployment/my-app --timeout=180s

# 4. Confirm the pods are new
kubectl -n prod get pods -l app=my-app -o wide

steps.title: Declarative triggers: checksum annotation or hashed ConfigMap
steps.description: For GitOps, make the config content part of the Pod template so any change produces a new template hash and a normal rolling update.
items: Helm checksum annotation: add the pod annotation checksum/config with the sha256 of the rendered ConfigMap template. When the ConfigMap changes, the annotation changes, and helm upgrade rolls the Deployment.

Kustomize generator: configMapGenerator appends a content hash to the name and rewrites references, so every edit creates a new ConfigMap and a new rollout. Old ConfigMaps can be garbage-collected later.
Benefit: rollback is a Git revert, because the previous config name is referenced by the previous Pod template.
Trade-off: a hash change restarts every pod even for a harmless comment edit, so keep volatile data out of the hashed object.
steps.codeBlock:
# Helm: deployment.yaml (pod template metadata)
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}

# Kustomize: kustomization.yaml
configMapGenerator:
  - name: my-app-config
    files:
      - app.properties
# renders my-app-config-<hash>; Deployment refs are rewritten automatically

steps.title: Controller-based reload with Reloader and hot reload
steps.description: If config changes outside the deployment pipeline, a controller can watch the objects and roll the workloads for you.
items: Reloader: the open-source Stakater Reloader watches ConfigMaps and Secrets and triggers a rolling update on annotated workloads, for example reloader.stakater.com/auto: "true". Review its RBAC, since it needs write access to workloads.

Hot reload instead of restart: apps that support SIGHUP or a file watcher (nginx reload, Prometheus /-/reload) can avoid restarts, using a sidecar to signal the main process. Test that the reload truly applies the setting.
Secrets: the same logic applies. Rotating a Secret does nothing until the pod restarts or re-reads the mounted file.
Blast radius: auto-restart on every change can cause a thundering herd if many workloads share one ConfigMap, so scope ConfigMaps per application.
steps.highlight: Always keep readinessProbe, maxUnavailable and a PodDisruptionBudget sane. A config-triggered rollout is a real deployment and will take traffic down if the new config is broken.

steps.title: Verification and failure modes
steps.description: Confirm that the new config is really in effect, not just that new pods exist.
items: Check the template: kubectl get deploy my-app -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.metadata.annotations}' should show the new checksum or restartedAt value.
Check the process: kubectl exec deploy/my-app -- env | grep LOG_LEVEL or read the mounted file to confirm the value the app really sees.

Bad config: a crash-looping new ReplicaSet leaves old pods running because rolling updates stop when new pods never become ready. Watch rollout status and alert on progressDeadlineSeconds being exceeded.
Validation: lint ConfigMaps in CI (schema or dry-run with kubectl apply --dry-run=server) so broken config never reaches the rollout.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Treat config as part of the Pod template (hash or checksum) so a config change is a normal, revertable rollout instead of a manual restart.
elevatorPitch: Pods only roll when the Pod template changes, so a ConfigMap edit alone never restarts anything; env vars are read at start, and mounted files update lazily.
I make config part of the template using a checksum annotation or a hashed ConfigMap name, and use kubectl rollout restart for ad hoc cases, then confirm with rollout status.
For config changed outside CI, I use a reload controller like Reloader with scoped ConfigMaps and keep probes and PDBs correct.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming editing a ConfigMap updates running pods
mistakesToAvoid.why: Env vars are fixed at container start, and subPath mounts never refresh, so the app keeps stale values.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Deleting pods manually to pick up config
mistakesToAvoid.why: It bypasses rolling-update safeguards and can drop capacity below the PodDisruptionBudget.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Sharing one giant ConfigMap across many workloads with auto-reload
mistakesToAvoid.why: A single edit restarts every consumer at once and creates a thundering herd.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Not testing the config before rolling
mistakesToAvoid.why: A bad value creates crash-looping pods; the rollout stalls and you must undo under pressure.

title: Kubernetes Q85: A CronJob job ran but the pod isnt showing in kubectl get jobs [L2]
summary: successfulJobsHistoryLimit may be 0 or 1 and old jobs were cleaned. Adjust to keep history.
question: A CronJob job ran but the pod isn't showing in `kubectl get jobs`.
intro: When a CronJob job ran but the pod isn't showing in kubectl get jobs, the first correction is that kubectl get jobs lists Job objects, not pods. A missing entry usually means the Job was garbage-collected (history limits or TTL), you are in the wrong namespace, or the CronJob never created a Job at all. Interviewers use this to test whether you know the CronJob to Job to Pod ownership chain and where each layer is cleaned up. The answer is a short diagnostic runbook: confirm the CronJob fired, find the Job, find the pod by label, then read events and logs.

steps.title: Mental model: CronJob creates Job creates Pod
steps.description: A CronJob does not run containers. It creates a Job on schedule, and the Job controller creates pods. Each layer has its own retention rules.
items: CronJob: records lastScheduleTime and lastSuccessfulTime in status. If these are empty or old, no Job was created and you debug the schedule, not the pod.
Job: kept according to successfulJobsHistoryLimit (default 3) and failedJobsHistoryLimit (default 1). Older Jobs and their pods are deleted by the CronJob controller.

Pod: belongs to the Job through ownerReferences and carries the label job-name=<job> (newer clusters also set batch.kubernetes.io/job-name). Pods vanish when the Job is deleted or when ttlSecondsAfterFinished expires.
Different commands: kubectl get jobs shows Jobs, kubectl get pods shows pods. Completed pods show Completed status and are hidden by some UIs and by --field-selector=status.phase=Running.

Ownership check: run kubectl get job <name> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].name}' to prove which CronJob created a Job, which helps when several CronJobs share similar name prefixes in one namespace.

steps.title: Hands-on: pod isn't showing in kubectl get jobs, find the run
steps.description: Work down the chain in the right namespace and widen the search before concluding the job did not run.
items: Namespace first: use -n or -A. CronJob objects and their Jobs always live in the same namespace.
CronJob status: kubectl describe cronjob shows last schedule time, active Jobs and Events such as SuccessfulCreate or MissSchedule.
All Jobs for it: Jobs are named <cronjob>-<timestamp>, so grep by prefix, and sort by creation time.
Pods by label: if the Job exists, list pods through the job-name label rather than guessing names.

Time window: compare lastScheduleTime with the current time and the cron expression. Cron schedules use the controller-manager's time zone unless spec.timeZone is set, so a job may have run at a different hour than you expected.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl -n prod get cronjob my-report -o wide
kubectl -n prod describe cronjob my-report | sed -n '/Events/,$p'

# Jobs created by this CronJob (newest last)
kubectl -n prod get jobs --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp | grep my-report

# Pods for a specific Job, including Completed ones
kubectl -n prod get pods -l job-name=my-report-28774000 -o wide

# Events survive a little longer than the objects (default ~1h)
kubectl -n prod get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | grep my-report

steps.title: Root causes when the Job or pod is gone
steps.description: Match what you see to a cause. Each one has a different fix.
items: History limit cleanup: with successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 0 the Job is deleted as soon as it finishes, so it can never be listed afterwards.
TTL after finished: spec.jobTemplate.spec.ttlSecondsAfterFinished removes the Job and its pods after the set seconds, which makes logs unrecoverable unless shipped elsewhere.
Never created: suspend: true, a wrong schedule or timeZone, concurrencyPolicy: Forbid while a previous run is stuck, or startingDeadlineSeconds exceeded after controller downtime.
Created but no pod: a ResourceQuota, LimitRange or admission webhook rejecting the pod. The Job events then show FailedCreate with the reason, even though no pod exists.

Concurrency skips: with concurrencyPolicy: Forbid the controller records a skipped run in events rather than creating a Job, and with Replace it deletes the still-running Job and its pods, which also explains pods that disappear mid-run.
steps.highlight: If the Job exists with COMPLETIONS 0/1 and no pods, read kubectl describe job Events first. FailedCreate messages name the quota or webhook that blocked it.

steps.title: Reproduce and verify
steps.description: Don't wait for the next schedule. Create a Job on demand from the CronJob template and watch it.
items: Manual trigger: kubectl create job --from=cronjob/my-report my-report-manual-1 uses the same pod template, so quota or RBAC problems reproduce immediately.
Watch: kubectl get pods -w -l job-name=my-report-manual-1 and then kubectl logs job/my-report-manual-1.
Failure states: ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff and exceeded backoffLimit all leave a failed Job whose pods remain until the failed history limit removes them.
Confirm the fix: after correcting the cause, check that lastSuccessfulTime advances on the next scheduled run.

Evidence after failure: if the run failed and you only need to see why, kubectl describe job and kubectl logs job/<name> --all-containers still work while the Job object exists, so capture output before retention expires.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl -n prod create job --from=cronjob/my-report my-report-manual-1
kubectl -n prod wait --for=condition=complete job/my-report-manual-1 --timeout=300s
kubectl -n prod logs job/my-report-manual-1
kubectl -n prod get cronjob my-report -o jsonpath='{.status.lastSuccessfulTime}'

steps.title: Production practice
steps.description: Make CronJob runs observable so you are never debugging after the evidence is deleted.
items: Keep enough history: use successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3 and failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3 or more for jobs you debug often, and avoid TTL values shorter than your alert response time.
Ship logs: send stdout to a log backend so output outlives the pod.
Alert on absence: with kube-state-metrics, alert when kube_cronjob_status_last_successful_time is older than the expected interval, not only on failures.
Set deadlines: define startingDeadlineSeconds, activeDeadlineSeconds and an explicit timeZone so skips and hangs are predictable.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Remember that jobs and pods are separate objects. Find the Job through the CronJob, then the pod via the job-name label, and check history limits and TTL before assuming it never ran.
elevatorPitch: kubectl get jobs lists Jobs, not pods, and a CronJob creates a Job which creates pods, each with its own cleanup rules.
I check the CronJob status and events, look in the right namespace, find the Job and its pods with the job-name label, and read FailedCreate events for quota or webhook blocks.
I automate it with generous history limits, shipped logs and an alert on stale lastSuccessfulTime.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting pods in the output of kubectl get jobs
mistakesToAvoid.why: The command lists only Job objects, so you must query pods separately by label.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Setting successfulJobsHistoryLimit to 0 or a tiny TTL, then debugging later
mistakesToAvoid.why: The Job and its pods are deleted immediately, so logs and events are gone.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
mistakesToAvoid.why: A hung previous run silently makes the controller skip new schedules.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Looking only at pod status for missing runs
mistakesToAvoid.why: If quota or a webhook blocked creation, no pod ever existed; the evidence is in Job events.

title: Kubernetes Q86: Your admission webhook is blocking all pod creation cluster-wide How do you recover [L3]
summary: If webhook server is down, set failurePolicy: Ignore on the webhook or delete the MutatingWebhookConfiguration object.
question: Your admission webhook is blocking all pod creation cluster-wide. How do you recover?
intro: When an admission webhook is blocking all pod creation, recover by removing or disabling the failing webhook configuration (or fixing its backend), then restoring it with a safe failurePolicy. This happens when a webhook with failurePolicy: Fail points at a service that is down, has an expired certificate, or depends on pods that cannot start because of the webhook itself, a circular dependency. Interviewers want to see calm triage: confirm the symptom from the error text, identify the webhook, break the deadlock using kubectl access to the API server, and add guardrails so it cannot recur.

steps.title: Recognise a webhook outage from the error
steps.description: The API server tells you exactly which webhook rejected the request, so read the error before changing anything.
items: Typical message: Internal error occurred: failed calling webhook "validate.example.com": Post "https://svc.ns.svc:443/validate?timeout=10s": no endpoints available. Other variants mention x509: certificate has expired or context deadline exceeded.
Scope: ReplicaSet events show FailedCreate with that text, so Deployments appear healthy but have zero new pods. Existing running pods are unaffected.
Mutating vs validating: both can block. Mutating webhooks run first, so check both configuration types.
Who is affected: only requests matching the webhook rules (resources, operations, namespace and object selectors). A webhook matching pods CREATE in all namespaces breaks everything.
Quick triage clue: if only some namespaces fail, look at namespaceSelector and objectSelector first. Cluster-wide failure points at a rule with no selector, which is the scenario in this question.

steps.title: Hands-on: admission webhook blocking all pod creation, find and inspect
steps.description: List the webhook configurations and read the rules, failurePolicy and backing Service.
items: List: both validatingwebhookconfigurations and mutatingwebhookconfigurations are cluster-scoped.
Match the name: use the webhook name from the error to find the owning configuration, and read its clientConfig.service.
Check the backend: confirm whether the Service has endpoints and whether the backing pods are running.
Look at policy: failurePolicy: Fail plus broad rules is the dangerous combination, while Ignore would have let requests through.

Timing and audit: kubectl get events -A --field-selector reason=FailedCreate shows how many controllers are affected and since when, which helps estimate the incident window and the number of objects admitted during any bypass.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations

kubectl get validatingwebhookconfiguration my-policy -o yaml | \
  grep -E 'name:|failurePolicy|timeoutSeconds|namespace:|service:' 

# Is the backend alive?
kubectl -n policy get endpoints my-policy-webhook
kubectl -n policy get pods -l app=my-policy-webhook

steps.title: Recover: bypass the webhook safely
steps.description: Prefer the least destructive option that restores pod creation, and save the original configuration first.
items: Back up: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfiguration my-policy -o yaml > my-policy.yaml so you can restore it exactly.
Option A, fix the backend: if it is a plain outage, restart or scale the webhook Deployment, renew the certificate, or fix the NetworkPolicy. This is best when it works quickly.
Option B, relax policy: patch failurePolicy to Ignore so requests pass while the backend is down. Note that this also drops enforcement.
Option C, delete: deleting the configuration is the last resort when the webhook's own pods cannot start. Controllers will recreate stuck ReplicaSet pods once admission succeeds.
Order of operations: disable or relax the webhook that is down, not every webhook. Other healthy webhooks keep enforcing policy, so avoid deleting all configurations in panic.
steps.codeBlock:
# Save the config first
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfiguration my-policy -o yaml > my-policy.yaml

# Option B: fail open for the first webhook entry
kubectl patch validatingwebhookconfiguration my-policy --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/webhooks/0/failurePolicy","value":"Ignore"}]'

# Option C: remove it entirely (restore later with kubectl apply -f my-policy.yaml)
kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration my-policy
steps.highlight: If you cannot reach the API server at all, the problem is not an admission webhook. Webhooks only block write requests that match their rules, so get and delete on the webhook configuration objects themselves are normally never intercepted.

steps.title: Verify and restore enforcement
steps.description: Confirm pods can be created, then bring the webhook back in a controlled way.
items: Smoke test: kubectl run test --image=registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9 --dry-run=server exercises admission without creating anything.
Retry stuck workloads: ReplicaSets retry with backoff. A kubectl rollout restart speeds recovery for deployments that are stuck.
Re-enable: restore the saved configuration only after the backend has ready endpoints and a valid certificate, ideally in a staging namespace first.
Audit: review what was admitted without policy during the bypass window, using audit logs, since unvalidated objects may have slipped through.

Communicate: announce the temporary loss of enforcement, record the exact commands used, and set a ticket to review admitted objects and to restore the original configuration after the backend is healthy.

steps.title: Prevent a repeat
steps.description: Webhook design determines the blast radius. Most outages come from the same few configuration mistakes.
items: Exclude system namespaces: use namespaceSelector to skip kube-system and the webhook's own namespace, so it can never block its own pods or critical components.
Short timeouts: set timeoutSeconds low (default is 10 seconds, maximum 30) so a hung backend does not stall every request.
Choose the failure mode deliberately: use Fail only for real security controls, and run the backend with several replicas, a PodDisruptionBudget and anti-affinity.
Certificate automation: manage the serving certificate with cert-manager or the controller's rotation, with an alert on expiry, and alert on webhook latency and error metrics from the API server.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Back up the webhook configuration, switch failurePolicy to Ignore or delete it to restore admission, then re-enable it only with system namespaces excluded.
elevatorPitch: A webhook with failurePolicy Fail and a dead backend rejects every matching request, so no pods can be created even though running pods are fine.
I read the error for the webhook name, inspect its rules and Service endpoints, back it up, then fix the backend or patch it to Ignore or delete it, and prove recovery with a server-side dry run.
Afterward I exclude kube-system and its own namespace, set short timeouts, run replicas with a PDB, and automate certificate rotation.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Deleting the webhook configuration without saving it
mistakesToAvoid.why: You lose the exact rules and CA bundle, making a faithful restore difficult.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Letting the webhook match its own namespace
mistakesToAvoid.why: If its pods are down, they cannot be recreated, which produces a circular deadlock.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using failurePolicy Fail for non-critical checks
mistakesToAvoid.why: A routine outage of the policy service then blocks the whole cluster.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting to audit after a bypass
mistakesToAvoid.why: Objects created while enforcement was off may violate policy and go unnoticed.

title: Kubernetes Q87: How do you check if a service account has permission to create pods [L2]
summary: kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<sa-name>
question: How do you check if a service account has permission to create pods?
intro: To check if a service account has permission to create pods, run kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name> -n <namespace>. The command asks the API server's authorizer and returns yes or no without creating anything. Interviewers ask this to see whether you can debug 403 Forbidden errors systematically: verify the identity, test the verb and resource, trace the RoleBinding, and know that Pod creation can also be blocked by admission (Pod Security, quotas), which is a different layer from RBAC.

steps.title: Mental model: identity, verb, resource, scope
steps.description: RBAC is additive allow-only. A request is permitted if any binding grants the verb on the resource in that namespace.
items: Identity: a service account is the user system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>, plus the groups system:serviceaccounts and system:serviceaccounts:<ns>.

Verb and resource: creating a pod is verb create on resource pods in the core API group (empty string). Controllers like Deployments create pods through the controller-manager's identity, not your service account.
Scope: a Role plus RoleBinding applies in one namespace, whereas a ClusterRole bound with a ClusterRoleBinding applies everywhere. A ClusterRole bound via RoleBinding is limited to that namespace.
Default: a new service account has no permissions beyond those given to the system:authenticated and discovery groups.

Aggregated roles: built-in ClusterRoles such as edit and admin include create on pods, and they can be extended through aggregation labels, so a service account may gain permission indirectly through a role you never edited.

steps.title: Hands-on: check if a service account has permission to create pods
steps.description: Use impersonation with kubectl auth can-i. Your own user needs the impersonate permission for serviceaccounts, which cluster admins have.
items: Basic test: run the command with --as and the namespace.
Explain the result: add -v=6 for the API calls, or ask for the full permission list with --list to see everything allowed in that namespace.
Cluster-wide: use -A or --all-namespaces, or omit -n for a cluster-scoped resource check.
Exit status: the command exits 0 for yes and 1 for no, so it fits shell checks and CI.

Impersonation rights: if --as returns forbidden, your own user lacks the impersonate verb on serviceaccounts. Test from inside a pod using that service account's token instead, which is the most realistic check.
steps.codeBlock:
# Can the SA create pods in 'prod'?
kubectl auth can-i create pods \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:deployer -n prod
# yes / no

# Everything the SA may do in that namespace
kubectl auth can-i --list \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:deployer -n prod

# Check the related subresource used for exec
kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:deployer -n prod

# Check yourself or from inside a pod using the mounted token
kubectl auth can-i create pods -n prod

steps.title: Trace why the answer is yes or no
steps.description: If the result surprises you, locate the binding and the role rules that grant or deny it.
items: Find bindings: list RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings and filter for the service account subject, for example with kubectl get rolebinding,clusterrolebinding -A -o wide and a grep on the name.
Read the role: kubectl describe role or clusterrole and look for pods with create. Remember apiGroups: [""] for pods.
Wrong subject namespace: a binding subject must name the service account's namespace. A common mistake is omitting it, so the binding silently matches nothing.
Real-request test: kubectl auth can-i evaluates RBAC only. For an end-to-end check, run a server-side dry-run create as the service account.
Reverse lookup: use a plugin such as kubectl-who-can with kubectl who-can create pods -n prod to list every subject allowed, which is useful during access reviews and incident response.
steps.codeBlock:
# Dry-run a real create as the service account (includes admission)
kubectl run probe --image=registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9 \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:deployer -n prod --dry-run=server

# Grant it if missing
kubectl -n prod create role pod-creator --verb=create --resource=pods
kubectl -n prod create rolebinding deployer-pod-creator \
  --role=pod-creator --serviceaccount=prod:deployer

steps.title: Failure modes: allowed by RBAC, still rejected
steps.description: A yes from RBAC does not guarantee pod creation. Other layers evaluate the request after authorization.
items: Pod Security Admission: a namespace labelled pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted rejects privileged or root pods regardless of RBAC.
Quota and limits: ResourceQuota or LimitRange violations return 403 style errors with the quota name in the message.
Webhooks and policy engines: Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper or custom webhooks can deny pods that RBAC allowed.
Other subresources: creating pods does not cover pods/exec, pods/portforward or serviceaccounts/token, which need their own rules.

Authorization modes: RBAC may not be the only authorizer. Webhook authorizers or cloud IAM integrations can add or deny access, so remember that can-i reports the combined decision of the configured authorizers.
steps.highlight: Read the exact 403 message. RBAC denials say User ... cannot create resource "pods", while admission denials name the policy, quota or webhook.

steps.title: Production practice: least privilege and auditing
steps.description: Treat pod-creation rights as high privilege, because anyone who can create pods can often mount secrets or escalate.
items: Scope narrowly: prefer namespaced Roles, and avoid wildcard verbs. Use resourceNames where possible.
Automate checks: run kubectl auth can-i assertions in CI after applying RBAC manifests, and fail if privileged accounts gain create on pods unexpectedly.
Audit tools: kubectl-who-can or rakkess plugins answer the reverse question of who can create pods.
Short-lived tokens: rely on projected, time-bound service account tokens, and disable automounting with automountServiceAccountToken: false for pods that never call the API.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: kubectl auth can-i tests RBAC only; follow it with a server-side dry-run as the service account to catch Pod Security, quota and webhook denials too.
elevatorPitch: Use kubectl auth can-i create pods with --as=system:serviceaccount:namespace:name to ask the API server's authorizer directly.
If the answer is unexpected I trace RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings for that subject, then confirm end to end with a server-side dry-run create.
I automate can-i assertions in CI and keep pod-create rights narrowly scoped, since create pods is effectively a privileged permission.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Testing with your own admin credentials
mistakesToAvoid.why: You get yes because you are cluster-admin, which says nothing about the service account.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting the namespace in the binding subject
mistakesToAvoid.why: The RoleBinding then references a service account that does not match, and access is silently denied.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating can-i yes as proof pods will be created
mistakesToAvoid.why: Pod Security Admission, quotas and webhooks can still reject the request.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Granting create on pods broadly to fix a 403
mistakesToAvoid.why: Pod creation can be used to mount secrets and escalate, so over-granting is a security risk.

title: Kubernetes Q88: What is the difference between kubectl get and kubectl describe [L1]
summary: get = brief summary table. describe = full detail including events. Use describe for debugging.
question: What is the difference between `kubectl get` and `kubectl describe`?
intro: kubectl get vs describe: get returns the stored object (a table or the raw YAML/JSON) and is the right tool for lists, scripting and automation, while describe renders a human-readable summary that also pulls in related Events, which makes it the first stop when something is failing. Interviewers ask this to see whether you know that describe output is a presentation layer you should never parse, and that Events (not the spec) usually explain why a pod is Pending or crash-looping. A strong answer names both sides and says when each one fits.

steps.title: Mental model: stored object vs rendered summary
steps.description: One command reads the API object, the other assembles a report from several API calls.
items: kubectl get: fetches the resource (or a list) and prints a server-side table by default; -o yaml or -o json gives the full object including status, ownerReferences and metadata.managedFields (hidden unless --show-managed-fields).
kubectl describe: formats the object client-side in kubectl and adds related data such as the Events that reference it, for a Pod also its node, QoS class, probes, mounts and container states.
Stability: get -o json follows the API schema and is safe to script. describe text layout is not an API and can change between kubectl versions.
Scope: get works across many objects at once (-A, -l, --watch); describe is meant for one object or a small selected set.

steps.title: kubectl get: lists, filtering and scripting
steps.description: Use get when you need breadth, exact field values or machine-readable output.
items: Wide view: -o wide adds node and IP columns without leaving table form.
Extract a field: -o jsonpath or -o custom-columns returns exactly the fields you need for a script or a quick audit.
Watch rollouts: -w streams changes, handy while a Deployment rolls out.
Full truth: -o yaml shows status.conditions and ownerReferences, which describe only partially renders.
steps.codeBlock:
# Table of pods with node and IP
kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=my-app -o wide

# One field, script-friendly
kubectl get pod my-app-7d9c-xk2lp -n prod -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}{"\n"}'

# Custom table: pod name and restart count
kubectl get pods -n prod -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,RESTARTS:.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount

# Who owns this pod? (ReplicaSet -> Deployment chain)
kubectl get pod my-app-7d9c-xk2lp -n prod -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].kind}/{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].name}{"\n"}'

steps.title: kubectl describe: Events first, then conditions
steps.description: Reach for describe when you need to know why something is not happening.
items: Events section: at the bottom, shows scheduler and kubelet messages such as FailedScheduling, FailedMount, BackOff or image pull errors.
Container state: shows Last State, exit code, reason (OOMKilled, Error) and restart count in one place.
Node view: describe node shows allocatable vs requested resources, taints and conditions, the quickest way to see why a pod will not fit.
Cross-check events: events are namespaced and short-lived (retained for about an hour by default), so capture them early.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl describe pod my-app-7d9c-xk2lp -n prod
# Look at: State/Last State, Conditions, Events (bottom)

# Same events, filtered and sorted (kubectl 1.26+)
kubectl events -n prod --for pod/my-app-7d9c-xk2lp

# Older equivalent
kubectl get events -n prod --field-selector involvedObject.name=my-app-7d9c-xk2lp --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
steps.highlight: If a pod is Pending, run describe first: the FailedScheduling event names the exact reason (insufficient CPU, untolerated taint, unbound PVC) that get never shows.

steps.title: Combining both in a real triage
steps.description: Use get to find the object and confirm facts, describe to explain them.
items: Step 1: get pods -A with a field selector isolates the unhealthy pods quickly.
Step 2: describe on one representative pod gives the reason from Events.
Step 3: get -o yaml confirms the effective spec (resources, probes, nodeSelector) the controller actually produced.
Step 4: logs --previous adds application-level evidence for crash loops.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector status.phase!=Running
kubectl describe pod my-app-7d9c-xk2lp -n prod | sed -n '/Events:/,$p'
kubectl get pod my-app-7d9c-xk2lp -n prod -o yaml | grep -A8 resources:
kubectl logs my-app-7d9c-xk2lp -n prod --previous

steps.title: Pitfalls and what to automate
steps.description: Know where each command misleads you.
items: Do not parse describe: use -o json with jq or jsonpath in CI and runbooks.
Events expire: ship them to your logging stack so evidence survives the retention window.
Secrets: describe secret hides values but get secret -o yaml shows base64 data, so restrict RBAC on get.
Stale view: a table from get can lag a fast-changing object, so add -w or re-run.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Use kubectl get -o yaml (or jsonpath) as the source of truth and for scripts, and kubectl describe only to read Events when asking why a resource is unhealthy.
elevatorPitch: kubectl get returns the stored API object as a table, YAML or JSON and is what you script against.
kubectl describe renders a human-readable summary and adds related Events, so I use it first when a pod is Pending or crash-looping.
I never parse describe output; automation uses -o json or jsonpath, and I export Events because they expire.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Parsing kubectl describe output with grep/awk in scripts
mistakesToAvoid.why: Its text layout is not part of the API and changes between kubectl versions, which silently breaks automation.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running only get when a pod is Pending
mistakesToAvoid.why: The table shows the phase but not the scheduler reason; that lives in Events visible through describe.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Waiting too long to read Events
mistakesToAvoid.why: Events are retained only briefly by default, so the failure message may be gone by the time you investigate.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming describe shows the full spec
mistakesToAvoid.why: It is a summary; fields like managedFields, full ownerReferences and some annotations only appear in get -o yaml.

title: Kubernetes Q89: You want to run a one-off debug pod on a specific node How [L2]
summary: kubectl debug node/<node-name> -it --image=ubuntu or use nodeName field in pod spec.
question: You want to run a one-off debug pod on a specific node. How?
