intro: To run a one-off debug pod on a specific node, use kubectl debug node/<node-name> -it --image=busybox, or pin an ordinary pod with nodeName or a kubernetes.io/hostname nodeSelector. The first form creates a pod already placed on that node with the host filesystem mounted at /host. Interviewers ask because debugging node-level problems (disk, DNS, CNI, kubelet) needs a shell next to the node, yet SSH is often unavailable on managed clusters. A good answer compares the options, explains how taints and the scheduler interact, and remembers cleanup and security.

steps.title: Mental model: three ways to land a pod on a node
steps.description: Each option makes a different trade-off between convenience, scheduler involvement and host access.
items: kubectl debug node: creates a pod in the current namespace, scheduled directly onto the node, using host namespaces and mounting the node root filesystem read-write at /host. Needs kubectl 1.20+ for the node form, and profiles on newer versions.

nodeName: setting spec.nodeName assigns the pod directly and bypasses the scheduler, so scheduler constraints, including NoSchedule taints, are not evaluated. A NoExecute taint is still enforced by the kubelet.
nodeSelector: kubernetes.io/hostname: <node> goes through the scheduler, so taints, resource requests and quotas still apply, and the pod stays Pending if they do not fit.
Managed clusters: on EKS, GKE and AKS you often have no SSH, which makes kubectl debug node the standard approach.
Typical use cases: checking disk pressure under /var/lib/kubelet, reading container runtime logs, testing DNS from the node's network, or inspecting mounted volumes that only exist on that host.

steps.title: Hands-on: run a one-off debug pod on a specific node with kubectl debug
steps.description: This is the fastest method and requires only API access plus permission to create pods.
items: Start a session: pick an image that has your tools. busybox is tiny, while nicolaka/netshoot adds network utilities.
Use the host filesystem: inside the container run chroot /host to work as if logged into the node, then read /var/log or inspect kubelet files.

Pick a profile: on kubectl 1.30 and later, --profile=sysadmin gives a privileged container and --profile=general a limited one. Profile availability depends on kubectl version, so check kubectl debug --help.
Cleanup: the debug pod is not removed automatically. Delete it when finished, since it is a normal pod named node-debugger-<node>-xxxxx.
Image choice: pin a version or digest of the debug image. A tool image that includes tcpdump, dig and curl saves time, but a smaller image pulls faster on a node with limited bandwidth.
steps.codeBlock:
# Interactive shell on node worker-1
kubectl debug node/worker-1 -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot

# Inside the container: the node filesystem is at /host
chroot /host /bin/sh
journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager | tail -n 50

# When done
exit
kubectl get pods | grep node-debugger
kubectl delete pod node-debugger-worker-1-abcde

steps.title: Pinning an ordinary pod with nodeName or nodeSelector
steps.description: Use a manifest when you need a specific image, resources, volumes or a service account that the debug command does not give you.
items: Short-lived: set restartPolicy: Never and use kubectl run --rm -it style behaviour so the pod disappears on exit.
Scheduler path: prefer nodeSelector with the hostname label. If the node is tainted, add a matching tolerations entry.
Bypass path: nodeName works on a cordoned node, which is handy while investigating, because cordon only adds the unschedulable taint that the scheduler honours.
Host access on demand: only add hostNetwork, hostPID or a hostPath volume when needed, because each widens what the pod can see.

Namespace matters: the debug pod is created in the namespace you specify, so ResourceQuota, LimitRange and Pod Security there still apply. Pick a namespace where that is acceptable, such as a dedicated debug namespace.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: debug-worker-1
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  nodeSelector:
    kubernetes.io/hostname: worker-1
  tolerations:
    - operator: Exists          # tolerate any taint for this debug pod
  containers:
    - name: debug
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sleep", "3600"]

# Run it, then exec in and clean up
# kubectl apply -f debug.yaml
# kubectl exec -it debug-worker-1 -- sh
# kubectl delete pod debug-worker-1 --now

steps.title: Verify placement and handle failures
steps.description: Always confirm the pod landed where you intended and that it really sees the node state you want to inspect.
items: Check placement: kubectl get pod debug-worker-1 -o wide shows the NODE column, and kubectl describe pod shows scheduling events.

Pending pod: usually a taint without a toleration, insufficient resources on a full node, or a typo in the hostname label. The node name and its hostname label can differ on some clouds, so verify with kubectl get node worker-1 --show-labels.
Permission denied: a restricted Pod Security Admission level blocks host namespaces and privileged containers. Use a namespace such as a dedicated debug namespace with relaxed policy.
NotReady node: API-created pods do not start on a node whose kubelet is dead, so fall back to cloud provider tools like SSM or serial console.
Verify host view: after chroot, hostname should print the node name and ps aux should show kubelet and containerd, confirming you are looking at the intended host and not just the container.

steps.title: Production practice: controlled, audited node access
steps.description: A node debug pod is root on the host, so govern it like SSH access.
items: RBAC: restrict who can create pods in the debug namespace and who can use pods/exec there.
Audit logging: API audit logs record pod creation and exec, which gives you a trail that SSH often lacks.
Time-box: use activeDeadlineSeconds on pinned manifests so forgotten debug pods terminate themselves.
Prefer less access: if only network checks are needed, avoid mounting the host filesystem and use a normal pod pinned to the node.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: kubectl debug node gives host-level access without SSH, but nodeName bypasses the scheduler; use a nodeSelector when you want taints and quotas respected, and always delete the debugger pod.
elevatorPitch: I use kubectl debug node/<name> with a tool-rich image, which creates a pod on that node with the host filesystem under /host.
For custom needs I pin a pod using a hostname nodeSelector or nodeName, add tolerations if tainted, and verify with get pod -o wide.
I treat it as root access: restrict RBAC, rely on audit logs, set deadlines and delete the pod afterward.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using nodeName and expecting scheduler checks
mistakesToAvoid.why: nodeName bypasses the scheduler, so resource fit and NoSchedule taints are not evaluated.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Leaving node-debugger pods running
mistakesToAvoid.why: They are privileged-capable pods with host filesystem access and are not cleaned up automatically.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Debugging a NotReady node with kubectl debug
mistakesToAvoid.why: The kubelet must be alive to start the pod, so use cloud console or SSM instead.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming hostname label equals node name
mistakesToAvoid.why: On some providers they differ, which leaves the pod Pending.

title: Kubernetes Q90: Explain how kube-proxy implements Services using iptables [L3]
summary: kube-proxy implements Services using iptables by watching Services and EndpointSlices and programming NAT rules that rewrite a Service's virtual ClusterIP to a randomly chosen pod IP (DNAT).
question: Explain how kube-proxy implements Services using iptables.
intro: kube-proxy implements Services using iptables by watching Services and EndpointSlices and programming NAT rules that rewrite a Service's virtual ClusterIP to a randomly chosen pod IP (DNAT). There is no listening process on the ClusterIP: packets are rewritten in the kernel by netfilter before they leave the client's node. Interviewers ask this to check you understand that a Service is a set of rules, not a proxy, and that you can debug it by reading chains. A strong answer covers the chain layout, probabilistic load balancing, conntrack behaviour, masquerading, and the limits that led to IPVS and nftables modes.

steps.title: Mental model: watch, translate, program
steps.description: kube-proxy runs on every node as a controller with no data path of its own in iptables mode.
items: Inputs: it watches Services and EndpointSlices through the API server, and only ready endpoints are included in rules.
Output: it writes the nat table rules, typically using iptables-restore to apply changes in batches, and re-syncs periodically and on changes.
Data path: traffic from pods or the host hits the PREROUTING or OUTPUT chain, jumps into KUBE-SERVICES, matches the ClusterIP and port, then DNATs to a pod IP.
Replacement: some CNIs such as Cilium can replace kube-proxy entirely with eBPF, so first check which implementation your cluster uses.

Why no listener: because rewriting happens in netfilter, ss -lntp will not show anything bound to the ClusterIP. That is why you cannot curl-debug the ClusterIP from a machine outside the cluster network.

steps.title: Hands-on: how kube-proxy implements Services using iptables, read the chains
steps.description: Dump the NAT table on a node and follow one Service through its chains.
items: KUBE-SERVICES: the entry chain with one rule per Service port, matching destination ClusterIP, protocol and port.
KUBE-SVC-<hash>: one chain per Service. It holds one rule per endpoint, using the statistic --mode random --probability match so each pod gets an approximately equal share.
KUBE-SEP-<hash>: one chain per endpoint, containing the DNAT rule to podIP:targetPort.
Other chains: KUBE-NODEPORTS handles NodePort traffic, and KUBE-MARK-MASQ marks packets that need source NAT.

Probability maths: with three endpoints the first rule matches one third, the second matches one half of the remainder, and the last matches everything left, which yields equal shares. Ready-state changes rewrite these probabilities.
steps.codeBlock:
# On a node (root). Find the Service's rules by ClusterIP
kubectl get svc my-app -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}'
sudo iptables -t nat -S KUBE-SERVICES | grep 10.96.12.34

# Follow the chain: service -> endpoints -> DNAT
sudo iptables -t nat -S KUBE-SVC-XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX
#  -A KUBE-SVC-X ... -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.33333 -j KUBE-SEP-AAA
#  -A KUBE-SVC-X ... -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.50000 -j KUBE-SEP-BBB
#  -A KUBE-SVC-X ... -j KUBE-SEP-CCC
sudo iptables -t nat -S KUBE-SEP-AAA
#  -A KUBE-SEP-AAA -p tcp -m tcp -j DNAT --to-destination 10.244.1.7:8080

steps.title: Return traffic, masquerading and conntrack
steps.description: The first packet of a connection selects the endpoint. Everything after that relies on connection tracking.
items: Conntrack: the kernel stores the DNAT mapping, so later packets and replies are translated back automatically and stick to the same pod for the life of the connection.
Load balancing granularity: balancing is per connection, not per request. Long-lived HTTP/2 or gRPC connections can therefore pin to one pod.
Masquerade: KUBE-MARK-MASQ and KUBE-POSTROUTING perform SNAT for traffic that leaves the node or for hairpin cases, so replies return through the same node.
externalTrafficPolicy: Local preserves the client source IP and only routes to local endpoints, while Cluster may SNAT and balance across nodes.
Session affinity: with sessionAffinity: ClientIP kube-proxy uses the recent iptables match to keep a client on the same endpoint for the configured timeout, overriding random selection.
steps.codeBlock:
# Inspect tracked connections to the Service (conntrack-tools)
sudo conntrack -L -d 10.96.12.34

# Which mode is kube-proxy in?
kubectl -n kube-system get cm kube-proxy -o yaml | grep -E 'mode:|syncPeriod'
kubectl -n kube-system logs ds/kube-proxy | head

steps.title: Debugging and failure modes
steps.description: Most Service problems are visible in endpoints and rules, not in kube-proxy itself.
items: No endpoints: kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=my-app. An empty list means a selector mismatch or failing readiness, so there are no DNAT rules and the connection is rejected.
Stale rules: if kube-proxy is crashing or lagging, rules can stay out of date. Check its logs and the rule sync metrics.
Scale cost: iptables rules are evaluated linearly and rebuilt as a whole, so very large numbers of Services increase update latency and CPU. That is the motivation for IPVS and nftables modes.
Conntrack exhaustion: a full table drops new connections, so monitor conntrack usage on busy nodes and tune limits accordingly.

Terminating endpoints: EndpointSlices mark endpoints ready, serving and terminating, which lets newer kube-proxy versions drain connections gracefully. Combine this with a preStop hook and readiness probes to avoid dropped requests during rollouts.

steps.title: Alternatives and production practice
steps.description: Know the other proxy modes and how to operate kube-proxy safely.
items: IPVS mode: uses kernel IPVS hash tables with multiple scheduling algorithms, scaling better for large clusters. Newer Kubernetes releases add an nftables mode, so check release notes for the status in your version.
Monitoring: scrape kube-proxy metrics such as sync duration and rule counts, and alert on sync errors.
Upgrades: keep kube-proxy version aligned with the control plane skew policy.
Troubleshooting order: Service, EndpointSlices, pod readiness, node rules, conntrack, NetworkPolicy, then CNI.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Remember that a ClusterIP is only rules in the kernel, so debug a broken Service by walking KUBE-SERVICES, KUBE-SVC and KUBE-SEP, and check EndpointSlices first.
elevatorPitch: kube-proxy watches Services and EndpointSlices and programs iptables NAT rules so the kernel rewrites a ClusterIP to a pod IP; no proxy process sits in the data path.
Chains go KUBE-SERVICES to KUBE-SVC to KUBE-SEP, with random probability rules for balancing and conntrack keeping each connection on one pod.
I verify with iptables -t nat -S and EndpointSlices, and know IPVS, nftables or eBPF replacements for large clusters.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Thinking kube-proxy forwards the traffic itself
mistakesToAvoid.why: In iptables mode packets are rewritten by netfilter in the kernel; kube-proxy only programs rules.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting per-request load balancing
mistakesToAvoid.why: Selection happens per connection, so long-lived gRPC or keep-alive connections stick to one pod.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Debugging rules before checking endpoints
mistakesToAvoid.why: A Service with no ready endpoints has no DNAT target, and the cause is selector or readiness.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring conntrack limits
mistakesToAvoid.why: A full conntrack table drops new connections even though iptables rules are correct.

title: Kubernetes Q91: What is topology spread constraints and when would you use it over pod anti-affinity [L2]
summary: Topology spread constraints tell the scheduler to distribute matching pods evenly across failure domains such as zones or nodes, within a tolerated difference called maxSkew.
question: What is topology spread constraints and when would you use it over pod anti-affinity?
intro: Topology spread constraints tell the scheduler to distribute matching pods evenly across failure domains such as zones or nodes, within a tolerated difference called maxSkew. Pod anti-affinity instead repels pods from each other, which is all-or-nothing when set as required. Interviewers ask this to test high availability design: how do you keep replicas alive through a zone outage without making the Deployment unschedulable when replicas exceed domains? The short answer is to prefer spread constraints for even distribution and keep anti-affinity for strict separation rules.

steps.title: How topology spread constraints work
steps.description: The scheduler counts matching pods per topology domain and keeps the gap within maxSkew.
items: topologyKey: the node label that defines a domain, commonly topology.kubernetes.io/zone or kubernetes.io/hostname.
maxSkew: the maximum allowed difference in matching pod count between the fullest and emptiest domain.
whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule keeps the pod Pending, ScheduleAnyway treats it as a soft preference.
labelSelector: selects which pods are counted; it must match the pods of the workload, otherwise the constraint counts nothing.

steps.title: Spreading across zones and nodes
steps.description: Combine a hard zone constraint with a soft node constraint for a typical web service.
items: Zone (hard): survive one zone loss with replicas balanced across zones.
Node (soft): avoid stacking on one node but never block scheduling.
minDomains: forces a minimum number of domains to be considered when used with DoNotSchedule (check availability on your version, beta since 1.25 and stable in 1.30).
Rolling updates: matchLabelKeys with pod-template-hash keeps old and new ReplicaSets from skewing each other (version dependent, enabled by default in recent releases).
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: prod
spec:
  replicas: 6
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: my-app}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: my-app}
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
      - maxSkew: 1
        topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels: {app: my-app}
      - maxSkew: 1
        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
        whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels: {app: my-app}
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: registry.example.com/my-app:1.0.0

steps.title: Choosing between spread and anti-affinity
steps.description: Both influence placement, but they express different intent.
items: Anti-affinity required: at most one matching pod per domain. With 6 replicas and 3 zones, 3 pods stay Pending.
Anti-affinity preferred: a weighted hint with no guaranteed balance, so skew can still grow.
Spread constraints: allow several pods per domain while keeping counts balanced, so scale-out always works.
Use anti-affinity when: you need strict exclusivity or separation between different workloads, for example never co-locating a noisy batch job with a latency-sensitive database.
Scale note: inter-pod anti-affinity is more expensive for the scheduler in large clusters than spread constraints.
steps.codeBlock:
# Anti-affinity: different workload separation
affinity:
  podAntiAffinity:
    requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
    - labelSelector:
        matchLabels: {app: batch-worker}
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
steps.highlight: Rule of thumb: spread constraints for balance across domains, anti-affinity for exclusion rules between specific workloads.

steps.title: Verifying the distribution
steps.description: Confirm real placement rather than trusting the manifest.
items: Node per pod: list pods with the node column and map nodes to zones.
Zone labels: confirm nodes actually carry the topology label, since a missing label makes that node ineligible for the constraint.
Pending reason: describe pod shows didn't match pod topology spread constraints when a hard rule blocks placement.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=my-app -o wide
kubectl get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone
kubectl describe pod <pending-pod> -n prod | grep -A3 FailedScheduling

steps.title: Limits and production practice
steps.description: Spread is applied at scheduling time only.
items: No rebalancing: pods are not moved after scale-down, node drain or failures, so skew can drift. The Descheduler (RemovePodsViolatingTopologySpreadConstraint) can evict violators.
Cluster defaults: the scheduler can apply defaultConstraints through KubeSchedulerConfiguration for pods that define none.
Autoscaling: combine with a PodDisruptionBudget, and remember Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter must be able to add nodes in the needed zone.
Stateful data: zonal PersistentVolumes can pin a pod to one zone and conflict with the constraint.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Use a hard zone constraint plus a soft hostname constraint with maxSkew: 1, and add the Descheduler because the scheduler never rebalances after the pods are placed.
elevatorPitch: Topology spread constraints keep matching pods evenly spread across zones or nodes within a maxSkew tolerance.
I verify with kubectl get pods -o wide and node zone labels, and check FailedScheduling events for blocked pods.
I pair them with a PodDisruptionBudget and the Descheduler, and keep anti-affinity only for strict separation between workloads.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using required pod anti-affinity per zone for a large Deployment
mistakesToAvoid.why: Replicas beyond the number of domains stay Pending, while a spread constraint with maxSkew would place them evenly.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: A labelSelector that does not match the pod labels
mistakesToAvoid.why: The scheduler counts zero pods per domain so the constraint never actually spreads anything.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming spread is maintained over time
mistakesToAvoid.why: It is evaluated only at scheduling, so drains and scale-downs can leave a skewed layout without a descheduler.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using DoNotSchedule on a key some nodes lack
mistakesToAvoid.why: Nodes without the topology label are ignored, which can concentrate pods or leave them Pending.

title: Kubernetes Q92: A pod needs GPU resources How do you configure it [L2]
summary: When a pod needs GPU resources, you configure it by running a device plugin on GPU nodes and requesting the extended resource, for example nvidia.com/gpu: 1, in the container's resources.limits.
question: A pod needs GPU resources. How do you configure it?
intro: When a pod needs GPU resources, you configure it by running a device plugin on GPU nodes and requesting the extended resource, for example nvidia.com/gpu: 1, in the container's resources.limits. The scheduler only places the pod on a node that advertises that capacity. Interviewers ask because GPUs are not a built-in resource like CPU: they depend on host drivers, a container runtime hook and a device plugin, and they are expensive, so sharing, taints and cost control matter. The answer should cover the node stack, the pod spec, verification, and the failure modes.

steps.title: Mental model: the node stack that exposes a GPU
steps.description: A GPU appears to Kubernetes only after several layers on the node are healthy.
items: Driver: the vendor driver must be installed on the host, since containers use the host kernel module.
Container runtime: NVIDIA Container Toolkit configures containerd or CRI-O so GPU devices and libraries are injected into containers.

Device plugin: a DaemonSet registers the extended resource with the kubelet, which then reports nvidia.com/gpu in node capacity and allocatable. AMD and Intel have their own plugins and resource names.
Easiest path: the NVIDIA GPU Operator automates driver, toolkit, device plugin and monitoring, while managed clouds often provide GPU node images.

Runtime class: some setups require runtimeClassName: nvidia in the pod spec, depending on how the toolkit and containerd were configured. The GPU Operator documents which approach it sets up by default.

steps.title: Hands-on: configure GPU resources in the pod spec
steps.description: Request GPUs as an extended resource under limits and keep other requests realistic.
items: Limits are the request: extended resources are specified in limits. If you also set a request, it must equal the limit.
Whole numbers only: you cannot request a fraction like 0.5, and GPUs are not overcommitted. Sharing uses time-slicing or MIG configured on the node.
Tolerations and selectors: GPU nodes are usually tainted so ordinary pods stay off them, so add a matching toleration and, if needed, a nodeSelector label.
Image: use a CUDA-compatible image whose CUDA version is supported by the host driver.
Scheduling hints: add node labels from GPU feature discovery, for example the GPU product, so a workload can select an A100 class instead of any GPU. Label names depend on the labeller you deploy.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: gpu-test
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  tolerations:
    - key: nvidia.com/gpu
      operator: Exists
      effect: NoSchedule
  containers:
    - name: cuda
      image: nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-base-ubuntu22.04
      command: ["nvidia-smi"]
      resources:
        limits:
          nvidia.com/gpu: 1     # extended resource, integers only

steps.title: Verify the GPU is advertised and usable
steps.description: Confirm at three levels: node capacity, scheduling and inside the container.
items: Node capacity: kubectl describe node should list nvidia.com/gpu under Capacity and Allocatable.
Scheduling: a Pending pod with Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu in its events means no node has free GPUs or the toleration is missing.
Container: run nvidia-smi in the pod and check that the expected device and driver version appear.
Plugin health: check the device plugin pods and their logs if capacity shows zero.
Check allocation: kubectl describe node lists allocated extended resources under Allocated resources, which shows how many GPUs are claimed and by which pods.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,GPU:.status.allocatable.nvidia\.com/gpu'
kubectl apply -f gpu-test.yaml
kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded pod/gpu-test --timeout=120s
kubectl logs gpu-test
# Expect the nvidia-smi table listing the GPU model and driver version

steps.title: Failure modes and sharing options
steps.description: Most GPU incidents are node-stack or scheduling problems rather than pod spec errors.
items: Capacity zero: driver not loaded, toolkit not configured for the runtime, or the plugin DaemonSet not scheduled on the node (taints, selectors).
Driver mismatch: CUDA image newer than the host driver supports yields runtime errors, so align versions.
Exclusive allocation: one pod per GPU by default, so idle GPUs held by finished or stuck pods waste money. Use Jobs with TTL for batch work.
Sharing: NVIDIA MIG partitions supported GPUs into isolated slices, while time-slicing shares a GPU with no memory isolation. Both are configured on the node, not in the pod.

Multi-GPU jobs: request several devices in one container, for example nvidia.com/gpu: 4, and remember the scheduler needs all four on one node. Topology and interconnect awareness depend on additional tooling.
steps.highlight: GPU limits must be integers and extended resources cannot be overcommitted, so two pods asking for one GPU each need two physical (or MIG/time-sliced) devices.

steps.title: Production practice: cost and isolation
steps.description: GPU nodes are the most expensive part of many clusters, so control who lands on them.
items: Taint GPU nodes: use a taint such as nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule and only tolerate it in GPU workloads, often enforced with a policy.
Quota: apply requests.nvidia.com/gpu ResourceQuota per namespace to cap consumption.
Autoscale: scale GPU node groups from zero with the cluster autoscaler or Karpenter, and use priority classes for important jobs.
Observe: export GPU metrics (for example NVIDIA DCGM exporter) and alert on utilisation, temperature and ECC errors.

Idle detection: compare allocated GPUs with real utilisation from DCGM metrics. Pods that hold a GPU while sitting idle are a common source of waste, so review them regularly and consider automatic cleanup of finished notebooks and jobs.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: A GPU request is only as good as the node stack under it; check node allocatable for nvidia.com/gpu before debugging the pod, and taint GPU nodes with quotas to control cost.
elevatorPitch: GPUs are extended resources: the host needs the driver and container toolkit, and a device plugin advertises nvidia.com/gpu to the kubelet.
In the pod I set nvidia.com/gpu in limits as an integer, add a toleration for the GPU taint, and verify with node allocatable and nvidia-smi.
I automate the stack with the GPU Operator, use quotas, taints and autoscaling for cost, and monitor with DCGM metrics.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Requesting a fractional GPU like 0.5
mistakesToAvoid.why: Extended resources must be integers; sharing needs MIG or time-slicing on the node.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Putting the GPU only under requests
mistakesToAvoid.why: Extended resources must be set in limits, and any request must equal the limit.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting tolerations on tainted GPU nodes
mistakesToAvoid.why: The pod stays Pending even though GPUs are free.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using a CUDA image newer than the host driver
mistakesToAvoid.why: The container starts but CUDA calls fail at runtime.

title: Kubernetes Q93: Describe leader election in Kubernetes control plane components [L3]
summary: Leader election in the Kubernetes control plane lets several replicas of kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler run for high availability while only one actively makes decisions.
question: Describe leader election in Kubernetes control plane components.
intro: Leader election in the Kubernetes control plane lets several replicas of kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler run for high availability while only one actively makes decisions. Replicas compete to hold a Lease object in kube-system, and the holder must renew it regularly or another replica takes over. Interviewers ask because it explains control plane failover, split-brain avoidance and why two controller-managers do not fight each other. A complete answer separates this from etcd's Raft consensus and from the API server, which runs active-active without a leader.

steps.title: Mental model: which components elect a leader
steps.description: Only components that make cluster-wide decisions need a single active instance.
items: kube-scheduler: one active scheduler assigns pods, so two active would double-bind pods.
kube-controller-manager: one active instance runs all built-in controllers. The cloud-controller-manager does the same.
kube-apiserver: not leader-elected. All API servers serve traffic simultaneously behind a load balancer, since they are stateless over etcd.
etcd: has its own leader through the Raft consensus protocol, unrelated to the Lease mechanism described here.
Standby behaviour: non-leader replicas keep running, hold caches and watch the Lease, but perform no scheduling or reconciliation. This is why failover is fast: informers are already warm.

steps.title: Hands-on: leader election in Kubernetes control plane components via Lease
steps.description: Election uses the coordination.k8s.io Lease API and optimistic concurrency from the API server, with etcd as the source of truth.
items: Acquire: each replica tries to create or update the Lease and write its identity into spec.holderIdentity. Optimistic concurrency through resourceVersion means only one write wins.
Renew: the leader updates renewTime periodically. Followers watch and retry on a fixed interval.
Expire: if the lease is not renewed within the lease duration, a follower acquires it and becomes leader. The old leader stops work if it cannot renew in time.
Where: Leases are named kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager in kube-system.
Optimistic locking: updating the Lease uses resourceVersion in the update request, so two replicas racing for an expired lease cannot both succeed. The loser receives a conflict and stays a follower.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl -n kube-system get lease
kubectl -n kube-system get lease kube-scheduler -o yaml
# spec:
#   holderIdentity: control-plane-1_8f1c...   <- current leader
#   leaseDurationSeconds: 15
#   renewTime: "2026-10-25T10:00:03.000000Z"
#   leaseTransitions: 4                       <- number of leader changes

# Quick view of both leaders
kubectl -n kube-system get lease kube-scheduler kube-controller-manager \
  -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,HOLDER:.spec.holderIdentity

steps.title: Timing parameters and failover behaviour
steps.description: Three flags control how fast failover happens, and the relationship between them matters.
items: --leader-elect: enables election and defaults to true for both components.
--leader-elect-lease-duration: how long non-leaders wait before taking over, default 15s.
--leader-elect-renew-deadline: how long the leader keeps retrying to renew before giving up, default 10s, and it must be shorter than the lease duration.
--leader-elect-retry-period: how often candidates attempt acquisition or renewal, default 2s. Verify defaults for your version with --help.

Failover estimate: a crashed leader is replaced after roughly the lease duration plus the retry period, because followers only notice expiry at their next retry. Lowering the values speeds failover but raises API traffic and risk of flapping.
steps.codeBlock:
# Static pod flags (kubeadm: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml)
- --leader-elect=true
- --leader-elect-lease-duration=15s
- --leader-elect-renew-deadline=10s
- --leader-elect-retry-period=2s

# Worst-case failover is roughly lease duration after the last renew

steps.title: Failure modes and troubleshooting
steps.description: Most issues show up as no leader, flapping leaders or a leader that is alive but unhealthy.
items: Frequent transitions: a rising leaseTransitions count points to slow API server or etcd, CPU starvation or network delays, which stop renewals.
Stale holder: a renewTime far in the past with no new holder suggests all replicas are down or cannot reach the API server.
Clock skew: timestamps come from the holder, but expiry is judged by observed local time, so election is relatively robust. Still, keep NTP healthy.
Safety limit: election does not guarantee a deposed leader stops instantly, so controllers must tolerate brief overlap, using resourceVersion conflicts on writes.

Check control plane health: compare the Lease holder with kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide to find which node runs the active scheduler, and read that pod's logs when scheduling decisions look wrong.
steps.highlight: If the scheduler or controller-manager seems idle, find the holder first. A healthy standby doing nothing is expected, but a missing or stale leader is an outage.

steps.title: Production practice and custom controllers
steps.description: The same mechanism is available to your own operators.
items: client-go: the leaderelection package with a Lease lock is what most operators use, and controller-runtime enables it with LeaderElection: true.
Run replicas: two or three control plane nodes spread across failure domains, with a standby for every elected component.
Monitor: alert on leader changes, stale leases and the leader_election_master_status metric where exposed.
RBAC: custom controllers need get, create and update on leases in their namespace.

Upgrades and maintenance: when draining or upgrading control plane nodes one at a time, check the Lease holder first. Restarting the current leader triggers a short failover, so schedule it outside peak scheduling activity and confirm a new holder appears.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Check kubectl get lease in kube-system to see who leads right now; a climbing leaseTransitions count is an early warning of API server or etcd slowness.
elevatorPitch: Scheduler and controller-manager run several replicas but only the holder of a Lease in kube-system is active; the API server is active-active and etcd uses Raft.
The leader renews the lease every few seconds and a follower takes over if it expires, with 15s, 10s and 2s as default timings.
I inspect holderIdentity and leaseTransitions, alert on flapping, and use the same Lease pattern in custom operators.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Saying the API server has a leader
mistakesToAvoid.why: API servers are stateless and serve simultaneously; only etcd has Raft and only two components use Leases.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Mixing up etcd Raft with Lease election
mistakesToAvoid.why: They are separate mechanisms with different failure semantics.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Setting renew deadline longer than lease duration
mistakesToAvoid.why: The leader could keep acting after others consider the lease expired.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring leaseTransitions
mistakesToAvoid.why: Repeated changes reveal control plane resource or latency problems before a full outage.

title: Kubernetes Q94: What is a finalizer and when would you use one [L2]
summary: A finalizer is a string in metadata.finalizers that tells Kubernetes to keep an object until a controller finishes cleanup and removes that string.
question: What is a finalizer and when would you use one?
intro: A finalizer is a string in metadata.finalizers that tells Kubernetes to keep an object until a controller finishes cleanup and removes that string. When you delete an object that has finalizers, the API server only sets deletionTimestamp; the object stays in a Terminating state until the list is empty. You use one when deleting an object requires external or ordered cleanup, such as releasing a cloud load balancer or disk. Interviewers ask because stuck Terminating namespaces and PVCs are common incidents, and the wrong fix, force-removing finalizers, can leak resources.

steps.title: Mental model: two-phase deletion
steps.description: Finalizers turn deletion into a request that controllers get to complete, rather than an instant removal.
items: Delete request: if finalizers exist, the API server sets metadata.deletionTimestamp and keeps the object. It becomes read-mostly: you can remove finalizers but cannot add new ones.
Controller work: the owning controller sees the timestamp, performs cleanup, then removes its own finalizer entry with a patch.
Final removal: when the finalizers list is empty and a deletionTimestamp is set, the API server deletes the object for real.
Built-in examples: kubernetes.io/pvc-protection keeps a PVC while a pod uses it, and foregroundDeletion makes owners wait for dependents to be removed.

Owner references vs finalizers: ownerReferences drive garbage collection of dependents when the owner is deleted, while finalizers let a controller block deletion of the object itself until its own cleanup finishes. They solve different problems.

steps.title: Hands-on: what is a finalizer, inspect one on a live object
steps.description: Look at the metadata and see which controller owns the pending cleanup.
items: Read: kubectl get <kind> <name> -o jsonpath shows finalizers and deletionTimestamp.
Identify the owner: the finalizer name usually encodes the controller domain, for example a storage, ingress or operator name.
Check the controller: events on the object and the controller's logs say why cleanup has not finished, so read them before touching the finalizer.
List stuck objects: filter by deletionTimestamp across a namespace to find everything waiting.
Deletion propagation: kubectl delete --cascade=foreground uses the foregroundDeletion finalizer so dependents are removed first, whereas --cascade=orphan leaves dependents behind.
steps.codeBlock:
# See finalizers and deletion state
kubectl -n prod get pvc data-0 -o jsonpath='{.metadata.finalizers}{"\n"}{.metadata.deletionTimestamp}{"\n"}'

# Everything in a namespace that is waiting to be deleted
kubectl -n prod get pods,pvc,svc -o json | \
  jq -r '.items[] | select(.metadata.deletionTimestamp) | .kind+"/"+.metadata.name'

kubectl -n prod describe pvc data-0 | sed -n '/Events/,$p'

steps.title: When you would use a finalizer
steps.description: Use one when deleting the Kubernetes object must trigger cleanup that cannot be done by garbage collection alone.
items: External resources: an operator that provisions a cloud database, DNS record or bucket adds a finalizer so the external resource is deleted before the custom resource disappears.
Ordered teardown: remove dependents or drain data first, then release the parent.
Protection: prevent accidental deletion of in-use objects, as PVC and PV protection do.
Not for everything: if ownerReferences and normal garbage collection suffice, a finalizer only adds a way for objects to get stuck.
PVC and PV protection: a PVC used by a running pod stays Terminating until the pod is gone, which is expected behaviour, not a bug, and the fix is to delete or stop the pod.
steps.codeBlock:
# Custom resource with a finalizer (the controller sets this when it creates the cloud resource)
apiVersion: example.com/v1
kind: Database
metadata:
  name: orders-db
  finalizers:
    - example.com/cleanup-cloud-db

# Controller logic (pseudocode)
# if obj.deletionTimestamp is set and finalizer present:
#     delete cloud database (idempotent)
#     remove finalizer via patch

steps.title: Failure modes: stuck in Terminating
steps.description: The usual cause is that the controller is gone, broken or unable to finish cleanup.
items: Controller uninstalled first: deleting an operator before its custom resources leaves objects with finalizers nobody removes.
Cleanup failing: external API errors, missing credentials or a blocked network keep the controller retrying forever.

Namespace stuck: a namespace waits for all contents to be gone. Find remaining resources, including custom resources, and fix the real blocker. Namespaces also have spec.finalizers handled through the /finalize subresource.
Last-resort removal: clearing finalizers deletes the Kubernetes object but skips the cleanup, so external resources may leak and must be checked manually.
Patch carefully: removing one entry from a finalizer list by merge patch replaces the whole list, so use a JSON patch or kubectl edit when other finalizers must stay in place.
steps.codeBlock:
# Preferred: fix the controller, or restore it, and let it finish

# Last resort: remove the finalizers (cleanup is SKIPPED)
kubectl -n prod patch pvc data-0 --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'

# Find what blocks a Terminating namespace
kubectl api-resources --verbs=list --namespaced -o name | \
  xargs -n1 kubectl -n stuck-ns get --ignore-not-found --show-kind
steps.highlight: Removing a finalizer by hand tells Kubernetes cleanup is done when it may not be. Verify external resources (volumes, load balancers, cloud records) afterward.

steps.title: Production practice for finalizer-based controllers
steps.description: Well-behaved finalizer code is idempotent and observable.
items: Add early, remove late: add the finalizer when you create the external resource, and remove it only after confirmed deletion.
Idempotent cleanup: cleanup may run many times, so treat a missing external resource as success.
Alerts: alert on objects whose deletionTimestamp is older than a threshold, for example with kube-state-metrics where available.
Runbook: document the owner and safe manual cleanup for each finalizer your platform uses, and uninstall operators only after deleting their resources.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: A stuck Terminating object is a controller problem first; fix or restore the owner, and only patch finalizers to null after confirming no external resource will leak.
elevatorPitch: A finalizer is a key in metadata.finalizers that blocks final deletion until a controller finishes cleanup and removes it; delete just sets deletionTimestamp.
I use it for external resources or ordered teardown, and I debug stuck objects by reading finalizers, events and the owning controller's logs.
Only as a last resort do I patch finalizers to null, then I check for leaked cloud resources.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Force-clearing finalizers as the first fix
mistakesToAvoid.why: It skips cleanup and can leak disks, load balancers or cloud records.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Uninstalling an operator before deleting its custom resources
mistakesToAvoid.why: Their finalizers have no controller to remove them, leaving objects stuck.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Adding a finalizer without idempotent cleanup
mistakesToAvoid.why: Retries or partial failures then block deletion forever.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using finalizers where ownerReferences suffice
mistakesToAvoid.why: It adds a failure mode with no benefit.

title: Kubernetes Q95: How does the Kubernetes garbage collector work [L3]
summary: The Kubernetes garbage collector is a controller in kube-controller-manager that deletes dependent objects once their owners are gone, using metadata.ownerReferences to build a dependency graph.
question: How does the Kubernetes garbage collector work?
intro: The Kubernetes garbage collector is a controller in kube-controller-manager that deletes dependent objects once their owners are gone, using metadata.ownerReferences to build a dependency graph. It is why deleting a Deployment also removes its ReplicaSets and pods. Interviewers ask it to check that you separate three things: owner-based cascading deletion, kubelet housekeeping of images and containers, and TTL cleanup of finished Jobs. Knowing the three deletion propagation modes and how finalizers interact is what marks a senior answer.

steps.title: The owner reference graph behind the garbage collector
steps.description: Every dependent records who owns it; the collector watches that graph.
items: ownerReferences: a list of apiVersion, kind, name and uid. Controllers set it automatically (Deployment to ReplicaSet to Pod).
Deletion trigger: when no owner with a matching UID exists any more, the dependent becomes garbage and is deleted.
Namespace rule: a namespaced owner cannot own objects in another namespace, and a namespaced dependent may have a cluster-scoped owner.
Not everything is owned: objects created by hand have no owner and are never collected automatically.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get rs -n prod -l app=my-app \
  -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,OWNER:.metadata.ownerReferences[0].name

kubectl get pod my-app-7d9c-xk2lp -n prod -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences}'

steps.title: Three cascading deletion modes
steps.description: The caller picks how dependents are removed.
items: Background (default): owner is deleted immediately, then the collector removes dependents asynchronously.
Foreground: the owner gets a foregroundDeletion finalizer and stays visible until dependents with blockOwnerDeletion=true are gone.
Orphan: the owner is deleted and the ownerReferences are removed from dependents, leaving them running.
kubectl flag: --cascade=background|foreground|orphan (older versions used --cascade=false for orphan).
steps.codeBlock:
# Default: background
kubectl delete deployment my-app -n prod

# Wait for pods to go first
kubectl delete deployment my-app -n prod --cascade=foreground

# Remove only the Deployment, keep ReplicaSet and pods running
kubectl delete deployment my-app -n prod --cascade=orphan
steps.highlight: Orphaning is a handy migration tool: a new controller with a matching selector can adopt the leftover pods or ReplicaSet without downtime.

steps.title: Finalizers and objects stuck in Terminating
steps.description: Finalizers delay actual removal until a controller finishes cleanup.
items: Mechanism: deletion sets deletionTimestamp; the object stays until every entry in metadata.finalizers is removed.
Foreground dependency: an owner waits on blocking dependents, so a stuck child keeps the parent in Terminating.
Diagnosis: check finalizers and dependents before touching anything.
Last resort: patching finalizers away skips cleanup and may leak cloud resources, so fix the responsible controller first.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get ns demo -o jsonpath='{.metadata.finalizers}{"\n"}'
kubectl get all -n demo
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.metadata.deletionTimestamp) | .metadata.name'

steps.title: Related cleanup that is not the same collector
steps.description: Clarify these separately in an interview.
items: Kubelet image GC: removes unused images when disk usage passes imageGCHighThresholdPercent (default 85) until it falls to the low threshold (80).
Kubelet container GC: cleans dead containers on the node.
PodGC controller: deletes terminated pods beyond --terminated-pod-gc-threshold and orphaned pods bound to missing nodes.
Job TTL: ttlSecondsAfterFinished in the Job spec removes finished Jobs and their pods through the TTL-after-finished controller.

steps.title: Production practice
steps.description: Design for predictable deletion.
items: Set ownerReferences in operators: custom controllers should use controllerutil.SetControllerReference so custom resources clean up their children.
Use foreground for ordered teardown: when dependents must finish before the owner disappears.
Guard Helm and GitOps: prune settings in Argo CD or Flux delete by ownership/labels, so review what a prune will remove.
Watch for leaks: alert on very old objects lacking owners, such as stray ConfigMaps or PVCs.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Before deleting a parent that is hard to recreate, use --cascade=orphan and verify ownerReferences on the survivors, then let a new controller adopt them.
elevatorPitch: The garbage collector is a kube-controller-manager controller that deletes dependents whose owner (by ownerReferences UID) no longer exists.
Deletion can cascade in background, foreground or orphan mode, and finalizers can hold objects in Terminating until cleanup completes.
I inspect ownerReferences and finalizers when deletes hang, and I keep kubelet image GC and Job TTL separate in my mental model.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Removing finalizers to unstick a delete without checking the controller
mistakesToAvoid.why: It skips external cleanup and can leak load balancers, disks or other cloud resources.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming deleting a Deployment always deletes its pods immediately
mistakesToAvoid.why: Background mode is asynchronous, and orphan mode keeps pods running.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Confusing kubelet image garbage collection with ownerReference collection
mistakesToAvoid.why: They run on different components with different triggers (disk thresholds vs object ownership).

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Setting cross-namespace owner references
mistakesToAvoid.why: They are invalid for namespaced owners, so the dependent may be treated as having a missing owner and be collected.

title: Kubernetes Q96: How do you run a privileged debug container on a running pod without modifying the pod spec [L2]
summary: kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=ubuntu --share-processes --copy-to=debug-pod — creates a copy of the pod with an extra debug container.
question: How do you run a privileged debug container on a running pod without modifying the pod spec?
intro: To run a privileged debug container on a running pod without modifying the pod spec, use kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=<tools-image> --target=<container> with a privileged profile. This adds an ephemeral container to the live pod through the ephemeralcontainers subresource, so your workload's containers are not restarted and the Deployment template is untouched. Interviewers ask because production images are often distroless with no shell, and you still need to inspect processes, network and files. A strong answer covers profiles, namespace sharing, the Pod Security and RBAC limits, and cleanup.

steps.title: Mental model: ephemeral containers
steps.description: Ephemeral containers are a special container type added to an existing pod for troubleshooting only.
items: What they are: containers added through a dedicated subresource to a running pod. They have no ports, probes or resource guarantees and are never restarted.

What is not changed: the pod's regular containers keep running, and the owning Deployment or StatefulSet template is not modified. The Pod object itself does record the ephemeral container in its status and spec.
Availability: generally available since Kubernetes 1.25, and requires kubectl with the debug command.
Permanent record: an ephemeral container cannot be removed or edited. It lives until the pod is deleted, so the pod stays 'dirty' afterwards.
Why not edit the Deployment: changing the template to add a debug sidecar triggers a rollout and replaces the very pod you want to investigate, destroying in-memory state and the symptom.

steps.title: Hands-on: run a privileged debug container on a running pod
steps.description: Attach a tools image, share the target container's process namespace, and choose a profile that grants the privileges you need.
items: --target: shares the process namespace with the named container, so ps and /proc/<pid>/root show the application's processes and files.
--profile: in kubectl 1.30 and later, sysadmin gives a privileged container, netadmin adds network capabilities, and general is the default for most uses. Check kubectl debug --help for your version.
Custom security context: on older versions or special needs, use --custom with a JSON file that sets the container securityContext.
Copy alternative: --copy-to makes a new pod, which leaves the original pod untouched but loses the original's runtime state.

Stateful investigation: because the app container keeps running, you can capture live behaviour such as open sockets, memory maps and DNS answers at the moment of the problem, which a restarted copy could not show.
steps.codeBlock:
# Privileged ephemeral container attached to the 'app' container
kubectl -n prod debug -it my-app-7d9c6b5f4-x2k8p \
  --image=nicolaka/netshoot \
  --target=app \
  --profile=sysadmin

# Inside the debug container
ps aux                      # sees the target's processes
ls /proc/1/root/etc         # target filesystem via /proc
ss -tnlp; tcpdump -i any -c 20 port 8080

# Older kubectl: custom security context
echo '{"securityContext":{"privileged":true}}' > custom.json
kubectl -n prod debug -it my-app-7d9c6b5f4-x2k8p --image=busybox --target=app --custom=custom.json

steps.title: Requirements: RBAC, Pod Security and runtime
steps.description: Several controls can stop a privileged debug container, which is intentional.
items: RBAC: you need patch or update on pods/ephemeralcontainers, plus pods/attach or pods/exec to attach.
Pod Security Admission: in a namespace enforcing baseline or restricted, privileged ephemeral containers are rejected. Use a controlled exception, not weaker namespace labels for everyone.
Runtime support: the container runtime must support ephemeral containers, which containerd and CRI-O do on supported versions.
Target limits: shared process namespace via --target needs runtime support. If unsupported, you will see only the debug container's processes.
Image tooling: choose an image with the tools you need, for example strace, tcpdump, dig and curl. Tracing another process may need extra capabilities such as SYS_PTRACE, which the profiles can add.
steps.codeBlock:
# Check your rights
kubectl auth can-i patch pods/ephemeralcontainers -n prod
kubectl auth can-i create pods/attach -n prod

# See the ephemeral container recorded on the pod
kubectl -n prod get pod my-app-7d9c6b5f4-x2k8p \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.ephemeralContainers[*].name}'

steps.title: Limits and alternatives
steps.description: Know when this technique does not fit.
items: Pod can't be cleaned: once added, the container remains in the pod spec until the pod is replaced. A rollout restart or deleting the pod removes it.
Node-level issues: if you need the host (kubelet, disk, CNI), use kubectl debug node/<name> instead.
Cannot reproduce state: for crash loops, --copy-to with a changed command (for example sleep) lets you debug a failing container.
Evidence handling: be careful with tools that dump memory or traffic, as they may expose secrets and customer data.
Resource impact: ephemeral containers have no resource guarantees, but they still consume node CPU and memory. A heavy capture on a busy pod can affect the application, so time-box it.
steps.highlight: Debugging with a privileged ephemeral container is effectively root on that pod. Treat access as break-glass, with approvals and audit logging.

steps.title: Production practice: break-glass debugging
steps.description: Make debugging possible without weakening everyday security.
items: Dedicated role: create a ClusterRole for ephemeral container access and bind it to an on-call group, ideally with time-limited access.
Audit: API audit logs record patches to pods/ephemeralcontainers, so alert on use in production namespaces.
Approved images: use a vetted internal debug image from your registry, scanned and pinned by digest, not an arbitrary public image.
Clean up: delete or restart the pod after investigations so an unusual privileged container does not remain.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: kubectl debug with --target and --profile=sysadmin gives root-level visibility into a live pod without touching its template, but it needs pods/ephemeralcontainers RBAC and a permissive Pod Security level.
elevatorPitch: I use kubectl debug to add an ephemeral container with a tools image, targeting the app container so it shares the process namespace.
For privileges I choose the sysadmin profile or a custom security context, subject to RBAC and Pod Security Admission, then verify with ps and /proc.
I treat it as audited break-glass access and restart the pod afterwards because ephemeral containers cannot be removed.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming the pod is not modified at all
mistakesToAvoid.why: The ephemeral container is recorded on the Pod and stays until the pod is deleted, though workload templates are unchanged.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting --target
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without it you do not share the app's process namespace and cannot see its processes.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Weakening namespace Pod Security labels permanently to allow debugging
mistakesToAvoid.why: It lowers the security of every workload there; grant narrow break-glass exceptions.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using an unvetted public image
mistakesToAvoid.why: A privileged container running unknown code is a serious supply chain risk.

title: Kubernetes Q97: What is the Kubernetes watch mechanism and how do informers use it [L3]
summary: The Kubernetes watch mechanism is a long-lived HTTP request that streams change events (ADDED, MODIFIED, DELETED) for resources starting from a given resourceVersion, and informers build a local cache and event handlers on top of.
question: What is the Kubernetes watch mechanism and how do informers use it?
intro: The Kubernetes watch mechanism is a long-lived HTTP request that streams change events (ADDED, MODIFIED, DELETED) for resources starting from a given resourceVersion, and informers build a local cache and event handlers on top of it. Controllers rely on this instead of polling, which keeps API server load low and reaction time fast. Interviewers ask because every controller, scheduler and operator is built on it, and failures (410 Gone, dropped watches, stale caches) explain odd cluster behaviour. A good answer walks through list-then-watch, the reflector, the store and work queue, and recovery behaviour.

steps.title: Mental model: the watch protocol
steps.description: A watch is a GET with watch=true that the server keeps open and answers with a stream of events.
items: Event stream: the response is a chunked stream of JSON objects with a type (ADDED, MODIFIED, DELETED, BOOKMARK, ERROR) and the object.
resourceVersion: an opaque version taken from etcd. Clients should treat it as opaque, pass it back to resume, and never compare numerically.
List then watch: a client lists to get state plus the list's resourceVersion, then watches from that version so no change is missed.
Server cache: the API server serves most watches from an in-memory watch cache, so many clients do not each hit etcd directly.
Efficiency: one watch replaces thousands of list calls. Each event contains the full changed object, so clients rarely need an extra GET to know the new state.

steps.title: Hands-on: the Kubernetes watch mechanism with kubectl and raw HTTP
steps.description: You can observe the same stream controllers receive.
items: kubectl: kubectl get pods -w is list followed by watch. Add --output-watch-events to show event types.
Raw API: use kubectl proxy and curl with ?watch=true to see JSON events.
Resume from a version: pass resourceVersion from a previous list so you get only newer events.
Bookmarks: allowWatchBookmarks=true asks the server to send periodic BOOKMARK events so clients can keep an up-to-date resourceVersion cheaply.

Selectors: add -l app=my-app or --field-selector to kubectl get -w to see how a scoped watch only delivers matching events, and note that a label change can appear as ADDED or DELETED for that selector.
steps.codeBlock:
# Human view with event types
kubectl get pods -n prod -w --output-watch-events

# Raw stream
kubectl proxy --port=8001 &
RV=$(curl -s localhost:8001/api/v1/namespaces/prod/pods | jq -r .metadata.resourceVersion)
curl -N "localhost:8001/api/v1/namespaces/prod/pods?watch=true&resourceVersion=$RV&allowWatchBookmarks=true"
# {"type":"MODIFIED","object":{"kind":"Pod", ...}}

steps.title: How informers use watch
steps.description: An informer, as in client-go, packages list-watch, caching and event dispatch so controllers do not reimplement it.
items: Reflector: performs the initial list and then the watch, pushing changes into a queue and re-listing when needed.
DeltaFIFO and indexer: deltas update a thread-safe local store with optional indexes, so controllers read from memory (listers) rather than the API server.
Event handlers: OnAdd, OnUpdate and OnDelete usually enqueue an object key to a rate-limited work queue, which deduplicates and retries.
Shared informers: one informer per resource type is shared by many controllers in a process, so there is a single watch connection per type.

Work queue semantics: the queue stores keys, not objects, so ten updates to one pod collapse into one reconcile that reads the latest cached state. This is what makes controllers level-triggered rather than edge-triggered.

steps.title: Failure modes and recovery
steps.description: Watches break. Informers are designed to heal, but you need to understand the symptoms.
items: 410 Gone: if the requested resourceVersion is too old (compacted from the watch history), the server returns 410 and the reflector must re-list, which costs a full list.
Dropped connections: timeouts, load balancer idle limits and API server restarts close watches. The reflector re-establishes from its last version.
Stale or slow consumers: a slow handler delays processing, so keep handlers fast and push heavy work to workers.
Resync: a periodic resync replays cached objects to handlers and does not contact the API server, it helps repair missed reconciliation, not cache staleness.

API server side: when many watchers exist, API Priority and Fairness and watch cache sizing decide who is slowed first, and very large clusters tune --watch-cache-sizes. Check the documentation for your version.
steps.highlight: Informer caches are eventually consistent. Read-after-write from a lister can return old data, so reconcile loops should tolerate stale reads and use resourceVersion conflicts on updates.

steps.title: Production practice for controller authors and operators
steps.description: Watching efficiently is what keeps large clusters healthy.
items: Scope the watch: use namespaces, label or field selectors so the controller caches only what it needs, reducing memory and API load.
Avoid polling: never loop on list calls from many clients, since it multiplies etcd and API server work.
Observe: monitor apiserver_registered_watchers, workqueue depth and retries, and relist counts for controllers.
Set sensible resync: a long or zero resync period is usually fine, and API Priority and Fairness protects the server from noisy clients.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Always list then watch from the returned resourceVersion, handle 410 Gone by re-listing, and scope informers with selectors to keep API server and memory cost low.
elevatorPitch: Watch is a long-lived HTTP stream of change events from a resourceVersion, served mostly from the API server's watch cache.
Informers wrap it: a reflector lists and watches, a DeltaFIFO updates a local indexed cache, and handlers enqueue keys to a work queue for reconciliation.
I handle 410 Gone with a re-list, scope watches with selectors, and monitor watchers and queue depth.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Polling the API with repeated list calls
mistakesToAvoid.why: It multiplies load on the API server and etcd, and is slower than a watch.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating resourceVersion as a number to compare
mistakesToAvoid.why: It is opaque, and ordering or arithmetic on it is unsupported.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Doing heavy work inside informer event handlers
mistakesToAvoid.why: It blocks event processing and makes the cache fall behind.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming lister reads are always current
mistakesToAvoid.why: Caches are eventually consistent, so logic must tolerate stale data.

title: Kubernetes Q98: Explain the difference between kubectl apply with a file vs kubectl apply -k (kustomize) [L2]
summary: kubectl apply -f vs apply -k: -f applies the manifest files exactly as written, while -k first builds a directory containing a kustomization.yaml (adding overlays, patches, name prefixes, image overrides and generated ConfigMaps).
question: Explain the difference between `kubectl apply` with a file vs `kubectl apply -k` (kustomize).
intro: kubectl apply -f vs apply -k: -f applies the manifest files exactly as written, while -k first builds a directory containing a kustomization.yaml (adding overlays, patches, name prefixes, image overrides and generated ConfigMaps) and then applies the rendered result. Both use the same declarative apply mechanism afterwards. Interviewers ask this to see whether you understand template-free configuration management and when plain files are enough. The right answer covers both sides: simple, single-environment manifests fit -f, multi-environment variation fits -k.

steps.title: What each flag does
steps.description: Same apply semantics, different input.
items: apply -f: reads a file, directory (non-recursive unless -R) or URL and sends each object as given.
apply -k: takes a directory with kustomization.yaml, renders it through the Kustomize library built into kubectl, then applies the output. Files not listed in the kustomization are ignored.
Exclusive: -f and -k cannot be combined in a single command.
No templating language: Kustomize patches and transforms valid YAML, unlike Helm which templates it.

steps.title: A base and overlay layout
steps.description: Keep shared manifests in a base and environment differences in overlays.
items: base: common Deployment and Service with no environment details.
overlay: sets namespace, replica count, image tag and patches per environment.
Image and name transforms: images, namePrefix and commonLabels edit every matching object without touching the base.
Generators: configMapGenerator appends a content hash to the name and rewrites references, so a config change triggers a rollout.
steps.codeBlock:
# overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: prod
resources:
  - ../../base
images:
  - name: registry.example.com/my-app
    newTag: 1.4.2
replicas:
  - name: my-app
    count: 6
configMapGenerator:
  - name: my-app-config
    literals:
      - LOG_LEVEL=info

steps.title: Commands: render, diff and kubectl apply
steps.description: Always preview what Kustomize produces before applying.
items: Render only: kubectl kustomize prints the final YAML without touching the cluster.
Diff: kubectl diff -k compares the rendered result to live state (exit code 1 means differences).
Apply: kubectl apply -k; add --server-side to use server-side apply and field ownership.
Plain files: apply -f with --dry-run=server validates against the API server without persisting.
steps.codeBlock:
# Plain manifests
kubectl apply -f deploy/ --dry-run=server

# Kustomize
kubectl kustomize overlays/prod | less
kubectl diff -k overlays/prod
kubectl apply -k overlays/prod
kubectl get deploy my-app -n prod
steps.highlight: The Kustomize bundled in kubectl lags the standalone kustomize binary; check kubectl version output for the embedded Kustomize version if a newer field is rejected.

steps.title: When to use which
steps.description: Match the tool to the amount of variation.
items: Choose -f when: one environment, a handful of static manifests, vendor YAML you do not want to modify, or quick experiments.
Choose -k when: the same app deploys to dev, staging and prod with different replicas, images, namespaces or config.
Beyond both: Helm suits packaged, parameterised distribution; Kustomize suits patching YAML you own or a rendered chart.
GitOps: Argo CD and Flux render Kustomize natively, so the same overlays work from the CLI and in-cluster.

steps.title: Pitfalls and CI practice
steps.description: Most surprises are about file selection and hidden transforms.
items: Forgotten resources: a new YAML file does nothing under -k until it is added to resources:.
Pruning: --prune needs a label selector (-l) or --all and can delete objects, so test with --dry-run first.
Hash suffixes: generated names change on content updates, so reference them through Kustomize, never hard-code them.
Pipeline gate: run kubectl kustomize piped to a validator such as kubeconform in CI before deploying.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Run kubectl diff -k overlays/<env> in CI before every apply -k, so you review the rendered result that actually reaches the cluster rather than the base files.
elevatorPitch: apply -f sends manifests as written, apply -k renders a kustomization with overlays, patches and generators first and then applies the output.
I verify with kubectl kustomize and kubectl diff -k, plus a server-side dry run.
I use -f for simple single-environment YAML and -k for multi-environment variation, and I automate the render and diff in CI or GitOps.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Adding a new file to an overlay directory without listing it in resources
mistakesToAvoid.why: Kustomize ignores unlisted files, so the object never reaches the cluster.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Trying to use -f and -k together
mistakesToAvoid.why: kubectl rejects the combination; put plain files under resources: in the kustomization instead.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Hard-coding generated ConfigMap names
mistakesToAvoid.why: The content hash suffix changes with the data; only Kustomize-managed references are rewritten.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Applying overlays without previewing
mistakesToAvoid.why: Patches and image transforms can change many objects silently; render or diff first.

title: Kubernetes Q101: How do you expose a gRPC service in Kubernetes [L2]
summary: To expose a gRPC service in Kubernetes, put it behind a Service for in-cluster traffic and an HTTP/2-aware entry point (an Ingress or Gateway API route with TLS, or a Layer 4 load balancer) for external traffic.
question: How do you expose a gRPC service in Kubernetes?
intro: To expose a gRPC service in Kubernetes, put it behind a Service for in-cluster traffic and an HTTP/2-aware entry point (an Ingress or Gateway API route with TLS, or a Layer 4 load balancer) for external traffic. The catch is that gRPC multiplexes many calls over one long-lived HTTP/2 connection, so a plain ClusterIP Service balances connections, not requests, and one pod can end up with all the load. Interviewers ask this to see whether you understand HTTP/2, connection-level versus request-level load balancing, and how ingress controllers treat backend protocols.

steps.title: Mental model: why gRPC breaks default Service load balancing
steps.description: kube-proxy balances at Layer 4, which is the wrong granularity for a protocol that reuses one TCP connection for thousands of calls.
items: Connection-level balancing: a ClusterIP Service picks a backend pod when a TCP connection is opened. A gRPC client that opens one channel and keeps it will stay pinned to that pod, even after you scale the Deployment out.

Request-level options: either use client-side load balancing against a headless Service (clusterIP: None, resolver dns:///, policy round_robin), or place an L7 proxy such as Envoy, NGINX, or a service mesh sidecar that understands HTTP/2 streams.
Protocol hint: set appProtocol on the Service port. kubernetes.io/h2c marks cleartext HTTP/2, and many controllers and meshes use it to pick the right behaviour.

External versus internal: east-west traffic is usually solved by headless Service plus client balancing or a mesh; north-south traffic needs an ingress, Gateway, or load balancer that speaks HTTP/2 end to end.
steps.highlight: If you scale a gRPC Deployment and one pod still shows all the CPU, you are looking at connection pinning, not a scheduler problem.

steps.title: Hands-on: expose a gRPC service in Kubernetes with a Service
steps.description: Declare the port as gRPC-capable and, for client-side balancing, add a headless twin of the Service.
items: Named port and appProtocol: expose the container port with a name and set appProtocol: kubernetes.io/h2c (or https when the pod terminates TLS itself).
Headless Service: clusterIP: None makes DNS return every ready pod IP, so the gRPC resolver can open one subchannel per pod.
Readiness matters: only Ready pods are published in the endpoints, so pair this with a proper gRPC readiness probe.

Client config: in grpc-go use a target like dns:///my-grpc-headless.prod.svc.cluster.local:50051 with the round_robin service config. Resolvers re-resolve on a timer, so new pods are picked up slowly; set a max connection age on the server to force reconnects.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-grpc
  namespace: prod
spec:
  selector:
    app: my-grpc
  ports:
    - name: grpc
      port: 50051
      targetPort: 50051
      appProtocol: kubernetes.io/h2c
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-grpc-headless
  namespace: prod
spec:
  clusterIP: None          # DNS returns all pod IPs
  selector:
    app: my-grpc
  ports:
    - name: grpc
      port: 50051

steps.title: Expose it externally: Ingress, Gateway API or a load balancer
steps.description: Pick the entry point based on whether you need L7 routing, TLS termination and host-based rules.
items: ingress-nginx: add nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol: "GRPC" (use GRPCS if the backend speaks TLS). gRPC over the controller requires HTTP/2, which in practice means the Ingress must have a tls section.
Gateway API: the GRPCRoute kind is part of the standard channel from Gateway API v1.1 onward and lets you match on service and method. Confirm your controller implements it before relying on it.
Layer 4 alternative: a type: LoadBalancer Service or NLB passes the TCP stream through. It is simple and fast but gives no per-request balancing and no path routing.
Timeouts: long-lived streaming RPCs need generous proxy read and send timeouts, otherwise the proxy resets streams that are merely idle.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: my-grpc
  namespace: prod
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/backend-protocol: "GRPC"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts: [grpc.example.com]
      secretName: grpc-example-tls
  rules:
    - host: grpc.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: my-grpc
                port:
                  number: 50051

steps.title: Verify with grpcurl and read the failure signals
steps.description: Test with a real gRPC client, because curl over HTTP/1.1 tells you nothing about the HTTP/2 path.
items: List services: grpcurl grpc.example.com:443 list works only if server reflection is enabled; otherwise pass -proto files.
Call a method: grpcurl -d '{"name":"test"}' grpc.example.com:443 my.pkg.Greeter/SayHello.
Check distribution: hit the endpoint in a loop and compare per-pod request counters or logs to confirm requests are spread, not pinned.

Typical errors: Unavailable with a 502 often means the ingress spoke HTTP/1.1 to the backend; Unimplemented means the path or service name is wrong; TLS handshake errors mean a hostname or certificate mismatch.
steps.codeBlock:
# in-cluster test without exposing anything
kubectl -n prod port-forward svc/my-grpc 50051:50051 &
grpcurl -plaintext localhost:50051 list
# external test
grpcurl grpc.example.com:443 grpc.health.v1.Health/Check

steps.title: Production practice: health, mesh and graceful shutdown
steps.description: Reliability for gRPC depends on connection lifecycle as much as on routing.
items: Health probes: use the native grpc probe or the health protocol so Ready means the gRPC server is actually serving.
Graceful shutdown: handle SIGTERM with GracefulStop() (or the equivalent) and set terminationGracePeriodSeconds long enough to drain streams.
Connection recycling: configure max connection age with a grace period on the server so clients rebalance after scale-out.
Mesh option: Istio and Linkerd balance gRPC per request out of the box, at the cost of sidecar or ambient-mode overhead.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: after scaling a gRPC Deployment, check per-pod request rates, not just pod count. Without client-side balancing, an L7 proxy, or a mesh, the new pods stay idle.
elevatorPitch: A gRPC service is HTTP/2 over long-lived connections, so I expose it through an HTTP/2-aware ingress, Gateway or L4 load balancer.
I avoid connection pinning with a headless Service and round_robin client balancing, or an L7 proxy or mesh, and verify with grpcurl and per-pod metrics.
I automate native gRPC probes, graceful shutdown and max connection age so rollouts and scale-outs do not drop streams.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on a ClusterIP Service to spread gRPC traffic
mistakesToAvoid.why: kube-proxy balances per connection, so a single long-lived channel keeps hitting one pod and new replicas stay idle.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Creating an NGINX Ingress for gRPC without TLS or the backend-protocol annotation
mistakesToAvoid.why: The controller then talks HTTP/1.1 or plaintext to the backend and clients see 502 or Unavailable errors.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Testing with curl instead of grpcurl
mistakesToAvoid.why: curl over HTTP/1.1 cannot prove the HTTP/2 path, trailers and framing that gRPC needs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Leaving default proxy timeouts on streaming RPCs
mistakesToAvoid.why: Idle bidirectional streams get reset mid-session when proxy read timeouts expire.
