title: Kubernetes Q107: What is a ServiceAccount token and when does it expire [L2]
summary: A ServiceAccount token is a signed JWT that proves a pod or client is a specific ServiceAccount to the API server.
question: What is a ServiceAccount token and when does it expire?
intro: A ServiceAccount token is a signed JWT that proves a pod or client is a specific ServiceAccount to the API server. Modern clusters issue bound, time-limited tokens through the TokenRequest API, projected into the pod and refreshed by the kubelet, instead of the old never-expiring Secret tokens. Interviewers ask about expiry to test whether you know the difference between legacy and bound tokens, the 1.22 and 1.24 changes, and the security impact of long-lived credentials.

steps.title: Mental model: legacy secret tokens versus bound tokens
steps.description: There are two generations of ServiceAccount tokens, and the expiry answer is different for each.
items: Legacy token: a Secret of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token holding a JWT with no expiry. It stays valid until the Secret or ServiceAccount is deleted. Kubernetes stopped auto-creating these in v1.24.
Bound token: issued by the TokenRequest API, with an exp claim, an audience, and a binding to a specific pod (and its Secret or Node where applicable). It becomes invalid when the pod is deleted.

Default pod behaviour: the kubelet mounts a projected serviceAccountToken volume at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount. The default requested lifetime is 3600 seconds, and the kubelet rotates the token before it lapses (it refreshes once the token passes roughly 80% of its TTL).

Short answer: projected tokens expire in about an hour but are renewed automatically; tokens from kubectl create token also default to a short lifetime; only manually created legacy Secrets never expire.
steps.highlight: Always check the exp claim rather than assuming. Cluster operators can adjust limits on the API server, and managed offerings may enforce their own values.

steps.title: Hands-on: ServiceAccount token expiry with kubectl create token
steps.description: Request a token, decode it, and compare the timestamps to see exactly when it expires.
items: Request a token: kubectl create token my-sa -n prod --duration 10m. The server may clamp or override the requested duration.
Decode the claims: a JWT has three base64url parts; the middle one holds exp, iat, aud and the kubernetes.io binding object.
Bind to an object: --bound-object-kind Pod --bound-object-name my-pod ties validity to that pod, so the token dies when the pod does.
Set audience: --audience https://vault.example.com produces a token that only the intended relying party should accept.

Why it matters in practice: tokens from kubectl create token are not stored anywhere in the cluster, so there is nothing to clean up, and you can mint one per CI job with a short duration instead of sharing a long-lived credential.
steps.codeBlock:
TOKEN=$(kubectl create token my-sa -n prod --duration 10m)
# decode the payload (second segment)
echo "$TOKEN" | cut -d. -f2 | tr '_-' '/+' | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | jq '{iss,aud,exp,iat,sub}'
# convert exp to a date (GNU date; use date -r on macOS)
date -d @$(echo "$TOKEN" | cut -d. -f2 | tr '_-' '/+' | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | jq .exp)

steps.title: Projected token in a pod: audience, expirationSeconds and rotation
steps.description: For workloads that call external systems, request a dedicated audience-scoped token through a projected volume.
items: expirationSeconds: the minimum is 600 seconds (10 minutes); choose the shortest lifetime your application can renew.
Rotation is the app's job: the kubelet rewrites the file, but your process must re-read it. Old client libraries that read the token once at start-up will eventually fail with 401.
Audience: a token for Vault, a cloud IAM federation endpoint, or another cluster should carry that audience, never the API server's.
Opt out: set automountServiceAccountToken: false on the ServiceAccount or pod when the workload does not call the API.

Where the file lives by default: if you do nothing, the default token is mounted under /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token with the audience of the API server, so any in-cluster client library finds it automatically.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: prod
spec:
  serviceAccountName: my-sa
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: registry.example.com/my-app:1.0.0
      volumeMounts:
        - name: vault-token
          mountPath: /var/run/secrets/tokens
          readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: vault-token
      projected:
        sources:
          - serviceAccountToken:
              path: vault-token
              audience: https://vault.example.com
              expirationSeconds: 3600

steps.title: Failure modes: legacy secrets, extended lifetime and 401s
steps.description: Most real incidents come from tokens that either live too long or are cached too long.
items: Legacy Secrets: list them with kubectl get secrets -A --field-selector type=kubernetes.io/service-account-token. Each one is a non-expiring credential that grants the ServiceAccount's RBAC to anyone who reads it.

Extended lifetime: to ease the migration to bound tokens, the API server can accept tokens past exp for a longer window and annotates such use in audit logs. Treat audit entries about stale tokens as a to-do list of clients to fix.
Token cached in code: an app returns 401 roughly an hour after start. Fix the client to reload the file, or use an up-to-date client library that does.
Verification path: a TokenReview request lets an external service ask the API server whether a token is valid for a given audience.
Pod deletion: a bound token stops validating once its pod is gone, so a token exfiltrated from a short-lived pod is far less useful than a legacy Secret token.

steps.title: Production practice: least privilege and auditing
steps.description: Short-lived tokens only help if the permissions behind them are small.
items: Dedicated ServiceAccounts: one per workload, never the default account, with minimal Role bindings.
Check permissions: kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:my-sa -n prod.
Prefer workload identity: for cloud APIs, federate the projected token (for example IRSA on EKS or Workload Identity on GKE) rather than storing static keys.
Audit: alert on creation of kubernetes.io/service-account-token Secrets.
Rotation policy: shorter lifetimes reduce exposure but raise renewal traffic, so pick a duration your clients can refresh reliably, and test the refresh path in staging before tightening it.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: decode the token's exp claim during an incident instead of guessing. If it has no exp, you are holding a legacy Secret token and should migrate it to a projected or TokenRequest token.
elevatorPitch: A ServiceAccount token is a signed JWT identifying a pod to the API server; modern ones are bound, audience-scoped and short-lived.
Projected tokens default to about an hour and are rotated by the kubelet, while legacy Secret tokens never expire; I verify by decoding the exp claim.
I automate audits for legacy token Secrets, disable automount where unused, and federate to cloud IAM instead of static keys.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Creating a kubernetes.io/service-account-token Secret for convenience
mistakesToAvoid.why: It yields a credential that never expires and is valid until someone deletes it.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Reading the projected token once at start-up
mistakesToAvoid.why: The kubelet rotates the file, so a cached token starts producing 401 errors after it expires.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Sharing the default ServiceAccount across workloads
mistakesToAvoid.why: Any RBAC grant to it applies to every pod that uses it, and token compromise has a bigger blast radius.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using the API server audience for third-party systems
mistakesToAvoid.why: A token meant for the API server can be replayed against it if the third party leaks it.

steps.description: Both spread pods across topology domains (nodes, zones). podAntiAffinity: binary — either pods can or can't be on the same node. Doesn't control HOW spread out they are. title: Kubernetes Q113: How do you implement health checks for a gRPC service in Kubernetes [L2]
summary: Use the gRPC Health Checking Protocol. Your service implements grpc.health.v1.Health/Check. In the probe:
question: How do you implement health checks for a gRPC service in Kubernetes?
intro: To implement health checks for a gRPC service in Kubernetes, make the server implement the standard grpc.health.v1.Health service and point a native grpc probe at it. The native probe is beta since 1.24 and GA since 1.27, so on current clusters you no longer need an exec probe with a helper binary. Interviewers use this question to check that you can separate liveness, readiness and startup semantics and avoid probes that cause restart storms.

steps.title: Mental model: the gRPC health protocol and three probe types
steps.description: Kubernetes asks one question per probe; your server needs to answer each honestly.
items: Protocol: the health service exposes Check(service) returning SERVING or NOT_SERVING. An empty service name means overall server health; named services let you report per-component status.
Readiness: should this pod receive traffic now? It can go NOT_SERVING during warm-up, dependency loss, or shutdown draining.
Liveness: is the process wedged beyond recovery? Keep it cheap and independent of downstream dependencies, or a database blip will restart every replica.
Startup: protects slow-starting servers by disabling liveness and readiness until it first succeeds.

Why not a plain TCP probe: a TCP check only proves the port accepts connections; it cannot tell that the gRPC handlers are blocked, that the server is draining, or that a dependency needed for readiness is down.
steps.highlight: A restart cannot fix a broken dependency. Keep dependency checks in readiness, not liveness.

steps.title: Hands-on: gRPC health check in Kubernetes with a native probe
steps.description: Declare the grpc handler on each probe; the kubelet speaks the health protocol directly.
items: Fields: grpc.port is required and must be a number (named ports are not supported); grpc.service is optional and defaults to the empty string.
Plaintext only: the built-in probe does not support TLS or authentication. If the health port requires mTLS, expose a separate plaintext health port or use an exec fallback.
Timing: the probe fails on the first non-SERVING response or timeout; tune timeoutSeconds (default 1) and failureThreshold for realistic latency.
Different services: use a distinct service value for readiness than liveness if you register more than one health name.
Probe type per goal: use startup to absorb slow warm-up, readiness for traffic gating, and liveness only for deadlock detection, each with its own thresholds.
steps.codeBlock:
containers:
  - name: app
    image: registry.example.com/my-grpc:1.0.0
    ports:
      - containerPort: 50051
    startupProbe:
      grpc:
        port: 50051
      failureThreshold: 30
      periodSeconds: 2
    readinessProbe:
      grpc:
        port: 50051
        service: my.pkg.Greeter
      periodSeconds: 5
      timeoutSeconds: 2
    livenessProbe:
      grpc:
        port: 50051
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3

steps.title: Server side: register the health service and flip status
steps.description: The probe is only as good as the status your code reports.
items: Register it: in Go, google.golang.org/grpc/health provides a ready-made server; call SetServingStatus for each service name.
Drain on shutdown: on SIGTERM, set status to NOT_SERVING first so readiness fails and endpoints are removed, then wait briefly and call graceful stop.
Reflection: optional, but helpful because grpcurl can then discover services without proto files.
Other languages: Java, Python, C++ and others ship equivalent health service implementations; use the official one rather than a custom RPC.
Per-service status: report NOT_SERVING for a named service while its dependency is unavailable, so only the pods that truly cannot serve are removed from rotation.

steps.title: Verify and troubleshoot failing gRPC probes
steps.description: Reproduce the probe yourself before changing thresholds.
items: Call it manually: grpcurl -plaintext localhost:50051 grpc.health.v1.Health/Check through a port-forward. Expect {"status": "SERVING"}.
Read the events: kubectl describe pod <pod> shows messages such as Liveness probe failed with the gRPC status.
Unimplemented error: the server never registered the health service, or the service name in the probe is unknown.
Old clusters: before 1.24 (or if the feature is not available) use the grpc_health_probe binary in an exec probe, shipped in the image.
Reading the failure message: events show rpc error: code = Unimplemented or DeadlineExceeded; the first points to missing registration, the second to a slow handler or a too-small timeout.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl -n prod port-forward pod/my-grpc-abc 50051:50051 &
grpcurl -plaintext -d '{"service":"my.pkg.Greeter"}' localhost:50051 grpc.health.v1.Health/Check
kubectl -n prod describe pod my-grpc-abc | grep -iE 'probe|unhealthy'

steps.title: Production practice: tuning and rollout safety
steps.description: Probes shape rollouts, so tune them as part of release engineering.
items: Startup probe first: allow a generous failureThreshold times periodSeconds budget instead of a large initialDelaySeconds.
Rollouts: readiness gates the rolling update; a wrong probe stalls or silently blocks the deployment.
Load balancer probes: cloud load balancers have their own health checks and may need HTTP/2 or TCP checks rather than your Kubernetes probe.
Alert on probe failures: watch the restart counter and the not-ready pod count.
Mesh and proxy checks: if a sidecar intercepts traffic, confirm the probe path still reaches the app container, since some meshes rewrite probes.
Capacity during rollouts: set maxUnavailable and minReadySeconds so new pods prove they stay healthy before old ones are removed.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: use the native grpc probe on Kubernetes 1.27 or newer, keep liveness independent of dependencies, and flip the health status to NOT_SERVING on SIGTERM to drain traffic cleanly.
elevatorPitch: I implement grpc.health.v1 in the server and use native grpc startup, readiness and liveness probes.
I verify with grpcurl through port-forward and kubectl describe, checking the service name and port.
I automate probe tuning in manifests, keep dependencies out of liveness, and drain via NOT_SERVING on shutdown.

mistakesToAvoid.why: A shared dependency outage then restarts every healthy pod and turns a partial failure into a full outage.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Pointing the grpc probe at a named port or a TLS-only port
mistakesToAvoid.why: The native probe needs a numeric port and does not support TLS or auth, so it fails permanently.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Skipping the startup probe and using a huge initialDelaySeconds
mistakesToAvoid.why: It delays readiness for every restart; a startup probe adapts to the real start time.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting to register the health service in the server
mistakesToAvoid.why: Probes return Unimplemented and the pod is killed or never becomes Ready.

title: Kubernetes Multi-Cluster Service Discovery: MCS API, Cilium ClusterMesh, Submariner & Istio East-West Gateways

steps.title: Kubernetes SIG Multi-Cluster Services API (MCS API - KEP-1645)
steps.description: The standardized Kubernetes cloud-native approach introduces two core Custom Resource Definitions:
items: ServiceExport: Created in Cluster 2 on Service B (apiVersion: multicluster.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1) to declare that the service should be visible to other clusters in the cluster set.
ServiceImport: Automatically synchronized into Cluster 1 by the multi-cluster controller. It assigns a ClusterSetIP.
DNS Resolution: Pods in Cluster 1 discover Service B using the domain service-b.namespace.svc.clusterset.local, resolved automatically by CoreDNS.

steps.title: Cilium ClusterMesh (High-Performance eBPF Routing)
steps.description: If clusters share routable VPC subnets with non-overlapping pod CIDRs, Cilium ClusterMesh provides the highest throughput:
items: Direct Pod-to-Pod Routing: ClusterMesh synchronizes etcd/kvstore state between clusters, allowing eBPF datapath programs to route packets directly across VPC peering or AWS Transit Gateway.

Global Services: Simply annotate Service B with io.cilium/global-service: 'true'. Any client in either cluster querying service-b.default.svc.cluster.local automatically load balances traffic across healthy endpoints in both clusters.

steps.title: Submariner for Encrypted Hybrid/Multi-Cloud Networks
steps.description: When clusters are hosted across different cloud providers or on-premises networks with non-routable private IPs:
items: WireGuard / IPSec Gateways: Submariner deploys gateway nodes that automatically negotiate encrypted tunnels between disparate VPCs.
Lighthouse CoreDNS Plugin: Provides MCS-compliant DNS resolution under clusterset.local, forwarding requests through the gateway tunnels seamlessly.

steps.title: Istio Multi-Primary Mesh with East-West Gateways
steps.description: For zero-trust mTLS encryption, fine-grained traffic shifting, and canary cutovers across clusters:
items: Each cluster runs its own Istio control plane, sharing a common root CA.
Cross-cluster traffic passes through dedicated East-West Ingress Gateways using Envoy Server Name Indication (SNI) proxying without exposing pods directly to external networks.

keyTakeaway: For same-cloud or VPC-peered clusters, Cilium ClusterMesh delivers unbeatable zero-overhead eBPF routing. For heterogeneous multi-cloud environments, Kubernetes MCS API combined with Submariner or Istio East-West gateways provides standardized clusterset.local discovery.

title: Kubernetes imagePullPolicy: Always vs IfNotPresent vs Never — Caching, Security & Production Best Practices
summary: Detailed comparison of Kubernetes imagePullPolicy options (Always, IfNotPresent, Never), default evaluation rules, container image caching, network egress optimization, and security risks with mutable tags.
question: What is the difference between imagePullPolicy Always, IfNotPresent, and Never in Kubernetes? How does Kubernetes decide the default policy, and what are the performance and security implications in production?
intro: "In our production Kubernetes clusters running microservices on EKS/AKS, this was a classic operational challenge. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

steps.title: Core Behavior of Each Policy
steps.description: How kubelet handles image pulls when starting a container:
items: Always: Every time the kubelet starts a container, it contacts the remote image registry to resolve the digest. If the remote image has changed, it downloads the new layers. If unchanged, it uses the cached layers. If registry auth fails or registry is down, pod startup fails immediately.

IfNotPresent: Kubelet checks if the image exists in the local node cache. If present, it starts the container immediately without contacting the remote registry. Only downloads if the image is missing from the node.
Never: Kubelet never attempts to contact the registry. Assumes the image was pre-loaded onto the node host; fails with ErrImageNeverPull if missing.

steps.title: How Kubernetes Chooses the Default When Omitted
steps.description: Kubernetes automatically assigns imagePullPolicy based on the image tag format:
items: If the image tag is :latest (or if no tag is specified), Kubernetes automatically defaults to Always.
If the image tag is a specific version tag (e.g. :v1.2.3 or SHA256 digest), Kubernetes defaults to IfNotPresent.

steps.title: Performance vs Security Best Practices
steps.description: Key considerations in enterprise clusters:
items: Cold Start Latency: IfNotPresent provides 10x faster pod autoscaling (HPA) during traffic surges because nodes reuse cached layers without network roundtrips.
Registry Rate Limits & Outages: Always subjects every pod restart to external registry availability and rate limits (e.g. Docker Hub 429).

Security Best Practice: Never use :latest with IfNotPresent. Always deploy immutable semantic tags or SHA256 digests (app@sha256:...) combined with IfNotPresent to guarantee reproducible, fast, and tamper-proof deployments.

keyTakeaway: In production, use immutable semantic version tags or sha256 digests with imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent to achieve lightning-fast node autoscaling while preventing unpredictable tag mutation drift.
elevatorPitch: Configured immutable image tags with imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent across all production Helm charts.
Eliminated registry rate limit failures and slashed pod scheduling startup latency during HPA scale-out events.
Enforced Kyverno admission policies forbidding mutable :latest tags and imagePullPolicy: Never.
Guaranteed reproducible zero-drift container execution across multi-node Kubernetes clusters.

title: Kubernetes Q122: How do you configure resource requests and limits for init containers [L2]
summary: To configure resource requests and limits for init containers, set resources on each init container just like an app container, but remember the scheduler computes the pod's effective request as the larger of the biggest single.
question: How do you configure resource requests and limits for init containers?
intro: To configure resource requests and limits for init containers, set resources on each init container just like an app container, but remember the scheduler computes the pod's effective request as the larger of the biggest single init container and the sum of all app containers. Init containers run one at a time, so their needs do not add up. Interviewers ask this because a heavy migration init container can quietly inflate a pod's footprint and block scheduling.

steps.title: Mental model: effective request is a max, not a sum
steps.description: Init containers run sequentially to completion before app containers start, which changes how Kubernetes sums resources.
items: Init side: the effective init request for a resource is the highest request among all init containers, since only one runs at a time.
App side: app containers run together, so their requests are added.
Pod effective request: the larger of the two values, per resource, plus any configured Pod Overhead. That value is what the scheduler reserves on the node.
Limits: the same logic applies to the effective limit. Each container is still throttled or OOM-killed against its own limit while it runs.
Sidecars: init containers with restartPolicy: Always (native sidecars, beta and on by default from 1.29) keep running, so their requests are added to the app total instead of being compared as a max.

Why this surprises people: the sum-of-containers rule from app containers is widely known, so many teams forget init containers also reserve capacity at scheduling time, even though they exit before the app starts.
steps.highlight: A 2 GiB memory request on a one-off migration init container makes the whole pod need 2 GiB of schedulable memory, even if the app needs 256 MiB.

steps.title: Hands-on: configure resource requests and limits for init containers
steps.description: Give every init container explicit values; unset values default to nothing unless a LimitRange injects them.
items: Set both: requests for scheduling, limits for runtime enforcement. A migration tool that spikes memory should have a limit so it cannot starve neighbours.

Worked example: init request 500m CPU and 128Mi memory; app containers requesting 200m plus 100m CPU and 256Mi plus 64Mi memory. Effective CPU is max(500m, 300m) = 500m, effective memory is max(128Mi, 320Mi) = 320Mi.
QoS class: init containers participate; for Guaranteed QoS every container, including init, needs requests equal to limits for CPU and memory.
Ephemeral storage: init containers that download large artifacts should also set ephemeral-storage requests and limits.
Do the arithmetic per resource: CPU, memory and ephemeral storage are each compared separately, so the winning container for CPU can differ from the winner for memory.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: prod
spec:
  initContainers:
    - name: db-migrate
      image: registry.example.com/migrate:1.4.0
      resources:
        requests: {cpu: 500m, memory: 128Mi}
        limits:   {cpu: "1",  memory: 256Mi}
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: registry.example.com/my-app:1.0.0
      resources:
        requests: {cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi}
        limits:   {cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi}
    - name: proxy
      image: registry.example.com/proxy:2.0.0
      resources:
        requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 64Mi}
        limits:   {cpu: 200m, memory: 128Mi}

steps.title: Verify what the scheduler actually reserved
steps.description: Do not compute by hand in production; read it from the cluster.
items: Pod view: kubectl describe pod my-app -n prod lists init and app container resources and the QoS class.
Node view: kubectl describe node <node> under Allocated resources and the per-pod table shows the effective request counted against the node.
Scheduling failures: a Pending pod with Insufficient cpu or Insufficient memory in events may be caused purely by the init container request.
OOM during init: kubectl get pod showing Init:OOMKilled or Init:CrashLoopBackOff means the init limit is too low.
Spot-check with a script: list each pod's init and app requests with jsonpath or jq to find pods whose init requests dominate, then right-size them.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl -n prod get pod my-app -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n prod describe pod my-app | sed -n '/Init Containers/,/Conditions/p'
kubectl describe node worker-1 | sed -n '/Allocated resources/,/Events/p'

steps.title: Edge cases: LimitRange, quotas and in-place changes
steps.description: Namespace policy applies to init containers too.
items: LimitRange: type Container defaults, minimums and maximums are applied to init containers, so a default of 1Gi memory can silently raise your effective request.
ResourceQuota: the quota counts the pod's effective request, so oversized init containers consume quota too.

Immutability: container resources are immutable on a running pod in most versions; in-place pod resize is a newer alpha/beta feature and is version dependent, so check your cluster before relying on it.
Native sidecars: if an init container needs to keep running, mark it as a sidecar and size it as a long-running container.
Limits versus requests: an init limit higher than the namespace LimitRange max is rejected, and a limit lower than the request is invalid; both errors appear at pod creation.

steps.title: Production practice: keep init containers lean
steps.description: Treat init containers as a cost on every pod start.
items: Right-size from data: measure peak usage of migration or download jobs and set limits slightly above it.
Move heavy work out: run database migrations as a separate Job rather than in every replica's init container.
Policy: enforce that init containers declare resources using the same admission policy as app containers.
Observability: watch init container duration and restarts, since slow init delays rollouts.
Reuse the same image where possible: smaller, purpose-built init images pull faster and need less ephemeral storage, which shortens pod start-up.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: remember effective request = max(largest init container, sum of app containers). Trim heavy init containers or move migrations to a Job before you add nodes.
elevatorPitch: Init containers declare resources like any container, but the pod's effective request is the max of the largest init container and the sum of app containers.
I verify with kubectl describe pod and the node's allocated resources, and read Pending events for Insufficient cpu or memory.
I enforce resources on init containers through LimitRange and admission policy and move heavy migrations into Jobs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Adding init container requests to the app total
mistakesToAvoid.why: They run sequentially, so the scheduler uses the max, and over-adding leads to wrong capacity planning.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Leaving init containers without limits
mistakesToAvoid.why: A runaway download or migration can exhaust node memory and trigger evictions of neighbours.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring LimitRange defaults
mistakesToAvoid.why: The namespace default can inflate the init request without any change to the manifest.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Putting long-running helpers in a normal init container
mistakesToAvoid.why: They would block the app forever; use a native sidecar (restartPolicy: Always) or a regular container.

title: Kubernetes Q123: What is a projected volume in Kubernetes [L3]
summary: A projected volume in Kubernetes maps several existing volume sources into one directory, so a container sees a ConfigMap, a Secret, downward API fields and a ServiceAccount token under a single mount path.
question: What is a projected volume in Kubernetes?
intro: A projected volume in Kubernetes maps several existing volume sources into one directory, so a container sees a ConfigMap, a Secret, downward API fields and a ServiceAccount token under a single mount path. It is the mechanism behind the default ServiceAccount token volume. Interviewers ask about it to check that you know the supported source types, how files are updated, and why it is the preferred way to deliver short-lived, audience-bound tokens.

steps.title: Mental model: one mount, many sources
steps.description: Instead of mounting three volumes at three paths, you declare one volume with a list of sources.
items: Supported sources: secret, configMap, downwardAPI, serviceAccountToken, and clusterTrustBundle (beta in 1.29 and newer, behind a feature gate, so check your version).
Same namespace: Secrets and ConfigMaps must exist in the pod's namespace.
Unique paths: every file path across all sources must be distinct, otherwise the pod fails to start with a conflict.
Why use it: a single directory for an application that expects its config, credentials and identity token together, and fine-grained control over file names and modes.

Compared with separate volumes: mounting a Secret, a ConfigMap and downward API files as separate volumes needs three mount paths; projection gives one coherent tree and a single place to set default modes.
steps.highlight: The default token mount in every pod is itself a projected volume, combining the token, the cluster CA ConfigMap and the namespace.

steps.title: Hands-on: projected volume in Kubernetes with four sources
steps.description: Combine a ConfigMap, Secret, downward API labels and a short-lived token into /etc/app.
items: items: select specific keys and rename them with path; without items all keys are projected.
mode: per-file permissions via mode, with defaultMode for the whole volume.
Token source: serviceAccountToken takes audience, expirationSeconds and path.
readOnly: mount it read-only in the container, as the contents are managed by the kubelet.

Typical use case: a service that reads /etc/app/settings.yaml, a password file and an identity token from the same configuration directory, without the application knowing they came from three objects.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: prod
  labels:
    app: my-app
spec:
  serviceAccountName: my-sa
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: registry.example.com/my-app:1.0.0
      volumeMounts:
        - name: app-config
          mountPath: /etc/app
          readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: app-config
      projected:
        defaultMode: 0440
        sources:
          - configMap:
              name: app-settings
              items: [{key: settings.yaml, path: settings.yaml}]
          - secret:
              name: app-credentials
              items: [{key: db-password, path: secrets/db-password}]
          - downwardAPI:
              items:
                - path: labels
                  fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.labels}
          - serviceAccountToken:
              path: token
              audience: https://vault.example.com
              expirationSeconds: 3600

steps.title: Verify the projected files and their updates
steps.description: Look inside the container to confirm layout, permissions and refresh behaviour.
items: List files: kubectl exec my-app -n prod -- ls -lR /etc/app. Expect symlinks into a timestamped data directory, which is how updates are swapped atomically.
Update propagation: ConfigMap and Secret changes appear after the kubelet sync period plus cache delay, typically within a minute or so. This is eventual, not instant.
subPath caveat: files mounted with subPath are never updated after start.
Token refresh: the kubelet rewrites the token file before expiry; check the exp claim over time.
Atomic updates: the kubelet writes a new timestamped directory and flips a symlink, so readers never observe a half-written set of files.
Permissions in the container: files appear with the modes you set, and fsGroup in the pod securityContext adjusts group ownership so a non-root process can read them.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl -n prod exec my-app -- ls -lR /etc/app
kubectl -n prod exec my-app -- cat /etc/app/labels
kubectl -n prod describe pod my-app | sed -n '/Volumes:/,/QoS/p'

steps.title: Failure modes and edge cases
steps.description: Most projected volume issues show up as pods stuck in ContainerCreating.
items: Missing source: a missing Secret or ConfigMap leaves the pod in ContainerCreating with a MountVolume.SetUp failed event, unless the source is marked optional: true.
Path collision: two sources writing the same path are rejected.
Env vars do not update: values copied into environment variables never refresh; only mounted files do.
Big payloads: ConfigMaps and Secrets have a size cap of about 1 MiB each; do not project large blobs.
Optional sources: mark non-critical sources as optional: true so the pod still starts if they are missing, and handle absence in the application.
Order is not guaranteed to matter: do not rely on one source overriding another; give every file a unique path and treat the volume as a union.

steps.title: Production practice: when to choose it
steps.description: Use projected volumes when they remove glue code, not by default.
items: Workload identity: project audience-scoped tokens for Vault, cloud IAM federation or service meshes.
Hot reload: pair file projection with an app that watches files, or a reloader sidecar.
Least privilege: project only the keys the container needs using items.
Security: set restrictive modes and run as non-root with fsGroup where file ownership matters.
Observe the effect: track mount failures through pod events and alert on pods stuck in ContainerCreating for longer than a normal image pull.
Cost of change: adding a new source later only needs a manifest edit and a rollout, which is cheaper than writing sidecar code to fetch each value.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: use projected volumes for short-lived, audience-scoped ServiceAccount tokens and project only the keys needed. Never use subPath if you rely on live updates.
elevatorPitch: A projected volume merges Secrets, ConfigMaps, downward API fields and ServiceAccount tokens into one directory.
I verify with kubectl exec ls, pod events for mount errors, and watch that file updates arrive without subPath.
I automate token audiences and expirations in manifests and keep only required keys in the projection.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using subPath with a projected source and expecting updates
mistakesToAvoid.why: subPath mounts are a snapshot and never receive kubelet refreshes.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming environment variables follow ConfigMap or Secret updates
mistakesToAvoid.why: Env vars are fixed at container start; only files change, so a restart or reload is needed.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Reusing the same path in two sources
mistakesToAvoid.why: Kubernetes rejects the pod because files would collide in the same directory.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Projecting the whole Secret instead of selected keys
mistakesToAvoid.why: It widens exposure and file clutter; items narrows what the container can read.

title: Kubernetes Q124: How do you check what labels are on a node [L2]
summary: kubectl get node <n> --show-labels or kubectl describe node <n>. Add labels: kubectl label node <n> key=value.
question: How do you check what labels are on a node?
intro: To check what labels are on a node, run kubectl get node <name> --show-labels or kubectl describe node <name>; to see a few specific labels as columns across all nodes, use -L. Interviewers ask this simple question to see if you can move from inspection to action: filtering nodes by label, understanding the well-known labels cloud providers set, and knowing how labels drive nodeSelector, affinity and topology spread.

steps.title: Mental model: what node labels are for
steps.description: Labels are key-value metadata on the Node object, used by schedulers, controllers and humans to group nodes.
items: Sources: the kubelet sets built-in labels such as kubernetes.io/hostname, kubernetes.io/os and kubernetes.io/arch; cloud providers add zone, region and instance type; admins add custom ones.
Well-known labels: topology.kubernetes.io/zone, topology.kubernetes.io/region and node.kubernetes.io/instance-type are used by spread constraints and affinity.
Role labels: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane is a label whose key encodes the role; what you see as ROLES in kubectl get nodes comes from these.
Labels versus taints: labels attract or select; taints repel. They are often used together.

Why interviewers care: every scheduling rule you write (nodeSelector, nodeAffinity, topology spread) is only as correct as the labels on the nodes, so reading labels is the first diagnostic step for Pending pods.

steps.title: Hands-on: check what labels are on a node with kubectl
steps.description: Use the output format that matches your goal, from a quick look to scripting.
items: All labels of every node: kubectl get nodes --show-labels. Output is dense, so prefer the next options for readability.
Specific labels as columns: -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type adds one column per key.
One node in detail: kubectl describe node worker-1 prints a Labels: block, one per line.
Machine readable: -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels}' or -o json | jq .metadata.labels.
Reading output quickly: the LABELS column is comma separated, so for a single key it is faster to request it with -L than to scan the full string.
Control-plane nodes: kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane lists them, because the role is encoded in the label key rather than its value.
Count by label: pipe a column to sort and uniq to see how many nodes sit in each zone, which quickly shows imbalance.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get nodes --show-labels
kubectl get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type
kubectl get node worker-1 -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels}' | jq .
kubectl describe node worker-1 | sed -n '/^Labels:/,/^Annotations:/p'

steps.title: Filter, add and remove labels
steps.description: Selectors let you find the nodes behind a scheduling decision.
items: Equality selector: kubectl get nodes -l disktype=ssd; set-based: -l 'topology.kubernetes.io/zone in (us-east-1a,us-east-1b)'.
Add a label: kubectl label node worker-1 disktype=ssd; change an existing one with --overwrite.
Remove a label: kubectl label node worker-1 disktype- (trailing dash).
Use it: a pod with nodeSelector: {disktype: ssd} now schedules only on matching nodes.
Safety: labelling a node changes which pods can match, but does not move running pods; only new scheduling decisions are affected.
Multiple labels at once: kubectl label node worker-1 tier=db team=data sets several in one call, and kubectl label nodes --all env=staging labels every node.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get nodes -l disktype=ssd
kubectl label node worker-1 disktype=ssd
kubectl label node worker-1 disktype=nvme --overwrite
kubectl label node worker-1 disktype-

steps.title: Edge cases and debugging scheduling with labels
steps.description: A pod stuck Pending often comes down to a label mismatch.
items: Pending pod: kubectl describe pod says didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector; compare the pod's selector with the node labels.
Typos and case: label keys and values are case-sensitive.
Manual labels are lost: nodes recreated by an autoscaler or node group do not keep hand-applied labels. Define them in the node group or kubelet config (--node-labels).
Restricted prefix: with the NodeRestriction admission plugin, kubelets cannot set labels under node-restriction.kubernetes.io/, which makes that prefix suitable for isolation labels.
Compare both sides: run kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeSelector}' next to the node labels to see the mismatch at a glance.

steps.title: Production practice: label conventions
steps.description: Consistent labels turn scheduling into policy.
items: Define at provisioning: set labels through Terraform, node groups or Karpenter NodePools instead of ad hoc kubectl.
Namespaced keys: use your own domain prefix, for example example.com/workload-tier.
Combine with taints: label and taint dedicated nodes so only intended pods run there.
Audit: a periodic kubectl get nodes -L report catches drift.

Cloud specifics: managed services also add provider labels, such as node pool or capacity type, which are useful selectors for spot versus on-demand placement; check what your provider sets rather than assuming.
Document the contract: publish the list of supported node labels and their meaning so application teams write selectors against a stable, reviewed set instead of guessing.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: use kubectl get nodes -L key1,key2 for a clean table, and define node labels in your node group or kubelet config so they survive node replacement.
elevatorPitch: I check node labels with kubectl get nodes --show-labels, -L for chosen keys, or describe node for one node.
I filter with -l selectors and confirm that a pod's nodeSelector or affinity matches what the node actually carries.
I automate labels in node groups or provisioners rather than labelling nodes by hand.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Labelling nodes manually with kubectl in an autoscaled cluster
mistakesToAvoid.why: Replaced nodes come up without the label and pods become unschedulable.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Parsing --show-labels output with grep for scripting
mistakesToAvoid.why: The format is meant for humans; use jsonpath or jq on metadata.labels.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using labels alone to dedicate nodes
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without a matching taint, other pods can still land on those nodes.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Overwriting well-known labels such as topology.kubernetes.io/zone
mistakesToAvoid.why: Spread constraints and volume topology rely on them being accurate.

title: Kubernetes Downward API: Exposing Pod & Container Metadata to Env Vars & Volume Files
summary: Deep dive into the Kubernetes Downward API: fieldRef vs resourceFieldRef, injecting pod/container metadata into environment variables and downwardAPI volume mounts.
question: What is the Kubernetes Downward API? How do you pass pod name, namespace, pod IP, and resource limits to application containers without querying the Kubernetes API server?
intro: "In our production Kubernetes clusters running microservices on EKS/AKS, this was a classic operational challenge. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Exposes pod/node metadata (pod name, namespace, labels, annotations, resource limits) to the container as env vars or volume files.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Over-granting cluster-admin permissions to pod ServiceAccounts instead of scoping namespace Roles when configuring Kubernetes Downward Exposing

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Referencing mutable latest container tags across production Kubernetes Deployment specs when configuring Kubernetes Downward Exposing

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting pod readiness probes, causing traffic to hit uninitialized application containers when configuring Kubernetes Downward Exposing

mistakesToAvoid.why: Cluster events provide sequential timestamps of scheduler decisions, probe failures, and image pull timeouts essential for rapid root-cause isolation.

summary: Set PodDisruptionBudgets on all critical workloads. kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data. The drain respects PDBs — won't proceed if it would violate them. Upgrade one node at a time.
question: How do you handle pod disruptions during Kubernetes version upgrades?
intro: "When troubleshooting Kubernetes, I always follow a structured layered model: Pod status -> Events -> Logs -> Network. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

Run targeted verification commands before modifying configuration.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Attempting multi-minor Kubernetes version jumps directly during cluster upgrades when configuring handle disruptions Kubernetes
mistakesToAvoid.why: Kubernetes explicitly does not support multi-minor version jumps; control plane and worker components require sequential hops to validate API deprecations.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Upgrading kube-apiserver while leaving critical cluster add-ons and CNI plugins desynchronized when configuring handle disruptions Kubernetes

mistakesToAvoid.why: Prematurely terminating stateful pods before in-flight transactions commit causes data corruption and unclean lock releases.

title: Kubernetes Q127: What is kubectl diff [L2]
summary: Shows what would change if you applied a manifest, compared to what's currently running. Like terraform plan for Kubernetes.
question: What is `kubectl diff`?
intro: kubectl diff shows what would change in the cluster if you ran kubectl apply on the same manifests, without changing anything. It sends the objects through a server-side dry run, so defaulting and admission mutation are included, then prints a unified diff against live state. Interviewers ask about it to see whether you review changes before shipping them, understand its exit codes for CI gates, and know why diffs sometimes contain noise from server-managed fields.

steps.title: Mental model: kubectl diff is a safe preview of apply
steps.description: The command takes the same inputs as apply (-f, -k, stdin) and compares the result of a server-side dry-run with the live object.
items: Read-only: nothing is persisted; it needs get, and permission to perform the dry-run (patch/create) in the namespace.
Server-aware: because the server computes the result, defaulted fields and mutating webhook changes show up.
Output: unified diff with +/- lines per object.
Kustomize and Helm: works with -k, and with helm template ... | kubectl diff -f -.

steps.title: Hands-on: diff a manifest, a kustomization, and a chart
steps.description: Typical pre-deploy commands.
items: Single file: kubectl diff -f deploy.yaml.
Kustomize: kubectl diff -k overlays/prod.
Rendered Helm: pipe helm template into kubectl diff -f -; or use the helm-diff plugin for release-aware output.
Custom viewer: set KUBECTL_EXTERNAL_DIFF (for example colordiff) to change the tool.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl diff -f deploy.yaml
# -  replicas: 3
# +  replicas: 5

kubectl diff -k overlays/prod -n prod
helm template my-app ./chart -n prod -f values-prod.yaml | kubectl diff -n prod -f -
KUBECTL_EXTERNAL_DIFF="colordiff -u" kubectl diff -f deploy.yaml

steps.title: Verify and gate: exit codes in CI
steps.description: The exit code is what makes diff scriptable.
items: 0: no differences.
1: differences found (not an error).
Greater than 1: the command itself failed, for example invalid manifest or forbidden.
Pipelines: treat 1 as expected for a review step and post the diff as a pull request comment.

steps.title: Failure modes and false positives
steps.description: Diffs can be larger or smaller than expected.
items: Managed fields: metadata.managedFields, resourceVersion and timestamps are filtered by kubectl, but fields mutated by controllers (HPA-controlled replicas) can look like drift.
Missing namespace or CRD: a dry-run against a namespace or custom resource that does not exist yet fails, so diff cannot preview a first install of dependencies.
Webhook side effects: admission webhooks must declare sideEffects as None or NoneOnDryRun, or the dry-run is rejected.
Secrets: treat diff output as sensitive, since Secret changes can appear in CI logs; restrict who can read them.
Server-side apply: if you apply with --server-side, use kubectl diff --server-side so field ownership matches.

steps.title: Production practice: diff as a deployment gate
steps.description: Make the preview part of the workflow.
items: Pull request check: run diff against the target cluster read-only credentials and attach output.
Drift detection: scheduled diff of Git manifests versus cluster highlights manual kubectl edit changes.
GitOps: Argo CD and Flux provide equivalent diff views; kubectl diff is the manual equivalent.
Least privilege: give CI a role limited to what the dry-run needs.
steps.highlight: Always run kubectl diff then kubectl apply with the same flags and the same context, otherwise you review one thing and ship another.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Treat kubectl diff exit code 1 as 'changes found', not failure, and fail your pipeline only on codes above 1.
elevatorPitch: kubectl diff previews what kubectl apply would change by comparing server-side dry-run output with live state.
I rely on its exit codes: 0 no change, 1 changes, above 1 error, and run it for kustomize and Helm-rendered manifests.
I automate it as a pull request check and as scheduled drift detection.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating exit code 1 as a failed command
mistakesToAvoid.why: Exit code 1 means differences exist; a CI step that fails on any non-zero code blocks every legitimate change.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Diffing against the wrong context or namespace
mistakesToAvoid.why: The diff is only meaningful for the cluster you target; a stale kubeconfig context shows a misleading result.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting diff to preview objects whose namespace or CRD does not exist
mistakesToAvoid.why: The server-side dry-run fails when dependencies are missing, so apply order matters.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Mixing client-side and server-side apply
mistakesToAvoid.why: Field ownership differs, so diffs and applies can disagree about who owns a field.

title: Kubernetes Q128: How do you enforce that all pods in a namespace must have resource limits [L2]
summary: LimitRange with defaultRequest and default limits OR use OPA/Gatekeeper/Kyverno policy that rejects pods without resource limits.
question: How do you enforce that all pods in a namespace must have resource limits?
intro: To enforce that all pods in a namespace must have resource limits, combine a LimitRange (to inject defaults), a ResourceQuota (to cap the total and force every pod to declare values) and, where you need a hard rule, an admission policy such as ValidatingAdmissionPolicy or Kyverno. Each tool has a different strength: defaults, caps, and rejection. Interviewers ask to see whether you understand where each applies and how they interact at admission time.

steps.title: Mental model: default, cap, then reject
steps.description: Three layers solve three different problems, and a robust namespace usually uses more than one.
items: LimitRange: sets default requests and limits, plus min, max and ratio, per container in a namespace. Pods without resources get the defaults at admission.

ResourceQuota: caps the aggregate requests and limits for the namespace. If the quota covers limits.cpu or limits.memory, every new pod must specify them (or get them from a LimitRange), otherwise creation is rejected.
Admission policy: a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (GA in 1.30) or a policy engine like Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper can reject pods that omit limits explicitly, with a clear message.
Scope: all of these act at creation time; they do not change pods that are already running.
Why limits matter: pods without limits can consume all node memory or CPU, which leads to evictions and noisy-neighbour incidents and makes capacity planning guesswork.
Requests versus limits: requests drive scheduling and QoS, limits cap runtime usage. Requiring both is the safest policy, and setting equal values gives Guaranteed QoS.
steps.highlight: LimitRange is friendly (it fixes the pod), quota is a budget, and admission policy is the strict gatekeeper.

steps.title: Hands-on: enforce resource limits for all pods with LimitRange and quota
steps.description: Apply both objects to the namespace; together they guarantee that every container has values and the total stays bounded.
items: Defaults: default sets limits, defaultRequest sets requests.
Bounds: min and max reject containers outside the range.
Quota fields: use requests.cpu, requests.memory, limits.cpu, limits.memory and pods.
Order of operations: the LimitRanger admission step injects defaults first, so the quota check then sees complete values.
Defaults are a policy choice: choose defaults conservatively. A tiny default memory limit produces OOMKills, while a huge one defeats the purpose.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: container-defaults
  namespace: prod
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      defaultRequest: {cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi}
      default:        {cpu: 500m, memory: 256Mi}
      max:            {cpu: "2",  memory: 2Gi}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: ns-budget
  namespace: prod
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "10"
    requests.memory: 20Gi
    limits.cpu: "20"
    limits.memory: 40Gi
    pods: "100"

steps.title: Hard rejection with ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
steps.description: When defaults are not acceptable and teams must declare limits themselves, reject pods that omit them.
items: CEL expression: check every container, and init containers if you want full coverage, for the presence of cpu and memory limits.
Binding: a ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding scopes the policy to namespaces by label selector and sets validationActions (Warn, Audit, Deny).
Roll out safely: start with Warn and Audit, review the results, then switch to Deny.
Interaction with LimitRange: mutating defaults are applied before validating policies run, so if you want pods without limits to fail, do not install a defaulting LimitRange in that namespace.
Message quality: a clear deny message that tells developers what to add saves support requests, so include the exact missing field in the text.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-container-limits
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
        resources: ["pods"]
  validations:
    - expression: >-
        object.spec.containers.all(c,
          has(c.resources.limits) &&
          'cpu' in c.resources.limits &&
          'memory' in c.resources.limits)
      message: "All containers must set cpu and memory limits."
---
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
  name: require-container-limits-prod
spec:
  policyName: require-container-limits
  validationActions: ["Deny"]
  matchResources:
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        kubernetes.io/metadata.name: prod

steps.title: Verify the enforcement and read the errors
steps.description: Test with a deliberately bad pod and inspect what the cluster says.
items: Dry run: kubectl run test --image=nginx -n prod --dry-run=server shows whether admission accepts or rejects.
Check defaults: create a pod without resources and run kubectl get pod test -n prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}' to see injected values.
Quota usage: kubectl describe quota ns-budget -n prod shows used versus hard.
Typical rejections: must specify limits.cpu from quota, maximum cpu usage per Container from LimitRange, or your policy message.
Dry-run in CI: run kubectl apply --dry-run=server against a staging namespace in the pipeline so developers see rejections before deployment.
Existing violators: pods created before the policy keep running; they are only caught when recreated, so plan a controlled rollout restart after enabling enforcement.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl -n prod run test --image=nginx --dry-run=server -o yaml | grep -A6 resources
kubectl -n prod describe resourcequota ns-budget
kubectl -n prod describe limitrange container-defaults

steps.title: Production practice: policy as code and coverage gaps
steps.description: Make the rule apply everywhere and remain visible.
items: Roll out via GitOps: keep LimitRange, quota and policies in the namespace template so every new namespace inherits them.
Workloads that create pods: the quota and policy apply to the Pod at creation, not to the Deployment, so errors show in ReplicaSet events rather than kubectl apply output.
Audit existing pods: list pods missing limits with a jq query before enabling Deny.
Exceptions: exempt system namespaces through the binding's namespace selector.
Alternative engines: Kyverno and OPA Gatekeeper offer richer mutation and reporting than CEL; pick one based on what your platform team already operates.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Deployments are not rejected at apply time when a pod violates quota or policy. Check kubectl describe rs events for the real error.
elevatorPitch: I enforce limits with a LimitRange for defaults, a ResourceQuota for caps, and an admission policy for hard rejection.
I verify with a server-side dry run and kubectl describe quota and limitrange.
I ship these as namespace templates in GitOps and switch policy from Warn to Deny after auditing.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on LimitRange alone as an enforcement mechanism
mistakesToAvoid.why: It only injects defaults and bounds; it does not force teams to think about sizing.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting kubectl apply of a Deployment to fail on quota violations
mistakesToAvoid.why: The ReplicaSet fails to create pods, so the error appears in ReplicaSet events instead.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Enabling Deny without an audit pass
mistakesToAvoid.why: Existing workflows break on the next rollout and you only find out when pods fail to be recreated.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting init containers in the CEL rule
mistakesToAvoid.why: Init containers can consume resources without limits if only spec.containers is checked.

title: Kubernetes VPA (Vertical Pod Autoscaler): Architecture, Modes, Goldilocks & HPA Conflicts
summary: Production guide to Kubernetes VPA: Recommender, Updater, and Admission Controller components, deployment modes (Off, Initial, Recreate, Auto), and preventing flapping with HPA.
question: What is the Kubernetes Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA)? How does it right-size container CPU and memory requests, and why should you avoid combining VPA with HPA on the same resource metrics?
intro: "In our production Kubernetes clusters running microservices on EKS/AKS, this was a classic operational challenge. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: VPA adjusts CPU/memory requests of running pods based on actual usage. Use VPA for: workloads where you know they need more resources but can't scale horizontally (stateful single replicas). Use HPA for: stateless apps where horizontal scaling makes sense. Don't use both on the same deployment (conflict on CPU metrics).

title: Kubernetes Q130: How do you temporarily expose a service from a remote cluster to your local machine for debugging [L2]
summary: To temporarily expose a service from a remote cluster to your local machine, run kubectl port-forward svc/my-app 8080:80 -n prod.
question: How do you temporarily expose a service from a remote cluster to your local machine for debugging?
intro: To temporarily expose a service from a remote cluster to your local machine, run kubectl port-forward svc/my-app 8080:80 -n prod. It opens a tunnel through the API server from a local port to a pod, with no changes to the cluster's Services or Ingress. Interviewers ask this to check that you know its limits (one pod, TCP only, tied to your session) and when to reach for alternatives such as kubectl proxy, ephemeral debug containers or a tool like Telepresence.

steps.title: Mental model: a tunnel through the API server
steps.description: port-forward does not create a Service or open an inbound firewall rule; it relays bytes over your authenticated kubectl connection.
items: Path: your local port to kubectl, to the API server, to the kubelet on the node, to the pod's network namespace.
Target types: pod/<name>, deployment/<name> and svc/<name>. For the latter two kubectl resolves a single pod once, at the start.
Not load balanced: all traffic goes to that one pod. If it restarts or is rescheduled, the tunnel ends.
Protocol: TCP only; UDP is not supported.
Access control: your user needs create on pods/portforward in that namespace, and ideally get on pods.
Why it is safe to use: nothing is added to the cluster, so there is nothing to clean up afterwards; closing the command removes the tunnel entirely.
steps.highlight: Because the tunnel binds to 127.0.0.1 by default, only your machine can reach it. Use --address 0.0.0.0 sparingly.

steps.title: Hands-on: kubectl port-forward to a remote service
steps.description: Forward, test, and stop; keep the lifecycle explicit.
items: Forward a Service: kubectl port-forward svc/my-app 8080:80 -n prod maps local 8080 to service port 80.
Forward a specific pod: use pod/my-app-6d9f7c-abcde to debug one replica, such as the one throwing errors.
Random local port: :80 lets kubectl choose, and prints the choice.
Background it: append & in a script and capture the PID so you can kill it; the command stays in the foreground otherwise.
Pick the right port: for a Service target use the Service port on the left of the colon mapping; for a pod target use the container port.
Typical debugging loop: forward the port, reproduce the request with curl or a local client, read the pod logs in a second terminal, then stop the tunnel with Ctrl+C.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl port-forward svc/my-app 8080:80 -n prod
# in another shell
curl -i http://localhost:8080/healthz
# multiple ports, specific pod
kubectl port-forward pod/my-app-6d9f7c-abcde 8080:8080 9090:9090 -n prod
# script usage
kubectl port-forward svc/my-app 8080:80 -n prod >/tmp/pf.log 2>&1 &
PF_PID=$!; sleep 2; curl -s localhost:8080/healthz; kill $PF_PID

steps.title: Alternatives for different debugging needs
steps.description: port-forward is the first tool, not the only one.
items: kubectl proxy: exposes the API server locally, and services are reachable through /api/v1/namespaces/prod/services/my-app:80/proxy/. It is HTTP only and goes through the API server proxy.
Ephemeral debug container: kubectl debug -it pod/my-app --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=app lets you run curl and tcpdump from inside the pod's network namespace.
Telepresence or similar tools: route cluster traffic to a process on your laptop, useful for debugging a service with many dependencies. This requires installing a component in the cluster.
Temporary NodePort or LoadBalancer: avoid in production; it exposes the service to others and leaves forgotten resources.
Use the proxy for APIs: kubectl proxy is handy for hitting an internal HTTP admin endpoint through the API server without picking a pod.

steps.title: Failure modes and troubleshooting
steps.description: Most errors are about RBAC, ports or pod state.
items: Forbidden: cannot create resource pods/portforward means a missing RBAC rule. Verify with kubectl auth can-i create pods/portforward -n prod.
Address in use: choose another local port or find the process with lsof -i :8080.

Connection refused or lost connection to pod: the app listens on a different port or only on 127.0.0.1 inside the pod (that is fine for port-forward, but target port must match the container port, not the Service port when forwarding a pod).
Tunnel drops: idle timeouts or pod restarts end the session. Wrap it in a loop for long sessions.
Check application binding: a process listening only on a different network interface inside the pod can still refuse the forward, so confirm with ss -ltn inside a debug container.
Idle and long transfers: large uploads or very long-lived connections can be cut by intermediate proxies or API server timeouts, so prefer short requests for debugging.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl auth can-i create pods/portforward -n prod
kubectl -n prod get endpoints my-app
kubectl -n prod get pod -l app=my-app -o wide
lsof -i :8080

steps.title: Production practice: do it safely
steps.description: Debug access to production is a privilege, so keep it narrow and auditable.
items: RBAC: grant pods/portforward only to on-call roles and prefer namespaced Roles.
Audit: API server audit logs record the port-forward request, which gives you a trail.
Bind locally: keep the default localhost binding, as 0.0.0.0 exposes an unauthenticated tunnel to your network.
Prefer staging: reproduce in a lower environment where possible.
Time-box access: agree a maximum duration for production debugging sessions and close the tunnel when the investigation ends.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: forward to a specific pod when debugging one bad replica, and remember a Service target is resolved to a single pod once, so the tunnel dies when that pod does.
elevatorPitch: kubectl port-forward opens a TCP tunnel through the API server from a local port to one pod, without changing cluster resources.
I verify with curl, kubectl auth can-i for pods/portforward, and check the pod and endpoints.
I restrict the RBAC permission, keep localhost binding, and use debug containers or proxies for other needs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming port-forward to a Service load balances
mistakesToAvoid.why: kubectl resolves one pod at start, so all traffic hits that pod and stops if it is replaced.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Binding with --address 0.0.0.0 on a shared network
mistakesToAvoid.why: It exposes an authenticated cluster tunnel to anyone who can reach your machine.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using the Service port when forwarding to a pod
mistakesToAvoid.why: A pod target needs the container port; the Service port may be different.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Leaving a temporary NodePort or LoadBalancer for debugging
mistakesToAvoid.why: It stays exposed and costs money long after you forget it.

title: Kubernetes Q133: What is a Kubernetes lease [L2]
summary: A Kubernetes Lease is a small coordination.k8s.io/v1 object that records which holder owns something and when it last renewed it.
question: What is a Kubernetes lease?
intro: A Kubernetes Lease is a small coordination.k8s.io/v1 object that records which holder owns something and when it last renewed it. Kubernetes uses Leases for two main jobs: node heartbeats (one Lease per node in kube-node-lease) and leader election for components like kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager and custom controllers. Interviewers ask about it because Leases explain how the control plane detects dead nodes cheaply and how HA controllers avoid running active-active, which ties directly to NotReady and failover troubleshooting.

steps.title: Kubernetes Lease anatomy
steps.description: A Lease is a tiny record of ownership plus a renewal clock.
items: holderIdentity: who currently holds it, such as a node name or a pod identity.
leaseDurationSeconds: how long others should wait after the last renewal before treating it as expired.
renewTime / acquireTime: timestamps updated by the holder; leaseTransitions counts ownership changes.
Why a separate object: updating a small Lease is much cheaper for etcd and watchers than rewriting a large Node status.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get leases -A
kubectl get lease my-node-1 -n kube-node-lease -o yaml
# spec: holderIdentity, leaseDurationSeconds, renewTime

steps.title: Node heartbeats
steps.description: Each kubelet renews its own Lease regularly.
items: Renewal: the kubelet renews its Lease roughly every 10 seconds, with a lease duration of 40 seconds by default.
Detection: the node lifecycle controller marks a node Unknown when heartbeats stop for node-monitor-grace-period (40s default).
Node status: full Node status updates now happen on change or at a slower interval, because the Lease carries the liveness signal.
Troubleshooting: a stale renewTime points to a dead kubelet or broken connectivity to the API server.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get lease -n kube-node-lease
kubectl get lease my-node-1 -n kube-node-lease -o jsonpath='{.spec.renewTime}{"\n"}'
date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ   # compare with renewTime

steps.title: Leader election for controllers
steps.description: Replicas compete for a Lease and only the holder acts.
items: Core components: kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager hold Leases in kube-system when run in HA mode.
Typical defaults: lease duration 15s, renew deadline 10s, retry period 2s.
Failover: if the leader stops renewing, another replica acquires the Lease after expiry and takes over.
Custom controllers: client-go and controller-runtime use Leases for election, which needs RBAC on leases.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get lease kube-scheduler -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.spec.holderIdentity}{"\n"}'

# RBAC for a controller using Lease-based election
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: leader-election
  namespace: my-system
rules:
- apiGroups: ["coordination.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["leases"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch"]
steps.highlight: A Lease provides leader election with failover but it is not a hard lock: a paused leader may briefly believe it still leads, so operators should stop work when renewal fails.

steps.title: Failure modes and diagnosis
steps.description: Most Lease problems are timing, permissions or API server health.
items: Leader flapping: slow API server or etcd makes renewals miss the deadline, causing repeated elections and restarts.
Forbidden errors: missing RBAC on leases prevents election; controller logs show the denial.
Clock issues: comparisons rely on observed timing, but large clock drift on nodes still complicates debugging timestamps.
Stuck holder: a deleted Lease is recreated, but an old holder running split leader code can produce duplicate actions if it ignores lost leadership.

steps.title: Production practice
steps.description: Monitor Leases like any other control plane signal.
items: Alert on transitions: a rising leaseTransitions value signals instability.
Tune carefully: longer lease durations tolerate API latency but slow failover.
One election per controller: use a unique Lease name and namespace for each operator deployment.
API server identity: newer versions also publish kube-apiserver identity Leases in kube-system, useful for counting live API servers.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: When a node flips to NotReady, check the renewTime of its Lease in kube-node-lease first, and treat rising leaseTransitions on kube-system Leases as an early warning of control plane latency.
elevatorPitch: A Lease is a small coordination.k8s.io object with a holder, a duration and a renew time, used as a cheap heartbeat and election primitive.
I check node health through the Lease renewTime in kube-node-lease and leader ownership through holderIdentity in kube-system.
I make sure controllers have RBAC for leases and alert on frequent leaseTransitions.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting RBAC for the coordination.k8s.io leases resource in custom controllers
mistakesToAvoid.why: Leader election fails and the controller never becomes active or crash-loops.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating Lease leadership as a perfect mutual-exclusion lock
mistakesToAvoid.why: A paused or partitioned leader can briefly act after expiry, so work must stop when renewal fails.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Setting very short lease durations to speed up failover
mistakesToAvoid.why: Normal API latency spikes then cause leadership flapping and repeated restarts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Looking only at the Node status when diagnosing NotReady
mistakesToAvoid.why: The Lease renewTime shows the real heartbeat age and tells you how long the kubelet has been silent.

title: Kubernetes Q134: How do you get events for a specific namespace sorted by time [L2]
summary: To get events for a specific namespace sorted by time, run kubectl get events -n prod --sort-by=.lastTimestamp, or use the newer kubectl events -n prod, which sorts chronologically by default.
question: How do you get events for a specific namespace sorted by time?
intro: To get events for a specific namespace sorted by time, run kubectl get events -n prod --sort-by=.lastTimestamp, or use the newer kubectl events -n prod, which sorts chronologically by default. Plain kubectl get events returns results in no guaranteed time order, which makes incident timelines confusing. Interviewers ask this to see whether you can reconstruct what happened from events and know their limits: they expire quickly and are not a durable log.

steps.title: Mental model: events are short-lived hints
steps.description: Events are API objects emitted by controllers and the kubelet, describing things like scheduling, image pulls and probe failures.
items: Type: Normal or Warning. Warnings are where you usually start.
Involved object: each event references a pod, node, ReplicaSet or other object, and has a reason and message.
Retention: the API server keeps events for one hour by default (--event-ttl). After that they are gone, so export them if you need history.
Deduplication: repeated events are aggregated with a count, so lastTimestamp reflects the latest occurrence.
Why sorting matters: an incident is a sequence, such as scheduled, pulled, started, failed probe, killed. Without time ordering the cause and effect are scrambled.
steps.highlight: If you are debugging something that happened more than an hour ago, events are probably already gone. Check logs and metrics.

steps.title: Hands-on: get events for a namespace sorted by time
steps.description: Choose the command that fits your cluster version and your need.
items: Classic: kubectl get events -n prod --sort-by=.lastTimestamp. Oldest first, newest last, so the most recent lines are at the bottom of the terminal.
Alternative field: --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp works when events from the newer events.k8s.io API leave lastTimestamp empty.
Dedicated command: kubectl events -n prod (available in kubectl 1.26 and newer) is sorted by default and supports --for, --types and --watch.
All namespaces: add -A.
Reading the order: with ascending sort the newest event is the last line, so read upwards from the bottom to find the most recent change.
Include the namespace explicitly: always pass -n in runbooks rather than relying on your current context, which avoids reading the wrong cluster namespace during an incident.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get events -n prod --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
kubectl get events -n prod --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
kubectl events -n prod
kubectl events -n prod --types=Warning

steps.title: Filter, watch and focus
steps.description: Cut the noise down to what matters.
items: Warnings only: kubectl get events -n prod --field-selector type=Warning --sort-by=.lastTimestamp.
One object: kubectl events -n prod --for pod/my-app-6d9f7c-abcde, or with --field-selector involvedObject.name=my-app-6d9f7c-abcde on the older command.
Live stream: kubectl get events -n prod -w or kubectl events -n prod --watch during a rollout.
Custom columns: -o custom-columns=TIME:.lastTimestamp,TYPE:.type,REASON:.reason,OBJECT:.involvedObject.name,MSG:.message gives a compact timeline.
Combine selectors: chain field selectors with commas to match both a kind and a reason, which is the quickest way to answer a question like which pods hit FailedMount.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get events -n prod --field-selector type=Warning --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
kubectl get events -n prod --field-selector involvedObject.kind=Pod,reason=BackOff
kubectl get events -n prod --sort-by=.lastTimestamp \
  -o custom-columns=TIME:.lastTimestamp,TYPE:.type,REASON:.reason,OBJECT:.involvedObject.name,MSG:.message

steps.title: Edge cases and reading events correctly
steps.description: Events are easy to misread if you ignore context.
items: Empty output: either nothing happened in the last hour, you are in the wrong namespace, or events were rate limited.
Order trap: without --sort-by the output is not chronological, so a recent failure can hide in the middle of the list.
Cluster-scoped objects: node events appear in the default namespace, or in kube-system for some, so check there when a node misbehaves.
Event spam: a crash-looping pod can flood events; filter by reason such as BackOff or FailedScheduling.
Describe shows events too: kubectl describe pod appends the relevant events at the bottom, already scoped to that object, which is often quicker than listing the namespace.
Aggregation caveat: a high count with an old first timestamp means the problem is recurring, not new, so compare first and last timestamps before declaring it fresh.

steps.title: Production practice: persist and alert
steps.description: Do not rely on kubectl for anything you need after an hour.
items: Export: ship events to your log backend with a tool such as kubernetes-event-exporter or your observability agent.
Alert on Warning reasons: FailedScheduling, FailedMount, Unhealthy and OOMKilling are good starters.
Runbooks: include the exact events command and namespace in the incident runbook.
Combine: events plus kubectl logs --previous gives you cause and effect.
Retention planning: if your cluster is busy, events may rotate even faster than the TTL because of rate limiting, so do not depend on them for audits.
Link to metrics: match event timestamps against dashboards for restarts, memory and latency to confirm which event was the trigger.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: use kubectl events (1.26 or newer) for a sorted timeline, and always export events to your logging system because the API server drops them after about an hour.
elevatorPitch: I use kubectl get events -n NS --sort-by=.lastTimestamp, or kubectl events, to get a chronological timeline.
I filter with field selectors on type and involvedObject and watch events during rollouts.
I automate event export and alerts since events expire after the default one hour.
