mistakesToAvoid.why: The default order is not chronological, so you misread the sequence of failures.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Investigating an old incident with kubectl events
mistakesToAvoid.why: The default event TTL is one hour, so older events have already been deleted.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Looking in the wrong namespace for node events

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating Normal events as noise only
mistakesToAvoid.why: Events such as Killing, Pulled and Scheduled provide the timeline context for the warnings.

title: Kubernetes Q137: What is eBPF and how is it used in Kubernetes networking [L3]

title: Kubernetes Q138: What happens when you delete a namespace that has resources in it [L2]
summary: When you delete a Kubernetes namespace, the API server marks it Terminating and the namespace controller deletes every namespaced object inside it, then removes the namespace itself.
question: What happens when you delete a namespace that has resources in it?
intro: When you delete a Kubernetes namespace, the API server marks it Terminating and the namespace controller deletes every namespaced object inside it, then removes the namespace itself. Cluster-scoped objects are not deleted, and storage outcomes depend on reclaim policy. Interviewers ask this because deletion is destructive and sometimes hangs forever: you need to explain finalizers, aggregated API failures and why force-removing a finalizer is a last resort.

steps.title: Mental model: what the namespace controller does
steps.description: Deletion is asynchronous and ordered by object finalizers, not instant.
items: Phase change: kubectl delete ns demo sets a deletionTimestamp and phase Terminating; new objects cannot be created in it.
Cascade: the controller discovers every namespaced resource type and deletes all instances: Pods, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCs, Roles, custom resources.
Pods: get SIGTERM and honour terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30s).
Finalize: when empty, the kubernetes finalizer in spec.finalizers is removed and the namespace disappears.

steps.title: Hands-on: inspect before and after deleting
steps.description: Know what you are about to destroy.
items: Inventory: list all namespaced resource types, not only kubectl get all, which omits many kinds.
Storage: check PVCs and the PV reclaim policy: Delete removes the backing volume, Retain keeps it as Released.
Delete: kubectl delete ns demo --wait=false returns immediately; omit the flag to block.
Watch: kubectl get ns demo -w.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl api-resources --verbs=list --namespaced -o name \
  | xargs -n1 kubectl get -n demo --ignore-not-found --show-kind

kubectl get pvc -n demo
kubectl get pv -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,RECLAIM:.spec.persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy,CLAIM:.spec.claimRef.name

kubectl delete ns demo --wait=false
kubectl get ns demo -w

steps.title: Verify cleanup and what survives
steps.description: Not everything is removed.
items: Gone: every namespaced object, including Secrets and RoleBindings in the namespace.
Survives: cluster-scoped objects such as ClusterRoles, ClusterRoleBindings you created for it, CRDs, StorageClasses, and PVs with Retain.
Cloud resources: LoadBalancer Services release their cloud load balancers via the controller, which can take a minute; PVs with Delete remove disks.
Confirm: kubectl get ns and check cloud console or CLI for orphaned volumes and load balancers.

steps.title: Failure mode: stuck in Terminating
steps.description: The most common production complaint.
items: Read conditions: kubectl get ns demo -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}' names the blocker, such as NamespaceContentRemaining or NamespaceDeletionDiscoveryFailure.
Resource finalizers: a custom resource whose controller was uninstalled first keeps its finalizer, and nothing removes it.
Broken APIService: an unavailable aggregated API (for example metrics) stops discovery, so deletion cannot enumerate types: kubectl get apiservice | grep False.
Fix the cause: reinstall the controller or restore the APIService; remove a finalizer from the specific object only if you accept leaking external resources.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get ns demo -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}={.status} {.message}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl get apiservice | grep -v True
# last resort, on the specific stuck object:
kubectl patch <kind>/<name> -n demo --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":[]}}'
steps.highlight: Avoid editing the namespace's spec.finalizers through the /finalize endpoint as a first move: it skips cleanup and can orphan external resources.

steps.title: Production practice: make deletion safe
steps.description: Reduce blast radius.
items: RBAC: restrict delete on namespaces to a small group.
Labels and policy: use admission policy to block deletion of namespaces labeled protected=true.
Backups: take Velero or snapshot backups before removing stateful namespaces; set PV reclaim to Retain for important data.
GitOps: delete through Git and let Argo CD or Flux prune, with a review step.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Before deleting a namespace, list every namespaced resource with kubectl api-resources --verbs=list --namespaced and check PV reclaim policies, because kubectl get all hides most kinds and Delete policy destroys the data.
elevatorPitch: Deleting a namespace marks it Terminating and cascades deletion of every namespaced object, but leaves cluster-scoped resources.
I inventory resources and PV reclaim policies first, then watch conditions if it hangs on finalizers or a broken APIService.
I protect it with RBAC, admission policy, backups and Git-driven deletion.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using kubectl get all to see what will be deleted
mistakesToAvoid.why: It lists only a few core kinds; Secrets, ConfigMaps, PVCs and custom resources are omitted.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Force-removing finalizers immediately
mistakesToAvoid.why: Finalizers exist to clean external resources; stripping them can orphan disks, load balancers or DNS records.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting PV reclaim policy
mistakesToAvoid.why: With Delete the backing volume is destroyed along with the PVC; with Retain it lingers and costs money.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Uninstalling operators before deleting their namespaces
mistakesToAvoid.why: Custom resources keep finalizers that only the operator can clear, leaving the namespace stuck in Terminating.

title: Kubernetes Q142: How do you pass the pods own name to the app running inside it [L2]
summary: Use downward API:
question: How do you pass the pod's own name to the app running inside it?
intro: To pass the pod's own name to the app running inside it, use the Downward API: set an environment variable with valueFrom.fieldRef.fieldPath: metadata.name. The kubelet injects the value at container start, so your app reads it like any other environment variable and needs no API access. Interviewers ask this to see if you know the Downward API fields, the difference between env and volume delivery, and why you should not give pods API permissions just to learn about themselves.

steps.title: Mental model: the kubelet hands the pod its own metadata
steps.description: The Downward API exposes pod and container fields to the container without calling the API server.
items: Common fieldRef paths: metadata.name, metadata.namespace, metadata.uid, spec.nodeName, spec.serviceAccountName, status.podIP and status.hostIP.
Resource fields: resourceFieldRef exposes a container's requests and limits, for example to size a thread pool or JVM heap.
Two delivery modes: environment variables (fixed at start) and a downwardAPI volume (files).
The hostname shortcut: by default the container's HOSTNAME equals the pod name, but this depends on settings such as hostname, subdomain and hostNetwork, so explicit fieldRef is more reliable.
Why not call the API: querying the API server for your own pod requires a ServiceAccount token, RBAC and network access, and adds a failure mode at start-up for information the kubelet already has.

steps.title: Hands-on: pass the pod's own name to the app with env vars
steps.description: Declare each variable with valueFrom; no extra RBAC or ServiceAccount is required.
items: Pod name: metadata.name, also available as a combined identity with namespace for log fields.
Namespace and node: add metadata.namespace and spec.nodeName in the same way.
Dependent env vars: you can build values using $(POD_NAME) syntax in env entries defined later in the list, for example to compose an instance ID.
Check the app: print the variable at start-up and include it in structured logs and metrics labels.
Where the value shows up: expose it as a log field, a metric label, or a request header, so one pod's behaviour can be traced across systems.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: my-app}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: my-app}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: registry.example.com/my-app:1.0.0
          env:
            - name: POD_NAME
              valueFrom:
                fieldRef:
                  fieldPath: metadata.name
            - name: POD_NAMESPACE
              valueFrom:
                fieldRef:
                  fieldPath: metadata.namespace
            - name: NODE_NAME
              valueFrom:
                fieldRef:
                  fieldPath: spec.nodeName
            - name: INSTANCE_ID
              value: "$(POD_NAMESPACE)/$(POD_NAME)"

steps.title: Volume delivery for labels and annotations
steps.description: Some fields can only be consumed through a volume, and files can update while the pod runs.
items: Labels and annotations: metadata.labels and metadata.annotations can be exposed as files, and the kubelet refreshes them when they change. They cannot be consumed as a whole through env vars, although a single label can be via metadata.labels['app'].
Env limitation: environment variables are never updated after start; a changed label requires a restart.
Format: a labels file contains one key="value" line per label.
Mounting: mount the volume read-only at a path such as /etc/podinfo.
Single label via env: fieldRef.fieldPath: metadata.labels['app'] works for one label in an env var; the value is still fixed at start.
steps.codeBlock:
containers:
        - name: app
          image: registry.example.com/my-app:1.0.0
          volumeMounts:
            - name: podinfo
              mountPath: /etc/podinfo
              readOnly: true
      volumes:
        - name: podinfo
          downwardAPI:
            items:
              - path: name
                fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name}
              - path: labels
                fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.labels}

steps.title: Verify and avoid common failures
steps.description: Check inside the running container and know when the value changes.
items: Verify: kubectl exec -n prod deploy/my-app -- printenv POD_NAME returns the pod name such as my-app-6d9f7c-abcde.

Stable versus changing: a Deployment's pod name changes whenever the pod is replaced, while a StatefulSet pod keeps its ordinal name (db-0) across restarts. Container restarts inside the same pod keep the name.
Invalid field path: a typo in fieldPath is rejected at admission; an unsupported field leaves the pod unable to be created.
Do not parse names: do not extract the hash from the pod name for logic; it is an implementation detail.
Restart behaviour: if the container restarts but the pod stays, the pod name is unchanged, which matters when you use it as a lock owner or cache key.
Debug quickly: if the variable is empty, check the manifest indentation of valueFrom and describe the pod to confirm the env block was applied.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl -n prod exec deploy/my-app -- printenv POD_NAME POD_NAMESPACE NODE_NAME
kubectl -n prod exec deploy/my-app -- cat /etc/podinfo/labels
kubectl -n prod get pods -l app=my-app -o name

steps.title: Production practice: identity, logging and coordination
steps.description: Pod identity is most useful for observability and leader election.
items: Logging: add pod, namespace and node to every log line and trace resource attributes, which removes guesswork in dashboards.
Leader election: use the pod name as the holder identity in Lease-based election.
StatefulSets: derive a stable shard or broker ID from the ordinal suffix, an intentional use of the stable name.
Avoid API calls: do not grant the pod get-pod RBAC just to learn its own name; the Downward API is simpler and safer.
Resource-aware apps: combine with resourceFieldRef for limits.cpu and limits.memory so the runtime sizes its pools from the real limits.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: inject the pod name with fieldRef metadata.name instead of reading HOSTNAME or calling the API, and use a downwardAPI volume only for labels and annotations that must refresh live.
elevatorPitch: I pass the pod name with the Downward API: an env var using fieldRef metadata.name, with no API access needed.
I verify with kubectl exec printenv and remember env values are fixed at start while volume files can update.
I automate it in manifests so every log line, metric and leader-election lease carries the pod identity.

mistakesToAvoid.why: It adds credentials and permissions for something the Downward API provides for free.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting env vars to follow label changes
mistakesToAvoid.why: Environment variables are set once at container start; use a downwardAPI volume for live labels.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on HOSTNAME in every setup
mistakesToAvoid.why: It can differ with hostNetwork or a custom hostname, while fieldRef is explicit.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using a Deployment pod name as a durable identity
mistakesToAvoid.why: The name changes when the pod is replaced; use a StatefulSet if you need stable names.

title: Kubernetes Q144: How do you create a self-signed TLS certificate for an Ingress [L2]
summary: To create a self-signed TLS certificate for an Ingress, generate a key and certificate with openssl req -x509 including a SubjectAltName, store them as a kubernetes.io/tls Secret with kubectl create secret tls, and reference that.
question: How do you create a self-signed TLS certificate for an Ingress?
intro: To create a self-signed TLS certificate for an Ingress, generate a key and certificate with openssl req -x509 including a SubjectAltName, store them as a kubernetes.io/tls Secret with kubectl create secret tls, and reference that Secret in the Ingress tls block. It is a good fit for dev and test clusters. Interviewers ask it to see if you know the Secret and Ingress wiring, why SAN matters, and when to switch to cert-manager.

steps.title: Mental model: key, certificate, Secret, Ingress
steps.description: Four pieces connect, and the failure is usually in how they are linked.
items: Certificate and key: a self-signed certificate is its own issuer, so clients do not trust it unless you add it to their trust store or skip verification.
Secret: type kubernetes.io/tls with keys tls.crt and tls.key, in the same namespace as the Ingress.
Ingress: the tls section lists hostnames and secretName; the controller loads the certificate and serves it through SNI.
SAN requirement: modern clients ignore the Common Name and validate the SubjectAltName, so always include the DNS name there.
When it is appropriate: local clusters, CI environments and internal tooling where you control the clients and can distribute the certificate.
steps.highlight: Without a SAN entry, browsers and curl report a hostname mismatch even if the CN is correct.

steps.title: Hands-on: create a self-signed TLS certificate for an Ingress
steps.description: Generate the files and create the Secret.
items: One command: openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes creates the key and certificate together; -days sets validity.
SAN via -addext: supported in OpenSSL 1.1.1 and newer. macOS ships LibreSSL by default, where -addext may not work, so use Homebrew OpenSSL or a config file.
Create the Secret: kubectl create secret tls app-example-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key -n prod.
Wildcard: use DNS:*.dev.example.com in the SAN when several hosts share the certificate.
Key size and algorithm: RSA 2048 is widely compatible; ECDSA keys with -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:prime256v1 are smaller and also supported by common controllers.
Keep the private key private: do not commit tls.key to Git; create the Secret from the files and delete them, or generate them in CI.
steps.codeBlock:
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -sha256 -days 365 \
  -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt \
  -subj "/CN=app.example.com" \
  -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:app.example.com,DNS:www.example.com"

kubectl create secret tls app-example-tls \
  --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key -n prod
kubectl -n prod get secret app-example-tls -o jsonpath='{.type}{"\n"}'

steps.title: Wire the Secret into the Ingress
steps.description: Host names in tls.hosts must match the rule host and the certificate.
items: tls block: list the hosts and secretName; the Secret must be in the Ingress namespace.
ingressClassName: make sure the controller you expect handles the Ingress.
Redirects: ingress-nginx redirects HTTP to HTTPS by default when TLS is configured; adjust via annotation if needed.
Rotation: to replace the cert, update the Secret in place; most controllers reload it without a restart.
One Secret per host group: several Ingress objects in the same namespace can reuse one Secret if the SAN covers all their hosts.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: my-app
  namespace: prod
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - app.example.com
      secretName: app-example-tls
  rules:
    - host: app.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: my-app
                port:
                  number: 80

steps.title: Verify the served certificate and troubleshoot
steps.description: Check what the controller actually presents, not what you think you configured.
items: Inspect the file: openssl x509 -in tls.crt -noout -subject -dates -ext subjectAltName (the -ext flag needs OpenSSL 1.1.1 or newer).
Test without DNS: curl --resolve app.example.com:443:<ingress-ip> https://app.example.com -k -v; remove -k and add --cacert tls.crt to check proper trust.
SNI view: openssl s_client -connect <ingress-ip>:443 -servername app.example.com shows the presented certificate.
Default fake certificate: if you see the controller's 'Kubernetes Ingress Controller Fake Certificate', the Secret name, namespace, type or host does not match, and the controller log says why.
Controller logs: ingress-nginx logs messages such as an unexpected error loading the secret, which pinpoint a wrong type or missing keys.
Browser warnings: a self-signed certificate warns unless the certificate is imported as trusted, which is expected and not a cluster fault.
steps.codeBlock:
openssl x509 -in tls.crt -noout -subject -dates -ext subjectAltName
curl -v --resolve app.example.com:443:203.0.113.10 --cacert tls.crt https://app.example.com/
openssl s_client -connect 203.0.113.10:443 -servername app.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer

steps.title: Production practice: use cert-manager or a real CA
steps.description: Self-signed certificates do not scale beyond local use.
items: cert-manager SelfSigned or CA issuer: automates creation and renewal inside the cluster, with the Certificate resource producing the Secret.
Public hosts: use ACME with Let's Encrypt for internet-facing names.
Local dev trust: a tool like mkcert creates a local CA so browsers trust the certificate without warnings.
Expiry monitoring: alert on certificate expiry, since self-signed certs expire silently.
Trust distribution: for service-to-service calls, mount the CA certificate into clients through a ConfigMap instead of disabling verification.
Renewal drill: rehearse replacing the certificate before expiry, including updating the Secret and confirming the controller serves the new serial number.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: always include a SubjectAltName and keep the TLS Secret in the same namespace as the Ingress. If you see the controller's Fake Certificate, the Secret is not being picked up.
elevatorPitch: I generate a key and self-signed certificate with openssl including a SAN, then create a kubernetes.io/tls Secret.
I reference it in the Ingress tls block and verify with openssl s_client and curl --resolve.
I automate with cert-manager issuers and monitor expiry instead of hand-made certificates.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting the SubjectAltName from the certificate
mistakesToAvoid.why: Modern clients check the SAN and reject the certificate even when the CN matches.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Creating the TLS Secret in a different namespace than the Ingress
mistakesToAvoid.why: The controller cannot read it and serves its default fake certificate.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using -k permanently instead of trusting the certificate
mistakesToAvoid.why: It hides real problems and trains teams to ignore TLS errors.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using self-signed certificates for production traffic
mistakesToAvoid.why: Clients cannot verify them and renewal is manual, which leads to outages when they expire.

title: Kubernetes Q145: What is an Admission Controller and how does Kubernetes use them [L3]
summary: An admission controller is a piece of API server code that intercepts a request after authentication and authorization but before the object is persisted to etcd, and can modify it, reject it, or both.
question: What is an Admission Controller and how does Kubernetes use them?
intro: An admission controller is a piece of API server code that intercepts a request after authentication and authorization but before the object is persisted to etcd, and can modify it, reject it, or both. Kubernetes uses admission controllers to enforce defaults and policy: injecting sidecars, applying quotas, enforcing Pod Security Standards and blocking non-compliant manifests. Interviewers ask this to see whether you understand the request lifecycle, the difference between mutating and validating stages, and the operational risk of a misconfigured webhook, which can block every deployment in a cluster. A strong answer also covers the newer in-process ValidatingAdmissionPolicy that reduces the need for webhooks.

steps.title: Mental model: where an admission controller sits
steps.description: Every write to the API server passes through a fixed pipeline, and admission is the last gate before persistence.
items: Pipeline order: authentication, authorization (RBAC), mutating admission, object schema validation, validating admission, then the write to etcd. Reads (get, list, watch) are never admitted.
Mutating: may change the object, for example adding a default StorageClass, injecting a sidecar container or setting resource requests. Mutating plugins run first so validation sees the final object.
Validating: may only accept or reject. Examples are ResourceQuota, PodSecurity and your own policy checks. Any single rejection fails the whole request with a clear error message.
Scope: admission acts on create, update, delete and connect (exec, port-forward) operations. It does not retroactively fix objects that already exist in etcd.
steps.highlight: Authorization answers can this user do this? Admission answers is this specific object acceptable? Both must pass.

steps.title: Hands-on: inspect built-in admission controllers
steps.description: Built-in plugins compile into kube-apiserver and are toggled by flags, while dynamic ones are registered through API objects.
items: Built-in examples: NamespaceLifecycle, LimitRanger, ServiceAccount, ResourceQuota, DefaultStorageClass, NodeRestriction and PodSecurity (stable since 1.25, replacing PodSecurityPolicy).

Configure: on self-managed control planes use --enable-admission-plugins and --disable-admission-plugins on the kube-apiserver manifest. Managed services (EKS, GKE, AKS) usually do not let you change these.

Dynamic: MutatingWebhookConfiguration and ValidatingWebhookConfiguration point the API server at an HTTPS service you run, which receives an AdmissionReview and replies with allowed true or false plus optional JSON patches.
Defaults vary: the enabled-by-default list changes between minor versions, so confirm against your cluster instead of memorising it.
steps.codeBlock:
# See which plugins a kubeadm-style apiserver enables (flag may be absent = defaults)
kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o yaml | grep -i admission

# List dynamic webhooks registered in the cluster
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations

# Server-side dry run triggers admission without persisting anything
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml --dry-run=server

steps.title: Hands-on: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy with CEL
steps.description: Since Kubernetes 1.30 ValidatingAdmissionPolicy is GA, letting you express rules in CEL inside the API server with no webhook to run.
items: Policy: a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy holds matchConstraints and a list of CEL validations with messages.
Binding: a ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding activates the policy, selects namespaces and sets validationActions such as Deny, Warn or Audit.
Rollout tip: start with Warn and Audit to see what would break, then switch to Deny.
Older clusters: on 1.28 and 1.29 the feature is beta and may need to be enabled; check your version before relying on it.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-replicas-limit
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
    - apiGroups: ["apps"]
      apiVersions: ["v1"]
      operations: ["CREATE","UPDATE"]
      resources: ["deployments"]
  validations:
  - expression: "object.spec.replicas <= 10"
    message: "replicas must be 10 or fewer"
---
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
  name: require-replicas-limit-binding
spec:
  policyName: require-replicas-limit
  validationActions: ["Warn","Audit"]   # switch to ["Deny"] once clean

steps.title: Verify what admission did to a request
steps.description: When an apply is rejected or an object looks different from your manifest, confirm which stage acted.
items: Read the error: rejections name the source, for example admission webhook "x.example.com" denied the request or exceeded quota. The name points at the exact webhook configuration.
Compare objects: kubectl get pod my-pod -o yaml against your manifest shows mutations such as injected containers, default tolerations or added annotations.
Audit logs: API audit events and the apiserver metric apiserver_admission_webhook_rejection_count show which webhooks reject and how often.
Test safely: --dry-run=server runs the full admission chain, while --dry-run=client skips it, so only the server variant is a valid policy test.

steps.title: Failure modes and production practice
steps.description: Webhooks sit on the critical path of every write, so their reliability directly becomes cluster reliability.
items: failurePolicy: Fail blocks requests when the webhook is unreachable; Ignore lets them through. Security policies usually use Fail, but only with highly available webhook pods and a short timeoutSeconds.
Self-deadlock: a webhook that matches the pods or namespaces of its own deployment, or kube-system, can stop itself from restarting. Exclude them with namespaceSelector or objectSelector.
Side effects and ordering: declare sideEffects: None where true so dry-run works, and remember mutating webhooks can be re-invoked via reinvocationPolicy when another one changes the object.

Operate it: keep webhooks in GitOps, rotate serving certificates (cert-manager is common), alert on latency and rejection metrics, and prefer built-in plugins or CEL policies over custom webhooks when they can express the rule.
steps.highlight: If the API server cannot call a Fail-closed webhook, even kubectl delete of the webhook configuration may be needed to recover; keep that break-glass procedure documented.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Roll out any new admission policy in Warn/Audit mode first and exclude kube-system and the webhook own namespace, because a Fail-closed webhook that cannot start itself can freeze deployments cluster-wide.
elevatorPitch: An admission controller is API server logic that runs after authN/authZ and before etcd persistence, mutating or validating each write request.
I verify behaviour with kubectl apply --dry-run=server, by diffing the live object against my manifest, and by checking webhook rejection metrics.
I automate policy as code, using ValidatingAdmissionPolicy or a policy engine in GitOps, rolled out in Warn mode with HA webhooks and tight failurePolicy settings.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Confusing admission with RBAC
mistakesToAvoid.why: RBAC decides who may act; admission inspects the object itself. A user with full RBAC rights can still be rejected by quota or policy.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Letting a webhook match its own namespace
mistakesToAvoid.why: If the webhook pods go down and the policy is Fail-closed, they cannot be recreated because their own creation request is blocked.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Testing policy with client-side dry run
mistakesToAvoid.why: --dry-run=client never contacts the API server, so no admission plugin or webhook runs and the test proves nothing.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using Fail with a single webhook replica and long timeout
mistakesToAvoid.why: A slow or crashed replica stalls every matching write until the timeout, turning a policy tool into a cluster-wide outage.

title: Kubernetes Q146: How do you retrieve only the logs from a specific container in a pod that has multiple containers [L2]
summary: kubectl logs <pod> -c <container-name>. Get container names: kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[].name}'.
question: How do you retrieve only the logs from a specific container in a pod that has multiple containers?
intro: To get the logs from a specific container in a pod that runs several containers, pass the container name with kubectl logs <pod> -c <container>. Without -c, kubectl either picks a default container and prints a notice or fails, depending on version and annotations. Interviewers use this simple question to check that you know a pod is a group of containers, that init containers and crashed containers need different flags, and that you can debug sidecar-heavy workloads such as service-mesh or logging agents without scraping everything. A complete answer includes how to discover container names, filter by time, follow streams and read the previous crashed instance.

steps.title: Step zero: list the containers in the pod
steps.description: You cannot select a container you cannot name, so start by discovering the names, including init and ephemeral ones.
items: Quick list: kubectl get pod my-pod -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}' prints the regular containers; use .spec.initContainers[*].name for init containers.
Human view: kubectl describe pod my-pod shows each container state, restart count, last termination reason and exit code.
Hint from kubectl: running kubectl logs my-pod on a multi-container pod prints Defaulted container "app" out of: app, istio-proxy on modern versions, which reveals the names.
Default container: the annotation kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-container on the pod sets which container kubectl picks when -c is omitted.

steps.title: Hands-on: logs from a specific container in a pod
steps.description: The core command is the same for every case: add -c, then layer flags for time, size and follow behaviour.
items: Basic: -c app returns only that container stdout and stderr as captured by the container runtime, leaving the sidecar noise out.
Bound the output: combine --tail=200, --since=15m and --timestamps so you do not download a huge log or lose time correlation.
Stream live: -f follows the log; pair it with --tail=0 to see only new lines during a reproduction.
Namespace: add -n prod, because a pod name alone resolves only in the current context namespace.
Multiple lines of context: -c app --tail=50 -f is the usual live debugging combination while you reproduce a request.
steps.codeBlock:
# Only the app container
kubectl logs my-pod -n prod -c app

# Last 200 lines from the last 15 minutes, with timestamps
kubectl logs my-pod -n prod -c app --tail=200 --since=15m --timestamps

# Follow a sidecar live
kubectl logs my-pod -n prod -c istio-proxy -f --tail=0

# Init container logs (they have already exited)
kubectl logs my-pod -n prod -c wait-for-db

steps.title: Crashed containers and many pods at once
steps.description: A restarting container hides its failure reason in the previous instance, and real incidents involve several replicas.
items: Previous instance: --previous (or -p) prints logs of the last terminated container, essential in CrashLoopBackOff where the current instance has just started.
Whole pod: --all-containers=true merges every container, and --prefix labels each line with pod and container so you can still tell them apart.
By label: kubectl logs -l app=my-app -c app reads from all matching pods; --max-log-requests caps parallel streams (default 5) when following many pods.
Via workload: kubectl logs deploy/my-app -c app selects one pod from the deployment, convenient but not a view of every replica.
steps.codeBlock:
# Why did it crash? read the previous run of the failing container
kubectl logs my-pod -n prod -c app --previous --tail=100

# All containers in all pods with this label, tagged by source
kubectl logs -n prod -l app=my-app --all-containers=true --prefix --since=10m

# Check exit code and reason first
kubectl get pod my-pod -n prod \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[?(@.name=="app")].lastState.terminated}'

steps.title: Verify and troubleshoot common errors
steps.description: Most failures come from a wrong name, a container that has not started, or logs that never reached the kubelet.
items: container not found: a typo or a name from another pod; recheck with the jsonpath listing and remember init and ephemeral containers use the same -c flag.
waiting to start: ContainerCreating or PodInitializing means no log exists yet; read kubectl describe pod events for image pull or volume problems.
Empty output: the app may log to a file instead of stdout; Kubernetes only exposes stdout and stderr, so run kubectl exec my-pod -c app -- tail /var/log/app.log for that case.
Logs vanish after deletion: kubectl reads from the node, so logs disappear when the pod is evicted or deleted and are subject to kubelet rotation limits.

steps.title: Production practice beyond kubectl logs
steps.description: kubectl is for live debugging; durable investigation needs centralised logging and sane sidecar design.
items: Ship logs: run a node-level agent (Fluent Bit, Vector or the Grafana Alloy agent) that tags records with container_name, so queries filter the same way -c does.
Structured output: emit JSON to stdout with a request ID so you can correlate the app with its proxy sidecar logs.
Rotation: tune kubelet containerLogMaxSize and containerLogMaxFiles so a chatty container cannot fill node disk.
Ephemeral debugging: when a distroless container offers no shell, attach one with kubectl debug -it my-pod --image=busybox --target=app.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: In CrashLoopBackOff always add --previous together with -c, because the current container instance has barely started and the real error lives in the previous one.
elevatorPitch: A pod can hold several containers, so I select one with kubectl logs <pod> -c <container>, using jsonpath or describe to find the names.
I verify with --since, --tail and --timestamps, add --previous for crashes, and check events if the container never started.
I automate this by shipping stdout to a central log stack labelled by container name and by setting a default-container annotation on sidecar-injected pods.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting --previous on a crash-looping container
mistakesToAvoid.why: The live container often has no useful output yet, so you miss the stack trace that explains the restart.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming deploy/my-app shows every replica
mistakesToAvoid.why: kubectl picks a single pod from the workload; use a label selector or central logging for all replicas.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Looking for file-based logs with kubectl logs
mistakesToAvoid.why: Only stdout and stderr are captured; an app writing to a file inside the container produces empty output.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Dumping full unbounded logs
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without --tail or --since a busy container returns huge output, slows the API server path and hides the relevant window.

title: Kubernetes Q147: What is kubectl apply --prune [L2]
summary: kubectl apply --prune makes kubectl apply delete live objects that were previously applied by kubectl but are no longer present in the manifests you pass, so the cluster converges to the files rather than only adding or changing.
question: What is `kubectl apply --prune`?
intro: kubectl apply --prune makes kubectl apply delete live objects that were previously applied by kubectl but are no longer present in the manifests you pass, so the cluster converges to the files rather than only adding or changing things. It works by comparing against the last-applied-configuration annotation within a label selector or the --all scope. Interviewers ask it because it is powerful and dangerous: a wrong selector can delete workloads, and the feature has long been documented as alpha with an ApplySet-based rewrite in progress. A senior answer explains the mechanics, the guardrails and when to use GitOps pruning instead.

steps.title: Mental model: how apply --prune decides what to delete
steps.description: Plain apply never deletes, so removed files leave orphans; prune closes that gap with a bounded comparison.
items: Without prune: deleting service.yaml from your repo and re-running kubectl apply -f . leaves the Service running because kubectl has no record that the file ever existed.
With prune: kubectl lists live objects of the allowed kinds that match your selector and carry the last-applied annotation, then deletes those not in the current input.
Scope is mandatory: you must give -l key=value or --all, otherwise the command refuses, which limits blast radius to that label set.

Status: classic prune is still flagged alpha in kubectl docs. A newer ApplySet design (--applyset, gated by KUBECTL_APPLYSET=true) exists since about 1.27 but is also alpha, so check your kubectl version.
Comparison: kubectl delete -f removes what is in files; prune removes what is not in the files, which is the reverse.

steps.title: Hands-on: kubectl apply --prune with a label selector
steps.description: Always label everything you manage, restrict kinds with an allowlist and look at a diff before deleting anything.
items: Label the set: put one unique label such as app.kubernetes.io/part-of: my-app on every manifest so the selector matches exactly your objects.
Allowlist kinds: --prune-allowlist=group/version/kind (older name --prune-whitelist, deprecated) limits what may be deleted. Without it a built-in default list of namespaced kinds applies.
Preview first: --dry-run=server prints pruned lines for would-be deletions without acting, and kubectl diff shows changes to existing objects.
Namespace: pass -n prod explicitly; pruning is evaluated within the namespace of the manifests.
steps.codeBlock:
# 1) Preview: see which objects would be pruned
kubectl apply -f manifests/ -n prod \
  -l app.kubernetes.io/part-of=my-app \
  --prune \
  --prune-allowlist=core/v1/Service \
  --prune-allowlist=apps/v1/Deployment \
  --prune-allowlist=core/v1/ConfigMap \
  --dry-run=server

# Example output
# deployment.apps/my-app configured (server dry run)
# service/old-api pruned (server dry run)

# 2) Same command without --dry-run to execute

steps.title: Verify safely before you prune
steps.description: Treat prune like a delete command, because it is one, and confirm the selector and the candidate list.
items: Inventory live set: kubectl get all,cm,ingress -n prod -l app.kubernetes.io/part-of=my-app shows exactly what the selector sees today.
Compare to files: every listed object that has no manifest in your directory is a deletion candidate; make sure that is intended.
Check annotation: only objects with kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration are prunable; objects created with kubectl create or by controllers are usually not.
Stage first: run the identical command in a non-production namespace or cluster before production, and require review of the dry-run output in CI.

steps.title: Failure modes and edge cases
steps.description: Most prune incidents come from broad selectors, incomplete manifests or mixed ownership of objects.
items: Partial input: applying a subset of files with prune deletes everything else under the label. Pass the whole directory every time, or never prune.
Shared labels: if another team or Helm release uses the same label, you can delete their objects. Use a label unique to your release.
Cluster-scoped and CRDs: pruning custom resources or cluster-scoped kinds requires allowing them explicitly; deleting a CRD cascades to all its custom resources, so keep CRDs out of the prune set.
Stateful data: pruned PVCs may delete volumes depending on reclaim policy. Never allowlist PersistentVolumeClaim casually.
steps.highlight: There is no undo: pruned objects are gone, and the secret values or PVC data may be unrecoverable. Keep manifests in Git and back up stateful data.

steps.title: Production practice: prefer declarative controllers
steps.description: In automated delivery, prune should be a feature of the deployment tool, with audit trails and approvals.
items: Argo CD: enable syncPolicy.automated.prune: true or sync with prune, and use PruneLast and per-resource Prune=false annotations to protect critical objects.
Flux: set prune: true on the Kustomization; Flux tracks inventory itself rather than relying on selectors.
Helm: helm upgrade already removes resources dropped from the chart, so you do not need kubectl prune for charts.
Guardrails: add RBAC limiting delete rights, namespace-scoped service accounts, and alerts for large delete counts in a single sync.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Pair --prune with a label unique to your release, an explicit --prune-allowlist and a --dry-run=server review, and move to Argo CD or Flux inventory-based pruning for anything production.
elevatorPitch: kubectl apply --prune deletes live objects, within a label selector, that were applied earlier but are missing from the current manifests.
I verify by running --dry-run=server first, listing the selector with kubectl get, and confirming the allowlist of kinds.
I automate this with GitOps tools such as Argo CD or Flux that track inventory, and I avoid raw kubectl prune in production pipelines.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Pruning with a partial set of files
mistakesToAvoid.why: Anything under the selector that is not in the input is deleted, so a single-file apply can remove the rest of the application.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using a generic label like app=web
mistakesToAvoid.why: The selector can match objects from other releases and delete them even though you never meant to manage them.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Allowlisting PVCs, CRDs or Namespaces
mistakesToAvoid.why: Deleting these can destroy data or cascade to every custom resource or object in the namespace.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating prune as stable and complete
mistakesToAvoid.why: The documented alpha status means behaviour and flags have changed; test on your exact kubectl version and read its help output.

title: Kubernetes Q148: How do you implement an egress gateway in a Kubernetes cluster [L3]
summary: Force all outbound traffic through a central point (useful for IP whitelisting at third-party APIs). With Istio: configure an EgressGateway service and VirtualService/DestinationRule to route external traffic through it.
question: How do you implement an egress gateway in a Kubernetes cluster?
intro: "Kubernetes is a declarative desired state system; understanding the reconciliation loop is how you diagnose this quickly. When addressing this question, I walk the interviewer through our production incident runbook: isolating the blast radius, checking diagnostic logs and metrics, and applying a safe fix."

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: Force all outbound traffic through a central point (useful for IP whitelisting at third-party APIs). With Istio: configure an EgressGateway service and VirtualService/DestinationRule to route external traffic through it. The gateway's pod IPs can be given static Elastic IPs on AWS. All external traffic appears from known IPs.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Force all outbound traffic through a central point (useful for IP whitelisting at third-party APIs). With Istio: configure an Egre.
elevatorPitch: Immediate Triage: Force all outbound traffic through a central point (useful for IP whitelisting at third-party A
Run targeted verification commands before modifying configuration.
Automate permanent guardrails (CI check, alerts, IaC policy) to prevent recurrence.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Over-granting cluster-admin permissions to pod ServiceAccounts instead of scoping namespace Roles when configuring implement egress gateway
mistakesToAvoid.why: Over-granting cluster-wide permissions violates least-privilege principles and allows compromised pods to escalate privileges across namespaces.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Referencing mutable latest container tags across production Kubernetes Deployment specs when configuring implement egress gateway
mistakesToAvoid.why: Deployments referencing `:latest` risk inconsistent versions across replica pods and break deterministic rollback capabilities.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting pod readiness probes, causing traffic to hit uninitialized application containers when configuring implement egress gateway
mistakesToAvoid.why: Readiness probes gate traffic delivery; missing probes cause Kubernetes to route user requests to pods before dependencies or caches are loaded.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Executing diagnostic triage without analyzing chronological cluster events and describe outputs when configuring implement egress gateway
mistakesToAvoid.why: Cluster events provide sequential timestamps of scheduler decisions, probe failures, and image pull timeouts essential for rapid root-cause isolation.

title: Kubernetes Q149: What is the significance of the --dry-run=server flag vs --dry-run=client [L2]
summary: kubectl --dry-run=server vs client comes down to where the request is processed: with client kubectl builds and prints the object locally and never contacts the API server for it, while with server the API server runs the full.
question: What is the significance of the `--dry-run=server` flag vs `--dry-run=client`?
intro: kubectl --dry-run=server vs client comes down to where the request is processed: with client kubectl builds and prints the object locally and never contacts the API server for it, while with server the API server runs the full request path (authentication, authorization, admission, validation) and then stops before persisting. Interviewers use it to test whether you know why a manifest can pass a client dry-run and still be rejected on a real apply.

steps.title: Mental model: three values, three behaviours
steps.description: The flag accepts none (default), client and server. The old bare --dry-run and --dry-run=true forms are deprecated.
items: client: no object is sent; useful for generating YAML with -o yaml and basic schema validation.
server: request is sent with the dry-run flag; the object goes through admission and validation but is not stored.
Response: server mode returns the object as it would be stored, including defaults and webhook mutations.
Side effects: none persisted in either mode.

steps.title: Hands-on: --dry-run=server vs client in practice
steps.description: Use each mode for what it is good at.
items: Scaffold manifests: kubectl create deploy ... --dry-run=client -o yaml prints YAML with no cluster needed beyond discovery.
Validate for real: kubectl apply -f x.yaml --dry-run=server hits admission and policy.
See defaults: add -o yaml to inspect the object the server would store.
Strict schema: --validate=strict rejects unknown or duplicate fields on current kubectl versions.
steps.codeBlock:
# client: generate YAML locally
kubectl create deployment my-app --image=registry.example.com/my-app:1.4.0 \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml

# server: run through admission without persisting
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml -n prod --dry-run=server -o yaml | head -n 30
# deployment.apps/my-app created (server dry run)

steps.title: Verify what each mode catches
steps.description: A concrete comparison shows the significance.
items: Client misses: missing namespace, name conflicts with immutable fields, ResourceQuota or LimitRange violations, Pod Security admission, validating webhooks, RBAC denial.
Server catches: all of the above because they run in the API server.
Test: apply a Pod that violates a Pod Security restricted namespace; client passes, server rejects.
Output marker: messages end with (dry run) or (server dry run).
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl apply -f privileged-pod.yaml -n restricted-ns --dry-run=client
# pod/priv created (dry run)

kubectl apply -f privileged-pod.yaml -n restricted-ns --dry-run=server
# Error from server (Forbidden): pods "priv" is forbidden: violates PodSecurity "restricted:latest"

steps.title: Failure modes and caveats
steps.description: Server dry-run is accurate but not free of constraints.
items: Webhooks: admission webhooks with sideEffects other than None/NoneOnDryRun are rejected for dry-run requests.
Permissions: the caller needs the real verb (create, patch) on the resource, so read-only CI users fail.
Dependencies: a namespace or CRD that is itself only in the same manifest set does not exist yet, so later objects fail validation.
Not runtime: a passing dry-run does not guarantee scheduling success, image pulls or probe health.
Generated names: generateName objects show placeholder results in dry-run.

steps.title: Production practice: layered validation in CI
steps.description: Combine cheap and authoritative checks.
items: Stage 1: offline schema checks (kubeconform, --dry-run=client) on every commit.
Stage 2: --dry-run=server against a staging or preview cluster before merge.
Stage 3: kubectl diff to show reviewers the change.
Policy: admission policy (Kyverno, Gatekeeper, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy) is only exercised by server dry-run.
steps.highlight: Use client dry-run to generate, server dry-run to validate. Only the server answers 'will my cluster accept this?'.

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
steps.description: Standard rsync -avz over SSH for millions of tiny files is extremely slow. The bottleneck becomes SSH encryption overhead and the serial nature of rsync analyzing one file at a time.
items: Parallelization: I would use find piped into xargs running multiple rsync processes in parallel, or use tools specifically designed for this like fpsync or GNU parallel.
Disable Compression: Remove the -z flag from rsync. Compressing already compressed files (like images) wastes CPU, and for tiny files, the compression overhead dominates.
Change Cipher: If I must use SSH, I'd use a faster cipher: rsync -e "ssh -c aes128-ctr".

steps.description: To optimize: Sender: tar -cf - folder | nc -l 1234 Receiver: nc 1234 | tar -xf -
items: Use Netcat/Tar (if secure): In a trusted backend network, pipe a parallel tar stream directly over unencrypted TCP via nc. It avoids SSH entirely.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: An inode (index node) is a data structure on a standard Linux filesystem that stores metadata about a file, like its size, permissions, ownership, and pointers to the disk blocks where the data is stored. It does *not* store the file name. If two different file names (paths) have the exact same inode number (verified via ls -i), it means they are Hard Links. Hard links cannot span different filesystems.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: strace relies on the ptrace system call. Every single time the application tries to do anything, ptrace forces the kernel to pause the application, do a context switch to the strace user-space tool, print the log, and context switch back. It intercepts the sys-calls securely at the kernel level, aggregates the data in memory, and only passes the summarized findings back to user space asynchronously. The overhead is virtually zero, making it completely safe for profiling high-load production servers.

steps.description: This operator manages file descriptors in Linux: 1 is Standard Output (STDOUT) and 2 is Standard Error (STDERR). title: Linux Q26: A database server has 64GB of RAM and Swap enabled Swappiness is set to the default of 60 You notice the database occasionally acts sluggish because Linux is using 5GB of Swap even though 10GB of RAM is perfectly free You disable Swap entirely via swapoff -a to force it entirely into RAM and sudden OOM Outages begin Explain this behavior [L3]
summary: Linux actively manages memory between Application Memory (Anonymous) and File Caching (Page Cache).
question: A database server has 64GB of RAM and Swap enabled. Swappiness is set to the default of 60. You notice the database occasionally acts sluggish because Linux is using 5GB of Swap, even though 10GB of RAM is perfectly free. You disable Swap entirely via `swapoff -a` to force it entirely into RAM, and sudden OOM Outages begin. Explain this behavior.
roleContext: Linux Scenario #26 (L3) · Linux / SRE — Scenario-Based Interview Questions
intro: "In an interview, I explain my systematic Linux troubleshooting methodology using Brendan Gregg's USE method. The interviewer is testing: `vm.swappiness`, Anonymous memory vs Page Cache, memory pressure.. I structure my answer around systematic triage first, root cause analysis second, and permanent remediation third."

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: Linux actively manages memory between Application Memory (Anonymous) and File Caching (Page Cache). A swappiness of 60 aggressively pages out idle, rarely used application memory to the relatively slow Swap partition to free up RAM so Linux can cache heavily requested disk files, speeding up overall I/O. When you ran swapoff, you ripped away the safety net. Now, when the database makes a sudden, massive memory allocation request, Linux has no Swap to move the idle pages to. It must furiously drop disk caches to find space. If the cache dropping isn't fast enough to satisfy the allocation speed, the kernel enters an Out Of Memory condition and the OOM Killer aggressively terminates the database to save the OS. *Fix:* Turn Swap back on, but drastically tune sysctl vm.swappiness=1 (or 10) to instruct the kernel to only swap out memory absolutely as a last resort before an OOM.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: No, the server is perfectly saturated, but not overloaded. Load Average represents the number of processes currently utilizing a CPU core, plus the processes waiting in the queue for a turn. If the load jumped to 8.00 on a 4-core machine, then 4 processes are running, and 4 are waiting—meaning the CPU is severely bottlenecked and users are experiencing delays.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: chroot (Change Root) modifies the root directory (/) for a specific running process and its children. If you chroot an app into /var/jail, the app believes /var/jail is the absolute bottom of the entire filesystem. It physically cannot cd ../../etc to steal system passwords. *Why it's insufficient:* chroot *only* isolates the filesystem view. The application can still see all other processes in the host OS, intercept network traffic, and access host hardware. If the app runs as root inside the jail, knowledgeable attackers can craft system calls to escape the chroot entirely. True isolation requires Linux Namespaces and Cgroups (e.g., Docker containerization), not just chroot.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: The specialized variable $? holds the numeric exit code of the absolute last command executed in the terminal. In Linux architecture, an exit code of 0 means success (the command executed perfectly without errors). Any numeric exit code greater than 0 (e.g., 1, 127, 255) means failure. This is why scripts often check if [ $? -eq 0 ] to decide whether to proceed to the next step or halt and throw an error.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: Yes. This is entirely supported by the /proc and /sys pseudo-filesystems. These are not real physical directories stored on the hard drive; they are dynamic illusions generated strictly in RAM by the kernel. When you run cat /proc/cpuinfo or cat /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp, you are not reading a file; you are actually making a direct system call right into the kernel space. The kernel instantly aggregates the hardware or process data and renders it as plain text output to your terminal, adhering strictly to the Linux philosophy that "everything is a file."

title: Linux Q39: A legacy cron job runs every 5 minutes (*/5 * * * *) It takes 6 minutes to complete so instances are overlapping locking the database and failing The developer wants to migrate it to systemd timers How does systemd solve this overlapping issue inherently [L2]
summary: Traditional cron is notoriously "dumb." It strictly fires by the clock regardless of the state of the previous job, requiring developers to write complex bash flock (file locking) wrappers to prevent overlap.
question: A legacy cron job runs every 5 minutes (`*/5 * * * *`). It takes 6 minutes to complete, so instances are overlapping, locking the database, and failing. The developer wants to migrate it to `systemd` timers. How does systemd solve this overlapping issue inherently?
roleContext: Linux Scenario #39 (L2) · Linux / SRE — Scenario-Based Interview Questions
intro: "We encountered this OS-level bottleneck during peak traffic and diagnosed it down to kernel and filesystem metrics. The interviewer is testing: Cron vs Systemd Timers, execution safety.. I structure my answer around systematic triage first, root cause analysis second, and permanent remediation third."

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: Traditional cron is notoriously "dumb." It strictly fires by the clock regardless of the state of the previous job, requiring developers to write complex bash flock (file locking) wrappers to prevent overlap. Systemd Timers solve this intrinsically. When you migrate it to a service.timer unit, the default behavior of systemd is that it will not trigger the linked service unit if that specific service is already actively running. steps.description: Modern Linux systems use systemd to manage services instead of SysVinit scripts. A systemd unit file (e.g., /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service) must configure restart behavior explicitly.
items: Type=simple (default): The process runs in the foreground. Systemd considers the service active when the process starts.
Type=forking: The process daemonizes itself (old SysVinit behavior). Systemd waits for the parent to exit before considering it active.
Restart=on-failure: Automatically restart if the process exits with a non-zero exit code.

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: Key directives: Example configuration: Then enable and start: systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl enable myapp && systemctl start myapp.

Type=simple

RestartSec=5

WantedBy=multi-user.target

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
steps.description: Namespaces and Cgroups are complementary isolation mechanisms:
items: Creates new namespaces for the process: unshare(CLONE_NEWPID | CLONE_NEWNET | ...)
Assigns the process to a cgroup: /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/docker// with memory.limit_in_bytes=512M
The container process thinks it's PID 1 (due to PID namespace) but the host sees it as PID 4567.

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: Namespaces isolate *visibility* (PID namespace hides other processes, network namespace creates a separate NIC, filesystem namespace provides a chroot-like view). Cgroups enforce *resource limits* (CPU shares, memory cap, I/O bandwidth, etc.). When a container starts, the container runtime (Docker/containerd): When the container process terminates, the cgroup persists because cgroups are kernel-managed resource accounting structures separate from process lifecycles. The kernel keeps tracking memory usage, I/O metrics, etc., even if the process exits. This allows inspecting historical resource consumption after a crash. Reusing the same cgroup name: If you spin up a new container and reuse the same cgroup path without cleaning up the old one, the new process joins the cgroup with the old memory limit still in place and metrics still aggregating. This can cause unexpected behavior (e.g., the old limit prevents the new container from starting). Container runtimes always clean up cgroups (or create unique names with container IDs) to prevent this collision.

steps.description: Disk latency has two distinct bottlenecks: read latency (affecting query performance) and write latency (affecting commits/fsync). They require different tools to diagnose.
items: r/s and w/s: Read and write operations per second (independently measured).
rareq-sz and wareq-sz: Average request sizes (small vs large).
r_await and w_await: Average latency for reads and writes (in ms).
svctm: Service time (how long the disk takes to serve one request).
%util: Percentage of time the disk is busy (100% = fully saturated).

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: Tool 1: iostat -x 1 shows: If r_await is 2ms but w_await is 500ms, writes are the bottleneck, not reads. Tool 2: blktrace + blkparse captures every disk I/O operation: Output shows timestamp, operation type (R/W), block address, size, queue depth, and latency for each I/O. You can see if writes are getting stuck behind a large read or being reordered by the scheduler. Root causes:
items: High write latency + queue depth > 1: Disk controller or SSD firmware throttling writes (e.g., NAND garbage collection).
High write latency + queue depth = 1: Single slow write (e.g., journal flush to slow media or encryption overhead).
Random writes slower than sequential: RAID write-back cache eviction or lack of RAID optimization for random workloads.

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
steps.description: TCP keepalive is a kernel-level mechanism that sends periodic probe packets on idle connections to verify the remote end is still alive.
items: net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time = 7200 (Wait 2 hours before sending the first probe)

net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_probes = 9 (Send 9 probes before declaring dead)

steps.description: During a RAID rebuild, the controller must read data from the surviving disks to reconstruct the missing disk's data onto the hot spare. This rebuild I/O competes directly with production I/O for the same physical disk heads, bus bandwidth, and controller queue slots.

Contention: The rebuild process and production queries fight for disk seek time, especially on spinning HDDs.
Write penalty: RAID-10 mirrors writes, so the rebuild adds extra write operations.

Throttle rebuild speed: Most RAID controllers allow setting rebuild priority (e.g., megacli -AdpSetProp RebuildRate -val 30 -a0 sets it to 30%). Lower values reduce rebuild impact but increase the vulnerable window.

items: Schedule rebuilds during low traffic: If possible, initiate manual rebuilds during off-peak hours.
Use SSDs: SSDs eliminate seek-time contention, making rebuild impact nearly negligible.
RAID controller cache: Ensure the battery-backed write cache is functioning—it absorbs write bursts during rebuild.

steps.description: Linux network bonding combines multiple physical NICs into a single logical interface for redundancy and/or throughput.
items: Mode 0 (balance-rr): Round-robin — packets are distributed across NICs sequentially. Increases throughput but requires switch configuration (EtherChannel/LACP).
Mode 1 (active-backup): Only one NIC is active; the standby takes over if the active fails. No switch configuration needed. Best for database servers where reliability matters more than throughput.
Mode 2 (balance-xor): XOR-based distribution. Requires switch support.

items: Mode 4 (802.3ad / LACP): Dynamic link aggregation using the IEEE standard. Provides both redundancy and increased throughput. Requires switch LACP support.
Mode 6 (balance-alb): Adaptive load balancing. No switch configuration needed, balances outgoing traffic.

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
steps.description: The du and df commands measure disk usage differently:
items: du walks the directory tree and sums up the sizes of files it can see (existing directory entries).
df queries the filesystem's superblock, which tracks total allocated vs. free blocks.

Deleted files still held open by processes: When a file is deleted (rm) but a process still has it open, du can't see it (directory entry is gone), but df still counts the blocks as used. Fix: lsof +L1 finds files with zero links (deleted but open). Restart the process or truncate via /proc//fd/.

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: Common causes of discrepancy:
items: Reserved blocks: ext4 reserves 5% of the partition for root by default. df accounts for these reserved blocks; du doesn't know about them. Check with tune2fs -l /dev/sda1 | grep "Reserved block count". Reduce if needed: tune2fs -m 1 /dev/sda1 (sets reserved to 1%).
Filesystem journal: The ext4 journal consumes space visible to df but not du.

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
steps.description: /dev/null is a special virtual device file known as the "bit bucket" or "black hole." Any data written to it is silently discarded, and reading from it immediately returns EOF (End of File).
items: Suppress output: command > /dev/null 2>&1 — discards both STDOUT and STDERR, running the command silently.
Suppress only errors: command 2>/dev/null — hides error messages while showing normal output.
Empty a file: cat /dev/null > /var/log/bigfile.log — truncates the file to zero bytes without deleting the inode (keeping processes that have it open happy).

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: Common uses: /dev/null is one of the "everything is a file" Unix primitives that makes shell scripting composable and clean.
items: Test write speed: dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/null bs=1M count=1000 — benchmarks pure throughput without disk involvement.
Conditional checks: if grep -q "pattern" file > /dev/null 2>&1; then ... — tests for a pattern without displaying matches.

Shared accountability: Product teams and SRE teams share the same budget. Product managers understand that pushing risky features consumes reliability budget.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: By definition, a private subnet does not have a route to the Internet Gateway (IGW) and the instances within it do not have public IPs. To allow outbound internet access (like downloading updates) while keeping the application secure from inbound connections, you must deploy a NAT Gateway (or NAT instance) in a *public* subnet. Then, you must update the private subnet's Route Table to point all default traffic (0.0.0.0/0) to the NAT Gateway. The NAT Gateway will translate the private IPs to its own public IP, fetch the update, and return the data to the instance.

question: What is the difference between an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and a Network Load Balancer (NLB)? When do you use which?
intro: "Networking issues can paralyze distributed applications. In our hybrid cloud architecture, we traced this packet path. steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
items: ALB (Layer 7): Operates at the Application layer. It understands HTTP/HTTPS headers, URLs, and cookies. You use it when you need path-based routing (e.g., /api to one target group, /images to another), WebSocket support, or advanced WAF integrations. It terminates the connection and creates a new one to the backend.

NLB (Layer 4): Operates at the Transport layer. It only understands IP addresses and TCP/UDP ports. It is incredibly fast, handles millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency, and provides a static IP address. You use it for non-HTTP traffic (like databases, SSH, or custom TCP protocols) or when you require end-to-end TLS where the backend terminates the certificate.

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: A 502 Bad Gateway from an ALB means the ALB tried to communicate with the target instance, but the connection dropped or the target returned an invalid response. The most common cause, aside from the app actually crashing, is a mismatch in Keep-Alive timeouts. If the backend web server (like Nginx or Node.js) has an idle timeout configured shorter than the ALB's idle timeout (default 60 seconds), the backend might close the TCP connection just as the ALB decides to send a new request down that established pipe. The ALB gets a connection reset and throws a 502. The fix is to ensure the backend application's idle timeout is greater than the ALB's idle timeout.

title: Networking Q7: Your database is in a private subnet with a Network ACL (NACL) that explicitly allows port 3306 inbound from the application subnet (10010/24) However the DB connections are timing out The Security Group allows 3306 What is wrong [L3]
summary: The problem is that Network ACLs are stateless.
question: Your database is in a private subnet with a Network ACL (NACL) that explicitly allows port 3306 inbound from the application subnet (10.0.1.0/24). However, the DB connections are timing out. The Security Group allows 3306. What is wrong?
intro: "In our multi-VPC setup, services in private subnets ran into this exact routing obstacle. The interviewer is testing: Ephemeral ports, stateful vs. stateless firewalls.. I structure my answer around systematic triage first, root cause analysis second, and permanent remediation third."

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: The problem is that Network ACLs are stateless. Security Groups are stateful (if you allow an inbound request, the outbound response is automatically allowed). Because NACLs are stateless, returning traffic is blocked unless explicitly permitted. When the application server hits the DB on port 3306, the database must reply to the application server's random Ephemeral Port (usually ranging from 1024-65535, typical Linux is 32768-60999). You must add an outbound rule on the database subnet's NACL to allow TCP traffic across the ephemeral port range back to the application subnet 10.0.1.0/24.

title: Networking Q8: Users resolve apimyappcom Half of them connect successfully to the new server and half keep hitting the old deprecated server even though you changed the Route53 DNS record an hour ago Why [L2]
summary: This is classic DNS caching behavior related to TTL (Time To Live).
question: Users resolve `api.myapp.com`. Half of them connect successfully to the new server, and half keep hitting the old deprecated server even though you changed the Route53 DNS record an hour ago. Why?
intro: "Isolating network failures requires proving whether packets are dropped by route tables, security groups, or stateless NACLs. The interviewer is testing: DNS propagation, TTL (Time To Live).. I structure my answer around systematic triage first, root cause analysis second, and permanent remediation third."

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: This is classic DNS caching behavior related to TTL (Time To Live). When the original DNS record was created, it had a TTL (e.g., 24 hours). When Local ISPs, recursive resolvers (like 8.8.8.8), and user browsers resolve the domain, they cache the IP address for that duration. Even though you updated the authoritative server in Route53, the downstream internet caches will not query Route53 again until their local TTL expires. To prevent this in the future, you must lower the TTL on the old record to something short (e.g., 60 seconds) at least 24 hours *before* the migration, do the migration, and then raise the TTL back up on the new IP.

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
steps.description: A SYN flood exhausts the server's TCP connections by sending SYN packets but never responding to the SYN-ACK, leaving half-open connections in the kernel's queue until it drops legitimate traffic.
items: Infrastructure Level: I would move the application behind a Layer 4/7 edge protection network like AWS Shield/WAF, Cloudflare, or an AWS ALB. These services independently handle the TCP handshake and only pass fully established HTTP connections to the backend, completely absorbing the SYN flood.

OS Level: If it's a bare-metal server, I would enable SYN Cookies via sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1. This tells the Linux kernel to stop allocating memory for half-open connections and instead encode the connection state cryptographically into the SYN-ACK sequence number, verifying it only if the final ACK arrives.

summary: This is absolutely an MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) mismatch issue.
question: We have a BGP VPN connection established over IPSec from our data center to AWS. The tunnel is "UP", but large file transfers keep freezing or failing halfway through, while small pings and SSH commands work fine. What is happening?
intro: "In our multi-VPC setup, services in private subnets ran into this exact routing obstacle. The interviewer is testing: MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit), MSS, Path MTU Discovery, IPsec header overhead.. I structure my answer around systematic triage first, root cause analysis second, and permanent remediation third."

steps.title: Initial Diagnostics & Root Cause Analysis
steps.description: This is absolutely an MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) mismatch issue.
items: Enable TCP MSS Clamping on the VPN router (modifying the TCP handshake to force a lower MSS, e.g., 1350).
Allow ICMP type 3 code 4 (Fragmentation Needed) on all firewalls.
Lower the MTU manually on the host interfaces.

steps.title: Remediation & Permanent Safeguards
steps.description: Standard ethernet MTU is 1500 bytes. However, IPsec VPN tunnels add encryption headers (ESP, tunnel mode) which consume ~50-80 bytes. If an application tries to send a full 1500-byte packet with the "Don't Fragment" (DF) bit set, the VPN router drops it because it exceeds the tunnel's inner MTU, and sends an ICMP "Fragmentation Needed" message back. However, if firewalls along the path are blocking these ICMP messages (breaking Path MTU Discovery), the application never slows down its packet size. Known as a "PMTUD Blackhole". To fix:

title: Networking Q14: What is Anycast DNS and why do CDNs and large DNS providers (like Route53 or Cloudflare 1111) use it [L2]
summary: In standard Unicast networking, one IP address points to exactly one server in the world.
question: What is Anycast DNS, and why do CDNs and large DNS providers (like Route53 or Cloudflare 1.1.1.1) use it?
intro: "When an interviewer asks how I diagnose network connectivity, I follow an outside-in OSI model approach. The interviewer is testing: BGP Anycast vs Unicast, global routing optimization.. I structure my answer around systematic triage first, root cause analysis second, and permanent remediation third."

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: In standard Unicast networking, one IP address points to exactly one server in the world. Anycast is a BGP networking technique where the *exact same IP address* is advertised by multiple servers across different geographic data centers globally. When a user in London queries 1.1.1.1, the internet's BGP routing tables route their packets to the closest (shortest path) Cloudflare data center in London. When a user in Tokyo queries the exact same 1.1.1.1, they are routed to Tokyo. This drastically reduces latency, improves high availability (if the London node dies, BGP withdraws the route and Tokyo takes over), and inherently mitigates DDoS attacks by distributing the traffic load globally.

steps.description: If the Australian user connects directly to the ALB, their TCP handshake and HTTP data traverse the public internet across multiple ISP hops, undersea cables, and peering points—which is slow, jittery, and packet-loss prone.
items: It uses Anycast IPs, so the Australian user's traffic is immediately routed to the closest AWS Edge Location in Sydney.
TCP Termination at the Edge: The TCP handshake completes instantly with the Sydney edge node, saving hundreds of milliseconds.
AWS Backbone: The data then travels from Sydney to us-east-1 strictly over AWS's dedicated, highly optimized, private fiber backbone, bypassing public internet congestion entirely.

title: Networking Q19: You see many connections in the TIME_WAIT state on your busy proxy server Is this an error What causes it [L2]
summary: TIME_WAIT is not an error; it is a normal part of the TCP teardown process.
question: You see many connections in the `TIME_WAIT` state on your busy proxy server. Is this an error? What causes it?
intro: "In our multi-VPC setup, services in private subnets ran into this exact routing obstacle. The interviewer is testing: TCP state machine, socket termination, socket reuse.. I structure my answer around systematic triage first, root cause analysis second, and permanent remediation third."

steps.title: Production Solution & Architecture
steps.description: TIME_WAIT is not an error; it is a normal part of the TCP teardown process. When the server closes a connection (by sending the first FIN packet), it enters the TIME_WAIT state for a period (usually 2 * MSL, around 60 seconds). This ensures that any delayed packets floating in the network are dropped and don't accidentally corrupt a new connection that happens to reuse the exact same source IP and port. However, on a very busy proxy, too many TIME_WAIT sockets can exhaust ephemeral ports, preventing new outbound connections. It can be mitigated by keeping connections alive longer (connection pooling), or tuning sysctl (tcp_tw_reuse=1 to safely reuse them for outbound connections).

title: Networking Q21: When architecting a new service how do you decide between using TCP or UDP [L1]
summary: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): Is a connection-oriented, stateful protocol. It guarantees delivery through acknowledgments, automatically retransmits lost packets, and orders packets correctly.
