title: Terraform Q24: What is a data source in Terraform [L2]
summary: A data source in Terraform is a read-only lookup, declared with a data block, that fetches information about something Terraform does not manage in the current configuration, such as an existing VPC, the latest AMI or the current.
question: What is a `data` source in Terraform?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #24 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: A data source in Terraform is a read-only lookup, declared with a data block, that fetches information about something Terraform does not manage in the current configuration, such as an existing VPC, the latest AMI or the current AWS account ID. Resources create and own infrastructure; data sources only read it. Interviewers ask this to check that you can integrate with existing infrastructure and other teams stacks without hard-coding IDs, and that you understand when the read happens, what happens if nothing matches and how data sources differ from variables and remote state. The answer should include a real example and the failure modes.

steps.title: Mental model: data blocks versus resource blocks
steps.description: The distinction is ownership: Terraform manages the lifecycle of resources and only queries data sources.
items: Resource: resource "aws_instance" "web" creates, updates and destroys a real object, and tracks it in state.
Data source: data "aws_vpc" "main" asks the provider API for existing information. Terraform never creates or deletes the thing it reads.
Reference syntax: read values with the data. prefix, for example data.aws_vpc.main.id.
State: results are stored in state so plans can use them, but they are refreshed on each plan and apply, so they reflect current reality.
Why interviewers care: data sources are how Terraform composes with infrastructure created by other teams, the console or a different state, without importing it.

steps.title: Hands-on: using a data source in Terraform
steps.description: Typical uses are looking up AMIs, networks, account context and outputs from another state.
items: Filter precisely: an aws_ami data source needs owners and filter blocks, otherwise it may match nothing or the wrong image.
Single match required: many data sources error if more than one result is found; use arguments like most_recent = true where offered.
Cross-stack: terraform_remote_state reads outputs from another state, though published outputs or SSM parameters create looser coupling.
Account context: aws_caller_identity and aws_region avoid hard-coding account IDs in ARNs.
Use with for_each: a data source can itself use for_each, for example to look up several subnets by ID.

steps.title: When data sources are read and how to verify
steps.description: Reads happen at plan time when arguments are known, otherwise they are deferred until apply.
items: Known arguments: the lookup runs during plan, so you can review the resolved value in the plan output.
Unknown arguments: if an argument depends on a resource not yet created, the read is deferred to apply and values show as (known after apply).
Validate results: use precondition and postcondition blocks in lifecycle (Terraform 1.2 and later) to assert a data source returned what you expect.
Quick check: terraform console evaluates expressions such as data.aws_ami.al2023.name against real state.
Refresh behaviour: terraform plan -refresh-only shows how data source results changed without proposing infrastructure edits.

steps.title: Failure modes and best practice
steps.description: Data sources are convenient, but they introduce hidden dependencies on infrastructure you do not control.
items: Nothing found: the plan fails with "no matching ... found". Check filters, region, account and permissions, since read permissions are also needed.
Drift of inputs: a most_recent AMI lookup can change on any plan and trigger instance replacement. Pin AMI names, or use SSM parameters, when stability matters.
Ordering: a data source that must read something created in the same run needs depends_on, which can defer the read to apply; prefer passing resource attributes directly.
Secrets in state: reading a secret value into a data source stores it in state, so protect and encrypt the backend.
Alternatives: if a value is a fixed setting rather than discoverable infrastructure, a variable is clearer than a lookup.
steps.highlight: Use a data source for things owned elsewhere. If your configuration owns the object, reference the resource attribute instead.

steps.title: Common data source patterns in real projects
steps.description: A few recurring patterns cover most real use.
items: Existing network: look up a shared VPC and subnets by tag so application stacks do not hard-code IDs that differ per environment.
IAM policy documents: aws_iam_policy_document builds JSON policies in HCL; it reads nothing remote but is a data source used for rendering.
Secrets and parameters: aws_ssm_parameter reads published values from another team; mark outputs sensitive and remember state storage.
Zones and availability: aws_availability_zones yields valid zones per region so modules stay portable.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Prefer stable identifiers (names, tags, SSM parameters) in data source filters and add postconditions, because a most_recent lookup can silently trigger replacements on the next plan.
elevatorPitch: A data source in Terraform is a read-only data block that looks up existing infrastructure or context, as opposed to a resource that Terraform creates and owns.
I verify it with terraform plan, terraform console and state list, and add pre or postconditions to assert the result.
I automate by replacing hard-coded IDs with data lookups and by pinning AMIs or reading published SSM parameters for cross-stack values.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using a data source for something the same configuration creates
mistakesToAvoid.why: Reference the resource attribute directly; a lookup adds an extra API call and can defer reads to apply time.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Loose filters that match multiple objects
mistakesToAvoid.why: Many data sources fail on multiple matches, and others pick an unexpected one, leading to wrong AMIs or subnets.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on most_recent for production AMIs
mistakesToAvoid.why: A new image publication changes the plan and can force instance replacement without any code change.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting the read permissions of the CI role
mistakesToAvoid.why: Data sources call real provider APIs, so a role with write-only scope fails during plan.

title: Terraform Q25: How do you manage Terraform provider credentials without hardcoding them [L3]
summary: To manage Terraform provider credentials without hardcoding them, keep secrets out of .tf files and state-adjacent code and let the provider obtain short-lived credentials from its environment: instance or workload identity, OIDC.
question: How do you manage Terraform provider credentials without hardcoding them?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #25 (L3) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: To manage Terraform provider credentials without hardcoding them, keep secrets out of .tf files and state-adjacent code and let the provider obtain short-lived credentials from its environment: instance or workload identity, OIDC federation from CI, an SSO profile or a secrets manager such as Vault. Interviewers ask this because leaked access keys in Git are a common incident cause, and because Terraform state itself can contain secrets. The best answer prefers identity-based, short-lived credentials over long-lived keys, scopes roles tightly per environment and protects the state backend.

steps.title: Mental model: how a provider finds credentials
steps.description: Providers read credentials from a defined chain, so your job is to supply one without writing secrets into code.
items: Provider block: keep it free of access_key and secret_key. Only non-secret settings such as region and assume_role belong there.
Environment chain: the AWS provider checks environment variables, shared config and credentials files, SSO, container credentials and instance metadata, in order.
Best order of preference: workload identity (EC2 role, IRSA, Pod Identity) or OIDC federation, then SSO profiles for humans, then Vault-issued dynamic keys. Static keys are last resort.
Other clouds: the same idea applies: Azure managed identity or workload identity federation, Google workload identity federation or impersonation.
Kubernetes and Helm providers: fetch cluster credentials via an exec plugin (for example aws eks get-token) instead of embedding tokens.
Backend credentials: the state backend needs its own access path; configure it through the same environment chain rather than keys in the backend block.

steps.title: Hands-on: provider credentials without hardcoding them
steps.description: Use assume_role and a named profile locally, and OIDC in CI so no secret is stored at all.
items: Local developers: run aws sso login --profile prod-admin then export AWS_PROFILE; credentials expire automatically.
Assume role: an assume_role block in the provider lets one identity switch into a per-environment role with limited rights.
Confirm identity: aws sts get-caller-identity before plan prevents applying to the wrong account.
Non-AWS secrets: pass sensitive variables through TF_VAR_name environment variables, not committed .tfvars files.

steps.title: Automation: OIDC federation from CI, no stored keys
steps.description: With OpenID Connect, the pipeline proves its identity to the cloud and receives temporary credentials for one job.
items: Trust policy: create an IAM OIDC provider for the CI system and a role whose trust policy restricts the repository, branch or environment claims.
GitHub Actions: grant permissions: id-token: write and use aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials with role-to-assume.
Least privilege: use a read-only plan role for pull requests and a separate apply role limited to the protected branch or environment.
No secrets to rotate: there are no stored access keys in repository settings, removing the largest leak surface.
Fork protection: never grant apply credentials to pull requests from forks; run those with read-only or no cloud access.
steps.codeBlock:
# .github/workflows/terraform.yml (excerpt)
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4
  - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
    with:
      role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/terraform-plan
      aws-region: us-east-1
  - run: terraform init -input=false && terraform plan -input=false

steps.title: Failure modes: secrets still leak through state and logs
steps.description: Removing hardcoded keys is only half the job, because Terraform records resource attributes in state.
items: State contains secrets: passwords, generated keys and some data source values are stored in plain text in state. Use an encrypted backend with tight access and versioning.
sensitive does not encrypt: marking a variable or output sensitive = true hides it from CLI output only; it still exists in state.
Logs and plans: avoid printing plan files or TF_LOG=DEBUG output in CI artifacts, which can expose tokens.

Secrets managers: prefer letting the application fetch secrets at runtime from Secrets Manager, Vault or External Secrets rather than injecting values through Terraform. Newer Terraform releases add ephemeral values to avoid state storage; check your version.
Rotation: if a long-lived credential is unavoidable, store it in a secrets manager, rotate on a schedule and alert on its use from unexpected networks.
steps.highlight: Scan the repository history with a tool such as gitleaks and rotate any credential that was ever committed, since deleting the line does not remove it from history.

steps.title: Governance and audit of provider access
steps.description: Credentials are only as safe as the policy around them.
items: Separate accounts: use one cloud account per environment with its own Terraform role, so a compromised dev pipeline cannot reach prod.
Audit trails: use session_name in assume_role and review CloudTrail events to see which pipeline run performed which change.
Pre-commit scanning: run gitleaks or detect-secrets in a pre-commit hook and in CI to block commits that contain keys.
Approval gates: require manual approval for apply on protected environments so credentials with write power are only used after review.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Prefer identity federation (OIDC, workload identity, SSO) over any stored key, and separate plan and apply roles; also remember that sensitive = true does not stop secrets from landing in state.
elevatorPitch: I keep provider blocks free of secrets and let the provider pull short-lived credentials from workload identity, SSO profiles, assume_role or OIDC federation.
I verify with aws sts get-caller-identity before plans, and secret scanners in CI to ensure nothing is committed.
I automate with GitHub OIDC roles per environment, an encrypted versioned state backend and Vault or Secrets Manager for any remaining secret values.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Committing terraform.tfvars with keys or passwords
mistakesToAvoid.why: Git history keeps the secret forever; use environment variables or a secrets manager and rotate anything already leaked.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming sensitive = true protects state
mistakesToAvoid.why: It only redacts CLI output; the values remain in the state file, so the backend must be encrypted and access-controlled.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: One broad admin role for every environment and for PR plans
mistakesToAvoid.why: A malicious pull request or a mistaken apply can then reach production; use separate least-privilege roles per environment and per action.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Long-lived static access keys in CI secrets
mistakesToAvoid.why: They must be rotated, can leak through logs, and are valid from anywhere; OIDC issues credentials that expire after the job.

title: Terraform Q27: How do you make Terraform wait for one resource before creating another [L2]
summary: To make Terraform wait for one resource before creating another, create a dependency edge: reference an attribute of the first resource (implicit dependency) or use depends_on when the relationship is not visible in arguments.
question: How do you make Terraform wait for one resource before creating another?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #27 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: To make Terraform wait for one resource before creating another, create a dependency edge: reference an attribute of the first resource (implicit dependency) or use depends_on when the relationship is not visible in arguments. When the provider reports a resource complete before it is truly usable, as happens with IAM or DNS propagation, add a deliberate delay with time_sleep or a proper retry mechanism. Interviewers ask this to see whether you understand Terraform dependency graph, parallelism and eventual consistency rather than reaching for sleeps. The senior answer is to prefer references, use depends_on sparingly and treat time-based waits as a last resort.

steps.title: Mental model: Terraform builds a dependency graph
steps.description: Terraform runs independent resources in parallel and orders only the ones with a known dependency.
items: Implicit dependency: using aws_iam_role.app.arn inside another resource tells Terraform to create the role first. This is the preferred form.
Explicit dependency: depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy_attachment.app] orders resources that share no attribute reference.
Parallelism: by default up to 10 operations run concurrently (-parallelism), so missing edges show up as race conditions.
Destroy order: dependencies reverse on destroy automatically, which is another reason to model them honestly.
Modules: outputs carry dependency information, so referencing module.network.subnet_ids already waits for the module resources behind that output.

steps.title: Hands-on: make Terraform wait for one resource
steps.description: Combine a reference, depends_on and a time_sleep where propagation delay is real.
items: IAM case: a role policy attachment can succeed before IAM is globally consistent, so the next service call may briefly fail with an access error.
time_sleep: from the hashicorp/time provider, it waits a set create_duration after its own dependencies complete.
Chain it: make the sleep depend on the policy attachment and make the consumer depend on the sleep.
Keep it short: choose the smallest delay that works and document why it exists.
Verify the delay is needed: remove the sleep in a scratch environment and apply; if it succeeds repeatedly, the wait was unnecessary.

steps.title: Better options than a fixed sleep
steps.description: A sleep is a guess. Use real readiness signals when the provider or tooling offers them.
items: Resource timeouts: many resources support a timeouts block, and providers often poll until the resource reaches the desired state; extend it for slow services.
Wait resources: some providers have dedicated waiters, for example certificate validation resources that wait for DNS validation to complete.
Provisioner as last resort: a local-exec that polls an endpoint can gate completion, but provisioners are discouraged and only run at creation.
Use terraform_data: terraform_data (Terraform 1.4 and later) with triggers_replace and a polling provisioner replaces older null_resource patterns.
Retries: some providers expose retry settings; for example the AWS provider supports max_retries for throttled API calls, which is different from waiting for readiness.

steps.title: Failure modes and verification
steps.description: Wrong ordering shows up as flaky applies, so verify with graphs and repeat runs.
items: Inspect order: terraform graph | dot -Tsvg > graph.svg visualises edges; a missing line between two resources explains a race.
Overusing depends_on: on modules or data sources it can force the data read to apply time and widen unknowns in plans. Prefer attribute references.
Time only at creation: time_sleep waits when created; it does not re-wait on later updates unless triggers change.
Verify idempotence: test in a clean account: apply once from scratch and expect success without a retry, then plan expecting no changes.
Failure signature: typical symptoms are access denied or not found errors that vanish on a rerun, which indicate eventual consistency rather than a real misconfiguration.
steps.highlight: Do not use -target to force ordering; it is for exceptional recovery and leaves the graph incomplete.

steps.title: Design guidance: when waiting is a smell
steps.description: Needing waits often points to a modelling problem that is better solved structurally.
items: Split stacks: if one layer must be fully ready before another starts, put them in separate root modules and apply them in order in CI.
Readiness belongs to the platform: for Kubernetes, rely on readiness probes and health checks rather than Terraform sleeps.
Document delays: add a comment naming the API behaviour that forces each wait, so a later engineer can remove it when the provider fixes it.
Observe in CI: track apply duration; sudden growth often reveals piled-up sleeps or very long timeouts.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Fix ordering with a real attribute reference first, then depends_on, and only add time_sleep for proven eventual-consistency gaps, with a comment explaining which API needs the delay.
elevatorPitch: I make Terraform wait by creating a dependency: reference the other resource attribute, or use depends_on when no attribute links them.
I verify with terraform graph and by applying from scratch in a clean account to prove it works without a retry.
I automate readiness with provider timeouts and waiters, and use time_sleep or a polling terraform_data only for documented propagation delays.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Adding time_sleep before trying references
mistakesToAvoid.why: A sleep hides a missing dependency, wastes time on every run and still fails when propagation is slower than the guess.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Putting depends_on on whole modules by habit
mistakesToAvoid.why: It makes every resource in the module depend on the target and can defer data reads to apply, producing noisy plans.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using -target to enforce ordering
mistakesToAvoid.why: It skips parts of the graph and can leave state inconsistent; model the dependency in code instead.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting provisioners to rerun on every apply
mistakesToAvoid.why: They run only when the resource is created or destroyed, so a later readiness check needs a trigger or a different design.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to pin required_providers versions, causing breaking provider upgrades in CI pipelines when configuring terraform apply failed
mistakesToAvoid.why: Unpinned provider versions automatically download breaking major upgrades during CI runs, introducing unexpected schema validation failures.

title: Terraform Q30: How do you test Terraform modules [L2]
summary: To test Terraform modules, layer cheap static checks first, then plan-level assertions, then real apply tests in a disposable account.
question: How do you test Terraform modules?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #30 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: To test Terraform modules, layer cheap static checks first, then plan-level assertions, then real apply tests in a disposable account. Use terraform fmt, validate and linters, then the native terraform test framework (Terraform 1.6 and later) with .tftest.hcl files, and reserve Terratest or full integration runs for behaviour you cannot assert from a plan. Interviewers ask this to see whether you treat infrastructure code like software: a test pyramid, safe cleanup, cost control and automation in CI. A strong answer explains what each layer catches and what it cannot.

steps.title: Mental model: a test pyramid for Terraform modules
steps.description: Cost and speed rise as you go from static checks to real infrastructure, so push most checks to the cheap layers.
items: Static: terraform fmt -check, terraform validate, TFLint rules and policy scanners such as Checkov or Trivy run in seconds without credentials.
Plan-level: terraform test with command = plan asserts planned values, conditions and variable validation without creating anything.
Apply-level: real apply in a sandbox account proves provider and API behaviour, outputs and idempotence, at the cost of time and money.
Consumer examples: keep an examples/ directory that uses the module like a caller would; tests and docs both use it.
Speed matters: static and plan tests finish in seconds to minutes, so developers actually run them locally before pushing.

steps.title: Hands-on: test Terraform modules with terraform test
steps.description: Native tests live next to the module and need no extra language or framework.
items: File layout: put *.tftest.hcl files in the module root or a tests/ directory and run terraform test.
run blocks: each run sets command (plan or apply), optional variables and one or more assert blocks.
Negative tests: use expect_failures to prove that variable validation rejects bad input.
Mocking: mock_provider (Terraform 1.7 and later) lets plan-style tests run without cloud credentials.
Run selectively: terraform test -filter=tests/bucket.tftest.hcl runs one file while you iterate, and -verbose prints plan output for debugging.

steps.title: Integration testing with Terratest and CI
steps.description: For multi-step scenarios and probing deployed endpoints, Go based Terratest is a common choice.
items: Terratest: a Go test calls terraform.InitAndApply, reads outputs, makes real checks (HTTP, SDK calls) and destroys with defer.
Isolation: use unique name suffixes and a dedicated sandbox account so parallel CI runs do not collide.
CI tiers: run static and plan tests on every pull request; run apply-based tests on merge or nightly to control cost.
Cleanup guard: add a scheduled job that deletes leftover resources by tag, because failed runs can skip destroy.

steps.title: Failure modes and what to verify
steps.description: Tests can give false confidence if they only exercise the happy path or leave debris behind.
items: Plan cannot see runtime behaviour: values known only after apply cannot be asserted at plan stage; use an apply run for those.
Idempotence: follow an apply with plan -detailed-exitcode; exit code 2 means the module produces a perpetual diff.
Version matrix: test against the minimum and latest supported provider versions declared in the module required_providers.
Cost and secrets: keep sandbox accounts with budgets, short-lived OIDC credentials and no production data.
Cleanup behaviour: terraform test destroys infrastructure created by apply runs at the end, but a crashed job can still leave resources, so tag them.
Flaky tests: retry only known transient API errors; blindly retrying hides genuine ordering bugs in the module.
steps.highlight: A passing test suite that never destroys what it creates is just a slow resource leak; always verify teardown.

steps.title: Policy and security testing for modules
steps.description: Functional tests do not prove a module is safe, so add policy checks to the same pipeline.
items: Scanners: Checkov, Trivy or tfsec flag public buckets, open security groups and missing encryption directly in HCL.
Policy as code: run OPA/Conftest or Sentinel against terraform show -json tfplan to enforce organisation rules on planned changes.
Secure defaults: write tests that assert encryption, logging and versioning are on by default, so a refactor cannot quietly remove them.
Documentation tests: run terraform-docs in CI and fail if the README is stale, keeping the module contract visible.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Put most coverage into fast plan-level terraform test runs with mock providers and validation negative tests, and keep real-apply tests for a small set of scenarios in a sandbox account with tag-based cleanup.
elevatorPitch: I test Terraform modules in layers: fmt, validate and linting, plan-based terraform test assertions, then apply tests in a sandbox.
I verify idempotence with a second plan using detailed-exitcode and verify outputs and behaviour with run assertions or Terratest.
I automate fast checks on every pull request, run apply tests on merge or nightly with OIDC credentials, and schedule tag-based cleanup.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Only running terraform validate
mistakesToAvoid.why: Validate checks syntax and types, not provider behaviour or logic, so broken conditions and wrong defaults still pass.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running apply tests in a shared or production account
mistakesToAvoid.why: Failed tests can leave or modify real resources and cost money; use a dedicated sandbox with budgets.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Skipping the second plan after apply
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without it you miss perpetual diffs caused by computed or normalised attributes.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Testing against a single provider version
mistakesToAvoid.why: Constraints allow a range, and a module can break on the minimum or newest version it claims to support.

title: Terraform Q31: What is the terraformlockhcl file and should you commit it [L2]
summary: The .terraform.lock.hcl file is Terraform's dependency lock file: it records the exact provider versions and package checksums selected by terraform init, and yes, you should commit it to version control.
question: What is the `.terraform.lock.hcl` file and should you commit it?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #31 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: The .terraform.lock.hcl file is Terraform's dependency lock file: it records the exact provider versions and package checksums selected by terraform init, and yes, you should commit it to version control. Interviewers ask because an uncommitted lock file means every laptop and CI runner can resolve a different provider version inside the same version constraint, which turns a routine plan into a surprise diff. A strong answer explains what the file contains, what it does not cover (modules), how hashes interact with multiple platforms, and how to upgrade deliberately through a reviewed pull request.

steps.title: What the .terraform.lock.hcl file records
steps.description: Think of it as a package-lock for providers: constraints say what is allowed, the lock file says what was chosen.
items: Contents: one provider block per provider with the selected version, the original constraints, and a set of hashes (h1: and zh: entries) used to verify the downloaded package.
Created by: terraform init when no entry exists for a provider. Later runs reuse the recorded version as long as it still satisfies the configuration.
Constraints vs lock: version = "~> 5.0" in required_providers permits many releases; the lock file pins exactly one of them until you ask for an upgrade.
Not covered: modules are not locked by this file. Pin them with an explicit version argument for registry modules or a git ref for git sources.

steps.title: Hands-on: should you commit the .terraform.lock.hcl file
steps.description: Commit it to the root module directory alongside your .tf files, and keep the .terraform/ directory ignored.
items: Commit: check that .gitignore contains .terraform/ but not .terraform.lock.hcl. Many generic Terraform gitignore templates were historically wrong about this.
Why: it gives reproducible provider selection across developers, CI and production applies, and it detects a tampered or substituted provider package through checksum mismatch.
Review it: a lock file change in a pull request is a provider upgrade. Reviewers should read the release notes, not just the hash noise.
Reusable modules: a child module that is never run on its own does not need its own lock file; the root module that runs init owns it.
steps.codeBlock:
# first-time setup
terraform init
git add .terraform.lock.hcl
git commit -m "Pin provider selections"

# confirm it is tracked and not ignored
git check-ignore -v .terraform.lock.hcl || echo "not ignored: good"
git ls-files .terraform.lock.hcl

steps.title: Upgrading providers and covering every platform
steps.description: Upgrades are explicit, and the file must carry hashes for every OS and architecture that runs Terraform.
items: Upgrade deliberately: terraform init -upgrade re-resolves versions within your constraints and rewrites the lock file; commit the result in its own PR.
Multi-platform hashes: if developers use macOS arm64 and CI uses Linux amd64, run terraform providers lock with every -platform so the file holds hashes for all of them.
Read-only in CI: terraform init -lockfile=readonly fails if init would need to change the lock file, which catches a forgotten commit.
Inspect: terraform providers shows which providers each module requires and terraform version lists the selected versions.
steps.codeBlock:
terraform init -upgrade

terraform providers lock \
  -platform=linux_amd64 \
  -platform=linux_arm64 \
  -platform=darwin_arm64

# CI: refuse to modify the lock file
terraform init -lockfile=readonly

steps.title: Failure modes and how to fix them
steps.description: Most lock file incidents are checksum mismatches or constraints that no longer match the recorded version.
items: Checksum mismatch: the error says the package "doesn't match any of the checksums previously recorded in the dependency lock file". It usually means the file only holds hashes for another platform; regenerate with terraform providers lock for all platforms.
Constraint conflict: if you raise the constraint above the locked version, init reports that the locked version does not match; run terraform init -upgrade.
Merge conflicts: resolve by picking one side, then re-running init (or providers lock) so the file is regenerated rather than hand-merged.
Mirrors: when using a provider mirror or private registry, hashes can differ from the public registry. Generate the lock file using the same installation source your CI uses.
Hash types: zh: hashes cover the zipped release package as published, while h1: hashes cover the unpacked contents and work across mirrors, which is why both appear.
steps.highlight: Never delete the lock file to "fix" an error without understanding why: you silently allow the next init to pick newer provider versions and change your plan.

steps.title: Automating lock file hygiene
steps.description: Treat provider upgrades as a routine, reviewed dependency update.
items: Automated PRs: Renovate and Dependabot can open pull requests that bump providers and refresh .terraform.lock.hcl; confirm your tool regenerates hashes for all platforms you use.
Plan on the PR: run terraform plan in CI for the upgrade PR so provider behavior changes appear as a visible diff before merge.
Supply chain: checksum verification plus pinned versions reduces the risk of a different package being installed than the one you reviewed.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Commit .terraform.lock.hcl, generate hashes for every platform with terraform providers lock, and use init -lockfile=readonly in CI so provider upgrades only happen through a reviewed PR.
elevatorPitch: The .terraform.lock.hcl file pins the exact provider versions and checksums chosen by terraform init, so it belongs in version control.
I verify with git diff on the file and terraform providers, and run init with -lockfile=readonly in CI.
I automate upgrades with Renovate or Dependabot PRs and refresh hashes for linux and darwin platforms.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Adding .terraform.lock.hcl to .gitignore
mistakesToAvoid.why: Each machine then resolves its own provider version, and plan results differ between laptops and CI.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Generating the lock file only on macOS
mistakesToAvoid.why: It will lack hashes for linux_amd64, so the CI runner fails with a checksum mismatch.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Deleting the lock file to clear an error
mistakesToAvoid.why: Terraform will select the newest allowed provider and may introduce unreviewed behavior changes.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming the lock file pins modules
mistakesToAvoid.why: It only covers providers; modules need their own version or git ref pinning.

title: Terraform Q32: How do you handle cross-region disaster recovery with Terraform [L3]
summary: Cross-region disaster recovery with Terraform means describing both the primary and the recovery region as code, using provider aliases and reusable modules, while the actual data replication is handled by the services themselves.
question: How do you handle cross-region disaster recovery with Terraform?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #32 (L3) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: Cross-region disaster recovery with Terraform means describing both the primary and the recovery region as code, using provider aliases and reusable modules, while the actual data replication is handled by the services themselves (S3 replication, Aurora Global Database, DynamoDB global tables). Terraform builds and keeps the DR footprint consistent; it does not fail traffic over by itself. Interviewers ask this to see whether you separate state per region, avoid making the DR region depend on the failed region, pick a pilot light or warm standby model deliberately, and rehearse the failover rather than just writing the code.

steps.title: Decide the DR model and isolate state
steps.description: The recovery tier (backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-active) drives cost, RTO and RPO, and therefore the Terraform layout.
items: Pilot light: data stores replicate continuously, compute exists at zero or minimal capacity, and you scale it up during failover. Cheap, but RTO includes scale-up time.
Warm standby: a scaled-down but running copy of the stack. Faster failover, higher steady-state cost.

State layout: keep a separate state per region (for example prod/us-east-1 and prod/us-west-2), and keep the DR state bucket outside the primary region so you can still run apply when the primary is down.
Shared code, different inputs: one module, two tfvars files, so the DR stack cannot drift from production.
RTO and RPO first: write down the recovery time and recovery point objectives per tier before choosing a model, because they decide whether continuous replication or periodic backups are acceptable.
steps.highlight: If your only state bucket and lock mechanism live in the primary region, a regional outage also blocks the Terraform run you need to recover.

steps.title: Hands-on: cross-region disaster recovery with Terraform
steps.description: Use provider aliases and pass each one into the same module.
items: Provider alias: declare a second aws provider with alias = "dr" and a different region.
Module providers map: use providers = { aws = aws.dr } so every resource in the module lands in the DR region.
Capacity variable: expose desired_capacity so DR runs at reduced size and can be raised during failover.
Global resources: IAM and Route 53 are global; create them once, not per region, to avoid duplicates and conflicts.

steps.title: Replicate data and wire traffic failover
steps.description: Terraform declares the replication and routing resources; the services move the data.
items: Object storage: enable versioning on both buckets and add aws_s3_bucket_replication_configuration with an IAM role that can replicate.
Databases: use Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB global tables where supported; check current regional support and promotion behavior for your engine.
Encryption: use multi-Region KMS keys or a destination-region key for each replicated store so replicas can be decrypted after failover.
DNS: create Route 53 failover records tied to health checks so traffic moves to the secondary endpoint when the primary is unhealthy.
Cross-region copies: use cross-region snapshot copies and AMI copies for tiers that tolerate a longer recovery time, which costs far less than a running standby.

steps.title: Failure modes to design out
steps.description: Most DR plans fail on hidden dependencies, not on the Terraform syntax.
items: Hidden regional dependencies: ECR images, secrets, AMIs, parameter store values and certificates must exist in the DR region. Copy or replicate them explicitly.
Split-brain on promotion: promoting a replica while the old primary is still writing risks divergence; define who can trigger failover and how the old primary is fenced.
Quota and capacity: check current service quotas in the DR region, and consider capacity reservations for critical instance types.
Drift: run a scheduled terraform plan -detailed-exitcode against the DR stack so manual changes are detected.
Config drift between regions: do not hand-tune the DR region. Every manual change should be backported into the shared module, otherwise failover day is the first time the stacks differ.

steps.title: Verify with drills and automate
steps.description: An untested DR stack is a hope, not a plan.
items: Game days: periodically fail traffic over in a non-production copy or a controlled window, measure the real RTO and RPO and record them.
Pipeline: apply primary and DR from the same pipeline with the same module version, gated by plan review.
Failback: document and rehearse returning to the primary, including data resynchronisation.
Runbook as code: keep the failover steps (promote database, switch DNS weight, raise desired capacity) in a scripted, reviewed procedure with a clear approval owner.
Observability: monitor replication lag and health checks from outside the primary region so the signal that triggers failover survives the outage.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Keep DR state and its locking outside the primary region, and treat the failover runbook (promotion, DNS, scale-up) as tested code, not a diagram.
elevatorPitch: Cross-region DR in Terraform is one module deployed twice through provider aliases, with per-region state and service-level replication.
I verify with scheduled plans for drift and regular failover drills that measure actual RTO and RPO.
I automate both regions from one pipeline and keep state and secrets available outside the primary region.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Storing the only state bucket in the primary region
mistakesToAvoid.why: A regional outage blocks the Terraform run you need to recover.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming Terraform replicates data
mistakesToAvoid.why: It only creates replication resources; promotion and consistency are service behaviors you must understand and test.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting regional copies of images, keys and secrets
mistakesToAvoid.why: The DR stack boots but cannot pull images or decrypt data.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Never rehearsing failover
mistakesToAvoid.why: Hidden dependencies and quota limits only appear under a real switchover.

title: Terraform Q33: What does terraform output do [L2]
summary: terraform output reads the output values of the root module from the current state and prints them, without planning or changing any infrastructure.
question: What does `terraform output` do?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #33 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: terraform output reads the output values of the root module from the current state and prints them, without planning or changing any infrastructure. It is the supported way for scripts, CI jobs and humans to consume values such as a load balancer DNS name or a cluster endpoint. Interviewers use it to check that you understand where outputs live (state, root module only), how sensitive values behave, and the difference between -json and -raw when you wire Terraform into shell pipelines.

steps.title: What terraform output reads and what it does not
steps.description: Outputs are computed during apply and stored in state; the command just reads them. Knowing this boundary explains most surprises, such as an output that exists in code but returns nothing yet.
items: Source: the root module's output blocks as recorded in the state of the current backend. It does not call cloud APIs and does not refresh.
Root only: outputs of child modules are not shown unless the root module re-exports them with its own output block.
No state, no output: before the first successful apply you get a warning that no outputs were found.
Cross-stack use: another configuration can consume the same values through the terraform_remote_state data source, which also exposes root outputs only.
Check before apply: because outputs come from state, a new output block does not appear in terraform output until you run apply (or apply -refresh-only) to store it.

steps.title: Hands-on: terraform output in scripts
steps.description: Pick the format that matches the consumer.
items: All outputs: terraform output prints every output in a human readable form; sensitive ones show as <sensitive>.
One value: terraform output alb_dns_name prints a single output; strings are quoted in this mode.
-raw: prints a string, number or bool with no quotes or newline decoration, ideal for shell variables. It fails for lists and objects.
-json: prints machine readable JSON for every output (or one) and is the right choice with jq.
steps.codeBlock:
terraform output
terraform output alb_dns_name          # "my-alb-123.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com"

URL=$(terraform output -raw alb_dns_name)
curl -fsS "https://$URL/healthz"

terraform output -json | jq -r '.alb_dns_name.value'
terraform output -json subnet_ids | jq -r '.[]'

steps.title: Sensitive outputs and what they really protect
steps.description: The sensitive flag controls display, not storage. Treat the sensitive flag as a courtesy to anyone reading terminal output, not as encryption.
items: Display: with sensitive = true the plan and the plain terraform output list hide the value.
Explicit read: naming a sensitive output, or using -json or -raw, still prints it. Do not run those in logged CI steps without masking.
State exposure: the value is stored in plaintext in the state file, so restrict and encrypt the backend and prefer a secrets manager for real secrets.
Propagation: a value derived from a sensitive input must itself be marked sensitive or Terraform raises an error.
Cleaning up: pipe sensitive values straight into the consuming command or a secure store, never into a log line, an artifact or a pull request comment.
steps.highlight: The sensitive flag is a display safeguard. Anyone who can read the state can read the secret.

steps.title: Failure modes and edge cases
steps.description: Most issues come from the wrong directory, backend or output type. Always confirm which backend and workspace you are reading before trusting what comes back.
items: Wrong working directory or workspace: you read another environment's outputs. Confirm with terraform workspace show and the backend config.
Backend not initialised: run terraform init first so the remote backend is configured.
Stale values: outputs reflect the last apply. If infrastructure changed outside Terraform, run terraform apply -refresh-only to update state first.
-raw on a list: fails with an error about unsupported type; use -json and jq.
Exit codes in scripts: terraform output returns a non-zero code when the named output does not exist, so use set -e in shell steps and fail loudly.

steps.title: Using outputs safely in pipelines
steps.description: Treat outputs as an interface between stacks and jobs. Outputs form a small public interface for your stack, so manage them like an API.
items: Stable contract: document output names and types; renaming one breaks downstream scripts and remote state consumers.
CI masking: mask values written to job variables and avoid echoing them.
Prefer data sources: for cross-stack lookups, a data source against the real resource is often less coupled than reading another stack's state.
Precondition style checks: in CI, run terraform output -json after apply and assert the expected keys exist before promoting the build to the next stage.
Documentation: add a description to each output so the purpose and expected consumers are visible to the next engineer.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Use terraform output -raw name for shell variables and -json with jq for structured data, and remember that sensitive outputs are still plaintext in state.
elevatorPitch: terraform output prints the root module's output values from the current state, with no refresh or infrastructure change.
I verify I am in the right workspace and backend, and use -raw for strings and -json for structured values.
I automate downstream steps from outputs in CI, mask sensitive ones, and keep a stable output contract.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting child module outputs to appear
mistakesToAvoid.why: Only the root module's outputs are shown; re-export them explicitly.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using -raw with lists or objects
mistakesToAvoid.why: The command errors because -raw supports only strings, numbers and booleans.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Believing sensitive = true encrypts the value
mistakesToAvoid.why: It only hides it in CLI display; the state file still contains it.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Reading outputs from the wrong workspace
mistakesToAvoid.why: Scripts then act on another environment's endpoints.

title: Terraform Q34: You want to create an S3 bucket name based on the account ID to ensure uniqueness How [L2]
summary: Use data "aws_caller_identity" "current" {} → bucket = "my-app-${data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id}".
question: You want to create an S3 bucket name based on the account ID to ensure uniqueness. How?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #34 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: To create an S3 bucket name based on the account ID in Terraform, read the account with the aws_caller_identity data source and interpolate data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id into the bucket argument. S3 bucket names are globally unique across all AWS accounts, so embedding the account ID, and often the region, avoids collisions and makes ownership obvious. Interviewers look for the data source (not a hard coded number), awareness of naming rules, and an understanding that changing a bucket name forces replacement.

steps.title: Why account ID in the bucket name works
steps.description: Uniqueness and traceability come from the prefix, not from secrecy. Treat the account ID as a uniqueness helper and a readable label, not as protection.
items: Global namespace: a bucket name must be unique across all accounts in an AWS partition, so generic names such as logs are almost always taken.
Account scoped names: company-app-logs-123456789012 is unique in practice and tells operators which account owns it.
Not a secret: account IDs are identifiers, not credentials. Do not rely on a predictable name for security; use bucket policies and Block Public Access.
Naming rules: 3 to 63 characters, lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens, starting and ending with a letter or number.
Region matters too: buckets are regional, but names are global within the partition, so adding the region helps humans and avoids collisions when one module deploys to several regions.

steps.title: Hands-on: S3 bucket name based on the account ID
steps.description: Read the identity of the credentials Terraform is actually using.
items: Data source: aws_caller_identity returns account_id, arn and user_id for the current provider configuration.
Known at plan time: the data source is read during plan, so the bucket name appears in the plan output rather than as "known after apply".

Add the region: include data.aws_region.current so the same module can be applied to several regions without a name clash. In recent AWS provider major versions the attribute is region; older ones use name, so check your provider docs.
Locals: compute the name once in locals and reuse it for tags and policies.

steps.title: Verify the generated name
steps.description: Confirm the value before and after apply. Checking in three places, the console, the CLI and the plan, catches wrong-account mistakes before data lands in the wrong bucket.
items: Console check: terraform console then evaluate local.bucket_name after init.
Identity check: compare with aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text to confirm the credentials target the expected account.
Resource check: after apply run aws s3api head-bucket --bucket <name>; no error means it exists and you can access it.
Length check: add a validation or precondition that the final name is at most 63 characters.
Plan output check: run terraform plan and confirm the bucket argument shows the full literal name, which proves the data source resolved at plan time.
steps.codeBlock:
terraform console
> local.bucket_name
"acme-app-logs-123456789012-us-east-1"

aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text
aws s3api head-bucket --bucket acme-app-logs-123456789012-us-east-1

steps.title: Failure modes and alternatives
steps.description: A name collision or an unintended rename are the usual problems. These problems are cheap to avoid when you design naming up front and expensive to repair after data exists.
items: BucketAlreadyExists: another account owns the name. Change the prefix; account IDs make this rare but a prefix like logs alone does not.
Wrong account: assuming a role changes the identity. The data source reports the role's target account, which is usually what you want, but verify the provider's assume_role block.
Rename means replace: changing bucket forces a new bucket, and Terraform cannot copy objects. Plan a migration if the bucket holds data.
Alternative: bucket_prefix lets AWS add a random suffix, which is unique but not predictable, so other systems must read the name from outputs.

steps.title: Governance and production practice
steps.description: Standardise naming so it cannot drift. A shared convention makes bucket names predictable for humans and consistent for tooling.
items: Naming module: put the convention in one module so every team produces consistent names.
Policy as code: use tflint rules, OPA or Sentinel to enforce the naming pattern and Block Public Access.
Export the name: expose it as an output so consumers do not rebuild the string.

Predictable names and squatting: a predictable name can be pre-created by someone else before you apply, so reference buckets by Terraform outputs and use bucket policy conditions, not name trust, for access control.
Multiple accounts: in a multi-account setup, run the same module per account via provider aliases or separate pipelines and let the data source supply each account's ID automatically.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Build the name from aws_caller_identity plus region in a single local, validate its length, and remember that renaming an existing bucket forces replacement.
elevatorPitch: Use the aws_caller_identity data source and interpolate account_id into the bucket argument, usually with the region as well.
I verify with terraform console, aws sts get-caller-identity and aws s3api head-bucket.
I centralise the naming in a module, enforce it with policy checks and export the name as an output.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Hard coding the account number
mistakesToAvoid.why: The code breaks when promoted to another account and invites mistakes.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating the account ID as a security control
mistakesToAvoid.why: Names are guessable; protect data with policies and Block Public Access.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Renaming a populated bucket in place
mistakesToAvoid.why: Terraform destroys and recreates it, which does not move the objects.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring the 63 character limit
mistakesToAvoid.why: Long prefixes plus account ID and region can exceed it and fail at apply.

title: Terraform Q36: What is terraform graph [L2]
summary: terraform graph prints Terraform's internal dependency graph in DOT format, which Graphviz can render as an image.
question: What is `terraform graph`?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #36 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: terraform graph prints Terraform's internal dependency graph in DOT format, which Graphviz can render as an image. Terraform builds this graph from references between resources, modules, variables and providers, and uses it to decide ordering and parallelism. Interviewers ask about it because it shows whether you understand how Terraform orders operations, and because it is the first tool to reach for when you see a dependency cycle error or an unexpected apply order. A good answer covers the command, rendering, the -type options and its limits.

steps.title: How Terraform builds the dependency graph
steps.description: Every reference creates an edge, and edges decide ordering. Understanding this model makes the output of the graph command easy to read, because every line is simply one of these relationships.
items: Implicit edges: referencing aws_subnet.a.id inside another resource makes that resource depend on the subnet, so the subnet is created first and destroyed last.
Explicit edges: depends_on adds dependencies that Terraform cannot infer from references.
Parallelism: nodes with no path between them run concurrently, limited by -parallelism (default 10).
Graph is a DAG: a directed acyclic graph. If your references form a loop, Terraform reports a cycle and refuses to continue.
Walk order: Terraform walks the graph from nodes with no dependencies outward, and walks it in reverse for destroys, which is why a subnet is deleted only after everything inside it.

steps.title: Hands-on: terraform graph with Graphviz
steps.description: Generate DOT text, then render it with the dot tool. Graphviz is a separate install and is not bundled with Terraform, so a missing dot binary is the most common first stumble.
items: Prerequisite: run terraform init in the root module first; the command needs the configuration and providers loaded.
Render: pipe the output into dot from Graphviz to produce SVG or PNG. Install Graphviz with your package manager.
Graph types: -type=plan, -type=plan-destroy and -type=apply show different phases; the default is plan style.
From a saved plan: terraform graph -plan=tfplan graphs the exact operations in a plan file.
steps.codeBlock:
terraform init
terraform graph > graph.dot
terraform graph | dot -Tsvg > graph.svg

# graph of a specific saved plan
terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform graph -plan=tfplan | dot -Tpng > plan-graph.png

steps.title: Using the graph to debug cycle errors
steps.description: A cycle means resource A needs B while B needs A.
items: Symptom: Error: Cycle: aws_security_group.a, aws_security_group.b listing the participating nodes.
Visualise: terraform graph -draw-cycles | dot -Tsvg highlights the cycle edges in colour.
Typical cause: two security groups referencing each other inline. Move the rules into separate aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule resources so the groups no longer depend on each other.
Also check: module outputs feeding inputs of a module that the first one depends on, and depends_on that points back.
Cross-checking: after breaking a cycle, re-run terraform validate and terraform plan; the cycle error disappears at graph construction time, so it is caught early.
steps.codeBlock:
terraform graph -draw-cycles | dot -Tsvg > cycles.svg

# fix: break the loop with standalone rule resources
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "a_from_b" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.a.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.b.id
  ip_protocol                  = "tcp"
  from_port                    = 8080
  to_port                      = 8080
}

steps.title: Limits and edge cases
steps.description: The raw graph is accurate but hard to read at scale. Knowing these limits keeps you from over-trusting a diagram when the plan is the real authority.
items: Noise: large configurations produce graphs with provider and root nodes that drown the useful edges. Filter with tools such as grep, or use a dedicated visualiser.
No values: the graph shows structure, not attribute values or whether a change will happen. Use terraform plan for that.
Expansion: count and for_each instances are not necessarily shown the same way in every graph type, so compare the plan-type and apply-type views when in doubt.
Format: output is plain DOT text; if dot is missing you will only see text, so verify Graphviz is installed with dot -V.
Large stacks: split the root module or generate per-module graphs, because a single image of hundreds of resources is rarely readable in a review.

steps.title: Where it fits in daily work
steps.description: Use it for explanation and troubleshooting, not as the source of truth for architecture. Used sparingly, the graph is a cheap way to turn an opaque ordering question into a visible one.
items: Documentation: attach a rendered graph artifact in CI for large stacks to help reviews.
Refactors: compare graphs before and after splitting modules to confirm dependencies did not change unexpectedly.
Ordering questions: if resources apply in a surprising order, inspect the graph before adding depends_on.
Teaching tool: showing a new teammate the graph for a small module is a fast way to explain why Terraform created resources in parallel and why one waited for another.
Pair with plan: use the graph for why an order exists and the plan for what will change; together they answer most ordering questions without guessing.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: When you hit a cycle error, run terraform graph -draw-cycles | dot -Tsvg to see the loop, then break it with standalone rule resources rather than adding more depends_on.
elevatorPitch: terraform graph prints the dependency graph as DOT text, which Graphviz renders into an image.
I verify structure with plan or apply type graphs and use -draw-cycles to debug cycle errors.
I generate graph images in CI for large stacks and compare them across refactors.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Expecting a ready made picture
mistakesToAvoid.why: The output is DOT text; you must render it with Graphviz.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Fixing cycles with more depends_on
mistakesToAvoid.why: Extra edges make cycles more likely; the fix is to remove a circular reference.

title: Terraform Q37: You need to change a resource attribute that forces replacement but you want to minimize downtime How [L2]
summary: Use create_before_destroy lifecycle:
question: You need to change a resource attribute that forces replacement but you want to minimize downtime. How?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #37 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: When a resource attribute that forces replacement must change, minimise downtime by making Terraform create the new object before it destroys the old one with lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }, avoiding name collisions, and shifting traffic gradually. The plan marks such attributes with # forces replacement. Interviewers ask this to test whether you read plans carefully, know that replacement is destroy plus create by default, and recognise resources like databases where replacement means data loss and needs a different strategy entirely.

steps.title: Understand what forces replacement
steps.description: Some attributes are immutable in the provider or the cloud API, so Terraform must recreate the object. Learning to spot these markers quickly is the single most useful habit for avoiding accidental outages from routine changes.
items: Read the plan: terraform plan shows # forces replacement next to the attribute and prints -/+ for destroy-and-recreate.
Default order: destroy first, then create. That is the source of the downtime for load balancers, security groups and instances.
Dependencies: everything that references the replaced object is updated too, which can cascade.
Data bearing resources: for databases and volumes, replacement deletes data unless you snapshot or migrate.

Common examples: renaming a resource with a fixed name, changing the subnet of an instance, or changing an immutable engine setting often trigger replacement; confirm with the provider documentation for that argument.
steps.highlight: Always read for -/+ in the plan before approving, especially on stateful resources.

steps.title: Hands-on: resource attribute that forces replacement with create_before_destroy
steps.description: Reverse the order, and make names unique so both objects can coexist.
items: Lifecycle: create_before_destroy = true builds the replacement first, updates dependents, then deletes the old object.
Name collisions: if the name is fixed, creation fails because the old object still exists. Use name_prefix or add a suffix that changes with the replacement.
Propagation: Terraform applies the same ordering to dependencies of that resource, which is usually required but can surprise you.
Typical fit: security groups, launch templates, ACM certificates, target groups and instances behind a load balancer.

steps.title: Control when and how replacement happens
steps.description: Use Terraform's own tools to rehearse and sequence the change. These options let you rehearse the replacement on one object before committing the whole fleet.
items: Force a rollout: terraform apply -replace="aws_instance.web[0]" replaces one instance deliberately, instead of the deprecated taint command.
Roll one at a time: for a fleet, replace a single instance, verify health, then continue, rather than changing all at once.
replace_triggered_by: make a resource replace when another changes (Terraform 1.2 and later), for example an instance refreshing when a related resource ID changes.
Preview: use terraform plan -out=tfplan and review it, then apply that exact plan.
Health checks: make sure the load balancer health check passes on the new target before the old one drains, otherwise create_before_destroy only moves the outage.

steps.title: Failure modes and alternatives
steps.description: Some resources cannot be made zero downtime by ordering alone. Decide before the change whether ordering alone is enough or a different migration pattern is needed.
items: Unique constraints: resources with fixed names, static IPs or unique ports fail with "already exists" under create_before_destroy.
Databases: do not replace in place. Take a snapshot, use blue/green or a read replica promotion, then repoint the application. Keep deletion_protection and a final snapshot enabled.
Avoid the change: if the attribute is not essential, use ignore_changes or keep the old value; accept drift knowingly.
Blue/green: create a parallel stack, shift DNS or load balancer weights, then remove the old stack in a later apply.
Dependents: replacing a resource changes its ID, so anything pinned to the old ID, such as allow lists or DNS records, must update in the same apply.

steps.title: Production safeguards
steps.description: Make destructive plans visible and hard to approve by accident. Guardrails matter most when a change is routine enough that reviewers stop reading the plan carefully.
items: Plan review gate: fail the pipeline or require extra approval when a plan contains deletes of tagged critical resources.
prevent_destroy: add it to critical stateful resources so a replacement attempt errors out instead of deleting.
Off-hours and canaries: schedule replacements and watch health checks and error rates during the change.
Staged rollouts: split the change into two pull requests when possible, first adding the new resource and shifting traffic, then removing the old one.
Backups and snapshots: take and verify a snapshot before touching any stateful resource, and know the restore time.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Pair create_before_destroy with name_prefix, and use prevent_destroy on stateful resources so a forced replacement stops the apply instead of deleting data.
elevatorPitch: A resource attribute that forces replacement makes Terraform destroy then create; I flip the order with create_before_destroy and unique names.
I verify by reading the plan for -/+ and forces replacement, and by rolling one instance with apply -replace.
I automate plan review gates and use prevent_destroy or blue/green for stateful resources.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Adding create_before_destroy with a fixed name
mistakesToAvoid.why: The new object collides with the old one and the apply fails midway.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Replacing a database in place
mistakesToAvoid.why: Terraform deletes and recreates it, losing data unless you migrate via snapshots or blue/green.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using terraform taint in new workflows
mistakesToAvoid.why: It is deprecated; use apply -replace so the plan is reviewable.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Approving the plan without searching for -/+
mistakesToAvoid.why: A single changed immutable attribute can destroy production resources.

steps.title: Standard terraform fmt vs terraform fmt -recursive
steps.description: Understanding directory traversal limitations:
items: Standard terraform fmt: Only parses and formats .tf and .tfvars files located directly in the current working directory. It completely ignores nested child modules or subfolders.

Recursive terraform fmt -recursive: Recursively scans every subfolder and nested module in the entire directory tree, applying canonical HashiCorp HCL style (2-space indent, equal-sign alignment, trailing commas).
In-Place Modification: Rewrites files in place and outputs the list of modified file paths to stdout.

steps.title: Automating Formatting Checks in CI/CD (-check & -diff)
steps.description: In automated pull request workflows, CI runners must verify formatting without silently mutating files:
items: The CI Command: terraform fmt -recursive -check -diff
-check: Returns exit code 0 if all files are properly formatted; returns exit code 3 if any files require formatting (failing the pipeline PR check).
-diff: Prints unified diffs directly into the CI build log showing the exact lines with spacing or indentation violations.

steps.title: Shifting Left with Git Pre-Commit Hooks
steps.description: Prevent unformatted code from ever entering Git repositories:
items: Add the Anton Babenko terraform-docs / pre-commit-terraform hook in .pre-commit-config.yaml:
- id: terraform_fmt with args: ['--args=-recursive'].
Developers receive instant feedback at git commit time, automatically reformatting staged files locally before push.

keyTakeaway: Always run terraform fmt -recursive -check -diff in CI pipelines to prevent unformatted IaC drift, and equip engineers with git pre-commit hooks for zero-friction local formatting.

title: Terraform Q40: How do you reference the output of one module in another in the same root module [L2]
summary: To reference the output of one module in another in the same root module, declare an output in the first module and pass it to the second as an input argument using module.name.output.
question: How do you reference the output of one module in another in the same root module?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #40 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: To reference the output of one module in another in the same root module, declare an output in the first module and pass it to the second as an input argument using module.<name>.<output>. Modules never read each other's internals; the root module wires them together, and Terraform infers the creation order from that reference. Interviewers use this question to check you understand module interfaces (variables in, outputs out), implicit dependencies, and how to avoid circular wiring when networking, compute and database modules depend on each other.

steps.title: The module interface: variables in, outputs out
steps.description: A module exposes only what its outputs declare. This separation is what lets teams swap or upgrade a module without touching its consumers, as long as the outputs keep their shape.
items: Child outputs: a resource attribute is invisible outside the module until an output block exposes it.
Child inputs: the consuming module declares a matching variable to receive the value.
Root wiring: the root module connects them with module.vpc.private_subnet_ids style expressions.
Implicit ordering: that reference adds a dependency edge, so the VPC module is applied before the app module without depends_on.
Terminology: the calling configuration is the parent, the called one is the child; the root module is the directory where you run terraform plan.

steps.title: Hands-on: reference the output of one module in another
steps.description: Three files: the producer's output, the consumer's variable and the root wiring. The example below is the complete pattern, and every cross-module reference in a real project follows the same three steps.
items: Producer: modules/vpc/outputs.tf exports the IDs the consumer needs.
Consumer: modules/app/variables.tf declares typed variables with descriptions.
Root: main.tf passes module.vpc.* into the app module call.
Types: keep outputs typed and minimal, for example a list of subnet IDs, not the whole resource object.
Run it: terraform init then terraform plan; Terraform shows the app module's inputs as known after apply until the VPC exists.

steps.title: Modules with count and for_each
steps.description: The reference syntax changes when a module call is expanded. Expanded modules are the most common source of confusing reference errors in larger codebases.
items: count: use module.vpc[0].vpc_id to pick an instance, or module.vpc[*].vpc_id for all. Pick the form that matches how the producer module is called.
for_each: use module.vpc["prod"].vpc_id, or build a map with a for expression: { for k, m in module.vpc : k => m.vpc_id }.
Sensitive: an output derived from a sensitive value must be marked sensitive = true, and consumers keep the flag.
Inspect: terraform console evaluates module.vpc.private_subnet_ids after the first apply.
Splat expressions: with count on the producer, module.vpc[*].private_subnet_ids returns a list of lists, so use flatten() when the consumer expects a flat list.

steps.title: Failure modes and fixes
steps.description: Most errors are missing outputs, wrong types or cycles. Reading the error message carefully usually tells you which side of the interface is missing or mismatched. Fix the interface rather than working around it.
items: Unsupported attribute: "This object does not have an attribute named ..." means the child module has no such output. Add the output block and re-run.
Type mismatch: passing a string where a list is expected. Check variable type and the output's value shape.
Cycle between modules: if networking needs a security group from compute and compute needs a subnet from networking, split the shared piece into a third module.
depends_on on modules: only add it for hidden side effects; references already create ordering.
Type conversion: use tolist() or toset() deliberately when an output is a set but the consumer variable is a list.

steps.title: Practice for maintainable modules
steps.description: Design outputs as a stable API. Good module interfaces are small, typed and documented, which keeps root modules readable.
items: Describe outputs: add description so the registry and docs are useful.
Avoid leaking internals: export IDs and ARNs, not entire resource objects, so refactors inside the module do not break consumers.
Version modules: when you rename or remove an output, treat it as a breaking change and bump the module version.
Naming outputs: choose names that describe the value, such as private_subnet_ids rather than subnets, so call sites read clearly.
Testing: use terraform test (Terraform 1.6 and later) or a small example directory to check that outputs keep their shape when the module changes.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Export only the IDs consumers need, and wire them in the root with module.name.output; if two modules need each other, extract the shared resource into a third module.
elevatorPitch: You expose a value with an output block in module A and pass module.a.output_name into a variable of module B in the root module.
I check wiring in terraform console and with plan, where a missing output fails immediately.
I treat outputs as a versioned API, describe them and avoid leaking whole resource objects.

mistakesToAvoid.why: It adds unnecessary coupling and can create cycles or delay planning.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Outputting entire resource objects

title: Terraform Q42: What does terraform state list do [L2]
summary: terraform state list prints the address of every resource and data source tracked in the current Terraform state, one per line.
question: What does `terraform state list` do?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #42 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: terraform state list prints the address of every resource and data source tracked in the current Terraform state, one per line. It is read-only and does not contact cloud APIs, which makes it the quickest way to see what Terraform believes it manages. Interviewers ask about it because it underpins safe state surgery: before you import, move or remove anything you must know the exact address. A strong answer covers filters, quoting for indexed resources, the companion commands, and the safeguards around state-changing siblings.

steps.title: What state list shows and what it does not
steps.description: It reads the state snapshot from your configured backend. Keeping this in mind prevents the classic mistake of assuming the state view matches what exists in the cloud.
items: Output: resource addresses such as aws_instance.web, module.vpc.aws_subnet.private[0] and data.aws_ami.ubuntu.
Scope: everything in state, including data sources and resources in child modules, but not output values (use terraform output) and not unmanaged cloud resources.
Read-only: no refresh, no plan, no changes. It does need a working backend and credentials to read remote state.
Source of truth: state is Terraform's record, not reality; a resource listed here may have been deleted outside Terraform.
Address format: addresses follow module.<name>.<type>.<name>[index or key], and the same string is what you use in -target, -replace and import blocks.

steps.title: Hands-on: terraform state list with filters
steps.description: Narrow the list to find the address you need.
items: Filter by address: terraform state list module.vpc lists only resources under that module; a resource type prefix works too.
Filter by ID: terraform state list -id=i-0abc123 finds the address that owns a provider ID.
Quote indexed addresses: in shells wrap keys in single quotes, for example 'aws_instance.web["a"]', so the shell does not strip the inner quotes.
Count: pipe to wc -l or grep for quick audits.
steps.codeBlock:
terraform state list
terraform state list module.vpc
terraform state list -id=i-0abc123def4567890
terraform state list | grep '^aws_s3_bucket'
terraform state list | wc -l

steps.title: Pair it with state show and the safe-change workflow
steps.description: List finds the address; the next commands inspect or modify it. Always inspect with the read-only commands before you reach for anything that rewrites state.
items: Inspect: terraform state show 'aws_instance.web["a"]' prints the recorded attributes of one resource.
Rename or move: terraform state mv changes an address, but in Terraform 1.1 and later a moved block is preferred because it is reviewable in code.
Forget a resource: terraform state rm removes it from state without destroying it; in 1.7 and later a removed block does this declaratively.
Backups: before any write command, pull a copy with terraform state pull > backup.tfstate.
Import check: after adding an import block and applying, run state list to confirm the new address appears and then run plan to confirm there is no diff.
