terraform state show 'aws_instance.web["a"]'
terraform state pull > backup-$(date +%F).tfstate

# preferred for refactors: declarative, reviewable
moved {
  from = aws_instance.web
  to   = module.web.aws_instance.this
}

steps.title: Failure modes and troubleshooting
steps.description: Empty or surprising output almost always points to the wrong backend or workspace. A quick checklist of backend, workspace and credentials resolves nearly every case of confusing output.
items: Empty output: you may be in the wrong directory, workspace or backend. Check terraform workspace show and the backend block, and run terraform init.
Access errors: reading remote state requires permissions on the bucket or workspace; check credentials and role.
Lock contention: listing is read-only, but a stale lock can still block commands that write. Use terraform force-unlock only after confirming no run is active.
Missing resource: if a resource you expect is absent, it was never imported or was removed; bring it under management with an import block.
Large states: state with thousands of resources makes plans slow; use state list counts by module to decide where to split the configuration.

steps.title: Production practice
steps.description: Treat state operations as controlled changes. State is critical infrastructure data, so changes to it deserve the same discipline as changes to production code.
items: Access control: restrict who can write state; state can contain secrets, so encrypt the backend and log access.
Audits: run state list in a pipeline to detect unexpected resource types or to confirm a migration moved everything.
Prefer config over CLI surgery: use moved, import and removed blocks so peers can review the change.
Drift detection: combine state list with cloud inventory queries to find resources that exist in the account but were never brought under Terraform.
Backend hygiene: enable versioning on the state bucket so a bad write can be rolled back to a previous object version.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Use terraform state list to find the exact address, quote indexed keys, take a state pull backup, and prefer moved blocks over state mv for reviewable refactors.
elevatorPitch: terraform state list prints the address of every resource and data source in the current state, read-only.
I verify with state show, and filter by module or -id when hunting for an address.
I back up state before changes and prefer moved, import and removed blocks to manual state surgery.

mistakesToAvoid.why: A listed resource may be gone in the cloud and an unlisted one may exist; state list reports only what Terraform tracks.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Forgetting to quote indexed addresses
mistakesToAvoid.why: The shell strips quotes and Terraform reports no matching resource.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running state rm or mv without a backup
mistakesToAvoid.why: A wrong address can orphan or later recreate real infrastructure.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running it in the wrong workspace
mistakesToAvoid.why: You inspect another environment's state and draw wrong conclusions.

title: Terraform Q45: How do you handle a situation where Terraform needs to create resources in a specific order (eg wait 30 seconds for IAM propagation) [L3]
summary: Use time_sleep resource from the hashicorp/time provider:
question: How do you handle a situation where Terraform needs to create resources in a specific order (e.g., wait 30 seconds for IAM propagation)?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #45 (L3) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: To make Terraform create resources in a specific order, express the order as dependencies: reference attributes so Terraform infers edges, add depends_on where no attribute links two resources, and use the time_sleep resource from the HashiCorp time provider when you must wait for eventual consistency, such as IAM propagation. Terraform does not run top to bottom; it walks a dependency graph in parallel. Interviewers want to hear that you reach for references first, use a delay only as a targeted last resort, and avoid local-exec sleeps.

steps.title: How ordering works in Terraform
steps.description: The file order is irrelevant; the dependency graph decides. Once you accept that ordering is a graph property, every fix becomes a question of adding the right edge.
items: Implicit dependency: using aws_iam_role.app.arn in another resource makes Terraform create the role first. This is the preferred mechanism.
Explicit dependency: depends_on = [ ... ] adds an edge when the relationship is real but invisible in arguments, for example an IAM policy that a Lambda needs at runtime.
Parallel by default: independent resources are created concurrently (default -parallelism=10), which exposes race conditions with eventually consistent APIs.
Destroy order: reversed automatically; dependents are destroyed before the things they depend on.
Why races happen: IAM is eventually consistent, so a role or policy can be accepted by the API but not yet visible to another service that tries to use it moments later.

steps.title: Hands-on: create resources in a specific order with time_sleep
steps.description: Insert a controlled wait between the IAM change and its first consumer.
items: Provider: hashicorp/time supplies time_sleep with create_duration and destroy_duration.
Wiring: the sleep depends on the IAM resource, and the consumer depends on the sleep. Both edges are needed.
Triggers: by default the sleep runs once; use triggers to wait again when the upstream value changes.
Scope it: keep the delay small and attached to one pair of resources, not global.
Version note: check the current hashicorp/time provider version on the registry and pin a constraint; the time_sleep resource has been stable for years.

steps.title: Verify the order and the fix
steps.description: Confirm both that the dependency exists and that the race is gone. Seeing the wait in the log and the edge in the graph together is good evidence that your fix is wired correctly.
items: Graph: terraform graph | dot -Tsvg shows the edge from the consumer to the sleep and from the sleep to the IAM resource.
Apply log: the output shows time_sleep.wait_30_seconds: Still creating... before the consumer starts.
Re-run: apply from a clean state in a test account several times; a race may only fail occasionally.
Error signature: messages like "role cannot be assumed" or "invalid principal in policy" right after creation point to eventual consistency.
steps.codeBlock:
terraform apply
# ...
# time_sleep.wait_30_seconds: Creating...
# time_sleep.wait_30_seconds: Still creating... [10s elapsed]
# time_sleep.wait_30_seconds: Creation complete after 30s
# aws_lambda_function.fn: Creating...

steps.title: Alternatives and failure modes
steps.description: A sleep is a guess; know when it is wrong. A delay hides the symptom of a race, so always understand which API is eventually consistent before adding one.
items: Fixed delay may be too short: propagation time varies. Check for provider retry behavior first, and keep the delay as a safety margin rather than a proof.
local-exec sleep: provisioner "local-exec" { command = "sleep 30" } works but is opaque, platform dependent and not modeled in the graph. Provisioners are a last resort.
Better signals: where the API offers a waiter or a data source that confirms readiness, use it instead of time.
Split applies: for rare cases, apply a foundational layer first in a separate state or pipeline stage.
Provider retries: many AWS provider resources already retry on known propagation errors, so a delay is only needed when you can reproduce a failure.

steps.title: Production practice
steps.description: Keep ordering explicit and documented. Explicit, commented ordering is easier to maintain than clever tricks that nobody remembers later.
items: Comment the why: note the failure that prompted each depends_on or delay so future readers do not delete it.
Review delays: periodically test removing them after provider upgrades, since providers often add retries.
Pipeline stages: separate foundation (IAM, networking) from workloads to reduce intra-apply races.
Cost of waiting: every sleep adds to total apply time, which matters in pipelines that provision many environments; measure before and after.
Testing in a clean account: run the full apply in a fresh sandbox periodically, since a warm account hides propagation races that appear on first creation.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Use references first, depends_on second, and a scoped time_sleep only for proven eventual-consistency races such as IAM propagation.
elevatorPitch: Terraform orders by dependency graph, so I use attribute references, depends_on, and time_sleep for IAM propagation.
I verify with terraform graph and apply logs, and test from a clean account to catch races.
I document each delay and revisit it after provider upgrades, avoiding local-exec sleeps.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on file order
mistakesToAvoid.why: Terraform ignores it; independent resources run in parallel.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Adding a sleep without a depends_on edge to it
mistakesToAvoid.why: The consumer may start before the sleep, so the wait does nothing.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using local-exec sleep as the default tool
mistakesToAvoid.why: It is invisible to the graph, platform dependent and brittle.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Setting one large global delay
mistakesToAvoid.why: It slows every apply and still does not guarantee readiness.

title: Terraform Q46: What is the Terraform Registry [L2]
summary: The Terraform Registry is the public index at registry.terraform.io where Terraform downloads providers and shares reusable modules, addressed as namespace/name for providers and namespace/name/provider for modules.
question: What is the Terraform Registry?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #46 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: The Terraform Registry is the public index at registry.terraform.io where Terraform downloads providers and shares reusable modules, addressed as namespace/name for providers and namespace/name/provider for modules. Terraform init resolves these sources automatically. Interviewers ask about it because it sits in your supply chain: you should know how sources and versions are pinned, how providers are verified, how publishing works, and what to use when you need a private registry or an air-gapped mirror.

steps.title: What the registry hosts
steps.description: Two kinds of artefacts share one index. Understanding the two artefact types and their addresses explains most init output you will ever read.
items: Providers: plugins that talk to APIs, such as hashicorp/aws. Tiers include Official (HashiCorp), Partner and Community.
Modules: reusable configuration, such as terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws, with documented inputs, outputs and versions.
Addressing: a provider source is [hostname/]namespace/type; the default host is the public registry.
Other registries: HCP Terraform and Terraform Enterprise offer private registries, and OpenTofu runs its own registry; the protocol lets you point at any compatible host.
Versioning: every module and provider release follows semantic versioning on the registry, which is what lets constraints like ~> 5.0 work predictably.

steps.title: Hands-on: using the Terraform Registry with pinned versions
steps.description: Declare sources and constraints so builds are reproducible. Version constraints are what turn the registry from a convenience into a reproducible supply chain.
items: Providers: list them in required_providers with source and a version constraint.
Modules: use source plus version; registry modules honour the version argument, git sources use ?ref=.
Lock it: commit .terraform.lock.hcl so provider selections and checksums are fixed.
Read docs: each registry page lists inputs, outputs, resources and examples; read them before using a module. Check the examples section and the supported provider and Terraform version ranges.
Search first: before writing a module, check the registry for a well maintained one, but compare download counts, release cadence and open issues before adopting it.

steps.title: Publishing modules and private registries
steps.description: The public registry has simple conventions; private ones add access control. Teams usually start on the public registry and add a private one once they have internal modules worth sharing.
items: Module naming: a public GitHub repository named terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME> with semantic version tags such as v1.2.0.
Provider publishing: providers are published with signed release artefacts; the registry verifies a GPG signature.
Private use: use a private registry (for example in HCP Terraform) or a git source for internal modules with controlled access.
Mirrors: in restricted networks configure the CLI to install from a mirror.
Documentation generation: the registry renders module README files and inputs and outputs automatically from the repository, so good descriptions pay off.

steps.title: Failure modes and risks
steps.description: Convenience in the registry becomes risk if sources are unpinned. Most registry incidents come from unpinned versions or from network paths that block the registry host.
items: Unpinned versions: without constraints, init may select a new major release with breaking changes. Constraints such as ~> 5.0 allow minor updates but block the next major release.
Unreviewed community modules: modules run with your credentials; review the code or pin to audited versions.
Network failures: Failed to query available provider packages usually means connectivity, proxy or mirror configuration; check CLI config and egress rules.
Checksum errors: mirrors or different platforms can trigger lock file mismatches; regenerate with terraform providers lock.
Provider trust: prefer Official and Partner providers where available, and review community providers carefully because they run with your credentials.

steps.title: Supply chain practice
steps.description: Treat registry dependencies like any third party package. Third party Terraform code is executable infrastructure logic, so apply the same scrutiny you give application dependencies. Pin, review and mirror what you depend on.
items: Dependency updates: use Renovate or Dependabot to propose provider and module bumps through pull requests.
Internal catalog: publish vetted modules to a private registry so teams do not copy and paste.
Scanning: run static analysis such as tflint and security scanners on module code before adopting it.
Pinned CI images: run Terraform from a pinned container image or version manager so the CLI version is as reproducible as the providers.
Vendoring: for strict environments, run terraform providers mirror to build a local mirror of the exact providers a configuration needs.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Pin every registry provider and module version, commit the lock file, and mirror or vendor dependencies for restricted environments.
elevatorPitch: The Terraform Registry is the public index of providers and modules that terraform init resolves from source addresses.
I verify by pinning versions, committing the lock file and reading module code before use.
I automate dependency updates with PRs and use private registries or mirrors for internal and air-gapped needs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Leaving module and provider versions unpinned
mistakesToAvoid.why: A new release can silently change behavior between runs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Trusting community modules without review
mistakesToAvoid.why: They execute with your cloud credentials and can create broad permissions.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming the registry is available everywhere
mistakesToAvoid.why: Air-gapped or proxied networks need a configured mirror.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Copying modules instead of consuming a versioned source
mistakesToAvoid.why: The copy drifts and misses security fixes.

title: Terraform Q47: How do you pass a list of values to a Terraform variable [L2]
summary: To pass a list of values to a Terraform variable, declare it with type = list(string) and supply it in a .tfvars file as subnets = ["a", "b"], or on the command line with -var or the TF_VAR_subnets environment variable using the.
question: How do you pass a list of values to a Terraform variable?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #47 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: To pass a list of values to a Terraform variable, declare it with type = list(string) and supply it in a .tfvars file as subnets = ["a", "b"], or on the command line with -var or the TF_VAR_subnets environment variable using the same HCL syntax. Interviewers ask this to test your grasp of variable types, the precedence order of inputs, shell quoting pitfalls, and the difference between lists and sets when later using for_each.

steps.title: Declare the list type first
steps.description: The type decides parsing, validation and how you can iterate. Choosing the right type up front gives clearer errors and prevents surprises when you later iterate over the values.
items: list(string): ordered, allows duplicates, accessed by index such as var.subnets[0]. It is the most common choice for subnet IDs, CIDR blocks and availability zones.
set(string): unordered and unique; required by for_each unless you convert with toset().
list(object): use for richer entries, such as name and size per item, with named attributes.
Defaults and validation: add a default for optional lists and a validation block for rules like non-empty.
Nested types: for items with several fields, list(object({ name = string, size = number })) documents the shape and gives clear type errors when input is wrong.

steps.title: Hands-on: pass a list of values to a Terraform variable
steps.description: Four supported input methods, all using HCL list syntax. All four routes feed the same variable, so the real question is which one fits your workflow and how they override each other.
items: tfvars file: put subnets = ["subnet-a", "subnet-b"] in terraform.tfvars, any *.auto.tfvars, or a file passed with -var-file.
CLI flag: -var='subnets=["subnet-a","subnet-b"]'; use single quotes outside so the shell keeps the inner double quotes. On Windows shells, quoting rules differ, so a file is safer.
Environment: TF_VAR_subnets='["subnet-a","subnet-b"]' is parsed the same way for complex types.
JSON: a terraform.tfvars.json file with {"subnets": ["a", "b"]} suits generated input from other tools.
Auto-loaded files: terraform.tfvars and files ending in .auto.tfvars load automatically; other names, like prod.tfvars, need -var-file.
steps.codeBlock:
# prod.tfvars
subnets = ["subnet-0aaa", "subnet-0bbb"]

terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars
terraform plan -var='subnets=["subnet-0aaa","subnet-0bbb"]'
export TF_VAR_subnets='["subnet-0aaa","subnet-0bbb"]'
terraform plan

steps.title: Verify the value Terraform received
steps.description: Do not guess how the input was parsed. Printing the parsed value takes seconds and removes any doubt about quoting or type conversion.
items: Console: terraform console -var-file=prod.tfvars then evaluate var.subnets and length(var.subnets).
Plan: review resources that consume the list; a wrong length shows as unexpected adds or removes.
Iteration: convert for use with for_each: for_each = toset(var.subnets) and refer to each.value.
Validation errors: a failed validation block stops plan with your message, a cheap early check. Add a clear error_message that tells the caller exactly what to fix.
Indexing: reading var.subnets[2] beyond the list length errors at plan, so pair indexing with a length validation or use try() or element() deliberately.
steps.codeBlock:
$ terraform console -var-file=prod.tfvars
> var.subnets
[
  "subnet-0aaa",
  "subnet-0bbb",
]
> length(var.subnets)
2

steps.title: Precedence and failure modes
steps.description: Several sources can set the same variable; later ones win. Knowing the precedence prevents the confusing situation where a value in a file is silently overridden elsewhere. Keep the number of sources small to stay predictable.
items: Order (low to high): defaults, environment variables TF_VAR_*, terraform.tfvars, terraform.tfvars.json, *.auto.tfvars, then -var and -var-file in the order given.
Quoting errors: unquoted brackets or missing inner quotes produce "Invalid value for input variable"; test the exact shell line.
Type mismatch: passing a plain string to a list variable fails; wrap in brackets.
Order changes: a list reorder changes indexed resources and may force recreation; prefer maps or for_each with stable keys.
Windows shells: PowerShell and cmd treat quotes differently from bash; prefer a tfvars file or a JSON file to avoid quoting problems in cross-platform teams.

steps.title: Production practice
steps.description: Keep inputs reviewable and environment specific. Consistent, typed inputs make the same code safe to run across many environments.
items: Per environment files: keep dev.tfvars and prod.tfvars in version control for non-secret values.
Secrets: do not place secrets in tfvars committed to git; inject them from the CI secret store as TF_VAR_* variables.
Typed objects: prefer list(object({...})) or a map with validation over loosely typed lists of strings.
Pipelines: store non-secret tfvars in the repository and pass the file name per environment with -var-file, so the same pipeline can promote dev to prod.
Documentation: give every variable a description and example so callers know whether to supply a list, set or map.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Prefer tfvars files with a typed variable and validation, and use toset() or a map with stable keys when iterating so reordering the list does not recreate resources.
elevatorPitch: You declare type = list(string) and pass it as an HCL list via tfvars, -var, TF_VAR_ or a JSON file.
I verify with terraform console and the plan, and I know that -var and -var-file override tfvars and env vars.
I keep per environment tfvars in git, inject secrets from CI and use validation blocks.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Mangling shell quotes on the -var flag
mistakesToAvoid.why: The inner double quotes get stripped and Terraform reports an invalid value.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using a list with for_each directly
mistakesToAvoid.why: for_each needs a set or map; wrap with toset() or the plan errors.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on list order for indexed resources
mistakesToAvoid.why: Reordering or removing an item shifts indexes and recreates resources.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Committing secrets inside tfvars
mistakesToAvoid.why: The values land in git history and in logs.

title: Terraform Q49: How do you manage multiple versions of Terraform itself in your team [L2]
summary: To manage multiple versions of Terraform in a team, declare a supported range in required_version, pin one exact version per repo with a version manager such as tfenv, and run the same pinned binary in CI.
question: How do you manage multiple versions of Terraform itself in your team?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #49 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: To manage multiple versions of Terraform in a team, declare a supported range in required_version, pin one exact version per repo with a version manager such as tfenv, and run the same pinned binary in CI. Interviewers ask this because Terraform state is forward-only: once a newer binary writes the state, older binaries refuse to read it, so one engineer running a different version can block everyone. A strong answer covers local tooling, the constraint in code, CI enforcement, and a controlled upgrade process for many root modules.

steps.title: Mental model: required_version versus the binary you run
steps.description: Terraform has three independent version axes, and confusing them is the most common source of team friction.
items: Core version: the terraform binary itself. Check it with terraform version. It decides which language features (import blocks, moved blocks, removed blocks) are available.
required_version: a constraint inside the terraform {} block that makes init, plan and apply fail fast when the binary is outside the allowed range. It documents intent but does not install anything.
Provider versions: pinned separately in required_providers and recorded in .terraform.lock.hcl. Upgrading core does not upgrade providers, and the reverse is also true.

State format version: the state file records the Terraform version that last wrote it. A newer writer can make the state unreadable for older binaries, which is why unsynchronised upgrades hurt teams.
steps.highlight: Use a range in required_version (the contract) and an exact version in a version file (what everyone actually runs). A range alone still lets two engineers run different minor versions.

steps.title: Hands-on: manage multiple versions of Terraform with tfenv
steps.description: A version manager lets each repository declare its exact version and switches the binary automatically when you change directories.
items: tfenv: reads a .terraform-version file in the repo root. tfenv install with no argument installs the version in that file, and tfenv use activates it.
Constraint-driven selection: tfenv install min-required and tfenv use min-required pick the lowest version that satisfies required_version, which is useful for verifying that your minimum is real.
Alternatives: asdf and mise (read .tool-versions) manage Terraform alongside kubectl, helm and others, so one file pins the whole toolchain. OpenTofu has its own manager, tofuenv.
Commit the file: check .terraform-version into git so a fresh clone and a CI runner resolve the same version without any wiki page.
steps.codeBlock:
# One-time per repo
echo "1.7.5" > .terraform-version
tfenv install            # installs the version in .terraform-version
tfenv use 1.7.5
terraform version        # Terraform v1.7.5 on darwin_arm64

# Several root modules on different versions
tfenv list               # shows installed versions, * marks active
cd ../legacy-network && tfenv use 1.5.7

steps.title: Pin the same Terraform version in CI
steps.description: Local discipline is not enough; the pipeline must be the source of truth and must fail when it drifts from the repo.
items: GitHub Actions: hashicorp/setup-terraform accepts terraform_version (an exact version or a constraint). Feed it the contents of .terraform-version so the file stays authoritative.
Containers: run Terraform from a pinned image tag, never latest, and bump the tag in the same PR that bumps the version file.
HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise: each workspace has its own Terraform version setting. Keep it in sync with the repo, or manage it as code with the tfe provider.
Guard step: add a job step that compares terraform version -json against the version file and fails with a clear message instead of a confusing state error later.
steps.codeBlock:
# .github/workflows/terraform.yml (excerpt)
- name: Read pinned version
  id: tf
  run: echo "version=$(cat .terraform-version)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

- uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
  with:
    terraform_version: ${{ steps.tf.outputs.version }}

- name: Verify binary matches pin
  run: |
    test "$(terraform version -json | jq -r .terraform_version)" = "$(cat .terraform-version)"

steps.title: Failure modes: state written by a newer version
steps.description: Most incidents here are one engineer applying with a newer binary and everyone else being locked out of the state.
items: Symptom: an error similar to state snapshot was created by Terraform vX, which is newer than current vY. The fix is to upgrade your binary, not to edit the state file.

Downgrade is not supported: after a newer version writes state you generally cannot roll back to the older binary. Restore from a versioned backend object only if you accept losing the changes made since.
Mixed modules: a child module may declare its own required_version. The strictest constraint across the whole tree wins, so a vendored module can silently raise your floor.

Licensing and forks: Terraform 1.6 and later is under the BUSL license, and OpenTofu is a separate fork whose versions do not map one-to-one. Do not mix terraform and tofu against the same state without an explicit migration plan.
steps.highlight: Enable versioning on the remote state bucket (for example S3 object versioning) so a bad upgrade can be investigated or reverted at the object level.

steps.title: Production practice: a controlled upgrade workflow
steps.description: Treat a Terraform core bump like a dependency upgrade with a blast radius, not like a laptop preference.
items: Read the changelog: check the upgrade guide for deprecations between your current and target minor versions before touching any repo.

Prove it with a plan: in a branch, bump the version file and required_version, run terraform init -upgrade=false and terraform plan for every root module. The goal is a no-op plan; any diff is a finding to explain.
Roll out in tiers: upgrade dev, then staging, then prod roots, and only raise required_version's lower bound once every environment has applied successfully.
Automate nudges: Renovate or Dependabot can open PRs for the version file and for pinned CI actions, so upgrades are small and routine.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Pair a range in required_version with an exact value in .terraform-version, and make CI fail when the two disagree; the state file only moves forward, so mismatches are cheaper to catch in the pipeline than in production.
elevatorPitch: I pin Terraform with a required_version range in code and an exact version in .terraform-version, installed through tfenv or mise.
CI installs the same version from that file and fails if terraform version differs, so local and pipeline runs are identical.
Upgrades go through a PR with no-op plans on every root module, rolled out dev to prod, with state versioning enabled as a safety net.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Setting required_version = ">= 1.0" and nothing else
mistakesToAvoid.why: An open-ended floor lets every engineer and runner use a different minor version, and the newest one that writes state locks out the rest.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using the latest tag for the Terraform container or action in CI
mistakesToAvoid.why: The pipeline silently upgrades core, and the first apply after a release can rewrite state in a version nobody tested.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Trying to downgrade after a newer version has applied
mistakesToAvoid.why: State written by a newer release is generally unreadable by older ones; the recovery path is a state backup, not a binary swap.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming a core upgrade also upgrades providers
mistakesToAvoid.why: Providers are locked in .terraform.lock.hcl; changing core without reviewing provider pins gives you two unrelated upgrade axes to debug at once.

title: Terraform Q50: What is terraform console [L2]
summary: The console loads your root module, then evaluates whatever expression you type in the same scope that a locals block would have.
question: What is `terraform console`?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #50 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: What is terraform console? It is an interactive read-only REPL that evaluates Terraform expressions against your configuration, variables and current state, so you can test functions, for expressions and resource attributes without running a plan. Interviewers ask because it separates engineers who guess at cidrsubnet or merge behaviour and wait for a failed pipeline from those who verify an expression in seconds. A good answer covers what it can see, how to script it, what it cannot do, and the state-lock side effect.

steps.title: Mental model: what terraform console can and cannot see
steps.description: The console loads your root module, then evaluates whatever expression you type in the same scope that a locals block would have.
items: Visible: input variables, local.* values, resource and data source attributes that already exist in state, module outputs, and the full built-in function library.
Not visible: attributes of resources that are not yet created. They evaluate as unknown, which mirrors the plan-time behaviour of (known after apply).
Read-only: it never changes infrastructure or state. It does need an initialised working directory, so run terraform init first if providers or modules are missing.
State lock: it reads state through the backend and takes the state lock, so a long-lived console session can block a teammate's plan on a locked remote backend.

Backends and credentials: the console needs the same backend configuration and provider credentials as a plan, because it loads state from the backend. A missing AWS profile or expired SSO session shows up as a backend error before you can type anything.
steps.highlight: Because the console holds the state lock on locking backends, close it when you are done, or pass -lock=false for a quick read when you accept the risk.

steps.title: Hands-on: terraform console for functions and expressions
steps.description: Use the REPL to settle the exact output of functions before committing them to a module.
items: Network maths: cidrsubnet and cidrhost are the classic uses, since a wrong newbits argument silently produces an overlapping subnet.
Collections: test merge, flatten, zipmap, and for expressions on your real locals to see the actual map keys that for_each will receive.
Type conversion: check tolist, toset, and type(...) output to understand why a set cannot be indexed like a list.
Multi-line input: the console accepts multi-line expressions, so you can paste a whole for expression. Type exit or press Ctrl-D to leave.
steps.codeBlock:
$ terraform console
> cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 2)
"10.0.2.0/24"
> cidrhost("10.0.2.0/24", 10)
"10.0.2.10"
> merge({a = 1}, {b = 2})
{
  "a" = 1
  "b" = 2
}
> [for k, v in local.buckets : upper(k) if v.enabled]
> type(local.buckets)
> exit

steps.title: Inspect real state values and pass variables
steps.description: The console shines when debugging why an interpolation produces an unexpected value in an existing environment.
items: Resource attributes: type aws_instance.web.private_ip or module.vpc.private_subnet_ids to see exactly what the current state holds.
Variables: supply the same inputs as production using -var or -var-file=prod.tfvars so locals evaluate with the real data.
Different state: -state=path targets a local state file, handy when examining a copy pulled with terraform state pull instead of touching the live backend.
Complex values: wrap output in jsonencode(...) to print a compact view of a deeply nested object, then pipe through jq.
steps.codeBlock:
terraform init
terraform console -var-file=prod.tfvars
> aws_security_group.app.id
"sg-0123456789abcdef0"
> jsonencode(local.tags)

# Inspect an offline copy without locking the live backend
terraform state pull > /tmp/prod.tfstate
terraform console -state=/tmp/prod.tfstate -lock=false

steps.title: Scripting: pipe expressions in for quick checks and CI
steps.description: The console reads standard input, which turns it into a one-shot evaluator suitable for scripts.
items: One-liners: echo 'cidrsubnet(var.vpc_cidr, 4, 1)' | terraform console prints only the result, with no prompt noise.
Assertions: a script can compare the output to an expected value as a lightweight guardrail on a shared locals file.
Prefer tests for permanence: for repeatable checks, terraform test (available from 1.6) or precondition blocks are the durable option; the console is for exploration.
Output formatting: strings print quoted. Use tostring and jq -r on JSON output when you need raw values for a shell variable.
steps.codeBlock:
echo 'cidrsubnet("10.20.0.0/16", 8, 3)' | terraform console
# "10.20.3.0/24"

echo 'jsonencode(local.common_tags)' | terraform console | jq -r 'fromjson'

steps.title: Limits, failure modes and when not to use it
steps.description: Knowing the edges stops you from trusting a console result that does not reflect what apply will do.
items: Unknown values: a value that depends on a not-yet-created resource shows as unknown; the console cannot predict it, so use terraform plan for the truth.
Stale state: results reflect the last applied state, not live infrastructure. If something drifted, run terraform plan -refresh-only first.
Secrets exposure: sensitive values may still be visible in the REPL and in your shell history when piped; do not paste console output into tickets.
Not a test framework: it checks a single expression once. It does not validate the dependency graph or provider behaviour.
Good habit: when a CI plan fails on an expression, reproduce it locally in the console with the same -var-file, fix the expression there, and only then commit the change.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Reach for terraform console before you write a for_each or cidrsubnet expression into a module, and remember it takes the state lock on remote backends, so exit the session as soon as you have your answer.
elevatorPitch: terraform console is a read-only REPL that evaluates HCL expressions against my variables, locals and current state.
I use it to verify functions like cidrsubnet and the exact keys a for_each will receive before running a plan.
I script it with piped input for quick checks, but move durable assertions into terraform test or precondition blocks.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Leaving a console session open against a remote backend
mistakesToAvoid.why: It holds the state lock, so teammates and CI plans fail with a lock error until you exit.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Trusting console output for values of resources that do not exist yet
mistakesToAvoid.why: Unknown values cannot be computed in the REPL; only a plan shows how they resolve at apply time.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running it before terraform init
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without installed providers and modules the console fails to load the configuration, and the error is easy to misread as a code bug.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using it as a substitute for automated tests
mistakesToAvoid.why: Manual REPL checks are not repeatable; encode important expectations in terraform test or preconditions.

title: Terraform Q52: A Terraform resource shows as (known after apply) for an attribute What does this mean [L2]
summary: (known after apply) in a Terraform plan means the value cannot be computed until the provider creates or changes the resource, for example an ARN, an ID, or a generated IP. It is normal for new resources and usually harmless.
question: A Terraform resource shows as `(known after apply)` for an attribute. What does this mean?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #52 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: (known after apply) in a Terraform plan means the value cannot be computed until the provider creates or changes the resource, for example an ARN, an ID, or a generated IP. It is normal for new resources and usually harmless. It becomes a problem when an unknown value feeds something Terraform must know at plan time, such as count or for_each. Interviewers use this question to see whether you understand the plan and apply phases, can read a plan critically, and know how to restructure code that depends on unknowns.

steps.title: Mental model: why a value is (known after apply)
steps.description: Terraform builds a plan from configuration and prior state, and every attribute is either known, or unknown until a provider returns it.
items: Computed by the provider: attributes such as id, arn, public_ip and creation_date are assigned by the remote API, so a plan for a new resource must show them as unknown.
Derived values: anything built from an unknown value is also unknown. An output that interpolates aws_instance.web.id is unknown until the instance exists.
On updates: an attribute that previously had a value and now shows -> (known after apply) means an upstream change will recompute it. Find the upstream change; do not assume a bug.
Deferred data sources: a data source whose depends_on includes a resource with pending changes is read during apply, so its attributes are unknown in the plan.

steps.title: Hands-on: read the plan and the JSON for unknown attributes
steps.description: The human-readable plan tells you what changes; the JSON plan tells you exactly which fields are unknown.
items: Save the plan: terraform plan -out=tfplan, then render it with terraform show tfplan for a readable version.
JSON view: terraform show -json tfplan exposes resource_changes[].change.after_unknown, a map marking each attribute that will be computed.
Filter with jq: list only resources whose planned change contains unknowns, to separate the harmless id from a surprising attribute.
Replacement hints: a changed attribute marked # forces replacement next to a known-after-apply value means a new resource, and therefore new IDs, will cascade downstream.
steps.codeBlock:
terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform show tfplan | grep -n "known after apply"

terraform show -json tfplan \
  | jq -r '.resource_changes[]
           | select(.change.after_unknown != {})
           | [.address, (.change.after_unknown | keys | join(","))] | @tsv'

steps.title: Failure mode: unknown values in for_each and count
steps.description: The error that actually blocks teams is Invalid for_each argument ... cannot be determined until apply.
items: Why it happens: Terraform must know the full set of instance keys at plan time to build the graph. Keys derived from a resource ID or ARN created in the same run are unknown, so planning fails.
Fix by design: key for_each on static values such as names from a variable or a map literal, and put the unknown value in the map's value instead of its key.
Split the stack: if the keys truly come from another resource, create that resource in a separate root module or layer and read it back with a data source or remote state.
Last resort: a two-phase terraform apply -target=... works, but it is a workaround that leaves your configuration unable to converge from scratch; document it or remove the dependency.
steps.highlight: Unknown values are allowed in resource arguments, but not in count, for_each, provider configuration blocks that need them to authenticate, or backend settings.

steps.title: Troubleshooting unexpected (known after apply) on an update
steps.description: When a stable attribute suddenly turns unknown on an existing resource, work through the cause in order.
items: Upstream replacement: check whether a dependency shows must be replaced. The new object will get a new ID, so every reference becomes unknown.
Provider computed fields: some attributes are recomputed whenever a sibling argument changes, for example a policy document hash or a rendered user data. Confirm with the JSON plan.
Data source timing: remove unnecessary depends_on on a data source, since it forces deferral. Prefer implicit dependencies by reference.
Module outputs: a module output built from an unknown value is unknown to every caller, so one deep change can ripple across stacks.

steps.title: Prevention and review habits
steps.description: Make unknowns visible in review so they are explained rather than discovered at apply time.
items: Review the plan, not the diff: reviewers should read the planned output, specifically for replacements that turn many values unknown.
Use lifecycle carefully: ignore_changes can hide an attribute from diffs, but it does not make an unknown value known.
Add preconditions: a precondition on a variable catches bad inputs before they create unresolvable graphs.
Keep layers small: separate network, identity and workload stacks so a replacement in one does not make the next unknown.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Treat (known after apply) on a brand-new resource as normal, but treat it on an existing attribute as a signal to trace upstream for a replacement, and use terraform show -json with after_unknown to prove it.
elevatorPitch: (known after apply) means the provider computes the value during apply, such as an ID or ARN, so the plan cannot know it yet.
I verify with terraform show -json and the after_unknown field, and trace unexpected unknowns to an upstream replacement.
I design configurations with static for_each keys so unknown values only appear as map values, never as keys or counts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Keying for_each on a resource ID or IP created in the same apply
mistakesToAvoid.why: Terraform needs all keys at plan time, so it errors out; use static keys and put the unknown in the value.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Fixing unknown-value errors permanently with -target
mistakesToAvoid.why: It hides a graph design problem, and a fresh environment cannot be built with a single apply.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Adding depends_on to data sources out of habit
mistakesToAvoid.why: It defers the read to apply time and turns the data source's attributes unknown across the plan.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring unknowns on an existing attribute
mistakesToAvoid.why: It usually means an upstream replacement is coming, which can destroy and recreate dependent resources.

title: Terraform Q54: What is the replace_triggered_by lifecycle argument [L2]
summary: Forces resource replacement when another resource changes. Example: replace EC2 instance whenever the launch template changes:
question: What is the `replace_triggered_by` lifecycle argument?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #54 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: The replace_triggered_by lifecycle argument, available from Terraform 1.2, tells Terraform to destroy and recreate a resource whenever another referenced resource or attribute changes. It solves cases where a dependency changes but the dependent object has no argument that changes, so Terraform would otherwise plan nothing. Interviewers ask it to check that you understand the dependency graph, can distinguish it from -replace, taint and create_before_destroy, and know the blast radius of automatic replacement.

steps.title: Mental model: what replace_triggered_by does
steps.description: By default Terraform only updates a resource when its own arguments differ. This argument adds an extra reason to replace it.
items: Trigger list: replace_triggered_by takes a list of references to managed resources or their attributes.
Resource reference: pointing at a whole resource (aws_launch_template.app) replaces your resource if that resource is updated or replaced.
Attribute reference: pointing at an attribute (aws_launch_template.app.latest_version) triggers only when that attribute changes, which is more precise.
Scope: references must be to managed resources, or to attributes of them, not to data sources or input variables; to react to a variable, route it through terraform_data.

Why it exists: before Terraform 1.2 teams used null_resource tricks or manual taint commands to force this behaviour. The lifecycle argument makes the rule explicit, reviewable and part of the dependency graph.
Version note: it requires Terraform 1.2 or newer, so set required_version accordingly before adopting it in shared modules.
steps.highlight: Replacement means destroy and create. For stateful resources such as databases this can mean data loss, so use it deliberately.

steps.title: Hands-on: replace_triggered_by in a real configuration
steps.description: A common use is rolling a resource that consumes a changed object without its own diff, such as an instance reading a rendered config.
items: Dependent resource: an EC2 instance should be rebuilt when its configuration object changes, because user data is only read at first boot.
Variable-driven trigger: wrap a version string in terraform_data and reference it, so bumping the variable forces replacement.
Plan output: the plan marks the resource as replaced and notes the reason, so reviewers can see which trigger fired. Always read this line in review.
Count and for_each: triggers can reference indexed instances, but be explicit about which instance you mean to avoid replacing an entire set.

steps.title: Compare with -replace, taint and create_before_destroy
steps.description: Interviews often hinge on knowing which tool expresses a permanent rule versus a one-off action.
items: replace_triggered_by: a declarative, permanent rule stored in code. Every future change to the trigger replaces the resource.
terraform apply -replace=ADDR: a one-time imperative action for a single run. It is recorded in the plan, and is the modern replacement for the deprecated terraform taint.
create_before_destroy: controls the order of replacement, not whether it happens. Combine it with replace_triggered_by for zero-gap swaps when names allow two copies to exist.
ignore_changes: the opposite intent, suppressing diffs on an attribute. Do not use both on the same attribute without a reason.
steps.codeBlock:
# one-off, imperative
terraform apply -replace="aws_instance.app"

# preview what a trigger would do
terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform show tfplan | grep -B2 -A2 "replaced"

steps.title: Failure modes and edge cases
steps.description: Automatic replacement is powerful, which is exactly why the failure modes matter.
items: Cascading replacements: if the trigger is a whole resource that changes frequently, your resource is replaced on every tag or minor update. Prefer a specific attribute.
Name collisions: with create_before_destroy, a fixed name argument collides because both copies exist briefly. Use name_prefix or generated names.
Cycles: a trigger cannot create a dependency loop. Terraform reports a cycle if the target also depends on the resource.
Stateful data: replacing a database, volume or queue loses data unless snapshots, retention or prevent_destroy are in place.
Chained triggers: if A triggers B and B triggers C, one change replaces all three. Draw the chain before merging and confirm the plan lists exactly the replacements you expect.

steps.title: Production practice and review
steps.description: Use it for immutable-infrastructure patterns, and gate the blast radius.
items: Immutable patterns: roll instances, ECS task roles or Lambda aliases when an upstream template or config changes and the resource has no changing argument.
Guardrails: add prevent_destroy = true to stateful resources; a trigger that would replace them then fails the plan instead of destroying data.
Review: require plan output in the pull request so replacements caused by triggers are visible before merge.
Document the trigger: add a comment explaining why the dependency forces replacement, so the next engineer does not remove it as unused.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Reference a specific attribute such as latest_version instead of the whole resource in replace_triggered_by, so only the change you care about forces replacement.
elevatorPitch: replace_triggered_by is a lifecycle argument from Terraform 1.2 that replaces a resource when a referenced resource or attribute changes.
I check the plan output to confirm which trigger fired, and use terraform_data to turn a variable into a trigger.
I pair it with prevent_destroy on stateful resources and use -replace for one-off needs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Pointing at a whole frequently-updated resource
mistakesToAvoid.why: Every update to it, even a tag change, replaces your resource; reference one attribute.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Referencing a data source or variable directly

title: Terraform Q56: What is terraform providers lock [L2]
summary: terraform providers lock is a command that records provider checksums for the platforms you choose in .terraform.lock.hcl, without needing to run on each platform.
question: What is `terraform providers lock`?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #56 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: terraform providers lock is a command that records provider checksums for the platforms you choose in .terraform.lock.hcl, without needing to run on each platform. By default terraform init only records hashes for the machine it runs on, so a lock file generated on a Mac can fail on a Linux CI runner. Interviewers ask this to test whether you understand supply-chain integrity, dependency locking and the classic checksum does not match error that appears when a team mixes laptops and pipelines.

steps.title: Mental model: what the dependency lock file records
steps.description: The lock file pins the exact provider version and a set of cryptographic hashes that must match any package Terraform installs later.
items: Contents: each provider block lists version, the version constraints, and a hashes list containing h1: and zh: entries.
h1 hashes: computed from the unpacked provider package contents, specific to one platform build. zh hashes: checksums of the release zip archives published by the registry.
Default behaviour: terraform init records only hashes for the current platform, plus the archive hashes the registry publishes, so other platforms may be unverifiable.
Purpose: a compromised or altered provider build will fail the hash check, giving you a trust-on-first-use guarantee that is then reviewable in a pull request.

Trust model: the first lock records what the registry served at that moment. It protects against later tampering, but it is not a signature check of the first download, which Terraform verifies separately through the registry's signing keys.
steps.highlight: Commit .terraform.lock.hcl to version control. It is the provider equivalent of package-lock.json, and it is only useful if every engineer and the pipeline share it.

steps.title: Hands-on: terraform providers lock for every platform
steps.description: Run the command once, on any machine, and list every platform your team and runners use.
items: Platforms flag: use -platform=OS_ARCH repeatedly, for example linux_amd64, linux_arm64, darwin_arm64 and windows_amd64.
How it works: it contacts the registry (or a mirror), downloads each requested platform package, computes its hash, and adds it to the lock file.
Mirrors: -fs-mirror=DIR and -net-mirror=URL source packages from a filesystem or network mirror, which matters for air-gapped environments.
Review the diff: a new run should only add hash lines. A changed version means you also upgraded the provider.
steps.codeBlock:
terraform init
terraform providers lock \
  -platform=linux_amd64 \
  -platform=linux_arm64 \
  -platform=darwin_arm64 \
  -platform=windows_amd64

git diff .terraform.lock.hcl     # expect extra h1:/zh: lines only
git add .terraform.lock.hcl && git commit -m "Lock providers for all platforms"

steps.title: Troubleshooting: checksum does not match the lock file
steps.description: The most common symptom is an init failure on a runner that differs from the machine that created the lock.
items: Error text: messages like the current package for registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws doesn't match any of the checksums previously recorded in the dependency lock file.
Cause 1, missing platform: the lock was generated on darwin_arm64 and CI runs linux_amd64. Fix by running providers lock with all platforms.
Cause 2, tampered or re-published build: investigate before overriding. Compare against the registry and avoid blindly deleting the lock file.
Cause 3, mirror differences: a corporate mirror can produce different hashes; run the lock command against the same mirror CI uses.
steps.codeBlock:
# CI failure
terraform init
# Error: Failed to install provider ... does not match any of the checksums

# Fix: add hashes for the runner platform, commit, re-run
terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64

steps.title: Upgrading providers and enforcing read-only locks
steps.description: Locking is only half the story; the other half is controlling when versions change.
items: Deliberate upgrade: terraform init -upgrade picks the newest version within your constraints and rewrites the lock file. Do this in a dedicated PR.
Read-only init in CI: terraform init -lockfile=readonly makes init fail if the lock file would need changes, preventing the pipeline from silently altering dependencies.
Constraints versus lock: version = "~> 5.40" defines the allowed range, while the lock file picks the exact version inside it. Both must be committed.
After an upgrade: rerun providers lock with every platform so the new version has complete hashes.
steps.codeBlock:
# Dedicated upgrade PR
terraform init -upgrade
terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64
terraform plan

# In CI
terraform init -lockfile=readonly

steps.title: Production practice: supply chain and automation
steps.description: Treat provider updates as dependencies that need review.
items: Automated updates: Renovate and Dependabot support Terraform and can open PRs that include lock file changes; ensure a job reruns providers lock for all platforms.
Private mirrors: use provider_installation in the CLI config with a network mirror for restricted networks, then lock against that mirror.
Validation: add a CI step that runs terraform providers to list requirements and fails if the lock file is absent.
Audit: review hash additions in PRs; unexpected new version lines deserve the same scrutiny as any dependency change.
Onboarding: document the supported platforms in the repo README next to the lock command, so a new engineer on a different architecture, such as Apple silicon, does not hit a mismatch.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Run terraform providers lock with every platform your laptops and runners use immediately after each provider upgrade, and use init -lockfile=readonly in CI so dependencies never change silently.
elevatorPitch: terraform providers lock pre-computes provider checksums for chosen platforms and writes them to .terraform.lock.hcl.
I run it with linux and darwin platforms after upgrades, and diff the lock file to confirm only hashes were added.
CI uses -lockfile=readonly, and Renovate opens version-bump PRs so provider changes are reviewed, not accidental.

mistakesToAvoid.why: It records hashes for that platform alone, so Linux runners hit checksum mismatch errors.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Deleting .terraform.lock.hcl to make an error go away
mistakesToAvoid.why: It discards the integrity guarantee and may pull a different provider version.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Adding the lock file to .gitignore
mistakesToAvoid.why: Every environment then resolves versions independently, which defeats locking.

mistakesToAvoid.why: It changes provider versions mid-pipeline; use -lockfile=readonly and upgrade in reviewed PRs.

title: Terraform Q57: How do you handle conditionally creating a resource in Terraform [L2]
summary: Use count:
question: How do you handle conditionally creating a resource in Terraform?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #57 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: Conditionally creating a resource in Terraform is done by setting count to 0 or 1 from a boolean, or by using for_each over an empty or single-element map. Terraform has no if statement for resources, so the pattern is to vary how many instances exist. Interviewers ask because the details matter: referencing a resource that may not exist, the unknown-value limit on count, address changes when toggling, and optional nested blocks all trip up real modules.

steps.title: Mental model: instances, not if-statements
steps.description: A resource block declares a template; count or for_each decides how many copies exist, and zero is a valid answer.
items: count toggle: count = var.enable_x ? 1 : 0 is the simplest and most common form. The resource is then addressed as aws_x.this[0].
for_each toggle: for_each = var.enable_x ? { main = true } : {} gives a stable string key instead of a numeric index, which survives reordering.
Modules: count and for_each on module blocks work since Terraform 0.13, so you can toggle an entire stack of resources at once.
Known at plan time: the condition must be known during plan. Base it on input variables or static locals, not on attributes of resources created in the same run.
Choosing between them: use count for a simple on or off switch, and for_each when you manage a collection or want a stable key that appears in the state address and in plan output.

steps.title: Hands-on: conditionally creating a resource in Terraform with count
steps.description: Show the toggle, and then the part most people miss: safely referencing the resource that might not exist.
items: Create: a boolean variable drives count. Give the variable a default and a description so callers know the toggle exists.
Reference safely: use one(aws_x.this[*].id) (Terraform 0.15 and later), which returns null when there are zero instances and the value when there is one.
Alternative: try(aws_x.this[0].id, null) also works but can mask unrelated errors, so prefer one().
Output: publish the nullable value as a module output so callers can handle absence explicitly.

steps.title: Optional arguments and nested blocks with dynamic
steps.description: Not everything conditional is a whole resource; sometimes only a block or argument should appear.
items: Optional argument: set it to null to omit it, for example kms_key_id = var.kms_key_arn with a null default.
Optional nested block: use a dynamic block iterating a list that is empty when the feature is off.
Nested toggles: keep dynamic blocks for small cases; heavy use makes plans hard to read, so consider two resource variants instead.
Validation: add a validation block so dependent variables (like a certificate ARN when HTTPS is on) cannot be left unset.

steps.title: Failure modes: unknown counts and shifting addresses
steps.description: Two problems account for most production issues with conditional resources.
items: Unknown count: The count value depends on resource attributes that cannot be determined until apply. Drive the toggle from a variable, or split the stack.
Index shifts: using count over a list means removing an item in the middle renumbers resources, causing destroy and recreate. Use for_each with stable keys for collections.
Toggling changes the address: moving from a plain resource to count turns aws_x.this into aws_x.this[0]. Without a moved block Terraform plans destroy and create.
Destroy on disable: flipping the toggle to false destroys the resource. Protect data with snapshots or prevent_destroy if that is unacceptable.

steps.title: Production practice: module design and tests
steps.description: Keep conditionals readable and verified.
items: One toggle per feature: expose a single boolean such as enable_flow_logs instead of scattering conditions across files.
Test both states: run terraform plan with the toggle on and off in CI, or use terraform test (1.6 and later) to assert counts.
Preconditions: use a precondition to fail early when a required companion variable is missing.
Prefer composition: if more than three or four resources share a condition, wrap them in a module and toggle the module.
Document defaults: state in the variable description whether the default creates the resource, because flipping a default in a shared module changes every caller's plan.
Interview angle: mention that you would rather expose a boolean and a clear module contract than let callers pass count directly, since count on module calls hides the toggle from readers.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Drive the toggle from an input variable (never from another resource's attribute) and reference the optional resource with one(resource.name[*].attr) so zero instances yield null instead of an index error.
elevatorPitch: Terraform has no resource-level if, so I set count to 0 or 1, or for_each to an empty or single map, from a boolean variable.
I reference optional resources with one(res[*].attr) and test the plan with the toggle on and off.
I use moved blocks when changing the shape of a resource so toggling never recreates real infrastructure by accident.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Basing count on a resource attribute created in the same apply
mistakesToAvoid.why: The value is unknown at plan time, and Terraform refuses to plan; use a variable.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using count over a list that can be reordered
mistakesToAvoid.why: Index renumbering recreates resources; use for_each with stable keys.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Indexing aws_x.this[0] directly in outputs
mistakesToAvoid.why: It errors when the count is zero; use one() or a splat expression.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Adding count to an existing resource without a moved block
mistakesToAvoid.why: The address changes to [0], producing a destroy and create plan.

title: Terraform Q59: How do you use Terraform to create IAM policies without hardcoding JSON [L2]
summary: Use the aws_iam_policy_document data source:
question: How do you use Terraform to create IAM policies without hardcoding JSON?
roleContext: Terraform Scenario #59 (L2) · Use VPC ID from another module
intro: To create IAM policies without hardcoding JSON in Terraform, use the aws_iam_policy_document data source, which builds policy JSON from HCL blocks, or jsonencode() on a native map. Both let you use variables, resource references and conditions instead of fragile heredoc strings. Interviewers ask because hardcoded JSON hides typos, ignores dependencies and tends to be over-permissive. A strong answer shows composition, least privilege, trust policies, validation with Access Analyzer, and how to avoid permissions drift.

steps.title: Mental model: HCL in, valid policy JSON out
steps.description: The data source does not call AWS; it is a pure renderer that converts blocks into a JSON string you pass to a policy resource.
items: Data source: data "aws_iam_policy_document" exposes a .json attribute containing the rendered policy.
Dependency aware: referencing aws_s3_bucket.data.arn inside the document creates an implicit dependency, so the policy follows the bucket rename or replacement.
Typed fields: actions, resources, principals and condition are lists and blocks, so Terraform catches shape errors at validate time rather than IAM catching them at apply.
Alternative: jsonencode({ Version = ..., Statement = [...] }) is valid too and good for short policies, but offers no merge helpers.

Why not heredocs: a heredoc is just a string, so Terraform cannot check structure, cannot track the references inside it, and shows any whitespace change as a diff. The data source removes all three problems.

steps.title: Hands-on: IAM policies without hardcoding JSON
steps.description: Build a least-privilege identity policy for an application role and attach it.
items: Statements: give each statement a sid for readability and for override merging.
Resource scoping: list the bucket ARN for bucket-level actions and "${arn}/*" for object-level actions, a distinction that many hand-written policies get wrong.
Conditions: add condition blocks (for example aws:SourceVpce or aws:PrincipalOrgID) to narrow the grant further.
Attach: pass data.aws_iam_policy_document.app.json to aws_iam_policy or aws_iam_role_policy.
Variables for scope: accept a list of ARNs as an input variable and splat them into resources, so callers choose the scope while the module owns the actions.
Partition and account: build ARNs with data.aws_partition.current.partition and data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id rather than hardcoding arn:aws or an account number.

steps.title: Trust policies, merging and dynamic statements
steps.description: Role trust policies and reusable policy fragments use the same data source.
items: Trust policy: use a principals block with type = "Service" and identifiers = ["ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com"], then pass the JSON to assume_role_policy.
source_policy_documents: merge several documents into one, so a base policy plus a team-specific add-on composes cleanly.
override_policy_documents: later documents replace statements with the same sid, giving environment-specific overrides.
dynamic statements: loop over a map of buckets with a dynamic "statement" block to generate one statement per entry from a variable.

steps.title: Verification: validate and simulate before apply
steps.description: A rendered policy can be syntactically valid and still be wrong; check it.
items: Plan review: read the planned policy JSON in the plan output; it is deterministic and reviewable in a PR.
Access Analyzer: run aws accessanalyzer validate-policy on the rendered JSON to catch security warnings and errors such as overly broad wildcards.
Simulate: use aws iam simulate-principal-policy after apply to confirm that an action is allowed or denied for the role.
Static analysis: run tflint, checkov or trivy config in CI to flag Action: * and Resource: *.
Review in PRs: because the plan prints the rendered policy, reviewers can read the exact permissions being granted, which is not possible when the JSON is assembled in a script.
steps.codeBlock:
terraform show -json tfplan \
  | jq -r '.resource_changes[] | select(.type=="aws_iam_policy") | .change.after.policy' \
  > policy.json

aws accessanalyzer validate-policy \
  --policy-document file://policy.json \
  --policy-type IDENTITY_POLICY

aws iam simulate-principal-policy \
  --policy-source-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/my-app-task \
  --action-names s3:GetObject \
  --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::my-data-bucket/file.txt

steps.title: Failure modes and production practice
steps.description: Know what goes wrong with generated policies, and how teams keep them tidy.
items: Perpetual diff: mixing heredoc JSON with reordered keys causes diffs on every plan. The data source emits canonical ordering, which avoids that.
Size limits: managed policies and inline policies have size limits (check current IAM quotas). Split policies by function instead of one giant document.
Wildcard creep: use variables for actions with validation, and require reviewers for any *.
Modules: publish a small internal module that takes a list of bucket ARNs and returns a policy JSON, so every team gets the same least-privilege shape.

Boundaries: for roles created by application teams, attach a permissions boundary policy, also rendered from aws_iam_policy_document, so even a mistaken statement cannot exceed the approved ceiling. Pair it with service control policies at the organization level for defence in depth.

keyTakeaway: Pro-Tip: Render policies with aws_iam_policy_document, split object-level and bucket-level resources correctly, and validate the output with aws accessanalyzer validate-policy in CI before it reaches an account.
elevatorPitch: I use aws_iam_policy_document to generate IAM JSON from HCL, referencing real resource ARNs so dependencies are tracked.
I compose policies with source_policy_documents and validate the rendered JSON with Access Analyzer and a policy scanner in CI.
I keep trust policies and permissions as separate documents and review the planned policy in every pull request.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Writing policy heredocs with literal ARNs
mistakesToAvoid.why: They break when a bucket is renamed and hide typos until an access denied appears in production.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using "${bucket_arn}/*" for s3:ListBucket
mistakesToAvoid.why: List actions apply to the bucket ARN, while object actions need the /* form; mixing them yields silent denials.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Granting Action: "*" or Resource: "*" for convenience
mistakesToAvoid.why: It defeats least privilege and fails most policy scanners.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming a valid policy is a correct policy
mistakesToAvoid.why: The data source does not check semantics; use Access Analyzer and simulation to confirm the effect.

title: Fine-Grained Service Discovery Across 1,000+ Microservices Using Envoy & Istio
summary: Architectural runbook for scaling Istio and Envoy service discovery across 1,000+ microservices without control-plane xDS push storms, memory bloat, or OOM crashes on sidecars.
question: How would you implement fine-grained service discovery across 1000+ microservices using Envoy or Istio?
roleContext: Staff Cloud Architect / Systems at Scale Loop
intro: At a scale of 1,000+ microservices and tens of thousands of pods, default 'flat mesh' service discovery causes catastrophic control plane saturation. By default, Istiod broadcasts every endpoint in the entire cluster to every Envoy sidecar via EDS (Endpoint Discovery Service). A cluster of 1,000 services with 10 replicas each forces every Envoy proxy to maintain 10,000 TCP connection pools and route tables, driving sidecar memory to 1GB+ per pod and triggering xDS CPU storms during routine pod churn. We solved this by decomposing the mesh using scoped discovery boundaries.

steps.title: Scope Egress Discovery Boundaries with Istio Sidecar Resources
steps.description: Never allow sidecars to watch the root namespace. Enforce strict egress host visibility per namespace:
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: Sidecar
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: payments
spec:
  egress:
  - hosts:
    - "./*"                  # Only discover services within the same namespace
    - "istio-system/*"       # Required telemetry and control plane
    - "auth/auth-service.auth.svc.cluster.local"  # Explicit cross-namespace dependency
items: Memory Drop: Drops sidecar footprint from ~950MB to <35MB per pod by discarding 98% of unneeded route tables and listener configs.
Control Plane Headroom: Istiod now only pushes updates to proxies that actually depend on the changing workload.

steps.title: Migrate from State-of-the-World to Delta xDS
steps.description: Configure Istiod and Envoy sidecars to use incremental (Delta) xDS protocol over gRPC instead of ADS (Aggregated Discovery Service) full snapshots:
steps.codeBlock:
# In IstioOperator or Helm values:
meshConfig:
  discoverySelectors:
    - matchLabels:
        istio-discovery: enabled
  defaultConfig:
    proxyMetadata:
      ISTIO_DELTA_XDS: "true"
items: Incremental Updates: When a pod restarts in service B, Envoy only receives the specific IP diff rather than the serialized 1,000-service cluster configuration.
Network Egress: Reduces mesh internal control plane traffic by over 85% during rolling deployment bursts.

steps.title: Partition Workloads with Discovery Selectors
steps.description: Use Istio Discovery Selectors to completely exclude high-churn ephemeral jobs, database replicas, and batch workers from the service mesh control plane:
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl label namespace batch-jobs spark-analytics istio-discovery=disabled
kubectl label namespace core-api checkout payments istio-discovery=enabled
items: Prevents batch jobs that cycle hundreds of pods per minute from triggering invalidation events across customer-facing API proxies.

steps.title: Diagnostic Verification Commands
steps.description: Verify endpoint synchronization and proxy memory consumption on the live cluster:
steps.codeBlock:
# 1. Inspect total clusters known to a specific Envoy sidecar (target: < 25, not 1000+)
istioctl proxy-config clusters <pod-name>.<namespace> | wc -l

# 2. Check sync latency between Istiod control plane and proxies
istioctl proxy-status

# 3. Check memory consumption of the Envoy sidecar container
kubectl top pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> --containers | grep istio-proxy
steps.highlight: In our benchmarks, scoping reduced P99 discovery synchronization latency from 4.8 seconds down to 110ms across 1,200 microservices.

keyTakeaway: At 1,000+ services, service discovery is an architectural partitioning problem, not a compute problem. You must treat the mesh as a federated set of localized dependency graphs using Sidecar egress hosts, Delta xDS, and Discovery Selectors.
elevatorPitch: By default, Istio pushes every cluster endpoint to every Envoy proxy, causing memory bloat (1GB+/pod) and xDS CPU storms at 1,000+ service scale.
We enforce strict 'Sidecar' CRDs in every namespace, restricting proxy egress discovery to intra-namespace peers plus explicit external dependencies.
We enable Delta xDS (incremental gRPC streaming) to transmit only endpoint diffs rather than full multi-megabyte cluster snapshots during pod churn.
We apply Discovery Selectors at the mesh level to isolate high-churn batch/analytics workloads from customer-facing API sidecars.
Result: Envoy sidecar memory dropped from 950MB to ~35MB, and control plane sync latency fell from 4.8s to 110ms.
