title: Secret Handling in Docker Builds: Eliminating ARG/ENV Leaks with BuildKit Secrets and SSH Forwarding
summary: Audit and eliminate credential leakage anti-patterns in Dockerfiles (`ARG`, `ENV`, multi-stage leaks). Implement BuildKit `--mount=type=secret` and `--mount=type=ssh` for secure private repo cloning.
question: During a routine compliance audit, a security researcher ran `docker history --no-trunc` against your production customer-facing API container and discovered raw GitHub Personal Access Tokens and AWS secret keys embedded in cleartext in the layer metadata. Developers used `ARG GITHUB_TOKEN` and `ENV AWS_SECRET` to download private npm packages and S3 config files during image builds. You must eliminate all secret leakage anti-patterns and mandate secure BuildKit secret mounts and SSH agent forwarding.
roleContext: Principal Docker Architect / Staff SRE Scenario
intro: Audit and eliminate credential leakage anti-patterns in Dockerfiles (`ARG`, `ENV`, multi-stage leaks). Implement BuildKit `--mount=type=secret` and `--mount=type=ssh` for secure private repo cloning.

steps.title: Expose the Flaws of ARG, ENV, and Multi-Stage Masking
steps.description: Understand why common workarounds fail: `ENV` persists variables permanently into runtime containers. `ARG` values are stored in plaintext inside the image configuration JSON and layer history. Even deleting the secret in a later multi-stage build does not prevent the secret from being extracted from intermediate cache layers or build logs.
steps.content: Understand why common workarounds fail: `ENV` persists variables permanently into runtime containers. `ARG` values are stored in plaintext inside the image configuration JSON and layer history. Even deleting the secret in a later multi-stage build does not prevent the secret from being extracted from intermediate cache layers or build logs.
steps.highlight: Expose the Flaws of ARG, ENV, and Multi-Stage Masking
steps.codeBlock:
# INSECURE ANTI-PATTERNS:
# Anti-pattern 1: ARG leaks into docker history
ARG GITHUB_TOKEN
RUN git clone https://$GITHUB_TOKEN@github.com/myorg/private-repo.git

# Anti-pattern 2: ENV persists in final container environment
ENV AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE

steps.title: Implement BuildKit Ephemeral Secret Mounts
steps.description: Use BuildKit's `--mount=type=secret` syntax. Secrets are exposed to a single `RUN` command as a temporary in-memory file (`/run/secrets/<id>`) and are completely excluded from layer diffs and image metadata.
steps.content: Use BuildKit's `--mount=type=secret` syntax. Secrets are exposed to a single `RUN` command as a temporary in-memory file (`/run/secrets/<id>`) and are completely excluded from layer diffs and image metadata.
steps.highlight: Implement BuildKit Ephemeral Secret Mounts
steps.codeBlock:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./

# Securely mount secret for npm authentication
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc \
    npm ci --omit=dev

COPY . .
CMD ["node", "index.js"]

steps.title: Utilize BuildKit SSH Agent Forwarding for Git Clones
steps.description: To clone private Git repositories during build without copying SSH keys into the Docker context, use `--mount=type=ssh` to forward the local host's SSH agent directly to the builder.
steps.content: To clone private Git repositories during build without copying SSH keys into the Docker context, use `--mount=type=ssh` to forward the local host's SSH agent directly to the builder.
steps.highlight: Utilize BuildKit SSH Agent Forwarding for Git Clones
steps.codeBlock:
# Dockerfile
FROM alpine:3.19
RUN apk add --no-cache openssh-client git
RUN mkdir -p -m 0700 ~/.ssh && ssh-keyscan github.com >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts

# Clone private repository using host's SSH agent
RUN --mount=type=ssh git clone git@github.com:myorg/core-lib.git /lib

# CLI Invocation:
# eval $(ssh-agent) && ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_rsa
# docker build --ssh default -t my-secure-app .

steps.title: Audit and Verify Zero Secret Artifacts in Final Image
steps.description: Verify that neither `docker history` nor `docker inspect` contains any secret artifacts, and that `/run/secrets` does not exist in the finished container image.
steps.content: Verify that neither `docker history` nor `docker inspect` contains any secret artifacts, and that `/run/secrets` does not exist in the finished container image.
steps.highlight: Audit and Verify Zero Secret Artifacts in Final Image
steps.codeBlock:
# Inspect layers for leaked secrets
docker history --no-trunc my-secure-app:latest | grep -i npmrc
# Output: Zero matches!

# Inspect container filesystem to verify secret directory is absent
docker run --rm my-secure-app:latest ls -la /run/secrets
# Output: ls: /run/secrets: No such file or directory

keyTakeaway: Never pass secrets via `ARG` or `ENV` in Dockerfiles. BuildKit's `--mount=type=secret` mounts volatile in-memory credentials exclusively during the required `RUN` step, and `--mount=type=ssh` securely forwards SSH agents without copying private keys into the build context.
elevatorPitch: We eradicated credential leaks from our container images by outlawing `ARG` and `ENV` for sensitive data. By adopting BuildKit `--mount=type=secret` and SSH agent forwarding, private dependencies are fetched securely during compilation without leaving a single trace in image layers or metadata history.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on legacy bucket ACLs instead of modern S3 Block Public Access and IAM bucket policies
mistakesToAvoid.why: AWS recommends disabling ACLs (Bucket Owner Enforced) in favor of centralized declarative bucket policies and account-level Block Public Access controls.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Confusing SSE-S3 encryption with KMS customer-managed key (SSE-KMS) authorization policies
mistakesToAvoid.why: Accessing SSE-KMS encrypted objects requires both `s3:GetObject` and `kms:Decrypt` permissions; neglecting KMS key policies causes silent 403 Forbidden errors.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using sequential timestamps or predictable prefixes for high-throughput S3 read and write keys
mistakesToAvoid.why: Sequential key prefixes limit S3 horizontal partitioning; randomized hash prefixes distribute workloads across partitions to achieve 3,500 PUT and 5,500 GET requests/sec.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to audit S3 object delete markers when troubleshooting missing versioned objects
mistakesToAvoid.why: Issuing a DELETE on a versioned bucket only adds a delete marker; engineers must retrieve previous versions or purge markers to restore data.

title: Tuning Linux Kernel Sysctls in Containers: Namespaced vs Unsafe Sysctls and Production Network Tuning
summary: Configure and tune Linux kernel sysctl parameters within Docker containers. Distinguish between safe namespaced sysctls (network/IPC) and dangerous node-level sysctls, optimizing high-concurrency TCP sockets.
question: Your high-throughput API gateway running in Docker handles 50,000 concurrent HTTP/WebSocket connections. During traffic surges, clients experience connection drops. Kernel logs show `TCP: request_sock_TCP: Possible SYN flooding on port 80. Dropping request`. The Linux default `net.core.somaxconn` (128) and `net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog` (512) are bottlenecking socket acceptance. You must tune container sysctl parameters without compromising host kernel stability or violating security policies.
roleContext: Principal Docker Architect / Staff SRE Scenario
intro: Configure and tune Linux kernel sysctl parameters within Docker containers. Distinguish between safe namespaced sysctls (network/IPC) and dangerous node-level sysctls, optimizing high-concurrency TCP sockets.

steps.title: Differentiate Namespaced Sysctls from Global Node Sysctls
steps.description: Understand Linux kernel sysctl classification: Namespaced sysctls are isolated to the container's network or IPC namespace (e.g., `net.*` and `kernel.msg*`). Modifying them only affects that specific container. Non-namespaced sysctls (e.g., `vm.max_map_count`, `fs.file-max`) affect the entire host OS kernel and all running containers.
steps.content: Understand Linux kernel sysctl classification: Namespaced sysctls are isolated to the container's network or IPC namespace (e.g., `net.*` and `kernel.msg*`). Modifying them only affects that specific container. Non-namespaced sysctls (e.g., `vm.max_map_count`, `fs.file-max`) affect the entire host OS kernel and all running containers.
steps.highlight: Differentiate Namespaced Sysctls from Global Node Sysctls
steps.codeBlock:
<!-- Sysctl Scope -->
Namespaced (Safe per container):
  ├── net.core.somaxconn (Socket listen backlog)
  ├── net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog (SYN queue size)
  └── net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range (Ephemeral port range)

Global / Non-Namespaced (Host-wide, requires privileged access):
  ├── vm.max_map_count (Required for Elasticsearch)
  └── fs.file-max (Total system open file limits)

steps.title: Configure Namespaced Sysctls via Docker CLI and Compose
steps.description: Pass namespaced sysctl parameters using `--sysctl` in `docker run` or the `sysctls` key in Docker Compose.
steps.content: Pass namespaced sysctl parameters using `--sysctl` in `docker run` or the `sysctls` key in Docker Compose.
steps.highlight: Configure Namespaced Sysctls via Docker CLI and Compose
steps.codeBlock:
# Docker CLI invocation with optimized network buffers
docker run -d \
  --name api-gateway \
  --sysctl net.core.somaxconn=65535 \
  --sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog=65535 \
  --sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1 \
  --sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range="1024 65535" \
  -p 80:80 \
  nginx:alpine

# Docker Compose configuration:
# services:
#   gateway:
#     image: nginx:alpine
#     sysctls:
#       - net.core.somaxconn=65535
#       - net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog=65535

steps.title: Handle Non-Namespaced Sysctls Safely in Kubernetes
steps.description: For databases like Elasticsearch that require global sysctls like `vm.max_map_count=262144`, avoid running the container as privileged. Use a privileged `initContainer` or node-level DaemonSet to set the sysctl on the host once at boot.
steps.content: For databases like Elasticsearch that require global sysctls like `vm.max_map_count=262144`, avoid running the container as privileged. Use a privileged `initContainer` or node-level DaemonSet to set the sysctl on the host once at boot.
steps.highlight: Handle Non-Namespaced Sysctls Safely in Kubernetes
steps.codeBlock:
# InitContainer setting host sysctl safely before main container starts
initContainers:
  - name: init-sysctl
    image: busybox:musl
    command: ["sysctl", "-w", "vm.max_map_count=262144"]
    securityContext:
      privileged: true

steps.title: Verify Kernel Socket Capacity and Monitor Drops
steps.description: Inspect `/proc/sys/net/core/somaxconn` inside the running container and monitor `netstat -s` for listen queue overflows (`times the listen queue of a socket overflowed`).
steps.content: Inspect `/proc/sys/net/core/somaxconn` inside the running container and monitor `netstat -s` for listen queue overflows (`times the listen queue of a socket overflowed`).
steps.highlight: Verify Kernel Socket Capacity and Monitor Drops
steps.codeBlock:
# Check active sysctl value inside container
docker exec -it api-gateway cat /proc/sys/net/core/somaxconn
# Output: 65535

# Verify listen queue drop counters
docker exec -it api-gateway netstat -s | grep -i overflow

keyTakeaway: Namespaced sysctls (`net.*`) can be tuned safely per container using `--sysctl` without impacting host stability. Non-namespaced sysctls alter the global host kernel and should be managed via host configuration or init containers rather than granting ongoing privileged rights to application containers.
elevatorPitch: We eliminated SYN flood packet drops and socket acceptance bottlenecks on our high-traffic API gateways by tuning namespaced kernel sysctls directly in Docker. By raising `net.core.somaxconn` and `tcp_max_syn_backlog` to 65,535 via `--sysctl`, our containers effortlessly handle 50,000 concurrent WebSocket connections while maintaining strict security boundaries.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Structuring Dockerfile instructions inefficiently by copying app source before package manifests when configuring Tuning Linux Kernel
mistakesToAvoid.why: Copying code before package manifests (`package.json`, `go.mod`, `requirements.txt`) invalidates the build cache on every commit, forcing slow full reinstalls.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Neglecting the PID 1 process reap problem and omitting proper SIGTERM signal forwarding when configuring Tuning Linux Kernel
mistakesToAvoid.why: If an application runs as PID 1 without an init system (like `tini`), it fails to reap zombie child processes and ignores `SIGTERM` signals, causing unclean 10s timeouts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assembling single-stage images containing compilers, build SDKs, and header files in production when configuring Tuning Linux Kernel
mistakesToAvoid.why: Single-stage builds bloat image size by gigabytes and expose extensive package vulnerabilities; multi-stage builds isolate artifacts into minimal distroless images.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Confusing container port forwarding on bridge networks with unisolated host networking mode when configuring Tuning Linux Kernel
mistakesToAvoid.why: Bridge networking utilizes iptables NAT translations which add latency overhead, whereas host networking bypasses the network namespace entirely.

title: Troubleshooting Docker Embedded DNS (127.0.0.11) Timeouts and resolv.conf ndots Latency
summary: Diagnose intermittent 5-second DNS resolution timeouts inside Docker containers. Understand Docker's internal 127.0.0.11 resolver, `resolv.conf` `ndots:5` search path amplification, and UDP socket drops.
question: Your microservices on a custom Docker bridge network experience intermittent 5,000ms latency spikes when making external API calls to AWS S3 and payment gateways. Application logs show sporadic `getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN` or `dns lookup timed out` errors. Direct `curl` commands to external IP addresses respond in 15ms. You must trace the container's DNS resolution path through the embedded Docker DNS server at `127.0.0.11`, identify UDP packet drops and search domain amplification, and implement a resilient DNS configuration.
roleContext: Principal Docker Architect / Staff SRE Scenario
intro: Diagnose intermittent 5-second DNS resolution timeouts inside Docker containers. Understand Docker's internal 127.0.0.11 resolver, `resolv.conf` `ndots:5` search path amplification, and UDP socket drops.

steps.title: Understand Docker Embedded DNS Resolver Mechanics
steps.description: On user-defined bridge networks, Docker injects an internal DNS server listening at `127.0.0.11:53`. This server intercepts DNS queries: container names are resolved via internal Docker daemon records, while external queries are forwarded to upstream DNS servers listed in the host's `/etc/resolv.conf`.
steps.content: On user-defined bridge networks, Docker injects an internal DNS server listening at `127.0.0.11:53`. This server intercepts DNS queries: container names are resolved via internal Docker daemon records, while external queries are forwarded to upstream DNS servers listed in the host's `/etc/resolv.conf`.
steps.highlight: Understand Docker Embedded DNS Resolver Mechanics
steps.codeBlock:
<!-- Docker DNS Path -->
Container App (getaddrinfo)
  └── Queries: 127.0.0.11:53 (Docker Embedded DNS)
        ├── Matches service name? -> Returns container IP (172.18.0.4)
        └── External domain?      -> Forwards UDP packet to Host DNS (e.g., 8.8.8.8)

steps.title: Diagnose the 5-Second Timeout and ndots Search Amplification
steps.description: Standard Linux glibc resolvers append every domain listed in the `search` directive of `/etc/resolv.conf` if the query contains fewer dots than `ndots` (default is often 5 in container environments). Querying `api.stripe.com` generates redundant queries like `api.stripe.com.default.svc.cluster.local`, causing upstream rate limiting or dropped UDP packets that trigger a 5-second timeout.
steps.content: Standard Linux glibc resolvers append every domain listed in the `search` directive of `/etc/resolv.conf` if the query contains fewer dots than `ndots` (default is often 5 in container environments). Querying `api.stripe.com` generates redundant queries like `api.stripe.com.default.svc.cluster.local`, causing upstream rate limiting or dropped UDP packets that trigger a 5-second timeout.
steps.highlight: Diagnose the 5-Second Timeout and ndots Search Amplification
steps.codeBlock:
# Inspect container resolv.conf
docker exec -it my-app cat /etc/resolv.conf
# Sample output:
# nameserver 127.0.0.11
# options ndots:5

# Trace DNS resolution using dig and tcpdump
docker exec -it my-app dig +trace api.stripe.com

steps.title: Capture DNS Packets and Detect Conntrack Race Conditions
steps.description: Use `tcpdump` inside the container or on the bridge interface. High-concurrency DNS lookups often trigger a known Linux kernel conntrack race condition where simultaneous A and AAAA DNS queries collide on the same UDP socket.
steps.content: Use `tcpdump` inside the container or on the bridge interface. High-concurrency DNS lookups often trigger a known Linux kernel conntrack race condition where simultaneous A and AAAA DNS queries collide on the same UDP socket.
steps.highlight: Capture DNS Packets and Detect Conntrack Race Conditions
steps.codeBlock:
# Monitor DNS traffic on Docker bridge interface
sudo tcpdump -i br-1a2b3c4d -n "udp port 53" -vv

steps.title: Configure Explicit Upstream DNS and Single-Request Options
steps.description: Fix the issue by specifying reliable upstream DNS servers and passing `single-request-reopen` via `--dns-opt` to force sequential UDP lookups, or lowering `ndots`.
steps.content: Fix the issue by specifying reliable upstream DNS servers and passing `single-request-reopen` via `--dns-opt` to force sequential UDP lookups, or lowering `ndots`.
steps.highlight: Configure Explicit Upstream DNS and Single-Request Options
steps.codeBlock:
# Docker run with hardened DNS options
docker run -d \
  --name resilient-api \
  --dns 1.1.1.1 \
  --dns 8.8.8.8 \
  --dns-opt ndots:2 \
  --dns-opt single-request-reopen \
  --dns-opt timeout:2 \
  my-api:v1.0

# Or globally in /etc/docker/daemon.json:
# {
#   "dns": ["1.1.1.1", "8.8.8.8"],
#   "dns-opts": ["single-request-reopen", "timeout:2"]
# }

keyTakeaway: Docker containers on bridge networks resolve DNS via `127.0.0.11`. High-concurrency lookups suffer 5-second timeouts due to `ndots` search list amplification and concurrent A/AAAA UDP socket collisions in kernel conntrack. Setting `single-request-reopen` and configuring explicit DNS servers resolves the latency.
elevatorPitch: We diagnosed intermittent 5-second latency spikes in external API calls by capturing DNS queries on Docker bridge networks. The issue stemmed from glibc appending search domains for external FQDNs and concurrent A/AAAA socket collisions in Linux conntrack. Configuring `single-request-reopen` and tuning `ndots:2` in `daemon.json` completely eliminated the DNS timeouts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on legacy bucket ACLs instead of modern S3 Block Public Access and IAM bucket policies
mistakesToAvoid.why: AWS recommends disabling ACLs (Bucket Owner Enforced) in favor of centralized declarative bucket policies and account-level Block Public Access controls.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Confusing SSE-S3 encryption with KMS customer-managed key (SSE-KMS) authorization policies
mistakesToAvoid.why: Accessing SSE-KMS encrypted objects requires both `s3:GetObject` and `kms:Decrypt` permissions; neglecting KMS key policies causes silent 403 Forbidden errors.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using sequential timestamps or predictable prefixes for high-throughput S3 read and write keys
mistakesToAvoid.why: Sequential key prefixes limit S3 horizontal partitioning; randomized hash prefixes distribute workloads across partitions to achieve 3,500 PUT and 5,500 GET requests/sec.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to audit S3 object delete markers when troubleshooting missing versioned objects in docker-embedded-dns-127-0-0-11-timeouts
mistakesToAvoid.why: Issuing a DELETE on a versioned bucket only adds a delete marker; engineers must retrieve previous versions or purge markers to restore data.

title: Hardening Docker Logging Drivers: Why Blocking Mode Freezes Containers and non-blocking Mode Tuning
summary: Understand how Docker's default blocking logging mode can deadlock container processes during log surges or remote logging outages. Configure `mode: non-blocking` with ring buffers.
question: During an outage of your centralized log aggregator (Fluentd / Splunk), several critical customer-facing microservices running in Docker completely froze and stopped accepting incoming HTTP requests. Application threads were stuck in `write()` syscalls to stdout/stderr. SREs were astonished that a failure in the logging aggregator could bring down business-critical production applications. You must explain the mechanics of Docker's logging pipe buffer, configure non-blocking logging, and size the ring buffer.
roleContext: Principal Docker Architect / Staff SRE Scenario
intro: Understand how Docker's default blocking logging mode can deadlock container processes during log surges or remote logging outages. Configure `mode: non-blocking` with ring buffers.

steps.title: Analyze the Architecture of Container Logging Pipes
steps.description: When a container starts, Docker redirects its stdout and stderr to Linux named pipes (FIFOs) managed by `containerd-shim`. In default `blocking` mode, if the logging driver cannot consume logs fast enough, the 64KB kernel pipe buffer fills up, causing application `write()` system calls to block indefinitely.
steps.content: When a container starts, Docker redirects its stdout and stderr to Linux named pipes (FIFOs) managed by `containerd-shim`. In default `blocking` mode, if the logging driver cannot consume logs fast enough, the 64KB kernel pipe buffer fills up, causing application `write()` system calls to block indefinitely.
steps.highlight: Analyze the Architecture of Container Logging Pipes
steps.codeBlock:
<!-- Logging Pipe Deadlock Flow -->
Application (writes to stdout) ───> Linux Kernel FIFO Pipe (64KB Buffer)
                                              │ (Buffer FULL!)
                                              └───> write() syscall BLOCKS!
                                              └───> Application Threads Freeze!
Logging Driver (Blocked / Slow Splunk / Disk I/O)

steps.title: Reproduce the Deadlock with a Slow Consumer
steps.description: Demonstrate how a process freezes when stdout cannot be drained by creating a container that outputs logs faster than a congested driver can process.
steps.content: Demonstrate how a process freezes when stdout cannot be drained by creating a container that outputs logs faster than a congested driver can process.
steps.highlight: Reproduce the Deadlock with a Slow Consumer
steps.codeBlock:
# Launch container with high-volume logging
docker run --rm alpine sh -c 'while true; do dd if=/dev/urandom bs=1024 count=1 2>/dev/null | base64; done' > /dev/null
# If pipe consumer stops, the process enters 'S' (interruptible sleep) stuck on write()

steps.title: Configure mode: non-blocking in daemon.json
steps.description: Switch Docker's logging mode to `non-blocking`. In non-blocking mode, Docker places an in-memory ring buffer between the container and the logging driver. If the buffer fills, older log messages are dropped rather than blocking the application.
steps.content: Switch Docker's logging mode to `non-blocking`. In non-blocking mode, Docker places an in-memory ring buffer between the container and the logging driver. If the buffer fills, older log messages are dropped rather than blocking the application.
steps.highlight: Configure mode: non-blocking in daemon.json

steps.title: Verify Non-Blocking Behavior and Monitor Dropped Log Metrics
steps.description: Launch containers and verify that during simulated collector downtime, application requests continue processing without interruption. Monitor Docker daemon log messages for buffer overflow warnings.
steps.content: Launch containers and verify that during simulated collector downtime, application requests continue processing without interruption. Monitor Docker daemon log messages for buffer overflow warnings.
steps.highlight: Verify Non-Blocking Behavior and Monitor Dropped Log Metrics
steps.codeBlock:
# Inspect container log configuration
docker inspect <CONTAINER_ID> --format '{{json .HostConfig.LogConfig}}' | jq .
# Output confirms "mode": "non-blocking", "max-buffer-size": "8m"

keyTakeaway: Docker's default blocking log mode causes application threads to deadlock when Linux pipe buffers fill up during logging subsystem slowdowns. Configuring `mode: non-blocking` with an 8MB buffer guarantees that container processes never freeze, prioritizing application availability over non-critical log retention.
elevatorPitch: We eliminated production application freezes caused by log pipeline congestion by configuring Docker's `mode: non-blocking` across all hosts. An 8MB in-memory ring buffer decouples application stdout/stderr from disk and remote log sinks, ensuring that a transient Fluentd or Splunk failure can never block application execution threads.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Bridge networking utilizes iptables NAT translations which add latency overhead, whereas host networking bypasses the network namespace entirely.

title: Mastering Container Memory and Swap Limits: --memory, --memory-swap, and swappiness Tuning
summary: Configure and calculate Docker container memory ceilings: `--memory`, `--memory-swap`, and `--memory-swappiness`. Prevent severe disk thrashing caused by excessive swapping and avoid sudden OOM kills.
question: Your Redis cache containers and Java JVM microservices run on multi-tenant Docker hosts with host swap enabled. When host memory pressure occurs, the Linux kernel aggressively swaps out JVM heap pages to host swap disk, degrading API response times from 5ms to 1,200ms due to disk paging thrashing. Meanwhile, engineers are confused by how `--memory-swap` interacts with `--memory`. You must formulate the mathematical relationship of Docker memory flags, disable swap for latency-critical caches, and tune swappiness.
roleContext: Principal Docker Architect / Staff SRE Scenario
intro: Configure and calculate Docker container memory ceilings: `--memory`, `--memory-swap`, and `--memory-swappiness`. Prevent severe disk thrashing caused by excessive swapping and avoid sudden OOM kills.

steps.title: Deconstruct the Mathematical Relationship of Docker Memory Flags
steps.description: Understand the precise calculation: `--memory-swap` represents total memory (RAM + SWAP combined), NOT swap alone. If `--memory=1g` and `--memory-swap=3g`, the container has 1GB of physical RAM and 2GB of swap space.
steps.content: Understand the precise calculation: `--memory-swap` represents total memory (RAM + SWAP combined), NOT swap alone. If `--memory=1g` and `--memory-swap=3g`, the container has 1GB of physical RAM and 2GB of swap space.
steps.highlight: Deconstruct the Mathematical Relationship of Docker Memory Flags
steps.codeBlock:
<!-- Docker Memory & Swap Formula -->
Total Container Memory Ceiling = --memory-swap
Physical RAM Allocation        = --memory
Actual Permitted Swap Space    = --memory-swap MINUS --memory

Rule Examples:
- Set RAM to 2GB, Swap to 1GB:     --memory=2g --memory-swap=3g
- Disable swap completely:         --memory=2g --memory-swap=2g (RAM == Total)
- Allow unlimited swap (Host max): --memory=2g --memory-swap=-1

steps.title: Completely Disable Swap for Latency-Critical Workloads
steps.description: For latency-critical in-memory databases (Redis, Memcached) or garbage-collected runtimes (Java/Go), swapping degrades throughput catastrophically. Set `--memory-swap` equal to `--memory` to strictly prohibit swap paging.
steps.content: For latency-critical in-memory databases (Redis, Memcached) or garbage-collected runtimes (Java/Go), swapping degrades throughput catastrophically. Set `--memory-swap` equal to `--memory` to strictly prohibit swap paging.
steps.highlight: Completely Disable Swap for Latency-Critical Workloads
steps.codeBlock:
# Prohibit swap paging for Redis
docker run -d \
  --name redis-cache \
  --memory="4g" \
  --memory-swap="4g" \
  redis:7-alpine

steps.title: Tune Container Swappiness (--memory-swappiness)
steps.description: Adjust the kernel's aggressiveness when swapping page cache versus anonymous memory using `--memory-swappiness` (0 to 100). A value of 0 instructs the kernel to avoid swapping process memory unless absolutely necessary.
steps.content: Adjust the kernel's aggressiveness when swapping page cache versus anonymous memory using `--memory-swappiness` (0 to 100). A value of 0 instructs the kernel to avoid swapping process memory unless absolutely necessary.
steps.highlight: Tune Container Swappiness (--memory-swappiness)
steps.codeBlock:
# Set swappiness to 0 to prioritize file cache reclamation over anonymous heap paging
docker run -d \
  --name java-api \
  --memory="2g" \
  --memory-swap="3g" \
  --memory-swappiness=0 \
  openjdk:21-slim

steps.title: Verify Cgroup Memory and Swap Limits in the Host Kernel
steps.description: Inspect the container's cgroup controllers to confirm limits are applied correctly by the kernel.
steps.content: Inspect the container's cgroup controllers to confirm limits are applied correctly by the kernel.
steps.highlight: Verify Cgroup Memory and Swap Limits in the Host Kernel
steps.codeBlock:
# In cgroups v2:
CONTAINER_ID=$(docker inspect redis-cache --format '{{.Id}}')
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/docker/${CONTAINER_ID}/memory.max
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/docker/${CONTAINER_ID}/memory.swap.max

# Inspect memory statistics and major page faults (disk paging)
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/docker/${CONTAINER_ID}/memory.stat | grep -E 'anon|file|pgpgin|pgpgout'

keyTakeaway: `--memory-swap` represents total memory (RAM plus Swap), not standalone swap. Setting `--memory-swap` equal to `--memory` prohibits swapping, preventing disk thrashing and maintaining microsecond response times for databases and garbage-collected runtimes.
elevatorPitch: We solved severe 1,000ms latency spikes in our containerized Java and Redis services by correcting their memory flags. Because `--memory-swap` defines total RAM plus swap, setting `--memory-swap` equal to `--memory` alongside `--memory-swappiness=0` completely prevented the kernel from paging application heaps to disk, restoring steady-state 5ms latency.

title: Hardening Linux Capabilities in Containers: Dropping ALL and Granting CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
summary: Implement principle of least privilege using Linux capabilities in Docker. Drop default capabilities (`--cap-drop=ALL`) and selectively restore only required capabilities like `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`.
question: Your security team conducted a penetration test and proved that default Docker containers retain 14 Linux capabilities, including `CAP_NET_RAW` (allowing ARP spoofing and packet sniffing) and `CAP_MKNOD` (allowing creation of device nodes). The CISO mandates that all production containers must drop ALL default capabilities by default, running as unprivileged users. However, your frontend Nginx proxy needs to bind to privileged port 80 and port 443 without running as root. You must configure granular capability hardening.
roleContext: Principal Docker Architect / Staff SRE Scenario
intro: Implement principle of least privilege using Linux capabilities in Docker. Drop default capabilities (`--cap-drop=ALL`) and selectively restore only required capabilities like `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`.

steps.title: Audit Docker's Default Linux Capabilities
steps.description: By default, Docker grants containers a subset of Linux capabilities: `CAP_CHOWN`, `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE`, `CAP_FOWNER`, `CAP_FSETID`, `CAP_KILL`, `CAP_SETGID`, `CAP_SETUID`, `CAP_SETPCAP`, `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`, `CAP_NET_RAW`, `CAP_SYS_CHROOT`, `CAP_MKNOD`, `CAP_AUDIT_WRITE`, `CAP_SETFCAP`. Many of these can be abused during container breakout attempts.
steps.content: By default, Docker grants containers a subset of Linux capabilities: `CAP_CHOWN`, `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE`, `CAP_FOWNER`, `CAP_FSETID`, `CAP_KILL`, `CAP_SETGID`, `CAP_SETUID`, `CAP_SETPCAP`, `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`, `CAP_NET_RAW`, `CAP_SYS_CHROOT`, `CAP_MKNOD`, `CAP_AUDIT_WRITE`, `CAP_SETFCAP`. Many of these can be abused during container breakout attempts.
steps.highlight: Audit Docker's Default Linux Capabilities
steps.codeBlock:
# Inspect granted capabilities of a default container
docker run --rm alpine capsh --print | grep Current
# Output: Current: = cap_chown,cap_dac_override,cap_net_raw,...

steps.title: Enforce the --cap-drop=ALL Security Baseline
steps.description: Always strip all capabilities first using `--cap-drop=ALL`. This establishes a zero-capability baseline, preventing unauthorized raw socket creation or ownership changes.
steps.content: Always strip all capabilities first using `--cap-drop=ALL`. This establishes a zero-capability baseline, preventing unauthorized raw socket creation or ownership changes.
steps.highlight: Enforce the --cap-drop=ALL Security Baseline
steps.codeBlock:
# Strip all capabilities
docker run --rm --cap-drop=ALL alpine capsh --print | grep Current
# Output: Current: = (empty, zero capabilities!)

steps.title: Selectively Add CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE for Unprivileged Port Binding
steps.description: Linux kernels require the `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` capability to bind to privileged ports below 1024 (e.g., 80, 443). Grant strictly this single capability to an unprivileged container user.
steps.content: Linux kernels require the `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` capability to bind to privileged ports below 1024 (e.g., 80, 443). Grant strictly this single capability to an unprivileged container user.
steps.highlight: Selectively Add CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE for Unprivileged Port Binding
steps.codeBlock:
# Run unprivileged container with only CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
docker run -d \
  --name secure-nginx \
  --user 1001:1001 \
  --cap-drop=ALL \
  --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE \
  -p 80:80 \
  nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:alpine

steps.title: Declarative Capability Hardening in Docker Compose and Kubernetes
steps.description: Apply the capability dropping and addition declaratively in `compose.yaml` and Kubernetes Pod `securityContext`.
steps.content: Apply the capability dropping and addition declaratively in `compose.yaml` and Kubernetes Pod `securityContext`.
steps.highlight: Declarative Capability Hardening in Docker Compose and Kubernetes
steps.codeBlock:
# Docker Compose
services:
  web:
    image: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:alpine
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    cap_add:
      - NET_BIND_SERVICE

# Kubernetes Pod SecurityContext
# securityContext:
#   capabilities:
#     drop: ["ALL"]
#     add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]

keyTakeaway: Default containers inherit dangerous capabilities like `CAP_NET_RAW`. Adhering to the principle of least privilege requires declaring `--cap-drop=ALL` and selectively re-enabling only necessary capabilities such as `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`.
elevatorPitch: We neutralized container privilege escalation risks by enforcing `--cap-drop=ALL` across our entire fleet. For web gateways requiring binding to ports 80 and 443, we selectively add `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` to unprivileged user accounts, ensuring our workloads have zero capability to forge raw packets, alter file ownerships, or touch kernel devices.

title: Automated Docker Host Maintenance: Safe System Pruning, Volume Protection, and BuildKit GC
summary: Design and automate recurring Docker host cleanup workflows. Use `docker system prune`, filters (`until`), BuildKit garbage collection, and safeguard stateful named volumes against accidental deletion.
question: A junior engineer executed `docker system prune -a --volumes -f` on a staging server to free up disk space, accidentally deleting production-mirror database volumes and wiping uncommitted test databases. On other CI nodes, unmaintained Docker hosts frequently run out of disk space due to hundreds of gigabytes of dangling images and BuildKit cache layers. You must design an automated, safe maintenance strategy that prunes stale resources using age filters without risking persistent volumes.
roleContext: Principal Docker Architect / Staff SRE Scenario
intro: Design and automate recurring Docker host cleanup workflows. Use `docker system prune`, filters (`until`), BuildKit garbage collection, and safeguard stateful named volumes against accidental deletion.

steps.title: Analyze the Scope and Risks of Prune Subcommands
steps.description: Understand command scopes: `docker image prune` removes dangling (`<none>`) images. `docker container prune` cleans stopped containers. `docker system prune -a` removes all unused images (not just dangling ones). Adding `--volumes` destroys all anonymous and unused named volumes, posing catastrophic data loss risks.
steps.content: Understand command scopes: `docker image prune` removes dangling (`<none>`) images. `docker container prune` cleans stopped containers. `docker system prune -a` removes all unused images (not just dangling ones). Adding `--volumes` destroys all anonymous and unused named volumes, posing catastrophic data loss risks.
steps.highlight: Analyze the Scope and Risks of Prune Subcommands
steps.codeBlock:
<!-- Prune Command Danger Levels -->
SAFE:        docker image prune                                (Removes dangling layers only)
CONTROLLED:  docker system prune --filter "until=168h"         (Removes stopped containers & untagged images > 7 days old)
DANGEROUS:   docker system prune -a                            (Removes ALL images not actively running!)
CATASTROPHIC: docker system prune -a --volumes                 (Destroys all unused persistent volumes!)

steps.title: Implement Age-Filtered Maintenance with --filter until
steps.description: Always qualify automated pruning scripts with the `until` filter (e.g., `until=72h` or `until=168h`), ensuring that recently stopped containers and recently downloaded base images are preserved for developer cache.
steps.content: Always qualify automated pruning scripts with the `until` filter (e.g., `until=72h` or `until=168h`), ensuring that recently stopped containers and recently downloaded base images are preserved for developer cache.
steps.highlight: Implement Age-Filtered Maintenance with --filter until
steps.codeBlock:
# Prune stopped containers older than 3 days
docker container prune --filter "until=72h" -f

# Prune unused images created more than 7 days ago (without touching volumes)
docker image prune -a --filter "until=168h" -f

steps.title: Configure Built-in BuildKit Garbage Collection in daemon.json
steps.description: Rather than relying on manual cron jobs, configure BuildKit's native garbage collector in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` to enforce strict disk storage ceilings.
steps.content: Rather than relying on manual cron jobs, configure BuildKit's native garbage collector in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` to enforce strict disk storage ceilings.
steps.highlight: Configure Built-in BuildKit Garbage Collection in daemon.json

steps.title: Deploy Automated systemd Timer for Routine Host Hygiene
steps.description: Create a hardened systemd service and timer running weekly that safely trims orphaned build layers and dangling images while strictly excluding `--volumes`.
steps.content: Create a hardened systemd service and timer running weekly that safely trims orphaned build layers and dangling images while strictly excluding `--volumes`.
steps.highlight: Deploy Automated systemd Timer for Routine Host Hygiene
steps.codeBlock:
# /etc/systemd/system/docker-prune.service
[Unit]
Description=Safe Docker Host Prune
[Service]
Type=Oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/docker system prune -f --filter "until=168h"

keyTakeaway: Never use `--volumes` in automated pruning scripts. Safe host maintenance relies on age-based filters (`--filter until=168h`) and native BuildKit garbage collection policies in `daemon.json` to keep disk usage bounded without threatening persistent data.
elevatorPitch: We prevented disk exhaustion across 200 build nodes while eliminating accidental data loss by deploying a strict pruning policy. We banned the `--volumes` flag in scripts, enabled BuildKit's native 20GB garbage collection in `daemon.json`, and deployed weekly systemd timers that prune dangling images older than 7 days using the `until` filter.

title: Enforcing Cryptographic Container Integrity with Docker Content Trust (DCT) and Notary
summary: Configure Docker Content Trust (DCT) to enforce digital signing and cryptographic verification of container images. Prevent deployment of untrusted or tampered images using `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1`.
question: Your enterprise security guidelines require that production environments execute only container images digitally signed by approved CI/CD release pipelines. If an adversary compromises an internal registry and overwrites a tag (such as `api:v1.0`) with a trojanized image, Docker engines must refuse to pull or execute the corrupted image. You must implement Docker Content Trust (DCT), manage Notary root and repository keys, and enforce image verification on production nodes.
roleContext: Principal Docker Architect / Staff SRE Scenario
intro: Configure Docker Content Trust (DCT) to enforce digital signing and cryptographic verification of container images. Prevent deployment of untrusted or tampered images using `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1`.

steps.title: Understand Docker Content Trust (DCT) Architecture and Notary
steps.description: DCT is based on The Update Framework (TUF) and Notary. It uses a hierarchy of cryptographic keys: the Root Key (offline key of trust), Targets Key (signs image tags/digests), Snapshot Key (prevents replay/freeze attacks), and Timestamp Key (ensures freshness).
steps.content: DCT is based on The Update Framework (TUF) and Notary. It uses a hierarchy of cryptographic keys: the Root Key (offline key of trust), Targets Key (signs image tags/digests), Snapshot Key (prevents replay/freeze attacks), and Timestamp Key (ensures freshness).
steps.highlight: Understand Docker Content Trust (DCT) Architecture and Notary
steps.codeBlock:
<!-- Key Hierarchy -->
Root Key (Kept Offline in HSM / Cold Storage)
  └── Targets Key (Signs image tags and hashes)
  └── Snapshot Key (Validates metadata consistency)
  └── Timestamp Key (Held by Notary server, prevents replay attacks)

steps.title: Generate Signing Delegation Keys and Initialize Trust
steps.description: Enable Docker Content Trust locally using `export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1`. Generate signing keys and initialize trust for your target repository.
steps.content: Enable Docker Content Trust locally using `export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1`. Generate signing keys and initialize trust for your target repository.
steps.highlight: Generate Signing Delegation Keys and Initialize Trust
steps.codeBlock:
# Enable Docker Content Trust in shell
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST_SERVER="https://notary.internal.company:4443"

# Build and push signed image (prompts to generate Root & Targets passphrases)
docker build -t registry.internal.company/security/auth:v1.0 .
docker push registry.internal.company/security/auth:v1.0
# Output: Signing and pushing trust metadata for registry.internal.company/security/auth

steps.title: Verify Trust Enforcement on Production Docker Daemons
steps.description: Enable `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1` on production hosts. Attempt to run an unsigned or tampered image, and verify that Docker aborts execution with `Error: remote trust data does not exist`.
steps.content: Enable `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1` on production hosts. Attempt to run an unsigned or tampered image, and verify that Docker aborts execution with `Error: remote trust data does not exist`.
steps.highlight: Verify Trust Enforcement on Production Docker Daemons
steps.codeBlock:
# On production host with DCT enabled:
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1

# Running signed image succeeds:
docker pull registry.internal.company/security/auth:v1.0
# Status: Downloaded newer image for registry.internal.company/security/auth:v1.0

# Running unsigned image is blocked:
docker pull untrusted-registry.com/app:latest
# Error: remote trust data does not exist for untrusted-registry.com/app

steps.title: Automate Delegation Signing in CI/CD Runners
steps.description: Configure CI/CD runners with delegation signing keys (`docker trust signer add`) so automated pipelines can sign images using short-lived delegation certificates without exposing the master Root Key.
steps.content: Configure CI/CD runners with delegation signing keys (`docker trust signer add`) so automated pipelines can sign images using short-lived delegation certificates without exposing the master Root Key.
steps.highlight: Automate Delegation Signing in CI/CD Runners
steps.codeBlock:
# Add CI delegation signer
docker trust signer add --key ci-signer.pub ci-builder registry.internal.company/security/auth

keyTakeaway: Docker Content Trust (DCT) enforces cryptographic image integrity using TUF and Notary. Setting `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1` ensures that production engines only pull and run images that have been signed by verified keys, preventing registry tag poisoning and supply chain tampering.
elevatorPitch: We secured our container deployments against image tampering and registry poisoning by enabling Docker Content Trust. With `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1` enforced on production nodes, the Docker engine verifies cryptographic signatures against our Notary server before pulling any layer, rejecting untrusted or altered images at the runtime gate.

title: Container Operations Command Reference: Mapping Docker CLI to crictl, nerdctl, and ctr
summary: Master the command-line mapping between standard Docker CLI commands and containerd debugging utilities: `crictl` for Kubernetes, `nerdctl` for Docker parity, and `ctr` for low-level runtime triage.
question: Your engineering organization migrated all Kubernetes nodes from Docker daemon (`dockershim`) to containerd. During on-call incidents, newly onboarded SREs repeatedly attempt to run familiar commands like `docker ps`, `docker logs`, `docker exec`, and `docker images`, which fail on containerd nodes. You must author a comprehensive operational command translation matrix and operational troubleshooting guide mapping Docker commands to `crictl`, `nerdctl`, and `ctr`.
roleContext: Principal Docker Architect / Staff SRE Scenario
intro: Master the command-line mapping between standard Docker CLI commands and containerd debugging utilities: `crictl` for Kubernetes, `nerdctl` for Docker parity, and `ctr` for low-level runtime triage.

steps.title: Understand the Purpose of Each Tool in the containerd Stack
steps.description: Differentiate tool scopes: `docker` manages the Docker daemon. `crictl` communicates through Kubernetes Container Runtime Interface (CRI) and understands Pod sandboxes. `nerdctl` provides full Docker CLI syntax compatibility for containerd. `ctr` interacts directly with containerd's internal gRPC APIs for low-level debugging.
steps.content: Differentiate tool scopes: `docker` manages the Docker daemon. `crictl` communicates through Kubernetes Container Runtime Interface (CRI) and understands Pod sandboxes. `nerdctl` provides full Docker CLI syntax compatibility for containerd. `ctr` interacts directly with containerd's internal gRPC APIs for low-level debugging.
steps.highlight: Understand the Purpose of Each Tool in the containerd Stack
steps.codeBlock:
<!-- CLI Hierarchy -->
Docker CLI   ───> dockerd ───> containerd ───> containerd-shim ───> runc
crictl       ───> CRI Plugin (inside containerd, k8s.io namespace)
nerdctl      ───> containerd (Docker CLI drop-in)
ctr          ───> containerd (Raw internal API)

steps.title: Master the Core Operational Command Translation Matrix
steps.description: Map standard daily operational commands across the four CLI tools.
steps.content: Map standard daily operational commands across the four CLI tools.
steps.highlight: Master the Core Operational Command Translation Matrix
steps.codeBlock:
# Task: List Running Containers
# Docker:   docker ps
# crictl:   crictl ps
# nerdctl:  nerdctl -n k8s.io ps
# ctr:      ctr -n k8s.io tasks list

# Task: View Container Logs
# Docker:   docker logs <id>
# crictl:   crictl logs <id>
# nerdctl:  nerdctl -n k8s.io logs <id>
# ctr:      (Not natively supported; logs must be read from /var/log/pods/)

# Task: Execute Interactive Shell
# Docker:   docker exec -it <id> sh
# crictl:   crictl exec -it <id> sh
# nerdctl:  nerdctl -n k8s.io exec -it <id> sh
# ctr:      ctr -n k8s.io tasks exec --exec-id test -t <id> sh

# Task: List Images
# Docker:   docker images
# crictl:   crictl images
# nerdctl:  nerdctl -n k8s.io images
# ctr:      ctr -n k8s.io images list

steps.title: Utilize Pod Sandbox Inspection Commands Unique to crictl
steps.description: Unlike Docker, `crictl` understands Kubernetes Pod Sandboxes (the pause container boundary). Use `crictl pods` and `crictl inspectp` to inspect pod-level networking, cgroup configurations, and annotations.
steps.content: Unlike Docker, `crictl` understands Kubernetes Pod Sandboxes (the pause container boundary). Use `crictl pods` and `crictl inspectp` to inspect pod-level networking, cgroup configurations, and annotations.
steps.highlight: Utilize Pod Sandbox Inspection Commands Unique to crictl
steps.codeBlock:
# List all pod sandboxes on the node
crictl pods

# Inspect pod sandbox network details
crictl inspectp <POD_ID> | jq .status.network.ip

# Stop and remove an entire pod sandbox directly
crictl stopp <POD_ID>
crictl rmp <POD_ID>

steps.title: Use nerdctl for Image Building and Rootless Containers
steps.description: When developers need Docker-like functionality on containerd hosts (e.g., building images or running Compose stacks), use `nerdctl` which leverages BuildKit and compose specifications natively.
steps.content: When developers need Docker-like functionality on containerd hosts (e.g., building images or running Compose stacks), use `nerdctl` which leverages BuildKit and compose specifications natively.

nerdctl build -t my-app:v1 .

# Run compose stack on containerd
nerdctl compose up -d

keyTakeaway: On Kubernetes containerd nodes, `crictl` is the primary tool for container and pod sandbox triage, `nerdctl` provides a drop-in replacement for the Docker CLI experience, and `ctr` provides raw daemon diagnostics when the CRI socket is unresponsive.
elevatorPitch: When our nodes transitioned from Docker to containerd, we provided our SREs with a clear CLI mapping guide. For pod-level troubleshooting, they use `crictl` which natively understands pod sandboxes. For Docker command parity and local builds, they use `nerdctl`, ensuring seamless incident triage without confusion.

title: Securing Remote Docker API: Hardening Port 2376 with Mutual TLS (mTLS) to Prevent Cryptojacking
summary: Secure remote Docker engine TCP sockets. Prevent unauthenticated remote code execution and cryptojacking worm attacks by configuring strict mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication on port 2376.
question: A development team exposed Docker's TCP socket on port 2375 (`-H tcp://0.0.0.0:2375`) to allow remote builds from a Jenkins server. Within 4 hours, internet botnets scanned the port, invoked the Docker API to launch privileged containers mounting the host root filesystem, and deployed Monero cryptominers across the server fleet. You must disinfect the servers, shut down unencrypted port 2375, and implement hardened mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication on port 2376 using client certificates.
roleContext: Principal Docker Architect / Staff SRE Scenario
intro: Secure remote Docker engine TCP sockets. Prevent unauthenticated remote code execution and cryptojacking worm attacks by configuring strict mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication on port 2376.

steps.title: Understand the Severity of Unauthenticated Docker API Exposure
steps.description: Exposing Docker's API without TLS on port 2375 allows anyone who can reach the port to execute arbitrary commands as host root. An attacker simply issues a POST request to `/containers/create` with a privileged Alpine container mounting `/` from the host.
steps.content: Exposing Docker's API without TLS on port 2375 allows anyone who can reach the port to execute arbitrary commands as host root. An attacker simply issues a POST request to `/containers/create` with a privileged Alpine container mounting `/` from the host.
steps.highlight: Understand the Severity of Unauthenticated Docker API Exposure
steps.codeBlock:
# Demonstration of the attack vector:
curl -X POST http://victim-node:2375/containers/create \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"Image":"alpine","Cmd":["sh","-c","echo pwned > /host/etc/motd"],"HostConfig":{"Binds":["/:/host"]}}'

steps.title: Generate CA, Server, and Client Certificates for mTLS
steps.description: Create a dedicated Certificate Authority (CA), a server certificate with the host IP/FQDN in the Subject Alternative Name (SAN), and a client certificate for authentication.
steps.content: Create a dedicated Certificate Authority (CA), a server certificate with the host IP/FQDN in the Subject Alternative Name (SAN), and a client certificate for authentication.
steps.highlight: Generate CA, Server, and Client Certificates for mTLS
steps.codeBlock:
# 1. Create CA
openssl genrsa -out ca-key.pem 4096
openssl req -new -x509 -days 365 -key ca-key.pem -sha256 -out ca.pem -subj "/CN=Docker-CA"

# 2. Create Server Key and Cert with SAN
openssl genrsa -out server-key.pem 4096
openssl req -subj "/CN=docker-host.internal" -sha256 -new -key server-key.pem -out server.csr
echo "subjectAltName = DNS:docker-host.internal,IP:10.0.1.50" > extfile.cnf
echo "extendedKeyUsage = serverAuth" >> extfile.cnf
openssl x509 -req -days 365 -sha256 -in server.csr -CA ca.pem -CAkey ca-key.pem \
  -CAcreateserial -out server-cert.pem -extfile extfile.cnf

# 3. Create Client Key and Cert
openssl genrsa -out key.pem 4096
openssl req -subj '/CN=client' -new -key key.pem -out client.csr
echo "extendedKeyUsage = clientAuth" > extfile-client.cnf
openssl x509 -req -days 365 -sha256 -in client.csr -CA ca.pem -CAkey ca-key.pem \
  -CAcreateserial -out cert.pem -extfile extfile-client.cnf

steps.title: Configure Docker Daemon for Mandatory TLS Verification
steps.description: Configure `/etc/docker/daemon.json` to bind to port 2376 with `tlsverify: true`, referencing the generated CA and server certificate.
steps.content: Configure `/etc/docker/daemon.json` to bind to port 2376 with `tlsverify: true`, referencing the generated CA and server certificate.
steps.highlight: Configure Docker Daemon for Mandatory TLS Verification
steps.codeBlock:
cat <<EOF | sudo tee /etc/docker/daemon.json
{
  "tls": true,
  "tlsverify": true,
  "tlscacert": "/etc/docker/certs/ca.pem",
  "tlscert": "/etc/docker/certs/server-cert.pem",
  "tlskey": "/etc/docker/certs/server-key.pem",
  "hosts": ["unix:///var/run/docker.sock", "tcp://0.0.0.0:2376"]
}
EOF

sudo systemctl restart docker

steps.title: Connect Securely from Remote Client Using TLS Flags
steps.description: Test the connection from the remote Jenkins runner. Verify that connecting without client certificates fails, and connecting with certificates succeeds.
steps.content: Test the connection from the remote Jenkins runner. Verify that connecting without client certificates fails, and connecting with certificates succeeds.
steps.highlight: Connect Securely from Remote Client Using TLS Flags
steps.codeBlock:
# Unauthenticated connection fails:
curl https://10.0.1.50:2376/version --insecure
# Output: Bad Request / Client sent an HTTP request to an HTTPS server

# Authenticated connection via Docker CLI succeeds:
docker --tlsverify \
  --tlscacert=ca.pem \
  --tlscert=cert.pem \
  --tlskey=key.pem \
  -H=tcp://10.0.1.50:2376 version

keyTakeaway: Never expose Docker port 2375 unencrypted. When remote API access is required, bind strictly to port 2376 with `tlsverify: true` and enforce mutual TLS using client certificates signed by an internal Certificate Authority.
elevatorPitch: We eradicated remote container takeover and cryptojacking vulnerabilities by shutting down unencrypted Docker port 2375 across all build hosts. We configured mutual TLS on port 2376 requiring valid x509 client certificates, ensuring that only authenticated CI runners presenting valid cryptographic credentials can interact with the Docker daemon.

title: Integrating Persistent Cloud Storage in Docker: CSI Plugins, RexRay, and AWS EBS/EFS Volume Mounts
summary: Architect persistent cloud block and file storage for Docker containers. Configure Docker volume plugins (RexRay / CSI plugins) to dynamically attach, format, and mount AWS EBS and EFS volumes.
question: Your team is running stateful database containers (PostgreSQL, MongoDB) on standalone AWS EC2 instances managed by Docker Compose. If an EC2 host suffers a hardware failure, an operator must provision a new instance, detach the AWS EBS volume from the dead host, reattach it to the new host, and mount it before starting the container. You need to implement an automated Docker storage plugin (using RexRay or Docker CSI) that dynamically attaches and mounts AWS EBS and EFS volumes on container startup.
roleContext: Principal Docker Architect / Staff SRE Scenario
intro: Architect persistent cloud block and file storage for Docker containers. Configure Docker volume plugins (RexRay / CSI plugins) to dynamically attach, format, and mount AWS EBS and EFS volumes.

steps.title: Understand Docker Volume Plugin Architecture
steps.description: Docker supports storage extensibility through managed volume plugins (V2 plugin architecture). When a container requests a named volume backed by a plugin, the plugin communicates with cloud provider APIs (e.g., AWS EC2/EBS APIs) to dynamically attach the cloud disk to the host and mount it to `/var/lib/docker/plugins/...`.
steps.content: Docker supports storage extensibility through managed volume plugins (V2 plugin architecture). When a container requests a named volume backed by a plugin, the plugin communicates with cloud provider APIs (e.g., AWS EC2/EBS APIs) to dynamically attach the cloud disk to the host and mount it to `/var/lib/docker/plugins/...`.
steps.highlight: Understand Docker Volume Plugin Architecture
steps.codeBlock:
<!-- Volume Plugin Flow -->
docker run -v my-ebs-vol:/data db:latest
  └── Docker Volume Plugin (RexRay / AWS EBS Driver)
        ├── Calls AWS API: DescribeVolumes & AttachVolume (vol-0a1b2c -> i-09876)
        ├── Waits for /dev/xvdf to appear on Linux host
        ├── Formats (mkfs.ext4 if new) & mounts to host
        └── Passes mountpoint into container /data

steps.title: Install and Configure Docker Cloud Volume Plugin
steps.description: Install the managed storage plugin using `docker plugin install`, granting necessary IAM permissions for AWS EBS and EC2 volume management.
steps.content: Install the managed storage plugin using `docker plugin install`, granting necessary IAM permissions for AWS EBS and EC2 volume management.
steps.highlight: Install and Configure Docker Cloud Volume Plugin
steps.codeBlock:
# Install RexRay AWS EBS volume plugin
docker plugin install rexray/ebs \
  EBS_REGION=us-east-1 \
  EBS_MAXRETRIES=10 \
  --grant-all-permissions

# Verify active plugins
docker plugin ls

steps.title: Provision and Mount Persistent EBS Volume Declaratively
steps.description: Create a persistent named volume backed by the cloud driver specifying volume size, IOPS, and volume type (`gp3`). Mount the volume into the database container.
steps.content: Create a persistent named volume backed by the cloud driver specifying volume size, IOPS, and volume type (`gp3`). Mount the volume into the database container.
steps.highlight: Provision and Mount Persistent EBS Volume Declaratively

# Create 100GB GP3 volume via Docker CLI
docker volume create -d rexray/ebs \
  --name prod-postgres-ebs \
  -o size=100 \
  -o volumeType=gp3 \
  -o iops=3000

# Run stateful container using the persistent cloud volume
docker run -d \
  --name db-primary \
  -v prod-postgres-ebs:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  postgres:16

keyTakeaway: Docker managed volume plugins bridge container lifecycles with cloud block and file storage. By leveraging storage plugins, containers automatically attach and mount persistent AWS EBS volumes across host failures without manual disk detachment.

Persistent databases mount named EBS volumes backed by the storage driver; if an underlying host fails, launching the container on a new instance automatically detaches the EBS volume and re-mounts it in seconds with zero data loss.

title: Calibrating Docker HEALTHCHECKs: Interval, Timeout, Retries, and Preventing Cascading Restarts
summary: Design and calibrate container `HEALTHCHECK` parameters (`interval`, `timeout`, `retries`, `start-period`). Prevent false-positive container flapping and cascading failures during traffic spikes.
question: During a flash sale, your frontend API containers experienced high latency spikes. Docker healthchecks configured with an aggressive 2-second timeout (`--timeout=2s`) and 2 retries began failing because the busy application took 2.5 seconds to reply to the health check probe. Docker marked the containers `unhealthy`, triggering orchestrator restart loops that killed healthy instances and amplified the traffic load on remaining nodes, causing a complete cascading system collapse. You must properly calibrate healthcheck parameters.
roleContext: Principal Docker Architect / Staff SRE Scenario
intro: Design and calibrate container `HEALTHCHECK` parameters (`interval`, `timeout`, `retries`, `start-period`). Prevent false-positive container flapping and cascading failures during traffic spikes.

steps.title: Understand the States and Mechanics of Docker HEALTHCHECK
steps.description: A container healthcheck has three lifecycle states: `starting` (during `start-period`), `healthy` (probe exit code 0), and `unhealthy` (probe exit code 1 or timeout). Crucially, during `start-period`, failing health checks do not count towards the retry limit.
steps.content: A container healthcheck has three lifecycle states: `starting` (during `start-period`), `healthy` (probe exit code 0), and `unhealthy` (probe exit code 1 or timeout). Crucially, during `start-period`, failing health checks do not count towards the retry limit.
steps.highlight: Understand the States and Mechanics of Docker HEALTHCHECK
steps.codeBlock:
<!-- Healthcheck Lifecycle -->
Container Starts ───> State: STARTING (start-period: 30s)
                          │ (Failures do not trigger unhealthy!)
                          └─── Probe succeeds -> State: HEALTHY
                                  │ (Normal monitoring begins: interval=10s)
                                  └── Failures >= retries -> State: UNHEALTHY

steps.title: Calibrate Parameters to Prevent False-Positive Flapping
steps.description: Avoid hair-trigger thresholds. Set `interval` to 10-15 seconds, `timeout` to 5 seconds, and `retries` to 3 or 4. Ensure `start-period` is long enough to accommodate slow application warm-ups and schema checks.
steps.content: Avoid hair-trigger thresholds. Set `interval` to 10-15 seconds, `timeout` to 5 seconds, and `retries` to 3 or 4. Ensure `start-period` is long enough to accommodate slow application warm-ups and schema checks.
steps.highlight: Calibrate Parameters to Prevent False-Positive Flapping
steps.codeBlock:
# Dockerfile
HEALTHCHECK --interval=15s \
            --timeout=5s \
            --start-period=40s \
            --retries=3 \
  CMD curl -f http://localhost:8080/health/liveness || exit 1

steps.title: Decouple Deep Readiness from Shallow Liveness Probes
steps.description: A common mistake is designing health checks that test heavy downstream dependencies (e.g., executing a database query or external API call). If the database slows down, all API containers fail their healthchecks and reboot simultaneously. Healthchecks should test internal container viability (liveness), not transitive dependencies.
steps.content: A common mistake is designing health checks that test heavy downstream dependencies (e.g., executing a database query or external API call). If the database slows down, all API containers fail their healthchecks and reboot simultaneously. Healthchecks should test internal container viability (liveness), not transitive dependencies.
steps.highlight: Decouple Deep Readiness from Shallow Liveness Probes

steps.title: Inspect Health Status and History in Docker Inspect
steps.description: Use `docker inspect` to view the timestamp, exit code, and stdout/stderr output of the last 5 health check executions.
steps.content: Use `docker inspect` to view the timestamp, exit code, and stdout/stderr output of the last 5 health check executions.
steps.highlight: Inspect Health Status and History in Docker Inspect
steps.codeBlock:
# View recent healthcheck execution logs
docker inspect --format '{{json .State.Health}}' my-app | jq .

keyTakeaway: Aggressive healthchecks cause catastrophic cascading failures when high load causes transient latency. Always configure a generous `start-period`, set `retries` to at least 3, and ensure the healthcheck tests local process viability rather than downstream database dependencies.
elevatorPitch: We stopped cascading restart outages during high-traffic events by recalibrating our container health checks. We decoupled deep dependency checks from container liveness, lengthened retry thresholds to 3 consecutive failures with a 5-second timeout, and added a 40-second `start-period`, preventing healthy but busy containers from being mistakenly terminated.

title: Capturing and Analyzing Linux Core Dumps from Crashing Containers with GDB
summary: Configure host Linux kernels and Docker containers to reliably generate core dumps during segmentation faults (`SIGSEGV`). Configure `/proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern`, ulimits, and debug with GDB.
question: A mission-critical C++ and Go payment gateway running inside Docker occasionally crashes with exit code 139 (`SIGSEGV` - Segmentation Fault). Because containers discard volatile state upon termination, no core dump file is produced, making postmortem debugging impossible. The development team is unable to locate the failing thread or memory address. You must configure the host kernel and container execution environment to capture full core dumps to a persistent host volume and analyze them using GDB.
roleContext: Principal Docker Architect / Staff SRE Scenario
intro: Configure host Linux kernels and Docker containers to reliably generate core dumps during segmentation faults (`SIGSEGV`). Configure `/proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern`, ulimits, and debug with GDB.

steps.title: Understand Linux Kernel Core Pattern Mechanics for Containers
steps.description: When a process crashes inside a container, the host kernel handles the core dump. If `/proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern` specifies a relative path (e.g., `core`), the file is written to the container's working directory and lost on container restart. To capture core dumps reliably, configure an absolute path on the host or pipe to a host handler.
steps.content: When a process crashes inside a container, the host kernel handles the core dump. If `/proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern` specifies a relative path (e.g., `core`), the file is written to the container's working directory and lost on container restart. To capture core dumps reliably, configure an absolute path on the host or pipe to a host handler.
steps.highlight: Understand Linux Kernel Core Pattern Mechanics for Containers
steps.codeBlock:
# Configure host kernel core dump pattern to write to a dedicated host directory
echo '/var/coredumps/core.%e.%p.%h.%t' | sudo tee /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern

# Ensure host directory exists and has permissive write permissions
sudo mkdir -p /var/coredumps && sudo chmod 1777 /var/coredumps

steps.title: Enable Unlimited Core File Size in Docker Container
steps.description: By default, Docker containers have a core dump ulimit of 0 (`ulimit -c 0`), which suppresses core dump generation. Pass `--ulimit core=-1:-1` at runtime to allow unlimited core dump sizes.
steps.content: By default, Docker containers have a core dump ulimit of 0 (`ulimit -c 0`), which suppresses core dump generation. Pass `--ulimit core=-1:-1` at runtime to allow unlimited core dump sizes.
steps.highlight: Enable Unlimited Core File Size in Docker Container
steps.codeBlock:
# Run container with unlimited core file size
docker run -d \
  --name payment-engine \
  --ulimit core=-1:-1 \
  -v /var/coredumps:/var/coredumps \
  payment-gateway:v3.2

steps.title: Simulate Crash and Verify Core Dump Generation
steps.description: Send `SIGSEGV` or `SIGABRT` to the running process inside the container. Verify that the Linux kernel generates a complete memory image in `/var/coredumps`.
steps.content: Send `SIGSEGV` or `SIGABRT` to the running process inside the container. Verify that the Linux kernel generates a complete memory image in `/var/coredumps`.
steps.highlight: Simulate Crash and Verify Core Dump Generation
steps.codeBlock:
# Send SIGSEGV to trigger segmentation fault
docker exec -it payment-engine kill -SIGSEGV 1

# Verify core dump file on host
ls -lh /var/coredumps/
# Output: -rw------- 1 1000 1000 482M Oct 06 12:00 core.payment-engine.1.container-host.1728216000

steps.title: Inspect Stack Trace with GDB Inside Debug Container
steps.description: Launch an ephemeral debugging container with GDB and debug symbols to inspect the backtrace and locate the exact crash line.
steps.content: Launch an ephemeral debugging container with GDB and debug symbols to inspect the backtrace and locate the exact crash line.
steps.highlight: Inspect Stack Trace with GDB Inside Debug Container
steps.codeBlock:
# Launch GDB to inspect thread backtrace
docker run --rm -v /var/coredumps:/dumps -v $(pwd)/symbols:/symbols ubuntu:22.04 \
  gdb /symbols/payment-engine /dumps/core.payment-engine... -ex "bt full" -ex "quit"

keyTakeaway: Capturing core dumps from containers requires configuring the host's `/proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern` with an absolute path and launching containers with `--ulimit core=-1:-1`. Mounting the dump directory allows immediate analysis with GDB.
elevatorPitch: We solved intermittent segmentation fault crashes in our native payment runtimes by configuring kernel core dump capture. By setting the host `core_pattern` to an absolute path and passing `--ulimit core=-1:-1` to containers, crash dumps are persisted automatically, enabling developers to pinpoint faulty memory pointers with GDB in minutes.

title: Triaging Containers Stuck in Terminating and Linux Kernel Uninterruptible Sleep ('D' State)
summary: Diagnose and resolve containers that cannot be stopped or killed with `docker rm -f` or `kill -9` because processes are trapped in Linux kernel Uninterruptible Sleep (`D` state) due to hanging NFS or block storage I/O.
question: Several production worker nodes report containers stuck in `Terminating` status. Executing `docker kill -s 9 <id>` or `docker rm -f <id>` has no effect; the CLI hangs or returns successfully while the container remains running. Running `ps aux` reveals application threads in state `D` (Uninterruptible Sleep). A shared NFS volume or AWS EBS disk stopped responding to SCSI requests. You must explain why `SIGKILL` cannot terminate processes in `D` state, safely unfreeze the kernel subsystem, and recover the node.
roleContext: Principal Docker Architect / Staff SRE Scenario
intro: Diagnose and resolve containers that cannot be stopped or killed with `docker rm -f` or `kill -9` because processes are trapped in Linux kernel Uninterruptible Sleep (`D` state) due to hanging NFS or block storage I/O.

steps.title: Understand the Linux Kernel 'D' State (Uninterruptible Sleep)
steps.description: A process enters `TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE` (`D` state) when waiting for hardware I/O (such as a disk read or NFS network RPC). In this state, the kernel guarantees data integrity by ignoring ALL signals, including `SIGKILL` (`kill -9`). The process cannot terminate until the kernel I/O call returns or times out.
steps.content: A process enters `TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE` (`D` state) when waiting for hardware I/O (such as a disk read or NFS network RPC). In this state, the kernel guarantees data integrity by ignoring ALL signals, including `SIGKILL` (`kill -9`). The process cannot terminate until the kernel I/O call returns or times out.
steps.highlight: Understand the Linux Kernel 'D' State (Uninterruptible Sleep)
steps.codeBlock:
<!-- Process Wait States -->
Interruptible Sleep ('S'):
  Process waiting for timer / event. Kernel delivers SIGTERM/SIGKILL -> Process terminates immediately.

Uninterruptible Sleep ('D'):
  Process waiting inside Kernel Driver for Disk / NFS I/O.
  Kernel IGNORES ALL SIGNALS! kill -9 has ZERO effect until I/O finishes or fails!

steps.title: Identify the Blocked Kernel Syscall using /proc and wchan
steps.description: Locate the stuck process PID and read `/proc/<pid>/wchan` and `/proc/<pid>/stack` to identify the exact kernel function where the thread is sleeping.
steps.content: Locate the stuck process PID and read `/proc/<pid>/wchan` and `/proc/<pid>/stack` to identify the exact kernel function where the thread is sleeping.
steps.highlight: Identify the Blocked Kernel Syscall using /proc and wchan
steps.codeBlock:
# Find processes in 'D' state
ps -eo pid,stat,wchan:25,comm | grep -w D
# Sample output: 4120 D   nfs_wait_client_call  app-worker

# Inspect kernel stack trace of the stuck thread
cat /proc/4120/stack
# Reveals: [<0>] nfs4_proc_getattr+0x65/0x90
#          [<0>] call_rwsem_down_read_failed+0x18/0x30

steps.title: Safely Release or Force-Unmount the Hanging Filesystem
steps.description: If the cause is a frozen NFS share, perform a lazy and forced unmount (`umount -l -f /mnt/nfs`). This disconnects the mount from the VFS hierarchy, causing pending I/O requests to fail with an error and allowing the kernel to wake the thread.
steps.content: If the cause is a frozen NFS share, perform a lazy and forced unmount (`umount -l -f /mnt/nfs`). This disconnects the mount from the VFS hierarchy, causing pending I/O requests to fail with an error and allowing the kernel to wake the thread.
steps.highlight: Safely Release or Force-Unmount the Hanging Filesystem
steps.codeBlock:
# Force and lazy unmount hanging storage
sudo umount -f -l /var/lib/docker/volumes/hanging_volume/_data

steps.title: Handle Blocked Block Devices (EBS / SAN)
steps.description: For hanging block devices, check `dmesg` for SCSI I/O timeouts (`task blocked for more than 120 seconds`). If the block device controller is completely unresponsive, rebooting the node is the only way to clear threads stuck in kernel space.
steps.content: For hanging block devices, check `dmesg` for SCSI I/O timeouts (`task blocked for more than 120 seconds`). If the block device controller is completely unresponsive, rebooting the node is the only way to clear threads stuck in kernel space.
steps.highlight: Handle Blocked Block Devices (EBS / SAN)
steps.codeBlock:
# Check dmesg for kernel hung task warnings
dmesg -T | grep -i "blocked for more than 120 seconds"

keyTakeaway: Processes in `D` state cannot be killed by `kill -9` because the kernel blocks signal delivery while waiting for hardware I/O to complete. Resolving hanging containers requires force-unmounting the underlying NFS/storage device (`umount -f -l`) or clearing disk timeouts.
elevatorPitch: When containers are stuck in `Terminating` and ignore `kill -9`, they are trapped in Linux kernel Uninterruptible Sleep (`D` state) waiting on unresponsive storage I/O. We diagnose this by checking `/proc/<pid>/stack` to identify the blocked kernel call. Force-unmounting the underlying volume (`umount -f -l`) aborts the pending I/O and instantly releases the trapped container.

title: Low-Overhead Container Observability with eBPF: Tracing Syscalls and Network Latency with bpftrace
summary: Achieve kernel-level observability into Docker containers without injecting code or restarting processes. Use eBPF and `bpftrace` to trace container filesystem latency, dropped packets, and DNS queries by cgroup.
question: A high-throughput microservice in production experiences periodic 200ms latency spikes. Traditional application APM agents and CPU profilers show normal CPU usage and no garbage collection pauses. Profiling with `strace` in production caused a 400% performance degradation and crashed client connections. You must use eBPF and `bpftrace` to trace disk I/O latency and network packet drops directly in the Linux kernel filtered by the container's cgroup ID with less than 1% overhead.
roleContext: Principal Docker Architect / Staff SRE Scenario
intro: Achieve kernel-level observability into Docker containers without injecting code or restarting processes. Use eBPF and `bpftrace` to trace container filesystem latency, dropped packets, and DNS queries by cgroup.

steps.title: Understand Why eBPF Outperforms strace for Container Observability
steps.description: `strace` relies on the `ptrace` system call, which intercepts every system call, pauses the target process twice (on entry and exit), and forces context switches to user space. eBPF executes sandboxed bytecode directly inside the Linux kernel on kprobes and tracepoints with sub-microsecond overhead.
steps.content: `strace` relies on the `ptrace` system call, which intercepts every system call, pauses the target process twice (on entry and exit), and forces context switches to user space. eBPF executes sandboxed bytecode directly inside the Linux kernel on kprobes and tracepoints with sub-microsecond overhead.
steps.highlight: Understand Why eBPF Outperforms strace for Container Observability
steps.codeBlock:
<!-- Performance Impact -->
strace:   Pauses container process on EVERY syscall! Overhead: 50% - 400% (Never run in Prod!)
eBPF:     JIT-compiled in-kernel verification. Copies only aggregated histograms. Overhead: < 1%

steps.title: Identify Container Cgroup ID for Scoped Filtering
steps.description: Obtain the container's 64-bit cgroup ID or namespace inode number to filter eBPF probes specifically to that container, avoiding host-wide trace noise.
steps.content: Obtain the container's 64-bit cgroup ID or namespace inode number to filter eBPF probes specifically to that container, avoiding host-wide trace noise.
steps.highlight: Identify Container Cgroup ID for Scoped Filtering
steps.codeBlock:
# Get container cgroup v2 ID
CONTAINER_ID=$(docker inspect my-app --format '{{.Id}}')
CGROUP_PATH="/sys/fs/cgroup/docker/${CONTAINER_ID}"
CGROUP_ID=$(python3 -c "import os; print(os.stat('$CGROUP_PATH').st_ino)")
echo "Filtering eBPF for cgroup ID: $CGROUP_ID"

steps.title: Trace Container Disk I/O Latency using bpftrace One-Liner
steps.description: Attach a `bpftrace` program to the kernel's block I/O tracepoints, generating a power-of-two histogram of disk latency specifically for the container.
steps.content: Attach a `bpftrace` program to the kernel's block I/O tracepoints, generating a power-of-two histogram of disk latency specifically for the container.
steps.highlight: Trace Container Disk I/O Latency using bpftrace One-Liner
