mistakesToAvoid.why: Senior SREs use Contributor Insights to pinpoint the exact partition keys and access patterns causing throttling rather than relying on average latency metrics.

title: Apache Kafka Consumer Group Rebalance Storm & Processing Lag Remediation
summary: Remediate catastrophic Kafka consumer group rebalance loops caused by processing timeouts on slow external APIs, and adopt the Cooperative Sticky Assignor to maintain streaming availability.
question: A 30-pod consumer group reading from an order processing Kafka topic experiences a catastrophic 'rebalance storm': pods continuously drop out and rejoin the group every 5 minutes, stopping all message consumption and ballooning consumer lag to millions of events. A slow external payment API is causing message processing batches to exceed the consumer poll timeout. How do you stabilize consumer heartbeats, migrate to cooperative sticky assignors, and eliminate rebalance loops?
roleContext: Staff SRE / Distributed Systems Engineer Interview Scenario
intro: In Apache Kafka, consumer groups dynamically distribute partition ownership across members. A consumer must periodically call `poll()` within `max.poll.interval.ms`. If a consumer thread is blocked (e.g. waiting for a downstream database or third-party HTTP call) and misses the interval, the Kafka coordinator assumes the consumer has died, evicts it, and triggers a group-wide rebalance. Under the legacy 'Eager' assignment protocol, all consumers stop processing and revoke all partitions during every rebalance, creating a vicious rebalance storm.

steps.title: Situation: Rebalance Storm Freezes Event Processing Pipeline
steps.content: During Black Friday traffic, downstream payment gateway latencies increased from 150ms to 4,200ms. With `max.poll.records = 500` and `max.poll.interval.ms = 300000` (5 minutes), processing a single batch took over 2,100 seconds (35 minutes), causing Kafka to repeatedly evict consumers and trigger continuous rebalance loops.

steps.title: Task: Decouple Heartbeats from Processing & Eliminate Stop-The-World Rebalances
steps.content: Prevent slow record processing from triggering consumer evictions, reduce batch processing durations, and configure zero-downtime incremental partition rebalancing.

steps.title: Action: Cooperative Sticky Rebalancing & Batch Rightsizing
steps.content:
1. **Migrate to CooperativeStickyAssignor**: Switched consumer configuration to `partition.assignment.strategy = org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor`. In Cooperative Rebalancing, unaffected partitions continue consuming data without pausing the entire cluster.
2. **Rightsize Poll Batches**: Reduced `max.poll.records` from 500 to 50 so that even during payment gateway degradation (4.2s per call), a full batch completes in under 210 seconds, well within the 300-second poll interval.
3. **Decouple Ingestion from Processing**: Refactored the consumer application to poll messages on a single thread and offload heavy processing to an asynchronous internal worker pool (Java `ThreadPoolExecutor` / Go worker goroutines) with manual commit on completion.

steps.title: Result: 100% Elimination of Rebalance Storms & Recovery of 2M Lag
steps.content: The consumer group stabilized instantly with zero member evictions. Partition rebalance durations fell from 180 seconds to 350 milliseconds, and the 2.4-million message backlog was drained within 25 minutes.

keyTakeaway: Rebalance storms happen when message processing times exceed `max.poll.interval.ms`. Always rightsize `max.poll.records`, use the modern `CooperativeStickyAssignor` to avoid stop-the-world pauses, and decouple Kafka poll loops from slow external HTTP calls.
elevatorPitch: Kafka evicts consumers when processing batches exceed max.poll.interval.ms.
Eager rebalancing revokes all partitions globally, halting all stream consumption.
Use CooperativeStickyAssignor and lower max.poll.records to allow incremental rebalancing without stopping consumers.

title: Zero-Downtime Expand-Contract Database Schema Migration for Mission-Critical APIs
summary: Design and execute an Expand-Contract database schema refactoring on a 40-million row table, avoiding ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks and application downtime.
question: A high-throughput PostgreSQL table ('users', 40 million rows) requires renaming column 'phone' to 'phone_number' and adding a NOT NULL constraint with default values, while maintaining 99.999% API availability. Running a standard 'ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL DEFAULT ...' or renaming the column locks the table with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, queuing thousands of web requests until the reverse proxy 504 timeouts. How do you design and execute a multi-phase Expand-Contract migration without downtime or table lock starvation?
roleContext: Lead DevOps / Platform Architect Interview Scenario
intro: In relational databases, destructive DDL commands like column renames, drops, and adding constrained columns acquire heavy table locks (e.g., `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` in PostgreSQL). Even if the DDL takes 100 milliseconds, any queued read or write query behind it is blocked, rapidly exhausting application connection pools and triggering cascading HTTP 504 gateway timeouts. The Expand-Contract (Parallel Run) pattern decouples database schema changes from application deployments across phased releases.

steps.title: Situation: Schema Migration Causes Severe Gateway Outages
steps.content: A junior engineer ran a migration script renaming `phone` to `phone_number` and adding `NOT NULL` on a 40-million-row production table. The statement queued behind an active analytical query, blocking all subsequent incoming `SELECT` and `UPDATE` statements for 45 seconds until 12,000 connections timed out.

steps.title: Task: Execute Phased Refactoring Without Table-Level Lock Contention
steps.content: Architect a zero-downtime migration pipeline that modifies the database schema, backfills 40 million rows, deploys application changes, and deprecates the old schema without blocking online queries.

steps.title: Action: Four-Phase Expand-Contract Execution
steps.content:
1. **Phase 1 (Expand - Schema Addition)**:
   Added the new column without default constraint lock:
   ```sql
   ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone_number VARCHAR(32);
   ```
   In PostgreSQL 11+, adding nullable columns without defaults is metadata-only (instantaneous).
2. **Phase 2 (Dual-Write Application Deployment)**:
   Updated application code to write to both `phone` and `phone_number`, while reading primarily from `phone`.
3. **Phase 3 (Backfill in Batches)**:
   Backfilled existing rows in batches of 5,000 using a background worker with `pg_sleep` intervals to avoid locking:
   ```sql
   UPDATE users SET phone_number = phone WHERE id BETWEEN :start AND :end AND phone_number IS NULL;
   ```
4. **Phase 4 (Add NOT NULL Validated Later)**:
   ```sql
   ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT check_phone_not_null CHECK (phone_number IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;
   ALTER TABLE users VALIDATE CONSTRAINT check_phone_not_null;
   ```
   `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` takes only a `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE` lock, allowing concurrent reads and writes!
5. **Phase 5 (Contract - Deprecate Old Column)**:
   Switched application code to read exclusively from `phone_number`, then dropped column `phone` in the subsequent release.

steps.title: Result: 100% Zero-Downtime Deployment & Zero Queued Locks
steps.content: All 40 million rows were successfully migrated across 3 continuous deployment cycles. Lock duration for each DDL operation stayed under 4 milliseconds, achieving 100% API uptime throughout the migration.

keyTakeaway: Never rename columns or add inline NOT NULL constraints directly in production relational databases. Always utilize the Expand-Contract pattern: add new column, dual-write in code, backfill in chunks, validate constraints asynchronously, and drop old columns in a subsequent release.
elevatorPitch: Destructive DDL like column renames and inline constraints acquire ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks.
Use the Expand-Contract pattern: add nullable column, dual-write in application, backfill in batches.
Add constraints with NOT VALID and validate later to avoid blocking concurrent database writes.

mistakesToAvoid.why: 502 indicates the backend target closed the TCP connection prematurely or returned malformed HTTP, whereas 504 means the target failed to respond before idle timeout.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Instant target deregistration severs in-flight HTTP requests during auto-scaling scale-in or rolling deployments, causing immediate user-facing drops.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Comparing load balancer generated errors against target generated errors immediately isolates whether the issue lies in the proxy tier or application runtime.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Target instances must explicitly permit inbound HTTP/HTTPS traffic from the ALB security group on the configured container/application port.

title: Point-In-Time Recovery (PITR) of a 10 TB PostgreSQL Database Under 45-Minute RTO
summary: Orchestrate a surgical Point-In-Time Recovery (PITR) of a 10 TB production database following an accidental DROP TABLE outage, restoring state to the exact second before data loss.
question: At 03:14:22 UTC, an automated cleanup script erroneously executes 'DROP TABLE customer_accounts CASCADE;' across primary billing tables. Midnight storage snapshots are 3 hours old, violating the company's 5-minute RPO. SRE leadership declares a P0 incident with a 45-minute RTO. How do you orchestrate a surgical Point-In-Time Recovery (PITR) using continuous WAL archives to restore state to exactly 03:14:21 UTC without overwriting the live database?
roleContext: Principal SRE / Disaster Recovery Lead Interview Scenario
intro: Point-In-Time Recovery (PITR) combines a physical baseline backup (via `pg_basebackup` or storage volume snapshot) with continuous Write-Ahead Log (WAL) archiving (using tools like `pgBackRest` or `wal-g`). By replaying WAL segments up to a specific recovery target timestamp or transaction ID, an SRE can restore a database to the exact millisecond preceding human error or data corruption.

steps.title: Situation: Erroneous DROP TABLE Triggers Catastrophic Data Loss
steps.content: At 03:14:22 UTC, critical account balance tables were dropped, impacting 4.2 million user accounts. Rolling back to the 00:00:00 UTC snapshot would cause 3 hours and 14 minutes of irreversible customer financial transaction data loss.

steps.title: Task: Restore Database to 03:14:21 UTC Under 45-Minute RTO
steps.content: Provision an isolated recovery instance, restore the most recent differential baseline backup, replay WAL archives up to `03:14:21 UTC`, extract the lost tables, and restore them to production without full database offline migration.

steps.title: Action: Fast EBS Snapshot Clone & pgBackRest WAL Replay
steps.content:
1. **Fast-Clone Primary Storage via EBS Snapshot**: Cloned the primary storage from the 03:00:00 UTC automated EBS volume snapshot in 4 minutes using AWS EBS Fast Snapshot Restore (FSR) on a dedicated recovery EC2 instance.
2. **Configure recovery.signal and Target Time**:
   Created `/var/lib/postgresql/data/recovery.signal` and configured `postgresql.conf`:
   ```ini
   restore_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=prod archive-get %f "%p"'
   recovery_target_time = '2026-10-06 03:14:21 UTC'
   recovery_target_action = 'promote'
   ```
3. **Replay WAL Segments**: Started PostgreSQL; it automatically fetched WAL files from S3 and replayed 14 minutes of write transactions, halting cleanly at `03:14:21 UTC`.
4. **Export Dropped Tables via pg_dump**: Dumped only `customer_accounts` table schema and data via `pg_dump -t customer_accounts`, and piped it directly into the production primary.
5. **Verify Data Integrity**: Verified record counts and checksums against customer ledger audit logs.

steps.title: Result: 0 Data Loss & RTO Met in 36 Minutes
steps.content: Database recovery completed in 36 minutes, beating the 45-minute RTO. Zero customer transactions were lost, achieving a verified 0-second RPO.

keyTakeaway: Never restore a 10 TB database by overwriting production directly. Use Fast Snapshot Restore (FSR) or differential backups to spin up an isolated recovery node, replay WAL logs to the exact second using PITR, and export only the affected tables back to production.
elevatorPitch: PITR combines base backups with continuous WAL archiving to restore to an exact timestamp.
Use storage snapshot cloning to provision an isolated instance rapidly instead of downloading 10 TB over network.
Replay WAL up to the second before the drop command, and extract affected tables with pg_dump.

title: Redis Sentinel Split-Brain & Unacknowledged Writes: Mitigating Data Loss During Failover
summary: Prevent silent data loss in Redis Sentinel clusters during network partitions by tuning quorum configurations and enforcing min-replicas-to-write rules.
question: During a transient network partition between AWS Availability Zones, a Redis master node is isolated from its Sentinel monitors and replica instances. The Sentinels detect quorum loss, declare the master dead, and promote a replica in AZ-b to become the new master. However, client applications in AZ-a still have network access to the old partitioned master and continue executing writes for 90 seconds. When the network heals, all writes made to the old master are irrevocably lost. How do you configure Redis min-replicas-to-write and quorum failover semantics to prevent split-brain write loss?
roleContext: Senior SRE / Infrastructure Engineer Interview Scenario
intro: Redis replication is asynchronous by default. When a network partition divides a Redis cluster, the Sentinel quorum promotes a replica to master in the majority partition. However, if clients in the minority partition continue writing to the partitioned old master, those writes cannot be synchronized. When the partition heals and the old master demotes to a replica, it resynchronizes from the new master by discarding its own local dataset, permanently deleting all unacknowledged minority writes.

steps.title: Situation: Asynchronous Failover Causes 90 Seconds of Lost Writes
steps.content: During an inter-AZ transit outage, AZ-a lost connectivity to AZ-b and AZ-c. Sentinel monitors in AZ-b/c elected a new master in AZ-b. However, client web pods in AZ-a continued issuing `SET` and `INCR` commands to the original master in AZ-a for 90 seconds. After network restoration, the original master reconnected, flushed its local keyspace, and erased 180,000 session tokens.

steps.title: Task: Enforce Strict Write Quorum Guardrails on Master Instances
steps.content: Configure Redis master instances to automatically reject writes if they lose contact with minimum replicas, limiting split-brain data loss windows to sub-second thresholds.

steps.title: Action: Configure min-replicas-to-write & Sentinel Down-After-Milliseconds
steps.content:
1. **Configure min-replicas Guardrails**:
   Configured on the Redis master:
   ```ini
   min-replicas-to-write 1
   min-replicas-max-lag 5
   ```
   If the master does not receive replication ACK heartbeats from at least 1 healthy replica within 5 seconds, it immediately rejects incoming write commands with `NOREPLICAS Not enough good replicas to write`.
2. **Tune Sentinel Quorum and Detection**:
   Reduced `down-after-milliseconds` from 30,000ms to 5,000ms so Sentinels detect partition failures within 5 seconds.
3. **Distribute Sentinels across 3 AZs**: Ensured Sentinel quorum is set to `2` across 3 availability zones, guaranteeing that minority partitions can never elect a master.
4. **Application Client Retry Logic**: Configured Redis client libraries (Lettuce / ioredis) with automated Sentinel refresh listeners to detect master failovers immediately.

steps.title: Result: 0 Data Loss During Partition Drills
steps.content: Simulated inter-AZ partition drills showed the old master automatically stopped accepting writes within 5 seconds. When the partition healed, resynchronization occurred with zero data inconsistencies.

keyTakeaway: Redis does not guarantee strong consistency during network partitions. Always configure `min-replicas-to-write 1` and `min-replicas-max-lag` so an isolated master stops accepting writes before Sentinels promote a new master, preventing split-brain data loss.
elevatorPitch: Network partitions can cause split-brain where clients write to an isolated master that gets wiped upon healing.
Configure min-replicas-to-write 1 and min-replicas-max-lag to reject writes on partitioned masters.
Keep down-after-milliseconds low and distribute Sentinel instances across at least 3 availability zones.

title: Deployment Succeeded but Traffic Still Going to Old Version: Systematic Diagnostic Runbook
summary: Step-by-step triage workflow when CI/CD reports a successful release, but live client traffic remains routed to the previous application version.
question: A deployment succeeded according to your CI/CD pipeline, but users are still receiving responses from the old version. Explain exactly where you start debugging and how you isolate the failure.
roleContext: Senior Platform Engineer / SRE Incident Response
intro: When a deployment reports green in CI/CD while production ingress still delivers the prior version, the failure is almost never in container building—it lies at the traffic routing and state convergence layer. I troubleshoot systematically from the user edge backwards: CDN caching, DNS routing, Ingress/Service endpoint registration, Deployment replica status, and GitOps sync state.

steps.title: Verify Edge CDN & Browser Caching
steps.description: Inspect HTTP response headers directly from the edge using curl. Check 'Age', 'CF-Cache-Status', 'X-Cache', or 'Cache-Control' headers. Frequently, static assets (JS bundles, HTML index files) or API responses are aggressively cached at Cloudflare, CloudFront, or client service workers even though backend pods were replaced.
steps.codeBlock:
curl -I -s -H "Cache-Control: no-cache" https://api.example.com/v1/version
# Check response headers:
# x-cache: Hit from cloudfront
# age: 84320

steps.title: Verify Ingress & Service Selector Endpoint Binding
steps.description: Check whether the Kubernetes Service or Ingress is actually pointing to the new Pod replicas. In Blue/Green or Canary deployments (Argo Rollouts, Istio, Flagger), the new ReplicaSet may be healthy but the Service selector, Istio VirtualService weight, or ALB Target Group weight never flipped to active.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get endpoints <service-name> -o yaml
kubectl get svc <service-name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'
# For Argo Rollouts:
kubectl argo rollouts status rollout <app-name>
kubectl argo rollouts get rollout <app-name>

steps.title: Check Pod Image Digest & Deployment Rollout Progress
steps.description: Verify what image digest is actively running inside the pods. If developers used mutable tags (e.g. ':latest' or ':staging') with 'imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent', the deployment updated its manifest, but the node continued running the cached old container image.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get deployment <app-name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[*].image}'
kubectl get pods -l app=<app-name> -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.status.containerStatuses[*].imageID}{"\n"}{end}'

steps.title: Validate GitOps Reconciliation & Pipeline Artifact Pinning
steps.description: Confirm whether ArgoCD, Flux, or Jenkins deployed the expected commit SHA. Ensure the pipeline didn't overwrite the manifest in a detached branch or experience silent git push rejection.
steps.highlight: Golden Rule: Always deploy immutable image tags pinned to git commit SHAs (e.g. app:v1.14.2-a8f3b9c) and enforce imagePullPolicy: Always to prevent silent image caching discrepancies.

keyTakeaway: A 'successful deployment' in CI/CD only means the API accepted the manifest. True release verification requires checking Edge cache -> Ingress weight -> Service endpoints -> Pod image sha256 digests.
elevatorPitch: Bypass CDN caching with curl -I to check Edge X-Cache and Age headers.
Inspect Service selectors and Ingress target groups to ensure traffic routing weights flipped to the new ReplicaSet.
Query running pod image digests using kubectl get pods -o jsonpath to confirm nodes pulled the new sha256 binary rather than a cached tag.
Verify GitOps sync status in ArgoCD/Flux to rule out out-of-sync branches or silent manifest rollbacks.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Promoting application releases to production without an automated, canary-validated rollback mechanism when configuring Deployment Succeeded Traffic
mistakesToAvoid.why: Pipelines that lack automated rollback mechanisms force engineering teams to scramble manual hotfixes during severe production regressions.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running concurrent deployment pipeline jobs without stage mutex locking on shared target environments when configuring Deployment Succeeded Traffic
mistakesToAvoid.why: Concurrent pipeline runs on the same environment race to apply state changes, causing out-of-order commits and unpredictable deployment state.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting dependency lockfiles (package-lock.json, go.sum, Cargo.lock) from continuous integration builds when configuring Deployment Succeeded Traffic
mistakesToAvoid.why: Omitting lockfiles allows upstream package updates to break builds unpredictably without any changes to application codebase.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to define dynamic cache invalidation keys for CI package managers and layer caches when configuring Deployment Succeeded Traffic
mistakesToAvoid.why: Stale build caches mask underlying dependency incompatibilities or pull outdated libraries, while un-cached runs slow feedback loops.

title: Kubernetes Pods Healthy in kubectl get pods but Users Report 504 Gateway Timeouts
summary: Architectural diagnostic workflow for resolving 504 Gateway Timeout errors when pod readiness and liveness probes show 100% green.
question: A Kubernetes application is healthy according to 'kubectl get pods' (1/1 Running), but users report 504 Gateway Timeout errors. Walk me through your troubleshooting flow.
intro: A 504 Gateway Timeout means an edge proxy (ALB, NGINX Ingress, Cloudflare) established a connection to an upstream gateway or backend, but did not receive a timely HTTP response before its idle timeout expired. Because 'kubectl get pods' only reflects liveness/readiness probes (which often query a lightweight '/healthz' endpoint), the application worker threads can be completely deadlocked on downstream database queries while the health endpoint responds instantly.

steps.title: Differentiate Shallow Health Probes from Deep Application Starvation
steps.description: Verify what the probe actually tests. If '/healthz' simply returns HTTP 200 without testing database pools, external APIs, or message queues, the pod appears 1/1 Running while all actual business logic threads are blocked waiting on locked PostgreSQL rows or downstream microservices.
steps.codeBlock:
# Inspect pod liveness/readiness probe definitions
kubectl get pod <pod-name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].readinessProbe}'
# Exec into container or port-forward to test realistic requests
kubectl port-forward pod/<pod-name> 8080:8080 &
curl -v http://localhost:8080/api/v1/checkout

steps.title: Diagnose Keepalive & Idle Timeout Mismatches
steps.description: Check timeout alignment between your Ingress controller / ALB and the backend container runtime. If the Load Balancer has an idle timeout of 60s, but the application server (e.g. Node.js, Gunicorn, Tomcat) has a keep-alive timeout of 50s, the backend server will silently close the TCP connection right as the LB reuses it, resulting in 502/504 errors under high concurrency.
steps.highlight: Architecture Requirement: Application keep-alive timeout must ALWAYS be strictly greater than upstream Ingress/ALB idle timeout (e.g. ALB = 60s, App Server keep-alive = 65s).

steps.title: Inspect Ingress Controller Logs & Upstream Response Times
steps.description: Review NGINX Ingress or AWS Load Balancer access logs. Compare $upstream_connect_time, $upstream_header_time, and $upstream_response_time. If $upstream_response_time is exactly 60.000s, the container received the request but hung.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ingress-nginx --tail=200 | grep ' 504 '
# Output pattern:
# upstream_response_time: 60.004, upstream_status: 504, request_time: 60.005

steps.title: Check Thread Pool & Connection Pool Saturation Inside Pod
steps.description: Inspect socket queues and thread dumps. Use 'ss -lnt' to see if the Send-Q or Recv-Q on the listen port is backed up, indicating that the kernel accepted TCP SYN packets, but the application process is too slow to call accept().
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- ss -lnt '( sport = :8080 )'
# Check thread exhaustion / GC pause:
jstack <pid> | grep -E 'BLOCKED|WAITING' # For Java
kill -USR1 <pid> # For Node.js heap/CPU profile

keyTakeaway: Pod Running status only proves that container PID 1 is alive and '/healthz' returned 200. 504s are caused by upstream keepalive race conditions, database connection pool exhaustion, or downstream service hangs.
elevatorPitch: Recognize that shallow /healthz probes pass even when application thread pools are deadlocked.
Check ingress logs for upstream_response_time matching the exact proxy timeout threshold (e.g. 60s).
Verify keep-alive timeout hierarchy: backend container keepalive must be 5-10s longer than Ingress/ALB idle timeout.
Inspect socket listen queues (ss -lnt) and application connection pools to catch thread starvation.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Confusing ALB 502 Bad Gateway (target connection reset) with 504 Gateway Timeout (upstream response timeout) when configuring Kubernetes Pods Healthy
mistakesToAvoid.why: 502 indicates the backend target closed the TCP connection prematurely or returned malformed HTTP, whereas 504 means the target failed to respond before idle timeout.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Setting target deregistration delay to zero instead of allowing connection draining when configuring Kubernetes Pods Healthy
mistakesToAvoid.why: Instant target deregistration severs in-flight HTTP requests during auto-scaling scale-in or rolling deployments, causing immediate user-facing drops.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to query CloudWatch ELB metrics (`HTTPCode_ELB_5XX` vs `HTTPCode_Target_5XX`) during load balancer outages when configuring Kubernetes Pods Healthy
mistakesToAvoid.why: Comparing load balancer generated errors against target generated errors immediately isolates whether the issue lies in the proxy tier or application runtime.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Overlooking Security Group rules on backend EC2/ECS instances that block health check traffic from the ALB when configuring Kubernetes Pods Healthy
mistakesToAvoid.why: Target instances must explicitly permit inbound HTTP/HTTPS traffic from the ALB security group on the configured container/application port.

title: AWS Cloud Bill Spiked 300% Overnight With Zero Deployments: Incident Response & Cost Remediation
summary: Urgent incident response protocol to detect, stop, and remediate a 3x AWS cloud billing spike when zero code deployments occurred.
question: Your AWS bill spiked 3x overnight, but no deployments happened. What is your step-by-step response to identify the leak, stop the bleeding, and prevent recurrence?
intro: When an AWS bill spikes abruptly without code deployments, the culprit is almost always unmetered data transfer, runaway auto-scaling triggered by external traffic or health probe loops, S3 API request flooding, or compromised IAM credentials spinning up unauthorized GPU/crypto-mining instances. I treat unexpected billing spikes as a Sev-1 operational incident.

steps.title: Immediate Hourly Granularity Cost Breakdown in AWS Cost Explorer
steps.description: Open AWS Cost Explorer or query the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) with Athena. Group costs by 'Usage Type' and 'API Operation' over the past 24 hours to isolate the exact AWS service driving the surge (e.g. 'USE2-NatGateway-Bytes', 'DataTransfer-Out-Bytes', 'S3-Requests-Tier1', or 'EC2-BoxUsage').
steps.codeBlock:
aws ce get-cost-and-usage \
  --time-period Start=$(date -u -v-2d +%Y-%m-%d),End=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%d) \
  --granularity HOURLY \
  --metrics "UnblendedCost" \
  --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE

steps.title: Check Top 4 Silent Cloud Cost Drivers
steps.description: Investigate common non-deployment spend drivers: 1. NAT Gateway Data Processing: Internal pods pulling massive container images or dataset backups from external registries through NAT instead of VPC Endpoints ($0.045/GB). 2. Cross-AZ Data Transfer: Microservices communicating across Availability Zones without AZ-affinity ($0.01/GB each way). 3. S3 List/Put Request Storms: Recursive scripts or broken backup jobs generating billions of S3 API calls. 4. Security Breach: Compromised access keys launching EC2 GPU instances (p4d, g5) across unfamiliar regions (e.g. ap-southeast-2, sa-east-1).
steps.highlight: Security Alert: Always check AWS CloudTrail for 'RunInstances' and 'CreateUser' calls across ALL regions to rule out account compromise.

steps.title: Stop the Financial Bleeding (Emergency Triage)
steps.description: If runaway SQS/Lambda loop: throttle concurrency or disable event source mappings. If NAT Gateway traffic: deploy AWS Gateway Endpoints for S3/DynamoDB (which are 100% free) or VPC Interface Endpoints. If unauthorized compute: terminate rogue instances, revoke compromised IAM session tokens, and attach explicit deny SCPs.
steps.codeBlock:
# Provision free S3 Gateway Endpoint to bypass NAT Gateway immediately:
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \
  --vpc-id vpc-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3 \
  --route-table-ids rtb-0123456789abcdef0

steps.title: Implement Automated Cost Anomaly Detection & Guardrails
steps.description: Configure AWS Cost Anomaly Detection with SNS/Slack alerts triggering within 2 hours of deviation. Set AWS Budgets with action policies to automatically shut down non-production accounts when monthly spending limits are exceeded.
steps.codeBlock:
aws ce create-anomaly-subscription \
  --subscription '{"SubscriptionName":"Sev1-Cost-Spike","Threshold":500,"Frequency":"IMMEDIATE","Subscribers":[{"Type":"EMAIL","Address":"sre-alerts@company.com"}]}'

keyTakeaway: Billing spikes without deployments are almost always data transfer leaks (NAT Gateways, inter-AZ traffic) or rogue automation loops. Triage with hourly CUR queries, deploy free VPC endpoints, and enforce automated Cost Anomaly alerts.
elevatorPitch: Query AWS Cost Explorer with hourly granularity grouped by Service and UsageType to find the guilty resource within 5 minutes.
Verify NAT Gateway bytes and cross-AZ traffic; deploy free S3 Gateway Endpoints to instantly cut data processing fees.
Audit CloudTrail globally for RunInstances and CreateAccessKey to eliminate credential theft and crypto-mining.
Establish AWS Cost Anomaly Detection and Budgets with automated SNS/Slack escalations.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on legacy bucket ACLs instead of modern S3 Block Public Access and IAM bucket policies when configuring Bill Spiked 300%
mistakesToAvoid.why: AWS recommends disabling ACLs (Bucket Owner Enforced) in favor of centralized declarative bucket policies and account-level Block Public Access controls.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Confusing SSE-S3 encryption with KMS customer-managed key (SSE-KMS) authorization policies when configuring Bill Spiked 300%
mistakesToAvoid.why: Accessing SSE-KMS encrypted objects requires both `s3:GetObject` and `kms:Decrypt` permissions; neglecting KMS key policies causes silent 403 Forbidden errors.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using sequential timestamps or predictable prefixes for high-throughput S3 read and write keys when configuring Bill Spiked 300%
mistakesToAvoid.why: Sequential key prefixes limit S3 horizontal partitioning; randomized hash prefixes distribute workloads across partitions to achieve 3,500 PUT and 5,500 GET requests/sec.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to audit S3 object delete markers when troubleshooting missing versioned objects when configuring Bill Spiked 300%
mistakesToAvoid.why: Issuing a DELETE on a versioned bucket only adds a delete marker; engineers must retrieve previous versions or purge markers to restore data.

title: CI/CD Pipeline Takes 40+ Minutes: How to Cut Execution Under 10 Minutes Without Adding Hardware
summary: Proven platform engineering strategy to slash monolithic CI/CD pipeline runtime from 40+ minutes to under 10 minutes strictly using software, caching, and pipeline refactoring.
question: Your CI/CD pipeline is taking 40+ minutes to complete. Your CTO demands it run under 10 minutes without spending a dime on additional runner hardware. What exact architectural optimizations will you implement?
intro: Slashing pipeline duration without adding hardware requires attacking the three biggest time sinks: redundant dependency downloading, serial stage bottlenecks, and cache-busting Docker builds. By optimizing Docker layer caching, parallelizing unit tests, caching package managers, and executing flaky end-to-end tests asynchronously, we achieve 4x-5x speedups on identical compute.

steps.title: Leverage Docker BuildKit Multi-Stage Builds & Inline Cache
steps.description: Order Dockerfile instructions from least-frequently changed to most-frequently changed. Copy dependency manifests (package.json, go.mod, pom.xml) first and download dependencies BEFORE copying source code. Enable BuildKit cache mounts (`--mount=type=cache`) so package managers reuse local disk caches across builds.
steps.codeBlock:
# Hardened Dockerfile with BuildKit Cache Mounts
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.4
FROM golang:1.24-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod go mod download
COPY . .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build go build -o server ./cmd/server

steps.title: Deconstruct Serial Stages into Parallel Fan-Out / Fan-In Topology
steps.description: Most 40-minute pipelines run Lint -> Security Scan -> Unit Tests -> Integration Tests sequentially. Transform these into parallel matrix jobs. Linting, SAST scanning (Trivy/SonarQube), and frontend/backend unit tests can run concurrently on the same runner node.

steps.title: Shard Test Suites Across Worker Threads
steps.description: If unit/integration tests take 25 minutes, split tests into balanced shards based on historical execution duration. Use test runner native sharding (`jest --shard=1/4` or pytest-xdist) to utilize all CPU cores on the existing runner rather than running tests single-threaded.
steps.codeBlock:
# Sharding pytest across existing runner CPU cores
pytest -n auto --dist loadfile tests/

steps.title: Decouple Heavy E2E Smoke Tests into Async Post-Deploy Stages
steps.description: Separate the gating PR pipeline from the post-merge regression pipeline. The PR build should only run fast unit tests and container builds (under 6 mins). Heavy browser-based Selenium/Playwright end-to-end tests should run on staging or nightly schedules.
steps.highlight: Platform Rule: Developer pull request gates should never exceed 8 minutes. Reserve heavy end-to-end test suites for post-merge or ephemeral staging environments.

keyTakeaway: You do not need more runner hardware to cut pipeline times by 75%. Implement Docker BuildKit cache mounts, optimize layer ordering, shard test execution across CPU cores, and run non-critical tests asynchronously.
elevatorPitch: Restructure Dockerfiles to copy dependency files first and enable Docker BuildKit --mount=type=cache.
Convert serial stages into parallel fan-out jobs for linting, security scanning, and unit testing.
Shard long-running test suites across multi-core CPUs using native test runners (pytest-xdist, jest --shard).
Move heavy end-to-end regressions out of the critical PR merge path into asynchronous staging triggers.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Promoting application releases to production without an automated, canary-validated rollback mechanism
mistakesToAvoid.why: Pipelines that lack automated rollback mechanisms force engineering teams to scramble manual hotfixes during severe production regressions.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running concurrent deployment pipeline jobs without stage mutex locking on shared target environments
mistakesToAvoid.why: Concurrent pipeline runs on the same environment race to apply state changes, causing out-of-order commits and unpredictable deployment state.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting dependency lockfiles (package-lock.json, go.sum, Cargo.lock) from continuous integration builds
mistakesToAvoid.why: Omitting lockfiles allows upstream package updates to break builds unpredictably without any changes to application codebase.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to define dynamic cache invalidation keys for CI package managers and layer caches in batch4-q004-cicd-pipeline-40-min-optimize-under-10-min
mistakesToAvoid.why: Stale build caches mask underlying dependency incompatibilities or pull outdated libraries, while un-cached runs slow feedback loops.

title: Infra Monitoring Shows Green but Devs and Users Report System Slowness: Who to Believe and First Checks
summary: How to resolve the classic production paradox where infrastructure dashboards show all green, yet developers and users complain of acute system slowness.
question: An SRE says the infrastructure is stable, the dev team says the system is slow, and monitoring dashboards show everything is GREEN. Who do you believe — and what do you check first?
intro: I always believe the users and the developers. Traditional infrastructure dashboards only monitor host-level resource utilization (CPU < 50%, Memory < 60%, Disk < 40%) and average latency (p50). A system can have 10% CPU usage while 95% of users experience 10-second timeouts due to lock contention, DNS latency, thread pool starvation, or tail latency (p99/p99.9) hidden by averages.

steps.title: Replace Average (p50) Metrics with High-Percentile Latency (p95, p99, p99.9)
steps.description: Averages hide catastrophic outages. If 900 users complete requests in 20ms and 100 users time out at 30,000ms, the mathematical average is ~3 seconds (which might look 'acceptable' on a coarse dashboard), but 10% of users are completely blocked. Query p95 and p99 latency immediately.
steps.codeBlock:
# PromQL query to expose tail latency
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, path))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, path))

steps.title: Analyze Edge-to-Backend Latency Discrepancy
steps.description: Compare metrics recorded at the client edge (CDN / CloudFront / ALB) against metrics recorded inside the backend application pods. If ALB latency is 5 seconds but application code reports 50ms execution time, the delay is happening in the queuing network layer: TLS handshake overhead, reverse-proxy backlog drops, or slow client transfer.
steps.highlight: SRE Axiom: Never trust internal pod metrics without verifying client-facing Synthetic Monitors and edge access logs.

steps.title: Inspect Resource Saturation vs. Resource Exhaustion (USE Method)
steps.description: Green CPU doesn't mean healthy compute. Check for CFS CPU Throttling (`container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total`) where Kubernetes throttles a container due to strict CPU limits even when the node has 80% free CPU. Check database connection pool wait queues and thread lock contention.
steps.codeBlock:
# PromQL: Detect hidden CPU throttling on Kubernetes pods
sum(rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total[5m])) by (pod) 
/ 
sum(rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total[5m])) by (pod) * 100

steps.title: Trace End-to-End Distributed Tracing Spans (OpenTelemetry)
steps.description: Pull up Jaeger/Tempo distributed traces for affected requests. Look at the waterfall visualization: identify whether time is spent waiting on PostgreSQL row locks, DNS resolution, Redis socket connect timeouts, or third-party API gateways.

keyTakeaway: Always believe user complaints over green infrastructure graphs. Green graphs usually mean servers aren't crashing, not that requests are succeeding fast. Inspect p99 tail latency, CPU CFS throttling, and distributed trace waterfalls.
elevatorPitch: Believe the users and developers immediately: host averages mask severe tail-latency outages.
Switch dashboards from average latency to p95 and p99 percentiles to expose degradation.
Check for CFS CPU Throttling where containers are artificially choked despite low node CPU.
Use OpenTelemetry distributed traces to pinpoint the exact microservice span or database lock causing delays.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Injecting high-cardinality label dimensions (such as user IDs or request UUIDs) into Prometheus metrics when addressing observability
mistakesToAvoid.why: High-cardinality label values cause exponential time-series growth, consuming gigabytes of TSDB memory and crashing Prometheus servers.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Evaluating application performance solely through arithmetic mean or p50 latency while ignoring tail latency (p99)
mistakesToAvoid.why: Averages hide catastrophic tail latency outages where 1% of high-value user transactions suffer severe timeouts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to inject and extract W3C distributed trace context across message brokers and RPC calls
mistakesToAvoid.why: Breaking distributed trace context propagation fragments end-to-end transaction waterfalls into disconnected, un-correlatable trace segments.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Configuring alert rule evaluation intervals without sufficient duration damping (for: 5m), inducing alert flap
mistakesToAvoid.why: Instant alerts triggered by transient sub-second CPU or latency blips page on-call engineers unnecessarily and dilute response urgency.

title: Terraform Apply Fails Due to Drift on Live Critical Infrastructure: Zero-Downtime Reconciliation
summary: Production runbook for safely reconciling configuration drift during a failing terraform apply on mission-critical live infrastructure without risking service interruption.
question: A terraform apply is failing due to configuration drift, but the underlying infrastructure is live and mission-critical. How do you reconcile state and fix the drift without causing downtime?
roleContext: Senior Platform Engineer / Cloud Infrastructure Lead
intro: Configuration drift occurs when live cloud resources are modified outside of Terraform (via cloud console, automated autoscalers, or emergency hotfixes), causing Terraform's expected state to diverge from reality. When `terraform apply` fails or threatens destructive replacement on critical systems, you must never force apply. You must isolate the drift, refresh the state safely, backport modifications, and protect against unintended destruction.

steps.title: Run Non-Destructive Speculative Plan & Backup Remote State
steps.description: Immediately create a backup snapshot of the current remote state file before running any write operations. Run `terraform plan` and analyze every resource flagged with `~` (update in-place), `+` (create), and especially `-` or `- / +` (destroy and recreate).
steps.codeBlock:
# Backup remote state
terraform state pull > terraform-state-backup-$(date +%s).json
# Run targeted speculative plan without touching live infrastructure
terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -out=tfplan.binary
terraform show -json tfplan.binary > plan_analysis.json

steps.title: Isolate Why the Resource Threatens Destruction
steps.description: If Terraform plans to destroy and recreate a live resource, identify the argument forcing recreation (e.g. changing an EC2 AMI, RDS storage type, or VPC subnet CIDR). Add `lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }` or `lifecycle { ignore_changes = [ ... ] }` in your HCL code to block destructive replacements.

steps.title: Refresh State from Reality and Backport Manual Changes into HCL
steps.description: Run `terraform apply -refresh-only` (in Terraform 1.1+) to update Terraform's state file with real-world infrastructure attributes without applying configuration changes. Once state matches cloud reality, inspect the diff and update your Terraform HCL code to mirror the live configuration.
steps.codeBlock:
# Inspect and approve state refresh safely
terraform apply -refresh-only
# Update HCL code to match newly refreshed attributes

steps.title: Execute Targeted Apply on Verified Non-Breaking Blocks
steps.description: Once HCL matches live state, run `terraform plan` to confirm that the diff is zero (`No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration`). If minor unmanaged resources exist, adopt them cleanly using `terraform import`.
steps.highlight: Golden Rule: Never run blind 'terraform apply' when drift is detected. Use 'terraform apply -refresh-only', inspect HCL differences, and apply code updates until 'No changes' is achieved.

keyTakeaway: Reconcile drift by backing up state, using 'terraform apply -refresh-only' to pull cloud reality into state without modifies, updating HCL to match reality, and locking resources with lifecycle prevent_destroy.
elevatorPitch: Back up remote state immediately with terraform state pull.
Inspect the plan to see which arguments are triggering in-place updates vs destructive replacement (-/+).
Use lifecycle prevent_destroy and ignore_changes on critical blocks to eliminate downtime risk.
Execute terraform apply -refresh-only to sync state with reality, then backport changes into HCL code until plan shows zero diff.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Executing Terraform applies without inspecting '# forces replacement' warnings in plan output
mistakesToAvoid.why: Attributes that force resource replacement destroy and recreate critical infrastructure (databases, load balancers), inducing unannounced production outages.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting remote state locking mechanisms (DynamoDB or backend native locks) for shared state files
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without state locking, concurrent CI/CD pipeline executions or team applies create race conditions that corrupt the state file.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Structuring entire enterprise cloud footprints into a single monolithic Terraform root module
mistakesToAvoid.why: Monolithic state files slow plan execution dramatically, increase blast radius during failed applies, and create severe pipeline locking contention.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to pin required_providers versions, causing breaking provider upgrades in CI pipelines in batch4-q006-terraform-apply-drift-live-critical-infra-reconcile
mistakesToAvoid.why: Unpinned provider versions automatically download breaking major upgrades during CI runs, introducing unexpected schema validation failures.

title: Rollback Script Fails During Production Outage With 5 Minutes Before SLA Breach: Incident Commander Decision
summary: High-stakes SRE decision framework when an automated rollback script fails during a production outage with only 5 minutes remaining before an enterprise SLA breach.
question: Your rollback script fails during an active production outage. You have 5 minutes before breaching customer SLAs. Walk me through your decision-making framework and exact actions.
roleContext: Incident Commander / Staff Site Reliability Engineer
intro: When an automated rollback script fails during an active outage with minutes before SLA breach, trying to debug the rollback script is an anti-pattern. As Incident Commander, my singular mandate is service restoration and blast radius mitigation, not fixing deployment automation. I immediately pivot to macroscopic traffic diversion: CDN maintenance fallbacks, DNS/ALB failover to DR/standby, or shedding non-critical load.

steps.title: T+0:00: Stop Script Debugging & Assert Incident Command
steps.description: Call a hard stop on debugging the broken script. Announce on the bridge: 'We are halting rollback script triage. We have 4 minutes to SLA breach. Executing traffic diversion protocol.' Ensure one person holds command while delegates execute predefined recovery actions.
steps.highlight: Incident Command Axiom: Never debug deployment tooling during an SLA-critical outage. Pivot immediately to traffic diversion or manual failover.

steps.title: T+1:00: Route Traffic Away from the Poisoned Cluster (DNS / CDN Failover)
steps.description: If running multi-region or active-standby, immediately flip Route53 ARC routing controls or Cloudflare load balancer weights to send 100% of user traffic to the healthy secondary region. If single region, switch Cloudflare/ALB to return a static maintenance page or cached response rather than throwing HTTP 500/504 errors.
steps.codeBlock:
# CLI Route53 Application Recovery Controller Failover
aws route53-recovery-control-config update-routing-control-states \
  --routing-control-states-entries "[{\"RoutingControlArn\":\"arn:aws:...:control/primary\",\"RoutingControlState\":\"Off\"},{\"RoutingControlArn\":\"arn:aws:...:control/secondary\",\"RoutingControlState\":\"On\"}]"

steps.title: T+2:30: Imperative Workload Rollback at the Compute Layer
steps.description: Bypass the broken CI/CD pipeline entirely and execute an imperative rollback directly on the container orchestrator. In Kubernetes, run `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>` or patch the Deployment image directly to the prior stable Docker digest.
steps.codeBlock:
# Bypass CI/CD and rollback deployment directly via kube-apiserver
kubectl rollout undo deployment/api-gateway -n production
kubectl rollout status deployment/api-gateway -n production --timeout=90s

steps.title: T+4:30: Validate Service Health & Post-Incident Reflection
steps.description: Validate 200 OK responses from synthetic canaries. Update customer status page. Once the system is stable, initiate a blameless post-mortem: analyze why the deployment failed, why the rollback script failed, and why pre-flight rollback testing was not automated in CI.

keyTakeaway: Under imminent SLA breach, do not debug deployment scripts. Pivot immediately to macroscopic recovery: reroute traffic to secondary regions or execute imperative orchestrator rollbacks (kubectl rollout undo).
elevatorPitch: Assert incident command and stop engineers from wasting time debugging the failed script.
Shift traffic immediately via Route53 ARC, CDN, or load balancer to secondary clusters or warm standby.
Bypass CI/CD pipelines to trigger imperative rollbacks directly at the cluster layer (kubectl rollout undo).
Enable edge maintenance mode or graceful degradation to preserve SLA uptime metrics.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Issuing immediate kill -9 (SIGKILL) commands rather than allowing graceful termination via kill -15 (SIGTERM) when configuring Rollback Script Fails
mistakesToAvoid.why: SIGKILL immediately halts execution without allowing processes to flush memory buffers, commit database transactions, or remove stale PID locks.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Overlooking file system inode exhaustion (df -i) when diagnosing 'No space left on device' errors when configuring Rollback Script Fails
mistakesToAvoid.why: Millions of small files or unrotated session tokens can exhaust available file system inodes even when standard disk storage (`df -h`) shows ample free space.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Exhausting open file descriptor allocations (ulimit -n) under intensive concurrent socket connections when configuring Rollback Script Fails
mistakesToAvoid.why: Reaching file descriptor exhaustion throws 'Too many open files' errors, preventing services from accepting new TCP client socket connections.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Permitting defunct zombie processes to accumulate without fixing parent process SIGCHLD waitpid reaping when configuring Rollback Script Fails
mistakesToAvoid.why: Zombie processes consume process table entries; accumulating zombies can exhaust the system maximum PID limit (`pid_max`).

title: Production Secret Accidentally Committed to GitHub and Already Cloned: Immediate Remediation Protocol
summary: Complete enterprise DevSecOps incident response runbook for a production credential leaked into a Git repository that has already been cloned.
question: A production secret was accidentally committed to a GitHub repository and developers have already cloned the commit. What are your exact step-by-step actions?
roleContext: Senior DevSecOps Engineer / Security Incident Responder
intro: The moment a secret is pushed to a remote Git repository—especially if already cloned—it must be treated as 100% compromised. Rewriting Git history or deleting the commit does NOT protect you because the plaintext credential is already stored on external workstations, GitHub internal caches, and potentially scrape bots. The golden rule is: Rotate First, Invalidate Second, Clean Git History Last.

steps.title: Step 1: Immediate Credential Revocation & Emergency Rotation
steps.description: Do NOT waste time deleting the commit. Immediately log into the cloud/identity provider (AWS IAM, Database, Stripe, GitHub PAT) and revoke the compromised key or generate a replacement credential. Update production services with the new secret via Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or Kubernetes Secrets.
steps.codeBlock:
# Example: Instantly deactivate compromised AWS IAM Access Key
aws iam update-access-key --access-key-id AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE --status Inactive
aws iam delete-access-key --access-key-id AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE

steps.title: Step 2: Inspect CloudTrail & Audit Logs for Unauthorized Exploitation
steps.description: Search security audit logs (AWS CloudTrail, database query logs, API access logs) from the timestamp the commit was pushed to the moment the key was revoked. Search for any unauthorized API calls or IP addresses originating outside corporate CIDR blocks.
steps.codeBlock:
# CloudTrail lookup for actions taken by the compromised key
aws cloudtrail lookup-events \
  --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=AccessKeyId,AttributeValue=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE \
  --start-time $(date -u -v-24H +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)

steps.title: Step 3: Scrub Git Commit History and Force-Push
steps.description: Use `git-filter-repo` (recommended over legacy BFG or filter-branch) to purge the secret from all commits, tags, and tree objects. Force-push the cleansed history and notify all developers to re-clone the repository to prevent pushing old commit history back.
steps.codeBlock:
# Purge the sensitive file or string from entire git history
pip install git-filter-repo
git filter-repo --replace-text <(echo 'regex:AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}==>REDACTED')
git push origin --force --all
git push origin --force --tags

steps.title: Step 4: Install Preventative Shift-Left Pre-Commit & CI Gates
steps.description: Deploy automated pre-commit secret detection tools (`gitleaks`, `trufflehog`) across developer workstations and enforce GitHub Secret Scanning with Push Protection on all organization repositories so commits with raw keys are blocked at `git push` time.
steps.highlight: Security Law: Secret deletion in Git is cosmetic. The only real fix is immediate revocation and rotation at the identity provider.

keyTakeaway: Assume the credential is breached. Prioritize: 1) Revoke and rotate the secret at the provider, 2) Audit access logs for compromise, 3) Purge Git history with git-filter-repo, 4) Enable GitHub Push Protection.
elevatorPitch: Treat the secret as compromised immediately; never waste time scrubbing Git before rotating.
Deactivate and rotate the credential in AWS/Vault/Database within 2 minutes.
Query CloudTrail and audit logs for the compromised Key ID to confirm whether external attackers executed API calls.
Scrub repository history using git-filter-repo and install Gitleaks push protection to permanently prevent future leaks.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Revoking compromised credentials immediately without analyzing forensic audit trails for active exploitation when configuring Secret Accidentally Committed
mistakesToAvoid.why: Deactivating a compromised access key prevents abuse while preserving forensic identity for CloudTrail investigations to assess blast radius.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Terminating compromised instances immediately during incident triage without isolating volatile RAM state when configuring Secret Accidentally Committed
mistakesToAvoid.why: Terminating compromised instances immediately destroys volatile memory evidence (RAM dumps) required to establish intrusion timelines.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Injecting plaintext secrets into container environment variables rather than fetching from dynamic secret vaults when configuring Secret Accidentally Committed
mistakesToAvoid.why: Container environment variables are visible via `docker inspect` or Kubernetes API queries, leaking sensitive API tokens to developers.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to enforce automated credential rotation for third-party SaaS integration tokens when configuring Secret Accidentally Committed
mistakesToAvoid.why: Static long-lived API tokens shared across internal services represent the highest-probability vector for supply-chain credential compromise.

title: Kubernetes Cluster Upgrade Works in Staging but Corrupts CoreDNS in Production: Emergency Restoration
summary: Root cause analysis and emergency restoration procedure when a Kubernetes cluster upgrade breaks CoreDNS in production despite passing in staging.
question: A Kubernetes cluster upgrade works perfectly in staging, but when applied to production, it corrupts CoreDNS and breaks internal name resolution. How do you approach patching and restoring service?
intro: CoreDNS breakages during minor or major Kubernetes upgrades almost always occur due to deprecated Corefile plugin syntax (e.g. 'upstream', 'ready', or 'forward' plugin changes), ConfigMap schema discrepancies between staging and production (such as custom stub-domains or rewrite rules in prod that staging lacked), or iptables/IPVS conntrack packet loss. Because all microservices rely on CoreDNS for service discovery, this represents a cluster-wide Sev-1 outage.

steps.title: Immediate CoreDNS Pod Logs & Crash Diagnosis
steps.description: Inspect CoreDNS pod events and container logs in `kube-system`. If CoreDNS pods are in CrashLoopBackOff, check the exit logs. Deprecated plugins in the Corefile will cause CoreDNS to refuse initialization with a syntax validation error.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=100
# Common failure: 
# plugin/ready: this plugin can only be used once
# Corefile:5 - Error during parsing: Unknown directive 'upstream'

steps.title: Restore Known Good CoreDNS ConfigMap & Plugin Directives
steps.description: Compare production's `coredns` ConfigMap against staging. Edit or restore the valid Corefile configuration, removing deprecated directives while maintaining internal forward resolvers. Trigger a rollout restart of CoreDNS pods.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl edit configmap coredns -n kube-system
# Remove unsupported plugin lines, verify valid Corefile:
# .:53 {
#     errors
#     health
#     ready
#     kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
#         pods insecure
#         fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
#     }
#     forward . /etc/resolv.conf
#     cache 30
#     loop
#     reload
#     loadbalance
# }
kubectl rollout restart deployment coredns -n kube-system

steps.title: Bypass CoreDNS via NodeLocal DNSCache or Direct IP Emergency Override
steps.description: If CoreDNS binary itself is broken, deploy or fallback to NodeLocal DNSCache. In extreme emergencies where pods cannot resolve databases, temporarily patch critical application Service environment variables or /etc/hosts with ClusterIP addresses while fixing CoreDNS.
steps.highlight: Cluster Resilience: Always run NodeLocal DNSCache in enterprise Kubernetes clusters to provide high-speed local caching and isolate applications from CoreDNS control plane upgrade hiccups.

steps.title: Verify Post-Fix DNS Resolution Across All Namespaces
steps.description: Spin up a transient debug container to execute DNS lookups across cluster.local, external domains, and reverse in-addr.arpa entries.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup kubernetes.default
kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup google.com

keyTakeaway: Production CoreDNS failures post-upgrade stem from undocumented ConfigMap differences and deprecated plugins. Quickly inspect pod logs for syntax rejections, roll back the Corefile ConfigMap, restart coredns pods, and enforce NodeLocal DNSCache.
elevatorPitch: Inspect kube-system CoreDNS pod logs to identify rejected Corefile directives.
Compare production vs staging coredns ConfigMaps to spot un-migrated plugins.
Revert the Corefile ConfigMap to clean, forward-compatible syntax and rollout restart coredns.
Deploy NodeLocal DNSCache as a permanent architectural safeguard against cluster-wide DNS failures.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Draining cluster worker nodes without auditing PodDisruptionBudget availability and replica headroom
mistakesToAvoid.why: Unconditional node draining without checking PDB `maxUnavailable` can evict quorum-critical pods, causing cascading service outages.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Skipping deprecated API manifest validation tools (Pluto, Kubent) prior to initiating cluster upgrades
mistakesToAvoid.why: Kubernetes regularly graduates and removes beta APIs; deploying modern cluster versions with outdated manifest API versions causes immediate deployment rejections.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Initiating control plane upgrades without verifying etcd snapshot backups and quorum health
mistakesToAvoid.why: If control plane state becomes corrupted during an upgrade, restoring etcd snapshots is the sole disaster recovery mechanism.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring kubelet daemon configuration deprecations across newly provisioned worker node instances
mistakesToAvoid.why: Kubelet flags and container runtime interfaces evolve across versions; unvalidated flags prevent worker node registration with the API server.

title: Describe a Real Incident Where You Introduced Infrastructure Failure: Root Cause, Lessons, and Postmortem
summary: Master-level behavioral and technical narrative answering the classic senior interview question: 'Tell me about a time you broke production, what you learned, and what changed.'
question: Tell me a real scenario where YOU introduced a failure in infrastructure. What happened, what did you learn, and what changed after?
roleContext: Principal SRE / Staff Platform Engineer Interview
intro: Senior interviewers ask this question not to penalize failure, but to measure accountability, crisis composure, and engineering maturity. Junior engineers blame others or claim they've never broken production. Senior engineers candidly describe a complex production outage they triggered, walk through the fast recovery, and explain the automated guardrails they built to make that failure class impossible for anyone in the future.

steps.title: The Situation & The Incident (What I Broke)
steps.description: During a routine Terraform refactoring of our AWS networking layer, I was renaming a security group module to follow new company naming standards. While `terraform plan` showed changes to security group descriptions and tags, I missed that changing the resource identifier in HCL caused Terraform to plan a destructive replacement (`destroy and then create`) of the primary Redis ElastiCache security group instead of an in-place update. Upon running apply, Terraform dropped the existing security group before the replacement provisioned, instantly severing 40,000 active web client connections and causing 500 Internal Server Errors across checkout.

steps.title: Immediate Actions & Blast Radius Containment
steps.description: I did not panic or attempt a convoluted rollback. I immediately joined the incident channel, announced: 'I just ran a Terraform apply on the Redis security group that destroyed the ingress rule; I am manually attaching the prior security group right now.' Using AWS CLI, I re-attached the legacy security group to the ElastiCache cluster within 90 seconds, restoring customer checkout. Total outage duration: 2 minutes 15 seconds.

steps.title: Root Cause Analysis (Why the Failure Occurred)
steps.description:
The failure was not merely 'human error.' The systemic weaknesses were:
1. Terraform lacked `create_before_destroy = true` lifecycle rules on networking dependencies.
2. CI pipeline did not enforce automated plan checking for destructive actions (`-` or `- / +`).
3. Applying Terraform changes to production was permitted from local engineer workstations rather than strictly through an automated GitOps pipeline with approval gates.

steps.title: What Changed After: Systemic Guardrails Implemented
steps.description: I authored a blameless post-mortem and implemented three permanent platform safeguards: 1. Policy as Code (OPA Conftest / Sentinel): Blocked any PR from merging if the plan contains destructive replacements of stateful resources (`aws_security_group`, `aws_db_instance`, `aws_elasticache_cluster`). 2. Mandatory State Move Procedures: Established runbooks requiring `terraform state mv` when renaming resources to guarantee in-place refactoring. 3. Atlantis GitOps Gateways: Revoked local AWS apply permissions; all production Terraform changes now run strictly via Atlantis with two peer approvals.
steps.highlight: Interview Golden Standard: Own the mistake completely, focus on systemic organizational improvements rather than personal blame, and demonstrate how you made the system permanently safer.

keyTakeaway: Engineering maturity is measured by ownership and architectural remediation. Frame your failure around: 1) What broke and why, 2) Fast containment, 3) Systemic root causes, 4) Automated guardrails (Policy as Code, GitOps gates) implemented.
elevatorPitch: Own the mistake transparently without shifting blame to teammates or ambiguous tools.
Highlight immediate crisis composure: quickly diagnosing the break and restoring service within minutes.
Perform a deep systemic root cause analysis: look at CI/CD gaps, missing lifecycle policies, and lack of guardrails.
Demonstrate permanent platform impact: implement Policy as Code (OPA/Conftest) and GitOps controls so the entire organization is protected from that failure mode forever.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Millions of small files or unrotated session tokens can exhaust available file system inodes even when standard disk storage (`df -h`) shows ample free space.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Reaching file descriptor exhaustion throws 'Too many open files' errors, preventing services from accepting new TCP client socket connections.
