title: CI/CD Failed Deployment Rollback Framework: Detect, Analyze, Rollback, Validate, Monitor, and RCA
summary: End-to-end operational guide for rolling back failed deployments in CI/CD pipelines, based on the Detect → Analyze → Rollback → Validate → Monitor → RCA lifecycle.
question: How do you perform a rollback of a failed deployment in your CI/CD pipeline? Walk me through your complete operational workflow from failure detection to post-incident prevention.
intro: When a production deployment fails, my primary priority is restoring service safely and minimizing downtime before investigating root cause. I follow a structured 7-stage lifecycle: Detect → Analyze → Rollback → Validate → Monitor → RCA → Prevent. Rollback restores stability; RCA prevents recurrence.

steps.title: Stage 1 & 2: Rapid Failure Detection & Scope Analysis
steps.description:
Detect anomalies via pipeline health checks and live monitoring:
- Pipeline logs (Jenkins / GitHub Actions / GitLab CI)
- Application error logs (Elasticsearch / Loki / Datadog)
- Container status (`CrashLoopBackOff`, `OOMKilled`)
- Alertmanager & PagerDuty error rate alerts
Quickly identify the last known stable deployment artifact (Git commit SHA, Docker image digest, or Helm release revision).
steps.codeBlock:
# Identify previous stable Helm release or Kubernetes rollout revision
helm history my-app -n production
kubectl rollout history deployment/my-app -n production

steps.title: Stage 3: Execute Controlled Rollback
steps.description: Trigger automated or manual rollback according to infrastructure target: - Kubernetes: Run `kubectl rollout undo deployment/` or roll back Helm chart. - Docker Standalone: Re-deploy the previously validated container image tag (e.g. `myapp:v1.4.1` replacing `myapp:v1.4.2`). - GitOps: Revert the Git commit on the main branch, allowing ArgoCD/Flux to auto-synchronize the previous manifest.
steps.codeBlock:
# Fast rollback commands
kubectl rollout undo deployment/my-app -n production
# Or via Helm:
helm rollback my-app 42 -n production

steps.title: Stage 4 & 5: Post-Rollback Validation & Active Monitoring
steps.description:
Validate that the rolled-back revision is healthy:
- Synthetic HTTP health checks (`/healthz` returning 200)
- Pod container ready status (`kubectl get pods -l app=my-app`)
- Error rate drops back below SLO thresholds in Grafana/Datadog
- CPU and memory usage return to normal baselines

steps.title: Stage 6 & 7: Root Cause Analysis (RCA) & Preventative Safeguards
steps.description: Conduct blameless post-mortem answering four fundamental questions: 1. What failed? (Exact component or code line) 2. Why did it fail? (Configuration drift, schema mismatch, unhandled null pointer) 3. Why wasn't it detected earlier? (Missing integration test or staging disparity) 4. What preventive action is required? (Automated canary analysis, pre-flight DB checks, or contract tests)
steps.highlight: Operational Axiom: Never leave a rollback as the final step. Always pair every rollback with a rigorous RCA to implement permanent preventative gates.

keyTakeaway: Follow Detect → Analyze → Rollback → Validate → Monitor → RCA → Prevent. Prioritize fast automated rollback via 'kubectl rollout undo' or Git commit reverts, followed by rigorous post-incident RCA.
elevatorPitch: Execute an immediate rollback to the last verified image tag or Helm revision.
Verify service restoration across synthetic health probes, pod statuses, and error rates.
Maintain continuous monitoring post-rollback to ensure performance stabilization.
Conduct blameless RCA addressing why the regression bypassed pre-deployment CI test gates.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Promoting application releases to production without an automated, canary-validated rollback mechanism when configuring CI/CD Failed Deployment
mistakesToAvoid.why: Pipelines that lack automated rollback mechanisms force engineering teams to scramble manual hotfixes during severe production regressions.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running concurrent deployment pipeline jobs without stage mutex locking on shared target environments when configuring CI/CD Failed Deployment
mistakesToAvoid.why: Concurrent pipeline runs on the same environment race to apply state changes, causing out-of-order commits and unpredictable deployment state.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting dependency lockfiles (package-lock.json, go.sum, Cargo.lock) from continuous integration builds when configuring CI/CD Failed Deployment
mistakesToAvoid.why: Omitting lockfiles allows upstream package updates to break builds unpredictably without any changes to application codebase.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to define dynamic cache invalidation keys for CI package managers and layer caches when configuring CI/CD Failed Deployment
mistakesToAvoid.why: Stale build caches mask underlying dependency incompatibilities or pull outdated libraries, while un-cached runs slow feedback loops.

title: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Pod Fails Health Checks Randomly: End-to-End Triage Runbook
summary: End-to-end troubleshooting methodology to diagnose and resolve intermittent liveness and readiness probe failures in Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS).
question: You’ve deployed an application to Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) and it fails health checks randomly. How do you debug this end-to-end?
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Technical Deep Dive
intro: Intermittent health check failures on AKS typically point to four architectural issues: probe timeout thresholds too aggressive under burst traffic, node-level CPU throttling starving kubelet worker threads, Azure CNI IP exhaustion/conntrack packet drops, or application garbage collection (GC) stop-the-world pauses blocking the health check endpoint.

steps.title: Inspect Kubelet Events & Probe Configuration
steps.description: Check whether failure events report 'Unhealthy' or 'Connection refused'. Examine `timeoutSeconds`, `periodSeconds`, and `failureThreshold` in the pod manifest. If `timeoutSeconds` is set to the default 1s and the application experiences brief GC pauses or database latency, kubelet immediately registers a failure.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n production
# Look for Events:
# Warning  Unhealthy  Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 500 or timeout

steps.title: Check Node & Container CPU Throttling (CFS Quotas)
steps.description: When container CPU limits (`resources.limits.cpu`) are too low, the Linux Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) throttles the application threads periodically. When throttled, the application process cannot respond to the kubelet HTTP GET probe within 1 second.
steps.codeBlock:
# Check if container is throttled via cgroup
kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.stat
# nr_throttled: count of periods where application was throttled

steps.title: Verify Azure CNI Networking & Conntrack Table Limits
steps.description: In AKS with Azure CNI, verify whether the node's VNet subnet has IP exhaustion or if the node kernel conntrack table (`nf_conntrack_count`) is approaching `nf_conntrack_max`. When conntrack overflows, kubelet packets to pod IPs are silently dropped.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get nodes -o wide
az aks show -g rg-banking -n aks-prod --query "networkProfile.networkPlugin"
# Check node conntrack count
kubectl get node <node-name> -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}'

steps.title: Isolate Endpoint Logic from Heavy Business Workloads
steps.description: Ensure the readiness probe endpoint does not execute deep blocking database queries (`SELECT 1 FROM massive_table`) or external API calls. Move deep dependencies to startup probes and keep readiness probes strictly evaluating local process health and connection pool availability.
steps.highlight: Best Practice: Separate startup probes (for initial bootstrapping) from readiness probes. Increase timeoutSeconds to 3s-5s and failureThreshold to 3.

keyTakeaway: Intermittent AKS probe failures stem from aggressive 1s probe timeouts, CFS CPU quota throttling, or heavy queries inside health endpoints. Tune timeout thresholds and verify cgroup throttling metrics.
elevatorPitch: Check pod describe events to determine whether failures are timeouts or connection resets.
Verify container CPU limits to ensure CFS throttling is not pausing application threads.
Inspect Azure CNI networking and conntrack table saturation on the host node.
Decouple heavy database checks from readiness probes; rely on lightweight process health endpoints.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Configuring Service selector labels that mismatch underlying Pod manifest metadata when configuring Azure Kubernetes Service
mistakesToAvoid.why: A typo in `spec.selector` causes the Service endpoints list (`kubectl get endpoints`) to remain empty, resulting in `503 Service Unavailable` or timeouts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting explicit ingressClassName specifications when running multiple ingress controllers when configuring Azure Kubernetes Service
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without an explicit `ingressClassName`, ingress resources are either ignored or picked up unpredictably by competing controllers.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Depleting worker node subnet IP address allocations under VPC CNI or Azure CNI when configuring Azure Kubernetes Service
mistakesToAvoid.why: Direct VPC pod networking allocates real subnet IPs; failing to monitor IP pools causes new pods to stay stuck indefinitely in `ContainerCreating`.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Attempting network triage without inspecting kubectl describe service and EndpointSlice resources when configuring Azure Kubernetes Service
mistakesToAvoid.why: Verifying EndpointSlice population immediately determines whether a connectivity failure is caused by pod labeling, readiness probes, or routing.

title: Canary Deployment Returns 502 Bad Gateway for 50% of Traffic: Troubleshooting Approach
summary: Diagnostic framework for resolving split-traffic 502 Bad Gateway errors during a canary deployment rollout in Kubernetes.
question: In a canary deployment to production, half the traffic returns HTTP 502 Bad Gateway, while the other half succeeds. Walk us through your troubleshooting approach.
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Scenario 2
intro: When exactly 50% of requests return HTTP 502 during a canary deployment while the remaining 50% succeed, traffic is splitting evenly between two upstream target groups: one healthy (stable version) and one failing (canary version). A 502 indicates that the Ingress controller or Service Mesh reverse proxy received an invalid response or connection reset (RST) from the canary backend.

steps.title: Confirm Traffic Split Routing & Upstream Targets
steps.description: Inspect the Ingress, VirtualService, or Load Balancer configuration to confirm how the 50/50 split is allocated. Identify the exact Pod IP addresses belonging to the canary ReplicaSet.
steps.codeBlock:
# Identify Pods in canary ReplicaSet
kubectl get pods -l app=payment-service --show-labels
kubectl get endpoints payment-service-canary -o wide

steps.title: Inspect Upstream Connection Resets & Port Mismatches
steps.description: Common causes of 502 on newly deployed canaries: 1. Container Port Mismatch: Service targetPort does not match the actual port exposed by the new container image (e.g. Service routes to 8080, but new Dockerfile exposes 8000). 2. Immediate Crash on Connection: The canary pod binds the socket but crashes on the first incoming request due to missing environment variables or secret misconfigurations. 3. TLS Mismatch: Ingress expects plaintext HTTP upstream, but canary was configured with HTTPS (or vice versa).
steps.codeBlock:
# Test canary pod directly from within the cluster bypassing ingress
kubectl exec -it <debug-pod> -- curl -v http://<canary-pod-ip>:<target-port>/healthz

steps.title: Halt Canary Progression & Route Traffic Back to 100% Stable
steps.description: Before deep-dive debugging, mitigate user impact immediately. Roll canary traffic back to 0% in Argo Rollouts or patch the Istio VirtualService weights.
steps.codeBlock:
# Rollback canary immediately via Argo Rollouts
kubectl argo rollouts abort payment-service
# Or update Istio VirtualService weight to 100% stable
kubectl patch virtualservice payment-service --type merge -p '{"spec":{"http":[{"route":[{"destination":{"host":"payment-stable"},"weight":100},{"destination":{"host":"payment-canary"},"weight":0}]}]}}'

steps.title: Extract Canary Logs & Core Dump
steps.description: Check the canary pod logs and previous container logs (`kubectl logs <canary-pod> --previous`) to analyze application exceptions, uncaught startup errors, or missing runtime configurations.

keyTakeaway: 50% 502 errors indicate that all traffic reaching the canary pool fails. Immediately halt the canary and route 100% of traffic back to stable, then verify targetPort mismatches, missing secrets, or HTTP/HTTPS protocol mismatches.
elevatorPitch: Recognize that a 50% failure rate maps directly to the canary replica pool failing completely.
Immediately abort the canary rollout to direct 100% of user traffic back to the stable deployment.
Verify container targetPort mapping against the Kubernetes Service spec.
Curl the canary pod IP directly from a cluster debug pod to isolate whether the app is crashing or misconfigured.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Confusing ALB 502 Bad Gateway (target connection reset) with 504 Gateway Timeout (upstream response timeout) when configuring Canary Deployment Returns
mistakesToAvoid.why: 502 indicates the backend target closed the TCP connection prematurely or returned malformed HTTP, whereas 504 means the target failed to respond before idle timeout.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Setting target deregistration delay to zero instead of allowing connection draining when configuring Canary Deployment Returns
mistakesToAvoid.why: Instant target deregistration severs in-flight HTTP requests during auto-scaling scale-in or rolling deployments, causing immediate user-facing drops.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to query CloudWatch ELB metrics (`HTTPCode_ELB_5XX` vs `HTTPCode_Target_5XX`) during load balancer outages when configuring Canary Deployment Returns
mistakesToAvoid.why: Comparing load balancer generated errors against target generated errors immediately isolates whether the issue lies in the proxy tier or application runtime.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Overlooking Security Group rules on backend EC2/ECS instances that block health check traffic from the ALB when configuring Canary Deployment Returns
mistakesToAvoid.why: Target instances must explicitly permit inbound HTTP/HTTPS traffic from the ALB security group on the configured container/application port.

title: Enterprise CI/CD Pipeline Takes 40 Minutes for Small Change: Bottleneck Isolation & Caching
summary: Enterprise pipeline optimization methodology to reduce build and deployment cycles from 40 minutes to under 8 minutes for minor code changes.
question: A CI/CD pipeline takes 40 minutes to deploy a small change. What would you do to optimize it?
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Technical Deep Dive
intro: When a small one-line change takes 40 minutes to traverse a pipeline, the system suffers from non-incremental workflows: re-downloading gigabytes of dependencies from scratch, re-building un-cached Docker layers, running monolithic integration test suites sequentially, and using slow ephemeral agent provisioning.

steps.title: Profile Pipeline Stages & Identify the Critical Path
steps.description: Generate a timeline flamegraph of the pipeline. Measure durations for checkout, dependency resolution, linting/SAST, unit tests, container packaging, integration tests, and artifact upload to locate the 80/20 bottleneck.

steps.title: Implement Distributed Dependency & Package Caching
steps.description: Use persistent cache mounts or remote object storage caches for package managers (Maven/Gradle local repository, npm/yarn cache, pip wheel cache). Only re-download dependencies when the lockfile (`package-lock.json`, `pom.xml`, `go.sum`) changes.
steps.codeBlock:
# Azure Pipelines Cache Task Example
- task: Cache@2
  inputs:
    key: 'maven | "$(Agent.OS)" | **/pom.xml'
    restoreKeys: |
       maven | "$(Agent.OS)"
    path: $(HOME)/.m2/repository

steps.title: Leverage Docker BuildKit Remote Layer Caching
steps.description: Utilize BuildKit inline cache or registry cache (`--cache-to type=registry`, `--cache-from type=registry`). Re-architect the Dockerfile so that OS package updates and base dependencies are layered first, while application binaries are copied last.
steps.codeBlock:
docker buildx build \
  --cache-from type=registry,ref=myacr.azurecr.io/app:cache \
  --cache-to type=registry,ref=myacr.azurecr.io/app:cache,mode=max \
  --tag myacr.azurecr.io/app:$(Build.SourceVersion) \
  --push .

steps.title: Execute Test Impact Analysis & Test Parallelization
steps.description: Integrate Test Impact Analysis (TIA) to run only the unit test suites affected by the modified code files in Pull Requests. Run tests concurrently across agent cores instead of single-threaded execution.
steps.highlight: Banking Standard: Keep PR fast feedback loops under 7 minutes. Move 30-minute end-to-end integration and penetration test suites to asynchronous staging triggers.

keyTakeaway: Optimize slow pipelines by profiling stage durations, implementing remote dependency caching, enabling Docker BuildKit registry caching, and running tests in parallel shards.
elevatorPitch: Audit pipeline execution timeline to pinpoint whether dependencies, tests, or Docker packaging dominate runtime.
Inject dependency caching (Maven .m2, npm cache) keyed on lockfile hashes.
Utilize Docker BuildKit remote registry caching so unchanged layers build in seconds.
Parallelize test suites and enforce Test Impact Analysis for PR verification.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Promoting application releases to production without an automated, canary-validated rollback mechanism when configuring Enterprise CI/CD Pipeline
mistakesToAvoid.why: Pipelines that lack automated rollback mechanisms force engineering teams to scramble manual hotfixes during severe production regressions.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running concurrent deployment pipeline jobs without stage mutex locking on shared target environments when configuring Enterprise CI/CD Pipeline
mistakesToAvoid.why: Concurrent pipeline runs on the same environment race to apply state changes, causing out-of-order commits and unpredictable deployment state.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting dependency lockfiles (package-lock.json, go.sum, Cargo.lock) from continuous integration builds when configuring Enterprise CI/CD Pipeline
mistakesToAvoid.why: Omitting lockfiles allows upstream package updates to break builds unpredictably without any changes to application codebase.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to define dynamic cache invalidation keys for CI package managers and layer caches when configuring Enterprise CI/CD Pipeline
mistakesToAvoid.why: Stale build caches mask underlying dependency incompatibilities or pull outdated libraries, while un-cached runs slow feedback loops.

title: High CPU Usage in One Kubernetes Pod With Clean Application Logs: Deep Diagnostic Flow
summary: Root cause analysis workflow for diagnosing a Kubernetes pod pinning 100% CPU when application logs contain zero errors or anomalies.
question: You see high CPU usage in one pod, but logs look clean. What next?
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Technical Deep Dive
intro: When a pod consumes 100% CPU while logging nothing, the application is stuck in a silent CPU-bound spin: an infinite loop, JVM garbage collection thrashing (Stop-The-World full GC), regex catastrophic backtracking, deadlock spinning on busy-wait locks, or an unhandled exception loop that silently swallows errors.

steps.title: Identify Whether All Cores or Single Core Are Pinned
steps.description: Exec into the pod or the underlying host node. Run `top` or `htop` and press `1` to see per-core CPU usage, and `H` to show thread-level CPU usage. Identify the exact thread ID (TID) consuming the CPU.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- top -H
# Note the high CPU PID/TID: e.g. PID 42 using 99.8% CPU

steps.title: Capture Thread Dumps or CPU Stack Traces
steps.description: Convert the thread ID to hexadecimal and inspect thread stacks: - Java / JVM: Use `jstack ` and search for the hexadecimal TID (`nid=0x2a`). - Go / Node / Python: Capture a pprof or async-profiler flamegraph.
steps.codeBlock:
# For JVM:
printf "%x\n" 42  # Output: 2a
jstack <pid> | grep -A 20 "nid=0x2a"
# For Go:
curl http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30 > cpu.pprof
go tool pprof -http=:8080 cpu.pprof

steps.title: Check Garbage Collection Thrashing & Memory Pressure
steps.description: Inspect memory allocation. If the application heap is 98% full and JVM Garbage Collector threads (`VM Thread`, `GC task thread#0`) are running continuously attempting to reclaim unreachable objects, CPU will pin at 100% while application code is suspended.
steps.codeBlock:
jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000 5
# Inspect FGC (Full GC count) and FGCT (Full GC time)

steps.title: Inspect Kernel Syscalls with strace / perf
steps.description: If thread dumps cannot be gathered, attach `perf` or `strace` from the node to see what system calls the thread is executing (e.g. spinning on `futex` or non-blocking socket reads).
steps.highlight: Production Tip: Always capture thread dumps and profiler flamegraphs BEFORE killing or restarting the pod, otherwise the root cause evidence is permanently lost.

keyTakeaway: Clean logs with high CPU point to silent CPU loops, regex backtracking, or GC thrashing. Capture thread dumps (jstack) or CPU profilers (pprof/perf) to identify the spinning thread ID before restarting.
elevatorPitch: Run top -H inside the container to identify the exact thread ID (TID) consuming CPU.
Capture thread dumps (jstack) and correlate the hex TID to find the exact code line.
Verify memory utilization to rule out continuous JVM Garbage Collection thrashing.
Preserve thread dumps and heap telemetry for post-incident root cause analysis before pod restarts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Restarting a crashing container without examining preceding termination logs via kubectl logs --previous when configuring High Usage Kubernetes
mistakesToAvoid.why: Restarting the pod flushes ephemeral container runtime state, destroying vital panic stack traces and fatal initialization logs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Misdiagnosing an application boot crash as a failure of aggressive liveness probes when configuring High Usage Kubernetes
mistakesToAvoid.why: Liveness probes with short timeouts or high failure thresholds kill slow-starting applications repeatedly, causing false `CrashLoopBackOff` loops.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Neglecting node taints, tolerations, and resource quotas when diagnosing pods stuck in Pending when configuring High Usage Kubernetes
mistakesToAvoid.why: Pods remain `Pending` when scheduler predicates fail; `kubectl describe pod` reveals whether CPU/memory exhaustion or taints prevent placement.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Invoking kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0 indiscriminately on unready pods when configuring High Usage Kubernetes
mistakesToAvoid.why: Forced deletion bypasses kubelet cleanup and can cause multi-attach errors on PersistentVolumes (PVs) or split-brain on stateful workloads.

title: Highly Available Logging System for 100+ Microservices Across 3 Regions: Architecture Blueprint
summary: Enterprise architectural design for a multi-region, resilient logging platform ingesting terabytes of logs from 100+ microservices without cross-region data transfer bottlenecks.
question: You’re asked to design a highly available logging system for 100+ microservices across 3 cloud regions. What tools and architecture would you suggest?
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Technical Deep Dive
intro: Designing an enterprise logging pipeline for 100+ microservices across 3 cloud regions requires balancing four core pillars: zero log loss during infrastructure outages, minimizing expensive cross-region egress costs, ensuring strict PCI/SOC2 compliance, and supporting sub-second query latency for on-call engineers.

steps.title: Regional Ingestion & Buffering (Decoupled Architecture)
steps.description: Deploy a local ingestion layer within each of the 3 regions to eliminate cross-region egress fees during ingestion: 1. Edge Collector: Deploy Vector or Fluent Bit as a DaemonSet on every Kubernetes node. Buffers logs in memory with local disk fallback. 2. Regional Buffer: Stream logs to a local Apache Kafka or AWS Kinesis cluster in each region to absorb ingestion spikes (e.g. 100k events/sec) without backpressuring application containers.

steps.title: In-Stream PII Masking & Schema Normalization
steps.description:
Stream logs through stream processors (Vector transforms or Kafka Streams) in each region to:
- Mask banking PII/PCI data (credit cards, IBANs, SSNs) using regex transformations.
- Parse unstructured text into OpenTelemetry / ECS JSON format.
- Drop debug logs in production to save indexing costs.
steps.codeBlock:
# Vector PII Masking Transform
[transforms.mask_pii]
type = "remap"
inputs = ["kafka_source"]
source = '''
.message = replace(.message, r'\b\d{4}[- ]?\d{4}[- ]?\d{4}[- ]?\d{4}\b', "[REDACTED_CARD]")
'''

steps.title: Tiered Storage Architecture (Hot / Warm / Cold)
steps.description: Store logs across tiered storage engines: - Hot Tier (1-7 days): Regional OpenSearch / Elasticsearch or Grafana Loki clusters for fast querying. - Warm Tier (8-30 days): Read-only indices backed by EBS/gp3. - Cold / Compliance Tier (30 days - 3 years): Raw compressed Parquet files shipped directly to S3 / Azure Blob Storage with Object Lock (WORM compliance for banking regulations) at 95% lower cost.

steps.title: Global Federated Search & Disaster Recovery
steps.description: Provide a single Grafana or OpenSearch Dashboards pane that queries regional clusters via cross-cluster search (CCS). If one region experiences an outage, logs remain buffered in local Kafka without data loss.
steps.highlight: Banking Compliance: Never ship unredacted raw logs across regions. Process and mask PII within the originating region before archiving.

keyTakeaway: Ingest locally per region using Vector and Kafka buffers to eliminate cross-region network egress costs and prevent log loss. Enforce in-stream PII masking, store 7 days in Hot OpenSearch/Loki, and archive 3 years in S3/Blob storage.
elevatorPitch: Deploy regional Vector DaemonSets and Kafka streaming buffers in all 3 regions to absorb traffic spikes without cross-region egress charges.
Implement in-stream PII scrubbing to redact sensitive banking account numbers and credit cards before storage.
Adopt tiered storage: Hot OpenSearch for 7-day fast queries and cold S3/Blob storage for 3-year regulatory compliance.
Enable cross-cluster federated search through Grafana to query logs across all 3 regions from a single UI.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Injecting high-cardinality label dimensions (such as user IDs or request UUIDs) into Prometheus metrics when addressing elasticsearch
mistakesToAvoid.why: High-cardinality label values cause exponential time-series growth, consuming gigabytes of TSDB memory and crashing Prometheus servers.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Evaluating application performance solely through arithmetic mean or p50 latency while ignoring tail latency (p99)
mistakesToAvoid.why: Averages hide catastrophic tail latency outages where 1% of high-value user transactions suffer severe timeouts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to inject and extract W3C distributed trace context across message brokers and RPC calls
mistakesToAvoid.why: Breaking distributed trace context propagation fragments end-to-end transaction waterfalls into disconnected, un-correlatable trace segments.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Configuring alert rule evaluation intervals without sufficient duration damping (for: 5m), inducing alert flap
mistakesToAvoid.why: Instant alerts triggered by transient sub-second CPU or latency blips page on-call engineers unnecessarily and dilute response urgency.

title: Production App Works Fine for Internal Users but Fails for External Users (403 Error): Isolation Runbook
summary: Step-by-step diagnostic strategy to isolate why an enterprise banking application succeeds for corporate network users but returns HTTP 403 Forbidden to public external clients.
question: A production application works fine for internal users but fails for external ones with a 403 Forbidden error. How will you isolate and resolve the issue?
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Scenario 6
intro: When an application serves internal users cleanly while returning HTTP 403 Forbidden to external users, the core application code is healthy. The failure resides at the edge boundary where security policies differentiate between internal and external request headers, IP source ranges, Web Application Firewall (WAF) rule evaluations, or mTLS / OAuth authorization scopes.

steps.title: Inspect HTTP Response Headers to Identify the Rejecting Component
steps.description: Run `curl -v` against the public endpoint. Examine the 'Server' and custom error headers in the 403 response. If the response header contains `Server: Cloudflare`, `Server: awselb/2.0`, or `x-azure-ref`, the request was rejected at the edge proxy, not by the backend pod.
steps.codeBlock:
curl -i -k https://api.banking.company.com/v1/accounts
# Response analysis:
# HTTP/2 403 
# server: Microsoft-Azure-Application-Gateway/v2
# x-ms-forbidden-reason: WAF-GeoBlock

steps.title: Audit Web Application Firewall (WAF) & Geo-Blocking Rules
steps.description: Check WAF logs (Azure WAF, AWS WAF, Cloudflare). Banking platforms enforce strict IP whitelisting, Rate-Limiting rules, and Geo-Blocking. External clients may originate from non-whitelisted geographical regions or trigger OWASP Core Rule Set (CRS) false positives due to specific cookie formats or User-Agent strings.
steps.codeBlock:
# Query Azure Application Gateway WAF logs via Log Analytics
AzureDiagnostics
| where Category == "ApplicationGatewayFirewallLog"
| where action_s == "Blocked"
| project TimeGenerated, clientIp_s, ruleId_s, message_s

steps.title: Check Ingress Controller CIDR Whitelisting & Reverse Proxy Headers
steps.description: Verify whether the Kubernetes Ingress manifest or NGINX configuration contains `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/whitelist-source-range`. If external clients traverse an intermediate load balancer that does NOT preserve the client IP via X-Forwarded-For, the Ingress sees the load balancer's private IP (or vice-versa).
steps.codeBlock: kubectl get ingress <ingress-name> -o yaml | grep -i whitelist

steps.title: Verify API Gateway Authentication & OAuth Scope Policies
steps.description: Internal users may authenticate automatically via intranet Kerberos/NTLM tokens or trusted mTLS certificates, whereas external clients require Bearer JWT tokens from an external Identity Provider (Azure AD / Okta). If the API gateway fails to parse the external token or missing scope, it returns 403 Forbidden.
steps.highlight: Diagnostic Rule: If curl -v returns 403 within 15ms, the edge proxy or WAF blocked it. If it takes >200ms, the application or API gateway evaluated auth tokens and rejected permissions.

keyTakeaway: Isolate the layer generating the 403 by inspecting response headers. Differentiate between WAF rule triggers, Ingress IP whitelist restrictions, and API Gateway OAuth authorization token scope mismatches.
elevatorPitch: Inspect curl response headers to identify whether WAF, Ingress, or the application backend returned the 403.
Query WAF logs to check for triggered OWASP rules, Geo-blocking, or rate-limiting filters.
Verify Ingress IP whitelist annotations and X-Forwarded-For client IP preservation.
Audit API Gateway OAuth2 token scopes to ensure external identity claims have appropriate permissions.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating stateless Network ACLs as stateful firewalls without specifying outbound ephemeral return ports when addressing application
mistakesToAvoid.why: Security Groups track connection state automatically, whereas stateless Network ACLs require explicit ephemeral port rules (1024-65535) for return traffic.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Opening short-lived non-pooled TCP client connections, exhausting ephemeral ports in TIME_WAIT state when addressing networking
mistakesToAvoid.why: Rapidly opening and closing short-lived TCP sockets without connection pooling exhausts ephemeral ports, causing connection refusal errors.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Directing load balancer health checks to heavy computational endpoints rather than dedicated health routes
mistakesToAvoid.why: Deep health check paths amplify database load during traffic spikes and risk cascading eviction of healthy application nodes.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Triggering BGP route dampening by rapidly announcing and withdrawing multihomed network prefixes
mistakesToAvoid.why: Rapidly flapping BGP route announcements triggers upstream ISP route dampening, effectively blackholing network traffic for hours.

title: Secure and Dynamic Secret Rotation in Azure DevOps Pipelines: Architecture Blueprint
summary: How to design dynamic, zero-trust secret rotation in Azure DevOps CI/CD pipelines eliminating static passwords and long-lived service principal keys.
question: How do you ensure secure and dynamic secret rotation in Azure DevOps pipelines?
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Technical Deep Dive
intro: In modern enterprise banking infrastructure, storing static secrets or long-lived service principal passwords inside CI/CD variable groups is a major compliance risk. I eliminate long-lived secrets using OpenID Connect (OIDC) Workload Identity Federation between Azure DevOps and Azure AD, paired with automated Azure Key Vault dynamic secret rotation and short-lived tokens.

steps.title: Eliminate Passwords via OIDC Workload Identity Federation
steps.description: Configure Azure DevOps Service Connections with Workload Identity Federation instead of static client secrets. When a pipeline runs, Azure DevOps generates a short-lived cryptographically signed OIDC token that Azure Active Directory exchanges for a temporary, 1-hour Azure access token.
steps.codeBlock:
# Azure DevOps YAML using federated service connection
steps:
- task: AzureCLI@2
  inputs:
    azureSubscription: 'Azure-DevOps-WorkloadIdentity-ServiceConnection'
    scriptType: 'bash'
    scriptLocation: 'inlineScript'
    inlineScript: |
      az account show

steps.title: Dynamic Secret Retrieval from Azure Key Vault
steps.description: Never store application database credentials in pipeline YAML. Use the `AzureKeyVault@2` pipeline task to dynamically pull the latest active secret version directly into agent memory at execution time. Secrets are masked in logs automatically.
steps.codeBlock:
- task: AzureKeyVault@2
  inputs:
    azureSubscription: 'Azure-DevOps-WorkloadIdentity-ServiceConnection'
    KeyVaultName: 'kv-prod-banking'
    SecretsFilter: 'DB-PASSWORD,STRIPE-SECRET'
    RunAsPreJob: true

steps.title: Automate Secret Rotation via Event Grid & Azure Functions
steps.description: Configure Azure Key Vault automatic rotation policies. When a database password reaches its 30-day lifecycle expiration, Key Vault triggers an Azure Event Grid event to an Azure Function, which generates a new password, updates PostgreSQL/SQL Server, and stores the new secret version in Key Vault with zero downtime.

steps.title: Enforce Dual-Credential Overlap for Zero-Downtime Rotation
steps.description: During rotation, configure the database with two active users (User A and User B). When User A's password rotates, services gracefully transition to User B without connection drops before User A's credentials are wiped.

keyTakeaway: Replace static pipeline secrets with Azure DevOps OIDC Workload Identity Federation. Retrieve secrets dynamically from Azure Key Vault and automate database credential rotation via Event Grid and dual-credential pairing.
elevatorPitch: Migrate Azure DevOps service connections to OIDC Workload Identity Federation to eliminate static client secrets.
Fetch secrets dynamically in pipeline memory via AzureKeyVault@2 rather than storing them in variables.
Automate rotation policies in Key Vault using Event Grid and Azure Functions for automated 30-day key updates.
Implement dual-credential rotation patterns to ensure zero downtime while database passwords cycle.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Revoking compromised credentials immediately without analyzing forensic audit trails for active exploitation when configuring Secure Dynamic Secret
mistakesToAvoid.why: Deactivating a compromised access key prevents abuse while preserving forensic identity for CloudTrail investigations to assess blast radius.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Terminating compromised instances immediately during incident triage without isolating volatile RAM state when configuring Secure Dynamic Secret
mistakesToAvoid.why: Terminating compromised instances immediately destroys volatile memory evidence (RAM dumps) required to establish intrusion timelines.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Injecting plaintext secrets into container environment variables rather than fetching from dynamic secret vaults when configuring Secure Dynamic Secret
mistakesToAvoid.why: Container environment variables are visible via `docker inspect` or Kubernetes API queries, leaking sensitive API tokens to developers.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to enforce automated credential rotation for third-party SaaS integration tokens when configuring Secure Dynamic Secret
mistakesToAvoid.why: Static long-lived API tokens shared across internal services represent the highest-probability vector for supply-chain credential compromise.

title: Architecting Azure Application Gateway v2 with WAF for Sensitive Banking Workloads
summary: Enterprise architectural pattern for implementing Azure Application Gateway v2 with Web Application Firewall (WAF) CRS 3.2 rules, SSL offloading, and mTLS for banking applications.
question: Explain how you’d use Azure Application Gateway with Web Application Firewall (WAF) for a sensitive banking application.
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Technical Deep Dive
intro: In financial services, Azure Application Gateway v2 with WAF serves as the first defensive perimeter, enforcing PCI-DSS, OWASP Top 10 mitigation, end-to-end TLS 1.3 encryption, and granular Layer 7 routing to private AKS backend pools without exposing pods to the public internet.

steps.title: Deploy in Dedicated Subnet with Private Backend Integration
steps.description: Provision Application Gateway v2 in a dedicated `/24` subnet within the hub VNet. Route incoming traffic exclusively to private IP endpoints in the AKS spoke VNet (via Private Endpoint or VNet Peering), ensuring zero public IPs on backend worker nodes.
steps.codeBlock:
# Backend pool configured with private AKS internal load balancer IP
az network application-gateway address-pool create \
  --gateway-name agw-prod-banking \
  --resource-group rg-banking \
  --name aks-private-backend \
  --servers 10.240.0.100

steps.title: Harden WAF with OWASP Core Rule Set (CRS 3.2) & Custom Rules
steps.description: Enable WAF in `Prevention` mode running CRS 3.2. Implement custom rules ahead of CRS: - Geo-Filtering: Block traffic from non-compliant foreign jurisdictions. - Rate Limiting: Restrict login/transfer endpoints to 50 requests per minute per IP. - IP Whitelisting: Restrict administrative API endpoints to corporate ExpressRoute / VPN ranges.
steps.codeBlock:
# Azure WAF Rate Limit Custom Rule
az network application-gateway waf-policy custom-rule create \
  --policy-name waf-banking-policy \
  --resource-group rg-banking \
  --name RateLimitLogins \
  --priority 10 \
  --rule-type RateLimit \
  --action Block \
  --rate-limit-duration OneMinute \
  --rate-limit-threshold 50

steps.title: Enforce End-to-End TLS 1.3 Encryption & Mutual TLS (mTLS)
steps.description: Do not terminate TLS to plaintext in banking. Terminate external client TLS at the Gateway with EV certificates managed in Key Vault, then re-encrypt traffic over a dedicated internal TLS connection to the AKS ingress controller. Enforce mutual TLS (mTLS) for B2B API integrations.
steps.highlight: Compliance Mandate: Strict PCI-DSS Section 4.1 mandates strong cryptography: disable TLS 1.0/1.1, disable weak ciphers, and enforce TLS 1.2/1.3 with Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS).

steps.title: Enable Centralized Diagnostic Streaming to Azure Sentinel / SIEM
steps.description: Stream all WAF access logs, firewall blocks, and performance metrics in real time to Azure Log Analytics and Azure Sentinel for automated threat hunting and SOC anomaly detection.

keyTakeaway: Architect Azure App Gateway v2 in Prevention mode with OWASP CRS 3.2, geo-blocking, end-to-end TLS re-encryption to private AKS subnets, and real-time streaming to Azure Sentinel.
elevatorPitch: Deploy App Gateway v2 in a dedicated subnet routing strictly to private backend AKS IP pools.
Enforce WAF Prevention mode with custom rate-limiting rules on sensitive transaction routes.
Mandate end-to-end TLS encryption with TLS 1.3 and mTLS client certificate verification.
Stream WAF telemetry to Azure Sentinel for real-time security operations monitoring.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Attaching wildcard permissions ('Action: *', 'Resource: *') to production IAM policies and roles when addressing architecting
mistakesToAvoid.why: Wildcard IAM grants violate least-privilege principles, allowing unauthorized lateral movement and privilege escalation across account boundaries.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying exclusively on edge network perimeters while neglecting zero-trust pod network isolation
mistakesToAvoid.why: Perimeter-only security allows attackers to move laterally unhindered once a single edge proxy or worker node is compromised.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Bypassing container image vulnerability scanning gates (Trivy/Grype) for emergency production patches
mistakesToAvoid.why: Deploying un-scanned emergency patches introduces critical CVE vulnerabilities and unpatched base OS exploit vectors.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting automated audit logging on sensitive secret reads and key vault decrypt requests
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without audit logs on secret access, security teams cannot determine which microservices or credentials were accessed during a security breach.

title: Intermittent DNS Resolution Failures During Azure Deployment: Diagnostic Runbook
summary: Root cause analysis and resolution runbook for intermittent DNS resolution timeouts during Azure application deployments.
question: During an Azure deployment, you receive intermittent DNS resolution issues. What can be the causes and how do you resolve them?
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Scenario 9
intro: Intermittent DNS failures in Azure usually stem from three architectural limits: hitting the Azure VM DNS resolution limit of 1024 packets per second (pps), CoreDNS connection throttling inside AKS, missing or improperly linked Azure Private DNS zones across VNets, or single-point-of-failure custom DNS virtual appliances.

steps.title: Diagnose the 1024 PPS Azure WireServer DNS Limit
steps.description: Every Azure VM interface has a hard limit of 1,024 UDP/TCP packets per second to Azure WireServer DNS (`168.63.129.16`). High-concurrency container clusters without local caching easily exceed this limit, causing Azure to drop subsequent DNS queries silently resulting in 5-second timeout retries.
steps.codeBlock:
# Check dropped DNS queries via Azure Network Watcher or VM metrics
# PromQL in AKS to check CoreDNS forward errors:
sum(rate(coredns_dns_request_duration_seconds_count[5m])) by (server)

steps.title: Deploy NodeLocal DNSCache in AKS
steps.description: Implement NodeLocal DNSCache as a DaemonSet. It runs a local DNS caching agent on every Kubernetes node listening on `169.254.20.10`, intercepting DNS requests before they leave the node. This eliminates UDP conntrack races and cuts WireServer requests by over 90%.
steps.codeBlock:
# Enable NodeLocal DNSCache in AKS cluster
az aks update -g rg-banking -n aks-prod --enable-node-local-dns

steps.title: Verify Azure Private DNS Zone VNet Link Configurations
steps.description: If resolving internal private endpoints (e.g. `privatelink.database.windows.net`), check whether the VNet containing the deploying VMs has an active Virtual Network Link attached to the Private DNS Zone. If auto-registration is overloaded or links are missing across peered VNets, resolution intermittently falls back to public IPs.
steps.codeBlock:
az network private-dns link vnet list \
  --zone-name "privatelink.database.windows.net" \
  --resource-group rg-dns

steps.title: Tune ndots and Single-Request-Options in resolv.conf
steps.description: By default, Linux `resolv.conf` has `ndots:5`, forcing the resolver to search multiple cluster search domains before resolving external hostnames. Optimize pod DNS configurations with `single-request-reopen` and reduced `ndots`.
steps.highlight: Architecture Fix: Always enable NodeLocal DNSCache on AKS and configure Azure Private DNS resolver rulesets across all peered hub-and-spoke VNets.

keyTakeaway: Intermittent Azure DNS resolution timeouts are primarily caused by hitting the Azure WireServer 1024 PPS limit or CoreDNS conntrack races. Resolve by enabling NodeLocal DNSCache and validating Private DNS VNet links.
elevatorPitch: Check if the workload exceeds Azure's 1,024 packets/second VM DNS WireServer ceiling.
Deploy NodeLocal DNSCache in AKS to handle DNS caching locally on every worker node.
Validate Azure Private DNS Zone VNet links across hub-and-spoke virtual networks.
Optimize pod resolv.conf options with single-request-reopen and lower ndots values.
