title: Application on AKS Experiences 10-Second Delays Every 15 Minutes: Root Cause Analysis
summary: Forensic root cause analysis workflow to track down predictable, periodic 10-second latency spikes occurring on a strict 15-minute cadence without code deployments.
question: A user reports 10-second delays every 15 minutes in an application running on AKS. No code changes happened. How would you begin root cause analysis?
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Technical Deep Dive
intro: When latency spikes occur on a strict, mathematical interval (e.g. exactly every 15 minutes), the root cause is virtually guaranteed to be a scheduled periodic background task: a Kubernetes CronJob executing on the same node, an internal application cache flush/warmup routine, periodic JVM major garbage collection, or cloud storage snapshotting.

steps.title: Correlate Latency Spikes with Cluster CronJobs & DaemonSets
steps.description: Inspect Kubernetes scheduled workloads. Search for any CronJob or batch task running with the schedule `*/15 * * * *` in any namespace on the cluster. A scheduled database backup or cache warm-up running on the same worker node can saturate node disk I/O or CPU bandwidth.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get cronjobs -A
# Look for SCHEDULE column matching: */15 * * * * or 0,15,30,45 * * * *

steps.title: Analyze Internal Application Background Threads & Cache Eviction
steps.description: If no external CronJob exists, inspect the application's internal scheduler (e.g. `@Scheduled(cron = '0 */15 * * * *')` in Spring Boot, Celery beat, or Go ticker). Applications frequently refresh an in-memory cache every 15 minutes; if the refresh runs synchronously with a global read-write lock, all user threads freeze for 10 seconds.
steps.codeBlock:
# Capture thread dump right during the 15-minute spike
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- jstack <pid> | grep -E 'locked|waiting to lock'

steps.title: Inspect Node-Level I/O Bursting & EBS/Managed Disk Credits
steps.description: Check Azure Managed Disk throttling metrics in Azure Monitor. If the AKS node uses standard burstable SSDs (P10/P20) and a periodic log rotation or OS indexing job exhausts IOPS burst tokens, disk operations stall until credits replenish.
steps.codeBlock:
# Check node disk I/O wait times
kubectl exec -it <debug-node> -- iostat -xz 1 10
# High %iowait and %util indicate disk starvation

steps.title: Correlate Downstream Database & External API Scheduled Syncs
steps.description: Query database slow query logs for queries executing every 15 minutes. Heavy analytical batch queries holding table-level shared locks will cause fast transaction queries to queue behind them.

keyTakeaway: A strict 15-minute latency cadence points directly to scheduled jobs: CronJobs on the node, internal cache eviction holding synchronized locks, disk IOPS burst credit exhaustion, or periodic DB batch locks.
elevatorPitch: Search for cluster CronJobs configured with schedule */15 * * * *.
Inspect application source code for internal scheduled cache-refresh routines holding write locks.
Monitor Azure Managed Disk IOPS and credit throttling metrics on the node hosting the pod.
Check database slow query logs for periodic analytical queries locking active transaction tables.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Injecting high-cardinality label dimensions (such as user IDs or request UUIDs) into Prometheus metrics when configuring Application Experiences Second
mistakesToAvoid.why: High-cardinality label values cause exponential time-series growth, consuming gigabytes of TSDB memory and crashing Prometheus servers.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Evaluating application performance solely through arithmetic mean or p50 latency while ignoring tail latency (p99) when configuring Application Experiences Second
mistakesToAvoid.why: Averages hide catastrophic tail latency outages where 1% of high-value user transactions suffer severe timeouts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to inject and extract W3C distributed trace context across message brokers and RPC calls when configuring Application Experiences Second
mistakesToAvoid.why: Breaking distributed trace context propagation fragments end-to-end transaction waterfalls into disconnected, un-correlatable trace segments.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Configuring alert rule evaluation intervals without sufficient duration damping (for: 5m), inducing alert flap when configuring Application Experiences Second
mistakesToAvoid.why: Instant alerts triggered by transient sub-second CPU or latency blips page on-call engineers unnecessarily and dilute response urgency.

title: Jenkins Build Jobs Randomly Failing at Artifact Upload Step: Network & Storage Triage
summary: Triage runbook for diagnosing intermittent failures during artifact uploads (Nexus, Artifactory, S3) from Jenkins pipeline agents.
question: Jenkins jobs are randomly failing at the artifact upload step. What layers would you check?
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Scenario 11
intro: When artifact uploads fail intermittently in enterprise CI/CD pipelines, the build itself succeeded, but the network transfer of heavy multi-hundred-megabyte binaries (JARs, tarballs, container layers) breaks. I isolate the failure across four distinct layers: Agent Disk/Memory, Network Egress & NAT timeouts, Artifact Repository HTTP quotas, and Storage Backend contention.

steps.title: Layer 1: Inspect Jenkins Agent Local Ephemeral Disk & Inodes
steps.description: Check whether the ephemeral agent node ran out of disk space or inodes during the build. Upload tools often stage tarball archives in `/tmp` before transmitting; if the agent disk hits 100%, the process throws an unhandled I/O exception.
steps.codeBlock:
df -h /tmp
df -i /tmp

steps.title: Layer 2: Network Firewalls, Idle Timeouts & MTU Fragmentation
steps.description: Examine firewall and load balancer logs between Jenkins agents and JFrog Artifactory / Sonatype Nexus. If uploading a 2 GB file over a slow network takes 10 minutes, intermediate stateful firewalls or reverse proxies with an idle timeout of 300s will drop the TCP session midway with 'Connection reset by peer'.
steps.codeBlock:
# Test sustained bandwidth and latency from agent to repository
curl -w "@curl-format.txt" -T large-test-file.bin -u user:pass https://nexus.internal/repo/

steps.title: Layer 3: Artifact Repository Server Thread Pool & Connection Limits
steps.description: Inspect the Artifactory/Nexus server metrics. If multiple concurrent Jenkins jobs complete simultaneously and attempt parallel uploads, the repository's HTTP server (NGINX/Tomcat) exhausts its max worker threads, returning HTTP 503 or 429.
steps.highlight: Repository Best Practice: Increase client connection timeouts and implement automated retry loops with exponential backoff on artifact upload steps.

steps.title: Layer 4: Storage Backend Quotas & IAM Token Expiry
steps.description: Check if the underlying artifact storage backend (S3 bucket or Azure Blob) is hitting rate limits or if the temporary cloud IAM role credential (AWS STS / Azure OIDC token) expired during a long-running build right before the upload step began.

keyTakeaway: Intermittent artifact upload drops are caused by reverse proxy idle timeouts dropping long TCP connections, Artifactory thread pool saturation, or agent /tmp disk exhaustion.
elevatorPitch: Check reverse proxy (NGINX/ALB) client_max_body_size and idle connection timeout settings.
Verify Jenkins ephemeral agent /tmp disk space and inode availability.
Inspect Artifactory/Nexus thread pool saturation and storage backend quotas under peak build traffic.
Configure upload clients with automated retry mechanisms and exponential backoff.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Promoting application releases to production without an automated, canary-validated rollback mechanism when configuring Jenkins Build Jobs
mistakesToAvoid.why: Pipelines that lack automated rollback mechanisms force engineering teams to scramble manual hotfixes during severe production regressions.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running concurrent deployment pipeline jobs without stage mutex locking on shared target environments when configuring Jenkins Build Jobs
mistakesToAvoid.why: Concurrent pipeline runs on the same environment race to apply state changes, causing out-of-order commits and unpredictable deployment state.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting dependency lockfiles (package-lock.json, go.sum, Cargo.lock) from continuous integration builds when configuring Jenkins Build Jobs
mistakesToAvoid.why: Omitting lockfiles allows upstream package updates to break builds unpredictably without any changes to application codebase.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to define dynamic cache invalidation keys for CI package managers and layer caches when configuring Jenkins Build Jobs
mistakesToAvoid.why: Stale build caches mask underlying dependency incompatibilities or pull outdated libraries, while un-cached runs slow feedback loops.

title: Designing an Automated Rollback Strategy in Kubernetes for Failed Production Deployments
summary: Architecture blueprint for designing metric-driven automated rollback pipelines in Kubernetes using Argo Rollouts, Prometheus analysis templates, and deployment health gates.
question: How would you set up an automated rollback strategy in Kubernetes for failed deployments?
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Scenario 12
intro: Relying on human engineers to manually run 'kubectl rollout undo' during an outage is too slow for tier-1 financial platforms. I architect automated rollback pipelines using Argo Rollouts combined with Prometheus AnalysisTemplates to evaluate real-time error rates and latency metrics, automatically triggering sub-minute rollbacks if SLI thresholds are breached.

steps.title: Adopt Progressive Delivery Controller (Argo Rollouts)
steps.description: Replace standard Kubernetes `Deployment` manifests with `Rollout` custom resources. Define structured canary steps (e.g. 10% traffic for 5 minutes, then 30%, then 100%) to restrict the failure blast radius.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: payment-engine
spec:
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
      - setWeight: 10
      - pause: { duration: 3m }
      - analysis:
          templates:
          - templateName: success-rate-metric
      - setWeight: 50
      - pause: { duration: 5m }
      - setWeight: 100

steps.title: Define Metric-Driven Prometheus AnalysisTemplates
steps.description: Configure automated metric queries that execute continuously during the rollout. If HTTP 5xx error rate exceeds 1% or p99 latency spikes above 500ms, the analysis job marks the deployment as Failed, halting traffic progression instantly.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: success-rate-metric
spec:
  metrics:
  - name: success-rate
    interval: 30s
    failureLimit: 2
    successCondition: result[0] >= 0.99
    provider:
      prometheus:
        address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
        query: |
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="payment-engine",status!~"5.*"}[1m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="payment-engine"}[1m]))

steps.title: Automate Instant Traffic Cutback & GitOps Reversion
steps.description: When the AnalysisTemplate fails, Argo Rollouts immediately routes 100% of user traffic back to the stable ReplicaSet via Ingress/Service mesh within seconds. Simultaneously, an event webhook notifies GitHub/GitLab to create an automated revert commit on the GitOps repository.

steps.title: Configure CrashLoop & Liveness Automated Fallbacks
steps.description: If pods crash immediately (`CrashLoopBackOff` or failed liveness probes), Kubernetes native `progressDeadlineSeconds` aborts rollout progression and notifies alerting channels.
steps.highlight: Platform Rule: Automated rollbacks must be metric-driven (Prometheus SLIs) rather than strictly process-driven to catch silent business logic regressions.

keyTakeaway: Implement automated rollbacks using Argo Rollouts with Prometheus AnalysisTemplates. Automatically divert traffic back to stable when error rates exceed 1% and trigger automated GitOps commit reversions.
elevatorPitch: Use Argo Rollouts instead of standard Deployments to manage granular canary traffic shifts.
Bind Prometheus AnalysisTemplates that continuously evaluate 5xx error rates and p99 latency.
Configure automatic aborts that shift traffic back to stable within seconds upon threshold breach.
Dispatch automated webhooks to Git to revert the deployment commit and maintain GitOps state integrity.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Over-granting cluster-admin permissions to pod ServiceAccounts instead of scoping namespace Roles when configuring Designing Automated Rollback
mistakesToAvoid.why: Over-granting cluster-wide permissions violates least-privilege principles and allows compromised pods to escalate privileges across namespaces.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Referencing mutable latest container tags across production Kubernetes Deployment specs when configuring Designing Automated Rollback
mistakesToAvoid.why: Deployments referencing `:latest` risk inconsistent versions across replica pods and break deterministic rollback capabilities.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting pod readiness probes, causing traffic to hit uninitialized application containers when configuring Designing Automated Rollback
mistakesToAvoid.why: Readiness probes gate traffic delivery; missing probes cause Kubernetes to route user requests to pods before dependencies or caches are loaded.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Executing diagnostic triage without analyzing chronological cluster events and describe outputs when configuring Designing Automated Rollback
mistakesToAvoid.why: Cluster events provide sequential timestamps of scheduler decisions, probe failures, and image pull timeouts essential for rapid root-cause isolation.

title: Cost-Optimized Cloud Architecture for Nightly Batch Reporting App with 3-Year Log Retention
summary: Design an enterprise cloud architecture for an internal reporting workload that runs exclusively once per night and must retain compliance logs for 3 years at lowest cost.
question: Design a cost-optimized cloud architecture for an internal reporting app that runs every night and stores logs for 3 years.
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Technical Deep Dive
intro: An internal reporting application that runs once per night has a utilization duty cycle of roughly 4-8% (1-2 hours per 24 hours). Running persistent VMs or databases is a huge waste of money. I design a 100% serverless / ephemeral architecture utilizing Spot instances, auto-pausing compute, and automated tiered object storage lifecycle rules.

steps.title: Ephemeral Compute: Spot Instances / Serverless Batch
steps.description: Do not run continuous virtual machines. Use AWS Batch or Azure Container Instances (ACI) / Azure Functions running on Spot compute instances (up to 80-90% discount). A scheduled cloud timer (AWS EventBridge / Azure Logic Apps) triggers the container job at 2:00 AM; the compute spins down to exactly $0.00 upon job completion.

steps.title: Database Optimization: Serverless Auto-Pausing Engine
steps.description: If a relational database is required, deploy Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 or Azure SQL Database Serverless with auto-pause enabled (`min_capacity = 0`). The database automatically sleeps when idle and resumes only during the nightly reporting execution window.
steps.highlight: FinOps Savings: Ephemeral Spot compute + auto-pausing Serverless database reduces monthly infrastructure costs by over 92% compared to 24/7 dedicated instances.

steps.title: Tiered Log Storage: S3 Glacier Deep Archive / Azure Archive Storage
steps.description: Because logs are required for 3-year compliance and rarely queried, stream raw compressed JSON/Parquet logs directly to object storage with an aggressive lifecycle transition policy: - Days 1-30: Standard S3 / Blob Storage (fast audit access if immediate issues arise). - Day 31: Transition to Glacier Flexible / Cold Tier. - Day 90 to Year 3: Transition to S3 Glacier Deep Archive ($0.00099 per GB/month) or Azure Archive Storage. - Day 1096: Automated deletion rule.

steps.title: Compliance & Immutability (WORM Lock)
steps.description: Enable S3 Object Lock or Azure Immutable Blob Storage in Compliance Mode to guarantee that logs cannot be deleted or overwritten by anyone (including root accounts) for the mandatory 3-year statutory audit period.

keyTakeaway: Run nightly batch compute on ephemeral Spot instances (AWS Batch/ACI) triggered by EventBridge. Store compliance logs using S3 Glacier Deep Archive lifecycle rules with Object Lock for 95% storage savings.
elevatorPitch: Use AWS Batch or Azure Container Instances backed by Spot instances that terminate immediately upon completion.
Deploy serverless auto-pausing databases that sleep during the daytime.
Transition logs to S3 Glacier Deep Archive or Azure Archive storage after 30 days to slash storage bills to under $1/TB/month.
Enforce WORM (Write Once, Read Many) compliance locking to meet strict banking audit mandates.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Engineering bespoke in-house developer tools instead of adopting standardized platform Golden Paths when configuring Cost Optimized Nightly
mistakesToAvoid.why: Bespoke internal tools create long-term maintenance debt and fragmented workflows, whereas standardized Golden Paths accelerate delivery.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Overlooking infrastructure cost visibility and FinOps allocation tagging across multi-tenant environments when configuring Cost Optimized Nightly
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without granular resource tagging, engineering organizations cannot attribute cloud infrastructure costs to specific teams or business units.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to define explicit Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and Error Budgets to balance feature velocity with reliability when configuring Cost Optimized Nightly
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without agreed SLOs, engineering and product teams lack an objective data-driven framework to prioritize technical debt over new features.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Neglecting automated continuous drift detection between declarative configuration and deployed cloud state when configuring Cost Optimized Nightly
mistakesToAvoid.why: Unmanaged drift accumulates over time, causing future automated deployments to fail or overwrite emergency manual adjustments.

title: Zero-Downtime Database Migrations in Distributed Applications: Expand/Contract Pattern
summary: Step-by-step architectural execution of the Expand and Contract pattern to migrate database schemas across distributed microservices with zero downtime.
question: How do you handle zero-downtime database migrations in a distributed application?
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Scenario 14
intro: In distributed microservices, running synchronous schema migrations (like renaming columns or adding NOT NULL constraints) during deployments breaks active service replicas. Zero-downtime database migrations mandate the Expand and Contract (Parallel Change) pattern across multiple decoupled deployment phases so that both old and new application versions function simultaneously.

steps.title: Phase 1: Expand (Additive Non-Breaking Schema Change)
steps.description: Add new columns or tables without destructive constraints. Never rename a column directly. If transitioning from `phone` to `phone_number`, add `phone_number` as a nullable column. Run this migration in CI before deploying code.
steps.codeBlock:
-- Step 1: Add new column safely
ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN phone_number VARCHAR(32);

steps.title: Phase 2: Dual-Writing Application Release
steps.description: Deploy Application Version 2.0. The code writes new data to BOTH `phone` and `phone_number`, but continues reading from `phone`. If a rollback to Version 1.0 is required, Version 1.0 remains 100% operational because `phone` is still updated.

steps.title: Phase 3: Backfill Historical Data in Batches
steps.description: Run an asynchronous background worker to copy historical values from `phone` to `phone_number`. Execute backfills in small indexed batches (e.g. 5,000 rows with sleep intervals) to prevent table locking or replication lag.
steps.codeBlock:
-- Batch backfill query with sleep to avoid locks
UPDATE customers 
SET phone_number = phone 
WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 5000 AND phone_number IS NULL;

steps.title: Phase 4 & 5: Switch Read Traffic & Contract (Deprecate Old Column)
steps.description: Deploy Application Version 2.1 to read exclusively from `phone_number`. Add NOT NULL constraints using `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` (which avoids table locks in PostgreSQL). In a subsequent sprint, drop the legacy `phone` column once zero services query it.
steps.highlight: Golden Rule: Never bundle a breaking database schema migration and an application code release in the same deployment step.

keyTakeaway: Execute database migrations using the Expand and Contract pattern across separate releases: 1) Add nullable column, 2) Dual-write in code, 3) Backfill historical rows in batches, 4) Switch reads, 5) Drop old column.
elevatorPitch: Apply the Expand-Contract pattern to ensure database backward compatibility at all times.
Make all database schema additions non-breaking (nullable columns without defaults).
Deploy dual-writing application versions so both legacy and modern replicas remain functional.
Backfill historical records in rate-limited background batches before deprecating old columns.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Applying exclusive-lock DDL table migrations on live production databases during peak traffic windows when configuring Zero Downtime Database
mistakesToAvoid.why: DDL migrations that acquire an exclusive table lock block all concurrent queries, queuing connections until the database connection pool exhausts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Allowing high-frequency queries to trigger full table scans without appropriate composite indexing when configuring Zero Downtime Database
mistakesToAvoid.why: Sequential table scans saturate database CPU and disk I/O, evicting frequently queried data from the buffer cache and causing cascading timeouts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Disabling referential integrity constraints during bulk ETL imports without post-import consistency validation when configuring Zero Downtime Database
mistakesToAvoid.why: Skipping relational consistency checks risks introducing orphaned records and referential integrity violations into production tables.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on database snapshot backups that have never been verified through automated restoration drills when configuring Zero Downtime Database
mistakesToAvoid.why: Backups that have never been tested with automated restore verification frequently fail during real disaster recovery scenarios.

title: Disaster Recovery Strategy for Stateful Applications Running on Containers
summary: Comprehensive disaster recovery framework for stateful containerized applications running on Kubernetes, achieving strict RTO and RPO targets across cloud regions.
question: What’s your approach to disaster recovery for stateful applications running on containers?
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Technical Deep Dive
intro: Containerized stateful applications (PostgreSQL, Kafka, Elasticsearch) cannot be treated like stateless web pods. A disaster recovery strategy requires decoupling data persistence from ephemeral compute, establishing continuous cross-region asynchronous storage replication, and utilizing Kubernetes-native backup controllers like Velero to orchestrate automated cluster restoration.

steps.title: Decouple Heavy State from Kubernetes Compute Where Feasible
steps.description: Evaluate workload state requirements. For primary relational databases, prefer managed cloud engines with native cross-region replication (AWS Aurora Global Database / Azure SQL Auto-Failover Groups) over running self-managed monolithic databases on EBS/PVCs.
steps.highlight: Architectural Principle: If state can be externalized to managed multi-region services, do it. Reserve StatefulSets for distributed engines designed for container clustering (Kafka, CockroachDB, Cassandra).

steps.title: CSI Volume Snapshot Replication & Velero Automation
steps.description: For workloads requiring persistent volumes (PVCs), implement the Kubernetes Container Storage Interface (CSI) Snapshotter coupled with Velero. Take hourly volume snapshots and sync metadata manifests to cross-region S3/Blob storage.
steps.codeBlock:
# Velero scheduled backup with CSI volume snapshotting
velero schedule create hourly-stateful-backup \
  --schedule="0 * * * *" \
  --include-namespaces production \
  --snapshot-volumes \
  --volume-snapshot-locations default

steps.title: Active-Passive Warm Standby Cluster Configuration
steps.description: Maintain a warm standby Kubernetes cluster in a secondary cloud region. Use GitOps (ArgoCD) to maintain identical manifests across both clusters. In disaster declaration, Velero restores PVC volume snapshots into the secondary cluster and ArgoCD scales StatefulSets from 0 to target replicas.

steps.title: Execute Automated Failover Drills & RPO/RTO Validation
steps.description: Conduct quarterly automated disaster recovery drills. Validate that recovery point objectives (RPO < 15 minutes) and recovery time objectives (RTO < 30 minutes) are met without data corruption.

keyTakeaway: Manage container state by externalizing to managed databases where possible, automating CSI snapshots via Velero into secondary regions, and maintaining warm standby clusters orchestrated by GitOps.
elevatorPitch: Externalize relational data to managed multi-region cloud services (Aurora Global / Azure SQL Failover Groups).
Use CSI volume snapshots and Velero to replicate PersistentVolume data and cluster manifests to secondary regions.
Maintain a warm standby Kubernetes cluster with scaled-to-zero replicas via ArgoCD.
Conduct quarterly automated failover fire drills to strictly validate RTO and RPO metrics.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Over-granting cluster-admin permissions to pod ServiceAccounts instead of scoping namespace Roles
mistakesToAvoid.why: Over-granting cluster-wide permissions violates least-privilege principles and allows compromised pods to escalate privileges across namespaces.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Referencing mutable latest container tags across production Kubernetes Deployment specs
mistakesToAvoid.why: Deployments referencing `:latest` risk inconsistent versions across replica pods and break deterministic rollback capabilities.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting pod readiness probes, causing traffic to hit uninitialized application containers
mistakesToAvoid.why: Readiness probes gate traffic delivery; missing probes cause Kubernetes to route user requests to pods before dependencies or caches are loaded.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Executing diagnostic triage without analyzing chronological cluster events and describe outputs in jpmorgan-q015-disaster-recovery-stateful-apps-containers
mistakesToAvoid.why: Cluster events provide sequential timestamps of scheduler decisions, probe failures, and image pull timeouts essential for rapid root-cause isolation.

title: Azure Function Being Throttled: Detection, Scaling Limits, and Mitigation Strategies
summary: Root cause detection and architectural remediation runbook for resolving concurrency throttling and cold-start failures on Azure Functions under production load.
question: An Azure function is being throttled. How will you detect and fix it?
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Scenario 16
intro: Azure Functions throttling occurs when execution requests exceed the compute plan's scale limits, when downstream databases exhaust connection pools under rapid fan-out, or when storage account IOPS limits are exceeded by the Function Scale Controller. I troubleshoot by querying Application Insights metrics and adjusting plan configurations.

steps.title: Detect Throttling Signatures in Application Insights
steps.description: Query Azure Application Insights and Azure Monitor for HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests), HTTP 503 (Service Unavailable), or event queue lag. Inspect the `FunctionExecutionCount` and `ThrottledCount` metrics.
steps.codeBlock:
# Kusto (KQL) Query to identify Function Throttling
requests
| where resultCode in ("429", "503")
| summarize count() by bin(timestamp, 5m), resultCode, operation_Name
| order by timestamp desc

steps.title: Identify Scale Controller Bottlenecks & Consumption Limits
steps.description: On the standard Consumption Plan, Azure Functions scale up to a maximum of 200 instances, but the Scale Controller adds new instances incrementally (e.g. 1 instance every few seconds). A sudden spike of 20,000 requests immediately overwhelms instances before scaling completes.
steps.highlight: Plan Reality: Consumption plans cannot handle sudden, steep spikes due to cold-starts and progressive Scale Controller rate limits.

steps.title: Migrate to Elastic Premium Plan or Set Pre-Warmed Instances
steps.description: Upgrade critical production functions to the Azure Functions Elastic Premium Plan. Elastic Premium provides pre-warmed instances to eliminate cold starts, unlimited compute scale, and VNet integration.
steps.codeBlock:
# Update Azure Function App to Premium plan with minimum pre-warmed instances
az functionapp plan update \
  --name plan-banking-premium \
  --resource-group rg-banking \
  --min-instances 5 \
  --max-instances 50

steps.title: Throttle Concurrency & Decouple via Message Buffers
steps.description: If downstream databases are choking, throttle the function's maximum concurrency in `host.json` (`maxConcurrentRequests`) and buffer incoming requests through Azure Service Bus queues or Event Hubs to flatten traffic bursts.

keyTakeaway: Detect Azure Function throttling via KQL queries in Application Insights for 429/503 errors. Fix by migrating to Elastic Premium with pre-warmed instances and buffering traffic through Service Bus queues.
elevatorPitch: Query Application Insights with KQL to track HTTP 429/503 codes and scale controller delays.
Upgrade from Consumption Plan to Elastic Premium to eliminate cold starts and scale bottlenecks.
Configure pre-warmed instances to instantly absorb burst traffic.
Buffer bursty traffic using Azure Service Bus queues to protect downstream databases from connection exhaustion.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Purging compromised IAM user credentials immediately prior to querying CloudTrail forensic event logs when configuring Azure Function Throttled
mistakesToAvoid.why: Deactivating a compromised key prevents abuse while preserving identity records for CloudTrail forensic queries to assess blast radius.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Conflating local IAM Permissions Boundaries with organizational Service Control Policies (SCPs) when configuring Azure Function Throttled
mistakesToAvoid.why: SCPs define maximum permission guards at the AWS Organization level across accounts, whereas permission boundaries limit delegate privileges within a single account.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Deploying single-AZ cloud infrastructure for production workloads without multi-AZ failover resilience when configuring Azure Function Throttled
mistakesToAvoid.why: Availability Zone hardware failures or localized network partitions cause complete service downtime when resources are not distributed across >=2 AZs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Jumping straight to SSH or instance restarts without reviewing CloudWatch metrics and AWS Systems Manager logs when configuring Azure Function Throttled
mistakesToAvoid.why: Senior SREs triage control plane and hypervisor metrics via CloudWatch and SSM Session Manager before executing invasive host-level actions.

title: Blue/Green Deployment Architecture With Instant Rollback on Azure Using Terraform and Pipelines
summary: Production blueprint for implementing Blue/Green zero-downtime deployments with instant traffic rollback on Azure using Terraform, App Service deployment slots, and Azure DevOps.
question: Define a plan for blue/green deployment with rollback on Azure using Terraform and pipelines.
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Scenario 17
intro: Blue/Green deployment eliminates downtime by maintaining two identical production environments: Blue (active live traffic) and Green (staging/idle). Using Terraform to declare infrastructure and Azure App Service Deployment Slots or Azure Front Door to swap traffic, we achieve instant cutovers and sub-second rollbacks without redeploying code.

steps.title: Declare Blue and Green Slots with Sticky Settings in Terraform
steps.description: Provision Azure App Service with a dedicated `staging` slot alongside `production`. Crucially, configure database connection strings and environment flags as `sticky_settings` so that when slots swap, configuration stays bound to the slot.

steps.title: CI/CD Pipeline Deploys to Staging (Green) & Runs Warmup Probes
steps.description: The Azure DevOps pipeline packages the build artifact and deploys it exclusively to the Green (`staging`) slot. Execute automated smoke tests and verify warm-up health checks while Blue continues handling 100% of public traffic.
steps.codeBlock:
# Azure DevOps Pipeline Step
- task: AzureWebAppDeployment@4
  inputs:
    azureSubscription: 'Azure-OIDC'
    appName: 'app-prod-banking'
    deployToSlotOrASE: true
    slotName: 'staging'
    package: '$(Pipeline.Workspace)/**/*.zip'

steps.title: Zero-Downtime Slot Swap (Virtual IP Cutover)
steps.description: Trigger an Azure slot swap. Azure manages the cutover seamlessly at the reverse-proxy routing layer by redirecting DNS/VIP bindings: Green becomes Production and Blue becomes Staging with zero dropped TCP connections.
steps.codeBlock:
- task: AzureAppServiceManage@0
  inputs:
    azureSubscription: 'Azure-OIDC'
    Action: 'Swap Slots'
    WebAppName: 'app-prod-banking'
    ResourceGroupName: 'rg-banking'
    SourceSlot: 'staging'
    SwapWithProduction: true

steps.title: Instant Sub-Second Rollback Protocol
steps.description: If post-swap telemetry reveals error spikes, trigger an immediate second slot swap. Because the previous stable Blue code is still alive in the staging slot, swapping back restores stability instantly without building or deploying.
steps.highlight: Production Value: Instant rollback takes under 10 seconds because the previous version is already warm and running in the alternate slot.

keyTakeaway: Provision App Service staging slots and sticky connection strings in Terraform. Deploy to Green, run smoke tests, perform an automated slot swap in the pipeline, and reserve the previous slot for instant rollback.
elevatorPitch: Use Terraform to declare primary and staging slots with sticky configuration parameters.
Deploy new releases into the staging slot and execute automated health checks.
Execute an Azure slot swap to redirect production traffic with zero downtime.
Execute an instant reverse slot swap if error rates spike post-cutover.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Executing Terraform applies without inspecting '# forces replacement' warnings in plan output when configuring Blue/Green Deployment Instant
mistakesToAvoid.why: Attributes that force resource replacement destroy and recreate critical infrastructure (databases, load balancers), inducing unannounced production outages.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting remote state locking mechanisms (DynamoDB or backend native locks) for shared state files when configuring Blue/Green Deployment Instant
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without state locking, concurrent CI/CD pipeline executions or team applies create race conditions that corrupt the state file.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Structuring entire enterprise cloud footprints into a single monolithic Terraform root module when configuring Blue/Green Deployment Instant
mistakesToAvoid.why: Monolithic state files slow plan execution dramatically, increase blast radius during failed applies, and create severe pipeline locking contention.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Unpinned provider versions automatically download breaking major upgrades during CI runs, introducing unexpected schema validation failures.

title: End-to-End SLA Monitoring Across Multi-Service Payments Pipelines: SLIs, SLOs & Distributed Tracing
summary: Design an end-to-end SLA and error budget monitoring architecture for a mission-critical multi-hop payments processing pipeline.
question: How would you monitor end-to-end SLA for services involved in a payments pipeline?
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Technical Deep Dive
intro: In a payments pipeline (Auth -> Fraud Check -> Ledger Debit -> Settlement -> Notification), monitoring individual microservice metrics in isolation is inadequate. An SLA breach occurs if the composite end-to-end transaction duration exceeds contractual boundaries or fails silently mid-flight. I design an end-to-end monitoring architecture based on distributed trace correlation, composite Service Level Indicators (SLIs), and synthetic transactions.

steps.title: Define Composite Multi-Hop Service Level Indicators (SLIs)
steps.description: Establish the core SLIs for the payments pipeline: - Availability SLI: `Successful Payments (HTTP 200 / Approved) / Total Initiated Payments` >= 99.99%. - Latency SLI: `p99 End-to-End Payment Duration (from client request to bank confirmation)` < 1,500ms. - Freshness SLI: Asynchronous settlement event queue lag < 5 seconds.

steps.title: Propagate Distributed Trace Context via OpenTelemetry (W3C TraceContext)
steps.description: Enforce W3C `traceparent` context propagation across all microservices and asynchronous message queues (Kafka / SQS). Every payment carries a unique `payment_id` and `trace_id` span attribute, enabling instant lookup of any degraded transaction.
steps.codeBlock:
# OpenTelemetry baggage propagation in HTTP headers
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
tracestate: payment_id=pay_998124,tier=enterprise

steps.title: Multi-Window Multi-Burn-Rate Alerting on Error Budgets
steps.description: Implement Google SRE multi-window burn-rate alerts in Prometheus / Alertmanager. Trigger page alerts only when the rate of error budget consumption threatens the monthly SLA (e.g. burning 2% of the budget in 1 hour), eliminating false alarm pager fatigue.
steps.codeBlock:
# PromQL Multi-Burn-Rate Alert Rule
expr: |
  (sum(rate(payment_failures_total[1h])) / sum(rate(payment_attempts_total[1h])) > (14.4 * 0.0001))
  and
  (sum(rate(payment_failures_total[5m])) / sum(rate(payment_attempts_total[5m])) > (14.4 * 0.0001))
for: 2m
labels:
  severity: critical
  team: payments-sre

steps.title: Deploy Synthetic Payment Probes in Production
steps.description: Execute continuous synthetic end-to-end transactions every 60 seconds using test credit card numbers against internal banking mock targets to detect pipeline degradation before real customers are impacted.

keyTakeaway: Monitor payments pipelines by tracking composite end-to-end SLIs with OpenTelemetry trace context propagation across all microservices. Implement multi-window burn-rate alerts and synthetic transaction probes.
elevatorPitch: Define composite availability and latency SLIs spanning the entire multi-hop payment lifecycle.
Enforce OpenTelemetry W3C trace context propagation across HTTP services and Kafka queues.
Implement multi-window burn-rate alerting to track monthly error budgets and prevent alert fatigue.
Run continuous synthetic transactions to detect pipeline regressions before customers do.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Setting static resource threshold alerts (e.g., CPU > 80%) instead of tracking user-facing SLO breaches when addressing multi-service
mistakesToAvoid.why: Static infrastructure alerts induce alert fatigue and miss critical user-impacting outages where CPU is low but requests are failing.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Writing unstructured plaintext log output instead of JSON format with injected trace and span IDs
mistakesToAvoid.why: Unstructured logs cannot be efficiently indexed, filtered, or aggregated in log management systems like OpenSearch, Loki, or Datadog.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to monitor metric scrape failures and exporter agent disconnects during network partitions
mistakesToAvoid.why: When agents or exporters fail to scrape targets, missing metrics can be falsely interpreted by alerting rules as zero errors.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting trace sampling strategies and log retention tiers, driving unsustainable telemetry storage costs
mistakesToAvoid.why: Ingesting high-volume debug logs indefinitely in production scales cloud log storage costs exponentially without operational benefit.

title: Scaling Strategies for Compute-Intensive vs. I/O-Intensive Enterprise Workloads in Azure
summary: Architectural comparison and scaling strategies for compute-heavy workloads versus storage/network I/O-heavy workloads in Microsoft Azure.
question: Explain the difference in scaling strategies for compute-intensive vs I/O-intensive workloads in Azure.
roleContext: J.P. Morgan Senior DevOps Engineer Interview · Scenario 19
intro: Compute-intensive workloads (cryptographic hashing, algorithmic trading, machine learning inference) bottleneck on CPU cores and mathematical floating-point operations. In contrast, I/O-intensive workloads (database transactional engines, streaming Kafka brokers, log aggregators) bottleneck on storage IOPS, disk throughput, and network interface packet limits. Their scaling topologies must be fundamentally different.

steps.title: Compute-Intensive Scaling Strategy
steps.description: Key characteristics and optimizations: - Azure SKUs: Select Fsv2 or FX-series instances (high CPU-to-memory ratio, up to 3.7 GHz clock speed). - Autoscaling Metric: Scale horizontally using CPU utilization (`Percentage CPU > 70%`) or custom queue depth metrics. - Optimization: Run lightweight OS kernels, disable unnecessary background daemons, and pin threads to vCPUs via CPU core pinning (`isolcpus` / NUMA architecture).
steps.codeBlock:
# Azure VMSS Compute Autoscaling Rule based on CPU
az monitor autoscale-rule create \
  --resource-group rg-compute \
  --autoscale-name autoscale-algo-trading \
  --scale out 2 \
  --condition "Percentage CPU > 75 avg 5m"

steps.title: I/O-Intensive Scaling Strategy
steps.description: Key characteristics and optimizations: - Azure SKUs: Select Ebdsv5 or Lsv3-series instances (high memory-to-CPU ratio, up to 260,000 IOPS and local NVMe storage). - Autoscaling Metric: Never scale on CPU. Scale on storage IOPS consumption, disk queue depth, or network bandwidth saturation. - Disk Architecture: Enable Premium SSD v2 or Ultra Disk with disk bursting. Crucially, turn on Host Caching (Read-Only / Read-Write) to serve queries directly from the VM's RAM cache without consuming disk IOPS.
steps.highlight: Storage Trap: An I/O-intensive VM will freeze if it exceeds the VM's uncached disk throughput limit, even if the attached Premium SSD has thousands of available IOPS.

steps.title: Network I/O Scaling: Accelerated Networking
steps.description: For high packet-per-second workloads, enable Azure Accelerated Networking (SR-IOV bypasses the hypervisor host switch, slashing network latency to under 30 microseconds and eliminating packet drops).
steps.codeBlock:
# Enable Accelerated Networking on Azure NIC
az network nic update \
  --name nic-banking-db \
  --resource-group rg-banking \
  --accelerated-networking true

steps.title: Architectural Summary: Horizontal vs Vertical
steps.description: Compute-intensive tasks scale horizontally across cheap ephemeral instances with high elasticity. I/O-intensive workloads typically scale vertically (larger memory and local NVMe storage) or shard partitioned data horizontally across specialized stateful clusters.

keyTakeaway: Scale compute workloads horizontally on Fsv2 instances using CPU thresholds. Scale I/O workloads vertically or via NVMe Lsv3 instances using IOPS queue depth, Premium SSD v2, and Accelerated Networking.
elevatorPitch: Use Fsv2-series for compute-intensive apps; scale horizontally based on CPU metrics and queue depth.
Use Ebdsv5/Lsv3 NVMe series for I/O-intensive apps; scale based on disk queue depth and IOPS limits.
Enable Host Caching and Premium SSD v2 to maximize disk throughput.
Mandate Azure Accelerated Networking (SR-IOV) to bypass hypervisor network latency on high-throughput workloads.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Purging compromised IAM user credentials immediately prior to querying CloudTrail forensic event logs when configuring Scaling Strategies Compute
mistakesToAvoid.why: Deactivating a compromised key prevents abuse while preserving identity records for CloudTrail forensic queries to assess blast radius.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Conflating local IAM Permissions Boundaries with organizational Service Control Policies (SCPs) when configuring Scaling Strategies Compute
mistakesToAvoid.why: SCPs define maximum permission guards at the AWS Organization level across accounts, whereas permission boundaries limit delegate privileges within a single account.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Deploying single-AZ cloud infrastructure for production workloads without multi-AZ failover resilience when configuring Scaling Strategies Compute
mistakesToAvoid.why: Availability Zone hardware failures or localized network partitions cause complete service downtime when resources are not distributed across >=2 AZs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Jumping straight to SSH or instance restarts without reviewing CloudWatch metrics and AWS Systems Manager logs when configuring Scaling Strategies Compute
mistakesToAvoid.why: Senior SREs triage control plane and hypervisor metrics via CloudWatch and SSM Session Manager before executing invasive host-level actions.

title: EC2 Intermittent Unresponsiveness Between 2 PM and 5 PM: High Queue Length With Normal CPU and Memory
summary: Deep troubleshooting runbook for an EC2 instance that becomes unresponsive during specific afternoon hours with normal CPU/memory metrics but rising disk queue length.
question: Assume an EC2 instance becomes intermittently unresponsive between 2 PM and 5 PM IST. When you check disk, CPU, and memory utilization, everything appears normal, but the system queue length is increasing. How would you troubleshoot and resolve this issue?
intro: When an EC2 instance experiences increasing system queue length (run queue or disk I/O queue) while CPU and RAM utilization appear normal, the operating system threads are blocked in an uninterruptible sleep state (`D` state in Linux). This indicates that processes are waiting on storage I/O, EBS burst balance exhaustion, network bandwidth throttling, or hypervisor CPU credit exhaustion.

steps.title: Correlate with EBS IOPS & Throughput Burst Balance
steps.description: Check Amazon CloudWatch metrics for the attached EBS volumes (`VolumeQueueLength`, `BurstBalance`, `VolumeReadOps`, `VolumeWriteOps`). If using `gp2` volumes, burst credits may deplete precisely between 2 PM and 5 PM due to an afternoon batch process, throttling throughput down to baseline and causing I/O requests to queue up indefinitely.
steps.codeBlock:
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics \
  --namespace AWS/EBS \
  --metric-name BurstBalance \
  --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --start-time 2026-10-06T08:00:00Z \
  --end-time 2026-10-06T12:00:00Z \
  --period 300 \
  --statistics Average

steps.title: Inspect Instance-Level EBS Bandwidth Throttling
steps.description: Every EC2 instance type (e.g. `t3.medium`, `m5.large`) has a maximum EBS-optimized bandwidth limit separate from the volume limit. If the instance hits `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%` limits in CloudWatch, disk operations stall even if the gp3 volume itself is within limits.
steps.codeBlock:
# On the Linux EC2 instance:
iostat -xz 1 10
# High await (e.g. >50ms) and high %util with low CPU indicates disk bottleneck

steps.title: Identify Uninterruptible Sleep (D-State) Processes
steps.description: Run `ps -eo state,pid,cmd | grep '^D'` during the 2 PM - 5 PM window. This displays processes waiting on kernel disk locks, NFS mounts, or network sockets.
steps.codeBlock:
ps -eo state,pid,user,cmd | awk '$1 ~ /D/ {print $0}'
# Inspect what file the process is blocked on:
cat /proc/<pid>/stack

steps.title: Migrate to gp3 / Provisioned IOPS & Upgrade Instance
steps.description: Upgrade the volume from `gp2` to `gp3` (which provides dedicated baseline 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s with no burst balance depletion) and resize the EC2 instance to a higher EBS-optimized bandwidth tier.
steps.highlight: Production Fix: Migrate legacy gp2 volumes to gp3 immediately. gp3 provides guaranteed baseline IOPS without relying on burst credit balances.

keyTakeaway: Normal CPU and RAM with rising queue length indicates threads blocked in uninterruptible disk I/O sleep (D state). Check EBS BurstBalance and instance-level EBS bandwidth throttling, and migrate to gp3.
elevatorPitch: Check CloudWatch VolumeQueueLength and BurstBalance metrics to confirm EBS I/O throttling.
Run iostat -xz and inspect D-state processes (ps -eo state,pid,cmd) on the Linux host.
Verify instance-level EBS-optimized bandwidth saturation.
Migrate from gp2 to gp3 to obtain consistent baseline IOPS and throughput without credit exhaustion.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Subscribing an Amazon SQS queue to an SNS topic without attaching an explicit queue access policy when configuring Intermittent Unresponsiveness High
mistakesToAvoid.why: SNS lacks permission to write to SQS by default; without an IAM resource policy granting `sqs:SendMessage` to the topic ARN, messages drop silently.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Confusing standard SQS queues with FIFO queues regarding strict ordering and deduplication when configuring Intermittent Unresponsiveness High
mistakesToAvoid.why: Standard SQS provides at-least-once delivery with best-effort ordering; strict FIFO ordering requires `MessageGroupId` and deduplication IDs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using short polling instead of SQS long polling (`WaitTimeSeconds: 20`) in high-volume consumers when configuring Intermittent Unresponsiveness High
mistakesToAvoid.why: Short polling queries single partition subsets and returns empty responses, dramatically inflating AWS API billing and consumer CPU usage.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to monitor `ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible` and `ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage` in CloudWatch when configuring Intermittent Unresponsiveness High
mistakesToAvoid.why: Queue depth and message age are primary SLI signals for consumer backlog saturation, far superior to consumer CPU utilization.

title: EC2 SSH Connectivity Sev-1 Incident: Application Running but SSH Failing Triage
summary: Sev-1 incident response procedure when an EC2 instance application operates normally, but operations engineers cannot establish SSH sessions.
question: An EC2 instance is running normally, and the application is also working as expected. However, the application team has raised a Sev-1 incident because they are unable to SSH into the EC2 instance. You have joined the Sev-1 call. What areas would you check to restore SSH connectivity?
roleContext: Senior Cloud Engineer L2 Interview · Sev-1 Live Scenario
intro: Because the application is functioning normally, the underlying EC2 hardware, hypervisor, OS kernel, and primary application ports are healthy. The failure is isolated strictly to the SSH management path. I troubleshoot in order from external network perimeter to host OS configuration.

steps.title: Check Security Group & Network ACL (NACL) Ingress Rules
steps.description: Verify port 22 ingress rules on the EC2 instance's Security Group. Check if someone modified the corporate VPN CIDR or accidentally deleted the port 22 rule. Verify that the subnet NACL allows inbound port 22 and outbound ephemeral ports (1024-65535).
steps.codeBlock:
# Verify Security Group rules via AWS CLI
aws ec2 describe-security-groups \
  --group-ids sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --query "SecurityGroups[*].IpPermissions[?ToPort==\`22\`]"

steps.title: Verify Routing Table & Bastion / VPN Path
steps.description: If engineers connect via a Bastion host or AWS Client VPN, verify that the Bastion instance is operational and its route table directs traffic through the Internet Gateway or Transit Gateway.
steps.codeBlock: aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters "Name=association.subnet-id,Values=subnet-01234567"

steps.title: Bypass SSH via AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Session Manager
steps.description: Do NOT waste precious Sev-1 time debugging port 22 if you need immediate terminal access. Connect directly using AWS SSM Session Manager. SSM relies on the outbound SSM agent and does not require port 22, public IPs, or security group ingress rules.
steps.codeBlock:
# Instantly connect via SSM bypassing SSH entirely
aws ssm start-session --target i-0123456789abcdef0

steps.title: Inspect Host sshd Daemon, iptables, and Disk Space
steps.description:
Once inside via SSM or EC2 Serial Console:
1. Check `systemctl status sshd` (is sshd running or listening on an alternate port?).
2. Check `journalctl -u sshd -n 50` for authentication failures or MaxStartups drops.
3. Check `df -h` (if root `/` is 100% full, sshd cannot allocate pty sessions and immediately terminates connections).
steps.highlight: Sev-1 Fast Recovery: During an active incident, use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager or EC2 Serial Console to gain terminal access in 30 seconds without debugging network firewall rules.

keyTakeaway: Application working means the instance is healthy. Check Security Group port 22 rules, but immediately bypass SSH using AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Session Manager or EC2 Serial Console to gain shell access and inspect sshd, disk space, and iptables.
elevatorPitch: Check Security Group and Subnet NACL ingress rules for port 22 and corporate VPN CIDRs.
Use AWS SSM Session Manager to immediately bypass SSH and access the terminal within seconds.
Use the EC2 Serial Console if the network stack is completely unresponsive.
Inspect sshd daemon status, root disk space (/tmp and /), and host iptables/firewalld rules.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Deactivating a compromised key prevents abuse while preserving identity records for CloudTrail forensic queries to assess blast radius.

mistakesToAvoid.why: SCPs define maximum permission guards at the AWS Organization level across accounts, whereas permission boundaries limit delegate privileges within a single account.

title: AWS Auto Scaling Group Delay: New Instances Not Launching Within Required Timeframe
summary: Diagnostic guide to identify and eliminate latency bottlenecks in AWS Auto Scaling Groups when new compute capacity fails to launch quickly during traffic surges.
question: Auto Scaling is not working as expected, and new instances are not being launched within the required time frame. How would you troubleshoot and resolve this issue?
intro: When an AWS Auto Scaling Group (ASG) takes too long to launch instances during traffic surges, the delay is split into two phases: Metric Detection Delay (CloudWatch evaluation periods and cooldown timers) and Instance Bootstrapping Delay (slow user-data scripts, AMI baking, and health check grace periods).

steps.title: Check ASG Activity History for Scaling Failures
steps.description: Review the Auto Scaling Group's Activity History. Look for failed launch attempts due to subnet IP exhaustion, account vCPU service quotas exceeded (`InsufficientInstanceCapacity`), or invalid Launch Template configurations.
steps.codeBlock:
aws autoscaling describe-scaling-activities \
  --auto-scaling-group-name asg-production-web \
  --max-records 10
# Check for: "Failed" activities and Description messages

steps.title: Audit Metric Evaluation Periods & Cooldowns
steps.description: Standard CloudWatch metrics report on a 5-minute schedule. If using Step Scaling or Simple Scaling with 5-minute metric periods and a 300-second cooldown, Auto Scaling can take 10 to 15 minutes to trigger the first new instance. Switch to 1-minute detailed monitoring and Target Tracking policies.
steps.codeBlock:
# Enable detailed 1-minute CloudWatch monitoring for ASG Launch Template
"Monitoring": { "Enabled": true }

steps.title: Optimize EC2 User-Data Execution Time (Golden AMI Pattern)
steps.description: Inspect the instance user-data bootstrap script (`/var/log/cloud-init-output.log`). If instances run `yum update -y`, download 2 GB Docker images, or compile binaries at launch, boot time will exceed 10 minutes. Pre-bake all dependencies, packages, and container images into a Golden AMI using HashiCorp Packer.
steps.highlight: Golden AMI Rule: An auto-scaled EC2 instance should boot and register healthy behind a load balancer in under 90 seconds. Bake dependencies into AMIs instead of downloading during boot.

steps.title: Implement AWS Auto Scaling Warm Pools
steps.description: Enable ASG Warm Pools. A Warm Pool maintains pre-initialized, stopped EC2 instances that have already completed OS updates and bootstrap scripts. When scaling occurs, instances transition from `Stopped` to `Running` in under 30 seconds.

keyTakeaway: ASG launch delays stem from 5-minute CloudWatch metric evaluation intervals, bloated user-data scripts, or service quota limits. Fix by enabling 1-minute detailed monitoring, baking Golden AMIs, and deploying ASG Warm Pools.
elevatorPitch: Check ASG Activity History for failed launch events or EC2 vCPU service quota limits.
Switch CloudWatch metrics from 5-minute basic monitoring to 1-minute detailed monitoring.
Replace long-running user-data scripts with pre-baked Golden AMIs using Packer.
Enable ASG Warm Pools to launch pre-initialized instances in under 30 seconds.

mistakesToAvoid.why: Deactivating a compromised key prevents abuse while preserving identity records for CloudTrail forensic queries to assess blast radius.
