title: SSH Connection Failing Even After Enabling Password Authentication on Server: Root Cause Triage
summary: Troubleshooting checklist when password-based SSH authentication fails to function despite editing /etc/ssh/sshd_config to set PasswordAuthentication yes.
question: SSH connection is failing even after enabling password authentication on the server. What could be the possible causes, and how would you troubleshoot and resolve the issue?
intro: When SSH password authentication fails despite setting `PasswordAuthentication yes` in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`, the issue typically stems from configuration overrides in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/`, un-restarted sshd daemons, cloud-init overwriting settings, locked user accounts, or PAM / SELinux security policy rejections.

steps.title: Check for Modular Drop-in Configs in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/
steps.description: In modern Linux distributions (Ubuntu 22.04+, RHEL 9+, Amazon Linux 2023), `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` includes drop-in files from `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf`. Cloud providers often drop a `50-cloud-init.conf` file that explicitly sets `PasswordAuthentication no`, which overrides the main file.
steps.codeBlock:
# Inspect effective sshd configuration
sshd -T | grep passwordauthentication
grep -rn "PasswordAuthentication" /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/

steps.title: Verify Daemon Restart & Syntax Validation
steps.description: Editing `sshd_config` has no effect until the service is restarted. Validate configuration syntax before restarting to avoid getting locked out.
steps.codeBlock:
sshd -t  # Validate syntax
systemctl restart sshd || systemctl restart ssh

steps.title: Verify User Account Password Status & Shadow Lock
steps.description: On cloud instances (AWS EC2, GCP), default users (`ec2-user`, `ubuntu`) are created with no password or a locked password (`!` or `*` in `/etc/shadow`). Password authentication will reject the login until an actual password is set via `passwd`.
steps.codeBlock:
passwd ec2-user
# Verify shadow file status (P = valid password, L = locked, NP = no password)
passwd -S ec2-user

steps.title: Inspect PAM Authentication & SELinux Contexts
steps.description: Ensure `UsePAM yes` is enabled in `sshd_config`. Check `/etc/pam.d/sshd` and review system audit logs for SELinux denials.
steps.codeBlock:
# Check sshd failure logs in real time
journalctl -u sshd -f
# Look for: "Failed password for invalid user" or "User ec2-user not allowed because account is locked"

keyTakeaway: Check the effective configuration using 'sshd -T', verify drop-in files in '/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/', confirm the user account has a set password in '/etc/shadow', and verify sshd was restarted.
elevatorPitch: Run sshd -T | grep passwordauthentication to verify the actual evaluated configuration.
Check /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ drop-in directory for cloud-init override files.
Verify the user account actually has a password set using passwd -S (cloud accounts are locked by default).
Review journalctl -u sshd logs to see exact PAM or shadow authentication rejection reasons.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Issuing immediate kill -9 (SIGKILL) commands rather than allowing graceful termination via kill -15 (SIGTERM) when configuring Connection Failing Even
mistakesToAvoid.why: SIGKILL immediately halts execution without allowing processes to flush memory buffers, commit database transactions, or remove stale PID locks.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Overlooking file system inode exhaustion (df -i) when diagnosing 'No space left on device' errors when configuring Connection Failing Even
mistakesToAvoid.why: Millions of small files or unrotated session tokens can exhaust available file system inodes even when standard disk storage (`df -h`) shows ample free space.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Exhausting open file descriptor allocations (ulimit -n) under intensive concurrent socket connections when configuring Connection Failing Even
mistakesToAvoid.why: Reaching file descriptor exhaustion throws 'Too many open files' errors, preventing services from accepting new TCP client socket connections.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Permitting defunct zombie processes to accumulate without fixing parent process SIGCHLD waitpid reaping when configuring Connection Failing Even
mistakesToAvoid.why: Zombie processes consume process table entries; accumulating zombies can exhaust the system maximum PID limit (`pid_max`).

title: RDS Performance Running Very Slowly After Cloud Migration: Troubleshooting & Root Cause Analysis
summary: Root cause analysis runbook for database query degradation after migrating an on-premises database to AWS RDS.
question: After migrating an application to AWS, the RDS instance is running very slowly. How would you troubleshoot the performance issue and identify the root cause?
intro: When a newly migrated database on RDS performs significantly worse than on-premises, the degradation is rarely caused by the AWS cloud itself. It is caused by architectural mismatches: ungathered post-migration optimizer statistics, undersized storage IOPS, missing parameter group tuning, network latency across AZs, or missing indexes that were omitted during dump/restore.

steps.title: Analyze AWS Performance Insights & Database Load (AAS)
steps.description: Open RDS Performance Insights. Inspect Average Active Sessions (AAS) against the Max vCPU line. Break down load by: - Wait States: Are sessions waiting on `io/table/scan`, `Lock:row`, `CPU`, or `Client:ClientRead`? - Top SQL: Identify the top 3 queries consuming 80% of database time.

steps.title: Check Table Statistics & Execute VACUUM / ANALYZE
steps.description: During standard database migrations (pg_dump/restore or AWS DMS), table data is imported but query optimizer statistics are empty. Without updated histogram statistics, the query planner chooses catastrophic Sequential Scans instead of Index Scans.

steps.title: Verify Storage IOPS & gp2/gp3 Volume Bottlenecks
steps.description: Check CloudWatch metrics: `ReadIOPS`, `WriteIOPS`, `ReadLatency`, `WriteLatency`, and `DiskQueueDepth`. If average read latency exceeds 10ms, storage is bottlenecking. Upgrade storage to gp3 with provisioned 12,000 IOPS or io2.
steps.codeBlock:
# Check CloudWatch RDS Latency
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics \
  --namespace AWS/RDS \
  --metric-name ReadLatency \
  --dimensions Name=DBInstanceIdentifier,Value=prod-db \
  --start-time $(date -u -v-2h +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) \
  --end-time $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ) \
  --period 300 --statistics Average

steps.title: Audit Network Placement (Multi-AZ & Application Colocation)
steps.description: Ensure the application EC2/EKS pods are located in the same AWS Region and Availability Zone as the primary RDS instance. If the app is in `us-east-1a` and primary RDS is in `us-east-1b`, every database round-trip incurs 1-2ms of cross-AZ network latency.

keyTakeaway: Slow RDS performance post-migration is primarily caused by missing optimizer statistics (run ANALYZE immediately), insufficient storage IOPS, default parameter group limits, or cross-AZ network latency.
elevatorPitch: Use RDS Performance Insights to analyze Average Active Sessions and dominant wait events.
Run ANALYZE immediately: newly restored databases lack optimizer statistics and default to table scans.
Inspect storage read/write latency in CloudWatch to detect IOPS throttling.
Verify that application servers and the primary database reside in the same Availability Zone.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Applying exclusive-lock DDL table migrations on live production databases during peak traffic windows when configuring Performance Running Slowly
mistakesToAvoid.why: DDL migrations that acquire an exclusive table lock block all concurrent queries, queuing connections until the database connection pool exhausts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Allowing high-frequency queries to trigger full table scans without appropriate composite indexing when configuring Performance Running Slowly
mistakesToAvoid.why: Sequential table scans saturate database CPU and disk I/O, evicting frequently queried data from the buffer cache and causing cascading timeouts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Disabling referential integrity constraints during bulk ETL imports without post-import consistency validation when configuring Performance Running Slowly
mistakesToAvoid.why: Skipping relational consistency checks risks introducing orphaned records and referential integrity violations into production tables.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on database snapshot backups that have never been verified through automated restoration drills when configuring Performance Running Slowly
mistakesToAvoid.why: Backups that have never been tested with automated restore verification frequently fail during real disaster recovery scenarios.

title: AWS Transit Gateway vs. VPC Peering: Architectural Decision Framework and Trade-offs
summary: Deep architectural comparison between AWS VPC Peering and AWS Transit Gateway, covering routing complexity, bandwidth, pricing, and scaling limits.
question: When would you choose AWS Transit Gateway versus VPC Peering, and why?
intro: The choice between AWS VPC Peering and AWS Transit Gateway comes down to scale, operational complexity, transitive routing needs, and cost. VPC Peering is a point-to-point, non-transitive connection with zero hourly cost and highest performance. Transit Gateway is a centralized cloud router that simplifies complex multi-VPC and hybrid-cloud topologies at the cost of hourly attachment fees and data processing charges.

steps.title: Architecture & Transitive Routing Comparison
steps.description: VPC Peering does NOT support transitive routing (VPC A cannot talk to VPC C through VPC B). For N VPCs to communicate fully via peering, you require `N*(N-1)/2` peering connections (e.g. 50 VPCs require 1,225 peering links), creating an unmanageable routing table mesh. Transit Gateway acts as a central hub (hub-and-spoke), supporting transitive routing across hundreds of VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect links.
flow: VPC B / On-Prem Direct Connect / Inspection VPC

steps.title: Performance & Bandwidth Comparison
steps.description: VPC Peering has no bandwidth limits or single-point-of-failure choke points; traffic flows over the AWS global backbone at line rate with zero added latency. Transit Gateway has a limit of 50 Gbps per VPC attachment burst (expandable via ECMP) and introduces a negligible sub-millisecond hop.
steps.highlight: Performance Rule: For massive data transfer pipelines between two high-throughput VPCs, VPC Peering provides higher throughput and zero data processing fees.

steps.title: Cost Model Breakdown
steps.description: Cost structures are fundamentally different: - VPC Peering: $0.00 base cost per hour. Standard inter-AZ data transfer fees apply ($0.01/GB). Same-AZ peering is completely FREE. - Transit Gateway: $0.05/hour per attachment ($36.50/month per VPC) + $0.02 per GB data processing fee ON TOP of standard data transfer fees.
steps.codeBlock:
# Cost Example: 20 VPCs transferring 50 TB/month
# VPC Peering: ~$500 in data transfer
# Transit Gateway: (20 * $36.50) + (50,000 GB * $0.02) + data transfer = ~$2,230/month

steps.title: Centralized Network Security & Inspection
steps.description: Transit Gateway allows routing all east-west and north-south traffic through a centralized 'Security/Inspection VPC' containing AWS Network Firewall or Palo Alto appliances before forwarding to destinations. VPC Peering cannot achieve this without complex proxying.

keyTakeaway: Choose VPC Peering for small, high-throughput VPC topologies (under 5-10 VPCs) where lowest cost and highest bandwidth matter. Choose Transit Gateway for large enterprise multi-account environments (10+ VPCs), hybrid on-premises connectivity, and centralized firewall inspection.
elevatorPitch: Use VPC Peering for 1-to-1 high-bandwidth connections with zero hourly cost and line-rate performance.
Use Transit Gateway for hub-and-spoke architectures connecting 10+ VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect.
Transit Gateway enables transitive routing and centralized firewall traffic inspection.
Consider cost: Transit Gateway charges $0.05/hr per attachment plus $0.02/GB data processing fees.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating stateless Network ACLs as stateful firewalls without specifying outbound ephemeral return ports when configuring Transit Gateway Peering
mistakesToAvoid.why: Security Groups track connection state automatically, whereas stateless Network ACLs require explicit ephemeral port rules (1024-65535) for return traffic.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Opening short-lived non-pooled TCP client connections, exhausting ephemeral ports in TIME_WAIT state when configuring Transit Gateway Peering
mistakesToAvoid.why: Rapidly opening and closing short-lived TCP sockets without connection pooling exhausts ephemeral ports, causing connection refusal errors.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Directing load balancer health checks to heavy computational endpoints rather than dedicated health routes when configuring Transit Gateway Peering
mistakesToAvoid.why: Deep health check paths amplify database load during traffic spikes and risk cascading eviction of healthy application nodes.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Triggering BGP route dampening by rapidly announcing and withdrawing multihomed network prefixes when configuring Transit Gateway Peering
mistakesToAvoid.why: Rapidly flapping BGP route announcements triggers upstream ISP route dampening, effectively blackholing network traffic for hours.

title: Kubernetes Service vs. Ingress: Architectural Differences and Traffic Routing Use Cases
summary: Clear, senior-level distinction between Kubernetes Services (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer) and Ingress controllers with real-world architecture examples.
question: What is the difference between a Kubernetes Service and an Ingress? When would you use each one?
intro: In Kubernetes, a Service operates at Layer 4 (Transport layer - TCP/UDP), providing stable internal networking and load balancing across dynamic pod IP addresses. An Ingress operates at Layer 7 (Application layer - HTTP/HTTPS), acting as an intelligent reverse proxy that routes external internet traffic to internal Services based on hostnames and URL paths.

steps.title: Kubernetes Service Types & Layer 4 Mechanics
steps.description: A Service creates a static virtual IP (ClusterIP) managed by kube-proxy iptables or IPVS rules: - ClusterIP: Exposes the service internally inside the cluster (default). - NodePort: Opens a dedicated static port (30000-32767) on all node IP addresses. - LoadBalancer: Provisions a cloud provider Layer 4 load balancer (AWS NLB / Azure Basic LB). Creating 50 LoadBalancer Services provisions 50 expensive cloud load balancers.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: payment-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: payment
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080

steps.title: Kubernetes Ingress & Layer 7 Routing Mechanics
steps.description: Ingress is a set of routing rules evaluated by an Ingress Controller (NGINX, Traefik, AWS ALB Controller). It consolidates routing for multiple microservices behind a single public cloud Load Balancer and single public IP address.
steps.codeBlock:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: main-ingress
spec:
  rules:
  - host: api.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /payments
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: payment-service
            port:
              number: 80
      - path: /users
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: user-service
            port:
              number: 80

steps.title: Key Capabilities Comparison Table
steps.description: Feature trade-offs: - Protocols: Service handles TCP, UDP, SCTP. Ingress handles HTTP, HTTPS, WebSockets, gRPC. - SSL Termination: Ingress terminates SSL/TLS and manages certs (cert-manager). Services do not terminate SSL. - Path Routing: Ingress routes by domain and URI path (`/payments` vs `/users`). Service knows nothing about HTTP paths.
steps.highlight: Cost & Architecture Rule: Never expose multiple web microservices using Service Type LoadBalancer. Expose them internally as ClusterIP Services and unify them under a single Ingress Controller.

steps.title: When to Use Each
steps.description: - Use ClusterIP Service for internal pod-to-pod communication. - Use Ingress for external web/API traffic needing domain routing, SSL termination, and rate limiting. - Use LoadBalancer Service when exposing non-HTTP Layer 4 traffic (database proxies, gaming UDP servers, MQTT brokers).

keyTakeaway: Service is Layer 4 (TCP/UDP stable IP for pods). Ingress is Layer 7 (HTTP reverse proxy providing SSL termination, host/path routing, and consolidating public entry points behind a single load balancer).
elevatorPitch: A Service operates at Layer 4, providing stable cluster-internal virtual IPs for dynamic pods.
An Ingress operates at Layer 7, providing HTTP/HTTPS routing, SSL termination, and path-based routing.
Use Ingress to route traffic to multiple internal ClusterIP services behind a single cloud load balancer.
Use Type LoadBalancer directly only for non-HTTP Layer 4 workloads like TCP gaming or MQTT.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Configuring Service selector labels that mismatch underlying Pod manifest metadata
mistakesToAvoid.why: A typo in `spec.selector` causes the Service endpoints list (`kubectl get endpoints`) to remain empty, resulting in `503 Service Unavailable` or timeouts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting explicit ingressClassName specifications when running multiple ingress controllers
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without an explicit `ingressClassName`, ingress resources are either ignored or picked up unpredictably by competing controllers.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Depleting worker node subnet IP address allocations under VPC CNI or Azure CNI
mistakesToAvoid.why: Direct VPC pod networking allocates real subnet IPs; failing to monitor IP pools causes new pods to stay stuck indefinitely in `ContainerCreating`.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Attempting network triage without inspecting kubectl describe service and EndpointSlice resources
mistakesToAvoid.why: Verifying EndpointSlice population immediately determines whether a connectivity failure is caused by pod labeling, readiness probes, or routing.

title: Kubernetes Pod Stuck in Pending State Due to Storage: CSI and PVC Diagnostic Flow
summary: Complete troubleshooting workflow when a Kubernetes pod is stuck in Pending state due to PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) and CSI storage issues.
question: A Kubernetes pod is stuck in the Pending state due to a storage-related issue. What possible causes would you investigate, and how would you troubleshoot the issue?
intro: When a pod remains in Pending status with storage warnings, the Kubernetes scheduler cannot place the pod onto any node because persistent storage volume constraints cannot be satisfied. I troubleshoot by checking pod events, PVC status, StorageClass provisioners, and Availability Zone topology constraints.

steps.title: Inspect Pod Describe Events
steps.description:
Run `kubectl describe pod <pod-name>`. Check the Events section at the bottom. Common storage failure messages:
- `0/3 nodes are available: 3 node(s) had volume node affinity conflict`
- `pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims`
- `waiting for a volume to be created, either by dynamic provisioning or manual binding`
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n production
# Look for Events:
# Warning  FailedScheduling  pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims

steps.title: Investigate PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) Binding Status
steps.description: Check whether the PVC is `Bound`, `Pending`, or `Lost`. Describe the PVC to see why dynamic volume provisioning failed.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get pvc -n production
kubectl describe pvc <pvc-name> -n production
# Typical error:
# StorageClass "gp3" not found OR VolumeBindingFailed: waiting for first consumer to be created

steps.title: Top Storage Failure Causes
steps.description: Investigate the top 4 storage failure modes: 1. StorageClass Misconfiguration: StorageClass does not exist or the underlying cloud CSI driver (e.g. `ebs.csi.aws.com`) is crashed. 2. Availability Zone Affinity Conflict: EBS/Azure Disks are zonal resources. If an EBS volume exists in `us-east-1a`, but worker nodes with available CPU/RAM are in `us-east-1b`, the pod cannot schedule. 3. AccessMode Mismatch: Claim requests `ReadWriteMany` (RWX) on an EBS or Azure Disk volume that only supports `ReadWriteOnce` (RWO). 4. Volume Limits Exceeded: Worker node has reached maximum EBS volume attachments per EC2 instance (e.g. 28 volumes per nitro instance).
steps.highlight: StorageClass Tip: Always use volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer in StorageClasses so volumes are provisioned in the exact Availability Zone where the pod is scheduled.

steps.title: Check CSI Driver DaemonSet Pods
steps.description: Verify that the cloud storage CSI controller and node daemonset pods are healthy in `kube-system`.
steps.codeBlock: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=aws-ebs-csi-driver

keyTakeaway: Pending storage pods are caused by unbound PVCs, missing StorageClasses, multi-attach limits, or AZ affinity conflicts. Fix by checking 'kubectl describe pvc' and using 'volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer'.
elevatorPitch: Run kubectl describe pod and kubectl describe pvc to identify the exact storage scheduler error.
Verify whether the PersistentVolume is locked in a different Availability Zone than available nodes.
Check AccessModes: EBS volumes support ReadWriteOnce, not ReadWriteMany.
Verify that the cloud CSI driver pods are healthy and running in kube-system.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Conflating container cgroup OOMKill events (Exit Code 137) with node-level MemoryPressure evictions when addressing storage-related
mistakesToAvoid.why: Exit Code 137 indicates the container cgroup exceeded its `limits.memory`, whereas Node MemoryPressure triggers kubelet eviction of lower QoS pods.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Increasing memory limits arbitrarily without profiling application heap allocation and memory leak roots
mistakesToAvoid.why: Increasing limits for applications with memory leaks merely delays the inevitable OOMKill and increases host resource waste.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Overlooking imagePullSecrets and registry credential expiration during ImagePullBackOff triage
mistakesToAvoid.why: Missing or expired private registry authentication tokens block container image pulls before pod bootstrapping can begin.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting startup probes on slow-initializing JVM or inference workloads in Kubernetes
mistakesToAvoid.why: Startup probes protect slow-starting applications by pausing liveness and readiness probe evaluation until initial warmup completes.

title: Terraform Apply Fails Halfway After Partially Creating Resources: Safe Recovery and State Triage
summary: Incident runbook to recover state cleanly when a terraform apply crashes or fails mid-run after creating partial cloud resources.
question: You run terraform apply, but the deployment fails after successfully creating some resources. How would you troubleshoot the failure and safely recover?
intro: When `terraform apply` fails mid-deployment, Terraform automatically updates the state file with whatever resources were successfully provisioned prior to the error. However, the infrastructure is left in a partial, broken state. Safe recovery requires identifying the exact failure error, refreshing state, fixing the root cause, and re-applying or surgically destroying partial resources.

steps.title: Identify the Exact Failure Reason in the Apply Log
steps.description: Inspect the failure output. Common causes: - API Permission Errors: Missing IAM actions (e.g. `AccessDenied` on KMS key creation). - Invalid Arguments: Resource naming collisions or unsupported CIDR blocks. - Cloud Service Quotas: Hit max VPCs or Elastic IPs in the region. - Network Timeouts: Resource provisioning timed out (e.g. RDS Aurora cluster creation).
steps.codeBlock:
# Inspect Terraform state to confirm what actually persisted
terraform state list

steps.title: Back Up Current Remote State Before Any Action
steps.description: Never run modifications on an unstable state without a snapshot backup.
steps.codeBlock: terraform state pull > terraform.state.backup.$(date +%s).json

steps.title: Decision: Roll Forward (Preferred) vs. Roll Back
steps.description: - Roll Forward (Recommended): Fix the root issue (e.g. grant missing IAM permission or update the failing parameter in `.tf` code). Re-run `terraform apply`. Because Terraform is declarative and idempotent, it detects the already-created resources in state and only creates the remaining resources. - Roll Back: If the deployment must be discarded, target the partially created resources and remove them using `terraform destroy -target=` to avoid deleting unaffected live infrastructure.
steps.codeBlock:
# Surgical targeted cleanup of partially created resources if rolling back
terraform destroy -target=aws_instance.broken_worker

steps.title: Reconcile Orphaned Resources with terraform import
steps.description: If a cloud resource was created by the cloud provider API right before network timeout dropped the connection, the resource exists in AWS but is missing from Terraform state. Import the resource into state before running apply again to prevent 'ResourceAlreadyExists' errors.
steps.codeBlock: terraform import aws_s3_bucket.data_bucket prod-analytics-data-bucket-unique

keyTakeaway: Terraform persists successful resources into state before failing. Backup state immediately, fix the error, and roll forward with another apply. If orphaned cloud resources exist, import them with 'terraform import'.
elevatorPitch: Back up remote state immediately using terraform state pull.
Analyze the apply log to identify whether permissions, quotas, or syntax caused the break.
Prefer Rolling Forward: fix the HCL configuration and re-run terraform apply (declarative idempotency).
Use terraform import if resources were created in the cloud but missed in state due to network timeouts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Manually modifying remote .tfstate JSON files by hand to resolve state drift or lock conflicts
mistakesToAvoid.why: Direct manual edits corrupt state checksums and risk desynchronizing real cloud infrastructure from Terraform's dependency graph.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Storing unencrypted API tokens or database credentials directly inside Terraform manifest files
mistakesToAvoid.why: Committing plaintext credentials into version control violates security compliance; sensitive inputs should be injected via environment variables or secret vaults.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using count indices rather than for_each mapping when creating variable collections of cloud resources
mistakesToAvoid.why: Removing an item from the middle of a `count` list re-indexes all subsequent resources, prompting Terraform to unnecessarily recreate unchanged infrastructure.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running terraform state rm on live resources without accounting for underlying infrastructure dependencies
mistakesToAvoid.why: Removing resources from state leaves orphaned cloud resources running unmanaged, accumulating cloud costs and creating naming collisions on re-creation.

title: Kubernetes Readiness vs. Liveness Probes: Internal Differences and Pod Restart Behavior
summary: Deep dive into the operational differences between Kubernetes readiness, liveness, and startup probes, with a detailed breakdown of pod restart mechanics.
question: What is the main difference between readiness and liveness probes? Does a readiness or liveness probe cause a pod to restart? Explain the behavior.
intro: The core distinction between readiness and liveness probes is the action kubelet takes upon failure. A failing Liveness probe restarts the container. A failing Readiness probe NEVER restarts the container—it removes the pod's IP address from the Service endpoints to stop receiving network traffic until the probe recovers.

steps.title: Liveness Probe Behavior (Process Health & Deadlocks)
steps.description: Purpose: Detects when an application is stuck in an unrecoverable state (e.g. fatal deadlock, corrupted JVM memory) where a container restart is the ONLY remediation. - Failure Action: Kubelet kills the container and initiates a restart according to the Pod's `restartPolicy: Always`. The pod restart count increments.
steps.codeBlock:
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 15
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3

steps.title: Readiness Probe Behavior (Traffic Eligibility & Warmup)
steps.description: Purpose: Detects whether the application is currently capable of handling client requests (e.g. warming up caches, loading datasets into memory, temporary downstream DB latency). - Failure Action: Kubelet marks `Ready: False`. The Kubernetes Endpoints controller removes the Pod IP from all Service endpoints. Traffic is diverted to other healthy pods. The container is NOT restarted.
steps.codeBlock:
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /ready
    port: 8080
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 2

steps.title: The Cascading Outage Trap (Misconfigured Liveness Probes)
steps.description: A classic production disaster occurs when engineers configure liveness probes to check external dependencies (database connectivity). If the database becomes slow, all pods fail their liveness probes simultaneously, kubelet restarts all containers, and the entire cluster enters a death spiral of restarts.
steps.highlight: Architectural Rule: Never check external databases or third-party APIs inside liveness probes! Liveness probes must only check local container process liveness.

steps.title: The Startup Probe (Solving Slow Initialization)
steps.description: Use `startupProbe` for legacy or JVM applications that take minutes to initialize. Startup probes disable liveness and readiness checks until the application has fully started, preventing kubelet from prematurely killing slow-booting pods.

keyTakeaway: Liveness probe failures trigger container restarts. Readiness probe failures remove the pod from Service endpoints without restarting. Never check external dependencies in liveness probes.
elevatorPitch: Liveness probes restart containers when they enter unrecoverable deadlock states.
Readiness probes remove pods from Service traffic endpoints without restarting containers.
Never check downstream databases in liveness probes to prevent cascading cluster restart storms.
Use startup probes to protect slow-starting applications from premature liveness kills.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Over-granting cluster-admin permissions to pod ServiceAccounts instead of scoping namespace Roles when configuring Kubernetes Readiness Liveness
mistakesToAvoid.why: Over-granting cluster-wide permissions violates least-privilege principles and allows compromised pods to escalate privileges across namespaces.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Referencing mutable latest container tags across production Kubernetes Deployment specs when configuring Kubernetes Readiness Liveness
mistakesToAvoid.why: Deployments referencing `:latest` risk inconsistent versions across replica pods and break deterministic rollback capabilities.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting pod readiness probes, causing traffic to hit uninitialized application containers when configuring Kubernetes Readiness Liveness
mistakesToAvoid.why: Readiness probes gate traffic delivery; missing probes cause Kubernetes to route user requests to pods before dependencies or caches are loaded.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Executing diagnostic triage without analyzing chronological cluster events and describe outputs when configuring Kubernetes Readiness Liveness
mistakesToAvoid.why: Cluster events provide sequential timestamps of scheduler decisions, probe failures, and image pull timeouts essential for rapid root-cause isolation.

title: How to Pass Sensitive Data to Terraform Without HashiCorp Vault or Cloud Secrets Manager
summary: Secure architectural patterns for injecting secrets into Terraform when dedicated secret vaults or cloud Secrets Managers are unavailable.
question: How would you pass sensitive data to Terraform if there is currently no Vault or cloud-based Secrets Manager available?
intro: When dedicated enterprise secrets management systems (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) are not deployed, sensitive values (database passwords, API tokens) must still NEVER be committed to Git in plaintext `.tf` or `.tfvars` files. I use environment variables (`TF_VAR_`), Mozilla SOPS with PGP/KMS encryption in Git, and Terraform `sensitive = true` variable masking.

steps.title: Pattern 1: Environment Variables via TF_VAR_ Injection
steps.description: Terraform automatically reads environment variables prefixed with `TF_VAR_`. In CI/CD pipelines (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI), inject secrets from masked pipeline variables into the runner environment at runtime.
steps.codeBlock:
# In CI/CD runner script:
export TF_VAR_db_password="$SECRET_FROM_CI_RUNNER"
terraform plan

steps.title: Pattern 2: Encrypted Git Repositories Using Mozilla SOPS
steps.description: Use Mozilla SOPS (Secrets OPerationS). SOPS allows encrypting values inside `.tfvars.json` or `.yaml` files using local PGP keys or age keys while keeping keys in plaintext. The encrypted file is safely committed to Git, and decrypted on-the-fly during pipeline execution.
steps.codeBlock:
# Encrypt secret tfvars file
sops --encrypt --in-place secrets.enc.tfvars.json
# Decrypt during terraform run:
terraform apply -var-file=<(sops -d secrets.enc.tfvars.json)

steps.title: Mark Variables as Sensitive in HCL
steps.description: Declare `sensitive = true` on all input variables in Terraform. This prevents Terraform from printing plaintext passwords in console logs, pipeline terminal streams, and `terraform plan` outputs.

steps.title: Protect Remote State File (State Encryption)
steps.description: Remember that Terraform state files store sensitive variables in plaintext JSON! Always enable server-side encryption (SSE-KMS) on the S3 remote state bucket and restrict bucket access with strict IAM policies.
steps.highlight: Security Alert: Even if variables are passed via TF_VAR_, they are stored in plaintext inside terraform.tfstate. Remote state encryption and IAM access controls are mandatory.

keyTakeaway: Pass secrets via TF_VAR_ environment variables from masked CI runners or use Mozilla SOPS to encrypt files in Git. Mark HCL variables with sensitive = true and encrypt the remote state backend.
elevatorPitch: Use TF_VAR_ environment variables injected dynamically from masked CI/CD pipeline stores.
Use Mozilla SOPS to encrypt secrets committed to Git using PGP or Age keys.
Flag all secret variables with sensitive = true to redact values from console outputs.
Enforce SSE-KMS encryption and strict IAM policies on the remote S3/GCS state file backend.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Manually modifying remote .tfstate JSON files by hand to resolve state drift or lock conflicts
mistakesToAvoid.why: Direct manual edits corrupt state checksums and risk desynchronizing real cloud infrastructure from Terraform's dependency graph.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Storing unencrypted API tokens or database credentials directly inside Terraform manifest files
mistakesToAvoid.why: Committing plaintext credentials into version control violates security compliance; sensitive inputs should be injected via environment variables or secret vaults.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using count indices rather than for_each mapping when creating variable collections of cloud resources
mistakesToAvoid.why: Removing an item from the middle of a `count` list re-indexes all subsequent resources, prompting Terraform to unnecessarily recreate unchanged infrastructure.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running terraform state rm on live resources without accounting for underlying infrastructure dependencies in cloud-l2-q011-passing-sensitive-data-terraform-without-vault-secrets-manager
mistakesToAvoid.why: Removing resources from state leaves orphaned cloud resources running unmanaged, accumulating cloud costs and creating naming collisions on re-creation.

title: Large Jenkins Pipeline Optimization: Parallel Stages, Ephemeral Agents, and Shared Libraries
summary: Engineering blueprint for refactoring large, monolithic Jenkins pipelines to reduce execution duration and eliminate agent queuing bottlenecks.
question: You have a large Jenkins pipeline that takes a long time to complete. How would you optimize the pipeline and reduce its execution time?
intro: Monolithic Jenkins pipelines slow down due to serial execution of independent stages, single-node workspace bloat, rebuilding unchanged layers, and agent scheduling queues on static VM workers. I optimize pipelines by restructuring stages for parallelism, running ephemeral container agents on Kubernetes, and caching dependencies.

steps.title: Parallelize Independent Stages in Declarative Pipeline
steps.description: Deconstruct sequential stages. Security scanning (SonarQube/Trivy), unit tests, and linting do not depend on each other and can execute concurrently in parallel stages.

steps.title: Migrate from Static VM Agents to Ephemeral Kubernetes Pod Agents
steps.description: Replace fixed EC2 VM agents with ephemeral Kubernetes pod agents via the Jenkins Kubernetes plugin. Pods spin up in seconds on demand with exact CPU/memory requests, eliminating agent queue wait times.

steps.title: Persist Shared Cache Volumes for Package Managers
steps.description: Mount persistent storage volumes (EFS / hostPath / NFS) into Jenkins agent pods for Maven `.m2` repository or npm cache directories so agents don't re-download dependencies on every run.
steps.highlight: Optimization Rule: Ephemeral agents eliminate queuing, while shared persistent cache mounts eliminate redundant internet downloading.

steps.title: Implement Stash / Unstash Hygiene and Prune Workspaces
steps.description: Only stash required build artifacts (e.g. compiled `.jar` files) rather than stashing entire node_modules or target folders across nodes.

keyTakeaway: Optimize Jenkins by converting serial stages into parallel blocks, migrating from static agents to ephemeral Kubernetes pod agents, and mounting persistent cache volumes for package managers.
elevatorPitch: Restructure independent lint, test, and security scanning steps into parallel stages.
Deploy the Jenkins Kubernetes plugin to spin up dynamic, ephemeral container agents on demand.
Mount persistent cache volumes for Maven and npm to prevent re-downloading packages.
Minimize stash/unstash payloads to only include essential compiled binary artifacts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Promoting application releases to production without an automated, canary-validated rollback mechanism when configuring Large Jenkins Pipeline
mistakesToAvoid.why: Pipelines that lack automated rollback mechanisms force engineering teams to scramble manual hotfixes during severe production regressions.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running concurrent deployment pipeline jobs without stage mutex locking on shared target environments when configuring Large Jenkins Pipeline
mistakesToAvoid.why: Concurrent pipeline runs on the same environment race to apply state changes, causing out-of-order commits and unpredictable deployment state.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting dependency lockfiles (package-lock.json, go.sum, Cargo.lock) from continuous integration builds when configuring Large Jenkins Pipeline
mistakesToAvoid.why: Omitting lockfiles allows upstream package updates to break builds unpredictably without any changes to application codebase.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to define dynamic cache invalidation keys for CI package managers and layer caches when configuring Large Jenkins Pipeline
mistakesToAvoid.why: Stale build caches mask underlying dependency incompatibilities or pull outdated libraries, while un-cached runs slow feedback loops.

title: Moving Specific Code Changes to Another Git Branch: The git cherry-pick Workflow
summary: Production guide for selectively porting isolated commits and hotfixes between Git branches using git cherry-pick without merging unrelated code.
question: You have specific code changes in one Git branch and want to move only those changes to another branch. How would you do this?
intro: When you need to backport a specific bug fix, configuration change, or feature from a development or experimental branch into a release or production hotfix branch without merging the entire history, `git cherry-pick` is the standard tool. It extracts the diff introduced by specific commits and applies them as new commits onto the target branch.

steps.title: Identify Commit Hash on Source Branch
steps.description: Check the git log on the source branch to identify the exact commit SHAs you want to copy.
steps.codeBlock:
git checkout feature-branch
git log --oneline -n 5
# Output: a8f3b9c fix(auth): resolve token expiration race condition

steps.title: Switch to Target Branch and Execute Cherry-Pick
steps.description: Switch to the target branch (e.g. `main` or `release-v1.4`), ensure your working tree is clean, and run `git cherry-pick <commit-hash>`.
steps.codeBlock:
git checkout main
git pull origin main
git cherry-pick a8f3b9c

steps.title: Resolving Merge Conflicts (If Applicable)
steps.description: If the destination branch has divergent code, Git will pause with conflict markers. Resolve conflicts in your editor, stage the files, and continue the cherry-pick.
steps.codeBlock:
# Check conflicting files
git status
# After resolving markers:
git add auth/token.go
git cherry-pick --continue
# (Or run 'git cherry-pick --abort' to cancel cleanly)

steps.title: Cherry-Picking Multiple Commits or Ranges
steps.description:
To cherry-pick a contiguous range of commits from commit A to commit B:
`git cherry-pick A^..B` (includes commit A up to commit B).
steps.highlight: Production Best Practice: Always run unit tests after cherry-picking before pushing to remote, as dependencies from the source branch may be missing in the target branch.

keyTakeaway: Use 'git cherry-pick <commit-sha>' to apply specific commits onto a target branch without merging whole branches. Resolve conflicts if divergence occurs and run test suites before pushing.
elevatorPitch: Identify the commit SHA from git log on the source branch.
Checkout the target branch and run git cherry-pick <commit-sha>.
If conflicts occur, resolve conflict markers, stage changes, and run git cherry-pick --continue.
Use git cherry-pick A^..B to port a contiguous range of commits cleanly.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running raw git push --force rather than git push --force-with-lease on shared team feature branches when configuring Moving Specific Code
mistakesToAvoid.why: `git push --force` unconditionally overwrites remote commits made by teammates, whereas `--force-with-lease` aborts if the remote ref was updated.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Resolving complex merge conflicts with blind checkout overwrite strategies without running unit tests when configuring Moving Specific Code
mistakesToAvoid.why: Unilateral conflict resolution frequently clobbers complementary logic introduced in parallel feature branches, creating regression bugs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Discarding corrupted working directories prematurely instead of recovering lost state using git reflog when configuring Moving Specific Code
mistakesToAvoid.why: `git reflog` tracks every HEAD movement, allowing instant recovery of discarded commits, botched rebases, or deleted local branches.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Disabling branch protection rules and mandatory PR approval reviews on shared release branches when configuring Moving Specific Code
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without branch protection, developers can bypass CI validation gates and push untested code directly to production branches.

title: Kafka & Redis Clusters Report Healthy but Microservice Requests Intermittently Fail at Scale
summary: Forensic diagnostic path to isolate intermittent request failures in a high-throughput microservice dependent on healthy Kafka and Redis clusters.
question: A service depends on Kafka and Redis. Both clusters appear 100% healthy on monitoring dashboards, but service requests are intermittently failing. What is your debug path before escalating to application teams?
roleContext: Tesla DevOps Engineer Interview · Round 1: Systems Reliability & Edge Compute
intro: When upstream Kafka and Redis clusters report healthy CPU, memory, and cluster health while client requests intermittently drop, the problem almost always resides in the client-side transport layer: connection pool exhaustion, file descriptor limits, socket TIME_WAIT accumulation, or thread starvation on client event loops.

steps.title: Check Socket States & Ephemeral Port / File Descriptor Limits
steps.description: Log into the application pods or host nodes. Inspect socket connection allocation with `ss -s` and `lsof`. Look for thousands of sockets in `TIME_WAIT` or `CLOSE_WAIT` states. Check if the container process is approaching its max open files limit (`ulimit -n`).
steps.codeBlock:
# Inspect active socket connection states and file descriptors
ss -s
cat /proc/<pid>/limits | grep "Max open files"
ls -1 /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l

steps.title: Inspect Client-Side Connection Pool Starvation & Timeouts
steps.description: Verify client configuration (e.g. Jedis/Lettuce for Redis, librdkafka/confluent-kafka for Kafka). If the client connection pool has `maxTotal = 50` connections and 500 concurrent worker threads burst, threads block waiting for an idle connection until the client timeout (e.g. 1000ms) triggers, throwing intermittent timeout exceptions.
steps.highlight: Scale Reality: Redis and Kafka cluster metrics only show server-side health. A single saturated client pool will drop requests while the Redis server operates at 5% CPU.

steps.title: Analyze Redis Single-Thread Latency & Slowlog
steps.description: Run `redis-cli slowlog get 20`. Even if overall Redis CPU is low, Redis runs on a single core for command execution. A single O(N) command (like `KEYS *` or an unbounded `HGETALL`) blocks the event loop for 200ms, dropping incoming client TCP requests intermittently.
steps.codeBlock: redis-cli -h redis.internal.tesla.com slowlog get 25

steps.title: Examine Kafka Producer Buffer Pools & Socket Send Buffers
steps.description: Check if Kafka producers are hitting `buffer.memory` limits. When downstream network latency fluctuates, `max.block.ms` expires, causing the producer to drop messages before they reach Kafka brokers.

keyTakeaway: Healthy cluster dashboards don't reflect client-side health. Check file descriptor limits, socket TIME_WAIT exhaustion, client connection pool starvation, and Redis slowlog spikes.
elevatorPitch: Inspect socket states (ss -s) and file descriptors (ulimit -n) on client service pods.
Verify client connection pool capacity (Jedis/Kafka producers) to detect pool exhaustion under burst traffic.
Check redis slowlog for blocking O(N) commands choking the single-threaded event loop.
Monitor Kafka client buffer.memory saturation and max.block.ms producer timeouts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Injecting high-cardinality label dimensions (such as user IDs or request UUIDs) into Prometheus metrics when configuring Kafka Redis Clusters
mistakesToAvoid.why: High-cardinality label values cause exponential time-series growth, consuming gigabytes of TSDB memory and crashing Prometheus servers.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Evaluating application performance solely through arithmetic mean or p50 latency while ignoring tail latency (p99) when configuring Kafka Redis Clusters
mistakesToAvoid.why: Averages hide catastrophic tail latency outages where 1% of high-value user transactions suffer severe timeouts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to inject and extract W3C distributed trace context across message brokers and RPC calls when configuring Kafka Redis Clusters
mistakesToAvoid.why: Breaking distributed trace context propagation fragments end-to-end transaction waterfalls into disconnected, un-correlatable trace segments.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Configuring alert rule evaluation intervals without sufficient duration damping (for: 5m), inducing alert flap when configuring Kafka Redis Clusters
mistakesToAvoid.why: Instant alerts triggered by transient sub-second CPU or latency blips page on-call engineers unnecessarily and dilute response urgency.

title: Designing a Secure CI/CD Pipeline for Simultaneous Cloud and On-Premises Factory Edge Deployments
summary: Architecture blueprint for securely deploying code simultaneously to multi-region cloud environments and thousands of on-premises factory and edge compute devices.
question: Walk me through how you’d design a secure CI/CD pipeline that pushes code to both cloud infrastructure and on-premises edge environments.
roleContext: Tesla DevOps Engineer Interview · Round 1: Edge Compute Architecture
intro: Pushing code to edge devices (such as factory robotics, Superchargers, or car telemetry nodes) using traditional push-based CI/CD is an operational anti-pattern. Edge devices reside behind strict corporate NATs, have intermittent connectivity, and must never expose inbound SSH/API ports to public runners. I design a pull-based GitOps architecture combining cryptographic artifact signing, local edge caching, and staged canary rollouts.

steps.title: Centralized Build & Cryptographic Image Signing (Sigstore/Cosign)
steps.description: Cloud CI runners (GitHub Actions / GitLab CI) compile binaries and container images. Before publishing to registries, sign every artifact using Cosign / Sigstore with private keys stored in cloud KMS. Generate a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) with Syft.
steps.codeBlock:
# Sign container image with KMS key in CI
cosign sign --key awskms:///arn:aws:kms:...:key/... myregistry.tesla.com/edge-firmware:v2.4.0
cosign verify --key awskms:///... myregistry.tesla.com/edge-firmware:v2.4.0

steps.title: Adopt Pull-Based Edge GitOps Agents (No Inbound Firewall Holes)
steps.description: Edge nodes run local lightweight GitOps agents (such as ArgoCD, Flux, or lightweight edge daemons like open-balena or K3s system-upgrade-controller). Edge nodes pull manifests via outbound HTTPS/mTLS connections to the Git repository, eliminating inbound firewall rules into factories.

steps.title: Deploy Local Factory Artifact Mirrors & P2P Caching
steps.description: In factories with 500 edge nodes, do NOT allow all 500 nodes to pull 2 GB images across the WAN link simultaneously. Deploy a local Harbor registry mirror or Dragonfly P2P distribution node inside each factory to cache images locally.
steps.highlight: Bandwidth Guardrail: Distribute container images via local edge registry mirrors or P2P distribution to prevent saturating factory WAN uplinks.

steps.title: Automated Canary Rings with Instant Hardware Rollback
steps.description: Deploy using ring topology: Ring 0 (Canary lab nodes in 1 factory) -> Ring 1 (10% edge devices) -> Ring 2 (Global fleet). Edge daemons enforce A/B partition updates with hardware watchdog timers: if the new firmware fails health checks within 5 minutes, the bootloader automatically reboots into the previous OS partition.

keyTakeaway: Use pull-based GitOps with mTLS rather than push-based CI/CD. Sign all artifacts cryptographically with Cosign, distribute images via local factory registry caches, and enforce A/B partition rollbacks with hardware watchdogs.
elevatorPitch: Never push directly to edge nodes over open inbound firewalls; use pull-based GitOps agents.
Cryptographically sign all container binaries and firmware using Cosign and Sigstore in CI.
Deploy local registry caching proxies in each factory to prevent WAN bandwidth saturation.
Enforce ring deployments with A/B dual-boot partitions and automated hardware watchdog rollbacks.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Promoting application releases to production without an automated, canary-validated rollback mechanism when configuring Designing Secure CI/CD
mistakesToAvoid.why: Pipelines that lack automated rollback mechanisms force engineering teams to scramble manual hotfixes during severe production regressions.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running concurrent deployment pipeline jobs without stage mutex locking on shared target environments when configuring Designing Secure CI/CD
mistakesToAvoid.why: Concurrent pipeline runs on the same environment race to apply state changes, causing out-of-order commits and unpredictable deployment state.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting dependency lockfiles (package-lock.json, go.sum, Cargo.lock) from continuous integration builds when configuring Designing Secure CI/CD
mistakesToAvoid.why: Omitting lockfiles allows upstream package updates to break builds unpredictably without any changes to application codebase.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to define dynamic cache invalidation keys for CI package managers and layer caches when configuring Designing Secure CI/CD
mistakesToAvoid.why: Stale build caches mask underlying dependency incompatibilities or pull outdated libraries, while un-cached runs slow feedback loops.

title: Kubernetes Pod Stuck in ContainerCreating: Triage Flow and the Next 3 Diagnostic CLI Commands
summary: Immediate root cause diagnosis and the exact 3 CLI commands to execute when a Kubernetes pod is stuck indefinitely in the ContainerCreating state.
question: How would you debug a pod stuck in 'ContainerCreating' during deployment? What are your next 3 CLI commands?
roleContext: Tesla DevOps Engineer Interview · Round 1: Systems Reliability
intro: When a pod is stuck in `ContainerCreating`, the Kubernetes control plane has already scheduled the pod to a worker node, but the local `kubelet` or container runtime (containerd/CRI-O) cannot assemble the runtime sandbox. This is caused by persistent volume mount timeouts, missing Secrets/ConfigMaps, CNI IP allocation failures, or image pull throttling.

steps.title: Command 1: Inspect Pod Events (kubectl describe pod)
steps.description: The first command reveals the exact subsystem blocking initialization: Volume Mount, Secret, ConfigMap, or Network Sandbox.
steps.codeBlock:
# Command 1:
kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>
# Look at Events table:
# MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "pvc-storage" : rpc error ...
# FailedCreatePodSandBox: failed to setup network for sandbox ... IPAM error

steps.title: Command 2: Inspect Kubelet Host Logs (journalctl -u kubelet)
steps.description: If pod events are silent or generic, log into the specific node and query kubelet system logs to see the underlying CRI or CNI failure.
steps.codeBlock:
# Command 2:
journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager -n 50
# Reveals containerd socket errors, disk space full, or device mapper timeouts

steps.title: Command 3: Inspect Containerd Runtime & CNI Plugin Logs
steps.description: If kubelet is waiting on the runtime sandbox, query containerd directly via `crictl` to inspect failing container tasks and CNI allocations.
steps.codeBlock:
# Command 3:
crictl pods --name <pod-name>
# And check containerd logs:
journalctl -u containerd --no-pager -n 50

steps.title: Top Root Causes & Fast Resolution
steps.description: 1. Volume Attachment Timeout: The previous pod replica is still holding an exclusive lock on an EBS/PersistentVolume. Manually terminate the dead pod or detach the stale cloud volume. 2. Missing Secret/ConfigMap: Pod spec references an optional=false Secret that does not exist in the namespace. 3. CNI Subnet Exhaustion: Node cannot allocate an IP address from the VPC/Calico subnet pool.
steps.highlight: Three Command Sequence: 1) kubectl describe pod, 2) journalctl -u kubelet, 3) crictl pods / journalctl -u containerd.

keyTakeaway: Execute: 1) kubectl describe pod for event errors, 2) journalctl -u kubelet for CRI/CSI errors, and 3) crictl / journalctl -u containerd for sandbox runtime failures. Resolve volume locks and CNI IP pool exhaustion.
elevatorPitch: Execute kubectl describe pod to inspect the Events log for volume mount or CNI errors.
Run journalctl -u kubelet on the host node to see CRI runtime and sandbox errors.
Run crictl pods and journalctl -u containerd to check container runtime timeouts directly.
Triage common root causes: stale volume locks from previous pods, missing secrets, or CNI IP exhaustion.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Conflating container cgroup OOMKill events (Exit Code 137) with node-level MemoryPressure evictions
mistakesToAvoid.why: Exit Code 137 indicates the container cgroup exceeded its `limits.memory`, whereas Node MemoryPressure triggers kubelet eviction of lower QoS pods.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Increasing memory limits arbitrarily without profiling application heap allocation and memory leak roots
mistakesToAvoid.why: Increasing limits for applications with memory leaks merely delays the inevitable OOMKill and increases host resource waste.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Overlooking imagePullSecrets and registry credential expiration during ImagePullBackOff triage
mistakesToAvoid.why: Missing or expired private registry authentication tokens block container image pulls before pod bootstrapping can begin.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting startup probes on slow-initializing JVM or inference workloads in Kubernetes
mistakesToAvoid.why: Startup probes protect slow-starting applications by pausing liveness and readiness probe evaluation until initial warmup completes.

title: Gradual Latency Spike Across NGINX Ingress Controller With Stable CPU and Memory
summary: Deep dive into NGINX Ingress controller latency regressions occurring under stable CPU and memory utilization due to socket backlog saturation and upstream connection churn.
question: You see a gradual increase in latency across an NGINX ingress controller, but CPU and memory are completely stable. What’s your next move?
roleContext: Tesla DevOps Engineer Interview · Round 1: Edge Compute & Ingress
intro: When NGINX Ingress latency climbs steadily while CPU and memory remain flat, NGINX is not bottlenecking on computation. It is bottlenecking on socket connection management: upstream TCP connection thrashing (lack of upstream keepalives), worker connection pool exhaustion, Linux kernel socket listen backlog overflow (`somaxconn`), or DNS resolution delays on upstream service endpoints.

steps.title: Check Upstream Keepalive Configuration (Connection Churn)
steps.description: By default, NGINX Ingress establishes a brand new TCP connection (and TLS handshake) for EVERY request sent to backend pods unless `upstream-keepalive-connections` is explicitly enabled. Under high RPS, this triggers massive ephemeral port exhaustion and TCP handshake latency spikes while CPU remains low.
steps.codeBlock:
# Enable upstream keepalive in Ingress ConfigMap
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: ingress-nginx-controller
  namespace: ingress-nginx
data:
  upstream-keepalive-connections: "100"
  upstream-keepalive-timeout: "60"
  upstream-keepalive-requests: "10000"

steps.title: Inspect Socket Listen Backlog & Drops (netstat -s / ss -lnt)
steps.description: Check if the operating system is dropping incoming TCP SYN packets because the socket listen backlog is saturated.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl exec -it <nginx-ingress-pod> -- netstat -s | grep -i "listen"
# Look for: "times the listen queue of a socket overflowed" or "SYNs to LISTEN sockets dropped"

steps.title: Inspect NGINX Worker Connections & Event Loop Limits
steps.description: Check whether NGINX is hitting `worker-connections` (default 16384). If saturated, new client requests queue up in OS buffers, causing perceived latency to soar.
steps.codeBlock: kubectl logs <nginx-ingress-pod> -n ingress-nginx | grep -i "worker_connections"

steps.title: Verify Dynamic Upstream Service Endpoint Churn
steps.description: If backend application pods are frequently scaling or restarting, NGINX Ingress constantly reloads or queries the kube-apiserver endpoints controller. Enable Lua-based dynamic upstream routing to eliminate configuration reload latency.
steps.highlight: Golden Configuration: Setting upstream-keepalive-connections cuts NGINX Ingress latency by up to 70% during traffic surges.

keyTakeaway: Ingress latency with flat CPU points to TCP connection thrashing. Enable upstream-keepalive-connections, increase max worker connections, and tune kernel net.core.somaxconn backlog queues.
elevatorPitch: Inspect upstream keepalives: NGINX defaults to opening a fresh TCP connection per request, choking on handshakes.
Check kernel socket listen queue overflows via netstat -s in the ingress pod.
Verify NGINX worker-connections limits and tune net.core.somaxconn.
Ensure dynamic endpoint routing is enabled to avoid frequent configuration reloads during autoscaling.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Treating stateless Network ACLs as stateful firewalls without specifying outbound ephemeral return ports when configuring Gradual Latency Spike
mistakesToAvoid.why: Security Groups track connection state automatically, whereas stateless Network ACLs require explicit ephemeral port rules (1024-65535) for return traffic.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Opening short-lived non-pooled TCP client connections, exhausting ephemeral ports in TIME_WAIT state when configuring Gradual Latency Spike
mistakesToAvoid.why: Rapidly opening and closing short-lived TCP sockets without connection pooling exhausts ephemeral ports, causing connection refusal errors.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Directing load balancer health checks to heavy computational endpoints rather than dedicated health routes when configuring Gradual Latency Spike
mistakesToAvoid.why: Deep health check paths amplify database load during traffic spikes and risk cascading eviction of healthy application nodes.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Triggering BGP route dampening by rapidly announcing and withdrawing multihomed network prefixes when configuring Gradual Latency Spike
mistakesToAvoid.why: Rapidly flapping BGP route announcements triggers upstream ISP route dampening, effectively blackholing network traffic for hours.

title: Vehicle Firmware Build Pipeline Fails During S3 Artifact Upload: Silent Jenkins & S3 Triage
summary: Triage runbook for resolving high-value firmware build pipeline upload failures where AWS S3 shows no error logs and Jenkins output is truncated.
question: A new firmware build pipeline starts failing during artifact uploads. S3 shows no error, Jenkins logs are incomplete. Where do you start?
roleContext: Tesla DevOps Engineer Interview · Round 2: Incident Simulation
intro: When a build pipeline producing large binaries (such as multi-gigabyte vehicle firmware images) fails silently during S3 upload without S3 errors or complete Jenkins logs, the failure occurs client-side before the HTTP request completes: Jenkins agent out-of-memory (OOM) killed by the Linux kernel, ephemeral disk space depletion, or AWS CLI multi-part upload timeout.

steps.title: Check Linux Kernel dmesg for OOM-Killer Execution
steps.description: When Jenkins logs truncate abruptly without a stack trace, the process was killed violently by `SIGKILL` (signal 9) rather than exiting gracefully. Check `dmesg` or system logs on the build node for `Out of memory: Killed process`.
steps.codeBlock:
# Check for OOM killer termination on Jenkins agent
dmesg -T | grep -i -E 'oom[-_]killer|killed process'
# If on Kubernetes runner:
kubectl describe pod <jenkins-agent-pod> | grep -i 'OOMKilled'

steps.title: Inspect Agent Ephemeral Disk Space & Temp Inodes
steps.description: The AWS CLI and SDKs buffer large multi-part uploads in the local temporary directory (`/tmp`) before splitting into 5 MB chunks. If the agent disk hits 100%, the process crashes instantly.
steps.codeBlock:
df -h /tmp
df -i /tmp

steps.title: Enable Verbose AWS CLI Debug Telemetry
steps.description: Re-run the upload command with `--debug`. This exposes exact TCP socket timeouts, SSL handshake failures, and IAM STS token expiration during long-running uploads.
steps.codeBlock: aws s3 cp firmware.bin s3://tesla-firmware-builds/ --debug > upload_debug.log 2>&1

steps.title: Tune Multi-Part Upload Concurrency and Chunk Size
steps.description:
Adjust AWS S3 CLI configurations to handle massive firmware binaries safely:
Increase `multipart_chunksize` to `64MB` and tune `max_concurrent_requests` to avoid saturating agent memory and file descriptors.
steps.codeBlock:
aws configure set default.s3.multipart_threshold 64MB
aws configure set default.s3.multipart_chunksize 64MB
aws configure set default.s3.max_concurrent_requests 10

keyTakeaway: Incomplete Jenkins logs indicate the runner process was killed violently by the Linux kernel OOM-killer or ran out of /tmp disk space during S3 multipart upload buffering. Check dmesg and tune S3 chunk sizes.
elevatorPitch: Check dmesg -T on the agent for Linux OOM-killer terminating the upload process with SIGKILL.
Verify local agent /tmp disk space and inode availability.
Execute the upload with the aws s3 --debug flag to uncover socket resets or expired STS tokens.
Tune AWS S3 multipart_chunksize to 64MB and control concurrency to reduce memory overhead.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to configure lifecycle expiration rules for incomplete multipart S3 uploads
mistakesToAvoid.why: Aborted or incomplete multipart upload parts remain in storage indefinitely, accumulating storage costs without appearing in standard console bucket listings.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Attempting cross-account S3 object copies without configuring destination bucket ownership overrides
mistakesToAvoid.why: By default, objects uploaded across accounts remain owned by the uploader account unless `bucket-owner-full-control` is explicitly enforced.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Relying on public internet S3 endpoints from inside private VPC subnets instead of S3 Gateway Endpoints
mistakesToAvoid.why: VPC S3 Gateway Endpoints eliminate NAT Gateway data processing fees and ensure high-throughput storage traffic remains entirely on the private AWS network.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Enabling S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) without verifying versioning status on both source and destination buckets in tesla-q005-firmware-build-pipeline-s3-artifact-upload-failure
mistakesToAvoid.why: CRR strictly requires S3 Versioning to be enabled on both source and destination buckets to synchronize object revisions and delete markers.

title: Cilium CNI Update Breaks Inter-Pod Communication for One Namespace: Triage and BPF Map Verification
summary: Production triage runbook when a Cilium eBPF CNI update breaks pod-to-pod network traffic selectively across a single namespace.
question: You deployed a Cilium update, and suddenly inter-pod communication breaks for one namespace. What’s your triage approach to confirm root cause?
roleContext: Tesla DevOps Engineer Interview · Round 2: Incident Simulation
intro: When a Cilium CNI update selectively breaks networking for only one namespace while others function normally, the core CNI daemon and host kernel eBPF subsystem are operational. The failure is isolated to namespace-specific NetworkPolicies, Cilium Endpoint identity desynchronization in BPF maps, or strict ingress/egress default-deny rule enforcement triggered by schema changes.

steps.title: Use Cilium CLI to Inspect Namespace Endpoints & Identity Maps
steps.description: Run `cilium-dbg endpoint list` on the node hosting affected pods. Verify whether pods in the broken namespace have valid Cilium Security Identities or are flagged in `WaitingForIdentity` or `Disconnecting` states.
steps.codeBlock:
# Inspect endpoints and security identities
cilium-dbg endpoint list
# Or via Kubernetes CLI:
kubectl get ciliumendpoints -n <broken-namespace>

steps.title: Audit NetworkPolicies & CiliumNetworkPolicies in the Namespace
steps.description: Cilium updates frequently introduce stricter parser validations for `CiliumNetworkPolicy` or `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy`. An existing policy with deprecated selectors or malformed port definitions may suddenly compile into a default-deny BPF filter.
steps.codeBlock:
kubectl get cnp,netpol -n <broken-namespace>
# Temporarily inspect policy drop events via Cilium monitor
cilium-dbg monitor --type drop

steps.title: Inspect BPF Map Drops & Packet Trace with Hubble
steps.description: Leverage Hubble (Cilium's eBPF observability engine) to trace dropped packets in real time. Hubble displays the exact dropped TCP flow, the source/destination pod identity, and the exact policy rule verdict.
steps.codeBlock:
hubble observe --namespace <broken-namespace> --verdict DROPPED
# Output pattern:
# TIMESTAMP: default/pod-a -> broken-ns/pod-b: DROPPED (Policy denied by cnp: deny-all-ingress)

steps.title: Re-synchronize Cilium Endpoint BPF Maps or Roll Back Policy
steps.description: If BPF maps are corrupted or out of sync with etcd, regenerate the endpoint BPF programs without restarting pods.
steps.codeBlock: cilium-dbg endpoint regenerate <endpoint-id>

keyTakeaway: Selective namespace packet drops post-Cilium update indicate NetworkPolicy compilation changes or BPF identity desynchronization. Use 'hubble observe --verdict DROPPED' to pinpoint the denying policy immediately.
elevatorPitch: Use hubble observe --verdict DROPPED to see real-time packet drops and the exact policy rule responsible.
Check cilium-dbg endpoint list to ensure pods have assigned security identities.
Review CiliumNetworkPolicies in the namespace for newly enforced syntax rules.
Regenerate BPF endpoint maps via cilium-dbg endpoint regenerate to restore connectivity.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Configuring Service selector labels that mismatch underlying Pod manifest metadata when configuring Cilium Update Breaks
mistakesToAvoid.why: A typo in `spec.selector` causes the Service endpoints list (`kubectl get endpoints`) to remain empty, resulting in `503 Service Unavailable` or timeouts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting explicit ingressClassName specifications when running multiple ingress controllers when configuring Cilium Update Breaks
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without an explicit `ingressClassName`, ingress resources are either ignored or picked up unpredictably by competing controllers.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Depleting worker node subnet IP address allocations under VPC CNI or Azure CNI when configuring Cilium Update Breaks
mistakesToAvoid.why: Direct VPC pod networking allocates real subnet IPs; failing to monitor IP pools causes new pods to stay stuck indefinitely in `ContainerCreating`.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Attempting network triage without inspecting kubectl describe service and EndpointSlice resources when configuring Cilium Update Breaks
mistakesToAvoid.why: Verifying EndpointSlice population immediately determines whether a connectivity failure is caused by pod labeling, readiness probes, or routing.

title: 30% of Superchargers Report Backend Unavailable While Dashboards Are Green: DNS, TLS & Routing Triage
summary: Incident isolation framework when 30% of European Superchargers report backend connectivity failure while core cloud monitoring displays 100% green.
question: 30% of Tesla Superchargers in Europe report 'backend unavailable', but cloud dashboards show all green. How would you isolate whether it’s DNS, TLS, or routing drift?
roleContext: Tesla DevOps Engineer Interview · Round 2: Energy Grid Fire Drills
intro: When 30% of edge devices in a specific continent fail to communicate while central cloud dashboards report all green, the problem is not in the central backend application. The failure is partitioned along the edge network path: localized BGP Anycast routing drops, regional ISP recursive DNS poisoning, or expired intermediate TLS CA certificates on older firmware revisions.

steps.title: Isolate Geographical & ISP Distribution
steps.description: Map the 30% failing Supercharger telemetry by cellular carrier / ISP (e.g. Vodafone, Orange, Deutsche Telekom) and geographic country. If 100% of affected chargers share a single cellular carrier or Point of Presence (PoP), the issue is upstream ISP routing, not Tesla software.

steps.title: Isolate DNS Resolution Failure
steps.description: Execute remote diagnostic probes from Supercharger cellular modems. Test if the edge device can resolve `backend.supercharge.tesla.com`. If queries return `NXDOMAIN` or SERVFAIL on regional ISP DNS servers while succeeding on `8.8.8.8`, it is DNS cache poisoning or DNSSEC validation failures.
steps.codeBlock:
# Remote diagnostic curl from edge modem
curl -v --dns-servers 8.8.8.8 https://backend.supercharge.tesla.com/healthz

steps.title: Isolate TLS Handshake & CA Certificate Chain Expiry
steps.description: If DNS resolves, inspect the TLS handshake. Check whether a recent certificate rotation introduced an intermediate CA certificate that older Supercharger firmware root stores do not recognize, causing client-side SSL handshake rejections.
steps.codeBlock:
openssl s_client -connect backend.supercharge.tesla.com:443 -servername backend.supercharge.tesla.com
# Look for: "verify error:num=20:unable to get local issuer certificate"

steps.title: Isolate BGP Anycast Routing Drift & MTU Black Holes
steps.description: If running BGP Anycast across European Edge PoPs (Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam), run `mtr` / traceroute from affected cell towers. Check for BGP route flapping, asymmetric routing drops, or PMTU (Path MTU) discovery drops where packets over 1400 bytes are silently discarded.
steps.highlight: Edge Reality: When edge hardware reports outages but servers are green, the network path between the cellular carrier and cloud edge PoP is compromised.

keyTakeaway: Isolate by correlating failure to cellular carrier and region. Systematically test: 1) DNS resolution via cellular DNS vs 8.8.8.8, 2) TLS certificate trust chain compatibility on older firmware, 3) BGP Anycast PoP drops and MTU black holes.
elevatorPitch: Correlate affected Superchargers by geographic country and cellular carrier to identify localized network boundaries.
Test DNS resolution from edge modems against public resolvers to rule out ISP DNS cache poisoning.
Verify TLS certificate chain validity against older firmware trust stores to catch SSL validation rejections.
Run MTR/traceroute to identify BGP Anycast routing drops or Path MTU packet fragmentation black holes.
