keyTakeaway: Store secrets encrypted in Git with Ansible Vault, inject passwords into ephemeral in-memory files (/dev/shm) in CI/CD runners, and enforce no_log: true on all sensitive tasks to guarantee zero credential leakage in build logs.
elevatorPitch: Encrypt sensitive variables with AES-256 using 'ansible-vault' or 'encrypt_string' and version control them in Git.
Store the vault decryption key in CI/CD masked secret vaults (GitHub Secrets / HashiCorp Vault).
Inject the key at runtime into in-memory temporary storage (/dev/shm/.vault_pass) or pass ANSIBLE_VAULT_PASSWORD_FILE.
Enforce 'no_log: true' on all template, URI, and database tasks to suppress secret output from CI console logs.
Rotate credentials seamlessly using 'ansible-vault rekey group_vars/all/vault.yml'.
Use separate vault-ids (e.g. --vault-id dev@prompt, --vault-id prod@file) for fine-grained multi-environment access.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting no_log: true on secret-consuming tasks
mistakesToAvoid.why: CI/CD build logs permanently store task inputs in plaintext, exposing rotated database credentials to anyone with repository read access.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Storing vault password files permanently on disk or inside Docker images
mistakesToAvoid.why: Defeats the purpose of encryption if build containers or runner disks can be snapshotted or inspected.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using a single global vault password for dev, staging, and production
mistakesToAvoid.why: Violates least-privilege security principles. Use Ansible vault-id to maintain separate keys across environments.

title: Ansible Q4: Why is an Nginx restart handler not firing even though a template configuration task notified it and how do you prevent broken configurations from reloading [L2]
summary: Handlers only fire at the end of a play if all previous tasks succeed. If an intermediate task fails, handlers are skipped by default. Fix by setting force_handlers: yes or meta: flush_handlers, and validate configs before reloading with validate directives.
question: In Ansible, a critical task in a playbook failed midway through execution, preventing service notification handlers from triggering. Why did this happen, and how do you enforce handler execution on failure?
roleContext: Senior DevOps / SRE Scenario #4 · Handlers & Error Handling
intro: "In production web tier rollouts, service restarts must only occur if configuration files are syntactically valid and all preceding dependencies succeed. Interviewers use this question to test understanding of Ansible's task execution lifecycle, handler notification queues, and safety guardrails."

steps.title: Diagnose Handler Execution Lifecycle
steps.description: Handlers in Ansible do not run immediately when notified. Instead, they are added to an internal queue and only executed once at the very end of the play after all regular tasks finish successfully:
items: If any intermediate task fails before play completion, Ansible aborts and skips the handler queue entirely.
If multiple tasks notify the same handler (e.g. notify: Restart Nginx), the handler executes exactly once, preventing flapping.

steps.title: Force Handler Execution When Needed
steps.description: To ensure handlers run even when non-critical downstream tasks fail, declare force_handlers: yes:
items: Add force_handlers: yes at the play level in your playbook.
Or pass the CLI flag: ansible-playbook site.yml --force-handlers.
Alternatively, flush queued handlers immediately midway through the play using: - meta: flush_handlers.

steps.title: Prevent Corrupt Configuration Reloads
steps.description: Never restart services on unverified template outputs. Use module validate directives to test syntax before moving files into production paths:
items: template: src=nginx.conf.j2 dest=/etc/nginx/nginx.conf validate='nginx -t -c %s'
Ansible writes the template to a temporary path (%s), tests syntax, and aborts if invalid, leaving the existing production config untouched.

keyTakeaway: Handlers execute only at the end of successful plays. Use force_handlers: yes to ensure service reloads occur during partial task failures, and always enforce atomic pre-validation with validate: 'nginx -t -c %s' to prevent broken syntax from taking down live traffic.
elevatorPitch: Ansible handlers run once at the end of a play only if all preceding tasks succeed.
If any subsequent task fails, Ansible aborts the run and skips all notified handlers by default.
Enable 'force_handlers: yes' in the play header or pass '--force-handlers' to trigger handlers despite non-critical task failures.
Use '- meta: flush_handlers' to force immediate handler execution between dependent tasks rather than waiting for play completion.
Always include pre-flight validation on config templates: 'validate: nginx -t -c %s' to catch syntax errors before files are moved to /etc/.
Handlers are deduplicated automatically — 10 tasks notifying 'Restart Nginx' trigger exactly 1 restart.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Restarting services directly in tasks rather than using notified handlers
mistakesToAvoid.why: Causes cascading service restarts on every task, introducing unnecessary latency spikes and dropping live customer connections.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Deploying templates to /etc/nginx/ without a validate directive
mistakesToAvoid.why: If a template contains a Jinja2 rendering typo, Nginx fails to restart and the web server crashes completely.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Misunderstanding when meta: flush_handlers runs
mistakesToAvoid.why: Flushing handlers too early restarts services before supporting assets (SSL certs, upstream sockets) are placed.

title: Ansible Q5: Your team uses AWS EC2 Auto Scaling Static IP inventory breaks daily How do you implement aws_ec2 dynamic inventory with keyed groups and tags [L2]
summary: Replace static hosts files with the official amazon.aws.aws_ec2 YAML inventory plugin. Query live AWS APIs to discover instances dynamically, filter by running states, and organize hosts using keyed_groups based on AWS tags.
question: You manage 500+ AWS EC2 instances across multiple environments. How do you implement Ansible AWS dynamic inventories with keyed groups and tag filtering for zero maintenance?
roleContext: Senior DevOps / Cloud Engineer Scenario #5 · Dynamic Cloud Inventory
intro: "In modern autoscaling cloud environments, instance lifecycles are ephemeral. Static IP inventories result in immediate configuration drift and SSH unreachable errors. I solve this by configuring the amazon.aws.aws_ec2 inventory plugin with tag-based keyed groups and private IP resolution."

steps.title: Create Declarative aws_ec2.yml Config
steps.description: Configure the official AWS collection inventory plugin file (must end with aws_ec2.yml or aws_ec2.yaml):
items: Specify plugin: plugin: amazon.aws.aws_ec2
Define target regions: regions: [us-east-1, eu-west-1]
Filter out terminated or stopping instances: filters: { instance-state-name: running }
Resolve hostnames via private IP: hostnames: [private-ip-address]

steps.title: Construct Dynamic Groups Using AWS Tags
steps.description: Automatically classify instances into Ansible host groups based on their AWS resource tags:
items: keyed_groups:
- key: tags.Environment   prefix: env → creates env_production, env_staging
- key: tags.Role   prefix: role → creates role_webserver, role_api

steps.title: Verify and Target Dynamic Fleets
steps.description: Audit the discovered infrastructure tree before executing configuration updates:
items: Verify inventory tree: ansible-inventory -i aws_ec2.yml --graph
Inspect metadata in JSON: ansible-inventory -i aws_ec2.yml --list
Execute playbook against dynamic group: ansible-playbook -i aws_ec2.yml deploy.yml --limit 'role_webserver:&env_production'

keyTakeaway: The amazon.aws.aws_ec2 plugin queries AWS APIs in real time, eliminating static inventory decay. Grouping instances with keyed_groups allows precise, tag-driven targeting of autoscaling fleets across VPCs and availability zones.
elevatorPitch: Static inventory files fail in autoscaling architectures where instance IDs and IP addresses change constantly.
Deploy the 'amazon.aws.aws_ec2' inventory plugin configured in 'aws_ec2.yml' with live AWS API queries.
Filter instances to only running states: 'filters: instance-state-name: running'.
Generate dynamic host groups using 'keyed_groups' mapped to AWS tags (Environment, Role, Service).
Set 'hostnames: private-ip-address' for secure private VPC communication via bastion/VPN.
Validate discovered infrastructure with 'ansible-inventory -i aws_ec2.yml --graph' before launching playbooks.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Naming the inventory file without the required aws_ec2.yml suffix
mistakesToAvoid.why: Ansible's auto plugin detection ignores files that do not match the *aws_ec2.yml naming pattern.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Defaulting to public IP hostnames for instances in private subnets
mistakesToAvoid.why: Private EC2 instances lack public IPs; playbooks fail with connection timeouts unless private-ip-address is declared.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to filter instance-state-name: running
mistakesToAvoid.why: Ansible attempts to connect over SSH to stopped and terminating instances, causing timeouts and failed plays.

title: Ansible Q6: When would you use the serial keyword versus forks in Ansible playbooks and how does serial enable rolling zero-downtime canary deployments [L3]
summary: Forks governs task-level parallel concurrency across hosts. The serial directive controls batch size for rolling updates, executing the entire play across a subset of hosts (e.g. 10%, then 50%) to guarantee zero-downtime availability.
question: When would you use the serial keyword versus forks in Ansible playbooks, and how does serial enable rolling zero-downtime canary deployments?
roleContext: Staff DevOps / Platform Engineer Scenario #6 · Release Engineering
intro: "Deploying updates across high-traffic production web tiers requires rolling canary strategies. Interviewers evaluate whether candidates distinguish between raw process concurrency (forks) and orchestrated batch rolling releases (serial) that integrate with load balancer health checks."

steps.title: Distinguish Forks vs. Serial Execution
steps.description: Understand the fundamental operational difference between task parallelism and play batching:
items: Forks: Dictates how many worker processes communicate over SSH simultaneously for a single task. A play of 100 hosts with forks: 50 executes each task in 2 parallel batches, but all 100 hosts remain in the same play lifecycle.
Serial: Batches the entire play from start to finish. A play with serial: 25% completes all tasks and handlers on the first 25 hosts before moving to the next 25.

steps.title: Configure Progressive Canary Rollouts
steps.description: Use list syntax in serial to implement safe canary percentages:
items: Batch 1 tests 1 single canary host. If tasks fail or health checks drop, execution halts immediately.
Batch 2 expands to 10% of the fleet; Batch 3 expands to 50%; Batch 4 updates the remainder.

steps.title: Integrate with Load Balancer Draining
steps.description: Guarantee zero dropped connections by deregistering targets from the ALB prior to application restart:
items: Task 1: Deregister host from AWS Target Group using community.aws.elb_target.
Task 2: Wait for active connections to drain (e.g. pause: seconds=20).
Task 3: Upgrade app binary and restart service.
Task 4: Run local health check: uri: url=http://localhost:8080/health status_code=200.
Task 5: Re-register host with Target Group and verify healthy status before advancing to next batch.

keyTakeaway: Forks scales task execution speed; serial controls blast radius during rolling updates. Combining progressive serial percentages with load balancer target deregistration delivers robust zero-downtime canary deployments.
elevatorPitch: Forks controls how many hosts execute a single task in parallel (default 5).
Serial controls how many hosts execute the entire play end-to-end as a self-contained batch.
Use progressive serial percentages: 'serial: ["1", "10%", "50%", "100%"]' to catch production regressions on a single canary node.
Combine serial with AWS ALB target deregistration and connection draining before touching application binaries.
Perform local URI health checks on localhost before re-registering the node into the live load balancer pool.
Set 'max_fail_percentage: 0' to immediately abort the deployment if any single node in the canary batch reports failure.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Attempting rolling updates using only the forks parameter
mistakesToAvoid.why: Forks executes tasks across the whole inventory; all 200 nodes will restart their services at roughly the same time, causing total outage.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Re-registering instances into the load balancer without local smoke tests
mistakesToAvoid.why: Sends live production traffic to unhealthy instances before their runtimes have initialized.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Neglecting connection draining timeouts on the load balancer
mistakesToAvoid.why: Immediately killing application daemons drops in-flight HTTP requests, generating 502 Bad Gateway errors.

title: Ansible Q7: A junior engineer uses the shell module for every task in an enterprise playbook What are the security risks when should you use command vs shell and how do you enforce idempotency [L1]
summary: The command module executes binaries directly without spawning /bin/sh, preventing shell injection. The shell module invokes the remote shell, enabling pipes and redirects. Enforce idempotency on shell commands using creates/removes attributes.
question: In Ansible, a junior engineer uses the shell module for simple file copy and grep operations. Why is the command or native module preferred over shell, and what are the security risks?
roleContext: Junior / Associate DevOps Scenario #7 · Security & Best Practices
intro: "Relying on the shell module for every automation task is a common anti-pattern that introduces shell injection vulnerabilities, breaks idempotency, and circumvents Ansible's declarative state model. I structure my response around security isolation, module selection criteria, and state guardrails."

steps.title: Identify Security Risks of the Shell Module
steps.description: The shell module passes command strings through /bin/sh on the remote target. If any variable interpolated into the command originates from user input or external APIs, attackers can inject arbitrary shell commands via semicolons, backticks, or pipes (e.g. app_name: 'test; rm -rf /').
items: Shell Injection: Unsanitized variables allow arbitrary command execution.
Environment Bleed: Inherits user profile aliases and environment quirks that cause non-deterministic behavior.

steps.title: Apply Strict Module Selection Criteria
steps.description: Follow the Ansible module hierarchy rule:
items: 1st Choice: Native Modules: Always prefer native declarative modules (file, service, package, git) which guarantee cross-platform idempotency.
2nd Choice: command Module: Use command when calling existing binaries without shell operators (e.g. ansible all -m command -a "uptime").
Last Resort: shell Module: Use shell strictly when pipes (|), redirects (>), or stream processing are required.

steps.title: Enforce Idempotency on Shell Tasks
steps.description: Custom scripts executed via command or shell always return changed: true by default. Enforce idempotency using built-in attributes:
items: shell: /opt/setup.sh creates=/opt/app/.configured
shell: tar -xzf bundle.tar.gz creates=/opt/bundle/bin
Declare changed_when: false for read-only inspection commands.

keyTakeaway: Always prioritize native modules first, the command module second, and the shell module strictly as a last resort. Guard all custom scripts with creates or removes to guarantee idempotent behavior.
elevatorPitch: The shell module passes strings through /bin/sh, exposing systems to shell injection if variables are untrusted.
The command module bypasses /bin/sh and invokes binaries directly, ensuring faster, secure execution.
Always prefer native declarative modules (copy, file, package, service) over bash scripts.
Use the shell module only when stream processing, pipes (|), or redirection (>) are strictly necessary.
Enforce idempotency on shell commands using 'creates: /path/file' or 'removes: /path/file'.
Mark read-only diagnostic commands with 'changed_when: false' to prevent false positive configuration alerts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using shell to install packages (e.g. shell: apt-get install nginx)
mistakesToAvoid.why: Bypasses package cache management, GPG key validation, and Ansible's native error handling.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to sanitize variables passed into shell tasks
mistakesToAvoid.why: Enables critical shell injection exploits across managed fleet infrastructure.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Leaving command tasks without creates or changed_when definitions
mistakesToAvoid.why: Every playbook run falsely reports 'changed', triggering unnecessary downstream handlers and skewing CI metrics.

title: Ansible Q8: Before applying a disruptive network configuration change what is the difference between syntax-check and check diff and what are the limitations of check mode [L1]
summary: syntax-check parses YAML syntax and module arguments locally without connecting to hosts. Check mode (--check) connects over SSH and simulates execution against host reality. Combining --check --diff shows unified line-by-line diffs before applying changes.
question: Before rolling out changes to production, how do you utilize Ansible check mode (--check) versus --syntax-check, and what are the critical limitations of dry-run validation?
roleContext: Junior / Associate DevOps Scenario #8 · Verification & Testing
intro: "In zero-tolerance production environments like financial networks, touching configurations without pre-flight validation is a career-limiting move. Interviewers test whether you know what checks run locally versus what runs against live nodes, and why dry-run mode can sometimes produce false failures."

steps.title: Local Syntax Verification (--syntax-check)
steps.description: ansible-playbook site.yml --syntax-check verifies YAML formatting, task indentation, and module parameter spelling on the local controller. It never contacts managed nodes or queries cloud APIs.
items: Catches YAML tab errors, missing colons, and malformed task dictionaries.
Runs in under 1 second; ideal for pre-commit Git hooks and CI PR validation.

steps.title: Live State Dry-Run (--check --diff)
steps.description: ansible-playbook site.yml --check --diff connects over SSH to target inventory nodes and simulates execution against real-time system state:
items: --check: Simulates tasks without altering disk files or daemon states.
--diff: Prints unified line-by-line diffs showing exact lines added (+) and removed (-).
Allows engineers to review exact config changes before production execution.

steps.title: Recognize Check Mode Limitations
steps.description: Check mode has key architectural limitations that senior engineers must anticipate:
items: Dependency Breakage: If Task A creates a user and Task B deploys files owned by that user, Task B will fail in check mode because the user was never actually created.
Custom Scripts: Custom shell tasks do not support check mode unless configured with check_mode: false.

keyTakeaway: syntax-check validates code locally; check mode simulates execution against live nodes. Always combine --check with --diff for production previews, but anticipate that downstream tasks depending on simulated state may fail during dry runs.
elevatorPitch: --syntax-check validates YAML formatting and module schemas locally without touching remote servers.
--check connects over SSH and simulates task execution against real-time system state without committing changes.
--diff displays a unified line-by-line diff of configuration files that would be modified.
The gold standard pre-flight command is: 'ansible-playbook site.yml --check --diff'.
Limitation: Check mode fails when later tasks depend on resources that earlier tasks only simulated creating.
Override check mode behavior on read-only tasks using 'check_mode: false' to ensure facts are gathered accurately.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming --syntax-check verifies whether host variables or files exist
mistakesToAvoid.why: Syntax check only validates YAML code structure; it cannot detect missing files or unreachable IP addresses.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Running disruptive playbooks in production without reviewing --diff output
mistakesToAvoid.why: Dry-run previews prevent unintended mass overrides of shared configuration files.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Panicking when check mode fails on dependent tasks
mistakesToAvoid.why: Experienced SREs recognize that downstream tasks requiring real upstream artifacts will naturally report errors in dry-run mode.

title: Ansible Q9: During a maintenance window ansible all -m ping reports UNREACHABLE for 30 out of 100 Linux servers Walk me through your step-by-step diagnostic triage runbook [L1]
summary: Triage UNREACHABLE errors by isolating network connectivity, SSH authentication, bastion proxy hops, and Python interpreter paths. Use -vvvv to inspect raw SSH commands and ControlMaster sockets.
question: During a scheduled maintenance window, ansible all -m ping reports 'UNREACHABLE' for 30 out of 100 Linux servers. Walk me through your step-by-step diagnostic triage runbook using SSH verbosity, bastions, and ControlMaster.
roleContext: Junior / Associate DevOps Scenario #9 · Network & SSH Triage
intro: "In fleet management, 'UNREACHABLE' is the most common operational error. It typically stems from network security groups, expired SSH certificates, bastion proxy jumps, or missing remote Python interpreters. I approach this using systematic bottom-up network and SSH debugging."

steps.title: Run Maximum Verbosity to Inspect Raw SSH
steps.description: Execute the ping module against a single unreachable host with full -vvvv debug output:
items: ansible failed_host -m ping -vvvv
Inspect the exact OpenSSH command generated by Ansible.
Identify failure stage: TCP connection timeout, host key verification mismatch, or permission denied (publickey).

steps.title: Validate Layer 3/4 Network & Security Groups
steps.description: Confirm basic network reachability from the controller to the target node:
items: Check port 22 reachability: nc -zv -w 3 22
If timeout occurs: verify AWS VPC Security Groups, Route Tables, and NACLs.
Verify bastion ProxyJump configuration in ansible.cfg: ProxyJump=bastion.corp.internal.

steps.title: Verify Authentication and Python Interpreter
steps.description: If SSH connects but Ansible still fails, inspect permissions and runtime binaries:
items: Test direct SSH login with Ansible key: ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa user@target-ip
Verify remote Python path: Ansible requires Python 3 on target hosts. If located in non-standard paths, configure ansible_python_interpreter: /usr/bin/python3 in host variables.

keyTakeaway: An UNREACHABLE error points to network routing, SSH keys, or Python binary availability. Use -vvvv to isolate the exact SSH command, verify port 22 reachability, and check ansible_python_interpreter path definitions.
elevatorPitch: Isolate an unreachable host and run 'ansible host -m ping -vvvv' to view the raw OpenSSH handshake.
Check Layer 4 network connectivity using 'nc -zv <target-ip> 22' to rule out AWS Security Groups and NACLs.
Verify SSH key authentication and permissions (chmod 600 id_rsa) on the controller.
Check Bastion/Jump host ProxyJump settings in ssh_args within ansible.cfg.
Confirm that Python 3 is installed on the remote host and declare 'ansible_python_interpreter: /usr/bin/python3'.
Clear stale SSH ControlMaster sockets in ~/.ansible/cp/ that can cause persistent connection hangs.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Testing ping against all 30 hosts at once instead of isolating one host with -vvvv
mistakesToAvoid.why: Generates unreadable console noise; senior engineers isolate a single representative failure to identify root cause.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Assuming ping module uses ICMP packets
mistakesToAvoid.why: Ansible's ping module executes an SSH login and runs a small Python snippet; it requires SSH access and Python on targets, not ICMP.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Ignoring stale ControlMaster multiplexing sockets
mistakesToAvoid.why: Old sockets in ~/.ansible/cp/ cause persistent connection failures even after network issues are resolved.

title: Ansible Q10: How do you structure complex Ansible projects using Ansible Galaxy roles and collections for enterprise multi-cloud governance [L2]
summary: Structure enterprise Ansible repositories using modular Galaxy roles and declarative requirements.yml manifests. Separate roles (reusable task bundles) from collections (module and plugin distributions).
question: Multiple engineering teams are creating duplicate tasks across repositories. How do you design an enterprise Ansible architecture using Galaxy roles, collections, and requirements.yml for reusability and CI/CD governance?
roleContext: Senior DevOps / Platform Engineer Scenario #10 · Modular Architecture
intro: "Monolithic, copy-pasted playbooks create technical debt and maintenance nightmares. Enterprise platform engineering requires decoupling modules and plugins (Collections) from declarative task logic (Roles), governed by strict semantic versioning in requirements.yml."

steps.title: Differentiate Roles and Collections
steps.description: Establish clear architectural boundaries across the organization:
items: Roles: Reusable units of automation including tasks, handlers, variables, defaults, templates, and meta definitions (e.g. role: nginx).
Collections: The modern packaging format distributing modules, action plugins, filter plugins, and connection plugins (e.g. amazon.aws, kubernetes.core).

steps.title: Declare Dependencies in requirements.yml
steps.description: Pin roles and collections using exact version constraints committed to Git:
items:
collections:
  - name: amazon.aws
    version: '>=6.0.0'

roles:
  - src: git@github.com:org/ansible-role-hardening.git
    scm: git
    version: v2.1.0
Install non-interactively in CI/CD: ansible-galaxy install -r requirements.yml -p ./roles/

steps.title: Standardize Enterprise Repository Layout
steps.description: Maintain a production repository structure:
items: ansible.cfg, requirements.yml, site.yml at root.
inventory/ containing production/, staging/ with dynamic configs.
roles/ containing downloaded external roles (git-ignored) and internal roles.
group_vars/ and host_vars/ for environment variable overrides.

keyTakeaway: Decouple automation logic using modular roles and collections versioned in requirements.yml. Standardize repository structure and enforce automated linting to enable scalable multi-team governance.
elevatorPitch: Collections distribute modules and plugins; Roles package reusable tasks, variables, and templates.
Use a declarative 'requirements.yml' manifest to pin exact semantic versions of external dependencies.
Install dependencies non-interactively in CI/CD pipelines using 'ansible-galaxy install -r requirements.yml'.
Git-ignore external downloaded roles while version-controlling custom internal business logic.
Organize inventories cleanly by environment (production/staging) with separate group_vars.
Enforce linting and formatting across PRs using 'ansible-lint' and 'yamllint' in automated pipelines.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Committing third-party Galaxy role files directly into internal Git repositories
mistakesToAvoid.why: Bloats repo size and breaks upstream update tracks. Commit requirements.yml and install dynamically instead.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting version constraints in requirements.yml
mistakesToAvoid.why: Upstream breaking changes automatically pull into production builds, causing sudden deployment failures.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Hardcoding environment-specific IPs or passwords inside roles
mistakesToAvoid.why: Destroys reusability; roles must define variables in defaults/main.yml that can be overridden in group_vars.

title: Ansible Q11: Playbook execution against 500 servers takes 45 minutes on Gathering Facts How do you optimize fact gathering and implement fact caching [L2]
summary: Fact gathering against large fleets creates severe network and CPU bottlenecks. Optimize by disabling facts when not needed, filtering specific facts, or implementing persistent fact caching with Redis or JSON backends.
question: Ansible playbook runs take over 15 minutes across a fleet of 800 servers, with 70% of execution time spent during fact-gathering. How do you optimize fact gathering and caching?
roleContext: Senior DevOps / SRE Scenario #11 · Performance Engineering
intro: "Gathering facts executes the setup module across every host, returning hundreds of kilobytes of JSON per node. At scale across 500+ nodes, this consumes massive network bandwidth and controller CPU time. I optimize this by disabling unnecessary fact steps, pruning gathering subsets, or enabling Redis fact caching."

steps.title: Disable Facts When Not Required
steps.description: Most deployment playbooks only deploy pre-built packages and configurations, requiring zero host facts. Turn off fact gathering globally in the play:
items: gather_facts: false at the top of your play.
Saves 100% of the fact collection phase, reducing start times from minutes to seconds.

steps.title: Gather Only Specific Fact Subsets
steps.description: If your play only needs networking or OS family information, prune the gathering scope using gather_subset:
items: gather_subset: ['!all', '!min', 'network']
Avoids expensive disk partition, hardware, and virtual memory scans across large fleets.

steps.title: Implement Centralized Fact Caching (Redis/JSON)
steps.description: Cache gathered facts persistently on the controller or in Redis so subsequent runs bypass the setup module entirely:
items:
In ansible.cfg, configure Redis caching:
gathering = smart
fact_caching = redis
fact_caching_timeout = 86400
fact_caching_connection = localhost:6379:0
With gathering = smart, Ansible only collects facts if the cache has expired or host is new.

keyTakeaway: Fact collection across 500+ hosts is a major performance bottleneck. Disable facts when not needed (gather_facts: false), restrict scopes with gather_subset, or enable smart fact caching with Redis to cut execution times by over 80%.
elevatorPitch: The default setup module collects hundreds of facts per host, creating severe network bottlenecks on 500+ node fleets.
Set 'gather_facts: false' for standard application deployments that do not evaluate host conditions.
Use 'gather_subset: ["!all", "network"]' to collect only the specific facts your templates require.
Enable 'gathering = smart' in ansible.cfg to automatically skip fact gathering if facts are already cached.
Implement high-performance fact caching using Redis ('fact_caching = redis') with a 24-hour TTL.
For simple controllers, use file-based JSON caching ('fact_caching = jsonfile') stored in /tmp/ansible_facts.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Leaving gather_facts: true enabled on every single play in a multi-tier playbook
mistakesToAvoid.why: Repeats the expensive 500-node fact collection phase multiple times during a single playbook run.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Setting fact_caching_timeout to 0 or infinite without TTL expiration
mistakesToAvoid.why: Stale cached facts cause playbooks to evaluate outdated IP addresses and memory stats long after hardware changes.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Failing to secure the Redis fact caching backend
mistakesToAvoid.why: Redis stores complete system metadata and environment variables; expose it only on localhost or over TLS.

title: Ansible Q12: A custom shell script returns exit code 0 even when it fails and reports changed every time How do you fix it using register failed_when and changed_when [L1]
summary: Custom scripts frequently violate standard exit code conventions. Capture stdout and return codes using register, override failure logic using failed_when, and accurately enforce changed_when conditions to eliminate false positives.
question: In an Ansible playbook, a custom CLI command returns exit code 1 for non-fatal status warnings, causing the task to fail. How do you tune failed_when and changed_when conditions?
roleContext: Junior / Associate DevOps Scenario #12 · Task Conditioning
intro: "Third-party CLI utilities and legacy bash scripts often hide errors by returning exit code 0, or generate false 'changed' statuses that trigger unnecessary service restarts. I resolve this by capturing task execution telemetry with register and writing explicit failed_when and changed_when expressions."

steps.title: Capture Script Telemetry with register
steps.description: Capture the command's stdout, stderr, and return code into a variable:
items: - name: Run legacy database migration script
command: /opt/scripts/migrate.sh
register: migration_out

steps.title: Override Failure Logic with failed_when
steps.description: Define custom boolean conditions that mark the task as failed even when the exit code is 0:
items:
failed_when:
    - migration_out.rc != 0 or 'ERROR' in migration_out.stdout or 'FAILED' in migration_out.stderr
This halts execution immediately when error patterns appear in stdout, preventing silent failures.

steps.title: Refine Mutation Status with changed_when
steps.description: By default, command/shell tasks always report changed: true. Override this so changes only register when work was actually performed:
items: changed_when: "'MIGRATION_APPLIED' in migration_out.stdout"
If stdout contains 'NO_CHANGES_NEEDED', the task cleanly reports green (ok), preventing downstream restart handlers from firing.

keyTakeaway: Never rely solely on binary exit codes for custom scripts. Register task output and use failed_when to catch embedded error strings, while using changed_when to ensure only actual mutations trigger downstream handlers.
elevatorPitch: By default, Ansible determines success purely by exit code 0 and marks all command/shell tasks as 'changed'.
Use 'register: output_var' to capture stdout, stderr, and return code in task memory.
Use 'failed_when: "'FATAL' in output_var.stdout"' to fail tasks when legacy scripts return exit code 0 on errors.
Use 'changed_when: "'UPDATED' in output_var.stdout"' to prevent false positive 'changed' status on no-op runs.
Set 'changed_when: false' on read-only status and audit commands to maintain pristine idempotency metrics.
Combine conditions with YAML lists to evaluate multiple logical expressions cleanly without complex bash regex.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using ignore_errors: yes instead of failed_when
mistakesToAvoid.why: ignore_errors blindly continues execution on real catastrophic errors; failed_when allows fine-grained error evaluation.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Leaving changed_when undefined on diagnostic shell scripts
mistakesToAvoid.why: Causes monitoring tools and CI reports to show false configuration drifts on every single run.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Checking for substring matching without accounting for case sensitivity
mistakesToAvoid.why: A script outputting 'error' will not match 'ERROR' unless explicitly lowercased via Jinja2 filters.

title: Ansible Q13: Tasks requiring sudo hang indefinitely on remote Debian servers during automated pipeline runs How do you fix passwordless sudo and become timeouts [L2]
summary: Non-interactive CI/CD runs hang when sudo prompts for passwords without a TTY. Configure NOPASSWD in sudoers.d, verify become_user/become_method, and adjust connect/command timeouts in ansible.cfg.
question: Tasks requiring sudo are hanging indefinitely on remote Debian servers during non-interactive automated pipeline runs. What is the root cause, and how do you configure passwordless sudo, --ask-become-pass, and ansible.cfg timeouts?
roleContext: Senior DevOps / SRE Scenario #13 · Privilege Escalation & Auth
intro: "When running Ansible in automated headless pipelines like Jenkins or GitHub Actions, interactive terminal prompts cannot be fulfilled. If sudo requires a password or pty allocation, tasks hang until CI timeouts abort the build. I resolve this by auditing sudoers NOPASSWD policies, become configuration, and timeout settings."

steps.title: Diagnose Non-Interactive Sudo Prompts
steps.description: When become: true is executed, Ansible issues sudo -u root .... In a non-interactive CI runner without a pseudo-terminal (TTY), if the remote sudoers file requires a password, the process hangs waiting for stdin that never arrives.
items: Missing TTY / Prompt Hang: Remote system waits for password entry on stdin.
requiretty Directive: In older RHEL/CentOS systems, Defaults requiretty prevents execution without an interactive terminal.

steps.title: Configure Non-Interactive Sudoers Guardrails
steps.description: Provision a secure, isolated drop-in sudoers file for the Ansible automation service account:
items: Create /etc/sudoers.d/ansible-deploy with permissions 0440.
Declare: ansible ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL
Validate syntax before saving using visudo -cf /etc/sudoers.d/ansible-deploy to prevent syntax lockouts.

steps.title: Tune Become Parameters in ansible.cfg
steps.description: Configure explicit escalation parameters in the controller configuration:
items:
[privilege_escalation]
become = True
become_method = sudo
become_user = root
become_ask_pass = False
For local debugging: pass -K or --ask-become-pass to provide password manually.

keyTakeaway: Automated headless pipelines require passwordless sudo (NOPASSWD) in /etc/sudoers.d/ and become_ask_pass = False. Always validate drop-in sudoers configurations with visudo -cf to avoid catastrophic administrative lockouts.
elevatorPitch: Ansible hangs in CI/CD when sudo prompts for passwords without an active interactive TTY.
Configure NOPASSWD for the dedicated Ansible service user in a dedicated drop-in file: /etc/sudoers.d/ansible.
Always validate sudoers syntax using 'visudo -cf /etc/sudoers.d/ansible' to avoid locking out root access.
Set 'become_ask_pass = False' and 'become_method = sudo' in the [privilege_escalation] section of ansible.cfg.
Remove legacy 'Defaults requiretty' directives from sudoers on enterprise Linux distributions.
Use '-b -K' (--ask-become-pass) only when executing playbooks manually from local workstations.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Editing /etc/sudoers directly instead of using /etc/sudoers.d/ drop-in files
mistakesToAvoid.why: Package updates overwrite /etc/sudoers, and syntax mistakes lock all administrators out of sudo.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Passing plaintext sudo passwords via extra vars (-e 'ansible_sudo_pass=...')
mistakesToAvoid.why: Exposes administrative credentials in process tables (ps aux) and shell history.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Enabling become: true globally on the entire playbook
mistakesToAvoid.why: Violates least-privilege principles; declare become only on specific tasks requiring elevated root privileges.

title: Ansible Q14: A team member uses multiple lineinfile tasks to modify sshd_config Why does this lead to drift and why is Jinja2 templating superior [L2]
summary: Using lineinfile for multi-line configurations creates unpredictable file ordering, duplicate keys, and silent configuration drift. Jinja2 templates (template module) provide declarative, atomic, and auditable single-source-of-truth state.
question: In Ansible infrastructure automation, engineers are modifying configs using lineinfile and template modules. When should you use template versus lineinfile to prevent configuration drift?
roleContext: Senior DevOps / SRE Scenario #14 · Drift Prevention & IaC
intro: "Configuration drift is the enemy of reliable infrastructure. While lineinfile appears convenient for quick single-line changes, using it across complex configuration files turns declarative management into procedural mutation. I structure my answer around failure modes of regex-based line replacement versus declarative Jinja2 templating."

steps.title: Examine lineinfile Failure Modes
steps.description: lineinfile modifies files in-place using regular expression pattern matching. Over time, this introduces subtle production outages:
items: Duplicate Directives: If the regex does not match existing variations (whitespace, comments), lineinfile appends a new line, leaving duplicate conflicting parameters.
Ordering Hazards: In files like sshd_config where Match blocks change scoping for all subsequent lines, appending lines to the end breaks global security settings.
Ghost Configurations: It cannot delete orphaned settings that are no longer declared in the playbook.

steps.title: Adopt Jinja2 Templating (template Module)
steps.description: The template module treats configuration files as declarative, complete artifacts:
items: Single Source of Truth: The rendered output completely replaces the destination file.
Atomic Overwrite: Ansible writes to a temporary file, validates syntax, and swaps the file atomically, eliminating partial file writes.
Dynamic Logic: Supports loops, conditionals, and filters directly within the template.

steps.title: Implement Pre-Flight Validation and Backups
steps.description: Combine templating with built-in safety parameters:
items:
template:
  src: sshd_config.j2
  dest: /etc/ssh/sshd_config
  backup: yes
  validate: '/usr/sbin/sshd -t -f %s'
If template rendering produces invalid sshd syntax, Ansible halts, preserves the backup, and leaves active SSH connections undisturbed.

keyTakeaway: lineinfile is a procedural patch tool prone to regex bugs and orphaned settings. The template module enforces full declarative state, eliminates configuration drift, and supports atomic pre-flight validation.
elevatorPitch: lineinfile relies on fragile regex matching that frequently creates duplicate keys and misplaces scoped directives (like sshd Match blocks).
lineinfile cannot remove obsolete configuration parameters that are deleted from your playbook, causing silent drift.
The 'template' module renders Jinja2 files as complete, authoritative declarative configurations.
Templates are written atomically using temporary swap files, preventing truncated files during sudden outages.
Always include 'backup: yes' and 'validate: /usr/sbin/sshd -t -f %s' to guarantee invalid configs never hit disk.
Reserve lineinfile strictly for isolated one-line insertions in external vendor-managed files.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Managing files with 5+ consecutive lineinfile tasks
mistakesToAvoid.why: Massively slows execution down (5 SSH round-trips) and turns declarative config into unmaintainable procedural code.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Using lineinfile at the bottom of sshd_config containing Match Group blocks
mistakesToAvoid.why: Appended lines become scoped inside the Match block rather than global server configuration, causing major security holes.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting backup: yes when deploying system-critical daemon templates
mistakesToAvoid.why: Without backups, rolling back unexpected template variables during an outage requires rebuilding instances.

title: Ansible Q15: An in-place database schema migration fails halfway through a playbook How do you use block rescue and always to implement automated rollback [L3]
summary: Implement try-catch-finally error handling in Ansible using block, rescue, and always. When a critical database migration task in a block fails, the rescue section triggers automated rollbacks, and always executes telemetry and notification webhooks.
question: An in-place database schema migration task fails halfway through a playbook. How do you use Ansible block, rescue, and always directives to implement automated rollback runbooks and send alert webhooks?
roleContext: Staff DevOps / Platform Architect Scenario #15 · Chaos Engineering
intro: "In enterprise CI/CD pipelines, automated failure handling is the difference between an unnoticeable self-healing deployment and a 3 AM Sev-1 outage. Ansible's block, rescue, and always directives provide robust exception handling analogous to try-catch-finally in modern programming languages."

steps.title: Encapsulate Risky Tasks in a block
steps.description: Group the forward migration operations inside a logical block structure:
items: - name: Database Schema Migration Block
block:
- name: Create database snapshot
- name: Apply Flyway / Liquibase database schema migration
- name: Run post-migration sanity tests

steps.title: Trigger Automated Rollback with rescue
steps.description: The rescue section executes exclusively if any task inside the preceding block returns an error:
items: rescue:
- name: Revert schema to previous migration version
command: /opt/bin/migrate -rollback
- name: Post alert to Slack incident channel
uri: url="{{ slack_webhook }}" method=POST body_format=json ...
- name: Fail explicitly to halt deployment pipeline
fail: msg='Schema migration failed! Automated rollback successfully executed.'

steps.title: Guarantee Cleanup Operations with always
steps.description: Tasks declared in always run unconditionally regardless of whether the block succeeded or failed:
items: always:
- name: Remove temporary lock files and credentials
file: path=/tmp/db_migration.lock state=absent
- name: Publish execution metric to CloudWatch / Datadog

keyTakeaway: Use block, rescue, and always to build production-grade try-catch-finally automation. Execute migrations in block, trigger automated rollbacks and alerts in rescue, and guarantee cleanup of locks and temp files in always.
elevatorPitch: Ansible's 'block' groups tasks logically, functioning as a 'try' block in software engineering.
The 'rescue' block functions as a 'catch' handler, executing only if any task inside the block fails.
Use rescue to trigger automated rollbacks (e.g. reverting DB schemas, restoring config backups) and paging SREs via webhook.
The 'always' block functions as a 'finally' handler, executing unconditionally regardless of success or failure.
Use always to clean up temporary credential files, release mutex lockfiles, and export pipeline metrics.
Always include an explicit 'fail' task at the end of rescue to ensure the CI/CD pipeline registers the build failure.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Omitting a fail module task at the end of the rescue block
mistakesToAvoid.why: If all tasks in rescue succeed, Ansible considers the play successful (green), allowing broken builds to progress downstream.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Attempting rollbacks using ignore_errors: yes
mistakesToAvoid.why: Blindly ignores failures and proceeds with dependent tasks, corrupting live database states.

mistakesToAvoid.mistake: Neglecting lockfile cleanup in the always block
mistakesToAvoid.why: Leaves orphaned mutex lockfiles on target hosts, preventing future deployments until manual SSH intervention.
